"You're the one with the grandma in the photo."

Micah squinted at the poster the way his dad scrutinized the router whenever the internet died during a recession, which his dad claimed was every week lately. "She says Inuit all the time. Like, 'we are Inuit.' But she never says 'I am an Inuit.' She says..." He trailed off and marched toward the kitchen, where his grandmother was actually sitting, eating soup, which Eli took as a good sign.

She looked at the poster, then at Eli, then at her soup, in that order.

"Inuit means 'the people,'" she said. "One person is an Inuk."

"So it's 'an Inuk, in 1962,'" Eli said slowly, working it through. "One person, one word. Lots of people, the other word."

"You could put it that way," she said, and went back to her soup, which appeared to be more interesting than their poster.

Eli carried the poster back to the table, crossed out the wrong word, and rewrote it. Micah leaned over his shoulder, reading aloud in a news anchor voice. "Grandmother Olemaq, an Inuk, in 1962. Very dignified. She'd better see this before we glue anything."

"Better glue it fast, then," Eli said, and reached for the glue stick.

The price tag for Frosty Crunch cereal had jumped from four dollars to six, and Edouard stood in aisle five staring at it like it had insulted him personally. That cereal was the whole reason he had offered to come grocery shopping with his dad. He had plans for that cereal. He intended to consume an entire box by Sunday.

"Dad. Six dollars."

His dad picked up the box, checked the tag, and set it down beside its neighbor, Snow Puffs, which was still four dollars. "Interesting," he said, in the voice of a man who was not going to be interesting back.

Edouard looked at the shelf. The Frosty Crunch was nearly gone, one battered box left, while the Snow Puffs sat in a fat, untouched row. He narrowed his eyes with genuine skepticism. Frosty Crunch had been the popular one all year. Kids at school traded the prize toys at lunch. Maybe that was it. Everybody wanted it, there wasn't much left, and the store had raised the price. Meanwhile the shelf overflowed with Snow Puffs nobody loved, still cheap.

"So what do we do?" his dad asked. "You want the six-dollar box?"

Edouard picked up the Snow Puffs and studied the ingredients, the cartoon penguin, everything. It was basically the same food. Oats, sugar, a prize. "We buy this," he said. "It does the same job for four dollars."

"Since when do you eat Snow Puffs?"

"Since Frosty Crunch got expensive." He dropped it in the cart, feeling clever, and then he noticed something. Halfway down the aisle, the Kowalski twins were doing exactly the same thing, their mom pulling Snow Puffs off the shelf while one twin pointed sadly at the empty Frosty Crunch spot.

"Look at that," Edouard said. "Everybody's switching. The store's going to sell a million Snow Puffs."

"Congratulations," his dad said. "You've discovered the substitute."

Edouard frowned. "The what?"

At the checkout, the Kowalski twins were ahead of them in line. The older twin held up her box and said, "Frosty Crunch costs too much now, so we got the substitute. Same cereal, basically."

"Basically," Edouard agreed, and then, quietly, to his own box: "Better prize, though."

Addison pressed her sheet music flat on the riser and watched the piano keys instead of the words. The eighth graders were supposed to sing the high part while her row held the low one, and every time the two parts came together, hers wobbled like a rope bridge.

"Don't think about their part," whispered Marisol beside her. "Just count."

Easy for Marisol to say. In the last rehearsal, Addison had followed the high voices straight up like a balloon on a string, and Mrs. Okafor had stopped everything. Today she would hold the low line even if it felt like a rebellion against the whole choir. She decided to test an idea: instead of listening to the singers, she would hang every note on the piano, which never got pulled away.

The accompanist, a lanky tenth grader named Dev, played the tricky passage again. He slowed down beautifully where the page said "rit.," letting the notes stretch like taffy, and the high voices floated with him. Addison gripped her low line and stayed on the piano. It was working.

Then Dev turned the page and kept playing slowly, slow, slow, even though the music on her sheet said "a tempo."

"That means go back to the original speed," Marisol murmured, tapping the marking. "After it slowed down."

Addison's part suddenly felt wrong, and she realized why: it wasn't her. The piano was dragging everyone behind. She raised her hand. "Dev, the a tempo. You're still slow."

He flushed, found the marking, and lifted his hands. "Again from bar twenty."

This time the piano snapped back to the steady first speed, and the two parts landed on top of each other like hands stacking. Addison's low line held firm, and for three whole bars the sound was one wide, braided thing.

Afterward Mrs. Okafor asked Dev to move the music away from the stage lights, since the old backdrop was flammable and the bulbs ran hot. While he stacked the props safely at the back wall, he gave Addison a thumbs-up.

"You saved the whole passage," Marisol said.

Addison looked at the piano, still open to the same page. "Want to integrate our parts at recess and try it once more?"

Hunter had repainted his sunset four times, and every time the sky turned muddy. The craft shed smelled like pine and paint, and his wooden plaque sat in front of him with a sky the color of wet dirt.

Across the table, Marta leaned over her friendship bracelets and squinted at his project. "It was orange this morning," she said. "What happened?"

"I tried to make the part near the mountain darker, so I mixed in some blue," Hunter said. "Then I added orange again to fix it. Then more blue." He held up his brush like evidence. "Now it's brown."

Rafi, a veteran camper who had come to Lake Birch for six summers in a row, wandered past with a cup of juice. He looked at the plaque and winced. "That happened to my dragon one year. I never figured it out."

That was the problem, Hunter thought. He could see the mud, but not what was making it. It wasn't the brushes, because Marta had used the same jars and her flowers stayed bright. It wasn't the wood, because his practice stars on scrap wood had turned brown too, and they had been fine on paper.

He got a fresh scrap of wood and laid out four dabs: orange and blue, red and green, yellow and purple, blue and yellow. He mixed each pair with a clean craft stick. The blue and yellow cooperated beautifully, turning into a green that looked like the lake in July. The other three mixes all went dull and brownish, like somebody had spilled dirt in them.

"Look at this," he said, and Marta and Rafi crowded in.

"So some colors get along and some don't," Marta said.

Hunter found the paper color wheel taped inside the paint box lid, the one nobody ever used. He spun it around. Orange sat straight across from blue. Red sat straight across from green. Yellow sat straight across from purple. Every pair that had turned brown sat opposite each other.

"The ones across from each other make the mud," he said. He tapped the wheel. "I heard the word once. Complementary colors. They're opposites, like red and green, and mixing two complementary paints gives you a dull brown or gray."

"So your sunset turned brown because orange and blue are complementary," Marta said.

"Opposite each other," Rafi said, tracing the wheel with his finger. "I could have saved my dragon."

Hunter painted the dark part of his sky with a blue that leaned toward purple's side of the wheel, and only a whisper of it, keeping the orange far from the edge. The sky glowed. Down at the bottom, he painted the mountain gray on purpose, which felt almost like a joke.

"That's the best one in the shed," Marta said.

Hunter signed his name in the corner with the smallest brush.

The word list for the school spelling bee had forty words, and Hailey had read all forty of them eleven times by Tuesday night. Her little brother, Marco, kept drumming his pencils on the table, which began to irritate her so much that she finally slammed her list down. "Rereading isn't even working," she said. "I read the words and two seconds later I can't spell 'rendezvous.'"

Her dad looked up from his magazine. "Interesting. There's a thing in here about that."

He slid the magazine across the table. Hailey read the paragraph twice. "In 2006," she said slowly, "these researchers, Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke, found that testing yourself on material helps you remember it longer than simply rereading it." She frowned. "So instead of reading the list again, somebody should just quiz me."

"Want to try it?"

"Okay, but don't go in order," Hailey said. "If you go in order, I'll just remember which word comes next instead of the word itself. That would be a bias toward the list, not the spelling." That part seemed logical to her, and her dad agreed it was fair.

So every night he called out random words while she dried dishes or brushed her teeth. Marco turned it into a game, shouting words from the hallway like a game show host. On Thursday she missed "chrysanthemum" three times, and by Saturday she could spell it while hanging upside down off the couch.

Monday morning, Mrs. Tanaka's classroom smelled like whiteboard marker, and twenty-three chairs had been pushed back to make room for the finalists. Hailey's hands were cold even though the radiator was clanking. Devon, the boy who had won last year, stood beside her whispering the list to himself over and over, his lips moving like he was reading a secret letter.

"Rendezvous," said Mrs. Tanaka. "Devon."

Devon blinked. "R-e-n-d-e-z..." He stopped, stared at the ceiling, and started the whole list again in his head, searching for where the word had been on the page. "V-o-u-s?" It came out like a question.

The bell for the next round sounded, and Hailey touched his shoulder quickly. "Hey," she whispered, "want to come over tonight? My dad'll quiz us both." Devon nodded, and Mrs. Tanaka turned to Hailey with the card in her hand.

"Chrysanthemum," she said.

Aaron had been at Camp Winnow for four days, and his craft project was already a disaster. He was supposed to make a spinning color wheel, a cardboard circle painted with wedge-shaped sections of color. When you spun it fast, the colors were supposed to blur together. His first attempt had gone wrong because he'd painted the wedges in a random order, and when the disc spun, it looked like mud.

The problem, he decided, was the order of the colors. Something about how they sat next to each other mattered, but he couldn't see it directly. He could only see the muddy result. So he tried an experiment. He painted a second wheel with red next to green, and blue next to orange, opposite pairs facing each other across the circle. Then he spun both wheels side by side and compared them. The second one blurred into something smoother, less brown. There was a rule hiding in there somewhere, and he was going to find it.

He went looking for information. The craft shed had exactly one bookshelf, holding a bird guide, a mystery novel missing its last thirty pages, and a dusty paperback called Opticks by Isaac Newton. Aaron flipped through it, mostly to be polite to the bookshelf, and stopped at a diagram. It was a circle, and the colors of the spectrum were arranged around the rim, red blending into orange, then yellow, then green, then blue. Newton had done this, the title page said, in a book first published in 1704. "Guys," Aaron said to the two boys painting beside him, "Newton drew one of these. Isaac Newton. In Opticks, 1704, he put the spectrum colors in a circle."

"Newton?" said Marcus, who was building a rubber-band-powered propeller out of a ruler and two plastic spoons. "The gravity guy? Why would he care about paint?" Marcus had spent the whole week insisting that crafts were a waste of time and real science was the only thing worth doing. Now he leaned over Aaron's shoulder and studied the circle for a long moment. "Huh. Okay, crafts, science, same shed," he said, and abandoned his propeller to grab a blank cardboard disc.

That night Aaron wrote a letter home, because the camp had a no-phones rule and his mother had promised to send real stamps. "Dear Mom," he wrote. "You were vague about what camp would be like, and you were right not to explain, because I would not have believed it. I made a color wheel. Mine failed at first, so I isolated the problem by testing one thing at a time, and it turns out a man from 1704 had already figured out the order. Tomorrow Marcus and I are painting his wheel with the spectrum going around in a circle, exactly like Newton's. Also, nobody has fed the camp hamster since Tuesday and I think that is the counselors' plan to make us think it is a mystery. Your son, Aaron."

The next afternoon they finished Marcus's wheel and spun it with the drill Marcus had borrowed from the maintenance shed. The colors blurred into a pale shimmer, and Marcus whooped so loudly that a counselor came running from the lake. "We got it," Marcus said, holding up the spinning wheel. "Newton's circle, spinning."

Gabrielle stood at the kitchen counter on Monday night with a stack of index cards and a timer that kept beeping at her like a smug little rodent. On Friday she had to give a two-minute speech in English class, and Ms. Petro had been relentless about the rules: an opening hook, three points, a closing. Gabrielle had all of that. Her cards were perfect. The problem was that last week, when she had practiced for her little brother, he fell asleep somewhere around point two, face-down in his cereal.

"Your voice is like a robot reading a menu," Theo had told her, spitting out a Cheerio for emphasis.

At lunch on Tuesday, Gabrielle watched her best friend Priya perform a tiny drama across the table. Priya's lab partner had knocked her volcano project onto the floor, and when the teacher asked if she was okay, Priya said, "I'm fine." But her shoulders had slumped, her voice had gone flat, and she'd paused a long time before saying it. Everyone at the table knew she was not fine. Not one bit.

That afternoon, Gabrielle cornered Priya by the lockers. "How did you do that? You said fine, and I knew you weren't."

Priya grinned. "It's called subtext. It's what you mean under the words. My cousin's in theater, and she says actors show it with pauses, tone, and gesture. Like, watch." Priya straightened her back, smiled brightly, and chirped, "I'm fine!" Then she slouched, dropped her voice, waited a beat, and mumbled, "I'm fine." Same words, two completely different messages.

Gabrielle had a hypothesis: if subtext worked on real people, it would work on a speech too. Her speech was about why the school should keep its garden, and her three points were solid, but on Thursday she tried an experiment in front of Theo. For her hook, instead of starting with "Did you know the garden has forty kinds of plants?", she picked up an empty seed packet, turned it over slowly, and paused before saying anything. Then, quietly, she said, "This packet used to be full." Theo actually looked up from his video game.

"You're trying to trick me with sadness," he said, but he didn't leave the room, so she counted it as a win. She kept testing. A pause before her second point made Theo lean forward. A random hand gesture at the wrong moment, though, exposed her nerves completely, because Theo laughed and said she looked like a confused traffic cop. So she cut that one.

On Friday, Gabrielle walked to the front of the room holding the seed packet. She let the silence sit for two whole seconds, which felt like two hours, and then began. When she finished her closing line and looked up, half the class had their hands raised, and Ms. Petro was writing something in her notebook. Behind her, Priya gave a slow thumbs-up, then slouched, dropped her voice, and mouthed, "I'm fine."

The gym smelled like popcorn and floor wax, and the bleachers rattled every time the home crowd stomped. Lillian kept one eye on her sister's team and the other on her little brother, Dario, who was not watching basketball at all. He was hunched over a baseball card, scowling at it like it had insulted him personally.

"Reyes is the best player nobody talks about," Dario said, louder than he meant to. A man in front of them turned around, and Dario shrank, clearly intimidated. Lillian had compassion for him, mostly. She also wanted to watch the game.

"Then why does nobody talk about him?" she asked.

"Because his batting average is low. But it's wrong. It's not fair." He shoved the card at her. On the back, in tiny print, were numbers, and one row said AVG .243.

Lillian was systematic about things like this. She read the whole back of the card, row by row, while the crowd roared at a steal she missed. Hits. At-bats. Walks. She counted on her fingers, then counted again. "Wait. He has 60 walks and they're not in the at-bats."

"Walks don't count as at-bats," Dario said, shrugging. "That's just the rule."

"So the average is hits divided by at-bats." She tapped the card. "And walks aren't in there at all. He gets on base all those times and gets no credit for any of it. Not one."

Dario sat up straight. "Nobody at school believes me."

"Then write it down. Numbers in a note are harder to argue with than your face." She dug a pen out of her jacket. He grabbed a napkin from the popcorn bag and wrote, in huge letters, REYES GOT ON BASE 60 MORE TIMES THAN THE AVERAGE SHOWS. ASK ME HOW. He held it up so the man in front could see it.

The man read it, laughed, and turned back around. "Kid's got a point," he said to his friend.

The buzzer sounded, halftime, and the whole gym thumped with stomping feet. Dario folded the napkin carefully and tucked it into his pocket like a treasure map.

"Sixty," he whispered, grinning at the scoreboard for no reason at all.

Blake sat cross-legged on the grass with his sketchbook, a basketball on the picnic table in front of him, and one very strict art assignment: shade a sphere with a highlight, a shadow, and a cast shadow. The assignment was mandatory, due Monday, and his stomach did that hormone thing where it churned just enough to make him lean harder on his pencil. His art teacher had told them a "real artist observes before drawing." Blake had rolled his eyes at that in class. Now he rolled the basketball a few inches and watched how the shadow stretched and slid across the tabletop like it was alive.

The sphere itself went okay. He found the highlight where the late sun hit the ball, built a gray curve around it, and pressed darkest on the far side. The problem was the table. He'd drawn the tabletop's far edge sloping upward, and no matter how he shaded, the whole surface looked like it was floating away from the basketball, like a magic carpet with a ball parked on it. He frowned, erased, and drew the edge tilted up again. Same problem. His little sister Maya wandered over with a popsicle and said, "Your table's flying."

"Thanks. Very helpful." But she was right, and he knew it. He thought about last summer, when he'd tried to draw his bedroom and sloped the ceiling edges the same wrong way. He'd crumpled that drawing and shoved it in the desk drawer, too annoyed to figure out what had gone wrong. He still kind of regretted quitting instead of looking harder. He decided not to quit this time.

He stood up and looked straight at the table's far edge, then lowered himself slowly to a crouch. Something changed as his eyes went down past the level of the tabletop. Below his eye level, the far edge didn't slope up anymore. He straightened, crouched again, accelerated his knees all the way to the grass, and there it was: edges above his eye level sloped down toward their vanishing points, while edges below his eye level sloped up toward them. He'd been standing, so the tabletop was below his eyes, which meant its edges should slope up toward the vanishing point, not tilt off into the sky.

"Maya, come look," he said. She crouched next to him, popsicle dripping. "When you're above the edge, it goes down to the vanishing point. When you're below it, it goes up. That's why my table was flying. I was below the tabletop but I drew it like I was above it." Maya squinted, then said, "So if you drew the ceiling while sitting on the floor, it slopes down toward the vanishing point?" Blake grinned and redrew the table with the edges climbing gently toward the vanishing point, then set the basketball on it, highlight, shadow, cast shadow and all. It sat there. Solid. Maya tapped the page and said, "Okay, that one's not flying. That one's just fat."

Kaitlyn spread five sponge squares across the kitchen table, each one soaked in a different liquid: vinegar, salt water, lemon juice, cola, and plain water. Her question for the science fair was which liquid would erode a sponge fastest, and for two weeks she had weighed each square every night and written the numbers in her notebook. The sponges were polymers, her father had mentioned once, and apparently some liquids could wear that material down over time. Tonight she had to turn fourteen columns of numbers into one graph, because tomorrow morning the whole school would walk past her poster.

She drew her axes, taped on her labels, and stood back. Something felt wrong. Her bars climbed upward in a way that made cola look like it had no effect at all, when her notes clearly said the cola sponge had crumbled first. She flipped through her notebook, frowning, and flipped back.

The doorbell rang. It was Leo from down the street, holding his own poster under one arm. "Mrs. Talbot said you had the good markers," he said. "Can I borrow the red one? My volcano caption smeared." He came in, glanced at her graph, and then blinked at it. "Wait, why is time going up the side?"

Kaitlyn looked again. She had put the days along the vertical side and the sponge weight along the bottom, because the weight numbers had felt like the important part, the part that should stand tall. "Is that wrong?" she asked.

Leo set his poster on the counter. "My brother caught me doing that last week. The thing you change goes on the horizontal x-axis, and the thing that happens because of it goes on the vertical y-axis." He tapped her notebook. "You changed the days, and the weight happened because of that, right?"

Kaitlyn checked her notes. The days were what she had controlled. The weights were what had followed. "So the days go across the bottom," she said slowly, "and the weights go up the side." She pulled the tape off, rotated her labels, and redrew the bars. Now the cola line dropped steeply downward, and the plain water line barely bent at all, exactly the story her sponges had been telling her.

"That looks plausible now," Leo said, borrowing the red marker. "Want to come see whether my volcano still smokes?" She capped the marker and followed him out the door, poster under her arm.

William woke to a strange brightness and a text from school: SNOW DAY, BUILDING CLOSED. He was already dressed before his mom finished her coffee. The snow had postponed his math test, which felt like a bonus prize, and the backyard lay under an ominous gray sky that promised even more by afternoon. Then he spotted Mr. Alvarez next door, standing at the top of his driveway with a shovel, breathing hard after only one narrow path. That gave William an idea, and maybe a job.

"Five dollars if I do the whole thing?" he called over the fence. Mr. Alvarez, who was sixty-eight and lived alone, agreed so fast it made William pause. He grabbed his shovel and marched over, ready to attack the driveway like the snow was the antagonist in one of his video games. He scooped huge, heavy shovelfuls, flinging them sideways, and finished one whole row before his arms burned. He noticed Mr. Alvarez had gone inside. Why would a man who wanted his driveway cleared go inside halfway through?

A girl came around the corner of the house, pulling a second shovel behind her like a sled. "I'm Rosa," she said. "He's my grandpa. I check on him on snow days." She looked at William's giant pile of thrown snow and then at the old man's footprints, which stopped and started, stopped and started, all the way up the first row. William followed her eyes. The pattern was there if you looked: Grandpa hadn't wandered off. He had been resting, over and over. "His doctor told him shoveling heavy snow is hard work on the heart," Rosa said. "He's supposed to take breaks." She pointed at William's shovel. "And lift small loads instead of big shovelfuls."

William looked down at his aching arms and wondered if his own heart was pounding the same way. He had been doing the exact opposite of everything, all at top speed. "So the trick is little scoops," he said slowly, "and we postpone the race part?" Rosa laughed and dragged her shovel to the far side. "You take that half, I'll take this one, and we rest between rows. Like circuits in gym."

They worked in small, easy lifts, and after each row they stood together at the edge of the driveway, watching their breath cloud in the cold. Mr. Alvarez came back out with a thermos and three cups of hot chocolate, and the work went faster with the breaks than William's solo sprint had, which seemed backwards until he thought about it. When they finished, the driveway was bare and William's arms felt fine. Mr. Alvarez pressed a five and a warm cup into his hands.

"Same time next storm?" William asked.

"Only if you promise to rest between rows," said Mr. Alvarez, and raised his cup like a toast.

Alexandra stood in the wings of the school auditorium, holding her violin like it might bolt for the exit. Her mother had said stage fright wasn't hereditary, since Grandma apparently once sang a solo in front of four hundred people without fainting, but Alexandra suspected her knees hadn't inherited that gene. The principal, Ms. Okafor, was at the podium reading a citation for the music program, some long list of awards, and then it was time for the sound check. Alexandra was first.

She walked out, and the moment the microphone stand was set in front of her, a whistle tore through the auditorium, so piercing that kids in the third row covered their ears. Ms. Okafor winced and switched the mic off. "We'll try again in a minute," she called, but her voice was tight, and Alexandra could tell she was worried. The concert was in an hour, and every performer needed the mic tested.

Alexandra stared at the loudspeaker standing on the stage floor behind the microphone, then at the mic itself, then back again. She remembered how the whistle had swelled, louder and louder, like something feeding itself. Sound from that speaker, she thought, going straight back into the mic, getting amplified again, then back out the speaker, around and around, louder every loop. It was like a rumor growing each time it was repeated.

She decided to simulate the real concert instead of a timid little check. "Can we turn everything on?" she asked the sound helper, a sixth grader named Theo. "But I want to stand here, sideways, with the mic pointed away from the speaker." She angled the stand so the microphone faced the empty front rows and turned her shoulder to block the line between them. Theo flipped the switch. The speaker hummed to life. No whistle.

"Try talking," Theo said.

"Testing," Alexandra said, and the word came out clean and round through the speaker, no squeal at all. Theo gave her a thumbs up, and Ms. Okafor, watching from the third row, let out a breath and smiled. Then she waved the next performer over, and Alexandra, her violin tucked under her chin, drew her bow across the first bright, steady note.

The waiting room clock said 3:02, and Zoey had to be at band practice by 3:45, which gave the whole morning a squeezed, ticking feeling. She sat with her knees perpendicular to the floor, heels hooked on the chair leg, and reread the note her best friend Priya had slipped into her locker that morning. "Bad day. Lunch disaster. Mom working late again. Come find me before practice." Zoey had no idea what to write back, so she'd shoved it in her pocket and taken it out four times since.

She was here because of the stomachaches. Every Sunday night for a month, like clockwork, and then gone by Tuesday. That was the part that didn't make sense. She'd started keeping a list on her phone, and when she looked at the dates, a pattern jumped out: bad stomach, no sleep the night before. Sunday nights she lay awake until one, sometimes two. Monday nights she slept fine. She had a theory, and today she planned to test it by telling the doctor everything, straight out, before the clock hit 3:20.

Outside the window, a strip of hospital garden buzzed with bees that pollinated the rows of purple flowers, moving flower to flower like they had their own deadline. A poster near the fish tank read FEELING STRESSED? YOU'RE NOT ALONE. A man across from her read a magazine, and a little boy built a tower of blocks and knocked it down, over and over.

When the nurse called her name, Zoey unfolded her list. She told the doctor about the pattern, the Sundays, the sleepless nights. The doctor nodded slowly. "What you're describing sounds like anxiety," she said. "Stress that the body holds onto." Zoey's stomach flipped, but not in the bad way. A hidden cause, and it had a name.

"Coping," the doctor said. "It means the ways a person handles stress or hard feelings. Some ways are healthier than others."

On the drive to practice, Zoey texted Priya: "Exercise helps. Sleep helps. Talking helps. I'm testing all three. You first. What do you do after a bad day?"

Priya's reply came before Zoey reached the gym: "Hide in my room. Why?"

"New plan," Zoey typed, pushing through the doors. "Meet me at the track at 3:45."

Hailey had decided to try keeping Shabbat from Friday sundown to Saturday noon, the way her family did, even though her best friends were all at the pool by ten. In the kitchen, the last thing she did before sunset was tape a note over the light switch, because her mother said the rule was no electricity, and Hailey wanted to be systematic about it. No phone, no TV, no turning things on. She set a loaf of challah on the table and waited in the dimming light, wondering what would actually be different.

Saturday morning she sat at the same table with her two cousins, Maya and Dov, who had come for lunch. Bored already, Hailey asked the question she'd been carrying around for weeks: "What happens after you die?"

"Orthodox Jews believe there'll be a resurrection of the dead," Dov said, tearing his bread. "Like, actually, in the future. Bodies rising."

Maya shrugged. "At our synagogue, our rabbi says what matters is how you live now. That's the whole point."

"They can't both be right," Hailey said.

"Why not?" Maya said. "Nobody's seen it. It's not like you can check."

That stopped Hailey. She looked at the covered switch, the silent phone in the drawer, the candles burnt down to stubs. She couldn't see whether resting had changed anything inside her either, but she had a way to test it. She had gone all morning without checking her phone once, which had never happened on a normal Saturday, and she had noticed the smell of the bread and the sound of Dov chewing, small things the screen usually magnified into the only things in the room.

She thought about last winter, when she'd skipped her grandmother's shiva because a swim meet mattered more to her, and how she still couldn't decide if that had been a mistake or just a choice.

"Okay," she said at last. "Different answers to the same question. Maybe that's allowed."

Maya stole a piece of Hailey's challah and grinned. "Maybe that's the most Jewish answer of all."

Dov reached for the butter dish and knocked over the candle stub, and all three of them scrambled to catch it before it rolled off the table.

Juliette spread the topographic map of Miller Ridge across the library table and weighted the corners with four books from the return cart. Her plan for Saturday was simple: find the steepest slope on the hill before her family's hike, so she could tell her dad which side to avoid. She had read that close-together contour lines meant steep ground and far-apart lines meant gentle ground, and now she meant to test it.

At the next computer, a boy named Deshawn was watching a flight tracker site. "Flight 482, 40 degrees north, 73 degrees west," he read off the screen. "My grandma's on that one. Which number says she's almost here? This one or that one?" He pointed at the 40, then the 73.

Juliette looked over. The topographic map had numbers along its edges too, and she had been ignoring them. "Those are coordinates," she said, and then she stopped, because she was not actually sure which was which. She pulled the atlas over and found a page marked with a line labeled 0 degrees running top to bottom, with numbers climbing east and west from it. "Okay, so the up-and-down lines are longitude. Longitude measures how far east or west a place is from the prime meridian, from 0 degrees up to 180 degrees east or west." She traced it with her finger. "So 73 degrees west, your grandma is west of the prime meridian."

"Is west where we are?" Deshawn said. "Then she's on our side of the world. Good."

"That's the east-west number," Juliette said. "The 40 is the other one. North-south." She turned back to her map, and now the edge numbers made sense too, and she could see they told her nothing about steepness at all. The contour lines did that job, and she got to work counting them.

The west side of Miller Ridge had lines stacked so tightly they nearly touched, like the stripes on a candy cane. The east side had fat, lazy gaps. She marked the west face with a sticky note: STEEPEST, STAY OFF.

Deshawn leaned over. "Too bad. That's the side with the old fire tower."

Juliette checked the legend. The tower wasn't on the steep face at all. A thin dotted trail switchbacked up the east side, gentle all the way, and met the ridge behind the tower. She laughed. "The easy side gets you there anyway."

"Your dad will be relieved," Deshawn said.

"My dad will not cooperate until I tell him the fire road is closed," Juliette said. "He insists on vigorous uphill hiking. He calls it a vacation."

"Mine calls baggage fees a tariff and refuses to pay them," Deshawn said. "That's why Grandma flies alone."

Juliette peeled the sticky note off the map and moved it to the east face. "Enter from the easy side, end up at the tower anyway," she said, and pressed it down flat.

Alexandre spread his science fair poster across the library table and frowned at the empty middle section. His experiment, a taste test pitting name-brand Crunch-O's against the store-brand cereal, had a problem. Yesterday his friend Marcus had sworn the name-brand box tasted better, and then admitted he had never even tried the store kind. How could Alexandre trust any answers if people already believed one box was the winner?

His little sister Priya wandered over from the lush tropical mural by the windows, where the painted vines looked greener than any real plant in town. She was eating dry cereal from a cup and clearly had opinions. Alexandre eyed her cup, then the two cereal boxes in his bag, and an idea began to form.

"Okay," he said, pulling out the boxes. "I need you to pour two bowls for me, but you have to hide the boxes first. Label them A and B and don't tell me which is which."

"Why?" Priya asked, already suspicious.

"It's a blind test," Alexandre said. "If I don't know which sample is which, what I expect can't sway my answers."

Priya hid behind the reference shelf with the boxes, and he heard her snickering the whole time. She returned with two matching bowls marked A and B in her careful handwriting. Alexandre tasted each one slowly, taking notes. Bowl A was slightly sweeter. Bowl B had a better crunch. He ranked them and slid his paper across the table.

Priya revealed the boxes, grinning. Bowl A, his top pick, was the store brand. He whooped so loudly that the librarian glared, and he shrank into his seat, still smiling. He could not accuse Marcus of lying about the name-brand after all; he had just proven that expectations do the talking when people know what they are eating. On his poster he wrote the comparison in fat letters: participants who could not identify the samples chose the cheaper cereal.

"Wait," Priya said, jabbing the nutrition labels. "The store one has fewer carbohydrates. Does that mean it's healthier?"

Alexandre looked at her, looked at his poster, and started a brand new page titled Round Two. "Get more bowls," he said.

The puddle was back. Levi crouched beside the bathroom door in his socks and stared at the dark patch of tile, exactly where it had been yesterday morning. Nobody would confess. His sister Nadia wanted a new hamster cage and claimed a leaking pipe would finally wreck the floor enough that their parents would have to accommodate a whole renovation, which she said would be the perfect time for building shelves. Levi wanted the truth, and he had exactly one guess to test.

He spread flour in a thin white circle around the puddle, because whatever came through at night would leave tracks. He also set a cup under the sink pipe, in case the water came from there instead. His first idea, his best idea, was the cat. Before bed he told Nadia, "If the flour shows paw prints, I win."

At breakfast the flour told a different story. There were no paw prints at all. The cup under the pipe was bone dry, so that guess was dead too. But the flour itself had been disturbed, dragged in a long smear toward the bathtub, and there were marks in it that looked almost like small bare heels. Levi felt the hair on his arms rise. Nadia leaned over his shoulder and whispered, "Somebody walks in here at night."

They staked out the hallway at midnight. Levi's obligation was to stay awake, and he almost failed twice before the bathroom door creaked. Levi flicked on the light. Nadia stood at the sink, eyes open but somewhere far away, hands moving under the running tap. She had been sleepwalking. In the morning, embarrassed and fascinated, she flipped through the pamphlet from their last field trip and read aloud what the guide at the science centre had told her: "A theory is not a guess; it is an explanation that has been repeatedly tested and supported, while a hypothesis is an idea still being tested." Levi grinned. His sleepwalking idea had started as a hypothesis, and now, after the flour and the stakeout, it had support. Nadia shut the pamphlet and said, "Fine. But the shelves were still a fertile idea."

The lights died at 8:17, right in the middle of Arthur's homework, and the whole house went quiet the way it does when the refrigerator stops humming. He found a flashlight and padded to the garage, where the breaker box waited with its rows of little black switches. He flipped the main one off and on. Nothing. He tried it again, slower, listening for the click. Still nothing, which meant the problem was not in his house at all. It was somewhere up the line, out on the street, invisible.

"Power's out for the whole block," his dad called from the porch. "Might as well come outside while it lasts."

The street was strange without its orange porch lamps and glowing windows. Arthur and his sister Maya stood on the grass, and Maya was the first to notice. "Look up," she said. "There are way more stars than usual." Arthur looked. The sky was crowded with them, a pale smudged river of light running across the dark. They argued about whether that river of stars was real or a cloud, and their dad mediated by suggesting they figure it out instead of shouting.

Maya still had battery on her phone. She searched and read out loud: "A 2016 world atlas of light pollution estimated that about 80 percent of North Americans can't see the Milky Way from where they live." She frowned. "It's called the Milky Way. That smudge."

"So that's it," Arthur said, working it through. "The streetlights and everything, all that artificial light, they wash it out. But tonight everything's dark." He thought of it like a simple equation: less ground light, more stars visible. He wanted proof. He clicked his flashlight on and held it near his face, staring upward. The faint stars closest to the horizon seemed to fade. He clicked it off, and they crept back.

"Try it again," Maya said, holding out her phone with its bright screen.

He did, twice more, and each time the stars near the light dimmed. Overhead a skein of migratory geese crossed the Milky Way, stitching a dark line through the pale river, and Arthur kept watching until the last of them passed.

Mason laced his cleats in the locker room, but his eyes kept drifting to the girl sitting two benches down, pulling on a helmet just like his. Her name was Priya, and she was trying out for the boys' baseball team with everybody else. A boy named Derek stomped over and said, "This is the boys' team. You can't be in here."

"The gym is open tryouts for baseball," Priya said calmly. "It says so on the sheet."

"There's a girls' softball team," Derek insisted. "So why would they let you..."

Mason wondered about that too. Why would the school run open tryouts if there was a whole separate team for girls? There had to be a reason, some rule working behind the scenes that nobody could see, like a current under the ice. He thought about how you might deduce it. If the school offered softball, that might be one factor, but maybe it wasn't the only one. Maybe the school had to let her try out no matter what.

"Come on," Mason said to Derek, "let's just go. Tryouts start in two minutes."

Out on the field, Coach Ramos set up a hitting rotation. Priya stepped into the cage fourth and smashed a line drive into the gap in left field. Derek stared. Mason noticed that Coach didn't even blink, as if a girl trying out were the most ordinary thing in the world. That was a clue. Coaches follow rules, Mason thought, even rules that aren't posted on the gym door.

After tryouts, he checked the athletic handbook on the bulletin board outside the locker room, running his finger down the pages. There it was, plain as a box score: Title IX, a U.S. law signed in 1972, bans discrimination based on sex in schools that receive federal money. And it had been applied to their sports programs. So that was the hidden rule. It covered the whole school, which meant Priya's tryout wasn't a favor or an accident. It was the law doing its quiet work.

The next day Mason found Derek by the lockers. "I figured out the Priya thing," he said. "It's Title IX, a U.S. law signed in 1972, banning discrimination based on sex in schools that receive federal money. It got applied to sports programs too. She has the same right to try out as us."

Derek frowned. "So my hypothetical girls-only baseball world isn't happening?"

"Not at this school," Mason said. He slung his bag over his shoulder. "Rosters get posted at three. Want to walk down and see who made it?"

Derek snapped his locker shut and followed him down the hall.

Alexa sat cross-legged on her bed with her science fair notebook open, but instead of taking notes she kept rereading the same paragraph about cloud formation. Every time she imagined standing up in front of the class tomorrow, her heart thumped like a drum and her stomach squeezed into a hard little knot. She pressed her palm against it and wondered what was actually happening in there. Could an intestine really tie itself up like a shoelace just because of a speech? That seemed absurd, and yet here she was, doubled over on her quilt over something her brother would call trivial.

She set the notebook down and called Priya on her tablet. Priya's face filled the screen, her bedroom closet visible behind her. "Okay, weird question," Alexa said. "Do you ever feel like your stomach is staging a protest before something big?"

Priya laughed. "I used to, every single morning before school. It wasn't just nerves, though. My mom noticed I wasn't sleeping and I kept fake-coughing to stay home, so we went to the doctor." She held up a hand before Alexa could ask. "The doctor said feeling anxious sometimes is normal. But mine was intense, it lasted months, and it was getting in the way of school and everything, so she diagnosed an anxiety disorder." Alexa repeated the words slowly, anxiety disorder, like she was testing whether they fit. "And here's the part that changed things," Priya went on. "It's treatable. I talked to someone and learned ways to cope, and now it's like... a smaller dog barking instead of a giant one."

Alexa wrote treatable in her notebook next to her cloud diagram. Then she had an idea, a small experiment. She grabbed the timer on her nightstand, set it for five minutes, and tried her new coping trick: breathe in for four counts, out for six, while naming three things she could see, hear, and touch. The lamp's warm glow. Rain ticking against the window. The ridges of her quilt under her fingers. When the timer buzzed, the knot in her stomach had loosened, not gone, but looser, like a fist uncurling one finger at a time.

"So it's like budgeting," Alexa said into the phone balanced on her pillow. "I budget my allowance for games and snacks. Maybe I can budget my worry, too, give it five timed minutes and then close the door on it." Priya snorted. "Boundaries for your brain. I like it." A knock rattled Alexa's bedroom door and her brother's voice came through: "Alexa, can I borrow your markers?" She took a breath and said, "Only if you knock and wait next time. That's my rule now." Priya cupped her hands around her mouth and called through the screen, "Boundaries for brothers, too!" Alexa laughed, picked up her marker, and drew a big circle around the word treatable.

Arianna's backyard pool was barely nine metres long, and on Saturday she had to swim twenty-five metres of front crawl with side breathing in front of the whole swim club. Her father would have helped, but last spring he had twisted his knee on the driveway and bruised the cartilage so badly he still limped, so all he could do was stand at the edge and count laps. Arianna pushed off, took three strokes, turned her head, and got a mouthful of water. Again. She coughed, tried again, and choked a second time.

At the far side of the pool, her neighbour Theo was playing one-on-one against his cousin Marco on the driveway hoop. Theo set a screen, planting himself so his body would obstruct Marco's defender, and Marco drove past. But Theo just stood there, hands on his hips, while every passing lane closed. "Nobody's open!" Marco shouted. They ran it again. Same result. Arianna gripped the pool ledge, watching. Something was off, some rule she couldn't see. Theo set the pick, then froze, as if the play ended there.

"Roll!" she called across the fence. Theo stared at her. "After you set the screen, turn and move toward the basket," she said, "so you're ready for a pass from whoever has the ball." Theo ran it once more. He set the pick, rolled to the hoop, and Marco's bounce pass arrived just as he turned. Layup. Marco whooped like it was a buzzer beater.

Watching them, Arianna floated on her back, thinking. Theo had been stuck because he kept doing the same motion and expecting a different ending. So was she. Every time she breathed, she was lifting her head forward, out of the stroke, instead of turning it to the side. She pushed off the wall, counted three strokes, and let her cheek rest on the water as her face rotated sideways. Air, clean air, no coughing. She kept going, one length, then a turnaround, then another, her father's voice counting from the fence. At the far wall she stopped, dripping and grinning, and shouted to Theo, "Run it again. I want to see that pass."

Scarlett raced through the library doors with her sketchbook under her arm and exactly forty minutes before the poster contest entries were due. The task was to draw your favorite place, and she had chosen the reading corner right here, with its worn green chair and the tall window behind it. She plopped down, grabbed a pencil from the shared box on the craft shelf, and started sketching fast.

The poster had to be bold. Judges walking past a wall of entries would give each one about two seconds. But when she held up her sketch of the chair, her lines looked pale and tired, as if the drawing itself wanted a nap. She scrutinized the paper, then the pencil, and noticed tiny letters stamped on the barrel: 4H. Last week, in Mrs. Okafor's art bin, she had grabbed a pencil stamped 6B and it had made rich, velvety darks. She turned the box over and found a jumble of Hs and Bs, all mixed together like camouflage, hiding the one she needed.

"I bet it's the letters," she whispered. She lined up four pencils on the table: 4H, H, 2B, 6B. One by one she drew a short stroke with each, pressing the same way each time. The 4H stroke was faint. The 6B stroke came out dark and soft as charcoal dust, darker than the 4H by a mile. She grinned so wide a boy at the next table looked over. "What are you doing, science?"

"Sort of," Scarlett said. "H is hardness and B is blackness. So this 6B is my new best friend."

She remembered the library's "shelf of eloquent posters," the fancy ones the librarians made for book month, and how their dark lettering had jumped out from down the hall. That was the look she wanted. With the 6B she redrew the chair, layered the window shadow until the paper seemed to glow, and added a cat curled on the cushion that had not been in her plan at all.

At the front desk she slid her entry across the counter with two minutes to spare. The librarian held it up to the light.

"Now that," the librarian said, "you can read from across the parking lot."

Scarlett said, "6B. Blackness."

The petition had forty-three signatures when Elena walked into the town hall, and it needed fifty before she could hand it to a single councillor. She wanted the bylaw against skate ramps on residential driveways changed, because her brother's ramp had been confiscated last Tuesday and it sat now in a locked storage room behind the recreation centre. Councillor Marsh sat at the long table near the front, so Elena slid into a chair two rows back and began counting the room for anyone who might sign.

Before the meeting started, a boy about her age leaned over from the next seat. "Are you the one with the ramp petition? I'm Theo. We're here for the same reason, kind of. My class is doing a project on how citizens actually get bylaws changed, and my teacher said we could watch a real petition in action." He nodded at her clipboard. "Can I ask how you got started?"

"I found out the bylaw exists, then I found out which councillors voted for it," Elena said. "Then I wrote one page saying what I want changed and why, and I asked people to sign it. Fifty signatures means the clerk puts it on the agenda and a councillor has to move it. That's the rule." She paused. "I still need seven more."

Theo helped her work the room during the break. A woman in a green coat signed. Two teenagers signed. A man refused and said ramps were "subjective, a matter of taste," which made no sense to Elena until Theo whispered, "I think he means it's an opinion thing, not a fact thing." By the time the mayor called the meeting back to order, they had fifty-one.

During the open floor, Councillor Marsh waved Elena forward. She read her page out loud, her voice steadier than she expected, and handed over the clipboard. Marsh asked one question: why had she gathered signatures instead of just asking him directly? "Because one person can be ignored," Elena said. "Fifty-one people are a pattern." Marsh looked at the list for a long moment. "Petition's accepted. I'll move it at the next meeting."

Afterward, walking out, Theo told her about his mock election at school, where his small party had lost badly for the third year running. "Every year it's just the two big parties that ever win, and our teacher wouldn't say why. We vote the same way adults do, first past the post." Elena thought about that. "So everyone knows small parties lose, so nobody votes for them, so they lose." Theo stared at her. "That's actually a thing. A French political scientist figured it out. It's called Duverger's law." He wrote her inference down in his notebook, then said the names of the two big mock parties out loud, and laughed.

The ramp came home the following Friday. Elena had made one more inference on the walk home from the town hall: Councillor Marsh's name had appeared on the bylaw's original vote, listed with the minority who had opposed it. She had chosen him first, and she planned to persist with the other four councillors next. That night she taped the fifty-one signatures to the garage door beside the ramp.

Samuel stood at the counter with his mother's five dollar bill folded in his fist like a secret. "You can supervise from the porch," she said, "but you're doing it yourself. Milk, and bring me the change." From the porch she watched him march down the walk, and Samuel pretended not to notice, though he stood a little straighter anyway.

At Marta's Corner Market he found the milk, cold and sweating, and carried it to the register with both hands. Marta rang it up, took his five, and handed him a quarter, a dime, and two pennies. Samuel stepped aside, laid the coins on the edge of the counter, and counted. He counted again. If the milk was $4.56, he was owed forty-four cents, and thirty-seven cents was not forty-four cents. Either he was wrong or she was, and he did not think he was wrong, because he had done the subtraction twice in his head while walking past the blue house with the influential yellow mailbox, the one everybody in the neighborhood used when giving directions. "Excuse me," he said, holding up the coins. "I think I'm short seven cents." Marta squinted at the register, said, "The button sticks on the fours," and dropped a nickel and two pennies into his palm.

He was still grinning about that when he got home and found his little cousin Theo on the back steps, knee bleeding in a long red smear, sniffling. "I fell off the wagon," Theo said, which was his whole diagnosis and clearly enough for him. Samuel set the milk on the kitchen table and reached for Theo's knee, then stopped. Last year the school nurse had helped Samuel with a gashed palm, and the first thing she had done, before anything else, was walk to the sink and wash her hands. He had thought it was strange then, but now it clicked into place like the change problem: something you did before the touching, not after. Germs didn't get into the cut if they never got onto the hands that touched the cut.

"Wait right there," Samuel said. "I have to wash my hands first." Theo looked at him like he was crazy. "My knee is the problem, not your hands." "My hands are going to land on your knee," Samuel said, soaping up to the wrists, "so they're part of the problem now." Theo thought about that, frowned, and held still while Samuel rinsed, dried, and pressed a clean paper towel against the scrape.

Samuel carried the milk to his mother along with the exact change, forty-four cents, counted twice. She looked at the coins, then at Theo's bandaged knee, then at Samuel's still-damp hands. "Forty-four cents and one fixed cousin," she said. "Not bad for a first trip." Theo lifted his leg into the light to admire it. "He washed his hands before he even touched me," he announced. "Like a doctor."

The zit had appeared on Sunday, right on the end of Emmett's nose, and school pictures were on Wednesday morning. He leaned against the car window while his mom drove, tilting the visor mirror to study it again, as if it might have shrunk since breakfast. It had not. His little sister used to get chocolate on her face and it wiped off with a napkin. This thing was different, and it seemed unfair that his own face would betray him two days before the photographer.

"Mom, can we stop somewhere? Like a pharmacy?"

She glanced over. "For what, honey?"

"Nothing. Face stuff." He felt his ears go hot. "Dad appointed me to pick up his razors anyway," he added, which was technically true, since Dad had said "grab me some razors if you're out" last week. Mom pulled into the parking lot of the drugstore by the hardware shop.

Emmett found the razor aisle first, then drifted to the wall of face washes, which was bigger than he expected. He was scanning shelves when a girl from his grade, Priya, appeared beside him, holding two bottles and turning them over to read the backs.

"Picture day?" she asked. "Me too. I woke up with three of them on my chin." She held up a bottle. "This one says it removes excess oil. My brother says pimples show up because of puberty. Hormones make the oil glands in your skin produce more oil, and it's called sebum, and it clogs your pores."

"Oil glands?" Emmett said. "I thought it was like dirt or something."

"That's what I thought. But it starts inside." She compared labels again. "So washing a million times wouldn't even fix it, because the stuff is coming from under the skin." She put one bottle back and kept the stronger one.

Emmett picked up a wash labeled for oily skin and read the back. The instructions were explicit: use twice daily, avoid eyes, rinse thoroughly. Twice daily. He counted backward. Two days until pictures meant four washes, if he started tonight. One wash right now in the store bathroom, one before bed, two more tomorrow and Tuesday. It wasn't much of a plan, but it was a plan, and having one made his shoulders loosen.

He paid with his own money, and in the car he read the bottle the whole way home, checking the ingredients like they were a code he might crack.

"Did you get your dad's razors?" Mom asked as they turned onto their street.

"Razors," Emmett said. "Right." He'd forgotten them completely. He ran back inside the store, grabbed the razors, and caught up with his mom at the register, the face wash in one hand and the razors in the other, four washes left before Wednesday.

The lights went out at 7:40, right in the middle of Alexandra's homework, and the whole house sank into a black so complete she couldn't even find her own elbow. "The power's out," her little brother Marcus announced from the hallway, as if she might not have noticed.

Alexandra fished the flashlight from the kitchen drawer and did some thinking while Marcus bumped into the coffee table behind her. The streetlights outside were dark too, which meant it wasn't just their house. And on the walk home from school, after the storm, she had seen a wire lying across the sidewalk two blocks over. It had looked harmless, dull and quiet, not sparking or humming like wires in movies. But her science teacher had once said something Alexandra had never forgotten: a fallen power line can still carry deadly electricity even when it is not sparking, so it should be treated as live, kept well away from, and reported. Mr. Okafor had made them all repeat it twice, which had seemed ridiculous at the time and now seemed like the smartest thing anyone had ever done.

"Marcus, do not eat that cheese," she said, shining the flashlight on him. He froze with the block halfway to his mouth. "That's for dinner. It's the most nutritious thing we have until the fridge situation stabilizes." The situation, as far as she could tell, was that the temperature inside would fluctuate every time he opened the door to graze, and the cheese would not survive his snacking until morning.

Her phone was at nine percent, so she typed fast: "Mom. Power out on our street. I think it's the downed wire on Elm, two blocks from school. I saw it on the way home. I did NOT touch it, I stayed way back. Please call it in to the power company, my battery is almost dead." Send. The battery dropped to eight percent, then seven, as if to add commentary.

Twenty minutes later the porch lit up, the refrigerator hummed like a released prisoner, and headlights swept the window. Marcus cheered. Alexandra's phone buzzed once before it died: "Reported. Proud of you. Also I'm bringing pizza, keep your paws off the cheese." Alexandra laughed and hid the cheese behind the milk anyway.

Grace ran her monologue for the fourth time on the draft of a stage built from plywood scraps, but every time she reached the line "You never listen to me anyway," her arms hung stiff at her sides and the words came out flat as cardboard. The community theatre was so dilapidated that rain dripped into a bucket near the props table, and the director wanted pauses and gestures that showed real anger before Friday's audition.

Across the stage, Marco was struggling too. His partner hadn't shown up, so he was supposed to improvise a scene with a girl named Priya, but Priya stood frozen near the curtain, saying nothing, staring at her sneakers. Marco tried asking her questions. Nothing. He waved a hand in front of her face. Still nothing.

Then Marco turned, planted his feet, and barked, "Captain, the ship is taking on water! I need orders!" Priya's shoulders snapped back as if someone had pulled a string. "Seal the lower deck," she said at once, pointing toward the wings. "And send two men to the pumps. Move!" Grace watched from her plywood corner, and something clicked. He had made her the captain just by calling her one. Priya hadn't been stuck because she had no ideas; she'd been stuck because she had no part to play yet.

After rehearsal, Grace caught Priya by the costume rack. "That thing Marco did, what was it?"

"Endowing," Priya said. "Giving your partner a role or trait through what you say. Like if I say 'Doctor, my arm hurts,' I've just made you the doctor."

Grace tried it that night with her little brother, who was sprawled on the couch. "Grandfather, tell me again why you never listen to me." He sat up, wheezed in a creaky old voice, and said, "Because you mumble, child." Grace felt her fists find her hips on their own, and the anger line burst out of her with a pause before it that surprised them both.

"Again," her brother said, settling back into the cushions. "And this time, Grandfather, you'd better answer me."

Gavin raised his hand so fast his chair scraped the floor. Mr. Okafor had just asked whether anyone could settle the argument Gavin and Priya had been having since Tuesday, and Gavin was not going to let the moment slip away. "Priya says most students at our school walk to school," he announced. "I think that's wrong. Almost everybody gets dropped off. The car line every morning goes all the way past the gym."

"That's your opinion," Priya said, arms folded. "You can't prove a thing by looking at one line of cars."

Mr. Okafor didn't jump in, which annoyed Gavin, because usually teachers jumped in constantly. Instead the class sat there with the question hanging in the air like the smell of disinfectant from the hallway. Gavin stared at the sparse corkboard by the window, where only two faded posters hung, and tried to think. He remembered last fall, when he'd claimed the cafeteria ran out of pizza by Wednesday, and Maya had counted for a whole week and shown it lasted until Thursday. He'd been wrong then, too, and it had stung, but not as much as being wrong without knowing would have.

"Wait," he said slowly. "It's not just an opinion. It's a claim. Like, it could be checked. Nobody has checked it yet, but we could." Priya tilted her head. "How?" she asked. "Follow everybody home?" Someone laughed. "A survey," Gavin said. "We ask every student how they get to school and count it up. Then we'd know if most of them walk or not." The word felt good in his mouth, solid, like a handle on a door he could actually open.

Mr. Okafor suggested they postpone the debate until they had data, and the class agreed to run the survey at lunch on Thursday. On Thursday, Gavin stood at the cafeteria door with a clipboard, pencil shaking slightly from too much excitement and not enough breakfast. The first twenty kids mostly said "bus," which surprised him. By the time the third lunch period started, his tally sheet was a mess of slashes and smudged graphite, but a pattern was climbing out of it anyway, one he hadn't predicted and Priya hadn't either.

They counted the sheets in Mr. Okafor's room after school, the radiator ticking, the hallway outside gone quiet. Priya totaled the walkers; Gavin totaled everyone else. He looked at her total, then at his own, then out the window at the empty car line loop, still painted yellow. "So I was wrong," he said, "but I was right that we could find out." Priya grinned and spun the clipboard toward him. "Count them again," she said. "I want to see your face when you get to the end."

Michael stood at the counter of Delgado's Corner Store with four dollars and a math test folded in his back pocket, and he had a problem. The problem was that Mr. Pruitt had promised a pizza party for the whole class if anyone scored a hundred on Friday's test, and Michael was the only one even close. The other problem was the machine by the door.

It was an old claw machine, and today it held a single rubber ball with a coordinate grid printed on it, along with a few random prizes nobody wanted. Michael had already spent two dollars trying to grab that ball. The claw's grip seemed to evaporate every time it lifted, like his luck was steaming away into the air. If he could win the ball, he'd have the one study tool he actually wanted, because the ball showed equations and their lines, and lines were exactly the thing he couldn't picture.

"Four dollars," said Rosa, who worked the register and was in his sister Ana's grade. "You going to buy gum or feed that machine again?"

"Neither yet," Michael said. He unfolded the practice sheet Mr. Pruitt had given him. At the top, Ana had scrawled a battleship game from last night, where she'd sworn his shot at (3, 5) was a miss because he'd counted up three and over five instead of across first. They'd argued until their dad made them wash dishes.

Michael tapped the paper. If he solved for x, he'd get a number. Then he could put that number in the first slot of a pair and pick any number for the second slot, and plot the point. He tried it with 2x plus 1 equals 7. He subtracted the 1 from both sides in his head, then divided, and got x equals 3. So the pair started with 3, then across first, like Ana kept insisting. He drew a quick grid on the back of his receipt, marked (3, 5) by counting three across and five up, and marked (3, 0) too, and there they sat in a line going straight up and down, like a fence post.

"The first number is across," he said out loud. "The second one is up or down."

"So?" said Rosa.

"So the ball is the same thing." Through the scratched glass, every printed line on that rubber ball slanted upward at the same steady angle, and each label started with the x value. If he imagined the claw dropping at a spot three across from the left wall and five up from the bottom, he could aim it like a plotted point instead of guessing.

He fed in his last quarter, counted three across, five up, and pressed the button. The claw swung, dropped, and closed on the ball. It lifted. It held.

Rosa leaned over the counter. "Okay, that was not luck."

The claw carried the ball toward the chute, then stopped directly above it and opened its grip, one inch short of the drop. Michael stared. Then he grabbed the receipt, folded it into a tight wedge, reached through the prize flap, and nudged the ball the last inch until it tumbled into his hand.

"Friday," he told Rosa, holding it up. "Class pizza. Three across, five up."

Luca slid into the green plastic seat behind Dev and dropped his backpack like a gauntlet. Every kid on Bus 14 knew the rule: the last row belonged to whoever claimed it first, and all year Dev had conquered that row more than anyone else. His name sat at the top of the ranking Zuri kept on the fogged window with her finger, and Luca's name sat right below it, second, the way it had sat since October.

"Nine for Dev, eight for Luca," Zuri announced that morning, rewriting the tally marks. "Dev's winning sixty percent of the days so far. Luca's at fifty-three."

Dev grinned and stretched his legs across the whole row like a king. Luca stared at the tally marks instead of at Dev, because something about them had been bothering him for a week. The ranking said Dev was first and Luca was second, but the tallies said something the ranking didn't. He counted them twice, lips moving, while the bus jolted over the railroad tracks.

"Nine and eight," Luca said slowly. "You're only ahead by one day. One day out of thirty-some. But the ranking makes it look like you own the row." He tapped the fogged glass. "A ranking shows who's ahead. It doesn't show by how much. First and second could be a hundredth apart or a mile apart, and the list looks exactly the same."

"So?" Dev said, though his grin had gone a little brittle around the edges.

"So I'm not actually losing by much. I'm losing by exactly one day." Luca pulled out a notebook and wrote tomorrow's date at the top of a clean page. He had a plan: get to the stop ten minutes early, which was annoying, but one day would flip the ranking, and one day was all that separated them.

At the next stop, Marisol climbed on holding a crumpled paper. She'd been collecting signatures all week, and now she stood in the aisle and cleared her throat. "We took a ballot," she announced. "Vote on whether the back row gets rotated instead of raced for. It passed. Twenty-two to four."

Dev's mouth fell open. Ziri wiped the whole ranking off the window with her sleeve, tallies and all, and the fog closed over it like a curtain.

"Rotated," Dev repeated, staring at his sneakers.

Luca leaned back in the last row, which was suddenly nobody's row, and everybody's. "You know," he said, "I got here early today anyway."

"Yeah," Dev said. "By one minute."

"Thirty seconds," said Luca. "Check the tally."

Grandma Wei arrived on Thursday, and by Friday night Isla had a problem: what to wear to her cousin Marisol's wedding shower on Saturday. Grandma had barely unpacked before she started pulling clothes out of Isla's closet and sorting them into two piles, one for yes and one for no.

"Not the white dress," Grandma said, holding up Isla's favorite one like it was a wet sock.

"It's a wedding thing," Isla said. "Marisol's whole theme is white. The invitations are white. The cake is white. The bride even wears white."

Grandma set the dress on the no pile and smoothed it flat, as if to preserve its feelings. "White is for mourning at funerals," she said. "In traditional Chinese culture, that is what we wear. For the dead." Then she pointed at Isla's rust-colored skirt. "Wear this."

Isla stared at her. She had never heard anything like this. Her brain started running its usual algorithm for arguments with Grandma: state facts, provide evidence, lose anyway.

Dad came through with the lasagna, and Isla got her chance. "Dad, tell Grandma white is a wedding color."

Dad put down the dish and rubbed his neck. "Both are true," he said. "Lots of Western brides wear white. And in Grandma's tradition, white is worn for mourning. Different people, same color, opposite meanings." He gave the no pile a guilty glance. "At your Aunt Po's funeral, everyone wore white. Marisol's wedding, the bride will too. Nobody's wrong."

Isla chewed on that through half a plate of lasagna. Same color. Two meanings. That meant the shower was going to be a room full of people doing opposite things at the same time, and only some of them would know it. She imagined Marisol's grandmother from Mexico, her neighbors, her own grandma, all handing gifts and thinking completely different thoughts about identical white napkins.

So she tested it. "Grandma, what if everyone at the party wears white except me? Won't I look like I'm at the wrong event?"

"Then you will look like the only person there with respect," Grandma said.

"That's a rebellious plan," Isla said. "Wearing not-white to a white party."

"Rebellious," Grandma agreed, spearing a meatball.

Isla tried one more angle. "Grandma, Marisol asked me to hand out the favors. White boxes with white ribbons. If I wear the rust skirt, the pictures will look strange."

Grandma put down her fork. For a moment Isla thought the algorithm had finally found a winning input. Then Grandma said, "The boxes are white?"

"Every single one."

Grandma looked at the window for a while. "Then the boxes are for mourning," she said, "and Marisol must pick new boxes, or I must pick new eyes." She picked up her fork again and went back to the lasagna. "Hand me the bread, and on Saturday you wear the rust."

Hudson had a report due Monday on why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids, which would have been fine if the exhibit he needed hadn't been closed for cleaning. A paper sign, unbothered by his opinion, said so.

"Gift shop's open," said his little sister Priya, who had come along for the air conditioning and wanted a replica canopic jar she'd been guarding with her eyes since noon.

The museum guide, sweeping near the barrier, tipped her head toward a corridor. "Pioneer wing's open. There's a river model down there too. Sometimes the river helps with the Egypt questions."

Hudson doubted a covered wagon could explain a pyramid, but he followed the corridor anyway. He found a long table with water and silt, a model of the Nile flooding its banks, and a wall panel about fields turning green every year while the desert stayed brown. He pushed a wooden lever and watched the water rise, leave dark mud, then sink. The river was the signal, he thought, the thing farmers watched to know when to plant. That's why priests studied the flood, and why the pharaoh, whose pyramid sat above the sand like a promise, got credit when the harvest came in. Priya pressed the lever too, twice, just to see the mud decompose into the water like cocoa in milk.

Beyond the river table sat a glass case with a diary from 1837. Hudson read the line out loud because it stopped him. "The bank took the farm in the spring. We hear land out west is cheap and the soil is black as coal, so we will risk the trail."

"So they just left?" Priya asked.

"The Panic of 1837 ruined a lot of farmers," Hudson said slowly, connecting it. "Then they went west for the good land." Ruined farmers, black soil, a dangerous trail. People following a signal of their own.

Priya tugged his sleeve. "You owe me a jar."

He bought her the small one, not the big one. She held it up to the light, decided it was better anyway, and marched out the door ahead of him.

Benjamin stood at the edge of the school auditorium stage, the spotlights making him squint, and tried again. "My brother took my compass. My brother sailed away. My brother was swallowed by the sea." He had marked seven places to pause and seven gestures, one for every sentence, but when he finished, his friend Priya just blinked from the third row.

"I counted your moves," she called up. "It felt like a list, not a story."

"That's the problem!" Benjamin said, flapping his script. "Seven pauses, and they all cancel each other out." He had been sure that more gestures meant more feeling. Now he suspected the opposite, that the audience could only hold a few big things in their heads at once, but he needed proof.

In the library the next day he flipped through a book on Rome and stopped at a page about a battle. "Listen to this," he told Priya. "Julius Caesar reported a quick victory at the Battle of Zela in 47 BC with just three Latin words. 'Veni, vidi, vici.' I came, I saw, I conquered."

"Three words?" Priya said. "For a whole battle?"

"That's the trick. Three beats, not seven." Priya frowned, because she still believed more was more, but she agreed to watch one more rehearsal after school.

The auditorium was notorious for its squeaky third floorboard, so Benjamin avoided it entirely and stood dead center. He decided to use only three gestures, and to conceal his nerves by gripping the edge of his sleeve during the rest, letting his hands be still on purpose. Before he began, he and Priya had a quick negotiation: she would raise a finger at every move he made so he could count them himself.

He let the silence stretch. "My brother took my compass." One step forward. "My brother sailed away." One arm lifted toward the back wall. "My brother was swallowed by the sea." Both hands opened, then slowly closed.

Nobody said anything for a second. Then Priya stood up and clapped.

"Okay," she said, "I take it back. Three wins."

Benjamin grinned and looked out at the empty seats, imagining them full. "Tomorrow we run it for the whole class," he said. "Same three. Don't touch the third floorboard."

Jaxson sat at the kitchen table with a wastebasket between his knees and the family's last box of tissues in front of him, so depleted it held only four. He had blown his nose eleven times since breakfast, hard, the way you would to clear out anything clogged, and after every single blow his nose still felt packed shut, like a sock stuck in a doorway.

"Stop blowing so much," said his older sister, Priya, dumping soup into a pot. "You're going to make your ears pop."

"It's already blocked. Blowing is supposed to fix that." He folded the tissue, blew again, and listened. Nothing moved. He pinched his nostrils closed and breathed in through his mouth, then slowly released them, and there was still that stuffed, thick feeling, deep in there, where no tissue could reach. That was strange. If mucus were the problem, blowing should have cleared some of it. He grabbed the house tablet and typed why does blowing not help a stuffy nose.

The first answer stopped him cold. A stuffy nose during a cold is caused mainly by swollen blood vessels and inflamed tissue in the lining of the nose, not only by a buildup of mucus. He read it twice. So the blockage was puffy, swollen walls, not a pile of gunk. Blowing at swollen walls was like trying to unclog a straw by sucking on it when the straw itself was pinched.

He tried an idea. He ran a towel under hot water, wrung it out, and held it warm against the bridge of his nose for a few minutes, then breathed slowly through each side. When he lowered the towel, air actually moved. Not perfectly, but moved.

"Did you just nominate yourself chief of home medicine?" Priya asked, stirring.

"No. I changed my mind about the tissues. We don't need to buy six boxes. It's not a mucus problem." He slid the nearly empty box across the table to her. "Also, I decided the cold is not a monarchy. Nobody rules it. It just does whatever it wants."

"Poor kingdom," Priya said. "Impoverished, with four tissues left."

Jaxson laughed, then winced, then breathed in, one nostril at a time, counting. "Three," he said. "Four. It's opening up."

Alexis laced his skates in the bench area of Riverside Ice Arena and watched his best friend Dante glide past the tryout line with his usual speed. That was the strange part. Dante was the fastest skater in sixth grade, but this morning he had wobbled twice during warm-ups, and when Coach Reyes blew the whistle, Dante's stop was so abrupt that he nearly fell over backward. Alexis filed that away and took his own turn around the cones.

The tryouts were for the school hockey team, and thirty kids had shown up to participate.
