Alexis wanted a forward spot, but so did Marcus Tran, who had been talking all week about how he was going to take it. Marcus was fast, too. During the second drill, Alexis noticed something. Marcus kept yawning on the bench. When the puck came to him, he reacted late, half a second behind, like a video with bad lag.

Between drills, Alexis sat next to him. "You look like you're skating through glue," Alexis said.

"I was up till two playing Starfall Six," Marcus admitted. "I only slept six hours. I figured I'd be fine."

Alexis had spent a week researching sleep for a science project, mostly so he could win arguments about bedtime. "Kids our age are supposed to get nine to twelve hours a night," he said. "Even teenagers only get to drop down to eight to ten. Six isn't on the chart for anybody."

"Whatever," Marcus said, and skated off, wobbling on the first turn.

Alexis thought about it while he waited for the scrimmage. He had a theory, one he couldn't see directly: the problem wasn't skating skill, it was an invisible cause, missing sleep, slowing everyone who had it. He could test it. His own plan had been to stay up nervous and wake at six, but instead he had gone to bed at nine thirty, and his legs felt springy on every crossover. When the scrimmage started, he cut left, took the pass, and scored on a rebound while Marcus watched the play arrive a beat too late.

At the end, Coach Reyes posted the list on the rink door. Alexis made forwards. Dante, who had crashed into the boards twice, made alternates. Marcus's name was not on the paper at all.

On the walk out, Dante pulled his hood up. "My cousin said there's a supplement for this. He's basically an entrepreneur, he sells protein powder to eighth graders out of his locker."

"Forget the powder," Alexis said. "Try nine hours."

Dante groaned. "That's so much sleeping."

Alexis pointed at the scoreboard clock, which still glowed above the empty ice. "You've got tryouts again in March. That's like ninety nights. You could test it properly."

Dante squinted at the clock, did some visible math, and said, "Fine. But if I turn into a grandpa who goes to bed at eight thirty, you're carrying my bag."

Alexis swung his own bag over his shoulder and said, "Deal," and the doors hissed shut behind them.

Kayla read her story aloud at the kitchen table, alone, because yesterday she had read it aloud to the class and watched Marcus fall asleep with his eyes open. Not closed. Open. That took a kind of commitment.

She counted something on the draft. Every sentence she'd written was long. She'd written them long on purpose, because long sentences seemed like more sentence for the money. Her first one had fourteen words, the next one had fifteen, the one after that had thirteen. They marched. They marched like a line of identical bricks, and apparently a line of identical bricks could put Marcus to sleep in under a minute.

The dilemma was this: cut them down, or mix them up. She tried cutting the weak adjectives first, the ones her teacher had circled in red, the verys and reallys and nicelies. That helped a little. The sentences got cleaner but they still marched, thirteen, twelve, thirteen, like a metronome nobody had asked for.

So she tried the other thing. She broke one long sentence in half and left the piece of it standing there on its own. "Nobody answered." Three words. Then a long sentence after it, then another short one. She read the new version out loud in the empty kitchen, slowly, the way she'd read to the class, and she could hear something change. Her voice had somewhere to go now. It sped up, slowed down, sped up again, like she was driving a bike over hills instead of a parking lot.

"It has rhythm," she said to the refrigerator. The refrigerator did not disagree.

She read it one more time to calibrate, timing herself with the microwave clock, and the whole thing felt about a minute shorter and a hundred percent less like a lullaby. It seemed logical, anyway, that Marcus's open-eyed sleep had been caused by the march of same-length sentences, and that a person needed a few short ones to break up the long ones, like rest stops. She underlined the short sentences in blue so she could see the pattern down the page: long, long, short, long, short, long. A heartbeat, sort of. Not a march.

At school the next day she raised her hand before her nerve could change its mind. She read the first paragraph, got to "Nobody answered," and looked up. Marcus was sitting straighter. He was actually blinking.

"You're not asleep," Kayla said.

"I'm deciding whether to be," said Marcus. "Keep going."

The food bank shared a parking lot with the neighborhood cleanup, so Emily ended up doing both, hauling a bag of trash in one hand and a box of dented soup cans in the other. Inside the food bank, her job was sorting, which mostly meant excavating the bottom of a donation barrel to see what had been squashed flat back in March. That was where she found the envelope.

"Mail goes in the office," said Mr. Alvarez, a volunteer whose grandkid had dragged him along. Then he squinted at it. "Actually, that's addressed to us."

The letter was from a farm two towns over. The handwriting slanted uphill. "You called about surplus kale. Come Saturday and glean the back field. Whatever's left after the harvest is yours." Emily read it twice. "Glean" sounded like something you did to a fish.

"It's an old idea," Mr. Alvarez said. "My grandmother would say it. The Book of Leviticus tells farmers to leave the edges of their fields unharvested, for the poor and for strangers." He handed the letter back. "Never thought I'd see it in a note about kale."

Saturday, Emily rode along in the food bank van. The farmer, a woman named Dot, walked them past rows already picked clean, then stopped at the field's edge, where a fringe of kale and stray cabbage still stood. "Combines can't get this close to the fence," she said. "So it rots. Seems bizarre, all this waste two feet from hunger." Emily tested the idea with her fingers, snapping stem after stem, filling crate after crate. Forty pounds, the scale said at the end.

Dot signed the donation slip and read it over. "Funny thing. I got a letter from the food bank last spring asking for surplus. I never called them back." She looked at Emily. "You all got a letter from me, though. Mine." Emily pulled the envelope from her jacket. The date on the letter was three years old. Somewhere in that donation barrel, buried under soup, an old invitation had waited for the barrel to be dug out. "We'd better answer it," Emily said, and asked Dot for a pen.

Emile had been practicing the jarabe in his cousin Rosa's garage for three days, and his boots still tangled on the zapateado every fourth count. Rosa's quinceañera was on Saturday, and the whole family expected him to dance in the performance at the party. The trouble was that Rosa kept disappearing every Tuesday and Thursday afternoon, right when they were supposed to rehearse together, and he couldn't figure out where she went. "You can't fix a pattern you can't see," his grandfather always said, so Emile decided to test it. If Rosa was hiding from the dancing, she would be anywhere the music wasn't. If it was something else, there would be one consistent place.

He found her in the den, sitting under the attic's pink insulation that showed through a gap in the ceiling tiles, holding a folded piece of paper. She looked up, and her shoulders dropped. "You're going to think it's silly," she said. "Read it," said Emile. She stood and read a passage aloud, slowly, the way you'd read something that mattered. "The party isn't until eight," she said. "But the day starts with the Mass. It's a Mass of thanksgiving." Emile had assumed the quinceañera was just the party, and now the whole day rearranged itself in his head: church first, family giving thanks, and only then the food and the dancing.

He remembered last summer, when his other cousin Marisol had turned fifteen and he'd been bored through the ceremony, squirming in the pew, thinking it was something to get through before the cake. He'd changed his mind about a lot since then. Now he understood why the girls practiced their readings so seriously, why Marisol had carried a small crown that her mother said was meant to symbolize something passing from one generation to the next.

"I'll help you," Emile said. "You read, I'll be the congregation." Rosa smiled and started over, and Emile stamped a soft zapateado under the table to keep her rhythm steady. When she finished without stumbling, he clapped so hard the paper jumped right out of her hands.

Samantha taped the folded program to her bedroom mirror so she would see it while she practiced. The order of songs ran down the page, and at the bottom, in her music teacher's handwriting, was the note she kept rereading: "After the last song, exit stage left, row by row." She hummed the second verse of "Oh, Shenandoah," stopped, and looked at the note again.

The problem was the word "left." In the mirror behind her, her bedroom door appeared on the right, but Samantha knew it was really on the left, because a mirror flips things. The audience, she thought, would be like a mirror. They would face her. So when they looked at her, her left side would be on their right. If stage left meant the left side as the audience saw it, she would walk toward the piano. If it meant her own left, she would walk toward the drums. Two options, and no way to check the answer from her bedroom.

She needed a test. At school the next day, she found Marcus, who had been in last year's concert. "When Mr. Okafor said exit stage left, which way did you actually go?" Marcus pointed toward the gym's far side, the side away from the piano. Samantha stood where a singer would stand, faced the empty bleachers, and checked which hand was on that side. Her left. She worked it out on the spot: stage left and stage right are the performers' left and right as they stand facing the audience.

The night of the concert, the gym lights radiated heat down onto the rows of singers, and Samantha felt the last song approaching, imminent and unstoppable. When the final note ended, Mr. Okafor raised his hand toward the far wing. Row by row, the singers filed off. Priya, beside Samantha, started to turn toward the piano. Samantha caught her sleeve. "Stage left is our left," she whispered, "not the audience's." Priya turned, and they stepped off together into the dark wing, where Marcus was waiting with two bottles of water.

Mia stood in front of a painting of an orange with a single lamp shining on it, sketchbook clamped under her arm. She had come to the gallery because her art club's sketching day was mandatory, and because she wanted one thing: to make her drawings stop looking flat. She picked a spot on the bench, opened to a blank page, and drew a circle. Then came the hard part. Where exactly did the light go, and where did the dark?

She shaded one side of the sphere, leaving a bright spot where the lamp would hit it. Behind it she dragged a smudge of graphite for the cast shadow on the table. Then, to make the ball look round, she erased a pale curve along the bottom of the dark side. She held the sketchpad out at arm's length and squinted.

A boy on the next bench leaned over. "Why does yours look like it has two lamps?"

Mia looked again. He was right. The pale curve at the bottom glowed almost white, like a second light hidden under the table. "It's not supposed to be that bright," she muttered. She studied the painting on the wall instead. On the orange's dark side, near the bottom, there was a soft lightness, lighter than the deepest part of the shadow, but never as light as the sunlit side. She tested it: she darkened her pale curve two pencil steps, keeping the core of the shadow darkest of all and the lit side still the brightest.

"Better," the boy said. "It looks like it's sitting on something."

"It's the table bouncing light back up," Mia said. "You just can't let it win."

She decided to isolate that one strip of reflected light and practice it on a second sphere, then a third, building her values in order, brightest to darkest, like a hierarchy. Her eraser was nearly a stub by the time the guard announced closing. Mia packed up slowly, then turned back for one last look at the orange.

"Same model tomorrow," she told it.

Asher sat in the back row of his new classroom while the teacher talked about the election posters on the wall. "Some of these are propaganda," she said, "posters made to persuade you, not to inform you." Asher copied the word into his notebook, though his mind kept drifting to the moving truck parked outside his old house three states away. His whole life was in those boxes, and tomorrow he would have to face them.

He remembered the last night in the old house, when his sister Priya had dug through a mountain of boxes hunting for her bedsheets. "Nobody labeled anything," she had groaned, pulling out a frying pan, a lamp, and a box of comic books. Asher had stood in the doorway watching her work by flashlight, and an idea had started to digest slowly in his head. The boxes had no writing on them, just brown opaque flaps, all looking the same, so every single one had to be opened and searched. There had to be a better way.

Now, after his first day at the new school, he walked through the empty rooms of the new house. His parents wouldn't arrive with the truck until morning, but the first boxes, the ones they had shipped ahead, were stacked in the garage. Asher found a marker in his backpack and got to work. On each box he wrote two things: the room it belonged in, and what was inside. "Kitchen, pots and pans." "Priya's room, bedsheets." When the truck came, his uncle would only have to read a box once and carry it straight to the right place, instead of dropping everything in the living room like last time.

The next morning, the truck rumbled into the driveway. Asher handed boxes off the lift one by one, pointing with the marker. "Bathroom, up the stairs." "My room, second door." Priya grabbed a box, read the label, and grinned. "Bedsheets," she said. "You're a genius." By lunch, most of the boxes had already found their rooms, and Asher carried the last one, marked "My room, comic books," up the stairs two at a time.

Kate stood at Mr. Oliver's cheese stall on Saturday morning, a wooden spoon in her hand and a small pot on his portable burner. Last summer, at her grandmother's house, she had watched a pot of macaroni and cheese go from silky to lumpy in about ten seconds, and she had promised herself she would figure out why. Today was her chance, because Mr. Oliver had offered to teach her, and his sauces never had a single lump.

"Flour and butter first," he said. "Equal parts, stir until it smells like toast. Then the milk, a little at a time." Kate stirred the flour and butter together, and it looked like wet sand at the beach, the kind you'd use to build a doomed castle. She added the milk slowly, whisking, and held her breath. "The suspense is killing you," Mr. Oliver said, laughing. "You can let your shoulders down. It's just cheese." The sauce turned smooth, and Kate felt like she had uncovered a secret rule of the universe: add the liquid gradually, whisk hard, and the lumps never get a chance to form.

Two stalls over, her little brother Theo was helping their dad sell jars of jam, and every few minutes he darted back to check the pot of rice simmering on their camp stove. He lifted the lid, peered in, and clapped it back down. He did it again. And again. When he served sample cups of rice and beans to customers, one man chewed thoughtfully and said, "Bit crunchy, isn't it?" Theo's face went pink to the tips of his ears.

Kate carried a taste over and crunched her way through it. She remembered the toast smell of the roux, how the timing had mattered, and she thought about Theo's lid. "Theo," she said, "when you kept peeking, the steam escaped, and that leaves the grains undercooked." Theo stared at the pot as if it had betrayed him. "So the rice needed the lid on the whole time?" "The whole time. No peeking." She handed him a fresh pot to start over. "Want to make the roux with me while it cooks? Fair warning, though. You have to whisk until your arm wants to fall off." Theo grabbed a spoon. "My arm never wants to fall off," he said. "It's that kind of arm."

Emmett coasted to a stop in front of his grandfather's gate, one foot down on the gravel lane, and stared at the sign he'd never noticed before. "No skateboarding in Harrow Park," it said, in letters too tidy to have been scribbled by anybody who actually skated. The park was two blocks from Grandpa's house, and Emmett had been riding its smooth paths since he was eight.

He remembered last summer, the day he'd finally landed the kickflip on the park's long concrete curve. He'd been so proud that he'd rolled all the way to Grandpa's back garden, where the tomato vines grew lush and green along the fence, and announced it through the screen door. Grandpa had come out wiping his hands on a towel and said, "Do it again, then." Emmett had tried six times and landed it once, and Grandpa had clapped like it was a home run.

Now the sign was up, and Emmett pushed through the gate with the board under his arm, already halfway through the question. "Grandpa, who puts up a sign like that? Can they just decide?"

"They can if the town council decides it," Grandpa said from the porch. He was sorting a crate of tomatoes, turning each one over. "It's a bylaw. A rule made by the local government, and it applies only inside this town. You could ride that thing in the next county over and it wouldn't mean a thing to them."

Emmett sat down on the steps, spinning one of the board's wheels with his thumb. The wheels were a tough polymer, some kind of plastic his cousin had told him about, and they spun a long time on a clean bearing. So the sign wasn't a law of the whole country. It was a town rule, made by town people. Which meant, maybe, town people could change it. "How would somebody get them to change it?"

"Petition," Grandpa said. "You collect signatures, you show up at a council meeting, and you ask. Enough names can generate a fair bit of attention. I did it once, over the garbage pickup schedule." He held up a tomato, ripe and heavy. "Worked, too."

That was the thing Emmett hadn't known: Grandpa had wanted the pickup moved off Tuesdays because it clashed with his market day, and forty signatures had done it. Emmett turned the problem over the way Grandpa turned the tomatoes. If the ban was a bylaw, then the people who signed didn't have to be skaters, just townspeople. If the council made the rule, the council could unmake it.

He spent the afternoon at the kitchen table with a notebook, drafting a page headed "Petition to Allow Skateboarding in Harrow Park." Then he rode to the community center, where Mr. Deloach, who ran it, looked at the page for a long moment. "You know," Mr. Deloach said slowly, "I've wanted a skate afternoon in the gym for years. Nobody ever asked me the right way."

"Then sign here," Emmett said, and slid the notebook across the desk, pen already lying on top of it.

The glass doors of city hall were so translucent that Jaxson walked toward them too fast and nearly bumped his nose on the frame. He straightened his backpack, which held one petition sheet with eleven signatures, all from kids at Riverside Park who wanted the bylaw banning skateboards there changed. His teacher had said a citizen could bring a petition to a councillor, but she had not said how, exactly, and the hallway ahead of him split into three different corridors.

He picked the corridor with a sign that said COUNCIL CHAMBERS and found a display case outside the big double doors. Inside, under old photographs, hung a copy of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. He scanned it while he worked up his courage, and something caught his eye. Most of the document was marked as coming into force in 1982, but section 15, the equality rights, had a different date printed beside it: 1985. He read the little card next to it twice. The equality rights had waited three years, the card said, to give governments time to update their laws. So the whole Charter had started in 1982, and this one part had started later, in 1985, three years after the rest.

Jaxson had a thought, and it made him grin. If even a country's most important rules could need time to be updated, then maybe a small city bylaw could be changed too. Maybe things that seemed permanent were really just waiting for someone to point them out. He tested the idea right there, whispering it to himself: "Rules can catch up."

A woman with a lanyard came out of the chambers carrying a box of agendas. "Can I help you?" she asked.

"I want to give a petition to a councillor," Jaxson said. "About the skateboard bylaw at Riverside Park. I have signatures." He held up his sheet, and his face went hot, because eleven signatures suddenly felt small. The embarrassment made his voice thinner than he wanted.

She looked at the names. "Eleven's a start," she said. "Councillor Amadi handles parks. Third floor, office twelve. She's in until four."

Jaxson rode the elevator with two men in suits who ignored him completely, which he decided was fine. At office twelve the door was open, and a woman was stacking papers behind a desk cluttered with coffee cups. He knocked on the doorframe anyway.

"Are you the councillor for parks?" he asked.

"I am."

"I have a petition. Eleven people signed it. I know that's not a lot, but I can get more, and I can contribute the research too. I already looked some stuff up." He stepped forward and laid the sheet on her desk. "The whole Charter started in 1982, but section 15, the equality rights, didn't come into force until 1985, three years after the rest, to give governments time to update their laws. So rules can be updated. That's what I'm asking for."

Councillor Amadi set down her stack and read every signature, top to bottom, before she looked up. "Tell me exactly what happens at that park on a Saturday," she said, and pulled out a chair.

Colton's phone buzzed at 6:47 on Tuesday, right as he sat down to spaghetti. The skate park group chat had gone from three messages a day to forty, because someone had pasted a letter from the local paper.

The letter said the town should never have agreed to install the skate park behind the elementary school, and it ended with a sentence Colton read four times: "The new park, which cost two million dollars, is a waste." His dad leaned over his shoulder, fork in hand. "Half of that sentence you could check," Dad said, and went back to his pasta.

Colton scrolled. Ravi had written "SO TRUE what a waste of money!!" and Marisol had written "no way, the park is awesome," and then the two of them had started typing in all caps about whose fault it was. Nobody had typed anything about the two million dollars.

He put his fork down. He could not see the town's bank account from the dinner table, but a cost was the kind of thing somebody had to have written down. The Parks Department had a website. He found a page about the skate park, and there it was, a citation at the bottom pointing to the town budget, and the budget said two million dollars. So that half of the sentence was true, or at least checkable, which was not the same as agreeing with it.

But "a waste" was different. He stared at the two words. Ravi thought the money should have gone to a pool. Marisol thought the park was the best thing in town. There was no budget page for awesome. His little sister wandered through the kitchen and he asked her, out of pure curiosity, whether she thought the park was a waste. "It's where I learned to drop in," she said, and took a garlic bread stick with her.

Back in the chat, Colton typed slowly, then faster: "Two different things got mixed in one sentence. The two million dollars part checks out, I found it in the town budget. The waste part is just what the guy thinks. You can't look that one up." Ravi replied with a thinking face. Marisol replied, "wait, so we were fighting about which part?" and then, a minute later, "because I only care about the park part."

Colton looked at the two distinct arguments, one about money that could be counted and one about fun that could not, sitting there in the same sentence like they belonged together. He picked his phone back up and typed: "new rule. If you can check it, link it." Ravi sent a thumbs up. Then a link appeared, from Ravi, to a petition for the pool. "This one you can check," Ravi wrote. "It has zero signatures."

Benjamin's laptop was so dilapidated that it made a sound like a dying kazoo whenever he opened more than three tabs, but it still ran a spreadsheet, which was all he needed. The problem was this: his cousin Marcus had sworn, in the family group chat, that TJ Ruiz was a better hitter than Sam Okafor, and Benjamin had exactly one weekend to prove him wrong. Batting average said Marcus was right, and Benjamin did not enjoy that.

He started copying numbers into the spreadsheet, row after row, while eating chips over the keyboard. His mother paused at the doorway and remarked that the hygiene of a desk used as a cafeteria was not something she wanted to quantify, then left him to it. He was still sulking over the averages when he remembered Saturday at his uncle Ray's sports bar, the TV turned to a baseball classic, his uncle swirling his drink.

"Some smarty-pants wrote a book called Moneyball," Uncle Ray had said. "Michael Lewis, 2003. It was about how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players." Then he had gone back to his wings, as if he hadn't just handed over a weapon.

Benjamin sat up so fast the chair squeaked. On-base percentage. Not hits. Times a player reached base, walks included. He found the columns for walks, typed the formula, and dragged it down the whole sheet, watching new numbers appear like something rising to the surface of a lake.

When he re-sorted the players by the new column, Sam Okafor climbed from eleventh to third, and TJ Ruiz sank like a stone with a family. Sam walked constantly; it didn't look exciting, so nobody talked about it, but there he was on base, inning after inning, being quietly useful. Marcus was ranking players with half the picture. Benjamin spent another hour checking, re-checking, and making the chart prettier than it needed to be, because charts that looked official won arguments.

He pasted the chart into the group chat and waited, hands folded behind his head. Three dots appeared. Then Marcus replied: "ok but I was still right about the nachos." Benjamin typed back, "Send me the nacho data and we'll see," and hit send before he could reconsider his life choices.

Luca knelt at the edge of the inflatable pool his dad had set up on the grass, breathing hard. Twenty-five metres of front crawl with side breathing, that was the goal, and so far he had managed about six before his face came up like a startled frog. The pool wasn't even twenty-five metres long, so he had to swim laps, turning at each end, which made everything worse. His younger brother Marco was supposed to count laps but kept getting distracted by the basketball game on the portable TV by the fence, the one Marco had bought with two months of income from mowing Mrs. Petro's lawn.

"Two laps," Marco called, not looking up.

Luca tried again. Kick, pull, breathe, but when he turned his head he always lifted it too far, and his legs sank, and he ended up spluttering. He climbed out, dripping, and stood next to Marco to watch the screen while he caught his breath. On the play, one team's guard dribbled around a big teammate who blocked the defender chasing him, and the defenders swapped who they were guarding.

"Switch," Marco muttered. "They switched on the pick and roll."

Luca squinted. The shortest defender on the court was now guarding the tallest player, who was posting up right under the basket, and the tall defender had been left chasing the quickest guard out top. Both matchups looked wrong. Luca wondered: did the switching team plan that, or did they just get stuck with it? It was like something hidden had shifted underneath the visible play, a rule you couldn't see until you traced each defender's path.

The tall player caught the ball and scored easily over the short defender. On the next possession, the same thing happened in reverse, and the quick guard blew past the lumbering tall defender.

"They keep switching," Luca said, "and every switch makes a mismatch."

Marco nodded. "The point guard spots it. Smallest guy on their tallest player."

Luca looked back at the pool. He'd been thinking about his breathing all wrong, like it was one fixed problem. But maybe it was a chain: something invisible upstream caused the spluttering downstream. If his head position was the "blocker," then maybe his arm pull was the defender getting switched onto the wrong job. When he lifted his head to breathe, his pulling arm stalled, and his legs, unguarded, sank. He had to keep the pull going while he turned, like the offense kept moving through the switch instead of freezing.

He asked Marco to retrieve the orange cones from the garage so they could mark twenty-five metres along the grass first, then measure the pool exactly, so the count would be credible instead of a guess. Four and a half lengths, it turned out.

Back in the water, Luca kicked off, pulled with his right arm, turned his head just enough, and kept the left arm moving through the switch. Breathe. Pull. Breathe. His legs stayed near the surface, almost weightless. He touched the far side, turned, and went again, counting under his breath. On the fourth length he was tired but smooth, and when his hand slapped the vinyl wall at the end, Marco was on his feet.

"That was five," Marco shouted. "You went past it!"

Luca laughed, gasping, and pushed wet hair out of his eyes. "Run it back," he said. "I want to see if it works twice."

Raphael sat on the floor of Mateo's kitchen, a paper menu spread between them and a box of cookies pretending to be a restaurant. Mateo's grandmother had come from Lyon in the spring, and she spoke almost no English, which meant Mateo was teaching Raphael enough French to survive a meal at her table. Today they were practicing what Raphael would say when the meal ended.

"Ask me for the bill," Mateo said, folding his arms like a waiter. He had even put a dish towel over his arm.

"La facture, s'il vous plaît," Raphael said, feeling proud. He had looked up "bill" in his notebook the night before, and facture was what the dictionary gave first.

Mateo winced. "Grand-mère will look at you like you asked for a tax invoice. That's for paperwork, not for restaurants."

Raphael's ears went hot. Last month he had tried ordering in French at the bakery near his house, and when he'd asked for something in the wrong words, the man behind the counter had laughed before correcting him. The humiliation had been small, but it stuck to him like gum on a shoe, corrosive enough that he'd almost skipped this whole project. Now he studied the menu again, thinking. If facture was a paperwork word, then French must have a separate word just for restaurant bills, the way English had "check" as well as "bill." Languages liked to hide the right word in a special pocket.

"Wait," he said. "Does the restaurant word sound like anything English?"

Mateo's little sister Camille wandered in and stole a cookie before they could stop her. "It's addition," she said with her mouth full.

"Like math?" Raphael asked. That seemed absurd. He turned it over in his head, testing it the way he tested a rule. "You add up everything you ate, so the bill is the addition?"

"Maybe," Mateo said. "Grand-mère just says it." He never explained things further than he had to.

They dragged Grand-mère in from the garden, her hands smelling of tomatoes and rain-wet soil. Raphael stood as straight as he could, held out the empty cookie plate, and said, "L'addition, s'il vous plaît." The words meant "The bill, please," though nobody translated; he just knew it now.

Grand-mère's whole face lifted. She clapped once, said something fast and delighted, and pressed a euro coin into his hand as if he had truly paid for his cookies.

"Keep it," she said in her slow, careful English. "You earned."

Raphael closed his fist around the coin and grinned at Mateo. "Same time next week?"

Tyler had promised his mom the kitchen table would be clear by six, and it was now 5:15, with the table covered in marbles, peppercorns, toothpicks, and a poster board that still said ATOM in crooked letters. The science fair was tomorrow morning. He had a model to build and, more urgently, a claim to fix, because last week he had told his whole class that burning toast was "basically the same as ice melting, just warmer." Priya had looked at him the way you look at a rodent that has wandered into your lunch bag, and Mr. Okafor had assigned him a demonstration to prove he understood the difference before the fair.

He set up on the counter, since the table was a disaster zone. Two slices of bread went into the toaster: one he would watch melt butter on, and one he would, if necessary, burn. Melting was a physical change, because the stuff was still the same stuff, just softer. Burning was a chemical change, because it turned into something new that smelled terrible and could not be unburned. He remembered his dad's old iron kettle rusting on the porch one whole winter, and how no amount of scrubbing ever brought the shiny metal back. That was the flashback he'd put on the poster, drawn as a sad kettle.

But the model was the real problem. He had used a marble for the proton and a marble for the electron, and something about that had bothered him all afternoon. He found the fact in his science book, in a corner, in small print: a proton has about 1,836 times the mass of an electron. He read it three times. "Eighteen thirty-six," he said to the toaster. His little sister, Mia, wandered in looking for cheese.

"A proton has about 1,836 times the mass of an electron," he told her, pointing at the page. "So almost all of an atom's mass is in the nucleus."

"So your electron-marble is basically a lie," Mia said, and took her cheese elsewhere.

Tyler dumped the marble electron back in the bag and hunted through the junk drawer until he found a single poppy seed. He glued it to a toothpick, spun it far out from the marble nucleus, and stepped back. The atom looked suddenly enormous and mostly empty, like a robust orange with one tiny gnat orbiting it. Then the toaster screamed up burnt, and the second slice came out black and smoking, definitely a chemical change, definitely not reversible. He cracked the window so the kitchen wouldn't smell like a cave where something had gone to hibernate, opened the butter dish for the good slice, and wrote "DEMONSTRATION COMPLETE" on the poster in his most confident handwriting. At 5:58, he carried the whole thing to his room, and the table was clear by six, give or take a poppy seed.

Ellie had been on the couch for three days, and she was tired of soup. She propped herself up on the armrest and watched the vapor rise from her mug of lemon tea, curling and vanishing near the ceiling. Her throat still felt scratchy, and her nose was red from tissue after tissue. The math competition at school was on Friday, and she wanted more than anything to be back for it.

When Mom came home from the pharmacy, Ellie sat up with an abrupt bounce. "Did you get the medicine? The kind that kills germs?"

"Everything the doctor said to get," Mom said, holding up a bag of cough syrup, tissues, and popsicles.

"Not that. Antibiotics," Ellie said. "Lily's little brother had a sore throat, and he took antibiotics and got better fast. If I take them, I could be back at school by Friday."

Mom set down the bag. "That's for the doctor to decide. We have a video call with her in ten minutes."

When the call started, Ellie asked right away. "Can you prescribe antibiotics? I need to get better fast. I have a competition."

The doctor shook her head, not unkindly. "Antibiotics kill bacteria, but they have no effect on viruses, so they wouldn't help you. A cold or the flu is a virus. Antibiotics just don't work on it."

Ellie frowned at the screen. "Then how do I get better?"

"Rest, fluids, time. Your body does the work."

So Ellie made a plan to conserve her energy. She spent Thursday on the couch doing practice problems in her head, drinking tea, and sleeping whenever her eyes got heavy. She noticed that the more she rested, the less her throat hurt, and by Friday morning her fever was gone and her nose had almost stopped running.

At school, she slid into her seat just as the competition papers were handed out. Lily leaned over. "You made it."

"Rest and fluids," Ellie whispered, "and a lot of nothing." She picked up her pencil and read the first problem.

Hazel had forty dollars and a plan: new basketball shoes, the ones with the springy sole, if they went on sale before Saturday's tryouts. The mall food court smelled like pretzels, and above it all a video wall played the shoe ad on loop. "Everybody's switching," a deep voice said, while a hundred blurry feet stamped past the camera. A famous point guard Hazel kind of admired looked straight at her and said, "I don't lace up anything else." Then the screen flashed the words REVOLUTIONARY and UNSTOPPABLE in gold.

She stopped walking. Something about that ad was like the wartime posters she'd been digging through for her library project. She'd started with posters from the 1940s, stern faces and pointing fingers, and then found something better. In a dusty reference book she read that the Institute for Propaganda Analysis was founded in the United States in 1937 to teach the public how to recognize propaganda. She'd written the sentence on an index card, but she hadn't really believed people needed lessons in spotting tricks. Now, standing under a thirty-foot shoe ad, she thought maybe they did.

She tested it like a game. First ad: "Everyone's switching." Her social studies teacher would say that was a bandwagon appeal, the same move as a poster showing a whole town buying war bonds. Second: REVOLUTIONARY and UNSTOPPABLE, words so vague they meant nothing, just loaded words, the book's term for language built to push feelings instead of facts. Third: the point guard. Would he really wear those shoes if the company didn't pay him? Celebrity testimonial, she scribbled on her hand with a pen from her pocket. Three tricks in one minute. She despised feeling handled, like her forty dollars had a target painted on it.

Inside the shoe store she picked up the box. The springy sole felt the same as the plain pair on the next shelf, which cost eighteen dollars less. An ambiguous sign said SALE, but the tiny print said "selected styles," and none of the selected styles were her size. "Can I try both?" she asked the clerk, a teenager named Priya who was balancing a stack of boxes one-handed while helping an older man find wide sizes.

Priya set the boxes down. "Smart question. Half the spring is the price tag, honestly." The older man chuckled. Hazel ran the length of the aisle in each pair. The cheaper ones gripped better on the slick floor; she could feel her cuts quicker. It wasn't proof, exactly, one run down one aisle, but it was evidence.

She bought the cheaper shoes, and with the leftover money she bought a pretzel and slid half of it across the table to a boy from her school, a refugee named Amir who'd arrived in the fall and usually sat alone with nothing from the food court. "For tryouts?" he asked, pointing at the box. "For tryouts," she said, and laced them up right there, double-knotted.

"Everybody's switching," she muttered at the video wall on her way out, and walked past it in her new shoes.

The gym smelled like popcorn and rubber soles, and Alexandre had a problem: his cousin Theo, the best shooter on the Ravens, had gone cold for three games, and today Coach Ramirez was watching from the bleachers, deciding who would start in the tournament. Alexandre kept a small notebook with every shot Theo took, home and away, because the local paper only printed one number and he wanted to know how it was built.

By halftime Theo had made 4 of 10, and the scoreboard screen flashed his season average: 40 percent. In the third quarter he got hot, swishing five straight, and the average ticked up to 50. The announcer's voice boomed over the squeak of sneakers. "Theo Cardoso, up ten percentage points today, folks." Two rows down, a radio reporter said into her microphone, "That same jump is a 25 percent increase for the young guard."

Alexandre stopped chewing his popcorn. Ten and twenty-five, about the same shot? He wrote both numbers and stared at them, then leaned toward the reporter. "How can it be ten and also twenty-five?" She smiled but kept talking into her recorder, so he turned to his notebook instead. He counted the season totals again, slow and careful, the way he counted everything. Both phrases pointed the same direction, from 40 to 50. Maybe they were two doors into the same room. He wanted to disclose the trick to somebody before the buzzer.

Next to him, Marcus was scribbling a sign that said MARCUS SAW IT FIRST, because his older brother worked the scoreboard clock and Marcus wanted the whole gym to know. "Check this," Alexandre said, showing him the notebook. "Ten percentage points, or a 25 percent increase. Same change, different words." Marcus squinted, then grinned. "So when the paper says Theo improved 25 percent, he only made one more shot out of ten?"

"Exactly," Alexandre said. Coach Ramirez wrote something in a small book and underlined it twice, his face neutral as a locked door, though his prescription for winning was famous: defense first, always. Theo caught a pass at the top of the key, rose, and released.

The net snapped clean, and Marcus held his sign over his head.

The folding tables at Uncle Sam's house were crowded with mango sticky rice, spring rolls, and a whole tray of fried bananas, and nobody was eating any of it. Gavin stood in the kitchen doorway holding a plate, because it was two o'clock in the afternoon and his stomach had been growling since the car ride. His grandmother poured tea for the aunties and handed him a cup. "Tea is fine," she said. "No food today, not after noon."

Gavin looked down the table at his cousins, who were sipping water and playing cards like this was normal. He felt like the only protagonist in a story where everyone else had read the ending. When he asked his older cousin Mali, she shrugged and kept shuffling. "It's an observance day," she said. "Uposatha." That was all she offered, so Gavin had to devise his own way to find out what was going on.

He started with what he could observe. His grandmother had on her white blouse, the stiff one she only wore to the temple. At breakfast that morning, everyone had eaten a huge meal at ten, which had seemed strange at the time. Now it made sense: they had loaded up early because food was stopping at midday. He counted what he knew on his fingers. One, a special day. Two, special clothes. Three, a big early meal and nothing after noon. He tested the idea out loud at the card table. "So it's like a rule? A whole list of rules for today?"

Mali finally looked up. "Eight precepts," she said, laying down a queen. "Grandma took all eight this morning. One of them is not eating after midday."

Gavin put his plate back on the counter, washed his hands, and came back to the table. He picked up his cards and lost three hands in a row. Around four o'clock his stomach gave a loud growl, and Mali laughed so hard she knocked over her tea. "Tomorrow," Gavin said, "we eat the fried bananas first."

The door banged open before Marcus could knock twice. It was Tasha, Dev's older sister, and she didn't say hi. "Take your shoes off and don't touch the kitchen," she snapped, then stomped upstairs. Marcus stood in the doorway holding his model rocket kit until Dev pulled him inside.

"She's like that," Dev said, spreading the kit across the living room carpet. "Always mad about something. Last week she yelled at me for breathing too loud." Marcus nodded, but something felt off. Tasha had helped him build a launch pad just last month, laughing the whole time. People didn't flip like a light switch for no reason, he thought, unless they were just that kind of person. He decided to test it. "Hey Dev, is anything going on with her?"

Dev shrugged. "How should I know? She's just rude."

They glued fins and taped the nose cone. Through the ceiling came footsteps, back and forth, back and forth, then a phone buzzing, then a long silence. Marcus kept one ear on it while his hands worked. He was beginning to build a second idea in his head: maybe Tasha's mood had a hidden cause, something he couldn't see, the way you can't see the wind but you can watch the flag.

At the tense moment, the footsteps stopped right above them, and a voice said, very quietly, "I'm sorry, Grandma. I'll come Saturday." Marcus froze with the glue tube in his hand. Dev looked up too.

Tasha came down a few minutes later, eyes red. "Sorry I barked at you guys. I just got a call. Grandma's in the hospital." She looked at the rocket spread across the floor. "That's a good one. Spontaneous combustion in the engine, right? That's what makes it go?" Marcus said yes, that was basically the motive power, fuel burning all at once. She almost smiled and went to make them popcorn.

Later, Dev's cousin Renard showed up and started complaining that a kid at school had slammed a door in his face that morning. "Total jerk," Renard said.

"Maybe," said Marcus. "Or maybe something happened to him you don't know about." He told them what he'd read in his brother's psychology book, holding it up to the light. "Psychologist Lee Ross named it the fundamental attribution error in 1977. We blame people's personality and skip their situation. Kind of like ants colonizing a whole picnic because one crumb fell, we spread the blame everywhere." Renard frowned, thinking. Then he picked up the spare nose cone and asked, "So when does this thing fly?"

Max had claimed the shady end of the picnic table before anyone else was awake, because today the art teacher was going to let them draw with charcoal. "Sphere shading," she had promised, "highlight, shadow, cast shadow," and Max had been thinking about it all night. He pressed his thumb into the black stick and dragged a circle across his paper, then squinted at the orange he'd set on the table as a model. The brightest spot sat up and to the left, where the morning sun caught it, and a dark crescent curled along the bottom right. He smudged gray under the orange and a stretched oval of it on the paper beside it. "That's the cast shadow," said Priya, dropping onto the bench across from him. "It points away from your light."

"It's like the light is a factor you have to account for," Max said, darkening the crescent. "Move the light and everything moves." Priya held up her own orange, turning it slowly, and Max noticed that when she turned it, the highlight slid to a new place, like the orange had its own private sun. He filed that away.

The real test came after lunch, when the teacher set out photos of living rooms for a perspective challenge. Max chose one with a big TV on the back wall and an armchair angled toward it, not lined up with anything. He had drawn the room's walls first, and every set of parallel lines ran off to two points way out at the edges of his paper. He knew those were the vanishing points, and he knew they both sat on the horizon line he'd drawn first. Then he stopped, pencil hovering. The armchair wasn't parallel to the walls. Could it use the same points?

He tried it. The chair's arms swooped toward the wrong places and the whole thing looked like it was melting. Max flipped to a fresh sheet and tried the opposite idea: give the chair its own two points. He lined his pencil along the seat edge, along the armrest, along the back, and each pair of lines met in its own two new spots. His heart jumped. He checked twice, and both new points landed exactly on his horizon line, same as the walls' points. "Priya, look. Its own pair, but on the same horizon line." She leaned over, then checked it with her ruler. "They do. Symmetrical and everything."

At dinner Max was still buzzing, and he decided to petition the teacher for one more photo, a kitchen with a turned stool, so he could test it again tomorrow. She wrote his name at the top of her list and said, "First thing after breakfast." Max grinned and went to sharpen every pencil he owned, lining them up by the lantern light with the sphere drawing clipped above them, highlight, shadow, cast shadow, like a trophy.

Juliette lined up at the free throw line for the third drill in a row, and her knee sent up a small, hot signal, like a match struck under her kneecap. She made the shot anyway. Coach Ruiz blew the whistle and called for layups, twenty of them, and Juliette started to run.

By layup fourteen the match had become a torch. She stopped on the baseline, hands on her knees, and pretended to be catching her breath. Across the gym, Danny from the baseball team sat on the bleachers with his arm wrapped in ice, sulking. "Pitch count," he said when he caught her looking. "Coach says I hit my limit for today." He rolled his eyes. "My arm feels fine."

Juliette had heard Danny's older brother talking last week, something about growth plates, areas of growing cartilage near the ends of kids' bones. The weird part was what he'd said next: the cartilage is weaker than the bone around it. That was why young athletes had limits on repetitive stress, limits that felt pointless because nothing hurt yet. She had tuned most of it out, thinking it was baseball stuff. Now she stood in a gym doing her twentieth layup on a knee that only complained sometimes, and wondered whether the pain was the whole warning or just the part she could see. Maybe the real damage was quiet. The thought seemed to magnify every ache she had ignored since September, including the day she'd jumped rope for an hour on a sore ankle because quitting felt like despair.

She jogged to the sideline. "Coach, my knee's been aching after practice, and it's not going away. Can I sub out of the jumping drills?"

"Smart," Coach Ruiz said. "Ice it."

Danny raised his ice pack toward her like a toast. "Look at us. Bench buddies."

She hadn't solved anything. She still didn't know if she'd been reckless or just tired, and the doctor appointment on Saturday loomed like a full-court press. But when the team ran suicides, she sat, watching, and pressed the ice against her knee until it burned cold.

Nolan got to Desh's house first, so he had the best view of the disaster. The science club's robot, built over three weekends for the county fair, sat dead in the middle of the garage, and the four members who arrived after him were already shouting.

"It's the battery," Marcus insisted. "I tested it Friday. It drains way too fast, like something is consuming all the power in ten minutes."

"You're wrong," Amelia said. "I watched the wheels on Saturday. The left one jerks. It's a motor problem."

Desh shook his head. "The wiring is the problem. I checked the circuits, and the backup sensor cable is pinched."

Nolan had been out of town and had seen nothing but a group chat full of arguing. Then Priya, the fifth member, was absent, sick with the flu. At her mother's suggestion, Nolan called her, and she asked him to read her text out loud to the group. He held up his phone.

"I only ever worked on the sensor that detects toxic gas," Nolan read. "I know that part works. I tested it with vinegar fumes Sunday. But I never saw the whole robot running. Someone else has to tell me about the rest."

Everyone went quiet. Nolan looked around the garage at four people who had each seen exactly one piece of the machine, and the shape of the argument suddenly made sense to him. He remembered a story his grandfather told him, from ancient India, about blind men who each touch a different part of an elephant and then describe the animal completely differently. The one holding the trunk imagines a snake; the one at the leg insists it is a tree.

"It's the parable of the blind men and the elephant," he said. "That's us. We've each only touched one part."

Desh grinned slowly. "So nobody's wrong. Everybody's just holding a different piece." They ran the robot whole, with all systems on, and watched together. It lurched left because of the motor, and the motor strained because the pinched cable made the sensor draw too much power, which drained the battery and set off the toxic-gas alarm by the vinegar residue Priya had left inside.

"So Marcus's battery, Desh's cable, Amelia's wheel, and Priya's sensor were all real," Nolan said, unscrewing the pinched cable cover. "Just one at a time."

Twenty minutes later the robot rolled straight across the driveway, and Amelia whooped so loud that Desh's neighbor looked over the fence. Marcus filmed it on his phone to send to Priya, and at the end he added, "Your nose works. The whole elephant works."

Grandpa's creek had yielded exactly zero fossils in three days of searching, which Victoria considered a personal insult. She had a shoebox of rocks on the porch rail, and she spread them out now: speckled ones, banded ones, one gray lump with shiny flecks that looked like someone had spilled glitter into wet concrete.

Grandpa came out with two glasses of lemonade and peered over her shoulder. "Grandma wants to retire that shoebox, by the way. She says it's full of dirt and mystery."

"It's full of specimens," Victoria said. She picked up the glittery one. "This one's igneous, I think. It was melted once, like lava, and then it cooled." The banded one went in a second pile. "Metamorphic. Squished and cooked underground until it got stripes." The third pile was softer rock, layered like a stack of pressed sandwiches. "Sedimentary. Made from mud and sand piling up."

"That's a lot of science for a shoebox," Grandpa said.

She held up her favorite find, a black stone from the creek bend. "I checked this one four times for fossils. Nothing." She had checked the banded one too, and the glittery one, dragging her thumb over every surface like a detective looking for fingerprints. Nothing, nothing, nothing.

Then she turned over a piece of the layered sandwich rock, and there it was: a curl pressed into the stone, small and perfect, like a snail that had signed its name a very long time ago.

"Fossil!" She nearly knocked over the lemonade.

Grandpa leaned in. "How come it's in that one and not the fancy ones you kept checking?"

Victoria lined up the three piles side by side. "The melted kind was too hot, I bet. The squished kind too. Anything living in there would've burned up." She tapped the soft layered pile. "Only these. Fossils are almost only ever in sedimentary rock."

"So the glitter rock is controversial."

"It's a paperweight," Victoria said. She wrapped the fossil in her bandana like it was a visiting ambassador, and carried it inside to show her grandmother.

Autumn had read the last page of The Scarlet Ibis twice, and she still could not say what the book was about in one sentence. Mrs. Ruiz's book club met in the library on Thursdays, and today each member had to state a theme and back it up with a quotation. Autumn's hand was sweating against her notebook.

She assumed everyone else had figured it out already. Marcus was flipping through his copy with a smug little smile, and Priya had three sticky notes bristling from her pages. Autumn had one sticky note, stuck to a page about a red bird. When the storm blew the scarlet ibis into the family's garden and it died, she had felt something tighten in her throat, though she could not say why.

"It's about guilt," Marcus announced. "The narrator's conscience bothers him, so it's about a guilty conscience." He read his quotation in an eloquent, dramatic voice, wobbling his eyebrows at Priya, who snorted so hard she knocked over the pretzel bowl.

Then it was Autumn's turn. She opened to the red bird. "I think it's about fragility," she said. "When the scarlet ibis dies in the garden, it's like the book is telling you something before it happens." She read her quotation about the fallen bird, and her voice came out steadier than she expected. "Doodle is fragile too. And later, in the storm, when the narrator finds him under the tree with his neck bent, it's like the bird all over again." The room went quiet except for the radiator ticking. Priya leaned over and flipped back to the bird scene, her finger moving down the page.

"That's foreshadowing," Priya whispered, tapping the dead red bird. "You found it before me."

Mrs. Ruiz wrote "storm" on the board and underlined it twice. "Notice," she said, "that a storm brings the bird, and a storm takes Doodle."

Autumn copied the word foreshadowing into her notebook, pressing hard enough to dent the next page, and then tore off the corner and folded it into a tiny paper bird.

Mackenzie had read The Lighthouse of Hallow Bay three times, but for her book club report she needed something more than a summary. She carried the novel, a stack of yellow sticky notes, and a pencil to the reading nook by the window, where the afternoon light fell in a warm stripe across the cushion. She had decided on a small ritual: every time the blue door of the old boathouse appeared in the story, she would mark the page and write one sentence about what was happening there.

The first blue door showed up in chapter two, when the main character, Ivy, pressed her ear against it and dreamed of the father who had disappeared at sea. Mackenzie wrote "hope of his return" on the note and pressed it onto the page. In chapter five, Ivy hid behind the same door while her cousin searched for her, and in chapter nine, the door stood open, letting in the wind while the family argued inside. Mackenzie sat back and looked at her row of notes like a string of flags.

At the kitchen table that evening, her older brother Dev leaned over her shoulder. "What's with all the yellow paper?"

"Every time the blue door shows up, I mark it," Mackenzie said. "I'm trying to see if it means something different each time."

Dev nodded. "Recurring image like that is called a motif," he said, and went back to his sandwich.

In the nook the next morning, Mackenzie formulated a test. If the door really changed meaning, then the last time it appeared should be almost the opposite of the first. She found the final mention in chapter twenty: Ivy painting the door gray herself, the day she finally stopped waiting for news of her father. Mackenzie read the page twice, then peeled off her first sticky note and laid it beside the last one. Hope of his return, one said. Letting him go, said the other. Same door, same hinges, same blue paint, but by the end it meant something entirely different. She checked the middle notes and saw the pattern in order, hiding place, shelter, then farewell.

That afternoon Dev found her taping the sticky notes in a long line down the hallway, chapter by chapter, like train cars.

"You know that's going to leave marks on the wall," he said.

Mackenzie stood at the far end and looked down the row. "Look at it from here," she said. "It goes from blue to gray."

Eleanor set her fork down beside her meatloaf and stared at the newspaper folded next to her plate, because the draft for her current events report was due by email at eight o'clock tonight, and it was already six forty-five. The article she had chosen ranked quarterbacks by something called passer rating, and the numbers made no sense to her at all. One quarterback had 104.2. Another had 158.3, and the caption under his photo called it perfect.

"Why would a perfect score be a weird number like that?" she asked her brother Marcus, who was stacking green beans on his knife like he was building a wall.

Marcus shrugged. "It's just what it is. Football stuff." He wanted to finish dinner fast so he could colonize the whole living room couch before their cousin arrived, spreading his blanket and controller across every cushion like territory he claimed by sitting on it first.

"A hundred would be perfect," Eleanor insisted. "Like on a test. If the scale starts at zero and ends somewhere, perfect should end at one hundred." She flipped the paper over and ran her finger down the ranking column again, counting the quarterbacks listed there. Twelve names, twelve different numbers, all squeezed down from games she had never watched. Somewhere behind each number were completions and yards and touchdowns and interceptions, and all of it had been crushed together into a single figure, the way her school averaged test scores into one grade. But the top number still bothered her, hanging there like a picture she couldn't get to hang perpendicular to the floor.

"Maybe it's not out of a hundred," Marcus said through a mouthful of beans. "Maybe the whole scale is different."

Eleanor grabbed her mother's phone from the counter and typed "passer rating maximum" into the search box. She read, scrolled, and read again. "It says the passer rating combines several passing statistics into one number," she announced, "on a scale from zero to a maximum of 158.3." She set the phone down. "So a perfect rating isn't a hundred. It's a strange number, and it's the top of the whole scale."

Marcus had stopped stacking beans. "So that guy with 158.3 is literally the best you can be?"

"By the rating, yeah." Eleanor was already rewriting the first line of her report in her head. She had planned to argue that the rankings were unfair because her favorite team's quarterback sat seventh, but now she understood that his number was built from everything he had done all season, folded together. Seventh wasn't a judgment of him as a person. It was arithmetic. She picked her fork back up and speared a green bean off Marcus's abandoned wall.

At 7:58 she hit send, then carried her plate to the sink. Marcus had claimed the couch, blanket and all, and was waving the remote at her.

"Want to watch the highlights?" he asked. "That perfect guy plays tonight."

Eleanor dried her hands on the towel. "Show me the numbers at the end," she said, and sat down on the last free cushion.

The bus jolted over the pothole by the gym, and Peyton grabbed the seat in front of her before she slid into the aisle. In her backpack was the sign-up sheet for Saturday's three-on-three basketball tournament, and one blank line left: her third teammate. She had until the last stop to decide.

"I still say Dez," said Marcus, leaning over from the next seat. "He's got the same average as Priya. Ten points a game. I did the math twice."

Peyton pulled out her notebook, where she'd copied the numbers from the rec center's weekly sheets. "Same average, but look." She turned the page so he could see. "Priya scored ten, ten, nine, ten, eleven. Every single week. Dez scored twenty-two, then two, then eighteen, then zero, then eight."

Marcus squinted at the columns. Rain had begun to saturate the windows, blurring the parking lots and mailboxes into gray streaks, and he had to tilt the notebook toward the light. "So? They both average ten."

Down the aisle, Dez was holding court near the back, retelling last week's game in a loud voice. "Twenty-two points! It was a siege out there, they double-teamed me all night, and I still dropped twenty-two." A couple of kids laughed and pounded his shoulder. Priya sat quietly by the window, retying her shoelace the way she did before every game, careful and slow.

Peyton frowned at her numbers. The average treated Priya's week and Dez's week the same, but the weeks underneath weren't the same at all. She thought about Saturday. Three games guaranteed, maybe five if they kept winning. She needed somebody she could count on every game, not one brilliant game and then a collapse. She tested the idea on Marcus.

"Okay, forget averages. If I tell you our first game, Priya gives us ten points. Can you promise me Dez does?"

Marcus rubbed the back of his neck. "No. He might give us two. He might give us twenty."

"Right. An average hides how the games are spread out." She tapped the two columns. "Priya's all bunched together. Dez swings between great and terrible."

Marcus was quiet for a second. The bus hissed to a stop and two fifth graders clattered down the steps. "I wanted Dez because he's fun," he admitted. "But you're right, we need steady. Put Priya down."

Peyton wrote the name, then got up and walked back through the swaying aisle. She sat down across from Priya, who looked up, surprised.

"Want to be on our tournament team Saturday?" Peyton asked. "Three games minimum."

Priya's slow smile spread. "I'll be there. Every game."

"I know," said Peyton. "That's why I asked."

Marcus turned around in his seat and held out his fist, and Priya bumped it just as the bus lurched forward into the rain.

Clara had signed up to speak at the community centre because the city planned to pave over the little patch of wild grass behind the skating rink, and she despised that idea more than she despised group projects. Mr. Petrosian at the front desk handed her a form and said, "You're a delegation, dear. Fill this in and you get five minutes at the meeting on Thursday."

"Five whole minutes?" said a boy beside her, gripping his own form so hard it crumpled. His name was Dev, and his hands were shaking. He wanted a crosswalk painted on Maple Street because his little sister had nearly been hit there twice. "I've never even spoken in front of a class."

"Then you need practice," Clara said. "Tonight. My grandma lives near the centre and she makes the best snacks in the province."

That evening they took turns at Grandma's kitchen table, a timer shaped like an egg counting down five minutes while Grandma listened from the counter. Dev read his speech in one breathless rush and finished in ninety seconds. Clara went the other way and got cut off mid-sentence, which meant her best argument, that the grass patch was a distinct habitat where monarch butterflies stopped on their way north like a tiny tundra stopover for travelers, never got said at all.

She tried folding her notes into sections and putting a sticky note that said BUTTERFLIES at the top of the last page, so if she ran long, she could jump straight there. It worked. Dev tried pretending the kitchen chairs were council members, which helped until Grandma asked a question in a stern voice and he laughed so hard he knocked over the egg timer.

On Thursday they sat side by side in the meeting room, waiting for their names to be called. Dev's knee bounced. Clara slid him the last of Grandma's cookies.

"Delegation of Dev Mehta," the clerk announced.

Dev stood up, straightened his crumpled form, and said, "Good evening. I brought pictures."

Zoey had been building her Scratch game all afternoon, a dodgeball arena where a cat in a top hat dodged flying doughnuts. Every time the cat got hit, the score went up by one, and every time a doughnut sailed past, the cat earned a point instead. She had the loops spinning the doughnuts in circles and if-then blocks checking collisions so often that her brother Marcus, wandering through the kitchen, said the project looked like a census of every possible crash.

"Very funny," Zoey said. "At least my doughnuts don't invade my side of the couch like your socks do."

But now she had a second problem. She wanted a printed score table on the side, a neat row of numbers she could save and show her friend Priya, so she was writing a tiny Python program that printed the round scores one after another. When she ran it, the numbers marched straight down the screen, each one on its own line, like lethargic soldiers falling into single file. She stared at it. She had typed everything on one line in the code, so why did the output refuse to sit in a row?

She tried retyping it. She tried putting the numbers closer together. The column only got longer. Marcus leaned over her shoulder, chewing a granola bar. "Your table has a fear of intimacy," he observed.

Zoey ignored him and did what she always did when something invisible was misbehaving: she tested one small idea. She wrote a print for a single number, then another print right after it, and ran the program. Two numbers. Two lines. So each print started a new line after its output, all by itself, even when she hadn't asked for one. That was the hidden rule. She hunted through her book until she found the small lever for it, a setting called end, and set it to end=' ' so the next output would stay on the same line.

She ran the whole table again. This time the numbers lay side by side in one clean row, ten of them, neat as teeth.

"Ha," she said, and pushed the laptop toward Marcus. "Say something nice about my row."

Marcus squinted at it. "It's very horizontal," he said. "I'm proud of it."

Carter arrived at Deshawn's house with his backpack clanking, ready for history club, and found everyone arguing before he even got his shoes off. Three kids sat around the kitchen table with two photocopied pages in front of them, and the smell of burned popcorn hung in the air from an earlier disaster nobody would admit to.

"It says right here the British fired first," Priya said, tapping her page. "The colonist witness says so."

Deshawn shook his head. "My page is a British soldier's account, and he swears the colonists fired first. Same morning, April 1775, at Lexington. Somebody's lying."

Carter sat down and pulled both pages toward him. He read them twice, chewing the end of his pencil. Both accounts sounded certain. Both had details, the smell of gun smoke, the shape of the green, the shout of officers. If people on both sides each said the other side fired first, then either one witness lied, or both sides honestly remembered it differently. He wanted to know which, and he thought of a way to check.

"I want to replicate the argument," he said. "Kind of. Priya, you go stand by the sink. Deshawn, stand at the back door. Amelia, you're the shot. Slam the pantry door."

Amelia grinned and slammed it. "Who fired?" Carter asked. Priya pointed at the back door. Deshawn pointed at the sink. Neither had seen the pantry. They tried it again with different positions, and every time, each witness truly believed the other person's side had caused the bang.

"So that's it," Carter said slowly. "Nobody has to be lying." Historians still did not know who fired the first shot at Lexington, because the witnesses from each side each said the other side fired first, and maybe every one of them believed it. The kids sat quietly for a moment, letting that settle.

Deshawn's mom came in with a fresh bowl of popcorn, having noticed the earlier loss from the scorched smell drifting upstairs. "You kids want juice too?" She set down cups without waiting for an answer. Priya slid the biggest cup toward Carter, since he'd missed snack time entirely by reading twice.

"Next meeting," Deshawn said, "we find a case where the two sides actually agree. Something parallel to this one."

"Deal," said Carter, and reached for the popcorn.

The planetarium's rock table sat right beside the Moon exhibit, and Mia had been given the job of sorting the sample box into igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic. Igneous rocks came from cooling, sedimentary from pressed layers, metamorphic from heat and squeezing. She held up a gray stone striped like fudge and turned it over, hunting for clues about how it had formed, when her cousins Dev and Rosa stormed up from the dome theater, still arguing.

"It's getting bigger," Dev insisted. "We saw the Moon chart in the dome. The lit part's growing every night this week."

"It is not," Rosa said, arms crossed. "Grandpa's almanac says it's shrinking. Look, the picture from last night shows more light than tonight's."

Mia set down the striped rock. She could perceive the problem instantly, because there was only one way both of them could be right and only one way they could both be wrong. "What word did the dome chart use?" she asked. "Waxing or waning?"

Dev squinted at the ceiling, remembering. "Waxing. It said waxing."

"Then it's growing," Mia said. "A waxing Moon's lit part grows night by night. A waning one's lit part shrinks. If it's waxing this week, the almanac picture is from a waning Moon, a different month, or somebody's remembering it backward."

Rosa frowned at the dome's Moon poster, comparing the phases printed in a row. "So waning and waxing are opposites. Same Moon, opposite directions."

Mia pulled out her field notebook, drew four circles, and shaded the lit part a little wider each night. "Keep watching the sky all week," she said. "It's cumulative, like layers in sedimentary rock. Each night adds a little more light, until the whole thing shows and you can't argue anymore." Rosa copied the circles into her own notebook, and Dev asked to keep the page with the fattest Moon.

Mia got back to her sorting. The striped rock went into the metamorphic pile, its bands pressed and cooked long ago, and she slid the box toward her cousins so they could start learning too.

"Draw your Moon circles after dinner," Dev said, already heading for the exit sky.

Maya's dog, Biscuit, flattened himself under the coffee table the second the thunder cracked, and Peyton watched him shake. "He's scared," Maya said, not looking up from her phone. "It's happening right now, the storm. He's freaked out by the actual thunder."

Peyton nodded slowly. Maya had been quiet all afternoon, checking the weather app, then the soccer app, then the weather again. Her cleats sat by the door, already double-knotted, though the tryout was still four days away. "You keep doing that," Peyton said, pointing at the phone. "Is there thunder in there?"

"No. It's the tryout list. They posted the roster numbers and mine is eleven, which is fine, but what if they move me to defense, what if I trip in the first drill, what if Coach Reyes already decided." Maya set the phone face down, then picked it up again. Peyton thought about Biscuit under the table. He was shaking at the thunder that was actually booming outside. Maya was shaking at thunder that had not happened yet and might never happen at all. "So Biscuit is scared of the storm," Peyton said, testing the idea out loud, "and you're not scared, exactly, because nothing's happening right now. It's more like you're worried about what might happen Friday. My mom says that's anxiety. Fear is the reaction to a threat happening now, and anxiety is worry about a threat that might happen in the future."

Maya stopped scrolling. "So Biscuit has fear and I have anxiety."

"Basically."

"Great. The dog is more competent than me."

"He's hiding under a table," Peyton said. "You're sitting on a couch eating all my chips."

"That's my coping mechanism. Chips consume my stress." Maya held up the nearly empty bag as proof, and Peyton laughed and grabbed the last chip, calling a truce over the crumbs.

Maya stood, put the phone in a drawer, and closed it. "Okay. If it's about a might, not a happening, then I can practice instead of worrying. Want to go outside before the next rumble?"

They laced up their cleats on the back step. Maya had just struck the ball against the fence twice when the drawer, muffled, began to buzz.

Florence pressed her finger on the map of India spread across the counter of Around the World Travel. Her mother was booking tickets to visit Auntie Meera in Mumbai, so Florence had time to learn the numbers printed along the map's edges. "The top numbers go sideways," said Mr. Patel, the agent, "and the side numbers go up and down. Find where they cross, and you have your city." She slid her finger along latitude 19 degrees north, then up from longitude 72 degrees east, and her fingertip landed on a dot on the coast. "Mumbai," she said, and Mr. Patel stamped a small circle around it with his pencil.

"Here's your puzzle, then," he said. "Your auntie emailed that you arrive in June, when the heat is at its worst. Why would the rain arrive exactly then?" Florence frowned at the map. Mumbai sat on the edge of a big brown landmass, and to the west of it stretched nothing but blue ocean. She remembered her teacher saying the school thermometer had to be calibrated in ice water before anyone trusted its readings, and she thought about how different surfaces warm up. A parking lot burned your sandals in summer, but the lake stayed cool.

"Land heats up faster than the ocean," she said slowly. "So in summer the land gets hot, and the air above it gets hot too." She traced the coastline with her pencil. "Hot air rises, right? Like over a radiator." Mr. Patel nodded and said nothing, so she kept going. "If the warm air rises over the land, something has to flow in to take its place. Moist air from the ocean, coming in off the water toward the coast."

"Exactly," said Mr. Patel. "And that moist air brings the rain with it. That flow has a name, by the way. The monsoon." He wrote the word on a card and slid it across the counter.

Florence looked at her penciled circle on Mumbai, right where land met sea, and grinned. She decided her whole visit would be one spontaneous experiment: she would stand on Auntie Meera's balcony each morning, feel which way the breeze blew, and check it against the map. "In June," she told her mother on the way out, "the wind should be coming from the ocean, onto the land, every single day."

Her mother said, "Bring your umbrella," and held the door.

Raphael sat at the kitchen table with his laptop open to the tryout roster, refreshing it every thirty seconds like an organism that had learned one trick and could not stop performing it. His sister Dara leaned over his shoulder, though she was supposed to be researching her debate topic, which was whether the school should sell smoothies in the cafeteria, a cause she had championed for two weeks with rising passion.

The list appeared at 4:02. Raphael's name was not on it.

"I don't get it," he said. "I beat half those kids in the sprints."

Dara, who wanted his laptop the moment he stopped needing it, scrolled the page for him. "Look at the birthdays they posted. Weird."

He looked. Of the fifteen names, eleven had birthdays from January to June. Three were in fall. One, a kid named Osei, was in November. Not a single December birthday but his own, anywhere.

"You're the youngest kid in your whole grade, basically," Dara said. "You've told me that forty times."

Raphael started to argue, then stopped. It wasn't just his grade. The cutoff for school was January first, which meant kids born in that first month were almost a year older than kids born in December. Same tryouts, same drills, months and months of extra growing. He grabbed a scrap of paper and wrote the birthdays in two columns, old half and young half, and stared at the lopsided result. Then he searched "birth month sports team selection" and found it had a name.

"Relative age effect," he read aloud.

"What's that?"

"Players born early in the selection year get picked more than ones born late. It's a real thing. People study it."
