Dara was quiet for a moment, which for her was eloquent. "So you got cut partly because of your birthday?"

"Partly." He closed the laptop before she could reach for it. "There's a winter league with January tryouts. New year, new cutoff. I'll be the old one for once."

"That's your plan? Wait four months and get older?"

"I'm going to train the whole time," he said, and began clearing the table, moving fast, already perspiring.

Samuel's cleats were still damp from the morning dew when Coach Marisol dragged a thick rope out of the equipment shed and dropped it across the center circle. "Tug-of-war," she announced. "Championship Saturday has one at halftime, and we are going to win it."

Devon, who lived upstairs from Samuel in the apartment building where their families were tenants, threw both fists in the air. "I've been waiting all season for this!"

They pulled in pairs first, then four against four, then all eight. Samuel gripped the rope in the eight-on-eight round and noticed something strange. When it had been just him against Devon, his arms burned and his legs shook. Now, with the whole team heaving together, his pull felt easier. Lazy, almost. He glanced down the line. Marco was definitely leaning back less than before. When Coach blew her whistle and called the pull "sloppy," Marco's face went pink.

That night Samuel couldn't let it go. He pulled a strand of spaghetti from his dinner and tugged it, thinking. He could infer something from what he'd seen: the more people on the rope, the smaller each person's pull seemed to get. But was that real, or was he imagining it? The only way to find out was a test.

At Tuesday practice he begged Coach Marisol for the spring scale she used for fitness testing. She hooked it to the rope and the fence post. Devon pulled alone and the scale read ninety pounds. Then four boys pulled together, and Samuel did the math in his notebook. Devon's share of the four-man pull was smaller than his solo pull. Same for Marco. Same for everyone. The pattern held.

"You sound like my grandfather," Coach said, laughing. "In 1913 Max Ringelmann reported that as more people pulled on a rope together, each person's average pull became smaller."

"Ringelmann," Samuel repeated, writing it down. "So what do we do about it?"

Coach rubbed her chin. "That, scientist, is your problem."

On Saturday, the stadium smelled like popcorn and cut grass, and the stands were louder than any game all season. At halftime, Samuel gathered his team in the end zone. "Every pull is your pull," he told them. "Nobody's hiding on this rope." He pointed at the opposing team's biggest puller, a tower of a kid. "He's not the rope. He's just one guy."

The whistle blew. Samuel planted his feet, kept his arms straight, and pulled as hard as if he were alone in his backyard. Down the line he heard Devon growling like a guard dog, and the rope came, inch by glorious inch, until the red flag crossed the chalk line. Devon tackled Samuel into the grass, and the whole team piled on, shouting, "Ringelmann!" at the sky.

Amelia spread her notebook across the library table and wrote "Five Reasons the Library Should Stay Open Until Eight" at the top of the page. Below it she made her outline: introduction, three reason paragraphs, conclusion. The librarian, Mr. Okafor, had told her class that a persuasive essay was like a court case, and each paragraph had to prove something. Amelia thought that sounded manageable until she sat down and realized she had exactly one fact, which was that some kids couldn't come to the library until after five because of the bus schedule.

Her friend Dev sat down across from her with a stack of books about frogs, because he was doing a report on animals that hibernate. "What's your essay about?" he asked.

"The library should stay open later," Amelia said. "Kids check out forty percent more books when it's open late."

Dev frowned. "Says who?"

"Says me. I made it up. It sounds convincing."

"That's not how it works." Dev turned a page. "If you put a number in there, people want to know where it came from. Like, if I write that wood frogs freeze solid all winter, I have to say the wildlife federation said that, or nobody believes me."

Amelia tapped her pencil. She looked over at the front desk, where Mr. Okafor was stamping returns, and got an idea. She wrote her opening paragraph on a fresh sheet, left out any sources, and walked it over to him. "Mr. Okafor, can you read this and tell me what you think?"

He read it and pointed at her number. "Forty percent more books. Says who?"

Exactly as predicted. Amelia grinned, went back to the table, and found the library's annual report in the reference section, which listed checkout totals by month and hour. The real number was smaller than her made-up one, but it came with a name attached: the report was published by the city library board. She wrote the sentence again with the real figure and added "according to the city library board's annual report," then took it back to the desk.

Mr. Okafor read it and nodded. "Now I can go look that up myself if I want to. That's a competent piece of arguing."

"But my first number was bigger," Amelia said.

"Bigger and useless. The expense of staying open late is real, so your argument has to be real too."

Dev raised his hand without being asked. "Point of order. I changed my mind about frogs. They don't all hibernate. Some just slow down and lurk under mud, being dramatic."

"That's not a point of order," said Amelia.

"It is now," said Dev, and he crossed out a whole paragraph with great satisfaction.

The list went up on the community theatre door at four o'clock sharp: showcase auditions, Friday night, one monologue each. Chase had five days to make Director Voss believe he could hold a stage alone, and he'd picked the trickiest speech in the whole script room, a town council scene from an old play called The Long Meeting. The character, a kid named Pip arguing at a council hearing, had a page of lines and zero stage directions printed. Everything, Ms. Voss told him with a wave of her feathered pen, would have to come from his pauses and his hands. "The audience can't hear a comma," she said. "You have to show it."

By Wednesday Chase had the words memorized, but the scene felt flat. In it, Pip stands up and asks the council to shorten the town festival by one day so the park grass can recover. The council president then rises and thunders that Pip obviously wants to cancel the festival forever, shut down the vendors, and erase a hundred years of tradition. The crowd gasps. Pip gets shouted down. Chase ran it again in the empty green room and frowned. Why would the crowd gasp at something Pip never said?

He flipped through the script and found the answer tucked in the playwright's note. Pip's friend whispers a single line: "He's building a straw man argument." Chase read it twice. So that was the game. The president takes Pip's small request, blows it up into something weaker and sillier, a total ban, and then attacks that puffed-up version instead of what Pip actually said. Nobody fights the real Pip. They fight the fake one, because the fake one is easier to beat.

That was the key to performing it. On Thursday, in front of the mirror in the costume closet, Chase made his choice. When the president ranted, Chase froze Pip mid-step and let three full seconds of silence pass, then lifted one hand, slow and steady, like raising a question mark in the air. The pause would tell the audience something was wrong. The gesture would tell them what. He narrated the beat out loud to himself, experimenting, "Pip doesn't argue yet, he just lets them hear it," and the whole speech snapped into focus around that moment.

Friday night, the house lights dimmed and Ms. Voss called his name from the fifth row, tapping her pen against her clipboard. Chase walked to the center mark, planted his feet, and asked for one day, just one. From the wings, the girl playing the president thundered her wild exaggeration about banning the festival forever, and Chase stopped. One beat. Two. Three. His hand rose, slow and unmistakable, and in the dark he heard somebody in the audience whisper, "Oh, she's twisting it." He let the silence stretch one more second, then said Pip's next line, quiet and clear: "That's not what I said." Ms. Voss's pen stopped tapping.

Hazel pressed her nose against the display case in the corner of the science museum, next to a faded diorama of the tundra where a plastic caribou stood guard over a very real, very rusty horseshoe. "Melt or rust," she whispered. "That's the whole game." Her worksheet, stamped with the museum's slightly dilapidated logo, asked her to sort changes into two piles: physical, like ice melting, and chemical, like iron rusting. The winner got a free pass to the planetarium, and Marcus, her best friend, wanted that pass so badly he had already counted the questions twice.

"Question seven is impossible," Marcus groaned, flapping his sheet. "A burning candle. Physical or chemical? And don't say both, because there's one box."

"Burning is chemical," Hazel said. "The wax melts too, but the flame part makes something new." She tapped the glass over the horseshoe. "Rust is new stuff too. Ice is still water, just wearing a costume."

Question ten stopped her cold. A little station nearby held cups of mystery liquids, pH strips, and a sign reading TEST ME. The mystery cup was cloudy and slippery, and next to it sat a card about vinegar, pH around three, the sour side of the scale. Hazel dunked a strip, and it turned the deep blue that meant the opposite side, the basic side, way up near nine or ten.

"Grandpa's kitchen," Hazel said slowly. "This smells like grandpa's kitchen. This is soapy water. Bar soap." Marcus sniffed the cup and made a face like he'd licked a caribou. "So most traditional bar soaps are basic," Hazel went on, writing fast. "pH around nine or ten. That's all the way across the scale from vinegar. Grandma always said don't mix them."

Marcus grabbed her arm. "That's the last answer. We can still beat the Henderson twins to the planetarium desk." They ran past the melting-ice exhibit, sheets flapping, and slapped the paper down in front of the volunteer.

"Two free passes," the volunteer said, and Marcus held his up to the ceiling lights like a trophy. "First one to the projection room picks the seats."

Ellie divided the garden behind the barn into two square plots, drew a map on cardboard, and tried to classify the seeds into neat groups: roots, leaves, things that climbed. Her younger brother, Marcus, wanted the climbing ones, the beans, because he liked the way the pump handle rose and fell like a piston when Grandpa filled the trough, and he figured beans working their way up a string would be just as satisfying to watch.

"You can have the beans," Ellie said, "if you help water." Marcus agreed, but he preferred watering his own way, which was a light sprinkle from the green can every single morning, the way he sprinkled the dog in July. Ellie watered her plot differently. Twice a week, she let the hose run slowly until the ground was soaked deep down, and on the other mornings she did nothing at all.

For weeks both plots looked the same, and Marcus was smug about it. Then came the hot week. By Thursday his bean leaves hung limp at noon and stayed limp into the evening. Ellie's tomatoes drooped a little in the heat, but they lifted again by supper. On Saturday, before either of them watered anything, Ellie dug carefully at the edge of each plot with her trowel. In Marcus's soil she found the bean roots, thin and white, spread out just under the surface where the ground was already dry and cracked. In her own plot she had to dig twice as deep before she found roots, heading downward where the soil was still dark and damp.

"Look," she said, and Marcus crouched beside her, poking his finger into the hole. "Mine stayed up top because I only ever gave them a little drink. Yours went down hunting for water." He wiped his hands on his jeans and frowned at his wilting beans, then at the hose. "So if I soak them good, will they grow deeper roots and quit fainting every day?"

"Only one way to find out," Ellie said, and she handed him the hose. Marcus turned the nozzle to a slow trickle and held it steady at the base of the first bean plant while a predatory ground beetle, the kind that patrols for cutworms, crossed the wet dirt ahead of the spray. Ellie marked the spot with a popsicle stick so they would know exactly where the change had begun, and they sat in the shade of the barn to wait for the water to sink all the way down.

William had forty-one dollars and a plan that refused to germinate. The telescope at the science fair booth cost ninety dollars, and Mrs. Ruiz's class was running a six-week money simulation in which you could "borrow" classroom cash from the class credit card at an interest charge every week, or save up the slow way. He wanted it now. The card let him have it now.

"Interest is the cost of borrowing," Mrs. Ruiz said, and left it there, tapping the board where the simulation rules were posted. She never explained more than that; she just handed out the envelopes and let kids find out.

That same week, William's sister Priya came home scowling over her portfolio envelope from her own class project. She had bought stock in Greenfield Power, and its small dividend, her weekly allowance of pretend income, had simply stopped. "They cut it," she said. "Companies can cut or skip dividends whenever. Nothing happens to them." William had a bond from the exact same company, part of his own envelope, and he hadn't checked it yet. He slid the paper out slowly, almost not wanting to look, because if his payment had stopped too, his whole telescope math would fracture. He had counted on that money.

The bond line read: interest paid, week four, on schedule. He read it twice. Priya leaned over his shoulder and her eyebrows went up.

"Yours still pays?"

"Yours they can skip. Mine they can't miss," William said. "If they miss it, it's a default." He wasn't sure how he knew that; he had found it in the fine print at the bottom of his bond sheet, and now it was his.

He sat back and did the arithmetic again, slower this time. If he borrowed the missing forty-nine dollars on the card, the interest charges each week would eat most of the dividend-style income his bond paid in. Saving up would take five more weeks. Borrowing would cost him nearly the whole telescope again in charges. It felt extravagant, paying twice for one thing.

At the simulation table the next morning, he slid the credit card back across to Mrs. Ruiz, unspent. "I'll wait," he said.

She smiled and dropped it in the box. "Week five," she announced to the room, "interest charged on all outstanding balances." Priya's stock still paid nothing, and William's bond paid again, small and steady, into his hand.

Emilie stood in the middle of the living room holding a rubber-band airplane like a microphone. Her brother Theo sat on the couch winding its propeller tighter and tighter, letting it buzz loose every time she stopped talking.

"Again," he said. "Your speech is tomorrow, and I want the TV back by eight."

Emilie's problem was not the two minutes. It was the opening. Her teacher wanted a hook, three points, and a closing, and every hook she tried sounded like a school report. "What if I start with the most famous speech ever written?" she said. She had chosen Hamlet for her topic because her grandmother loved it, but she only knew one line of it, the one everyone knew.

"That's not a plan," Theo said. "That's a guess."

She borrowed her mom's phone and searched for the words "To be, or not to be." There it was. "It's a soliloquy in Act 3, Scene 1," she read aloud, "of Shakespeare's play." So the most famous speech in the English language sat right in the middle of the action, not at the beginning where she would have put it. She thought about that. The play hooked you for two whole acts before Hamlet said the words everybody remembers.

She tried an experiment. Instead of opening with the quote, she opened with a question, then told the audience the famous line, then isolated her three points one by one: who Hamlet was, what the speech asked, and why people still quote it four hundred years later. Her closing circled back to the opening question.

Theo held up the airplane as a timer. The propeller spun down just as she said her last line.

"Two minutes," he announced. "Actually good, too." He clicked on the TV, then turned the volume low. "One more time, so I can heckle you properly."

Emilie cleared her throat. "To be, or not to be."

Christopher sat on the back steps with a jar of water, a brush, and a sheet of heavy paper on a clipboard. His assignment from the art camp booklet said to paint a sphere with a light source, showing the highlight, the shadow, and the cast shadow. He had propped a tennis ball on the picnic table with the sun coming from the upper left, so he could see exactly where the shine sat, bright as a tiny moon on the ball's surface.

He drew a circle, mixed a pale gray, and worked his way around the ball, darker toward the lower right where the shadow curled into the crease. The cast shadow pooled sideways across the table, and he painted that too, long and soft. Then he leaned back and squinted. The shine was gone. His gray wash had swallowed it. He frowned, dipped his brush in white paint, and dabbed it onto the spot where the gleam should have been. The white sat there like a flat little pancake, dull and chalky, nothing like the living shine on the tennis ball.

His little sister Nadia wandered out with a bandage on her arm and a purple popsicle. "I got a vaccine," she announced, "and Mom said I earned this." She looked over his shoulder. "Your ball has a smudge."

"It's a highlight," Christopher said. "It's supposed to shine. It doesn't."

"Paint around it," Nadia said, licking the popsicle. "Duh."

Christopher opened his mouth to argue, then stopped. In transparent watercolour, the paint let the paper show through, and the thick paper was porous enough to drink the washes. Maybe the shine wasn't something you added at all. Maybe it was the paper itself, clean and untouched. He tore off a fresh sheet, drew the circle, and this time painted in a horseshoe shape, leaving a small island of bare white paper where the sun struck. He eliminated every stroke that crept toward that island, rinsing his brush whenever a gray tide threatened it.

The sphere glowed. The bare paper gleamed brighter than any paint could, exactly like the spot on the tennis ball, and the cast shadow stretched away to the lower right as if the ball were really sitting there. He held it up. "Look. The shiniest part is just paper."

Nadia studied it, popsicle dripping onto the grass. "Okay, I changed my mind. Your ball doesn't have a smudge anymore. It has an eyeball."

"It's a sphere," Christopher said, but he tilted the page toward the sun, and the white spot winked.

The group chat pinged at 9:14, right while Zack was supposed to be asleep. It was Maya: "someone posted my old blog in the school forum. with screenshots. my OLD blog."

Zack sat up in the dark, phone glowing under his blanket. "i thought you deleted it in fourth grade," he typed.

"i did. like, a hundred times. it's still THERE."

Three dots appeared, vanished, appeared again. Dev wrote, "deleted stuff can't just come back. unless somebody saved it."

Zack's stomach did a slow flip. Because he had a blog too, from back when he thought he was going to be a famous inventor, full of posts about his "unbreakable alloy spoon" project, which had actually snapped in half on day two. He had also, once, put up a photo of himself in front of his house. With the house number visible.

"hold on," he typed. He opened his laptop, keeping the screen tilted away from the door in case his dad checked on him. He searched his old blog's address, then tried something Maya had mentioned in the chat, something called the Wayback Machine. Since 1996, he read, the Internet Archive had been saving copies of public web pages, and anyone could look at old versions of many websites.

His heart was hammering by the time the page loaded. Slowly, line by line, his old blog rebuilt itself on the screen. There he was at nine years old, grinning in front of the house, number and all. There was his post about how the strength of his spoon would "fluctuate depending on the temperature of the soup." Maya commented on it. Total strangers could have commented on it. Total strangers could have read it, saved it, shared it.

He screenshotted nothing. He just sat there.

"Zack you still there?" Maya asked.

He typed with cold fingers: "found my blog too. the photo of my house is still up. and i found a page from my school's old site with the field trip schedule. anybody could have known where our whole grade was that day."

Dev wrote, "so deleting doesn't actually delete."

"not if it was ever public," Zack sent. He started a new list of things to fix, starting with telling his dad in the morning. Then Maya's name popped up at the top of the chat, and beside it, a stranger's account had just joined the group.

Dominic had been rehearsing his speech the whole bus ride, muttering "Honourable Councillor Perkins" until the driver told him to knock it off. He clutched his petition, forty-three signatures demanding the repeal of the bylaw that banned scooters from Miller Park, and marched into the town hall, which smelled like coffee and old carpet. His friend Priya squeezed in beside him. "You've got this," she whispered. "You have more stamina than anyone in Grade 6. Remember the read-a-thon?"

That gave Dominic his opening line. When the mayor called for public comments, he shot up his hand so fast his chair squeaked. "Honourable Councillor Perkins," he began, voice cracking only once, "forty-three citizens signed this petition asking you to review Bylaw 12. That's a real petition, with real names, and it's notarized by my mom." He held it up like a trophy. The room chuckled. Councillor Perkins leaned forward, actually interested, which was more than Dominic had dared hope.

Then she asked the question he'd been dreading. "Forty-three signatures, out of how many scooter riders in town?" Dominic froze. He didn't know. "Hundreds," he guessed. "Maybe more." She nodded slowly. "Then why do you think the bylaw passed in the first place? Someone must have wanted it."

That night Dominic lay awake, thinking. He couldn't see the votes, but he could see their shadow. He pulled out his notebook and sketched the last election for park board. Three candidates had run. Ms. Ortiz got 34 percent, Mr. Bell got 33 percent, and Ms. Grant got 33 percent, and Grant won, barely, because she edged out Bell by four votes. But Ortiz and Bell had both campaigned on the exact same promise: more scooter restrictions. Dominic added the numbers twice, then three times, because he didn't believe his own arithmetic. "They had way more votes together," he whispered to his ceiling. "And they still lost."

The next morning he collabed with Priya over cafeteria fries, laying out his notebook like a detective on TV. "It's called first-past-the-post," she said, tapping his page. "My sister taught me. Two similar candidates can split their supporters' votes, and a third candidate wins with fewer votes than both of them combined." Dominic stared at her. "That's it! That's why the bylaw passed. All the anti-scooter people split between Ortiz and Bell, and Grant squeaked through. If either one had dropped out, the other would've won easily." He grinned so wide a fry fell out of his mouth.

At the next town hall meeting, Dominic arrived early with a new petition and a one-page chart, drawn in three colors because he'd decided evidence should be versatile. "Councillor Perkins," he said, "forty-three people signed this, and I can show you why the bylaw only reflects a sliver of the town." She studied his chart, then looked up with a strange smile. "Funny you should mention that election," she said. "I'm Ms. Ortiz."

Mason slid a paperclip across the lab table and watched it catch the light. Mr. Okoye had written two lists on the board, one for physical changes like melting ice and bending metal, and one for chemical changes like rusting and burning. The trick, Mason decided, was figuring out whether you could get the old thing back. Melted ice could freeze again. Rusty metal was rusty forever. If only he could see what was actually happening down inside the iron, tiny piece by tiny piece.

His partner Priya had other plans. "We need the atom model for the poster," she said, dumping three bags of beads on the table. "Red, blue, and yellow. I want that blue ribbon at the science fair, so it has to be right." She held up a red bead. "Electrons," she announced, then pointed at a blue one. "Protons."

Mason frowned. "But what's the yellow bead for?"

"The neutrons, obviously."

"Why obviously?"

Priya sighed like he had asked why water was wet. "Protons have a positive charge. Electrons have a negative charge. Neutrons have no charge at all."

"So yellow is nothing?" Mason turned the bead in his fingers. A particle that had no charge at all. It just sat there in the middle of the atom, doing nothing anybody could measure directly. Wait. Could it? His mind jumped back to the rusty paperclip. He couldn't see the iron atoms trading partners with the air, but the rust proved something hidden had happened. The charge rule was the same kind of invisible cause.

He wrote a note and folded it into a paper airplane, flying it across the room to his friend Dario, whose class period transported mail down the hall between labs. The note read: "Burn a small piece of magnesium ribbon for me tomorrow. If it changes to white powder and can't change back, that proves a chemical change happened, even though we can't watch the atoms do it." Dario wrote back one word on the wing: "Deal." Priya glued the yellow beads into the nucleus and held up the finished atom. "Positive, negative, and nothing," she said. "The nothing ones are my favorites."

Everly sat in the waiting room of Hartley Driving School while her mom took her lesson behind the building. Through the window she could see the orange cones lined up like little traffic guards, and the radio on the desk would transmit her mom's instructor saying things like "wider turn" and "check your mirror." Everly was the only kid there. Three adult candidates for their road tests sat filling out forms, and nobody needed her, which meant she was free.

Free, with a mission. Her mom had left her a five-dollar bill and one instruction: walk to the corner store, buy a carton of milk, count the change. Everly had done the store with her mom a hundred times but never alone, and the whole way there she felt like a spy in her own neighborhood. She found the milk, watched the screen say $3.75, handed over the five, and counted the coins back into her palm until they made exactly $1.25. She said "thank you" in a voice that came out steadier than she expected.

Back at the driving school, she discovered the trouble. In her backpack, folded since morning, was her costume shirt for Friday's play, and it was a wreck. Her dad had ironed it in a hurry, with the iron still on the cotton setting, and the nylon had gone shiny in two long streaks, like someone had polished it with wax. She held it up under the light and turned it. "Shiny means hot," she said to herself. "Way too hot."

The driving school was an old house, and behind the counter there was a real ironing board where the staff pressed their uniform shirts. A woman named Deb, who ran the front desk, glanced at Everly's shirt. "You can use it if you're careful," Deb said, and went back to her paperwork, which was exactly the kind of not-explaining Everly appreciated.

The iron had a card taped to its cord. Everly leaned close and read it out loud. "Dots on the iron symbol set the highest safe iron setting. One dot is low, about 110 degrees Celsius. Two is medium, about 150. Three is high, about 200." She looked at her dad's iron at home in her mind, remembered it cranked up for cotton, and understood. Her shirt had been a casualty of three dots.

But the shine itself, could it be fixed? She had an idea and wanted to test it before she trusted it. She cut a tiny sliver from the shirt's inside hem, wet it, laid it flat, and set the iron to one dot, the low, 110-degree setting. She pressed for three seconds and checked. The sliver looked dull and normal, no new shine. She moved up to two dots, about 150, tried a second sliver, and checked again. Still fine, but she decided not to gamble on the rest of the shirt, and she certainly wasn't going to three dots, about 200, not after what cotton-setting heat had already done. She set the iron back to one dot, laid the shirt flat, and pressed each streak gently, in and out, in and out.

When her mom came in from the lot, flushed and holding her permit, Everly held up the milk, the change counted into a neat stack, and the shirt, smooth and dull and saved. "One dot," she said. "That's the whole secret."

Charlotte sat cross-legged on the living room rug with her aunt's ancient laptop, which was so eccentric that it hummed like a refrigerator whenever she opened more than one tab. Her problem was real: she had promised her class she would summarize the forty-one survey forms about cafeteria food, and tomorrow morning she had to distribute the results to everyone. The forms were just a mess of tally marks on paper.

First she needed to know how to sort so many answers at once, so she searched the web. She typed "food" into the search bar and got a page full of junk, including a big shiny box at the top shouting BEST SNACKS DELIVERED FREE! Her friend Priya had warned her about those boxes last week. "That's an ad," Priya had said. "It's trying to sell you something, not answer you." Charlotte remembered that lesson now. She deleted her search and tried specific keywords instead: "summarize survey results in Excel." The ad boxes still sat at the top of the page, but below them the real results appeared, and one of them said PivotTable.

She clicked through and found her grandfather's spreadsheet program already had one. On the right side of the screen a pane appeared with a list of her survey questions at the top and four empty areas below them, labeled Filters, Columns, Rows and Values. Charlotte dragged the word "Grade" into Rows, and the table instantly grew a list of grades down its side. She dragged "Rating" into Columns, and ratings spread across the top. When she dragged "Count" into Values, numbers filled the middle like magic, and the forty-one forms turned into one small, readable table. She pulled "Grade" back out of Rows and dropped it into Filters instead, and a dropdown appeared where she could choose one grade at a time.

She thought about last month, when she had handed out her book report as one giant unsorted paragraph and Mrs. Okafor had squinted at it for a whole minute before saying anything. Maybe she should have organized it then, too, or maybe the mess had taught her something the tidy version never would. She still wasn't sure. She dragged "Grade" back to Rows, printed two copies, and called out, "Priya! Come see what I found!"

Rachel's draft was covered in red circles, and she was proud of every single one. "Ten adjectives gone," she told Priya, sliding the paper across the cafeteria table where the writing club met on Tuesdays. "Mr. Okafor called them weak, so I cut them. 'Very big' became 'big.' 'Really exciting' became 'exciting.'" She paused. "Then I cut 'big' and 'exciting' too, just to see what happened. The sentences got shorter. Some of them were three words. Then I made one long sentence on purpose, with a comma, so the rhythm wouldn't be flat."

Priya read the essay, which argued for a later school start time, and frowned. "It's punchy. But my brother read it and said he still didn't believe you, because you never said anything about the buses."

Rachel thought about the buses. She couldn't see her readers, sitting at home, deciding whether to agree with her, but she could picture them, and she could simulate their objections in her head the way she simulated chess moves against her grandfather. Best candidate for the strongest attack: busing schedules would be a mess if school started an hour later. That was the argument that could sink hers.

"That's the thing," Priya said, tapping the margin. "My sister did this for her debate class. You admit the other side has a real point, fairly, and then you answer it. The answer is called a rebuttal."

So Rachel tried it. She wrote that bus schedules really would be harder to change, that drivers might have volatile morning routes that couldn't easily shift, and then she answered it: the district could stagger the three school levels, so buses ran in waves instead of all at once. She hadn't believed it would help. It felt like giving away points. But when Priya read it again, she set the paper down slowly and said, "Okay. Now I'm convinced."

Rachel remembered last month, when she'd refused to change a single word of her poem because revision felt like admitting the first version was a failure. She wasn't sure yet which version of herself had been right. Maybe neither. She picked up her pen and drew one more circle around the word "definitely."

"Cut," she said.

Grandpa's laptop sat on the kitchen table beside a glass prism that caught the afternoon light and threw little rainbows across Alice's notebook. She was building her first real game, a Python quiz where players typed answers to math questions and the program kept score.

"Type your answer here," she said, sliding the laptop toward Grandpa.

He peered at the screen, then carefully typed: seven.

The program stopped. Red letters spilled down the screen, and at the end of them Alice spotted a word she didn't know yet: ValueError.

"Did I break it?" Grandpa asked. "I only answered the question."

Alice scrolled up and read the error again. The question had been "What is 3 + 4?" and Grandpa had answered with the word instead of the digit. She remembered, suddenly, the Scratch maze she'd made back in September, the one where a cat orbited a giant cheese block forever because she'd forgotten to check if the player touched the edge. She had fixed it with an if-then block: if the cat touched the edge, then the game ended. Maybe this was the same kind of problem, just in a new language. If someone typed a word, then something needed to catch it.

She couldn't see the rule itself. It was hidden inside the program, like gravity hidden inside an orbit. So she tested it, the way she'd learned to test everything. She typed 7 into the game herself. It worked, and her score went up. She typed seven. Crash, red letters, ValueError, every single time.

"There it is," she said. "If you type the number as a word, it crashes."

Grandpa leaned in. "So my spelling broke your computer."

"Your spelling broke my computer." Alice laughed, then frowned at the screen. "But there has to be a way to handle it."

She searched her notebook, where she'd copied bits of code from the library book, and found a line the book called a try. She wrapped her question in it, added a line that said "please type the number with digits," and handed the laptop back.

Grandpa typed seven again. This time the game didn't crash. It just asked politely for the digit, and he typed 7, and his score climbed to three while the rainbows from the prism slid across his hands.

"You're very agile with that keyboard," Grandpa said, missing half the keys as he said it.

Alice saved the file twice, just in case, and spun her chair toward him. "Okay. Round two. And Grandpa, this time, no vocabulary words."

The bakery smelled like sugar and cinnamon, and Arianna bounced on her toes while her dad studied the pastries behind the glass. They had exactly forty minutes before the tour bus left for Seville, and Mom had given her a mission: order lunch for all four of them in Spanish. For two weeks Arianna had been practicing full sentences about her family, so she was ready. "Tengo un hermano menor," she announced to the man at the counter. "Tengo un perro que se llama Biscuit y un gato que se llama Reina. Mi mamá es alta y mi papá es divertido."

The man smiled, clearly delighted, and asked something rapid that she didn't catch. She pointed at four empanadas and a bag of churros anyway, and he nodded and waved them toward a table. When the food arrived, it came on heavy ceramic plates, with forks and knives arranged neatly beside them. Arianna stared at the plates. Ten minutes to the bus, and food meant to be eaten on a bus was sitting on dishes that belonged to the bakery.

She thought back to the market that morning, where she'd watched a woman ahead of them in line say "para llevar" when she paid. The vendor had wrapped everything in paper and handed over a bag. Arianna hadn't known what the words meant then, but the pattern implied something: say those words, and the food travels. Her brother was already unhappily chewing, indifferent to her discovery, but Arianna raised her hand anyway.

"Para llevar," she said, pointing at the plates, then miming putting things into a bag.

The man laughed, snapped his fingers, and called to someone in the back. Within a minute the empanadas were tucked into paper sleeves and the churros were in a warm bag with grease spots blooming on the bottom. On the bus, Dad gave her the last churro as a reward, and Arianna grinned and added a new sentence to her list. "Mi familia come en el autobús," she said, "para llevar."

Emily was supposed to have watered the lettuce seedlings in the greenhouse before breakfast, and she had forgotten. Now they lay against the soil in floppy rows, and her stomach dropped the way it did when she knew she was in trouble. Grandpa Ruiz did not yell. He just stood beside the flats with his hands in his pockets and said, "They'll probably come back if we water them now. But you ought to know why they went down."

Emily squatted and touched a leaf. Yesterday it had stood up stiff, like a tiny green soldier. Nothing had eaten it, nothing had snapped it, and no frost had come in the night. Something had changed inside it that she couldn't see, and that bothered her more than the forgetting did. She remembered a poster from science class, back in September, a diagram of a plant cell with a big pale bubble drawn in the middle, labeled central vacuole. Her teacher had said the words once, quickly, and Emily had written them down and thought nothing more of them. Now she stared at the wilted seedlings and wondered whether that bubble was the whole secret.

She formulated a plan to test it, writing it out like a lab sheet because she wanted to be objective instead of just hopeful. She would water half the flat and leave the other half dry, then check every hour. She texted her friend Nadia to keep herself honest: "Doing an experiment. If my idea is right, the watered half stands up and the dry half stays flat. Watch this." By noon the watered seedlings had lifted halfway, and by evening they stood almost straight. The dry half stayed flat as ribbon.

She found the answer in Grandpa's old botany book, in a chapter with curled corners: when a plant's central vacuoles are full of water, they press outward against the cell walls, and when they lose water, the plant wilts. The pressing outward, she realized, was what kept the leaves stiff, like air in a tire. She read the sentence twice, out loud, just to hear it. So a floppy leaf meant empty vacuoles, and standing leaves meant full ones.

The next morning she taped a diagram above the flats. At the bottom she drew the sun with careful rays, then an arrow to the lettuce, then a grasshopper, then a garter snake, then a red-tailed hawk at the top. She showed Grandpa. "The sun feeds the lettuce, the lettuce feeds everything else," she said, tapping the page. "But watch this." She folded the paper so the lettuce row was hidden, hawk and snake and grasshopper left hanging. "If the lettuce dies, the whole chain breaks, because there's nothing to pass the sun's energy along." Grandpa studied it, then picked up the watering can and held it out to her. "Then I'd say you've got a percentage of those seedlings to save," he said. "Better get to it before breakfast."

Evan had been building the same cardboard vessel at the park picnic table for three Saturdays, a sailboat with a mast he had cut so it stood perfectly perpendicular to the deck, and today Marcus was not sitting across from him. Marcus was all the way over by the duck pond, throwing pebbles, because yesterday Evan had told everyone in the cafeteria that Marcus still slept with a stuffed rabbit named Captain Fluff. Marcus had found out at lunch, and now here they were at opposite ends of the park on a Saturday morning.

Evan walked to the pond with the note he had written on notebook paper. He read it out loud instead of handing it over, because Marcus would not take anything from him. "Dear Marcus, I'm sorry if you were upset about what I said."

Marcus picked up another pebble and did not throw it. "That's a non-apology," he said. "You're sorry if I was upset. Like it's my fault for being upset."

Evan looked at the paper. He read the line again in his head. The "if" was the problem. He had written sorry about Marcus's feelings, not sorry about the thing he himself had said. He had said it out loud in the cafeteria on purpose, to get a laugh, and everyone had laughed, and Marcus had sat there with his tray.

"I have to do it over," Evan said. He went back to the picnic table, took out his pencil, and folded the old note into the boat's hull. He wrote a new one and walked back. "Dear Marcus. I'm sorry I told everyone about Captain Fluff. It was your private thing and I used it to make people laugh. That was wrong. I won't say anything about your stuff again. Do you want to finish the boat? I can't get the sail to stay up."

Marcus turned the pebble over in his hand. The wind came off the pond and smelled like mud and duckweed. "The sail keeps falling because the mast is too skinny for the hole," he said. "You need to wedge something in there. A rolled-up piece of paper."

"The old note," Evan said. He unfolded it, rolled it tight, and pushed it into the base of the mast while Marcus held the deck steady. The sail stood.

They carried the boat to the pond's edge and set it in the water. It heeled over, righted itself, and drifted out toward the ducks. "Still floats," Marcus said. "Even with a non-apology inside it."

At dinner Joseph pushed his lasagna around the plate and finally said it. "Grandpa, your fertilizer story doesn't prove anything." Grandpa set down his fork. Last summer he had told the story a dozen times: he'd sprinkled some blue powder on his tomato plant, and by August the plant had grown taller than the fence. "One plant, one summer, one story," Joseph said. "The company claims it works, and their claim is supposed to be backed by tested evidence. But how would we even test it ourselves?" His little sister, Mina, grinned around a mouthful of garlic bread, and his mother raised one eyebrow in a way that felt faintly sinister, like she already knew the answer and was waiting to see if he did.

The kitchen smelled of oregano and burnt cheese. Rain streaked the window, and the porch light refracted through the drops so that every bead glowed orange. Joseph stared at that glittering pattern while the problem turned over in his mind. He needed to know if the blue powder caused the growth, but a hundred things could make a plant tall: sun, water, luck. Then the idea arrived, so suddenly he knocked over his water glass.

"Two pots," he said, grabbing napkins while Mina shrieked about her poem notebook, the one with a stanza about tomatoes on the first page, which was now soaked. "Same soil, same seeds, same window, same water. Everything the same, except one pot gets the powder and one doesn't. Grandpa told me that's what scientists call the control group. It gets everything the test group gets except the thing being tested. So if the powdered pot grows taller, the difference has to come from the powder and nothing else."

Grandpa chuckled. "Six weeks, then. Winner picks the movie."

"Deal," Joseph said, and shook on it, blue powder already waiting in his pocket.

The text from Zoe had arrived at 7:04 in the morning, and Emily had read it four times before breakfast. "Can't do the project tonight. Something came up. Don't ask." Zoe never said "don't ask." Zoe asked questions constantly, about everything from cloud shapes to cafeteria pizza. Emily spread her cereal bowl, her phone, and her notebook across the kitchen table and started a list, which she labeled, in careful printing, ANAYLSIS OF ZOE, then crossed out the misspelling and wrote it again. Cancelled plans. "Don't ask." No exclamation points, when Zoe usually used three. Emily chewed her pencil. Something was wrong, and Zoe was hiding it.

But what? Emily's first idea felt almost naive now, looking back: she'd assumed Zoe was just tired, because tired people cancel things. That theory had lasted until she scrolled up through two weeks of messages and found the pattern hiding there like a shape under a blanket. Zoe stopped using exclamation points on Tuesday. Tuesday was the day she'd stopped sitting with Emily at lunch, too, and started eating in the library. Emily sat very still. Her grandmother had once taught her that smoke detectors chirp before they die, a small warning before the real trouble. People probably did the same thing. Zoe was chirping.

Emily needed one more piece of proof, so she ran a test. She wrote back: "Okay, no questions. But I'm leaving cookies in your mailbox at noon. You don't have to come outside." It was the kind of message Zoe would normally demolish with jokes, like "bring FIVE cookies, minimum." The reply came in nine minutes. "Thanks." Just that. One word, flat as a dropped pancake. Emily's stomach went cold. That was three warning signs, lined up like dominoes. Who was she supposed to tell? Not Zoe, who had said don't ask. Then she remembered her mother's rule, written on a sticky note above the washing machine: if a friend's signals point to trouble, tell a trusted adult, even if the friend gets mad. Friends get over mad. Trouble doesn't get over itself.

She found her mother in the garage, pulling weeds out of a flowerpot, the smell of damp soil sharp in the warm air. "Mom. Zoe's in trouble and she won't say what." Emily laid out the evidence, one piece at a time, the way she'd lay out cards. Her mother listened without interrupting, then picked up her phone.

On the drive to Zoe's house, her mother called Zoe's mother, and Emily caught the edge of another conversation coming through the speaker, some radio show about health she'd half-heard that morning while brushing her teeth. A teenager had asked why her uncle reached for a cigarette the moment he got stressed, and a voice had answered that when smoke is inhaled, nicotine reaches the brain within about 10 seconds. Emily stared out the window at the passing fences. Ten seconds. Bodies reacted fast, and so did trouble, which meant you couldn't afford to sit around hoping it fixed itself.

Zoe's front door opened before they even knocked. Zoe stood there with red-rimmed eyes, holding the bag of cookies, and Emily realized with a jolt what had been wrong all along: Zoe hadn't been hiding from her. Zoe had been waiting to see if anyone would notice.

"You counted my exclamation points," Zoe said.

"You chirped," said Emily, and held out the last cookie from the bag she'd saved in her pocket.

Naomi sat on the fence rail with her sketchbook balanced on her knees, drawing arrows from left to right: sun, grass, grasshopper, mouse, hawk. The assignment was due Monday, and the last arrow, the one that ended at the hawk, kept coming out crooked. What really bothered her, though, was the question Uncle Reyes had tacked onto the bottom of the page in his looping handwriting. What happens if you take one link away? She was skeptical that one missing arrow could matter much. There were so many mice in the hayfield that they probably couldn't all be counted, and so many grasshoppers that they chewed the garden rows to lace.

Last summer at the science museum, she remembered, a boy had pulled the middle stone from the top of a block arch, and the whole thing had come down, clattering across the floor. The guide hadn't lectured. She had just said, "That one's the keystone," and moved on. Naomi had thought about it for days, how one block among many could hold up everything. Now, watching the pasture, she wondered whether a food chain had a keystone too, some creature whose disappearance would change the whole farm.

She decided to test it. Uncle Reyes had mentioned last spring that the hawks had gone, driven off when the old cottonwoods near the creek were cut down, and nobody had intervened to bring them back. Naomi counted what she could see: field mice darting everywhere, tunnels under the squash, bark stripped from the young apple trees. The grasshoppers were thicker than she'd ever seen them, because the mice had multiplied and eaten everything green faster than the hawks ever had. Hawks were so few, just two pairs before, yet without them the field looked nothing like it had. She flipped to a fresh page and drew the chain again, this time leaving the hawk out, then drew what followed: more mice, fewer grasshoppers' predators of plants, bare rows.

At dinner she slid the sketchbook across to Uncle Reyes. "Two hawks used to live here," she said. "That's almost none. But when they left, everything changed anyway." He studied the arrows, turning the page sideways. "There's a word for that," he said. "Robert Paine came up with it in 1969, for a species whose removal changes its whole community way more than its numbers would suggest." Naomi leaned in. "What's the word?" He tapped the empty space at the top of her chain. "Keystone species." She grabbed her pencil and wrote it above the hawk, then drew a new bird on the cottonwood stump, wings open, its brown feathers like camouflage against the bark.

Rebecca sat on her bed with the family group chat open, typing and deleting the same message for the fourth time. Priya hadn't spoken to her in six days, not since Rebecca told the whole lunch table about Priya's disastrous audition for the spring musical. Priya had walked out of the cafeteria, and now her replies had gone from paragraphs to nothing at all. Rebecca finally sent, "Can we talk?" to the chat, along with, "Not to you guys. Just needed to say it out loud somewhere."

Her older brother Marcus answered first. "Then why post it here?" he typed, adding a shrugging emoji. Her mom sent a thumbs up, which was her way of saying she was listening. Rebecca stared at the screen. The real problem wasn't talking. The real problem was that she wasn't even sure what she wanted anymore. She wasn't angry at Priya for icing her out, not really. But the thought of sitting with her at lunch again, of everything going back to normal, made her stomach tighten. She typed, "I think I've forgiven her but I don't want to be best friends again yet. Is that even allowed?" Then, before anyone could answer, she searched the phrase on her phone, because she wanted to know before she had to hear an opinion.

The psychology page she found made her sit up straight. There were two different things, and they had two different names. She read it twice, then texted the chat a screenshot. "Look. Forgiving and reconciling," she wrote. Marcus replied within seconds. "So you can do the first one without the second one." Rebecca typed, "Yeah. Forgiving just means letting go of resentment. Reconciling means rebuilding the relationship. So the friendship doesn't have to go back to exactly how it was." Her mom sent a single message: "Both are yours to decide."

On Saturday, Rebecca walked to Priya's house and stood on the porch holding two hot chocolates, which was a feasible plan only because she lived three blocks away. Priya opened the door, saw the cups, and sighed. "I'm still mad," she said. "That's fine," Rebecca said. "Me too, a little. But I'm done being resentful about it. Can we just sit on the steps?" Priya considered the larger cup, the one with extra whipped cream, and stepped outside.

Justin spread the parts across the workbench: thirty-one red marbles for protons, thirty-eight gray ones for neutrons, and a spool of copper wire he planned to bend into three rings for the electrons. His science teacher had assigned each student an element, and Justin's card said gallium. He had never heard of it, which was part of why he'd picked it.

He needed to check where gallium belonged, so he pulled the old periodic table off the garage wall. It had belonged to his grandfather, a veteran of the Navy engineering corps, and it was so faded that half the numbers had gone pale. Justin ran his finger along the rows looking for Ga, but the spot where it should have been was blank. So were the spaces below it, little empty squares like missing teeth. He checked the chart twice, then flipped it over, thinking the print might be on the back.

"Grandpa, your periodic table is broken," he called through the door. "It's got holes in it."

His grandfather came out, wiped his hands on a rag, and looked at the wall. "Mendeleev left those gaps on purpose," he said, and went back inside. That was all.

Justin stared at the empty square. On purpose? He tested the idea the only way he could, by finding a newer chart. He ran to the kitchen, grabbed his sister's chemistry binder, and brought it back to the workbench. In her chart the square was filled. Gallium, Ga, atomic number 31, sitting exactly where the blank had been. So the gaps weren't mistakes, and they weren't missing prints either. The old chart had been made before gallium was discovered, and whoever built the table had left the space open, waiting. Justin had assumed the chart was wrong; now he could see it was more like a reservation, a saved seat for a guest who hadn't arrived yet.

He sorted his marbles into a lump for the nucleus and bent the first wire ring. His original plan had been to glue everything down as fast as the glue would permit, but he changed his mind and left the pieces loose in labeled cups until each ring was bent right. When his grandfather came back out to park the truck, Justin held up the finished model. "Gallium," he said. "The one that filled the gap."

Sawyer stood in the deodorant aisle at Hendrick's Pharmacy holding two sticks, one labeled "Arctic Blast" and one labeled "Sport Strength," and sniffed each one like a detective. Last week his older cousin Teo had leaned over during a basketball game and said, "Dude. Shower daily. Use deodorant. Your sweat glands just changed the game." Sawyer had laughed, but then he'd noticed it himself, a smell that followed him from the gym to class like a shadow he couldn't shake.

The pharmacy felt like a museum of growing up. Vitamins for stamina, razors behind the counter, signs about skin and hair and body changes he was only starting to understand. He'd brought a note from his mom, since she was waiting in the car with his little sister. "You can handle this one," it said. "Pick the unscented kind, and check the label so you're not buying something with an explicit ingredient list full of stuff we can't pronounce. Proud of you. Mom."

At the register, the pharmacist, Ms. Ruiz, glanced at his choices and nodded. "Good pick. Deodorant is like brushing teeth. It only works if you do it every single day." She slid a pamphlet across the counter, the same one his health teacher had shown the class. On the back was a fact that had stuck in Sawyer's head: according to the CDC, nearly 9 out of 10 adults who smoke cigarettes daily first tried smoking by age 18. He'd turned that over in his mind all week. Almost every adult smoker started as a kid, which meant the decisions made at his age could contract into habits that lasted decades. It worked both ways, he figured. If bad habits started young, good ones probably did too.

"Testing a theory," he told Ms. Ruiz. "One week of daily showers and deodorant, no missed days, then I check the results." She smiled and wrote something on the back of his receipt: "Day 1. Come tell me how the experiment ends."

Seven days later, Sawyer pushed through the door and slapped the receipt on the counter. "Theory confirmed," he announced. "Arctic Blast, every morning. Case closed."

Peyton had consumed nothing but water for twenty minutes, which was a record for someone who usually scavenged fries off her friend Mateo's plate. She was too nervous to eat. In her pocket was a folded piece of paper with one sentence on it, and she had promised Mateo she would say it to the waiter without falling back into English.

"You need the bookstore before it closes at five," Mateo said. "So you ask him how to get there. In Spanish. If you chicken out, I consume your dessert."

"That's my dessert."

"Scavenger rules."

The waiter came by, and Peyton's mouth went dry. "Por favor," she began, "¿cómo llego a la librería?" The waiter nodded and answered fast, too fast, a river of words. Mateo smiled like he had already won. But Peyton caught something. He said "va a estar" and "va a cerrar," and she remembered the pattern: va a, then the verb. Future. The bookstore was going to close. And then, slower, he held up two fingers. Dos. Two blocks. "A la izquierda," he said, pointing left, and she knew izquierda from the hand trick her aunt had taught her, the one that looked like an L. Left at the bank, and the bookstore was across from the library.

"¿La biblioteca está enfrente de la librería?" she asked, and when he said "Sí," she actually understood the whole thing.

Mateo stared at her. Then, quietly, he leaned in. "Okay, then answer me something. In Spanish we put an ending on the verb for the future. Estaré. I will be. What's the English future ending?"

Peyton opened her mouth. Closed it. She said the words under her breath. "I will go. I am going to go. There isn't an ending. English doesn't have one. We just put will, or going to, before the verb."

"That's so weird," Mateo said, delighted. "We have a whole ending and you have nothing."

"It's not weird, it's just different," Peyton said, and then the waiter, who had been stacking plates at the next table, set down two slices of flan without being asked.

"Your Spanish was very good," he said in perfect English. "I am Eduardo. Your teacher is my sister." He tapped the flan. "On the house, because you tried. And the spice on this dessert is mild, but taste is subjective."

Mateo pushed both plates toward Peyton. "Scavenger rules," he said.

Jade crouched over an old picture frame in the backyard, arranging pebbles, bottle caps, and broken tiles into a mosaic for the neighborhood art contest. Her little brother Leo sat on the porch steps eating a pickle and offering advice nobody asked for.

"Put the big blue cap in the middle," he said. "Middle is best. Middle is the boss."

Jade tried it. The blue bottle cap went dead center, surrounded by a tidy ring of white pebbles, like a donut staring at her. She frowned. It looked like something from a plumbing catalogue, all neat and dull, not like the lagoon she'd imagined. She slid the cap left, then right, then almost center again. Still boring. Still a donut.

"Your art has the personality of a sock," Leo announced.

"Your face has the personality of a pickle." But he had a point, and she knew it. She flipped through her mom's old photography book on the grass, hunting for ideas, and stopped at a page with pictures marked up in pencil. Someone had drawn lines over the photographs, two straight lines one way and two perpendicular, cutting each picture into nine boxes like a tic-tac-toe board. The interesting subjects sat along those lines, or right where the lines crossed, never in the exact middle. The book called it the rule of thirds.

Jade grabbed a stick and drew the same grid in the dirt beside her frame, imagining the lines stretched across her mosaic. If the lines crossed in the four corners of the center square, then the blue cap belonged on one of those crossing points. She moved the cap up and to the left until it sat just off center, on a crossing, then rebuilt the pebbles around it so they swirled toward the cap instead of circling it like a fence.

She stood back and squinted. The whole thing suddenly had a direction, like water flowing somewhere. It wasn't a donut anymore. It was a lagoon.

"Whoa," said Leo, pickle paused halfway to his mouth. "It's looking at me sideways."

Jade took a photo on her mom's old phone to preserve the design in case a squirrel attacked, then carried the frame to the shade so the glue wouldn't dry too fast in the sun. Leo followed, dragging his pickle.

"Teach me the tic-tac-toe trick," he demanded.

"First, throw away that pickle. It smells like regret."

Leo sniffed it, shrugged, and took another bite.

Jessica's little brother, Ben, had hijacked her science fair volcano for the third time, and now the teacher had let her come into the lab after school to rebuild it, with Ben trailing behind because their mom was still at work. The volcano itself had survived the hijackings. The question Ben kept asking had not.

"Where do the bubbles come from?" Ben asked, for maybe the ninth time, while Jessica measured baking soda into the paper cone.

"I don't know yet," she said. "That's the annoying part."

Ms. Rao had left two trays of samples out on the long counter, each with a card. One card said physical change and showed a melted ice cube and a crumpled foil sheet. The other card said chemical change and showed a browned apple slice and a rusty nail. Jessica picked up the rusty nail and turned it over. The rust didn't wipe off. It was part of the nail now, the way a dent was part of Ben's bike. No, she thought, a dent was different. A dent could be hammered out. Rust couldn't be un-rusted.

"You can flatten foil back out," she said, mostly to herself. "So that's still foil. The ice melts and it's still water. But rust is a new thing."

"What's rust?" Ben asked, reaching for the nail. His reflex was to grab anything on a counter, so she moved it out of range.

She set down the nail and looked at the baking soda, then at the vinegar bottle. An idea, possibly an extravagant one, occurred to her: if new bubbles appeared when two things mixed, that might be a sign of a chemical change, because a gas was a new thing being made. She poured vinegar over the baking soda in the volcano's crater. Foam hissed up and spilled down the sides in extravagant red streams, and Ben leaned in so far she had to hold his collar.

"Bubbles," Jessica said, watching them pop. "That's a chemical change."

"Can I do it?" said Ben.

When Nora arrived at Priya's house, she nearly stuck out her hand for a shake, but Priya's grandmother pressed her palms together and nodded instead, so Nora copied her, palms together, and the grandmother smiled. Nora had brought a gift, a box of chocolates, and she handed it over with her left hand because her right was holding her coat. The grandmother took it, but her eyebrows did something small and strange, and she passed the box to her other hand before setting it down.

At dinner, the table was crowded with dishes Nora had never eaten before, rice and chicken and something spicy that made her nose run. She noticed something while reaching for the serving spoon. Priya, Priya's father, even little cousin Danial, all of them ate with their right hands only. Every time Danial's left hand crept toward the plate, his mother tapped the table beside it until he moved it back. Nora quietly revised her theory that the grandmother's eyebrows had been about the chocolates. It was about the hand.

She decided to test it. When the rice dish came around, she lifted it with her right hand and offered it to Priya's father, even though her reach felt awkward and elastic across the crowded table. He took it with his right hand too, and this time the eyebrows stayed calm.

"In Malaysia we use the right hand for eating and for giving and receiving things," Priya said, leaning close. "It's a sign of respect."

Nora kept her left hand in her lap after that. When the tea came, she received the cup with her right hand, and when she passed the bread, she used her right hand again, even when it meant setting down her spoon first. The grandmother watched her across the table, then ladled an extra spoonful of chicken onto Nora's plate and said something to Priya in a language Nora didn't understand.

"She says you eat like a proper Malaysian," Priya translated.

Nora grinned and picked up her spoon with her right hand.

Sofia heard the crash before she even reached the garage, which meant the trash cans were down again. Her little brother Marcus was already crouched behind the workbench, notebook in hand, watching through the window like a detective in a movie.

"It's the Hendersons' dog," Marcus whispered. "Every single trash day. That's my hypothesis." He said the word slowly, the way their science teacher said it, like it was something you could hold. "A testable guess. If I'm right, he'll do it again today."

"You've seen him do it?" Sofia asked.

"No, but the cans are knocked over every trash morning. Nine times now." Marcus flipped through his notebook, nine dates with a crooked checkmark beside each one. "Nine mornings, nine crashes. I'm going to win the science club bet. We took a ballot, and everyone voted that a raccoon was doing it. Everyone except me. If I catch the dog on camera, they have to vote again, and Best Hypothesis is mine."

Sofia pulled the old camcorder off the shelf and wiped the dust from its lens with her sleeve. Nine crashes sounded like proof, but something about it nagged at her. She remembered last summer, when her cousin Deja had insisted that every cat on the block hated water, and how smug she had looked right up until Sofia's cat Mister Pudding leapt straight into the wading pool. Deja had to confess the whole thing afterward, that she'd counted a dozen cats avoiding rain and thought that settled it. "A hundred white swans can't prove all swans are white," Deja had said, staring at the dripping cat, "but one black swan proves that wrong." Sofia hadn't fully understood it then. She was starting to.

"Nine mornings isn't proof," she told Marcus. "It just means the cans fall on trash days. The dog is a guess. So is the raccoon. So is anything until we see it happen."

They set the camcorder on the workbench, aimed at the cans, and waited. The garage smelled like oil and cut wood, and Marcus bounced his knee the whole time. At 6:40 the crash came, louder than usual, and they both lunged for the window.

A garbage truck rumbled past, its mechanical arm swinging wide, clipping the cans and sending them rolling across the driveway. Not a dog, not a raccoon, not anything with legs. Marcus stood frozen with his notebook hanging open, nine checkmarks suddenly meaning nothing at all.

"So I lost the bet," he said finally.

"You lost the bet," Sofia agreed, "but you won the science. Nobody else even tested theirs." She rewound the tape, and the truck swung its arm again on the little screen. Marcus watched it twice, then grabbed his pencil.

"I'm writing this down," he said. "New hypothesis. The arm's too long."

Parker slid into the booth at Corner Cup Cafe with his notebook, two pencils, and a problem the size of a walrus. His persuasive essay was due Friday, and all he had written was "Dogs" and then, underneath, "good ones."

"What's the emergency?" asked Grandpa Joe, setting down a hot chocolate with extra whipped cream, which was how he said good afternoon.

"I have to write five whole paragraphs. Introduction, three reasons, conclusion. Like a sandwich with three fillings and nobody's hungry."

"Five paragraphs." Grandpa Joe whistled. "Rebellious of your teacher to demand such a thing."

Parker flipped his notebook open. "The hard part is the persuading. I want to convince the school we need a dog day, but I don't know how convincing works. It's invisible. Like the wind."

Grandpa Joe leaned over and tapped a page where Parker had scrawled three weird words he'd copied off a library book cover: ethos, pathos, logos. "Well, well. Greek. A fellow named Aristotle wrote about those in his Rhetoric. Three ways to persuade."

"You know Greek?"

"I know a Greek diner owner. Also, I know those three." Grandpa Joe counted on his fingers. "Ethos is whether people believe you. Pathos is their feelings. Logos is logic and evidence."

Parker wrote fast, then narrowed his eyes. His grandpa was known to joke, so this needed testing. He looked around the cafe and spotted Mrs. Alvarez, who ran the bookstore next door and had a tundra of frost on her window because her heater had died. Parker marched over, cleared his throat, and said, "Mrs. Alvarez, your store is freezing, and studies say a layer of foam panels would insulate it so well that your heating bill would drop. Numbers don't lie." That was logos, with evidence.

She blinked. "Interesting, but who are you again?"

So logos alone wasn't enough. Parker tried again, louder. "Also, there's a little girl in there reading with mittens on! Mittens, Mrs. Alvarez!"

She pressed a hand to her heart. "Oh, the poor lamb. Mittens. That settles it, I'll call the insulation people today." Pathos, one mittened girl, victory.

Back at the booth, Parker was grinning until Grandpa Joe said, "One problem. Ethos. Mrs. Alvarez didn't know you from a moose. If a kid tells her about insulation, why should she trust the kid?" Parker chewed his pencil. On his essay draft, the school wouldn't trust him either. He needed a grown-up with credibility, like a vet, to say dogs were safe for a school visit.

He wrote "Paragraph 2: get Dr. Chen the vet to sign a note" and underlined it twice.

"Look at that," Grandpa Joe said, stealing a sip of the hot chocolate Parker had abandoned. "Three Greek words and a plan. Aristotle would buy you a muffin."

"Then get in line behind him," Parker said, and pulled the notebook back.

The Hendersons' living room was packed by the second quarter, and the windows had gone humid from all the shouting and the popcorn. Carter had the best seat, the beanbag by the TV, because he had arrived first. That was the whole reason he was there: Coach Henderson ran a halftime trivia contest every year, and the winner got the giant chocolate basketball that sat on the mantel, untouched, waiting.

"At halftime," Coach Henderson announced during a timeout, "the question is about basketball itself. One question. First right answer wins. And no phones." She tapped the chocolate ball like a gong.

Carter wanted that ball so badly his teeth ached. The problem was that he had no idea what the question would be. Beside him, Mr. Alvarez's cousin Dev, who was fourteen and loud, was already claiming the prize. "Basketball facts are my whole life," Dev said.

The timeout ended, but Carter wasn't watching the players anymore. He was staring at the hoop on the screen. Why was it called a basket? A hoop wasn't a basket. A basket was a thing you carried peaches in. His grandfather had peach baskets in the garage, and Carter had hauled them every August at the orchard. If somebody had named the game, he thought, they must have named it after the first thing they used as a goal. Not a hoop. Something that actually held the ball.

"Hey, Coach," he called across the room, "who made up basketball in the first place?"

She smiled a coach smile, the kind that gives away nothing. "Halftime, Carter. Three minutes."

Two minutes later a storm knocked the power out, and the whole room groaned in the dark. Somebody found the emergency lamp and the little generator in the garage, and Mr. Alvarez yanked the cord until it coughed to life. The TV stayed dead, but the lamp lit the room, and Coach Henderson clapped her hands. "Halftime is halftime. Here's the question. Basketball was invented by a man named James Naismith. Where and when, and what did he use for goals?"

"Peach baskets!" Carter shouted before he could stop himself. "That's why it's called a basket!" The words were out, and now he had to back them up, fast, before Dev could contradict him with something confident and wrong. Carter closed his eyes and pictured the game being brand new, a gym, winter. "December 1891," he said. "A YMCA training school. In Springfield, Massachusetts."

The room went quiet except for the generator humming in the garage. Coach Henderson slowly lifted the chocolate basketball off the mantel and weighed it in her hands.

"Nobody," she said, "has ever gotten all of that."

She tossed it underhand toward the beanbag, and Carter caught it against his chest with both arms.

Colton tapped his pencil against the desk and stared at the problem on the whiteboard: 1/3 + 1/4. Mrs. Patel had said the answer was not 2/7, and half the math club had written 2/7 anyway, including Colton. Now she wanted them to figure out why that was wrong before the club's fraction challenge on Friday.

"You can't just add the tops and the bottoms," said Priya, drawing two rectangles. "Thirds and fourths aren't the same size pieces."

Colton thought about the poster in the hallway that depicted the tundra, all ice and flat gray sky, and how his grandfather had said the ground underneath stayed frozen solid. These fractions were like that, he decided. Something hidden underneath the numbers, an invisible rule you couldn't see but could still test.

He tried cutting both fractions into the same size pieces. Twelve worked: 1/3 became 4/12, and 1/4 became 3/12. Four pieces plus three pieces made 7/12. He wrote it down, but a cold, sinking feeling stopped him. What if he was wrong again? On Friday he would have to stand at the board in front of everyone.

Then he remembered last winter, when Priya had sat at his kitchen table with her homework, unsure about an equation she had solved for x. Before her grandfather came in to check it, she had plugged her answer back in place of the variable, and when both sides came out equal, she grinned and closed her notebook. "If it goes back in and both sides match," she had said, "the answer is right."

Colton looked at 7/12. He couldn't plug a sum into a variable, but he could test it the same way, by taking it apart. If 7/12 was right, then subtracting 3/12 should give back 4/12, which was 1/3. He ran his finger down his work, slowly, one step at a time, barely breathing. Seven minus three was four. Four twelfths, and that really did equal one third.

He subtracted the other way, too: 7/12 minus 4/12 was 3/12, which was 1/4. Both checks came out even. The hidden rule held.

"Mrs. Patel," he said, standing up so fast his chair scraped, "I think it's 7/12, and I checked it by taking it apart both ways. It goes back together right."

Mrs. Patel walked over, looked at his page, and circled the answer. "Resilient thinking, Colton. You checked your own work instead of waiting for someone to tell you."

At the board on Friday, Colton solved 2/5 + 1/2 in under a minute, wrote 9/10, and tapped the marker against it twice. "Check me," he told the room.

At dinner Tyler pushed his peas around his plate while his little sister talked about Maya's bracelet stand at the fair. Maya had sold out on Saturday, at four dollars a bracelet, and now everyone wanted some.

"Everybody keeps asking her for more," Emma said, "but she's out of beads."

Tyler remembered the fair, the smell of kettle corn drifting past Maya's table, the way she'd stacked her bracelets in rows, brittle little shells of painted macaroni that clicked when you touched them. He'd watched a woman buy three at once without even asking the price. He'd wanted one himself, but four dollars was more than his allowance could stretch to after the settlement he'd made with his dad over the broken garage window, two weeks of chores for the repair.

"That's why nobody had them," Tyler said suddenly. "She didn't have very many, and everyone wanted one. So she could charge a lot."

"So?" Emma rolled her eyes.

"So watch what happens now." He grabbed a napkin and drew a table on it, the way he categorized things for science class, sellers down one side and prices across the top. "Maya made a pile of money at four dollars. If you could make bracelets, wouldn't you start?"

By Thursday he had his answer. Three new stands had popped up on his street alone. Mrs. Okafor had a folding table at the end of her driveway, and the twins from two doors down were stringing beads on their porch every afternoon.

"They're all three dollars," Emma reported that night, chewing a mouthful of spaghetti. "And Mrs. Okafor said she'd do two-fifty if you buy two."

Tyler set down his fork. High price, and now more sellers than he could count, all offering bracelets because four dollars had made it worth their while. He thought about the napkin chart, still folded in his pocket, and about waiting too long at the fair.

"So are you going to buy one?" Emma asked. "They're cheap now."

"Yeah," Tyler said, pushing back his chair. "Let's go before everybody in town opens a stand."

The gym at the Maple Street Community Center felt like the inside of a rain cloud. Leo dribbled down the court, and sweat rolled off his elbows before he even reached the foul line. "Come on, one more quarter!" Coach Rivera shouted, but half the Rockets were bent over with their hands on their knees, gasping like fish.

Leo had played in a tournament last month on a day that hit ninety-six degrees, and it had been brutal but somehow easier than this. Today the thermometer said eighty-eight, yet everyone was dragging. He mentioned it to Marcus during a water break. "Maybe we're just tired," Marcus said. "I hibernated all weekend playing video games. My legs are noodles." Leo shook his head. "Last game was hotter. This doesn't add up."

Then he noticed the window. The air outside was thick and hazy, and the glass had a film of moisture on it, even though nobody had touched it. He grabbed his water bottle, poured a little on his forearm, and blew on it. Almost nothing happened. The drop just sat there, shiny and stubborn, refusing to dry. In the drier tournament gym, his soaked jersey had dried stiff in twenty minutes. He tried an experiment on his other arm with a paper towel, fanning it. His damp arm felt cooler than the one with the plain water drop. "Marcus! Come feel my arm. Both of them."

Marcus pressed a finger to each forearm. "Whoa. That one's colder. Why?" Leo grinned. "Sweat's supposed to dry off us to cool us down, right? Today it just sits there and doesn't go anywhere." He jogged to the bench and told Coach. "So in humid weather we overheat more easily, even when it's not that hot out. Can we sub more often?" Coach squinted at him. "That's actually a credible theory. Fine. Rotating every four minutes."

The rotations worked. Fresh legs flooded the court every few minutes, and the Rockets clawed back from eight points down. With ten seconds left, Leo stole the ball at midcourt, drove past two defenders, and laid it up off the glass. The net didn't even ripple. "That," Marcus panted, throwing an arm around him, "is the sweatiest win of my whole life."
