The astronomy club's nocturnal watch party was in six weeks, and Aiden wanted the red telescope in Mr. Ferris's catalog more than he had ever wanted anything. The price was one hundred twenty dollars. His allowance was five dollars a week, which meant saving every dime until roughly the end of never.

"I can fix that," said Marcus, waving a folded paper under Aiden's nose at lunch. "My cousin signed up for this credit card offer and bought a guitar the same day. You borrow the money now, pay it back later. Easy."

Aiden read the paper. The card came with a contract full of tiny words, and one line said that if he didn't pay the whole balance each month, extra money got added on top, month after month. He did the math on his napkin, slowly, twice. If he borrowed one hundred twenty dollars and paid it off five dollars a month, the added charges would pile up faster than he could pay them down. He would end up handing over more money than the telescope cost, and he still wouldn't own it for ages.

"That's like the opposite of what happened to you," Aiden said carefully, because Marcus's birthday money was a sore subject.

Marcus slumped. "I put all ninety dollars into one company everybody was hyping. Then the company failed completely and the stock price fell to zero. Every dollar I put in, gone. Zero." He flicked a pea across his tray. "At least your telescope can't be worth zero. It's a real thing, and it comes with a warranty."

That night Aiden taped a note above his desk: TO AVOID MARCUS MATH, PAY LESS, WAIT LONGER, OWN IT. He asked Mrs. Okafor down the street if she needed help raking leaves, and she said yes, ten dollars a weekend. He mowed the Hendersons' lawn for eight. He skipped the school store's eraser shaped like a shark, which nearly broke his heart.

On the morning of the watch party, he counted the jar: one hundred twenty-three dollars and a paper clip. He walked to the store himself and set the bills on the counter. The telescope came in a box with a handle, and he carried it to the field just as the sun went down.

Marcus was already there, wrapped in a blanket like a burrito. "Trade you a look for a bag of chips," he said.

"Two bags," said Aiden, and turned the lens toward Saturn.

Gavin slid a battered paperback across the counter of Halvorsen's Books, the shop his grandfather had passed down like a hereditary trait, so that owning it felt almost built into the family. The retired diplomat who ran it now, Mr. Okafor, frowned at the cover of The Monkey's Paw and then at Gavin's homework sheet.

"I need a theme," Gavin said, "and a quotation to prove it. But every quotation I pick feels wrong. Like it's just about a paw, not about anything."

Mr. Okafor tapped the cover. "Read me the part where the soldier comes back."

Gavin found the page, and the old paper smell rose up as he read aloud. Sergeant-Major Morris, the man who had carried the paw to England, told the White family that the wishes twisted into something terrible, that a man before him had wished and died in misery. Then, before anyone could stop him, he flung the paw straight into the fire.

"Stop there," Mr. Okafor said. "What did he do?"

"Threw it in the fire." Gavin frowned. "But Mr. White snatched it out. He rescued it."

"So the story warned them. Every single one of them, before the first wish was ever made." Mr. Okafor leaned forward. "If the warning was that clear, what is the story really asking?"

Gavin stared at the page. Was it about greed? No, the Whites weren't greedy, just sad about their son. The customers browsing near the window seemed to migrate toward the counter, drawn in by his silence. He read the soldier's line again, how the paw had caused so much trouble that its last owner wanted to burn it away. Then it clicked. Maybe the theme was that knowing a danger is not the same as believing it.

"That's it," Gavin said, and copied the quotation onto his sheet, the pencil scratching fast. "Warnings only work if you let them."

Mr. Okafor smiled and stamped the book with the shop's old rubber stamp. "Then let's make sure you believe this one," he said. "Homework first, cocoa second."

Emily leaned over the sink and pulled her bangs aside. There, in the mirror, sat a red bump on her chin, and school photos were tomorrow morning.

She thought about her cousin's wedding last summer, when she had skipped showers for three days because the hotel pool "counted." Her skin had erupted afterward, and she had blamed the chlorine. Now she wondered if she had blamed the wrong thing. She ran a finger along her hairline, where her scalp always felt greasy by evening, even on days she washed that morning. The oil seemed to come from somewhere she couldn't see, some place under the skin doing its own work.

Her older sister Maya knocked on the door. "Are you hogging the bathroom again?"

"Maya, come look at this." Emily pointed at her chin. "Where does the stuff even come from? I wash my face."

Maya came in and studied the bump. "It's sebum," she said. "Hormones during puberty make your skin's oil glands pump out more of it, and it clogs your pores." She shrugged. "That's why my face wash has an acne component. It's on the shelf, the blue bottle."

Emily uncapped the blue bottle and sniffed it, sharp and medicinal, like wintergreen. "If oil is the problem, oil should show up somewhere. If I blot my forehead in the morning and after school, I could anticipate when the breakout times are."

So she did. The next morning she pressed a tissue to her forehead, then again after gym class. The morning tissue came away clean; the afternoon one showed a faint shiny smudge, like grease from a slice of nutritious peanut butter toast. The pattern matched her chin getting oilier by evening, too. It wasn't the pool, and it probably wasn't just one skipped shower either, though she still counted that wedding weekend as a strike against her.

Tonight she washed carefully, rolled on deodorant, and set her alarm twenty minutes early so she could wash again before the photographer's flash.

Maya called through the door, "You're still in there?"

"Blotting," Emily said, and held the tissue up to the light.

Emilie stacked the strawberry quarts along the front of the farm stand, careful not to bruise the ones on top. It was July, and the berries were everywhere: overflowing crates in the back, buckets on the counter, a hand-lettered sign that said $2.50 a quart. In February, that same quart had cost six dollars, and customers had still snapped them up. Her job was to explain the difference to the city folks who asked, and she had gotten good at it. "Strawberries are everywhere right now," she would say, "so the price goes down. In winter they're scarce, so the price goes up. Supply and demand." Some people nodded. One woman had asked her to classify the stand's produce by season, just for fun, and Emilie had done it in her head in under a minute.

The problem was Danny. He worked the cash box on Saturdays, and he had two bank flyers spread on the counter between customers. Both banks offered the same rate, five percent, on savings accounts. One bank said interest compounded yearly. The other said interest compounded monthly.

"They're the same rate," Danny said. "I'm going with this one. Green logo. I like green."

Emilie's instinct said the flyers couldn't be identical, or why print two words differently. But she was also pessimistic about arguments with Danny, who once insisted for a whole afternoon that a tomato was a vegetable. "It's classified as a fruit," she had told him, and he had shrugged and kept eating.

"Look," she said, sliding the flyers side by side. "Same rate. But this one says monthly. Compounded monthly." She said the word slowly, like laying out cards. "It means the bank adds your interest every month instead of once a year." She thought of the strawberry crates. In summer the berries kept arriving, and the pile grew all season; in winter nothing came in until spring. Money, she guessed, might work like that too. If the interest landed every month, then each new piece could start growing right away, instead of waiting a year to be counted.

"Monthly pays a little more," she said. "Same rate, but the monthly one gets ahead, because each month's interest starts earning sooner than the yearly one does."

Danny squinted at the flyers. "How much more?"

"A little. Not a lot. But it's more." She thought of her grandmother, who had once chosen a bank by which one gave out free calendars, and had never mentioned regretting it. Emilie wasn't sure she'd have chosen differently back then either. Maybe small things didn't matter. Maybe they did.

Danny folded the green flyer and put it in his back pocket anyway. "I still like green," he said, and rang up the next quart of strawberries, $2.50, a price that would climb again in December.

Declan stood at Grandma's stove with a heavy pan and a bag of sugar, because tonight he was making the dessert and it had to be authentic caramel sauce, the kind his grandpa talked about from his childhood. Grandma had gone to pick up Aunt Rosa, so Declan had the kitchen to himself. He poured a layer of sugar into the dry pan and turned the heat to medium, watching the pale grains at the edges begin to melt.

His little sister Priya wandered in, drawn by the smell of the Sunday roast crisping in the oven. "That's browning just like the crust on the roast," she said, pointing at the pan. "Same thing, right?"

Declan thought about that. The roast was meat, and meat had no sugar to speak of, so how could plain sugar browning and meat crusting be the same reaction? He scraped the melting sugar with a wooden spoon and watched it turn amber. "This is caramelization," he said. "It's browning that happens when sugar alone is heated. The crust on the roast can't be this, because the Maillard reaction is different. That one also needs amino acids, and meat has those."

"So test it," Priya said, in the annoying way of little sisters who are sometimes right.

He spooned a little of the amber caramel onto a plate, then took a pinch of flour and a splash of milk, mixed them with sugar in a small bowl, and set the bowl beside the pan. He was reaching for a spoon when the pan hissed and a thread of smoke rose from the caramel. He jerked it off the burner too fast, and half of it seized into a hard, pale lump. Perfect dessert, ruined, and everyone due back in twenty minutes.

Priya leaned over the small bowl, sniffed it, and frowned. "Declan. Why is your roast all sweet?"

He spun around. Grandma's roast, the one with the famous crust, glistened under a thin glaze, and sitting beside the oven was Grandma's secret jar with a spoon in it. "That's her sugar glaze," he said slowly. "So the crust is caramelization and the Maillard thing, together." He grabbed the seized lump of caramel, broke it into pieces, and dropped them into a pot of cream to melt again. "Don't tell Grandma we found the jar."

"Too late," said Grandma from the doorway, holding up the jar. "Now stir, both of you."

"Grandma, read it again," Adam said, passing the note across the table. His cousin Tyler had slipped it under his door an hour before dinner, and Adam had been waiting all evening to deal with it. The note said, in Tyler's cramped handwriting: "Marcus keeps flipping the coin to decide who goes first in Galactic Racers, and he wins the flip every single time. It's not fair. Tell him tonight."

Adam had been reading about mediators all week for a school project, and here was a real case landing right in his mashed potatoes. He could hardly sit still. "Tyler, Marcus, after dinner we settle this," he announced. "I'm the mediator. That means the referee of arguments, basically, in our family dynasty of fairness."

"It means nothing," said Marcus, "because you made it up."

Tyler lunged straight into his complaint, but Marcus cut him off halfway through. "That's not even what happened, because the coin..."

"Stop," Adam said, holding up his fork like a gavel. He'd read one rule that stuck with him: in mediation, each person usually gets to tell their side without being interrupted while the other person listens. "Tyler talks first, all the way through, and Marcus, you don't say one word. Then you get your turn. That's how this works."

Marcus crossed his arms but kept quiet. Tyler explained that Marcus always called heads, heads kept coming up, and whoever went first in Galactic Racers usually won. When Tyler finished, Adam made him summarize the problem in one sentence. "The problem is that whoever picks the coin side decides the whole game," Tyler said.

Marcus's turn came. "I just like heads," he said, shrugging. "I didn't know it mattered."

"Then the rule can't be whoever wins the flip," Adam said. "That's arbitrary. New rule: coin flip decides who goes second instead."

Both cousins stared at him. Then Tyler grinned. "Deal," said Marcus, and shook on it over the butter dish.

Emilia sat at the kitchen table with three ruined greeting cards in front of her. Each one had cracked along the fold, the thick card splitting into bumpy white lines that crossed her careful drawings of tulips. She was making a birthday card for her grandmother, and it had to be perfect, so she pressed a fourth card flat and folded it anyway, watching the paper splinter down the crease.

"There has to be a reason," she said to her cat, Biscuit, who was asleep on the chair beside her. She looked closely at the cracked cards. The folds were straight, but the surface was rough and broken, as if the card had been forced. She thought about the thin paper she folded into paper airplanes, which never cracked. Maybe the thick card was too stiff to bend cleanly on its own.

She tested a small piece of scrap card first. She took a blunt spoon from the kitchen drawer and drew it firmly along a ruler's edge, pressing a shallow line into the card. Then she folded along that line, and the card bent straight and clean, with no crack at all. She blinked at it, then tried a second scrap without the pressed line, and it split like the others. It was not luck. She had been negligent about one small step, and the small step was everything.

The next card transformed under her hands. She scored a line with the spoon before folding, and the spine of the card came out smooth and sharp. On the front she drew tulips, then a border of little stars. Biscuit woke up, yawned, and put one paw on the envelope, as if signing it too.

"You can deliver it with me," Emilia said. She slid the card inside, and the white paper whispered against the edges. On the envelope she wrote her grandmother's name and, underneath, in small letters, "Folded with a spoon."

The smell arrived on Tuesday, and by Thursday it had claimed the entire row behind Nicolas in science class. Marcus opened the window even though it was January. Ms. Patel didn't say anything, but she did sniff once, pause, and then move the lab demo two tables away, which felt worse than a speech.

The health unit that week covered puberty, and Nicolas learned that sweat glands kick into higher gear around age eleven, and that bacteria, which nobody can see, are what actually make the smell. He turned this over at lunch. An invisible cause, producing a visible, or at least smellable, effect. There was a principle in there somewhere: if the cause was hidden, the fix had to target it anyway, not just the smell. Spraying body spray over it, the way his older cousin did, would be like painting over a leak.

"Testing a theory," he announced that night, and put deodorant, soap, and a clean shirt in his backpack like lab equipment.

The next morning his hands were shaking so much he dropped the deodorant twice in the locker room. Getting changed for gym had become its own problem; his heart hammered whenever it was his turn to be picked for teams, and he'd started pretending he felt sick to avoid it. He told Marcus this while they waited in the gym, in a low voice, expecting mockery.

Marcus shrugged. "That's a thing, you know. Anxiety. I had it about tests last year."

"You? You never worry about anything."

"I worried about everything, I just hid it. My mom took me to a counselor. Anxiety disorders are treatable, and the counselor used cognitive behavioral therapy. That's what it's called. It teaches you to notice anxious thoughts and change them, and she said it's one of the most effective treatments there is."

"Change them how?"

"Like, I'd think, 'I'll fail every question.' She'd have me write that down, then write what actually happened. I usually got a B. My brain couldn't argue with the paper."

Nicolas applied the method right there. His thought: everyone will laugh if I miss the ball. He looked around. Rashad had already tripped over air twice, and nobody had laughed, because they were all too busy being embarrassed themselves. The hammering in his chest dialed itself down a notch.

The principle seemed objective, almost like a rule of the universe: hidden causes, whether bacteria or worried thoughts, still responded to the right tool. The gym teacher, enforcing the everyone-plays rule, pointed at Nicolas. "You're up, serving."

Nicolas tossed the ball, and his serve clipped the net, wobbled, and dropped over. Rashad high-fived him. "See? Invisible bacteria, invisible worries," Nicolas said. "Same principle."

"Did you just compare your brain to armpit germs?"

"Basically."

Alex cracked the eggs into the bowl and glanced at the recipe card again, even though he had read it six times. Saturday mornings at the community kitchen meant baking with his grandmother, and today he was in charge of the blueberry muffins from start to finish. He turned the dial to three seventy-five, just like the card said, and slid the rack to the middle.

"These are the same muffins that burned at your house last month," he said, measuring the flour. "You said you followed the recipe exactly."

"I did," his grandmother said, tying her apron. "Three hundred seventy-five degrees, eighteen minutes. Black tops every time. I nearly boycotted baking altogether."

Alex mixed the batter, folded in the berries, and filled the paper cups while she wiped down the counter beside him without being asked. When the oven beeped, he slid the tray inside and set the timer. But he kept thinking about those burned muffins. Same recipe, same temperature. Something did not add up.

Then he remembered the drawer of kitchen tools near the sink. Among the whisks and spatulas was a round metal thermometer with a hook on top, the kind you hang from a rack inside an oven. He had walked past it every Saturday without a second look. If the oven here showed one temperature but was actually another, the thermometer would catch it. He hung it inside, closed the door, and waited two minutes, peeking through the glass.

"Grandma, come look." He pointed at the dial face behind the door. The oven was set to three hundred seventy-five, but the thermometer read four hundred.

"Four hundred," she said slowly. "Many home ovens run hotter or cooler than the temperature on the dial. That little thermometer just told us the truth."

"Skepticism," Alex said. "I had it about this oven the whole time. Now it's proof." He pulled the muffins out three minutes early, and they came out golden, with distinct domed tops, nothing like the black hockey pucks from her kitchen.

She broke one in half, steam curling up, and took a bite. "Alex. These are perfect."

"You need one of those thermometers at your house," he said. "Then we can turn the dial down until the inside says three seventy-five, even if the dial itself says something lower."

She wrote "oven thermometer" on the back of the recipe card and underlined it twice. "Next weekend, your kitchen," she said, and handed him the warm half of her muffin.

Alex took it and put the rest of the tray on the cooling rack, the sweet smell drifting across the whole community kitchen, where three other people were already drifting over to ask for one.

Landon had one hour before the rock-sorting contest at the science museum ended, and the prize was a summer geology scholarship that would cover the whole field camp. The rules were posted on the wall: sort the twelve mystery rocks into bins marked igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic, by how each rock was formed. His little sister Priya hovered at his elbow, holding the clipboard they had been given.

"Number five," Priya read. "Dark, glassy, with tiny bubbles." Landon turned the rock in his hand. Bubbles meant it had cooled from something molten, he decided, so into the igneous bin it went. The striped one with layers went to sedimentary, and the one that looked squished and swirl-patterned, like a candy cane caught in a press, went to metamorphic. He was halfway through when Priya frowned at the last rock, a pale gray chunk with a pattern of tiny speckles. "This one could violate your whole system," she said. "It's got layers and speckles."

Landon didn't panic. He remembered what an influential scientist in the hall of fame display had written: rocks tell you their story if you look at how they formed, not just how they look. He carried the speckled rock to the big wall chart near the astronomy wing, the one he'd read while waiting in line, and compared the speckles to the chart's pictures. Then he grinned. "Cooled from melt. Igneous. The layers fooled me."

"You're sure?" Priya asked.

"New moon sure," Landon said. She looked confused, so he pointed at the ceiling dome, where a moon exhibit glowed. "Last night I couldn't find the Moon anywhere and I thought it vanished. At new moon the Moon lies roughly between Earth and the Sun, so its lit side faces away from us and it looks dark. It was always there. We just couldn't see it." He dropped the last rock into the igneous bin just as the timer buzzed. The judge strolled over, checked the bins, and circled something on her clipboard.

"Twelve for twelve," she said, and stuck a gold star on Priya's clipboard too.

The phone had been dead since the last gas station, and Dad was still refusing to ask for directions. "Grandpa said the cabin is right on the lake, near a town called Eagle Point," he said, drumming the wheel. "I want to find it before dark. I promised him we'd fish at sunrise."

Bentley unfolded the big paper map across his knees, and it crinkled like an enormous candy wrapper. Across the top and down the side ran rows of numbers, and thin lines crossed the map into a grid. Next to Eagle Point he found a tiny pair of numbers in the index at the back: latitude 44 degrees and 12 minutes north, longitude 87 degrees and 30 minutes west. He stared at the word "minutes" for a long moment. "That can't be how long it takes to get there," he said. "It's not time." But then what was it?

He tested an idea. If the whole state sat between the 44 and 45 lines, and the town's number said 44 degrees and 12 minutes, then the 12 must be a way of measuring distance between the big lines, not minutes on a clock. He held the map up to the light and counted the small tick marks between the printed lines. There were sixty of them. So each degree had to be divided into sixty of these "minutes," and sure enough, some of the finer labels were broken down even further, into seconds. "Sixty seconds in a minute," he said slowly. "It's like the clock, but for space." Dad glanced over. "You figuring that out all by yourself?"

Bentley was secretly proud, and a little envious of kids who got to learn this in a classroom instead of in a hot car. He slid his finger along the 44 degree line, then up from the 87 degree line, and where his fingers crossed, there it was: a small dot labeled Eagle Point, tucked against a blue blot of lake. "Turn left at the next highway, then about twenty miles north," he announced. Dad raised his eyebrows. "That's your verdict?" "That's my verdict," Bentley said. "Unless you want to knock on a stranger's door and ask a random anonymous person in the middle of nowhere."

Dad laughed and took the left turn. The road climbed through pines, and Bentley tracked their progress with his finger the whole way, checking the line numbers at every crossroad. Then the trees broke open and the lake flashed silver in the late sun, with a small cabin at the near shore and a rowboat pulled up on the sand. Dad honked the horn twice, and Bentley folded the map into a neat square and held it up like a trophy as the gravel crunched under the tires. "Grandpa," Dad called through the open window, "we used a map, and my navigator got us here."

Anna stood on Platform 4, gripping a sign she had made in marker: WELCOME GRANDPA JOE. The 3:15 from the city hissed in, and among the crowd she spotted his gray cap bobbing like a buoy. He waved with both hands. "One whole week," he announced, hugging her. "And I want to ride every train line this station has, even the slow one nobody likes." Anna grinned, but a worry buzzed at the back of her mind. Last year, when Grandma Rosa visited, Anna had meant to write down her stories and never got around to it. Grandma Rosa couldn't travel anymore, and those stories about her childhood felt like water slipping through fingers. She didn't want that to happen twice.

The week flew by. They rode the slow line to the harbor, and Grandpa Joe told her about the rat he had kept as a boy, a pet rodent named Whiskers who stole buttons. "Was that voluntary, keeping him, or did Whiskers just refuse to leave?" Anna asked, laughing. Grandpa Joe shrugged. "He moved in on his own. Like he chose me." On Friday, the last night, Anna studied him across the dinner table and tried to assess how many stories were still in there. Hundreds, maybe. How could she keep them?

Then she remembered the poster in the library window. A man had been recording his mother in a little booth. The poster had said the recordings go somewhere important, that people interview family members and, with permission, the recordings are saved at the Library of Congress. Anna had walked past it twice. Now she stopped walking. She grabbed her tablet.

"Grandpa, sit here and tell me about Whiskers again," she said, pressing record. "Why?" "There's a project called StoryCorps," she said. "People record interviews with their family, and with permission the recordings get saved at the Library of Congress. Like your stories could live there forever." Grandpa Joe went quiet. "Forever in a library," he murmured. "Then ask me anything, starting from the beginning." He leaned toward the microphone and said, "I was eight years old, and the button was missing from my coat."

The summer pool test was on Friday, and Muhammad had promised his grandfather he would swim twenty-five metres of front crawl before the Fourth of July barbecue. Twenty-five metres meant one full length of the community pool, with side breathing, without stopping, and Muhammad could not yet make it past the flags. Between swim practices, he and his friends played running games on the empty baseball diamond behind the pool, tagging bases like bases on a stolen run.

On Wednesday, DeShawn guarded Muhammad so tightly in their tag game that Muhammad could not reach second base no matter how he spun or dodged. DeShawn stayed glued to him, always half a step ahead, reading every fake. Muhammad felt ready to give up when Priya jogged over. "Stand still," she whispered, and she planted herself right in DeShawn's path. Muhammad broke left, and when DeShawn tried to follow, he had to scramble around Priya's planted feet, which bought Muhammad the second he needed to slap the base. "That's called a pick," Priya said, grinning. "Or a screen." Muhammad filed the idea away, and it made him think about the pool, where he always lost his rhythm in the same spot.

He had been losing air near the middle of the lane, and he began to suspect a hidden cause. Maybe it was not his arms giving out at all. Maybe he was holding his breath too long, letting it pile up until his body panicked, the way DeShawn's body had been blocked by a still friend standing in the way. His swimming problem had an invisible obstacle, and his job was to find something to plant in its path. He could not see air, but he could test an idea about it: breathe every third stroke instead of every fifth, a steady rhythm instead of a spontaneous gasp whenever he felt desperate.

Friday afternoon, the coach stood at the pool's edge with a clipboard. Muhammad pushed off, and a memory flashed into his mind: last summer, his grandfather cheering at a neighborhood pool while a cousin earned a red ribbon, and Muhammad cherishing the hope that one day someone would cheer that way for him. His arms circled, he rolled his head to the side, and air came in small, regular sips. The invisible weight never piled up. He touched the far wall and looked back at twenty-five metres of water he had finally crossed.

DeShawn and Priya were jumping up and down behind the fence that separated the pool from the baseball diamond, and DeShawn was shouting, "Pick! Nice pick!" Muhammad laughed, slapped the water, and called back, "See you at second base!"

Colton clutched his note card so hard the corners curled. He had come to the town hall meeting for one reason: the old drainage ditch behind the school was going to be paved over, and the skate ramps his brother Denny used would be gone. Somebody at the council had said a bill would fix it, but Colton did not know what a bill actually was, except that it was not the kind that arrived in envelopes.

He squeezed into a seat beside his grandfather, who was frugal with words at meetings but generous with butterscotch candies from his coat pocket. Outside, rain hammered the windows like a monsoon, and people shook off their umbrellas as they filed in, stamping puddles onto the floor.

"The first reading is just the bill being introduced," the clerk narrated into the microphone, walking everyone through each stage. "Then a second reading, committee study, a third reading, and a vote in the legislature. Only after all of that does it become law." Colton wrote the steps on the back of his note card, printing each one so Denny could read it later. So that was the path. A bill had to travel through it, like a package with a route.

Then a woman near the front stood up, waving a newspaper. "What about rights?" she asked. "Couldn't the legislature just trample them?"

The clerk shook his head, then paused. "There is something called the notwithstanding clause," he said. "Section 33 of the Charter. It lets Parliament or a provincial legislature override certain rights, but only for up to five years. After that, the override has to be renewed if they want it to continue."

Colton's pen stopped. Five years, then a wall. Whoever wanted to keep overriding rights had to come back and say so again, out loud, in front of everyone. He thought of Denny's ramps and pictured the bill climbing its stairs, reading by reading, like a kid getting passed along a hallway.

When the public comment period opened, Colton raised his hand before his courage could melt. He stood, knees wobbling, and read his card: "Please add the skate ramps to the bill at committee stage. My brother can't speak here tonight, so I'm speaking for him."

The room went quiet, and then the woman with the newspaper started clapping.

The whole premise of the food bank, Dylan discovered, was not just giving food away but giving it away in the right order. He had enrolled as a volunteer that morning because his scout troop needed service hours, and Ms. Reyes had put him on the canned vegetable shelf. He worked fast, sliding the new donations from the big box right into the front of the shelf where his hand fit easiest. When he finished, the row looked full and neat, labels all facing out.

Ms. Reyes walked past, stopped, and frowned at his shelf. "Redo it, please. New cans go in back."

"But the front's the easy spot," Dylan said.

"The easy spot is for the old cans," she said. "First in, first out."

Dylan pulled the new cans out again and stared at the shelf, thinking. So whatever went in first had to come out first, which meant the old cans sat in front where the next volunteer would grab them. He tested it by checking the dates on a few labels. Sure enough, the cans already at the front expired sooner than the ones in his box. It was like a line at a water park: first person in line, first person down the slide. He slid the new cans behind the old ones, all the way to the back, and pushed the old cans forward until the dates ran in order.

By noon his arms ached, but the shelf had a system now, and he liked systems. When the afternoon crew came in, a girl named Priya started stacking a fresh box right into the front of his row. "Back," Dylan said, pointing. "Older stuff goes out first so less expires on the shelf."

"You figured that out yourself?" she asked.

"Sort of. I got it wrong first."

She laughed and carried her box around to the far side. "Race you on the soup aisle."

Clara pressed her nose against the glass case in Mr. Reyes's classroom, where the class store kept a pair of purple binoculars for sixty dollars. Sixty dollars might as well have been six hundred. Her allowance was five dollars a week, and at that rate the binoculars would take twelve weeks, which felt like forever.

Then Marcus leaned over her shoulder. "My sister got a store credit card," he said. "She just took the binoculars home the same day. The card people only charge you a little extra each year, like ten percent."

Ten percent of sixty was six dollars. That sounded almost free, and Clara's hand was halfway to the sign-up sheet on Mr. Reyes's desk before she stopped. A little voice in her head said that if borrowing were that cheap, everyone would do it, and the store wouldn't make money. She pulled out her pencil instead.

Mr. Reyes's poster said the yearly interest rate was twenty-four percent, not ten. Clara wrote the numbers down. Sixty dollars, times twenty-four percent, times one year, came to fourteen dollars and forty cents. She sat back. She would owe the store more than two months of allowance, just for the privilege of waiting to pay. If something prolonged the debt, say she couldn't pay it off for two whole years, the numbers doubled. She did that math twice to be sure. Twenty-eight dollars and eighty cents, almost half the price of the binoculars again.

"Eighty-eight dollars total," she said to Marcus, showing him the paper. "That's not a little extra."

Marcus frowned at her arithmetic. "Your numbers seem credible," he admitted, "but what's the chance you'd really take a year to pay it back?"

"There's a probability I'd be exactly as broke as I am now," Clara said.

She tore up the sign-up sheet, opened her notebook, and wrote at the top of a fresh page: "Binoculars fund, week one." Then she taped her first five dollars inside the cover and set the notebook on her desk where she could see it every morning.

The chalkboard at math club still had last week's problem on it when Daniel walked in: a fraction puzzle worth extra points at Friday's competition. One half plus one third. Everyone knew Daniel's reputation for slow, careful work, but slow would not win on Friday, and he wanted this. He tried adding them straight across and got two fifths, which felt wrong the moment he wrote it. You could not add halves and thirds directly any more than you could add apples and pencils. There had to be a hidden rule, something you could not see on the surface, and he meant to find it.

He cut paper strips. One strip folded in two, one folded in three, one folded in six. When he laid them side by side, one half of the six-strip matched exactly three sixths, and one third matched two sixths. Five sixths. The strips could not lie. He tested it again with one half minus one third: three sixths minus two sixths, one sixth left over. Same answer both ways he checked. Ms. Reyes had left a note taped to the board, and Daniel read it aloud. "Try your method on y equals 2x plus 1. If it works, you will see something worth seeing."

Here was the twist: the note was addressed to Priya, not him. But Priya waved him over anyway. "I only had time to plot two points," she said, tapping her paper, "but look." The points sat at (0,1) and (1,3), and she laid her ruler across them. The graph of an equation like y = 2x + 1 is always a straight line, so plotting just two correct points is enough to draw it with a ruler. Her line ran clean across the whole page, and every extra point she checked afterward landed right on it. "Two points," she said, "and the whole thing appears."

The bell was inevitable, so they packed up fast. Priya slid the note across the table toward Daniel. "Ms. Reyes writes these for anyone who solves the warm-up first. Maybe next week it's your name." Daniel folded his six-strips into his notebook and followed the crowd migrating toward the door, already planning to practice common denominators that night. "Friday," he called back to Priya, holding up the note. "We're ready."

Eli knelt at the edge of the pond with a notebook, a pencil, and a mission: draw a food chain from the sun all the way to a top predator, then explain what would happen if one link disappeared. The problem was that food chains were invisible. Nobody could watch sunlight hop into a plant and then into a bug and then into a fish. He would have to be a detective.

"Are you excavating the pond or drawing it?" asked Maya, who had come down to catch frogs and was now ankle-deep in muck, holding her net like a spear.

"Collecting evidence." Eli pulled up a strand of pondweed and held it toward the light filtering through the canopy of willow branches. Sun, plant, bug, fish, heron. That was his chain, and the heron that stalked the far bank every evening was his top predator. But he wanted proof the chain was real, not just a guess. So he had swiped the little bottle of iodine from his sister's science kit, and he dripped a drop onto the pondweed leaf. The leaf went dark, almost black.

"That's starch," Maya said, leaning over his shoulder. "My grandpa says that's how potatoes get so filling. Plants store extra food as starch." She flicked pond water at him. "So your weed is basically a French fry."

"But what about the fish?" Eli said, frowning. "Where does a fish keep its spare energy? Not starch, right? It's not a potato with fins."

Maya waved her net grandly. "Animals store it as glycogen. Everybody knows that." Then she wobbled, sat down in the mud, and announced, "I have radical news. Zero frogs. Not one. My net is empty and my dignity is gone."

Eli looked at the far bank. No heron tonight either. "Exactly what I was supposed to figure out," he said slowly. "If the frogs and the little fish disappear, the heron loses its food. The chain breaks and the top goes hungry." He began sketching fast, sun at the bottom, heron at the top, and then, with satisfaction, he drew a big tear right through the middle.

Maya held up her muddy net. "Draw me in as a broken link too."

Noemie spread the chapters of her novel across the kitchen table like crime scene evidence, which was more or less what they were. Her assignment, due at eight tomorrow morning, was to track one symbol through the whole book and show how its meaning shifted chapter by chapter. She had picked the lantern, mostly because there were lanterns on nearly every page, which had seemed efficient and now seemed suspicious.

Her little brother Theo wandered through with a bowl of cereal and planted himself at the edge of the table. He was supposed to be studying his Romeo and Juliet lines for a quiz on Monday, and the index cards were bent from being in his back pocket. "Can I use your table?"

"It's not my table, it's the landlord's," Noemie said, not looking up. "And no."

Theo read over her shoulder anyway. "That's not the right scene. In mine, Juliet says 'Wherefore art thou Romeo,' because she's, like, looking around for him behind a curtain."

Noemie's pencil stopped. "That's not what that means."

"It's a question," Theo said. "'Where art thou' is 'where are you.'"

"Then why would there be a 'fore' on it?" She pulled his index card toward her and squinted at it. The balcony scene made no sense with his version, because Romeo was standing right below her, in plain view, the whole time. Juliet would have to be extremely unobservant. "Wherefore means why," she said slowly, testing the weight of it. "She's asking why he has to be Romeo. Why he has to be a Montague, her family's enemy. Not where he is. He's right there."

Theo stared at his cards as if they had personally betrayed him. "So my whole paraphrase is wrong."

"Extinct," Noemie agreed. "Dead as anything."

She pushed the cards back to him and looked at her own notes again, and something snagged in her mind. On her chart, the lantern meant safety in chapter two, home in chapter five, and in chapter nine the hero snuffed it out on purpose. Her note said "symbol gone, meaning gone." But it wasn't gone. It had flipped, like Juliet's question flipping from where to why. The lantern in chapter nine didn't convey the opposite of safety. It conveyed that the hero no longer wanted safety, that he wanted the dark.

She wrote it down, then crossed out two arrows on her chart and redrew them pointing the other way. "Out of my notes," she told Theo, who was now reading her chart aloud in a dramatic voice. "Quiz's Monday. Essay's at eight."

"Deadline pressure really brings out your warmth," Theo said, and slid his cards off the table.

Noemie captioned the final column, "The symbol isn't extinguished. It's asking a different question." Then she read it back to the empty kitchen, twice, and drew a small lantern in the margin with the flame pointing down.

Edouard had been waiting for Grandpa's visit all summer, but by the second morning something felt wrong. At breakfast, Grandpa held the cereal box at arm's length and squinted at it like it was a distant bird. When Edouard showed him a comic from his favorite lush, tropical adventure series, Grandpa smiled and handed it back after one glance. "Nice cover," he said, which was a strange thing to say about a comic.

Edouard started watching. At the market café, Grandpa stretched the menu out so far he nearly knocked over the sugar bowl, and he ordered "whatever you're having" instead of reading the specials. In the guest bedroom, the book Grandpa claimed he was reading sat closed on the nightstand while he stared out the window. Edouard had a sinking feeling. Maybe Grandpa didn't actually like comics, or books, or him.

That night Edouard found a clue. Tucked into the suitcase in the guest room was a letter from Grandpa's neighbor back home, and the handwriting was enormous, the letters as big as his thumb. "Your eyes are getting worse," Edouard read, feeling like a spy. "Wear the glasses." There were no glasses anywhere in the room.

He remembered something from last summer, a flashback that rose up sharp and clear. Grandpa threading a fishing hook for him at the lake, holding the line far away and blinking, finally saying, "You do it, Edouard. Your eyes are younger than mine." Edouard had thought Grandpa was just being lazy that day. Now a new idea was forming, and it compressed everything he'd noticed into one tidy thought: Grandpa's eyes worked fine for far away, but not up close. He was hiding it because he didn't want to be a bother.

Edouard tested the idea the next morning. He wrote, in huge letters across a page, WOULD YOU LIKE TO GO TO THE BOOKSTORE? He held it up across the kitchen and watched. Grandpa read it instantly, and his whole face changed.

"Ah," Grandpa said quietly. "You've figured out my secret. After about age forty, the lens of the eye loses flexibility and cannot focus up close as well. It's called presbyopia. My reading glasses correct it, and I left them on the bus." He laughed at himself. "I was too proud to say so."

At the bookstore, Edouard picked out the comic he'd wanted to share and read it aloud in the café, doing all the voices while Grandpa leaned back, listening, easy and happy. When Edouard paused at a cliffhanger, Grandpa's hand shot out and turned the page, quick as a reflex.

"Keep going," Grandpa said. "I have to know if they escape the jungle."

Piper had been at Camp Juniper for eleven days, and she had figured out three things. One: the lake smelled like frogs. Two: the mess hall served spaghetti every Wednesday. Three: somewhere between June and July, her own armpits had turned against her.

She noticed it during capture the flag, when her counselor, Rex, jogged past and Piper caught a whiff of something sour and realized it was coming from her own shirt. That night she dug the travel deodorant out of her duffel, the one her mom had packed "just in case," and sniffed it suspiciously. At the health talk in the lodge, the nurse had explained that between ages ten and thirteen, bodies switch on new sweat glands, and that sweat from those glands feeds bacteria, which is what actually smells. So the rule was simple: shower daily, use deodorant, and the smell never gets a chance to build. Piper tested it like a science experiment. One week of consistent showering and swiping every morning, and the problem dissolved. Her bunkmates stopped opening the windows when she walked in, which Rex said was the highest compliment at Camp Juniper.

But her best friend Dree was having a different kind of problem. On the night before the sailing test, Dree sat on her bunk with her knees pulled up, breathing fast. "I can't do it," she whispered. "I'm going to tip the boat over and everyone will laugh and I'll lose my spot. My whole scholarship to come here next summer, gone."

"Just calm down," Piper said. "It's easy."

Dree's face crumpled. "Easy for you to say. You don't even get nervous." She turned toward the wall, and Piper stood there feeling like she had knocked over something she couldn't pick back up.

Piper sat down on the edge of the bunk and tried again, this time with no advice at all. "Tell me about the tipping thing."

So Dree told her. The lake, the wind, the sail swinging around, the other campers watching from the dock. Piper listened, nodded, and said, "That sounds scary." Dree talked some more, and slowly her shoulders came down from around her ears.

The next morning, Dree passed the sailing test. She came dripping up the beach, holding her certification card like a trophy, and flopped down beside Piper on the sand.

"You didn't fix me," Dree said.

"I know," said Piper. "You just needed somebody to hear the scary part first."

Dree wrung out her ponytail and grinned. "Also, you smell way better than last week."

"Daily showers," said Piper. "I'm a whole new camper."

Cooper had never slept over at anyone's house before, and by eleven o'clock he was starting to worry that he wouldn't sleep at all. Dex's mom had already knocked twice. "Six a.m.," she'd said through the door. "The fishing boat leaves the dock at seven, asleep or not." Now the room was dark except for the glow of Dex's tablet, where they'd been watching video after video since nine.

At midnight Dex shut it off and they lay in their sleeping bags. Cooper stared at the ceiling. His body felt tired, but his brain wouldn't switch off, like a motor still running after the key was turned. Beside him, Dex rolled over for the tenth time.

"I can't fall asleep," Dex whispered. "Me neither," Cooper whispered back. He thought about it. They'd been lying in the dark for half an hour, so being in bed wasn't the problem. What else had they done? He tried to remember something his sister had said once, about light tricking your brain into thinking it's still daytime. It sounded plausible, but he wanted to test it before he trusted it.

"I hypothesize it was the tablet," Cooper said. "All that bright light, right up until we turned it off." Dex sat up. "What's the mechanism, though? How would light keep you awake?" "I don't know exactly. Something about the brain holding back a sleep hormone when it sees light, especially blue light, because it thinks it's daytime. So the hormone never builds up enough to knock us out."

Dex groaned. "Great. So we ruined sleepover night." "Or not," Cooper said. "If light held it back, maybe darkness lets it come back. We just have to stop giving our brains any light at all. No screen, no phone, nothing. Total black." He pulled his sleeping bag over his head like a tent. After a moment, Dex did the same, and the two of them lay there in the warm dark, breathing slowly.

From inside the bag, Dex's voice came muffled. "If this works, we're doing it at every sleepover." Cooper smiled in the darkness and closed his eyes.

Addison pressed her forehead against the airplane window and watched the clouds condense into gray towers below them. Their flight east to Rome had landed two days ago, and she still felt like her body was full of sand. She had fallen asleep at dinner, woken up at four in the morning, and dragged herself through the Colosseum while her little brother, Theo, bounced ahead of her taking pictures of every rock.

"Look at this one," Theo said now, holding up his camera in the Rome airport on their way home. He had one clear objective for the whole trip: get a photo of a pigeon sitting on something ancient. He already had pigeens on a statue, a pigeon on a wall, and, that morning, his prize, a pigeon on a broken column with the Colosseum in the background. "Best trip ever."

Addison couldn't argue, but something bothered her. On the flight out, she had been exhausted. Yet when they landed in Rome, Theo's eyes had gone wide and awake, and even her dad had said he felt strangely fine. It was the days after that had been terrible. On previous trips, flying home, everyone had seemed fine right away. She turned the thought over while they boarded.

Halfway across the Atlantic, she took out her notebook and made two columns. Trip out: flying east, awful afterward. Trip home: flying west. She looked at the columns. Could the direction itself matter? She decided to test it. "Theo," she whispered, "tomorrow, when we land, tell me how you feel. Really tell me."

"Fine, probably," he mumbled into his pillow.

They landed home at six in the evening. Theo ran through baggage claim chasing a plastic water bottle he was kicking like a soccer ball. Addison felt wide awake too, almost too awake, and at midnight she lay in her own bed staring at the ceiling. Her mother passed her door. "Can't sleep either," her mom said. "Funny, coming home is easier."

"It's because we flew west," Addison said. "Going east is the hard one."

Her mom paused in the doorway. "You know, I think you're right."

From down the hall, Theo's voice floated out into the dark. "Does Rome have pigeons at night?"

Emily slid into her usual seat on the bus, wedged her backpack against the window, and pulled out The Great Gatsby so fast the cover snapped.

"Book club is fifth period," said Marcus, dropping down beside her. "You don't have to read it on the way there, you know."

"I do, because Priya's going to beat me again." Priya had won the last two rounds of their game, which was to name the theme of the book and back it up with a quotation, and the losing side had to carry the winner's tray at lunch for a week. The hierarchy of the sixth-grade book club was brutal, and Emily was tired of the bottom.

She had read the chapter twice already. On the very first night of the story, a man reaches out across the dark water toward a green light. She flipped pages, hunting.

"What's so great about Gatsby, anyway?" Marcus asked. "My brother says he throws parties and mopes."

"That's basically it, and it's amazing." Emily tapped the page. "Look. The light is green, it glows at the end of Daisy Buchanan's dock, and it's across the water from Gatsby's house. This book came out in 1925, Marcus. Ninety-nine years before us, Fitzgerald put that light there on purpose. It has to mean something. That's how you find a theme. You find the thing the writer keeps showing you."

"So the theme is... lights?"

"Shush. I'm testing something." She had a theory: if a detail showed up at the very beginning, the writer was planting it, the way you'd plant a flag. Her test was simple. Find the light on page one, find it again later, and see what the character wanted when he reached for it. Wanting was the key to theme. She wrote in the margin, "He wants what he can't reach?"

"Wanting what you can't have," Marcus read over her shoulder. "That's the theme of my whole life. I wanted pizza today. I got fish sticks."

"You are not the novel, Marcus."

At fifth period, Priya leaned across the table, buoyant with confidence, practically floating. "Theme is that you can't repeat the past," she announced, and read her quotation.

Emily stood. She felt like she was intervening in history itself. "The theme is wanting something just out of reach." She opened to the first chapter and read the line about Gatsby stretching out his arms toward the green light at the end of Daisy's dock, across the water from his house.

"Both," said Mr. Ruiz finally, "are true themes."

Both girls carried their own trays. On the bus home, Marcus passed her a folded note.

Emily, it read. Next book, I'm challenging Priya myself. Teach me your light trick. Fish sticks for life, Marcus.

She wrote underneath, Deal. Bring snacks.

The pizza place on Fifth Street had a screen as wide as the whole back wall, and tonight it showed the World Cup qualifier while everybody waited for their food. Camille's uncle Rafael leaned across the table toward her grandfather. "First World Cup, Brazil took it. Everyone knows that."

"Uruguay," Grandpa said. He had been a train conductor for thirty years, and he still spoke like he was announcing a departure. "Uruguay won the first one."

"Argentina, then," said Camille's cousin Mateo, because he had an Argentina jersey and he wanted Argentina to have won everything. "If Uruguay was even in it." Camille noticed that Mateo's argument changed shape whenever it needed to. Brazil, then Argentina, then whoever, as long as it kept the argument going until everyone gave up. That was the pattern, and she wanted to catch it in the open.

By the door stood the old trivia machine, the kind that ate quarters. Camille had watched a man at the counter win a free milkshake on it an hour ago, so she knew it worked and she knew it asked sports questions. If the machine was right, it could settle the table. She dug two quarters out of her jacket, slid them into the slot, and chose the sports category. The machine offered a wall mural that portrayed a 1930s stadium, old leather ball and all, above the words HISTORY OF FOOTBALL, so she picked that one.

The question came up: who won the first FIFA World Cup, held in Uruguay in 1930? The four answers glowed. She pressed Uruguay, and the screen answered in green, then added the detail: Uruguay beat Argentina 4 to 2 in the final. Four goals to two, which Mateo would notice was the equivalent of a two-goal lead the whole second half. She carried the machine's printed ticket back to the table and set it next to his plate.

"Uruguay," she said. "Nineteen thirty. Four to two over Argentina in the final."

Mateo picked up the ticket, read it twice, and put it face down. "Okay," he said, "but who's paying for dessert now?"

Sophia heard the words "snow day" from the hallway and was out of bed before her alarm finished ringing. By nine she was dragging her red sled up Miller's Hill, where her friend Marcus was already stomping a path along the ridge. He pointed at a long sled with runners he'd borrowed from his cousin. "I'm breaking the hill record today," he said. "Cousin Tyler did the whole slope in twelve seconds. I timed him."

"First you have to help me with something," Sophia said. She had noticed it the day before, when she'd dug into the drift at the bottom of the hill. The deeper she'd gone, the less cold it felt. Today she wanted to test it properly, like the experiments they did in science, except this one was hers. They scooped and packed snow until they had a fort with walls as thick as Sophia was tall, and she hung a thermometer from a stick inside it. Then she tucked a second thermometer into a bush out in the open wind.

While they waited, Marcus scrutinized the snow around the fort, crouched low, frowning. "Look at this," he said. A thin, winding groove ran along the surface of the drift and vanished into it, like a tiny tunnel with a roof of snow. "Something's living under here." They followed the groove, careful not to cave it in, and Sophia remembered something from a winter documentary she'd watched in October, about how fresh snow is mostly trapped air, which makes it a good insulator, and how some small animals survive the whole winter in tunnels under the snow. "That's probably a vole," she said. "The snow is like a blanket over its hallways." Marcus said his grandfather had once shown them a moth larva curled under tree bark in January, and Sophia said that was the same idea: small things hiding in warm pockets while everything above them froze.

They ran back to check the thermometers, and Sophia could hardly keep still while she read them. Inside the fort it was several degrees warmer than out in the wind, and neither of them had done anything but pile up snow. "It works," she said. "It actually works." Then came the twist. From inside the grooved drift came a scrabbling sound, and a gray shape burst out of a hole near their feet, agile as a dart, streaking across the snow and diving into the next drift over. A vole, fat and quick, using its tunnels like a secret highway.

Marcus stood with his sled in both hands, watching the hole. "The snow fort is basically a giant vole tunnel," he said. "That's the best thing I've ever heard." He set the sled at the top of the hill and pointed down the slope. "Twelve seconds. Count them out loud." Sophia planted her boots at the bottom, cupped her hands around her mouth, and shouted, "Three, two, one, go!"

Savannah stood at the edge of the community theatre stage, script rolled in her fist, and tried again. "And I never went back," she said, pausing the way she had practiced. Mr. Okafor had given her the monologue on Monday: learn it, then make the pauses and gestures show what the character felt. But every time she performed it, her hands just hung there like coat hangers.

Before her rehearsal slot, the younger group did improv warm-ups, and today Mr. Okafor paired Savannah with a small boy named Dex. Dex crouched, cast an invisible line across the stage, and reeled it in slowly, gritting his teeth. Savannah, still reciting lines inside her head, walked past him and announced, "Excuse me, I'm late for school." Dex reeled in silence. The scene sat there, dead, until Mr. Okafor called time. On the bus home, Savannah kept replaying it. Dex had shown her a fishing rod, a whole lake maybe, and she had talked about homework as if he were furniture. She tested a guess the next morning with her brother: he mimed stirring a pot, and when she said, "That soup smells burned," the scene jumped alive. When she ignored it and talked about the weather, it died again. There was a rule hiding in there, and she was starting to see its shape.

At Thursday's warm-up she got Dex again. He picked up an invisible fishing rod at once, clearly testing her. This time she sat beside him on an invisible dock. "Any luck? Grandpa says this lake hasn't given up a fish since the flood." Dex grinned so hard his ears moved. "You took my offer!" he said. "That's what my sister calls it. An offer is anything a performer says or does that gives information about the scene, like a place, a name or a problem." They fished for two full minutes, arguing about whether the flood had been real, and Mr. Okafor wrote something on his clipboard.

Savannah went home and read her monologue differently. The playwright had made offers too. "And I never went back" gave information: a place she was leaving, a problem she couldn't face. Her old plan, standing still with hanging hands, would ignore all of it, so she decided to abandon that plan entirely. On each line she found the hidden offer and answered it with her body. When the character said a name, Savannah's eyes would find someone in the empty seats. When the line hinted at the problem, she would turn half away, letting one hand rise and stop midair, ambiguous between reaching for someone and pushing them off.

Saturday, on the real stage with the lights up, she tried it. The pause before "and I never went back" felt like a canyon, and she let her hand fall slowly, as if setting down something heavy she had carried the whole play. Afterward Mr. Okafor didn't say much, only "Better," but Dex was waiting in the wings with his fishing rod.

"You took every offer," he said. "Even the invisible ones."

The farm stand smelled of warm dirt and crushed leaves, and Emilie wiped strawberry juice off the counter for the third time that hour. Mr. Ruiz paid her five dollars a morning to stack baskets, make change, and answer questions, but today her math homework sat folded in her back pocket like a stone. She was supposed to draw two lines that crossed like an X and write about why strawberries cost two dollars a basket in June and six dollars in January. The lines themselves she could copy from the book, but she could not figure out who had first dreamed them up, and that question itched at her all morning.

A woman came by near noon, a recent refugee from Syria who had started coming every week with her two small sons. She counted coins carefully, and Emilie noticed she always bought more strawberries in summer, sometimes three baskets, and in winter she walked past them. "In winter they cost too much," the woman said simply, and Emilie felt something click, like a key finding its lock. More berries in summer made the price sink; fewer in winter made it climb. The X shape in her homework was just that idea, drawn.

During her break she asked Mr. Ruiz if she could borrow the shop's old laptop, its porous speaker crackling as it hummed to life. She typed "who made the supply and demand curves famous" and chewed her thumbnail while the page loaded. There it was. A British economist named Alfred Marshall had made the two crossing curves famous in his 1890 book, Principles of Economics. She read the name twice, then copied it onto her homework sheet in careful letters.

"Find what you needed?" Mr. Ruiz asked when she handed back the laptop.

"Alfred Marshall," Emilie said, holding up her paper. "He made my homework famous first." Outside, the strawberry vines flourished in the July heat, heavy with fruit, and she went back to the counter to stack another row of two-dollar baskets.

Brielle stood in the wings of the music classroom, clutching her flute, and watched Marcus pace. He was two performers ahead of her, and his hands were shaking so hard that his sheet music rattled like a window in a storm.

"You okay?" she whispered.

"My voice is going to crack," Marcus said. He swallowed hard. "My mouth is so dry, and my heart is going like a million miles an hour." He held out one hand so she could see the tremble for herself.

Brielle had felt exactly the same thing at last month's audition, and it had nearly wrecked her. That afternoon she had gone home and scrutinized the notes she'd copied from a science magazine in the library, reading every line twice. The article said stage fright is the body's fight-or-flight response. Adrenaline, it explained, can cause a racing heart, a dry mouth, a shaky voice, and trembling hands. So her body wasn't breaking. It was doing what any organism does when it senses danger, even danger as harmless as forty kids with folding chairs. The weird part, the part she'd wondered about for days, was that her body couldn't actually tell the difference between a bear and a concert.

So she had tested an idea. At the audition, right before her turn, she had taken slow breaths and told herself, out loud in a tiny whisper, "Nothing here is attacking me. This is just a room." Her heart had still pounded, but her hands had gone steady enough to play.

She turned to Marcus now. "Try this," she said, and handed him her water bottle. "Sip. Then breathe with me, slow. And tell your body it's fight-or-flight stuff, that's all it is."

Marcus looked hesitant, but he sipped, and then they breathed together behind the curtain, in through the nose, out through the mouth, four slow times. Ms. Reyes called his name. He walked out, and Brielle watched his shoulders drop as he set his music on the stand.

His first note came out wobbly. His second one didn't. By the chorus he was singing full and clear, and when he finished, he grinned straight at the wings.

Then Ms. Reyes said, "Brielle, you're up."

Brielle walked to the front, lifted her flute, and whispered, "Just a room."

The group chat was called "Mud Dogs Rule," and it had been quiet all week until Tuesday night, when Marisol posted a screenshot of two baseball players with a single question: "Who's better?"

Harper sat cross-legged on her bed with her tablet balanced on one knee. She tapped into the stats page and started comparing. The first player was David Justice, the second was Derek Jeter. For 1995, Justice had the higher batting average. She checked twice, because Marisol's older brother had once told her that websites make mistakes. For 1996, Justice had the higher average again. Two years, two wins. She typed, "Justice. Easy," and dropped the tablet beside her.

A minute later Marisol sent a laughing emoji and then a link. "Look at the combined number for both years together." Harper picked the tablet back up. She found the row, read it, and read it again. For the two years combined, Jeter's average was the higher one. She stared at the screen while her ceiling fan ticked around and around above her.

"That's bizarre," she typed slowly. "Justice beats him both years and loses when you add the years up?" Marisol replied that her brother called it Simpson's paradox, and that it had a name because it happened in more places than baseball. Harper decided to test it herself. She pulled up her own basketball free throws from the rec league app, where she kept every practice logged. She sorted the sessions into two groups, took the percentages for each group, then the percentage for all of them together, and worked the numbers with a pencil on the back of her homework. Her percentages moved the same way when she combined groups, which meant the thing on the baseball site wasn't a typo. It was something numbers could just do.

She scrolled up through the chat and noticed something else. Dex, who never missed a chance to argue, hadn't posted at all. She sent him a private message: "You're quiet. You already knew about this, didn't you?"

His reply came as a long text. "OK yes. I found it last summer and I was going to use it to win an argument with you about whether our Mud Dogs season was really as bad as the league standings said. Our average runs per game over the whole season look fine, but that's because of two blowout games. I didn't want to say that out loud because everyone would say I was making excuses." Harper read it twice. She thought about the standings pinned to the gym door, one number standing for all those afternoons, and about how the team's snacks had started to deteriorate into just Dex bringing squashed granola bars, as if morale were a kind of food going stale.

She typed back, "Bring better granola tomorrow and I'll tell the chat the paradox myself." Then she pasted the link into the group chat with the message: "Justice had the higher average in 1995 and in 1996. Jeter had the higher average for the two years combined. Numbers can do that."

Dex answered in four seconds: "Treaty accepted. The granola will be fresh."

Matthew slouched at his table in room 12, staring at the photocopied page where Mr. Ruiz had typed the same question three times: What is the theme of the novel? Support your answer with a quotation. Last week Matthew had written "the theme is friendship" and gotten it back with a red circle around nothing, which felt worse than a circle around something wrong. At least a mistake could be diagnosed. This was just empty.

"You have to use the actual text," said Priya, leaning over. "Like, copy a line and connect it."

"I know that," Matthew said, though he did not. Their class novel was an old retelling of Romeo and Juliet, and half of it sounded like a foreign language. He flipped to his marked page and read aloud in a whisper: "'She hath not seen the change of fourteen years.'"

Priya squinted. "She hath not seen the change of fourteen years. What's hath?"

"Beats me. Maybe it's 'hates'?" He tried it. "She hates not seen the change of fourteen years." That collapsed instantly, like a tent with one pole missing. He read further and found "he doth keep the peace" and "what doth it profit a man." Doth kept showing up where a verb belonged. He tested a pattern, the way he tested cheat codes: swap doth for does. "He does keep the peace." That worked. He looked back at hath. If doth meant does, maybe hath meant has. "She has not seen the change of fourteen years." The whole sentence snapped into place.

"That's it," Priya said, writing it down. "So hath means has. That's, like, their word for it."

Matthew's hand shot up before he could talk himself out of it. When Mr. Ruiz called on him, he stood, ears hot, and read the quotation in both versions, the old words and the plain modern English underneath. "The theme is that kids grow up faster than the grown-ups want them to. She hasn't even turned fourteen yet, and the whole story is already happening to her."

Mr. Ruiz didn't smile, but he underlined something on his clipboard, and Priya kicked Matthew's chair leg under the table, twice, which was her way of cheering.

That night Matthew found his father's old copy of Shakespeare on the shelf at home, its cover soft from years of hands. He hadn't known why he'd avoided it before, and he didn't entirely know why he was opening it now, except that last week he'd looked at a page like this and seen a locked door, and today someone had handed him a key. The house smelled like burnt toast from the kitchen, and from downstairs his father called, "You reading that thing?"

"Yeah," Matthew said. "He doth write pretty good."

His father's laugh came through the floorboards.

Grandma had been at the house since Monday, and by Wednesday Laurence had given up saying whole sentences to her at the park. She would shout across the picnic table by the duck pond, loud enough that a man walking his dog turned to look, and Grandma would still tilt her head and say, "What's that, dear? Speak up." Laurence couldn't understand it, because Grandma heard the ice cream truck's jingle from three blocks away, and she caught every word the deep-voiced park ranger said when he warned everyone about the geese. It was only Laurence's own voice that vanished.

Sitting on the bench, Laurence turned the puzzle over. Grandma had said her hearing was "mostly there, just blurry." Blurry sound. She thought about how the pond's shallow edge bent the light so the stones looked displaced, the way a straw in a glass seemed to refract into two pieces. Maybe sound could get blurry too, and maybe not all sound the same way. The ranger's low voice had come through fine. The ice cream truck, the wind in the reeds, the men playing chess, all low, all clear. Her own voice, and the shrieking little kids near the swings, all high, all lost. She felt a flicker of skepticism about her own idea, because it seemed too simple, but simple was worth testing.

She slid closer to Grandma and dropped her voice into the low register she used for reading the villain's part in class plays. "Grandma. The ducks stole my sandwich." She kept it quiet, quieter than a normal sentence, almost a mumble.

Grandma laughed out loud. "Both of them? Those fundamental criminals of the pond, always after the bread."

"You heard me?" Laurence said, still low. "I barely said it out loud."

"Loud enough, dear. It just wasn't all fuzzy." Grandma shook her head. "The doctor told me years ago, high-pitched sounds go first. I thought he meant bells and whistles. I didn't know my own granddaughter would count."

For the rest of the week, Laurence practiced her low voice until it felt like a coat she could put on. On Friday at the park, she leaned toward Grandma and rumbled, "The ice cream man is coming. My treat."

Grandma was already holding out her hand for coins.

Sawyer refreshed the marketplace page for the third time that morning, and the Frost Dragon egg was still priced at four thousand gold. Last month it had been two thousand. He slumped in his chair, staring at the listing while his snow fox, Pip, curled up in the corner of the screen and began to hibernate, the way the game's pets always did when their owner ignored them too long.

Four thousand gold was impossible. He had been saving for weeks, selling bread from his bakery stall, because bread was a carbohydrate that every player's energy bar needed and it always sold. But at this rate, the dragon egg would stay out of reach forever. He scrolled through the listings and counted them. Only three eggs for sale in the whole market. Three weeks ago, when the price was two thousand, there had been nine.

He sat back. Fewer eggs, higher price. More bread, lower price, because bread was everywhere. Something invisible was pushing the numbers, like a hidden hand. He wanted to see if he was right, so he opened a notebook and started a chart: item, number of listings, price. Then his dad called from the hallway that they were driving to the hardware store.

At the gas station, while Dad filled the tank, a kid about Sawyer's age pointed at the sign. "Why did it go up since last week? It was cheaper." The station attendant, wiping his hands on a rag, shrugged. "Crude oil. The cost of crude oil is usually the biggest single part of the price of a gallon of gasoline, so when crude oil goes up, the pump price goes up too." The kid's dad nodded like this was ordinary news, and Sawyer stood there with his hand on the door of the car, thinking. A price could move because of something far away that you never saw. Crude oil for gasoline. Scarcity for dragon eggs. Maybe the same rule, wearing different clothes.

Back home, he tested his idea. He spent his gold on a cheap fertile soil seed instead of the egg, planted it in his garden plot, and waited three days while more players hatched dragon events. By Saturday, the marketplace showed eleven Frost Dragon eggs, and the price had slid to one thousand eight hundred. Sawyer bought one. In his notebook, under the chart, he wrote "scarce = up, plentiful = down" and drew an arrow. Then he set the egg beside the sleeping Pip, tapped it once, and whispered, "Okay, buddy, wake up. You're about to have company."

On her third day at Millbrook Middle School, Scarlett got a seat by the window and a lab partner named Dee who kept a bag of gummy worms in her pencil case. "Emergency rations," Dee said solemnly. "Science is hungry work." Scarlett laughed for the first time in a week. After school she walked home to the new house, where the moving boxes still leaned against the walls like tired visitors.

Her mother had told her something at dinner, almost in passing. "I filed the permanent change of address with the Postal Service, so our First-Class Mail gets forwarded to this house for twelve months." Scarlett had chewed on that all evening. If mail could find her here, then Zoe's letters could too. But Zoe hadn't written yet, and Scarlett had no way to know whether the system actually worked or whether her letters would vanish somewhere between Ohio and here. She had a premise: if forwarding was real, a letter sent to the old address should come back to this one. All she needed was a test.

She wrote a note to herself, sealed it in an envelope, and addressed it to the old house in Dayton. "Dear Scarlett," it began, "if you are reading this, the mail is smarter than you thought." At the post office she asked the clerk to confirm it was First-Class Mail, because that mattered, and the clerk nodded and stamped it. Every afternoon for a week she checked the mailbox, finding only a pizza menu and something for her mother. "Be resilient," Dee told her at school. "Also, gummy worm? It helps."

On the ninth day the envelope appeared in the new mailbox, slightly bent, her own handwriting staring up at her. Scarlett whooped so loudly a neighbor's dog barked. That night she wrote Zoe a real letter, explaining the twelve months, telling her to write to the old address, and adding, "P.S. My new friend thinks mail is food for scientists. She is mostly wrong." She sealed it, and in the morning she ran the whole way to the post office, envelope flapping.

Jace had planted his tomato, pepper and squash seedlings on the first warm Saturday of April, certain that warm meant safe. "You're my tenants now," he told the little green rows, patting the soil around them, "and I'm the landlord who waters you." For two weeks they grew, and he thought the hard part was over.

Then the radio said thirty-four degrees tomorrow night, and Jace stood in the backyard frowning at the sky. Warm days had fooled him. He tried to remember what his grandfather had said last summer while picking peppers: "Can't put these out till after the last spring frost. Freezing kills them." Frost. That was the hidden thing, the cold that came at night when nobody was watching.

He wasn't sure the cold would really reach his plants, so he tested it. He covered every bed with old sheets and buckets, except one squash seedling that he left open on purpose, the far corner of the yard away from the house wall. If that one drooped by morning, he would know for certain it was the cold and not something else, like the neighbor's cat or too much water.

Morning came gray and glittering. Under the sheets the tomatoes stood stiff and fine, leaves untouched. The uncovered squash lay flat, its edges blackened and thin as wet paper. Jace knelt beside it, sorry he had needed proof at all. "That wasn't trivial," he said quietly. "That was your whole life." He decided to revise his plan completely: no more planting until frost season was truly over, and he would keep a journal by the window to track each cold snap.

He buried the squash by the fence, then heard the back gate. His little sister Mira stood holding her blanket. "Is it safe now?" she asked. Jace draped his biggest sheet over the pepper bed one more time and nodded. "Safe," he said. "Come on, let's count buds."

The bell on the door of Delgado's Corner Store jangled, and Quinn went straight to the pizza counter, where her workbook already sat open next to the napkin dispenser. She had one hour before her mom picked her up, and one week before the retest, and the grade she needed to get into the spring math team. Mr. Delgado had let her study at the counter all winter as long as she bought something, so she slid two quarters across the glass and asked for a slice.

"Cutting fresh ones today," he said, pulling a whole pie from the oven. "Big slices, quarters." He scored the pizza into four and set one piece on a plate for her.

Her best friend Priya pushed through the door with snow on her hood and dropped her backpack on a stool. "Okay, quiz me," Priya said, because that was the deal: Priya helped with the equations, and Quinn shared the pizza. Quinn turned the workbook around.
