The problem was y equals two x plus four, and the instructions said to pick three values for x, solve, and plot the line. Priya was meticulous about graphs; she sharpened her pencil until the point looked dangerous, then drew the grid on a napkin.

Quinn tried x equals three. "Two times three is six, plus four is ten," she said, and marked the point. She tried x equals zero and got four, and marked that too. But when she reached x equals one half, she stopped. "Two times one half, plus four," she said slowly. "I don't like halves in my work."

Priya picked up Quinn's uneaten crust and a fresh slice Mr. Delgado had just cut when a family ordered their pie in twelfths instead of quarters. "Watch," Priya said, laying her small slice on top of Quinn's big quarter. Then she added two more small slices beside it. Three of the thin pieces covered exactly the same space as the one thick piece. Quinn grabbed a twelfth slice and laid it along the edge of her quarter to check, then another, then a third. They matched. No gap, no overhang.

"One quarter equals three twelfths," Quinn said. "So I can make my one half into six twelfths, and my equation looks normal." She wrote it out, doubled the six twelfths to twelve twelfths, added four, and got five and one twelfth. She plotted it between four and six, and the three points fell onto a straight line that climbed across the napkin like a ramp. Priya leaned over and tapped the line. "You just made a picture that depicts every single answer at once," she said.

Quinn felt a flicker of guilt about the crust she had abandoned, so she ate it, then copied the napkin graph into her workbook in careful blue ink. Mr. Delgado leaned on the counter and squinted at it. "Straight, huh?" he said. "My whole display shelf works like that. Every can two inches above the last." Quinn grinned, packed her pencil, and pointed at the twelfths pie. "Three of those for one of these," she said. "Deal?"

Lydia sat in the emergency room with her left wrist propped on a pillow, remembering the last time she had sat in this exact chair, two summers ago, holding the exact same wrist. Back then the doctor had called it an acute fracture, which meant it was a fresh break, and she had worn a cast for six weeks. She remembered the day they took it off.

"It looks wrong," she had said, staring at her left arm next to her right one. The left arm was skinny and pale, like it belonged to a younger kid. "Why is it so much smaller?"

Her older brother Theo had leaned in, squinting. "Muscles in a limb kept still in a cast weaken and shrink," he said. "That's why an arm often looks thinner when the cast comes off." He had read it somewhere, and Lydia had tested it right there in the exam room, squeezing a tennis ball with each hand. The right hand bounced the ball hard off the wall. The left hand barely held on.

Now, waiting for the X-ray results, Lydia ran her thumb along her right forearm, which was currently her good arm but would soon be her only arm. "Hey, Theo," she said. He looked up from the magazine he was pretending to read so she wouldn't be scared. "I'm going to simulate the next six weeks. Every day, I'll make my left hand do things on purpose. Open doors. Carry my backpack. Brush my teeth." She pointed at the arm that had stayed strong because it never got a turn being lazy. "Last time was an anomaly. This time I'll be ready before the cast even comes off."

The doctor came back with the X-ray and said what Lydia already guessed: broken, cast, six weeks. Theo helped her write LEFT ARM: WANTED FOR HARD LABOR on the plaster before the ink could smear.

"So," Lydia said, wiggling the fingers that stuck out of the cast, "who's bringing me the tennis ball?"

Victor wanted his grandmother's annual art contest entry to be perfect, mostly because his cousin Priya had won it two years running. At the kitchen table in his grandparents' house, he kept drawing the same beach ball and it kept looking flat, like a sticker of a ball instead of a ball. His grandmother nurtureed his habit of trying again, sliding him a fresh peach and saying that she couldn't help him herself, since she had an allergy to pencils, which was her joke for arthritis. Grandpa, reading in the corner, looked over the top of his glasses and said one thing: "Artists call that line the terminator."

"Like the robot?" Victor said, but Grandpa only shrugged and went back to his book. Terminator. Robots didn't seem to have anything to do with a peach.

Then Victor carried the peach to the window, where the morning sun hit it sideways, and turned it slowly in his fingers. There was a line, curving around the fruit, where the bright gold stopped and the dusky side began. It wasn't a drawn line. Nothing marked it. It was simply the edge where the light stopped reaching, and on the table below, the peach threw a second, darker pool of shadow that stretched away from the sun. He fetched the desk lamp and angled it high, then low, watching the line slide and the cast shadow shorten and stretch like something alive. What if his ball looked flat because he had skipped that line entirely, shading everything softly the same way?

Back at the table, he sharpened his pencil to an acute point and drew the beach ball again, this time finding the terminator first, laying a definite shadow on the far side and a crisp cast shadow beneath it, then gently blending toward a bright spot where the lamp would have been. Grandpa wandered over, peach in hand, and studied the page. "Huh," he said. "Priya's going to hate this." Victor turned the drawing toward the window to check it in better light.

Eli stood at the shallow end of the community pool with his goggles fogged and his heart going like a drum. Twenty-five metres, front crawl, side breathing, without stopping. That was the goal. The lane rope stretched away from him, and at the far end his sister Maya sat on the blocks, swinging her legs.

"Stop drowning your face," Maya called. "Rotate, don't lift."

Eli tried again. Three strokes, then he craned his head up like a turtle, swallowed a mouthful of pool water, and stood up coughing. The water tasted like it came from somewhere corrosive, sharp enough to strip paint, though he knew it was just chlorine doing its job on every microbe in the pool. The big kids in the deep end orbited past each other in lazy loops, surfacing and diving, and he wanted that to be him.

"You're counting your hurdles wrong," Maya said when he reached the wall, breathless.

"Hurdles?"

"Track camp. I kept hitting every hurdle on the wrong foot." She held up three fingers. "Coach had us count strides. With three strides between hurdles, a hurdler takes off from the same foot every time, because an odd number of steps keeps the same leg leading." She shrugged. "I fixed my steps and stopped crashing."

Eli hung on the rope, thinking. He couldn't see his own arms while he swam, couldn't watch himself the way he could watch a runner. But he could count. If he breathed after every third stroke, then the same side would come around every time, like the same leg leading off the same hurdle. Even numbers, and his breathing side would keep switching. He couldn't see the pattern underwater, but he could hear it, one-two-three, turn.

He pushed off. One, two, three, roll to the right and breathe. One, two, three, right again. The water slid past his ears and his arm reached for the far wall. At the flags, ten strokes to go, he lost the count somewhere, panicked, lifted his turtle head, and grabbed the rope halfway. Maya didn't laugh. She crouched at the edge and held out her water bottle.

"You had it for fifteen metres," she said. "That's the farthest yet."

He drank, spat, and reset his goggles. Then he pushed off again. One, two, three, breathe. One, two, three. The wall came up under his hand, and he heard Maya's feet hit the deck above him.

"Twenty-five!" she shouted down. "All of it!"

Zoe's grandmother had claimed the long stone ledge by the duck pond for her diyas, and she had brought forty of them, packed in a dented biscuit tin. The park was filling up with families for the Diwali celebration, and Zoe's job, assigned the moment they arrived, was to line the little clay lamps along the ledge before dark.

The problem appeared immediately. Her little brother Rohan, who Zoe had privately classified as a one-boy wrecking crew, kept walking the ledge like a balance beam, kicking diyas into the grass. She'd lined up twelve. Now there were nine standing and three in the pond, where a duck was inspecting one with genuine scientific interest.

Zoe crouched and thought. She couldn't watch Rohan and arrange lamps at the same time, and Mom was busy unfolding chairs near the pavilion. So she tested an idea. She moved the diyas from the top of the ledge to the ground beside it, leaving the flat surface empty. When Rohan came sprinting back for his next tightrope walk, he found a bare ledge, lost interest in about four seconds, and ran off toward the playground. It worked. The rule she'd guessed at, that her brother wanted the height and not the lamps, turned out to be true. It felt almost like a paradox: fewer diyas in the obvious place meant more diyas safe.

She was setting them back on the ledge when her grandmother returned with a box of matches and a thermos of chai. "Good, good," Grandma said, patting the row of small oil lamps. "Diyas, all ready for the five days of Diwali. Mr. Patel from the temple called me eccentric for bringing so many, but I told him, better too much light than too little."

"That's not eccentric," Zoe said. "That's just planning."

Grandma laughed so hard she nearly dropped the matches, then struck one and touched the flame to the first wick.

Dominic stared at the blank page in his notebook and tapped his pencil until the eraser bounced. His assignment was a five-paragraph persuasive essay, due Monday, with an introduction, three body paragraphs, and a conclusion. He had decided to argue that the old movie theater downtown should be saved from being torn down. He knew exactly what he wanted to say. Outlines were for kids who didn't know their own minds, so he skipped that part and started writing his first full paragraph right away.

By Saturday he had two paragraphs finished, and both of them were about how the theater was old and beautiful. On Sunday his mother drove him to Grandma Ruth's house for dinner, notebook stuffed in his backpack, because he still had three paragraphs to go and no ideas left. While the roast was in the oven, he sat at the kitchen table and groaned. "It's all mush," he said. "I keep saying the same thing."

Grandma Ruth slid a stack of napkins across the table and uncapped a marker. "When I had to write reports at the bank, I'd list my main points first, and next to each one, the evidence for it," she said. "Before drafting a single full paragraph." She drew three lines on a napkin. "Try it. Called it my map."

Dominic humored her. He wrote: Point one, the theater is historic. Evidence: built in 1927, photo in the library. Point two, the neighborhood needs it. Evidence: nothing. His marker hovered. He turned the napkin over, checked the back, looked under it as if the evidence might be hiding on the table. "Grandma. I have a whole paragraph, the best one, and there's no proof for it at all." She shrugged and went to check the oven, and he sat there feeling like a detective who had just found the empty safe.

He tested it. Across the napkin he wrote a new point: the theater brings people downtown on weekends, and next to it, evidence: the line around the block at last month's classic film night, which he had seen himself. That point had legs. The other one had nothing. If he had kept drafting, he would have spent his whole Sunday polishing a paragraph that couldn't stand up.

That night he cut his beautiful paragraph and rebuilt the essay on the napkin points. On Monday, Ms. Alvarez returned the papers and held one up. "Dominic," she said, reading aloud, "every claim in this essay is backed by something real. And this line, 'Our neighborhood is not affluent, but the theater makes it feel rich,' is the best sentence in the class."

"You should see the napkin," Dominic said, and grinned.

Muhammad stood in the living room holding a candle like it was a prestigious trophy, even though it was just dripping wax on a saucer. The power had cut out an hour ago, and his big sister Zainab was stretched on the couch reading by her phone light. Muhammad's stomach growled so loudly that they both heard it.

"Snack time," he announced, and marched to the refrigerator. He opened the door, stared into the dark cold shelves, saw nothing he wanted, and shut it. Two minutes later he opened it again. And again. On the fourth try, Zainab appeared beside him holding her candle.

"Muhammad, stop. The fridge only keeps food safely cold for about four hours in a power cut, if the door stays closed. Every time you open it, you're spending that time." Muhammad blinked at her, then at the fridge, doing the math in his head. He had opened it five times. "So we decide first, then open it once?" he said slowly. "Exactly once," Zainab said. "Like a game show. One pick, no changing your answer."

Muhammad felt his conscience poke him about all those openings, so he made it right. He sat by the candle and wrote a note by hand, which felt hilariously old-fashioned: "Dear Fridge, I have chosen the leftover biryani and one mango juice. I will not peek. Signed, Muhammad." Zainab read it over his shoulder and laughed so hard she nearly snorted out the candle flame. They folded the letter, tucked it under the fridge magnet for proof, and retired to the couch to wait out the dark like brave explorers.

When the clock showed the hour they'd agreed on, Muhammad leapt up, announced "One pick!", flung the door open, grabbed the biryani container and juice in a single sweep, and shut the door with a triumphant bang. "Nailed it," he said, raising the juice like a trophy. Zainab handed him a fork. "Game show champion," she said. "Now eat before the candle retires."

Brielle sat at Grandma's kitchen table with three sharpened pencils and a blank page. Her assignment was due Monday: a five-paragraph persuasive essay, with an introduction, three reasons, and a conclusion. She had chosen the best topic in the world, more recess time at school, and she knew her strongest reason already. She wrote it at the top of a planning page. "Everyone at school wants it."

"Grandpa, what are you doing?" she asked, because he was pulling a dusty blue book off the shelf in the den.

"Looking for my old arguing book," he said. "You said you were writing to persuade. There's a chapter in here about reasons that sound strong but aren't." He set the book beside her paper and went back to his crossword.

Brielle frowned at her planning page. Everyone at school wants it. That did sound strong. Two hundred kids, maybe more, all wanting the same thing. She flipped through the book until she found a page marked with a paper clip. There was a picture of a wagon crowded with people, and underneath it, a name. She read the page twice, then carried the book to Grandpa. "So it's called the bandwagon fallacy?"

"That's the one," Grandpa said, and filled in another crossword square.

Brielle went back to the table and thought it through. The bandwagon fallacy meant believing something must be right or good just because many people believed it or did it. She tested her own reason against it, like checking a math answer backward. Lots of people believing recess should be longer did not make recess longer a good idea. It just meant lots of people agreed. She crossed out her best reason with one hard pencil stroke, then sat staring at what was left.

She tried an experiment on Grandma, who was rolling dough at the counter. "Grandma, everybody in my class says spinach tastes like wet paper. So spinach must taste like wet paper, right?"

Grandma sprinkled flour without looking up. "Half this family descends from farmers who ate spinach every day, and your cousin thrives on the stuff. Millions of people love it. Does that prove it's good?"

"No," Brielle said slowly. "It just proves millions of people love it." She grinned and ran back to the table. She wrote a new first reason: longer recess helps kids focus afterward, and she would find real proof, not just voices. She wrote a second reason about exercise. For the third, she nearly wrote that even the teachers wanted it, caught herself, and laughed out loud at how sneaky the fallacy was, hiding in her pencil like that.

By evening she had a full draft, five paragraphs with a real introduction and a conclusion that did more than repeat everything. She read the essay aloud in the den, standing on the hearth like a lawyer. When she finished, Grandpa set down his crossword and applauded with just his knuckles against the armrest, which was his loudest kind of clapping. "Motion carries," he said. "Recess is now mandatory."

Dominic sat cross-legged on his grandmother's porch, trying to keep his mind on his breath while the smell of frying onions drifted through the screen door. Today was his first time keeping a day of practice with her, no phone, no meat, no running around, just sitting and a short walk to the little shrine in her garden. It was only until sundown, but it already felt like a week.

In his pocket was a folded note his friend Ravi had slipped to him at school, because Ravi's mother said phones were a bad lens for serious questions. "Ask your grandma this," the note read. "We believe the soul gets reborn, the same soul in a new body. Do Buddhists believe that too? I need a good answer by Friday or my cousin will humiliate me at the family dinner again. He thinks I don't know anything about other religions."

Dominic had assumed the answer was yes. Rebirth was rebirth, wasn't it? He watched his grandmother place an orange on the shrine, and he tested his idea out loud. "So when someone is reborn, the soul moves to the next life, right? Like Ravi's family says?"

His grandmother shook her head without turning around. "We call it anatta, no-self," she said. "There is no permanent soul to move."

Dominic frowned. "Then what gets reborn?"

She held up the candle she was lighting, then touched its flame to a second candle beside it. "What continues is karma, passing along like this. Not the same unchanging self."

Dominic stared at the two flames burning side by side, one passed on and one receiving, neither one the same thing exactly. He thought about how he had answered Ravi last month, confidently wrong, saying all religions believed the same thing about souls. He hadn't even asked. Now he pulled out Ravi's note and began writing on the back, feeling the porch boards warm under his knees.

"Got the answer," he wrote. "But ask your cousin what he thinks moves from candle to candle."

Maya woke to a strange brightness and found the window filled with white. School was closed, the radio said, and her little brother Theo came bouncing into her room in his dinosaur pajamas before she could even find her socks.

The backyard had turned into a flat white plateau, level and smooth, except where the picnic table poked through like a buried boat. Theo wanted to build a snowman right away, but Maya stopped at the porch steps and pulled on her dark wool mitten. Last week she had read one sentence in a library book, and now she wanted to check whether it was true. "Watch," she said. "I'm going to catch them."

She held her mitten out flat and let the snowfall settle on it. The first flakes melted almost instantly, but when she turned her hand toward the shaded side of the porch, where the air was colder, they held their shape. She bent close. Six arms. She brushed them off and caught more. Six arms again, arranged like tiny stars. Theo leaned over her shoulder, breathing fog onto her wrist, until she made him wait on the steps. "You're melting them," she said.

They caught eleven flakes in all, and Maya counted every one. A lacy one had six branching arms. A stubby one, barely bigger than a crumb, still had six. One looked like a tiny plate with six notched edges. "They're all six," Theo said. "Why?" Maya thought about the book's one sentence, which she now believed completely. "Water links up six-sided when it freezes," she said. "So the flakes come out with six sides. Six arms. Every single time." She looked up at the millions of flakes still falling, each one of them six-sided, and felt like she had a secret about the whole sky.

Later they built the snowman on the white plateau of the yard, and Theo insisted on giving it a red scarf because, he said, red was Dad's favorite color and would symbolize him being home early on snow days. When they went inside, their mugs of cocoa were waiting, and Mom warned them not to sniff the bottle of glass cleaner she was using on the window, because it was toxic. Maya drank her cocoa slowly. Before the flakes on her mitten vanished, she had scooped one last big lacy one onto a black notebook cover and carried it to the freezer, where it waited, six perfect arms intact, on the shelf next to the peas. "I'll show Ms. Alvarez on Monday," she said, and closed the freezer door.

The Farmers Market closed at noon, and it was already 11:20, so Ethan jogged up the bank steps two at a time. Gray lichen crusted the stone balustrade, and it crunched faintly under his fingers when he grabbed it for balance. His mother was already inside, waiting in line with the coin jar from his room, three months of quarters he had counted the night before.

Ethan had his own errand. In March, when his grandmother had visited, they had bought a basket of strawberries for five dollars, and he had carried it home like something precious. This morning, at the same grower's stand, the same basket had a card that said $2.50. He had stood there holding the card, then set it down and walked to the bank to get his money, because he had left his wallet at home. Now he had to get back before noon with enough quarters, and the line had seven people in it.

"It's fine," his mother said. "We have time. The closing isn't imminent until they lock that door." She pointed at the glass doors, where a teller was turning a small sign on a chain.

While they waited, Ethan laid it out on the back of a deposit slip. In March, five dollars. Now, half that. Same grower, same basket. He wrote: what changed? Not the basket. Not the grower's kindness. He remembered March again, the berries small and pale at the edges, flown in from somewhere far off because nothing ripened here yet. He looked out the window toward the market tents, where pickups were parked nose to tail, every bed stacked with flats of red.

"Next," the teller called. Ethan's mother dumped the quarters into the counting machine, and while it rattled, Ethan counted the window. Eight grower trucks. In March he had seen one.

At the market, with four minutes left, he handed over his quarters and asked the grower, "Did everybody's berries get ripe at the same time?"

"Early summer, they all come on at once around here," the grower said, sliding the basket across. "The whole local crop hits the stands together."

"So there's way more of them than in March," Ethan said. "And the price dropped to half." The grower nodded and started folding the tent flaps. Ethan tucked the basket against his chest and ran, eating the first berry before he even reached the corner.

Penelope spread the evidence across the kitchen table: a printed copy of Bylaw 47, a letter to Councillor Okafor, and two pencil stubs because one always vanished. Her assignment was to explain, in plain words, how a citizen could petition a councillor to change a local bylaw. The bylaw she had chosen was the one banning skateboards on the library plaza, which had ruined her summer before it even started.

"You can't conquer a bylaw with pencils," said her brother Milo, sliding into the other chair with his own agenda. Milo wanted to be the family's official envelope sealer, a job he had invented that morning and now defended like a knight. "Also I get to lick the envelope. That's my price."

"Sealing is not a skill," Penelope said, but she slid the envelope across anyway, because a petitioner needs allies, and Milo was the only one home. She picked up the bylaw and read aloud the part where it said the plaza was for "quiet enjoyment only." Her plan for the letter had three steps: state the bylaw, state the change she wanted, and collect twenty signatures, because Councillor Okafor's own website said petitions with twenty or more signatures got read at a council meeting. That part she understood. The confusing part was her teacher's extra challenge question about the mock parliament her class was running on Friday.

The mock parliament had three parties. Penelope's group, the Purple Party, had won eleven of thirty seats, and she had assumed that meant they were basically in charge. Her homework sheet asked who would form the government, and she had written "the Purples" with total confidence. But now she counted the seats again, tapping each tally mark with a pencil stub. Eleven, ten, nine. She counted the other direction too, in case counting backwards revealed something secret. It didn't.

"Milo," she said slowly, "what if nobody gets more than half?"

"Then you share," Milo said, and pressed his tongue along the envelope flap with enormous ceremony. "Like the last slice of pizza."

Penelope stared at him. Their election was proportional, so seats matched votes, and no single party had won more than half of either. She flipped her paper over and rewrote her answer: the Purples would have to join with another party and build a coalition. On Friday, that meant her group had to negotiate with the Orange Party, whose one demand was a motion to lower the thermostat in the gym because their leader, Devi, insisted the gym was "a sauna wearing a disguise." Penelope had agreed to that even though she liked the gym warm, because that was how coalitions worked: you gave something up.

The letter to Councillor Okafor went into Milo's expertly sealed envelope along with the signature page, all twenty names, including Milo's, which he had written with a flourish and a tiny drawing of an envelope. Penelope taped the whole packet to her backpack where she couldn't miss it.

"Delivery fee," Milo said, holding out his hand.

"One cookie," she countered.

"Two, and I carry the backpack to the mailbox."

Joseph had never walked so fast with a leash in his hand. Duke, the brown-and-white mutt from the shelter, trotted beside him with his ears up, and Joseph kept glancing down to make sure the dog was still there. "Two blocks to home," he told him, and Duke's tail swung like a piston pumping at top speed. A delivery truck rumbled past with its engine clattering, and Duke bolted, yanking the leash right out of Joseph's fingers.

Joseph tore after him, but the dog vanished behind the Hendersons' hedge and did not come out the other side. He ran his hands through the branches, ducked under, checked the drainage ditch. Nothing. He was about to presume the worst, that Duke was gone for good, when Mrs. Okafor called from her porch, "Your dog's in my garage! He knocked over my flowerpots and he's cowering behind the lawnmower." She added that he was harmless, not some venomous beast, though he was shaking like one.

Joseph knelt in the dim garage and coaxed Duke out with half the granola bar in his pocket. His hands were still trembling when Mrs. Okafor asked how the shelter would even know the dog was his. "That's the chip," Joseph said. "The microchip." He told her it was about the size of a grain of rice, and it held an ID number. A scanner read the number and pulled up the owner's contact details. That was how the shelter had found Duke's first family, and how, when they couldn't keep him, they had known to call Joseph's mom the moment a spot opened up.

Mrs. Okafor leaned close to Duke's shoulder. "A grain of rice? In there?" "Yep," Joseph said, clipping the leash back on, twice as tight this time. "They scanned him at the shelter and his whole file came up in minutes." He scratched Duke's ears and stood. "Come on, boy. Home's that way, and I'm not letting go again."

The camp bus smelled like granola bars and bug spray, and Carson had the window seat, which felt like winning something. Across the aisle, a boy named Dev held up his phone to illustrate the problem: a photo of his older cousin at Camp Windrow last summer, arms glowing an angry, luminous pink. "Put sunscreen on at seven in the morning," Dev said, "and by dinner he looked like a lobster. Explain that."

Carson leaned over the seat. He liked problems you couldn't see the answer to right away, the hidden kind. "Was he outside all day?"

"At the lake," Dev said. "From lunch till five. Swimming, mostly."

The bus rattled over a pothole, and Carson thought hard. Sunscreen went on once, but the sun kept going all afternoon. If the sunscreen washed off in the lake, or just wore off over hours, then one morning application couldn't last a whole day. That would explain the lobster photo without needing anything mysterious. "I think it's a schedule thing," Carson said. "You have to redo it. Like an algorithm. Apply, wait, apply again."

"How long is the wait?"

"That's the part I don't know," Carson admitted, which bothered him the whole rest of the ride. When they pulled into camp, a tall counselor with a whistle and a clipboard climbed aboard and announced that lake time started after lunch, cabins first. In the cabin, one boy named Marcus, who turned out to be that exact cousin from the photo, now a junior counselor himself, dug through his duffel and pulled out a battered tube of sunscreen. "Rule from the doctor," Marcus said, tossing it to the nearest bunk. "Reapply about every two hours outdoors, and right after swimming or heavy sweating. Learned that the hard way."

Carson felt the whole thing click into place like a puzzle snapping shut. Every two hours. Right after swimming. That was the missing line of the algorithm, and the lobster photo was the proof.

At the lake, Carson set a timer on Dev's phone and they swam until the whistle blew. When the buzzer went off, they clambered onto the dock, dripping, and slathered on another coat while the other campers stared. "What are you doing?" a girl asked.

"Following the two-hour rule," Carson said, holding out the tube. "Want in?"

The twist came at dinner. Dev's phone buzzed with a text from his mother, and his face fell. "It's my cousin. The other one. She's at a different camp." He turned the screen around: a photo of a girl, shoulders bright pink, holding up a sad thumbs-up. "She put it on this morning and forgot."

"Send her the rule," Carson said, already reaching for the phone. "Every two hours. Right after swimming. She can start tonight."

Dev typed it out, then looked up and grinned. "Camp doctor in training, huh?"

"Camp bus detective," Carson said, and hit send.

Avery discovered the problem before breakfast, when she went out to shovel the front steps in yesterday's snow pants. Dad had scattered rock salt across the porch on Tuesday, and the icy patches under it had not shrunk one bit. The salt just sat there, like glittery gravel doing absolutely nothing.

Weird, she thought. She checked the thermometer nailed by the door. It read minus 12 degrees Celsius, which her brother, Milo, said was about 10 degrees Fahrenheit, colder than the inside of a freezer. "Ha," Milo said from the doorway, still in pajamas. "Even the salt gave up and went back to bed."

"Salt doesn't have a bed," Avery said, but she was already drafting a plan. She scooped a spoonful of the leftover salt, carried it to the kitchen, and wrote a note to keep track, because science deserved paperwork.

EXPERIMENT, the note said. Fact I know: salt melts ice. Fact I see: our salt is NOT melting anything. Question: is it too cold for salt? Guess: yes. Test: bring the ice inside where it's warm and see if the same salt starts working.

She chipped a chunk of ice off the porch railing, dropped it into a bowl with the old salt, and set it on the table. While she waited, she drew an intricate diagram of the porch in the margins, complete of a drawing of Milo as a snowman, since he refused to come outside.

In twenty minutes the ice in the bowl had gone slushy, with the salt sitting in little holes it had melted. Same salt, same ice, different temperature. So it had to be the cold. Somewhere between the warm kitchen and the minus 12 porch, the salt crossed a line where it quit working. Later, checking a weather site, she found the number: ordinary rock salt stopped working well below about minus 10 degrees Celsius, which was 14 degrees Fahrenheit. Colder than that, and you were just decorating your steps.

The hill behind the school was calling, so Avery left the note on the table, propped against the salt box where Dad would find it: "Don't waste the salt, it's too cold. It stops working below about minus 10 Celsius, or 14 Fahrenheit. The formula for a good snow day is zero school plus one sled."

She pulled her sled up the hill twice, and on the third run Milo waved from the bottom and shouted, "Hey, scientist! Race you home for hot chocolate!"

The line for the Solar Hours concert wrapped twice around the arena, and Addison had been in it since 6:40 a.m., which she considered a meticulous use of a Saturday. Her plan was simple: fifty-dollar tickets went on sale at ten, and she had fifty-two dollars, the extra two for a bottle of water. The problem was that everyone in line wanted the same thing, and there were only so many tickets. She could see the scarcity without being told; she just had to count the people ahead of her and hope the math worked out.

By 9:15 the man in the neon vest came down the line with a sign, and Addison read it twice. Front section tickets now eighty dollars, it said, because demand was heavy. Eighty dollars was more than fifty, and Addison watched the effect ripple through the line in front of her. A boy three spots ahead put his money back in his pocket and left. Two girls behind him studied the sign, argued in low voices, and left too. Addison held her fifty-two dollars and did not leave, because the regular seats were still fifty, and fewer people buying the expensive ones meant the line moved faster.

She tested her idea at the hot dog cart near the gate. All morning the cart sold lemonade for four dollars, and only a few people bought it, even though the day was hot enough to make the pavement shimmer. Then the vendor, wanting to empty his cart before the show, called out that lemonade was now two dollars. Half the line turned around. Kids who had walked past it twice came back, and the vendor ran out in fifteen minutes, his ice buckets scraped clean. Addison bought one, mostly for research, and drank it slowly in the shade.

Her brother Theo texted her a message while she waited for the doors: "Did you get tickets? Mom says scalpers are selling front row for 200 outside." Addison typed back: "Not buying. When the price went up to 80, half the line walked away. When lemonade dropped to 2, it sold out in 15 min." Theo replied with a single thumbs up, which she felt understated her achievement.

Inside, a girl with green streaks in her hair overheard Addison explaining the ticket math to a friend. "Oh, that's the law of demand," the girl said. "Price up, people buy less. Price down, they buy more."

Addison nodded as if she had known the name all along, and lifted her two-dollar lemonade in a small toast to the empty cart.

Wyatt crouched over the camp stove, turning the bacon with a fork, while his little sister Nora arranged napkins on the picnic table for the third time. She had announced at breakfast that she was in charge of table decoration, and she intended to take the job seriously. "Move your elbow," she said. "You're blocking the centerpiece." The centerpiece was a pinecone on a rock.

Dad stood nearby rinsing a coffeepot at the water jug. The bacon had been going fine until Wyatt dropped in a new strip and the grease in the pan caught, a soft orange flame licking up the side. Wyatt's hand shot toward the water jug, but Dad got there first. He didn't splash. He turned the burner off, then slid a lid across the top of the pan, and the fire went out like someone had pinched it.

"What?" Wyatt stared at the lid. "Why not water?"

"Water on a grease fire turns to steam in a flash and throws the burning oil everywhere," Dad said. "Turn off the heat, cover it, and the fire smothers." He lifted the lid a peek to check, then set it back down. "Ask Grandpa about the kitchen curtain when he was my age."

Wyatt turned that over while the pan cooled. He tried to picture it: liquid water flashing into vapor, dragging drops of burning oil with it. It seemed backwards that water, which he thought of as the fire fighter's best friend, could make a grease fire worse. He decided the most probable explanation was that Dad was right and his own instincts were wrong, and that he'd better remember the exact order of things: heat off first, then lid.

Two nights later it was Wyatt's turn again, this time frying potatoes in oil while Nora elaborated on her centerpiece by adding two acorn caps and a twist of foil. Dad had hiked down to the lake with Mom. Wyatt turned away for one second to grab the salt, and when he looked back the oil had flared, flames curling over the pan's edge and Nora screaming his name.

His whole body wanted the water bottle on the table. Instead he made himself think of the curtain story, and the picture he'd built in his head: water flashing into vapor, oil flung in a burning ring. He snapped the burner knob off, grabbed the lid, and slid it over the pan. The flames died under the metal. Nora stood frozen with the water bottle in her hand, arm half raised, and Wyatt held up his palm.

"Not that," he said. "Cover it, don't drown it." He lifted the lid a crack, saw only dark oil and potatoes, and slid it back on. "Give me a minute, and then you can put the napkins out."

Florence had wanted all week to paint an orange that looked round enough to pick up, and now it sat on Grandma's windowsill in a pool of morning light, taunting her. Her first attempt lay flat on the paper, a pale circle with two dark smears where she had guessed the shadow might go. Grandma was under siege at her own easel across the room, racing to finish a portrait before Friday's exhibition, so Florence could not ask for help. She studied the orange instead. The lamp emitted a steady glow from the left, and where the light struck, the skin was almost white. Below and to the right, the colour sank into darkness, and behind the fruit a soft grey shadow lay on the sill. She dipped her brush, made a new circle, and laid down the orange base.

Then she wanted the shadow at once, while the paint still shone wet, because waiting felt unbearable. She brushed a thin wash of blue-grey over the right side of the cheek and watched it spread where she had not put it. The wet layer underneath pulled it sideways, and the two colours ran together into a bruised, muddy patch. She sat back, staring at it. The blue had not stayed put. The paper had still been damp, and the colours had mingled on the surface instead of sitting one over the other.

She tried again on scrap paper, painting a circle and forcing herself to wait. She touched the corner of a tissue to the paint until the tissue came away clean. Only then did she brush the grey wash over the dry layer, and this time the blue-grey settled like a veil, letting the warm orange glow through it. The colours mixed in her eye rather than on the paper. "Glazing," Grandma said from across the room, not looking up from her portrait. "That's what you just did."

"You knew I'd mess it up first?"

"Your grandpa has chronic impatience with his watercolours," Grandma said. "I watched it happen to him for forty years." She turned her portrait toward the window, checking a cheek she had glazed an hour before, and Florence saw the same veil of shadow there, soft and alive. Florence went back to her orange, laid the cast shadow behind it in one careful stroke, and held the paper up beside the real fruit on the sill.

"Look," she said. "It's round."

The rain had turned into a full monsoon by lunch, so the whole sixth grade was stuck inside, and the chess club had claimed the back tables. That was where the trouble started. Mr. Delgado had brought in one enormous chocolate chip cookie as a prize for the winner of the speed tournament, and Rose and her friend Dakota had tied for first.

"We could split it," Dakota said, eyeing the cookie like it might escape.

"You split it and you'll give yourself the big half," Rose said. "Obviously."

"Fine. You split it, then."

"And then you'd say I gave myself the big half. This is a trap." Rose studied the cookie, which was about the size of a personal pizza and twice as important. She thought about her little cousins at her grandmother's birthday party last summer, both of them shrieking over the last slice of cake until her grandmother had done something Rose still remembered. One cousin cut, the other cousin picked.

"Okay," Rose said slowly. "One of us breaks the cookie into two parts, and the other one picks which part they want first." She turned to Mr. Delgado. "Is that a real thing, or did my grandma invent it?"

"It's called divide and choose," he said, and went back to his crossword.

Dakota narrowed her eyes, which meant she was checking for tricks. She recruited Marcus from the next table to watch, so nobody could sneak a thumb onto the bigger piece. "You divide," she announced. "I pick."

So Rose broke the cookie, and she broke it carefully, turning the halves against each other, hunting for the hair-thin difference that would give one of them an extra chocolate chip. Marcus held a ruler over both halves like a customs officer. Dakota leaned in, examined each one twice, and finally grabbed the left half, which was maybe one crumb bigger, or maybe not.

"Happy?" she said, mouth already full.

Rose took the other half and tasted it. Somewhere in the middle of chewing, she realized she didn't even like chocolate chip that much, and that Dakota had known it, and that Dakota had been angling for the whole cookie until the picking rule closed that door forever.

"Rematch next Thursday," Rose said. "I'm bringing my own cookie."

"Bring two," said Dakota. "I'll divide."

Auntie Ru's car would pull into the driveway at six o'clock sharp, and Katherine still hadn't figured out what to do about the greeting. Her cousin Tama was coming all the way from New Zealand, and Mom had said, "He'll expect a hongi, so be ready." Ready for what? The word sat in Katherine's head like an opaque window she couldn't see through, and dinner was two hours away.

"Maybe it's a handshake," said her little brother Ben, who wanted nothing more than to be in charge of handing Tama his welcome gift, because handing people gifts meant being the center of attention for at least ten seconds. He had already claimed the job at breakfast. "Everybody does handshakes."

Katherine didn't think so. Mom had pressed her noses together in the air, twice, practicing in front of the hall mirror like a secret code. So it involved faces. Katherine tried it on Ben, leaning in forehead-first, and Ben dissolved into giggles and fell off the couch. Definitely faces, she decided, and probably not a kiss, because Mom never kissed anyone at the door except Grandpa.

At the table that night, which had been stretched with the good tablecloth and all three extra chairs, Katherine watched like a scientist. Tama arrived at 6:02 with a paper-wrapped parcel of chocolate fish for Grandma, and everyone murmured approval, because in this house you never arrived without something, whereas at her friend Priya's house you were scolded for bringing gifts, as if you doubted the host's generosity. Strange, Katherine thought. Same object, opposite meaning, like a coin with two faces.

Then it happened. Tama stood in front of her, tall and smiling, and leaned in. Katherine matched him. Their noses and foreheads touched, warm and brief, and stayed pressed together for one held breath. When they drew apart, Tama's eyes were bright, and Grandma made a small satisfied sound from her chair.

"What does it mean?" Katherine whispered as they sat down, because Ben was already unwrapping the chocolate fish without asking, elbows planted on the table, and Mom was clearing her throat at him in the family's universal signal for elbows off, which Tama noticed and seemed to file away like a rule for later.

"It's called a hongi," Tama said. "Sharing the breath of life."

Katherine looked at him across the breadbasket and wondered whether everyone he knew at home walked around carrying a piece of everyone else's breath inside them. "So we're kind of family now," she said.

"We were already," said Tama, and passed her the potatoes before Ben could reach them.

The bus dropped them at the science center at ten sharp, and Hudson had a plan folded in his back pocket. Last year, on this same trip, he had skipped the hardest clue on the scavenger hunt sheet to save time, and Marcus had won by two points. He'd been frugal with his minutes, and it had cost him everything. This year he told himself he would slow down and read every sign, even the boring ones.

"Prism room first," said Priya, tugging his sleeve. That was her want, and she made no secret of it: the exhibit where beams refract into rainbows, because she'd promised her little brother a photo of it. Hudson went along, mostly because the first clue wasn't far away, and partly because after last year he'd decided that racing ahead alone hadn't made him any smarter.

The fire-safety wing held an old hand-pumped engine, brass fittings gone soft with age, and beside it hung a painting of a white dog covered in black spots. "Why is there a dog?" Marcus asked, holding his clue sheet. "It's not even technology." The sheet asked the same thing: Why did firehouses keep spotted dogs?

Hudson studied the engine instead of the dog. Two long poles crossed at the front, and leather harnesses hung where horses would have stood. There were no horses in the painting, but there was a road, and the dog was painted running, always running, ahead of everything. He thought about the horses, invisible in every picture, and about how loud and crowded streets used to be. A slow idea formed. "They ran ahead," he said. "Like a scout."

Priya wasn't listening. She had found something behind the engine, a wooden model street with a tiny carriage and a lever. When Hudson pulled the lever, a small spotted dog slid out on a wire and crowds of tiny metal people scattered to the sides. He pulled it twice more, watching the same pattern each time. "The dog clears the road," Hudson said. "That's the whole job."

Marcus leaned over the model, unconvinced. "So firehouses kept them because they got along with the horses and ran ahead of the carriages?" Hudson nodded, then pointed to the harnesses, then to the dog's position in the painting, out in front, ears back. Marcus wrote it down slowly, the way he never wrote anything, and for once he looked less sure of winning than curious.

The final clue led to the gift shop, where Hudson counted his seven dollars and found nothing but postcards in his price range. Priya bought a glass prism that refract­ed the shop lights across the ceiling, and she held it up for Marcus's camera, laughing, while the shop attendant rang it up. "You only lost by two points because you skipped the dog last year," Marcus said, reading his old sheet from his pocket. Hudson stared at him. There had been a dog clue last year too, a different painting, and he had walked right past it. "Want to split the postcard?" Marcus asked, sliding one across the counter toward him.

Anthony's first speech at the tournament had lasted forty seconds, and the judge had written exactly one comment on his ballot: "Where is the rest?" His three note cards sat in his lap like cargo he'd forgotten to unload. He retreated to the cafeteria, where his teammate Maya was bouncing a stress ball off a wall.

"Coach says you have to narrate your points like a story," she said. "Hook, three points, close. Two minutes."

"I know the shape," Anthony said. "It comes out of me in one big rush, like a sneeze."

Down the table, a kid from another school was mumbling a speech at top speed, words piling on words, when his coach reached over and tapped the tabletop. Da-DUM. Da-DUM. Da-DUM. The kid slowed down, and Anthony leaned closer, because something about that tapping pulled at him.

"He's doing Shakespeare practice," Maya said. "The coach calls it iambic pentameter."

"What is that?"

"Ten syllables a line, five pairs, and in every pair the soft beat comes first and the hard one second." She tapped it herself, five times, da-DUM, and Anthony suddenly saw his own problem, the hidden rule underneath it: a speech needed a beat. His rush had no beat at all. If he tapped his foot and landed on his key words like drumbeats, maybe the two minutes would fill themselves out.

In the corner, the sparse cafeteria felt almost like a stage, lights humming overhead like floodlights. He stood, tapped his heel, and tried it out loud, hitting the important words. "Homework. Helps. Us. Practice. Thinking." The rhythm carried him, and the words stretched to fill the space the way his heartbeat filled his chest.

"Round two in five minutes," Maya called.

Anthony squared his cards, tapped once, da-DUM, and walked toward the room like a knight walking toward a dragon that owed him an argument.

The snow came down so thick overnight that school was canceled before Noah even finished his cereal, which meant the whole backyard was his. He pulled on boots, zipped his coat to his chin, and burst out the sliding door into a world that was white, quiet, and completely untracked. Ten degrees, his weather app said, but next to it was a smaller number that made him stop halfway down the steps: it felt like two below zero.

"Wind chill," his older sister Priya called from the porch, holding her phone up. "The air is ten degrees, but the wind makes it feel way colder." She wasn't even coming out. She was just there to deliver the news and go back inside to her cocoa.

Noah stomped a path to the fort he'd built from snow and branches back in November, when the yard had still been lush and green at the edges. The fort looked smaller under all the new snow, like something the winter had swallowed. He climbed in through the gap he'd left and sat on his overturned bucket throne. It was actually kind of warm in there, or at least not freezing, which gave him an idea.

If wind made cold air feel colder, then blocking the wind should make it feel warmer. That was testable. He crouched in the still air behind the fort wall for a whole minute, then stepped out into the open where the wind bit at his face, then went back behind the wall. His cheeks told him the answer before his brain did. Behind the wall his face stopped hurting. Out in the open, it stung like needles. Same ten degrees both places, but only one of them felt like two below zero.

He ran inside to nominate Priya as witness number one for his experiment. "Come feel this. Stand behind the fort, then stand in the open. It's the same temperature but your face doesn't believe it." Priya groaned but followed him out, and when she stepped around the wall she actually said "whoa," which from Priya was basically a standing ovation.

They fortified the fort together all morning, packing snow into every gap until the wind couldn't reach them at all. Noah rubbed his red ears, the cold gone from the stiff cartilage of them, and grinned.

"Tomorrow," he said, "we build a roof."

Paisley cracked the first egg into the bowl before she had measured anything else, and by nine thirty the counter looked like a flour bomb had gone off. "The muffins have to be out of the oven by eleven," her friend Ruby reminded her, "because Mr. Delgado, our upstairs tenant, comes down for coffee at eleven sharp, and he judges everything." Paisley raced to the pantry for baking powder, came back, and discovered she'd forgotten to preheat the oven entirely. "The oven's cold as a swimming pool," she groaned. Ruby peeked at the recipe card. "It says preheat first. Four hundred degrees. It also says something weird at the top."

The card read, in Grandma Cruz's handwriting: Mise en place. "It's French," Ruby said, squinting. "It means 'putting in place.' Measuring out every single ingredient before you start cooking." Paisley looked at her lumpy batter, then at the oven, then at the clock. Ten o'clock. If she kept hunting for cinnamon while things sat and oven temperatures climbed, nothing would be done by eleven, and Mr. Delgado would shake his head and call their kitchen impoverished, which was his word for anything missing blueberries.

"We start over," Paisley announced, dumping the batter into the sink with ceremony. "This time I test the French way." She turned the dial to four hundred, then lined up little bowls on the counter like soldiers: flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, oil, milk, one egg. Ruby rinsed blueberries and let them contribute to the cause by plopping them in a cup. "You look like a scientist," Ruby said. "I look like a person who knows where her cinnamon is," Paisley said, holding up the cinnamon like a trophy.

At eleven sharp the muffins came out golden, the tops cracked just right, and Mr. Delgado arrived downstairs sniffing the air like a bear at a picnic basket. He bit into one, chewed, and nodded slowly. "Not impoverished at all," he declared. "Who measured everything in advance?" Paisley raised her hand. "Mise en place," she said. "Second batch's on me," said Mr. Delgado, reaching for a second muffin.

Livia slammed the gym doors open with her shoulder, basketball bouncing against her hip, because tonight was the night she was finally going to beat Marisol in sprints. The gymnasium smelled like floor wax and ambition, and the whole seventh-grade team was already stretching by the bleachers.

But Marisol looked terrible. She was the fastest player Livia had ever seen, the girl who trained every single day, even Sundays, even during a blizzard in February. Tonight, though, she jogged the warm-up lap like her shoes were full of sand, and Coach Delgado's stopwatch caught her at a time so slow that Marisol stared at it and then at the clock on the wall, as if the clock were lying.

"That can't be right," Marisol said. "I never take a day off."

That was exactly the problem, Livia realized, standing there spinning the ball on one finger. She had read a science article for health class about how muscles grow stronger during recovery after training, not during the workout itself, which meant rest days were actually part of getting better. Marisol was skipping that whole part. Livia had a theory, and theories needed testing.

"Bet you a fruit roll-up," Livia said, "that if you rest tomorrow, completely rest, couch-level rest, you'll be faster on Thursday."

Marisol squinted. "My cousin works at a sports corporation and he says champions train more, not less."

"Your cousin also said glitter would be permanent on your sneakers if you sealed it with hairspray, and it was gone by Tuesday."

Marisol laughed so hard she snorted, which made the whole team turn around, which made her snort again. "Fine. One day. One fruit roll-up."

Thursday night, the gym was loud with squeaking shoes. Marisol lined up, coiled like a spring, and when Coach blew the whistle she flew down the court so fast the stopwatch practically gave up. She turned to Livia, breathless and grinning.

"I owe you a fruit roll-up," she said, "and an apology to my legs."

Hunter unfolded the note his friend Rex had taped to the slide that morning. "Gone until three. Save my vote for the new shovel. Rex." It was signed in green marker, and Hunter read it twice, because today the Trail Club was voting on how to spend its five dollars, and Rex's vote mattered.

Hunter, Marisol, and Dev were the only ones at the tire swing by three o'clock. The club had five members, but Rex was out and Priya had soccer until four. "We could just vote now," Dev said. "It's three to nothing for the flag, plus Rex's note makes four." Marisol frowned. "Priya would say it isn't fair. She's the one who wants the flag."

Hunter could perceive the problem even though Priya wasn't there to shout about it: a vote taken with most of the club missing would count only until Priya arrived, and then the whole fight would start over. He thought about the student council, where he'd once sat in the back row and watched them count heads before voting. Someone had said a word he'd looked up afterward. "It's called a quorum," he said slowly. "It's the minimum number of members who have to be present for the group's decisions to count."

Marisol crossed her arms. "Says who?"

"Says the dictionary, and I watched the student council do it. They wouldn't vote until enough people showed up."

"So what's our quorum?"

Hunter counted on his fingers. "Five members. We've got three bodies and one note." He thought Rex's written message should count for something, like testimony, but a piece of paper couldn't argue back or change its mind. "Let's say we need more than half. Three isn't enough."

Dev kicked the wood chips. "Then we can't buy anything today."

"We can agree on a fair rule," Hunter said. "Nobody votes until Priya gets here. And Rex's note gets read out loud, but he can change his vote if he shows up."

Priya came running at ten after four, cleats still on, and demanded to know what she'd missed. Hunter handed her Rex's note. "Nothing yet," he said. "We waited for a quorum. Now we've got one."

Noah discovered the problem halfway through "The River Song," and it nearly knocked him off the riser. The choir was singing in two parts for the first time, sopranos floating above the altos, and for three whole measures it worked. Then his alto line started to feel like it was dragging, like the melody was walking ahead of him and he was stuck in mud. He glanced sideways at Priya, who was also on alto, and she looked as confused as he felt.

"What happened back there?" he whispered as they filed off the riser.

"You slowed down," Priya whispered back. "I slowed down because you did. But the sopranos kept going."

At lunch, Noah picked apart his sandwich without tasting it, which his mom would have said was a crime against her cuisine, since she'd spent twenty minutes on it. He kept hearing the moment in his head. Why would he slow down when nobody was slowing down? He hadn't decided to. Then he remembered the piano accompaniment recording, and something clicked. The song had two spots marked "rit." in the sheet music, and the recording slowed down at those spots. Were those places he had subconsciously decided to slow?

"Ritardando means gradually slowing down," Priya said when he asked her. "Mr. Okafor mentioned it once. And accelerando means gradually speeding up."

Noah stared at the sheet music in the cafeteria. The sopranos must have ignored the rit. because they were following the melody's natural momentum, while he, listening to the accompaniment in his head, had slowed right along with it. Half the room slowed and half didn't, and the harmony fell apart. It was like the tempo was something invisible, and the word in the music was the hidden cause. He wondered: could you hear a rule you couldn't see?

He decided to test it. At the next rehearsal, he asked Mr. Okafor if they could mark every rit. and every accel. with a pencil arrow, long or short depending on how gradual. "An arrow length of slow," Priya called it, and Mr. Okafor laughed and said the sound was subjective anyway, so they needed something visual to agree on. Then Noah asked if the two sections could face each other for one run-through.

The experiment worked, mostly. When the arrows came, the whole choir bent together at the first rit., and the chord stayed locked. At the accelerando they surged like a river picking up speed, and for a second Noah's part pulled ahead and he heard the chord go thin. He held back, matched Priya's breath, and felt the two lines lock in again.

"That was it," Mr. Okafor said from the piano. "You held your part."

Noah grinned at Priya. "I was following the piano in my head," he said. "Now I'm following the arrows."

The four square court behind the gym had a line down the middle of one square where the paint had worn away, and that line was the whole problem. Jaxon had hit a ball that landed near it, and Marcus said out, and Jaxon said in, and they had been standing there arguing long enough for three other games to finish around them.

"Everybody saw it was in," Jaxon said.

"Nobody saw anything," Marcus said. "It was too fast."

Jaxon was about to argue harder when he noticed who was standing around them. Priya had stopped dribbling her ball. Two fifth graders were watching from the fence. Even the kid who usually migrated to the far corner of the blacktop when anything got loud had drifted closer. There were at least eight of them, all watching, all silent.

He remembered something he had read in the library that week, a fact that had surprised him. "A study in 2001 watched kids on playgrounds," he told Marcus, "and other kids were there during 88 percent of bullying episodes."

"I'm not bullying you," Marcus said.

"I know. That's not the point." Jaxon kept his voice level, the way his grandmother did when she was working out a price at her shop. "The point is, we're almost never the only ones who see something. All these guys saw the ball. We're just not asking them."

He tested the idea right there, because an idea you don't test is only a guess. "Okay, hands up if it looked out," Jaxon said. Four hands went up. "Hands up if it looked in." Two went up. Two kids shrugged. So the witnesses disagreed, which meant the real problem was not the ball at all.

"Here's the problem," Jaxon said, and he made himself say it in one sentence. "There's a worn-out line on that square, and we don't have a rule for balls that land near it. So we both just claim whatever helps us." He pointed at the faded stripe. "We need one explicit rule, and it has to be fair even when it goes against you. That's the only kind that works."

Marcus looked at the line, then at the ball in his hands. "Replays don't exist here," he said slowly, "but the serve does. Any ball that lands on the worn part gets treated like a let in tennis. Do-over, no point. That's the rule, starting now."

"Starting now," Jaxon agreed. "Even if the do-over goes against me."

"Even if it goes against me too," Marcus said, and bounced the ball once, hard, to show he meant it.

Priya wrote the rule on the back of her hand in pen, like it was the prototype for a real sign, and the game started up again. The next ball landed square on the worn stripe, against Marcus this time, and Marcus tossed it back to the server without a word.

"Do-over," he called out. "You heard the rule."

The snow arrived overnight with no warning at all, so when Marcus woke up and saw the school parking lot buried, the day felt like a spontaneous gift. He suited up and hurried down Maple Street toward the hill behind Mr. Delgado's building, where his friend Theo was already packing snow onto a sled runner. Their favorite run started at the top, but a fallen branch had begun to obstruct the path halfway down, so they took turns steering around it, each pass a little faster than the last.

After an hour of climbing and crashing, Marcus pulled off one glove to shake the snow out and noticed something odd. His fingers were white and stinging, his ears had gone numb enough that he could pinch them without really feeling it, and the tip of his nose had that prickly, half-asleep feeling. Yet his chest and legs, under all those layers, were toasty. He tested the idea on the next run. He kept his gloved hands tucked under his arms, and sure enough his fingers warmed up while his ears stayed cold.

"Why do my hands hurt but my stomach doesn't?" Theo asked, rubbing his own red ears.

"I think fingers, toes, ears and the nose are the parts of the body most likely to get frostbite," Marcus said. "Everything else stays warm longer. My mom's landlord lost a toe that way one winter, so she's always going on about it."

Theo looked down at his boots. "Toes too?"

"Toes too. So we cover all four and we're good."

They dug spare hats and an extra pair of socks out of Marcus's garage, and Mrs. Delgado, watching from her window, waved them in for cocoa when their sled run ended in her hedge. Marcus pressed his warm mug against his cheek and felt his nose wake up, tingling.

"Same time after lunch?" Theo asked, already carrying the sled toward the hill.

The list in Isla's pocket had exactly three words on it: deodorant, soap, courage. The first two were for her. The third, she suspected, was for Priya, who had not read aloud in class since the day her voice came out as a squeak and Mr. Harlan had asked if she needed the nurse.

At the pharmacy, Isla found the deodorant aisle between the shampoo and the vitamins. Her mother had told her that as bodies changed, sweat glands under the arms woke up and made a smell, and that daily showers plus deodorant kept it under control. "You will comply with the new routine," her mother had said, "or your gym shirt will stage a controversy all by itself." Isla had laughed, though she had also spent three days being pessimistic about the whole thing, wondering if she was the only eleven-year-old in the world whose body was changing so fast.

She was reaching for a stick of deodorant when she heard someone breathing fast behind the toothpaste display. It was Priya, one hand pressed to her chest like she was holding her ribs together.

"Reading out loud tomorrow," Priya whispered. "English. Everyone. I practiced at home and it was fine, but my heart's already pounding and it's not even tomorrow. Why does my body act like it's in danger when it's just a paragraph?"

Isla thought about that. Danger. A pounding heart. Fast breathing. She had read the same thing in the body book her aunt had sent her, the one with the chapter about anxiety. "It's the fight-or-flight response," she said slowly, testing the idea as she said it. "Anxiety triggers it, and it releases adrenaline, and that speeds up your heart and your breathing even when there's no real danger."

"So my body is lying to me?"

"Sort of. It's just doing its job wrong." Isla turned the deodorant stick over in her hands. "Wait. That's why your gym shirt smells worse before presentations. Adrenaline makes you sweat."

Priya stared at her. "So the smell and the pounding are the same thing?"

Isla held up the stick of deodorant. "Proof. Tomorrow, we shower, we use this, and you read the paragraph. Your heart will hammer anyway, because adrenaline doesn't care about deodorant. But you'll smell calm."

Priya took a matching stick off the shelf and dropped both in the basket. "Deal," she said. "Now help me find the soap."

Ivy wanted the Slate Pro tablet more than she wanted her next birthday, and the poster in the library hallway knew it. It showed five glowing checkmarks: SHARPEST SCREEN, FASTEST CHIP, MOST APPS, LIGHTEST BODY, COOLEST COLORS. Above the checkmarks, a famous singer named Rae Delgado grinned and said, "I never leave home without mine." At the bottom, tiny letters announced that the Tech Store two blocks away would close at 5:00. Ivy checked the clock above the librarian's desk. It was 4:20.

Her best friend Marcus was already at a table, doing homework he should have finished three days ago. "Look at this," Ivy said, spreading the poster flat in front of him. "Rae Delgado uses one. And five great features. Five, Marcus." She tapped each checkmark. "Everyone at school is getting one. Even Priya, and Priya still uses a flip phone."

Marcus squinted at the poster. "Rae Delgado also gets paid to smile at things. That's her whole job." He turned a homework page over. "And 'sharpest' and 'coolest' aren't really facts. They're just loaded words. It's like when my brother calls his sandwich 'legendary' so I'll trade him my chips."

"Okay, but the screen is sharper." Ivy paused. "Sharper than what, though?" She read the poster again, slower this time. Something felt off, like a puzzle with a piece missing. The ad listed everything the tablet was good at and nothing else. "It says lightest body. It doesn't say anything about the battery." That seemed strange to her, because the battery was the first thing her mom asked about any device. It seemed logical that an ad with five checkmarks would add a sixth for battery life if the battery were any good.

She marched to the computer catalog, typed "Slate Pro review," and found a magazine article. The tablet's battery lasted four hours. Four. Her cousin's ancient tablet lasted nine. "Marcus," she whispered. "They stacked the deck. Five great facts, and they left out the bad one." Marcus nodded. "My language arts teacher calls that card stacking. Showing only the facts that support your side, so the message seems stronger than it is." Ivy wrote it on her hand, because some facts deserve ink.

At 4:45 Marcus asked, "Are we still buying it? The store closes in fifteen minutes." Ivy looked at the poster, at Rae Delgado's grin, at the five checkmarks marching in a row like they had somewhere to be. "No. But we can walk past the store on the way home and look through the window. That's free." Marcus zipped his backpack. "Now that's a feature they should advertise."

The ferry to Owl Lake Campground took forty minutes, and Brielle's little brother Theo turned green ten minutes in. He sat hunched against the rail inside the cabin, staring at the floor, holding a paper bag.

"I'm going to throw up," Theo said.

"Look out the window," Brielle said.

"I did. It made it worse."

That was the strange part, Brielle thought. Watching the water had made him feel sicker, not better. She remembered the museum trip last spring, when the bus had jolted over potholes and she had felt fine the whole ride. What had she done differently? She had sat by the window, but not at the passing trees. She had watched the mountains, far away, which never seemed to move.

"Come on." She took Theo's sleeve and pulled him toward the deck door. He was impulsive about most things, ice cream, puddles, wasps, but moving took persuasion now.

The wind on deck was cold. Brielle steered him to the rail. "Don't watch the water. Watch the shoreline, way out there. The far end, where it doesn't move."

Theo gripped the rail and fixed his eyes on the distant line of pines. A swell rolled under the hull, and another. Slowly his shoulders came down from around his ears. The gray went out of his face.

"It works," he said. "Why?"

Brielle considered lying, then didn't. "I don't know exactly. Something about your eyes and your ears agreeing when you look at the horizon." She pointed anyway. "Keep watching. Dad said the campsite is near that second point."

Their father came out with two granola bars, ready to intervene with crackers and ginger candy, but Theo waved him off and kept his eyes on the far shore.

When the ferry bumped the dock, Theo was the first one down the ramp, running. "Race you to the car," he called.

Brielle jogged after him over the gravel, her knee cartilage aching from a fall off her bike the week before, but not enough to slow her down.

Theo stood in the kitchen with dirt on his shirt and two days until the science fair. On the counter sat four bean seedlings in paper cups, and beside them his project board, which currently said, in giant letters, MUSIC IS GOOD FOR PLANTS. His little sister Maya wandered in, eating a pickle.

"That's your whole project?" she said. "Good for plants how? Also, plants don't have ears, so, nice work."

"Thanks for the exceptional feedback," Theo said. He stared at the board. The trouble was, he couldn't prove music was good for plants, because he couldn't even say what would prove him wrong. He remembered his notebook from class and flipped it open. There it was, in his own handwriting: a useful hypothesis must be testable, meaning an experiment could show it is wrong. Below it, the form it usually takes: If... then...

"So make it testable," Maya said, peering over his arm.

"I'm getting there." He crossed out the giant letters and wrote: If I play music for two seedlings and keep two seedlings in silence, then the music plants will grow taller in one week. He pointed at it. "An experiment could show that's wrong. The quiet plants could win, or it could be a tie. Either way, I'd know something."

"That's less exciting than my idea," Maya said. "My idea is that pickles are good for plants."

"Please don't elaborate."

She elaborated anyway, describing a pickle-watering system, until he handed her a prism from the junk drawer and aimed her at the window. Sunlight split into a stripe of rainbow across her hands, and she went quiet at last.

The next morning Theo measured the cups. The music plants had grown a centimeter. So had the others. He wrote down every number, even the boring ones, then set his ruler beside the cups for tomorrow.

"Tie so far," Maya reported from the window, holding the prism up so a green spot of rainbow landed on the tallest seedling. "Your plants are all winning, basically."

Elena spread her battery, bulb, switch and coiled wire across the picnic table at the edge of the skate park, because her brother Tomas refused to skip practice and she refused to fail Monday's science demonstration. She clipped the wire to the battery, flipped the switch, and the bulb stayed dark. She unclipped and reclipped every connection, but it was like arguing with the ramp: the same input, the same nothing. The skaters had started to migrate to the shaded half-pipe as the tropical afternoon heat pressed down, and a plague of gnats circled her table, but she kept working.

She took the bulb off and clipped the wire straight to a small meter instead. If current was flowing, the needle would move even though she could not see current itself. It did not move. "So the battery's fine or it's not," she said to herself, "but something between here and here is broken." She tested each piece of wire by touching its ends to the meter until one stretch, cracked where skaters had rolled over it, gave nothing at all. She replaced it, flipped the switch, and the bulb glowed. When her friend Dara rolled up, Elena held the lit bulb and said, "It lights because the switch closes the path, so current goes around the whole loop through the filament."

A text arrived from Tomas, on the far ramp: "Coach says graph beats guessing. Did you try the meter trick or just stare at it?" Elena typed back: "Meter trick. Found a dead wire. Also took five readings of voltage and current with the good wire, like the handbook said."

She plotted the five points on graph paper, voltage up the side, current along the bottom. The points fell into a straight line, and when she extended it backward with her ruler, it passed through zero, where no voltage meant no current. The line climbed steeply, which matched the way her bulb pushed back against the flow. Dara leaned over her shoulder and read the page. "That line means something?" Elena tapped the slope with her pencil and said, "The slope is the resistance." Dara nodded slowly, spun her board up onto the table, and said, "Show me the bulb again."

Grace wanted her own password for the family tablet, a real one, because her brother Theo had just changed his after something bad happened. A message from his friend Raj sat open on the screen: "Theo, someone got into my game account last night. I used the same password for everything, and now I have to fix all of it." Theo had read it out loud in an ominous voice, like a horror movie narrator, but Grace could tell he was genuinely worried.

She decided her password would come from her favorite song, a half-remembered line about rivers and roads. She typed the words into the search bar, but the results were a mess of pages about rivers, pages about roads, pages about rivers in general. Theo leaned over her shoulder. "Put quotation marks around it," he said. "Putting quotation marks around a phrase asks Google to find pages containing those exact words in that exact order." She typed the phrase again with quotes around it, and suddenly every result was the song itself. The line existed as one exact string of words, all together, in thousands of places.

That gave her an idea, and she tested it right away. She typed a made-up nonsense phrase in quotes, "purple otter settlement committee," and got zero results. Nothing on the whole internet had those exact words in that exact order. So a password made from a famous lyric was like hiding a key under a doormat that a million houses shared, but a mixed-up phrase was like no doormat anyone had ever made. She built hers from three unrelated words, some numbers, and a capital letter, and she wrote nothing down.

When Theo asked if she would just use it for everything, she shook her head. "If someone finds one, they shouldn't get all of them. That's what happened to Raj." To reassure him, she made up a second, completely different password for her game account and kept the two straight in her head. Then she slid the tablet across the table and said, "Your turn."

Grandpa's desk smelled like pencil shavings and old coffee, and Tyler sat in front of it holding a story he hated. He had written three pages about a dragon attack, and it was supposed to be his best work, but when he read it aloud that morning it sounded flat, like a sandwich without anything in it.

"Read me the first page," Grandpa said, folding his newspaper. He had been a newspaper editor for thirty years, and he wanted Tyler to love words the same way he did, though he promised not to fix the story for him. "I'll listen. You decide what to change."

Tyler read. "The big dragon flew over the very tall castle. It was scary. The brave knight drew his shiny sword. He was afraid but he was also brave."

Grandpa winced, and Tyler stopped. "It's bad, right?"

"It's all the same length," Tyler said suddenly, staring at the page. Every sentence marched along at exactly the same rhythm, like footsteps on a flat sidewalk. And half the words were decoration that did nothing. He crossed out big, very tall, brave, and shiny. Then he circled three short sentences in a row and rewrote one of them as a long sentence that rolled to the end of the line. When he read it again, the paragraph had snap to it.

Then he hit a line that stopped him cold. In his draft it looked like two sentences: "I know what you did," Mom said. "Last summer." He had learned that the period after said meant a new sentence started, so the second part needed a capital L. But it read wrong, because Last summer belonged with the first part. One thought, torn in half. He tried a lowercase l instead, and the whole thing became one continuing sentence, and it sounded right. "It's still the same sentence," he said, half to himself. "The tag just interrupts it."

Grandpa leaned over and squinted. "You figured that out yourself?"

"With a comma after did and a comma after said. Both halves are one sentence." Tyler pointed at the page, then noticed Grandpa staring at the desk.
