His grandfather had a stack of his own old columns in the drawer, ones he had never finished revising for a collection he dreamed of publishing. Tyler nudged the stack toward him. "Your turn. Pick one. I'll listen while you read."

Grandpa pulled out a yellowed page, cleared his throat, and began to read.

Kaylee dumped a box of dried beans, a bag of mini marshmallows, and three boxes of toothpicks onto the kitchen table and stared at them like they were going to arrange themselves. Her science project was due Friday: build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons, and electrons in the right places. The right places. That was the problem. She had drawn the nucleus and the electron shells on paper, but when she tried to start, she realized she didn't even know how many beans she needed.

"Protons are the ones that decide which element it is," her friend Priya said, dropping her backpack on a chair. "It's on the poster in Mr. Okafor's room. Every element has a number." Priya pointed at the folded page Kaylee had printed out, a strip of the periodic table with the elements marching across in squares. Kaylee smoothed it flat between the sugar bowl and the salt shaker.

"Look at the numbers," Priya said, tapping the top of each square. Hydrogen, 1. Helium, 2. Lithium, 3. Kaylee traced down and across with her finger, and her stomach did a small flip. "They count up by one. Every single one." She grabbed a pencil and checked carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine. "Six, seven, eight, nine. So oxygen has exactly one more proton than nitrogen, and nitrogen has one more than carbon."

"So if the table is in order like that," Kaylee said slowly, "each element has one more proton than the element before it." That gave her a way to test her model. She had chosen oxygen because she wanted to use the marshmallows as protons and she had exactly eight left. She counted out eight marshmallows, pushed them into a ball with eight beans for neutrons, and then froze. "Wait. If oxygen is number eight, does that mean eight electrons too?" She couldn't see electrons, couldn't see any of it, only the piles on the table and the numbers on the poster. But if the numbers counted protons, and protons were what made oxygen oxygen, then a whole atom had to balance.

She laid out eight toothpicks in two rings around the nucleus, two close in and six farther out, like the diagram in her textbook. "Hold this while the glue sets," she told Priya, and Priya pressed the marshmallow nucleus between her palms like an artisan shaping a lump of clay.

"It's kind of ironic," Priya said. "The part you can't see decides everything, and the part you can see is just beans." Kaylee slid a folded dish towel under the model to insulate it from the cold countertop so the glue wouldn't crack, then stepped back. The atom sat on the kitchen table, lopsided and sticky and, as far as she could prove, correct.

"One more proton than the one before it," Kaylee said, and tapped the poster. "Carbon, seven more toothpicks, and I'd have a whole different element."

The record player in Grandma Ruth's living room spun an old choir album while John practiced his part. On Thursday the community choir would sing in two-part harmony for the first time, and John had been assigned the lower line. He was determined to conquer it before then, mostly because the choir director had said, gently, that he drifted.

The sheet music had one strange word at the top: andante. John stared at it while Grandma molded tiny owls out of polymer clay at the kitchen table, baking them hard in her little oven. He assumed andante meant fast, because fast songs had fancy words. He marched into the living room and sang his line as quickly as he could, then tried to hold it against the higher part on the record.

It fell apart instantly. His line collided with theirs, tangled like headphone cords in a pocket. The intricate weaving of the two voices that the choir director had promised simply was not there. John flopped onto the couch and glared at the word again.

Then he noticed something. The record sleeve, propped against the shelf, listed all the tracks. One was marked largo, and that track had crawled by, slow as syrup, when he'd heard it earlier. Another was marked allegro, and that one had bounced along at a clip. He pulled out another album, and the pattern repeated. The words weren't decorations. They were instructions.

"Andante means a walking pace," he said slowly, testing it. "Largo means very slow, and allegro means fast and lively." Walking pace. Not sprinting.

He set the needle down again, stood tall, and sang at the speed of his own feet crossing the living room floor. The upper line rose above his like a staircase over steady ground, and for four whole bars the two parts held together.

Grandma appeared in the doorway, a clay owl in each hand. "Do that one more time," she said. "Exactly like that."

Samantha balanced the mixing bowl on the picnic table and read her grandmother's recipe card again, the one taped inside the camper where the wind couldn't steal it. The card was really a letter Gran had sent last spring, ending with "Save me a slice." Samantha had promised she would, and tonight she intended to bake her first loaf over the campfire.

She remembered the bakery visit from last summer, how Gran had let her poke a squishy lump of dough that seemed to breathe. "It's not magic," Gran had said, winking. "Yeast makes bread rise by feeding on sugars and releasing carbon dioxide gas, which gets trapped in the dough as bubbles." Samantha had thought that was the strangest thing she'd ever heard, a fungus burping bread into existence.

She mixed flour, sugar, and the packet of yeast, then reached for the kettle. The water had been sitting on the camp stove while Dad ran the generator to charge the lantern, so it was good and hot. She stirred it in, kneaded the dough, and set the bowl near the fire in a sheltered spot, safe from any draft, because Gran's letter said cold air would slow the rising. Then she waited. The dough sat there, round and lazy, as lethargic as her little brother Theo after a swim.

"That's a bread rock," Theo announced twenty minutes later. "You're making bread rocks for dinner."

"It's still waking up," Samantha said, but her stomach twisted. She leaned close and studied the dough. No bubbles. No puff. Nothing. She thought about Gran's letter again, feeding on sugars, releasing gas. The yeast should have been eating and puffing like tiny balloon artists, and it was doing nothing at all. Something had gone wrong before the bowl ever got set down. She touched the side of the mixing bowl where she'd poured the water in. Warm. Very warm. Hot, actually, still hot enough that she pulled her fingers back. The yeast hadn't been sleeping. The yeast had been cooked.

Theo, who had declared the whole project doomed, suddenly changed his mind and became her assistant. "New plan," he said solemnly, holding the fresh packet like it was treasure. They mixed everything again, and this time Samantha tested the cooled water on her wrist, the way you test a bottle for a baby, warm but not hot. They set the bowl by the fire and watched.

Ten minutes later Theo grabbed her sleeve. "Look, look! It's a balloon!" The dough had swelled up round and dome-shaped, and when Samantha pressed one finger gently against it, the surface sprang back like something alive. She grinned and shaped it into a loaf. "Gran," she said, "is getting the biggest slice of all."

"Only if I don't eat it first," said Theo, already reaching for a stick to poke the fire.

Brielle had planned the whole week before Grandpa's suitcase even reached the porch. She would show him the rope swing, the vegetable garden, and the dilapidated shed at the back fence where her old bike still leaned against a broken shelf. But on the second morning, the kitchen filled with smoke from toast nobody noticed, and Grandpa just sat at the table reading his newspaper while the slices turned black.

"Grandpa, the toast!" Brielle grabbed the fork and flipped them off the burner before the smoke alarm could intervene. She waved a towel at the ceiling and studied him. Last summer, he had smelled her burning marshmallow from across the entire yard. She tested him quietly, saying nothing about the cinnamon rolls she had hidden in the oven to surprise him at lunch. When she finally brought them out, warm and fragrant enough to make her own mouth water, he thanked her politely, as if she had handed him a paper napkin.

That afternoon she ran a careful experiment in the backyard. She set out five cups on the picnic table: vanilla, lemon, coffee, onion, and plain water. "Tell me what each one is," she said, and Grandpa, who loved games, agreed at once. He identified the coffee, slowly, and guessed wrong on everything else. The plain water he called "soap." Brielle sat back on the bench, thinking about her grandmother, who had always known it was raining before anyone else because she could smell it coming, and who had once found a gas leak that no one else had noticed. Maybe she, too, had stopped being able to smell near the end, and maybe everyone had mistaken it for not paying attention. Brielle wondered whether she should have visited more that year instead of choosing soccer camp.

That evening she typed her notes into the library computer and found a word waiting for her: presbyosmia. "The sense of smell naturally declines in old age," the screen said, "a change called presbyosmia." She read it twice, then printed it.

On the last day of his visit, Grandpa stood by the grill in the backyard while Brielle watched the hamburgers for him, flipping each one at exactly the right moment. He talked about his own grandfather's kitchen, and the bread that always seemed to come out of the oven a little too dark. "We teased him about it for years," he said, shaking his head. "Now I wonder."

"I'll be your nose while you're here," Brielle said, and handed him the spatula so he could do the honors himself.

Emma had spread her poster across the picnic table at Grandma's backyard reunion, and that was the problem. For her social studies project she had made a bar graph of the origins of people in Brampton, Ontario, using numbers from a government website. She had checked her addition three times, and the totals still came to far more than one hundred percent. "That's impossible," she muttered, jabbing her pencil at the poster. "A town can't be more than all of itself."

Her cousin Priya leaned over her shoulder, holding a paper plate of samosas. "Maybe the website made a mistake," she said. "Or maybe you did."

"I despise this graph," Emma said, which wasn't true, but it felt true right then. Uncles and aunts drifted past the table, some carrying chairs, some arguing about whose turn it was at the badminton net. Grandma arrived last, drying her hands on a dish towel, and studied the poster the way she studied a chessboard.

"Uncle Ray!" Grandma called across the yard. "Come and settle something." Uncle Ray, whom everyone agreed was the most competent person in the family at anything involving numbers, worked at the town hall. He set down his lemonade and looked at Emma's graph for a long moment. Then he laughed, not at her, but the way people laugh when a puzzle suddenly makes sense. "That's the census," he said. "It's not wrong. Canada's census has let people report more than one ethnic or cultural origin since 1981, so the origin totals add up to more than the country's population."

Emma stared at him. "More than one," she repeated slowly. In her head she tested the idea against her own family, sitting right there in folding chairs. Grandma cooked pierogi every Christmas and told stories about monsoon seasons in Sri Lanka, where she'd taught school for ten years before emigrating. Priya called herself both Guyanese and Canadian and refused to pick. Auntie Joan's family had come from Scotland four generations back, and she still put tartan napkins on the table every reunion. If every one of them could tick more than one box, then of course the bars would stack up past one hundred percent. Nobody had counted twice by accident; everybody had counted all of themselves.

She grabbed a marker and wrote across the top of the poster: "Why the numbers are bigger than 100." Then she drew a small pie chart of her own family, one slice for each thing they claimed, the slices overlapping in the middle like a Venn diagram. "Priya, hold this corner down," she said, reaching for her pencil case. "I'm going to interview everybody before the potato salad runs out."

Sofia stood in line outside the ticket kiosk in the west wing of the mall, third from the front, her fingers curled around the twenty dollars she had saved from dog walking. The kiosk sold tickets to the Bright Comet concert, and for one day only they were priced at ten dollars. Behind her, the line snaked past the pretzel stand, past the fountain where coins glinted under the water, and out toward the shoe store. She counted at least two hundred people.

At ten o'clock the metal shutter rattled up and the clerk began pulling tickets from a box. Sofia got hers, paper warm from the printer, and stepped aside to look at it. Behind her the box emptied fast. By the time the fiftieth person reached the counter, the clerk raised both hands and called out, "That's it, we're out." The rest of the line broke apart slowly, like ice melting. A girl near the fountain sat down on the rim and put her head in her hands.

"That's so unfair," said Malia, Sofia's neighbor, who had been two spots behind the shutter people. "Ten dollars, and they only had fifty tickets. Look at all these people." She swept her arm at the crowd still drifting, unwilling to leave. Sofia turned the ticket over in her hands. Half the people in that line had wanted a ticket and gotten nothing, because the price had been so low that everyone could afford one, and there weren't enough to go around. She remembered her brother once saying there was a word for that.

A man in a gray jacket moved along the edge of the crowd, speaking quietly. "Bright Comet, forty dollars, I've got two." Malia grabbed Sofia's sleeve. "That's the same ticket," she whispered. "Ten dollars at the kiosk, forty from him." Sofia watched a boy hand over the money and walk away holding the ticket like it was made of glass. Down the corridor, a cart selling phone cases sat stacked with hundreds of them, a sign reading five dollars, two for eight, and barely a customer stopping.

"My brother called it a shortage," Sofia said. "When the price stays low, more people want the thing than there are things to sell." She tested the logic in her head against what she had just watched: low price, long line, empty box. Then the phone case cart: plenty of cases, few buyers, price falling. It wasn't symmetrical, not exactly, but it fit both ways she looked at it.

Malia stared at the man in the gray jacket. "I was going to pay him forty," she said. "I had it in my pocket." She took out the bills, folded twice, and looked at them for a long moment. Then she put the money back in her pocket and straightened her shoulders. "Next time I'm getting here at seven," she said, "and I'm bringing a folding chair."

Megan sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with a notebook open on her knee, staring at a question she had written in big letters: WHEN? Her science fair beans were germinating in a damp paper towel beside her, tiny white roots curling like commas, and she was supposed to be recording their growth for her poster about a jar ecosystem. Instead she kept thinking about something Mrs. Alvarez's health packet had mentioned last week, something that had made half the class giggle and the other half go quiet.

The packet didn't say when anything would happen to her, only that it would, eventually. That was the problem. Megan liked problems with data. So she made a chart on the next page, like her bean chart, and wrote the names of every girl she could think of with an older sister: Priya, Jenna, Bree. At Priya's house on Saturday, she brought it up while they made popcorn. "Do you know how old your sister was when it happened? Her first period, I mean." Priya shrugged and yelled down the hall, and her sister shouted back, "Twelve and a half." Jenna's sister, texting from basketball practice, answered in a message Megan read off Jenna's phone: "i was 11!! still mad about it tbh." Bree's sister, who was in college, sent a note on lined paper she'd scribbled at the bus stop and left in the Mendozas' mailbox: "Almost 14. Everyone's different. Tell Bree to stop worrying." Megan copied each number into her chart.

Back in her bedroom, she laid the numbers out and stared at them. Eleven, twelve and a half, almost fourteen. They didn't match at all, which frustrated her until she remembered her beans. Some had sprouted on day three, some on day five, and one stubborn seed had waited until day eight, but all of them had sprouted. The differences weren't mistakes. They were just the range. She wrote that word in her notebook and underlined it, then added a line underneath: wide range is normal.

On Monday she showed the chart to Priya at lunch. "So there's no exact schedule," Megan said. "It's more like a middle age that lots of girls are near, and a big spread around it. Like my beans." Priya leaned over the chart, and her grin was contagious; by the time the bell rang, half the table was smiling at a page of bean data and sister stories. "You should put this in your poster," Priya said. Megan laughed. "My poster is about ecosystems." But she paper-clipped the chart into her notebook anyway, right next to the beans.

Anthony's problem was simple: someone had logged into his library account three times overnight and held every copy of the new space graphic novel until June. He had never told anyone his password, which was anthony123. In computer class that morning, Ms. Ruiz put a challenge on the board: create a password, then explain in one sentence why reusing it everywhere is a bad idea.

He typed anthony123 into the practice box, and a bar glowed red. Weak. He tried Anthony!2013! and the bar turned yellow, then green when he added the name of his eccentric neighbor's dog, Rickets, who wore a raincoat even in July. "A strong password has length, weird capital letters, and symbols," Anthony said to his partner, Divya. "So why can't I use the same strong one for everything?"

"Because if one site leaks it, they get all of you," Divya said. "Like a decomposer. One fungus gets into a fallen log, and the whole log goes." Anthony thought about the library account. Whoever guessed anthony123 might now try it on his game account too, since he had used it there since second grade. He tested it: he typed anthony123 into a fake login the class had set up, and the screen showed exactly which of his other pretend accounts would fall. All of them did.

That afternoon the class debated something Divya had found while researching: search engines. "In 2013 the US Federal Trade Commission told search engines that paid results must be clearly distinguishable from natural results," she read, "or they risk deceiving users." A boy named Marcus argued that ads dressed up as regular results were fair game. "No," Anthony said. "If you can't tell what's paid and what's natural, they violate the rule. It's like a password that looks strong but isn't." The class voted, and Marcus switched sides. Anthony copied his new password onto a scrap of paper, folded it twice, and tucked it deep in his backpack.

Grandpa's house had eleven rooms, and by Sunday morning Owen needed to have all eleven lines of the Sabbath blessing memorized. He spread the paper on the kitchen table and glared at it. "I can't keep a single line in my head, let alone eleven."

Grandpa slid a mug of cocoa toward him. "When I was your age, my tutor gave me a trick. You'll laugh, but it works."

"Try me."

"Put each line in a room of this house. The first line goes in the front hall, the second in the pantry, and so on. Then when you say the blessing, you walk the route in your mind and pick up each line where you left it." Grandpa sipped his tea. "The old scholars called it the method of loci. Latin for places, probably. Smart fellows, those Romans."

Owen decided to hypothesize. If the trick worked, then linking each part of a text to a place along a familiar route should let him walk that route in his imagination and recall everything in order. If it failed, he would know by lunchtime. He posted line one on the coat hook in the hall, whispered line two to the flour jar in the pantry, and tucked line three behind the bathroom mirror. He was diligent about it, marching from room to room like a soldier on a strange inspection.

At the dinner table he closed his eyes and started walking. Front hall, coat hook, first line. Pantry, flour jar, second. He got all the way to the guest room closet before he stumbled, because he'd put a line in the laundry basket and Mom had moved the basket to the washing room. "Wait," he said, eyes still shut. "The basket migrated. Line eight is doing laundry now."

Grandpa snorted into his soup. "Even the Romans never solved that problem."

Owen opened one eye. "Then line eight does laundry forever. It recites best with soap." He took a breath, finished the blessing clean through, and reached for the bread.

Anthony raised his hand so fast his chair squeaked. "Mr. Ruiz, why does my voice do that croaky thing now?" It had happened that morning in the shower, mid-song, and again at lunch when he'd yelled for the basketball. Mr. Ruiz only grinned and said, "Ask the choir teacher. That's her frontier, not mine." Frontier, Anthony thought. Like his voice was wild, unclaimed land.

Flashback: last spring, in this same room, Anthony had sung the solo in the spring assembly without a single wobble. His voice had been light and steady, and his grandmother had recorded the whole thing on her phone. Now, three months into seventh grade, he had signed up to audition for the winter concert, and the audition was Friday. He wanted that solo more than he'd wanted anything since the new skate park opened.

So he ran an experiment. He borrowed a notebook and made a tally: every time his voice cracked, he wrote down the note he'd been trying to hit. In the shower he sang up a scale. Low notes: smooth. Middle notes: fine. High notes: crack, crack, crack. There was a distinct breaking zone, like a fence across his range. He tried warming up first, then drinking cold water, then not talking all day. Nothing moved the fence. Whatever was happening was happening on its own, invisibly, somewhere inside.

On Thursday he brought his notebook to choir practice and showed the tallies to Ms. Park. "It's the larynx," she said simply. "It grows during puberty, and the vocal folds inside it get longer and thicker, so the voice may crack while this happens." Anthony stared at his tally marks. Longer and thicker. It wasn't a fence at all; it was construction. His voice was being rebuilt, bigger.

That night he wrote a note and left it on the kitchen counter for his dad, who worked late.

Dad, I audition tomorrow. Don't be intimidated by any weird sounds from the music room, it's just my larynx renovating. Wish me luck. Anthony.

At the audition Friday, Anthony chose a lower song than the one he'd sung in spring. He reached the highest note of the new arrangement, felt a small tremor pass through like a truck on a distant road, and kept going. Ms. Park circled his name. "Solo," she said. "Second verse, low key."

Anthony punched the air so hard his pencil flew across the music room and rolled under the piano.

Aurora had exactly one week to build a model of ancient Egypt for her history project, and so far all she had was a shoebox and a lot of regret. That was why she was in the city archive on a Saturday, hunting through a drawer labeled OLD MAPS, DO NOT RESHUFFLE, which she had immediately resuffled.

"There you are," she whispered, pulling out a wide map crisscrossed with a blue ribbon of river. The Nile. Next to it, a faded pamphlet showed the pyramids, those enormous triangles squatting on the desert's edge. Her problem, the one gnawing at her, was why. Why build such gigantic things there, of all places? Her older brother Theo, who was "helping" by eating chips over her shoulder, had a theory. "Aliens," he said. "It's the only factor that makes sense."

"It is not," Aurora said, and she turned back to the map, tracing the river's floodplain with one finger. The fertile land hugged the water in a thin green ribbon, and beyond it, nothing but sand. She noticed something: the pyramids stood close to that green edge, on high, dry ground, near where the floods would stop. The river gave the farms water and silt; the farms fed the workers; the dry plateau kept the stone from sinking. Theo's alien theory was just him being biased toward anything dramatic. She could incorporate the floodplain into her model with green paper and the pyramid plateau with sandpaper. It was a testable idea, and she was about to test it.

Then Theo, reaching for another chip, knocked a folder off the shelf. Out slid a brittle page about emperors. Aurora almost shoved it back, but a line caught her eye: in 395 CE, when Emperor Theodosius I died, the Roman Empire was permanently divided, and his two sons each took one half, east and west. She held it up.

"Hey, Theo. Two brothers once split a whole empire in half, and it stayed split forever."

He stared at the paper, then at her. "So when I said we should divide the bedroom with tape down the middle, I was being historical."

"You were being annoying," Aurora said, "but also, apparently, traditional." She smoothed the map flat, grabbed her green paper, and started cutting along the river.

James stared at the jumbled tray of foam balls on his workbench and realized, not for the first time, that his whole plan might have been built on a wrong idea. In his garage, with the door half open to let in the afternoon light, he had promised his little sister Maya that he would build her a model of an atom by dinnertime. The trouble was that he had assumed every atom needed the same parts, like every sandwich needed the same two slices of bread.

He had learned this the hard way last summer, and the memory still made him wince. At the science museum he had confidently glued one big ball, one small ball, and a clump in the middle for the neutron, only to have a kid next to him squint at it and say, "That's not hydrogen." James had argued, in a vain attempt to protect his work, until the kid pointed at the chart on the wall. He had walked away without finishing the model, and he still wondered whether he should have just asked someone instead of insisting he was right.

Now he spread out the chart he had copied into his notebook and tested his idea with actual balls instead of glue. He pushed the pieces around on the bench like a puzzle. "Okay," he said to himself, "the most common kind of hydrogen atom has just one proton and one electron and no neutron at all." He set down one large red ball, then one tiny blue ball, and deliberately left the gray clump sitting alone in the tray. It looked unfinished. It looked almost like camouflage, a half-built thing pretending to be complete, but the chart said otherwise, and the chart had been right before.

Maya wandered in, sneakers squeaking on the concrete, and picked up the gray ball. "What's this lonely one for?"

"Nothing," James said. "That's the weird part. Hydrogen doesn't need it." She frowned at the two lonely balls on the wire, so he handed her the glue and the paint. "You do the electron. I'll hold the wire."

She dipped her brush in blue, and the small ball slowly turned from white to bright, spinning between her fingers.

Amelia stood on the porch of Kanya's house holding a box of oranges in both hands, exactly the way her mother had shown her. When Kanya's grandmother opened the door, the old woman pressed her palms together and bowed slightly. Amelia had no idea what to do with her hands, so she just nodded fast and hoped that counted.

Inside, everyone had left their shoes in a row by the door, so Amelia nudged her sneakers into line with the rest. She watched Kanya's little brother, Santi, who was six, dart under the dining table like a fish under a canopy of chairs and tablecloth. He popped out near Amelia and grinned up at her with a gap where his front tooth used to be. Without thinking, Amelia reached down to ruffle his hair.

"Wait," Kanya said, catching her wrist. "Don't touch his head. In Thailand the head is sacred, so touching someone's head, even to pat a child, can be seen as rude."

Amelia pulled her hand back. Santi didn't look offended, only curious, but she took Kanya seriously. She began testing her theory as the evening went on, watching closely. Kanya's father passed Santi a dish and never once patted him. When Santi fell off a chair, his mother checked his elbow, his knee, and carefully not his head. Nobody touched anybody's head at all.

At dinner, Amelia kept noticing more. The spoon went in the right hand, the fork in the left, and the fork pushed food onto the spoon. She copied Kanya move for move, and when she almost used the fork directly, she caught herself and switched.

"You're learning fast," Kanya said.

"That's because I'm extremely sophisticated," Amelia said, and immediately dropped a grain of rice on her shirt.

Santi laughed so hard he slid off his chair again. This time, when he stood up, Amelia bowed to him, palms together, just like the grandmother at the door. Santi bowed right back.

Scarlett held the tuning fork against her knee, struck it, and listened until the hum faded to nothing. The music room smelled like rosin and old radiator dust, and Mr. Petra's note on the board said only: A above middle C, 440. Find it yourself. She plucked the A string on her violin. The two sounds wobbled against each other, a sour beating she could feel in her teeth even though she couldn't see it. Something hidden was making that wobble, and she suspected it was the string being slightly too low. She turned the fine tuner a hair, plucked again. The wobble slowed. Another hair. The wobble almost vanished, and when it did, the note felt round and steady, like two waves lying exactly on top of each other. She tuned the other strings from that A, matching each one to its neighbor, guessing and correcting.

Behind her, Dex was hammering the drum set at full blast, then dropping to silence, then blasting again. He wanted the drum solo in the spring concert more than he wanted lunch, and he'd been practicing like a startled thundercloud all week.

"That's not a crescendo," Scarlett said. "A crescendo means gradually getting louder. You're doing it all at once, like a door slamming."

Dex narrowed his eyes. "So what's the opposite called?"

"Decrescendo. Or diminuendo. It means gradually getting softer." She remembered her own first rehearsal in September, when she'd slammed into a loud passage and the whole violin section had flinched, and she still wasn't sure whether the look Mr. Petra had given her was amusement or disappointment. Probably both. "Watch."

She played a scale that grew from a whisper to a swell, then shrank back down like a tide going out. Dex copied her on the drums, rolling louder by careful degrees until the windows seemed to hum, then easing off until the sound deteriorated into a faint patter like distant rain.

"That analysis of yours," Dex said, "is annoyingly correct." He tapped the rim of the snare, a brittle little tick in the quiet room, and grinned. "Again, from the top. You count us in."

Scarlett lifted her bow and said, "One, two, three, four."

Brielle sat at the kitchen table with her left arm propped on a stack of cookbooks, the fresh white cast ending just below her elbow. The fall from the dilapidated porch railing had happened three days ago, and she was still turning over what Dr. Okafor had said. "The break missed the growth plate, which is the good news," the doctor had told them, and her mother had exhaled like she'd been holding her breath since the emergency room. Brielle hadn't asked why at the time, because asking felt like admitting she didn't understand something important about her own arm.

Her little brother Theo slid into the chair across from her, holding a jar of bean seeds he'd been trying to germinate on the windowsill all week. "When your cast comes off, we're playing catch," he announced. "Every day. I've been practicing my curveball so I can finally beat you." Theo had wanted to beat her at catch since spring, and now that she was benched, he kept repeating his plan like a promise.

"Growth plate," Brielle said slowly, watching him twist the jar lid. "That's what she called it. She said near the ends of long bones are growth plates made of cartilage, and that's where bones lengthen while you're still a kid." Theo wrinkled his nose. "Cartilage? Like your ears?" "Sort of, I think. So if a break goes through it, the bone might not grow right. Mine didn't, that's why it's good news."

She went to the hall closet and found the ball of twine. If her arm bone was still lengthening, like a bean seed swelling before it sprouted, she could catch it in the act. She looped the twine from her shoulder to her wrist on the right arm, cut it, and labeled the string with a marker: RIGHT, WEEK ONE. Then she did the same for the cast side, writing LEFT over the plaster instead.

"Do you actually think it's growing right now?" Theo asked, watching her tape both strings into her notebook.

"Seeds don't sprout while you stare at them either," Brielle said. "But the beans on the sill prove things happen slow." She closed the notebook and slid it to the end of the table, where they could both see it. "Six weeks. Then we measure again, and then, curveball or not, you're going down."

Theo grinned and set his jar beside it, fungus speckling the damp cotton inside. "Race you," he said. "Beans versus bone."

Samantha spread the giant world map across two airport chairs, which was against the rules of airports everywhere, probably, and made her brother Marcus climb over her feet to get to the window seat he had been guarding since check-in. Their flight to Santiago left in two hours, and Dad had given her a mission: figure out exactly where they were going, using only the map and the strange squiggling lines all over it.

"Those are latitude and longitude," Marcus said, without looking away from the window. "Dad told you that already. Twice."

"I know what they're called," Samantha said. "What I don't know is how they work. There's a difference." She traced a finger along a horizontal line labeled 20 and then a vertical one labeled 70. Somewhere they crossed, if the lines meant anything at all, was Chile. She found Santiago, then put her finger near a pale orange patch to the north and squinted at the tiny label. Atacama Desert.

Marcus leaned over, chewing a granola bar he'd been rationing since security like it was the last one on Earth. "What are you doing now?"

"I made a climate graph last week for school, for that desert," Samantha said. "Everybody else's graph had little bars for every month's rain. Half of mine was just empty space. I thought I messed up." She frowned at the map, then at the scribbled note in her notebook from the research: some weather stations there have never recorded rain. Not a little rain. Not rare rain. Never. "I spent an hour checking my math."

Marcus laughed so hard he almost lost his granola bar out the side of his mouth. "So your graph was right and the desert is just broken?"

"The desert isn't broken, it's just the driest place." She tapped the crossing point of her two lines. "See, 20 across, 70 down, give or take. That's how you say where a city is. Dad says pilots use numbers like that for everything." She wrote "20 S, 70 W, Atacama, zero rain ever" and underlined it twice, then drew a small triumphant camel in the margin, even though camels definitely did not flourish there. She doubted many organisms did, actually, in a place with no rain at all.

Marcus peered at her notebook. "Can I draw the camel a hat? Camels look versatile, they could pull off a hat."

Samantha handed him the pencil just as the gate agent called their row, and the two of them folded the map into a lopsided square and ran.

Julia slid her coordinate grid across the table until it bumped Mr. Okoye's tray of colored pencils, and the smell of sharpened wood drifted up as Marcus grabbed two and tossed her the green one. Math club met in the cafeteria every Tuesday, and today the whiteboard read "Two-Step Equations: y = 2x + 1." Julia's problem was y = 2x + 3, and she needed two points so she could draw the line. She picked x = 1 first, because one was easy, and got y = 5. Then she wanted x = one half, just to see what would happen.

"When x is one half, I get two times one half plus three," she said, talking it through. "So that's one plus three. Four." She plotted (1, 5) and then moved carefully to the halfway point between 0 and 1 on the x-axis, and up four. Marcus leaned over, chewing the eraser end of his pencil, which Julia could perceive was his thinking habit, because he only did it when a problem had him stuck.

"I wanted x = one third," Marcus said. "But then y equals two thirds plus three, and I can't add those." He scribbled, crossed out, scribbled again. "So I multiplied the denominators instead. Three times one is three, and I turned three into three over one, so three times one gives me three over one." He frowned at his paper. "Two thirds plus nine thirds is eleven thirds. It works, but it's ugly."

Julia tried it herself with different numbers, using the flat side of her ruler as a straightedge and making a quick adaptation to her method: instead of guessing, she multiplied the denominators every time. Each answer came out correct, and each time the fraction was bigger than it needed to be, waiting to be simplified. "It always works," she said slowly. "Multiplying the denominators gives you a common denominator. Just not always the smallest one."

"So it's like a shortcut that costs you later," Marcus said. "You get there, then you have to clean up."

Julia drew her line through both points, checked it against Marcus's paper, and pressed the green pencil down hard where the two lines crossed. "Same line," she said. "Different roads."

Parker scanned the field from the third deck, popcorn warm in his lap, and counted jerseys. His uncle had budgeted exactly enough cash for two hot dogs and one souvenir each, so Parker had chosen the popcorn to make his money last. He counted again, because the first count had to be wrong. "Maya, what numbers do you see out there?" he asked his cousin. She squinted through the railing. "Seventeen, thirty-one, six, nine, eleven." Parker checked the scoreboard roster. Every player had a number, and every number was there, except one. Nobody on either team wore 42. He wondered if 42 was bad luck, or against some rule nobody had told him.

Then the whole stadium went weird. The public address announcer said it was a special ceremony before the first pitch, and every single player on both teams jogged out wearing the same jersey, all with 42 on the back. "Why is everyone dressed the same?" Maya asked, tugging Parker's sleeve. "Did they lose their laundry?" Parker didn't laugh, because he was too busy thinking. Same number on every player, on every team, at the same time. That wasn't a coincidence. That looked like something people did on purpose, together, for one number.

The woman in the next seat, there with her grandson, leaned over. "You two look puzzled." She held up her grandson's tiny foam finger, which also had a 42 on it. Maya pointed at the field. "Why does everybody have that number?" The woman smiled. "In 1997, Major League Baseball retired Jackie Robinson's number 42 for every team. First time any professional athlete was honored that way." Parker whispered the words to himself so he would remember them. Retired, for every team. Not just one club, all of them. That was why he had never seen a 42 in any game he had watched on TV, not once. He had thought it was chance. It was the opposite of chance.

His uncle came back from the concession stand and handed Maya her hot dog before she even had to ask, because he always noticed who was waiting. Parker pointed at the field. "Uncle Theo, look. Every team in baseball gave up number 42 so one man could keep it forever." His uncle sat down slowly, looked at all those matching jerseys glowing under the lights, and put his cap over his heart. "Then let's stand up," he said. "All of us."

Liam sat cross-legged on Marcus's bedroom floor with Marcus's phone, because his own phone had died on the bus and Marcus never minded sharing. He was supposed to be looking up cheat codes for Rocket Racers, but when he typed his own name into the search bar just to see what would happen, the first result made his stomach drop. It was a comment he had written two years ago, back when he was eight, under a video of a soccer match. "The goalie is so bad he has an infection of the hands," he had written, misspelling everything, and there it was now, next to his full name, glowing on the screen like it had been waiting for him.

"That's weird," Liam said. "I posted that on my old account. I deleted the whole account last year."

Marcus leaned over, chewing the last of his pretzels. "Try my name," he said. Liam typed it in, and a picture came up that Marcus's mom had posted publicly years ago, of Marcus in a bird costume for the school's migratory animals play. It had spread from one page to another, and now a stranger's blog had it, with a caption underneath that called him "this brave little flamingo."

"Search engines use crawlers," Marcus said, reading from the top of the results page. "Automated programs that copy and index public web pages." He pointed at the small gray text. "So if it's public, it can turn up in search results."

Liam tested it, because it seemed too strange to just believe. He posted a fake comment on a public video, using his first name and a made-up last name, then searched for it. At first nothing came up, but after Marcus made them both quesadillas and they came back with crumbs on their shirts, the comment appeared, sitting there in the results like a photograph pinned to a wall. He deleted the comment immediately, then thought about the flamingo picture, which had already been copied and would not go away just because Marcus asked.

"We should tell your mom about the picture," Liam said. "Before the whole school searches your name." Marcus nodded slowly, and Liam handed him the phone first, letting him decide whether to show her now or after dinner. Down in the kitchen, Marcus's mom was saturating the counter with soapy water, scrubbing a pot and humming. Marcus took a breath and held the screen out to her. "Mom, can you look at something?"

Rebecca had signed up to speak at the town hall meeting because of the bench. The old stone bench outside the library had been tagged with a bylaw that banned anyone from sitting on the plaza after 6 p.m., and her grandfather, who read the newspaper there every evening, now had nowhere to wait for her after chess club. She stood in the lobby holding her petition form, watching the double doors of the council chamber.

Beside her, a boy named Dhruv was bouncing on his heels. "I'm here about the ice rink schedule," he whispered. "They cut open skate to two hours a week and I want it back. But speaking up there feels like an audition I didn't practice for." He exhaled, then seemed to inhale his nerves right back in. "You go first. Show me how it's done."

When the chair called her name, Rebecca walked to the microphone and pushed her form across the table toward Councillor Okafor. "I'm petitioning to change the plaza bylaw," she said. "I learned how at the courthouse on our class trip. The clerk showed us that a petition has to state the bylaw, say what change you want, and carry signatures from people who live here. I have ninety-one." She paused, because a thought she'd been testing all week had finally lined up. "The clerk also told us that when a federal bill passes, the Governor General gives royal assent, and a deputy, like a Supreme Court justice, can stand in for the monarch. So even the big rules get signed by someone filling the role. Which made me think: somebody must have written our plaza bylaw too, and somebody can change it. That's why I'm here instead of just being mad about it."

The councillor turned the form toward the light and read the signatures slowly, which was tedious for Rebecca, who could feel her heart thudding the whole time. "Ninety-one names," the councillor said at last. "Including, I see, Anton Ferreira, who taught me chess in this very building. I'll move it onto next month's agenda." She slid a blank petition sheet across the table. "You'll want signatures for the change wording. Bring it to my office any Tuesday."

Rebecca carried the blank sheet back down the aisle and pressed it into Dhruv's hands. "Your turn," she whispered. "Say the bylaw, say what you want, and count your people."

Dhruf stood, straightened his jacket, and walked toward the microphone.

Nolan set the recipe card on the counter and read it top to bottom twice, the way his older sister Priya had told him to. Preheat the oven to 375. Grease the muffin pan. Stir the wet ingredients and the dry ones in separate bowls, then fold them together. He twisted the oven dial and waited for the preheat light, feeling like he had finally been trusted with something real, because Priya had promised he could bake these blueberry muffins entirely on his own while she worked on her own project: the pasta sauce simmering on the back burner, which she was determined to make thick enough to cling to a spoon.

While the bowls came together, Nolan measured the flour carefully, level with the back of a knife. Last winter, he remembered, he had tried pancakes without measuring anything, and the batter had rebelled by turning into a gluey lump that refused to flatten even in the pan. Priya had laughed until she couldn't breathe, and then she had shown him how to scoop flour lightly and sweep the cup clean. "That's why recipes exist," she had said. He wasn't going to make that mistake again, and besides, the muffins were his proof that he could feed himself something that wasn't toast.

Priya lifted the lid off her sauce and frowned. "It's still soupy. It's been twenty minutes." She stirred it and sighed toward the window. Nolan glanced over while spooning batter into the pan, and something clicked. The lid had been clamped on the whole time. "Try it with the lid off," he said. She gave him a look. "Steam can't get out with the lid on," he said. "Try it and see."

She propped the lid against the sugar jar and let the sauce bubble uncovered. By the time his muffins had risen into golden domes and he was sliding the pan onto the rack, her sauce had gone from watery to thick enough to coat the wooden spoon. "Hey, it worked," she said, dipping the spoon and tilting it slowly. "Ours both worked." Nolan pulled the oven mitt, the one with the frail thumb worn almost through, onto his hand and opened the door. "Careful," Priya said. "Hot." He lifted the pan out and set it on the rack, and the smell of blueberries filled the whole kitchen.

The snow came down all morning, and by ten o'clock the school district had given up and called a snow day. Charlie yelled so loudly that her upstairs neighbor banged on the ceiling, but she was already pulling on her boots. She texted her friend Maya, and they met at the little park on Maple Street, where the slide was frozen solid and Mrs. Park, who lived nearby, was grumbling that her landlord was negligent and still hadn't fixed the gate, so it hung crooked in the snow.

"We're building a snowman," Charlie announced. "A huge one. Three balls high." Maya knelt down and started packing, but the snow wouldn't cooperate. Every time she pressed a handful together, it sifted back apart like sugar. Charlie tried too, squeezing until her mittens ached. The ball just crumbled in her palms. "This snow is broken," Maya said, kicking at it. The powder flew up in a dry puff and drifted down again without sticking to anything.

Charlie scooped two handfuls and held them side by side, one from the shadow of the bench and one from the sunny patch near the swing set. The sunny one felt heavier, almost damp, and when she squeezed it, it held. "Feel this," she said, and Maya pressed it into a rough little ball. "Snow near freezing has some water in it," Charlie said, turning the ball over. "It's the dry stuff that falls apart." Maya looked around. Half the park sat in shade, where the snow stayed powdery and useless, and half of it was wide open to the morning sun.

"So we wait," Maya said. "It's not even noon yet." They climbed the frozen slide until their mittens froze, then took turns dragging each other on the crooked gate like a sled. Back at home, Charlie's mom made cocoa, and they watched the chocolate dissolve into the milk while the sun climbed higher.

By two o'clock they tested the shady snow again, and this time Charlie could feel the difference before she even squeezed it. The top layer packed, then the next, and the next. Their snowman stood three balls high before the shadows came back, with a stick arm waving at the swing set, and Charlie said, "Same park, same snow. We just had to wait for the sun to do its part."

Emily slid her Spanish workbook across the library table and tried to ignore the fact that her presentation was tomorrow. Sra. Alvarez wanted each student to describe their family and pets in full sentences, spoken out loud, no notes. Emily could say "tengo un perro" in her sleep. The problem was her brother Marcus, and the verb.

"You look like you're defusing a bomb," said Priya, dropping into the chair across from her with a stack of books.

"Close. I wrote 'Mi hermano está alto' on my draft, and I don't know if it's wrong." Emily turned the notebook around. "Marco helped me after class, but he was in a rush, and he changed one of my sentences and didn't say why. I can't read his handwriting." The scribble in the margin looked like "es" or maybe "e's" or possibly "ews." Her flashcards, her textbook index, and the librarian's Spanish dictionary had given her three different vibes and zero answers.

Priya leaned in. "So ask someone who actually speaks it."

"The only person I know is my brother's friend Daniela, and she thinks I'm reckless because I fed the class fish over winter break. Twice." Emily had been trying to diminish that reputation for weeks, mostly by saying hello in a very small voice.

"You have forty minutes until the library closes," Priya said. "I'm going to find a book on deep-sea organisms for my science report. You're going to text Daniela."

Emily texted. Daniela replied fast, which was either a good sign or a trap. Emily typed the sentence, sent it, and turned her phone face down on the table so she couldn't watch the three dots appear and vanish, appear and vanish. She alphabetized Priya's flashcards. She counted ceiling tiles. When she finally flipped the phone over, the message was long.

"OK so," Daniela had written, "you said your brother is tired. Like, permanently tired. Forever."

Emily stared. Marcus had slept until noon on Saturday, but that hardly seemed like a criminal accusation. She scrolled up. There it was: she had written "Mi hermano está alto" when she meant tall, and somewhere between the draft and the final copy she had swapped her verbs. She typed back, "How do I say he IS tall? Like, all the time?"

"Es," Daniela answered. "Mi hermano es alto. Es for how he always is, like tall. Está for how he is right now, like tired. Estás vs es. Not the same."

Emily copied the rule onto a fresh card and held it up to the light. Then she built her sentences one at a time, testing each one before she wrote it down: Marcus es alto. Marcus está cansado. Her dog es pequeño and, after a bath, está mojado. She read the whole paragraph aloud in a whisper while Priya shelved her organism book and gave her a thumbs-up from between the stacks.

The next morning, Sra. Alvarez called her name third. Emily stood, took a breath, and said, "Mi hermano es alto. Mi hermano está cansado." From the back row, Marcus's friend Daniela nodded once, slowly, and mouthed, "¿Y el perro?"

"Mi perro es pequeño," Emily said, "y está mojado."

Evan stood on the porch of Kenji's house holding a gift bag so tightly the paper crinkled. Inside was a box of chocolate chip cookies, because you can't visit somebody's grandmother with empty hands, that much he'd figured out on his own. Kenji's grandmother opened the door, bowed, and said something quick and musical that Evan didn't understand. He panicked, stuck out his hand, and shook hers. She laughed, a big surprised laugh, and Kenji elbowed him. "You bow, doofus. Like this." Kenji bent from the waist, and Evan copied him so fast he almost head-butted the doorframe.

At dinner there were dumplings, rice, and a huge steaming pot of ramen. Evan was starving. He was also nervous, because Kenji's grandmother had gone quiet and formal, and Evan had a bias that quiet and formal meant "watch your manners or die of embarrassment." He remembered his own family's rule: no noises at the table, ever, or his aunt would raise one eyebrow at you until your appetite diminished on the spot.

Then Kenji picked up his bowl, put his face practically in it, and slurped. Loudly. It sounded like a pool drain. Evan froze with his chopsticks in the air, waiting for the eyebrow. Instead Kenji's father slurped. Then Kenji's little sister, who couldn't have been older than six, produced a slurp so tremendous that Evan's water glass rattled.

Evan studied them, thinking fast. Nobody's face was red. Nobody was apologizing. They were all doing it, even the grandmother, and they were smiling between slurps, which meant it wasn't rude here, it was normal. It had to be. He lifted his bowl, took a breath, and slurped his noodles with everything he had.

"Beautiful!" the grandmother shouted in English, clapping. "More soup for the boy!" She ladled a second helping into his bowl before he could even swallow. Kenji grinned across the table. "Told you this family's frugal," he whispered. "Nobody wastes broth."

"Neither do I," said Evan, and slurped again.

The waiting room clock ticked past 3:40, and Arianna's audition for the spring choir started at 4:15. She twisted a crumpled tissue in her lap, the third one since she'd sat down, each stained the same worrying shade of yellow-green.

"Look," she whispered to her dad, holding it up. "It's getting worse. What if I need antibiotics before I can sing?"

A boy across the aisle, maybe ten, leaned over his own pile of tissues. "Mine's green," he said, his voice brittle with worry. "Green means infection. My sister said so. I bet I need medicine today."

Arianna's name was called before she could answer. In the exam room, Dr. Patel listened to her lungs, looked in her throat, and said, "It's a virus. Rest, fluids, and you can sing tonight if your voice holds."

"But the mucus is yellow," Arianna said. "Practically green."

Dr. Patel smiled. "The color comes from your immune cells and an enzyme they release. Green or yellow doesn't tell us whether it's bacteria or a virus." She tapped the chart. "Your exam does, and this is viral."

Arianna folded the fact into her mind like a note she could pass along. On the way out, she stopped at the pharmacy counter to pick up tissues for the boy's mother, who was juggling a toddler and her purse.

"Hey," Arianna said to the boy, handing him the pack. "I asked the doctor about the green thing. It's just your immune cells and an enzyme they release. My doctor said the color alone can't tell you if it's bacteria or a virus. Mine's green too, and I don't need medicine."

The boy's shoulders dropped an inch. "Really? So I'm not super sick?"

"You're just full of germ fighters," Arianna said. "Same as me."

At 3:58 she and her dad raced for the car. In the parking lot she tested her voice on one soft scale, and the high note came out clean and clear, like a bell through an open window.

The tent smelled like pine and cold canvas when Lily unzipped her bag the first night in the park. She set her toothpaste, her sunscreen, and a half-eaten bag of trail mix in the corner by her sleeping pad, the way she did at home. Outside, her dad was hauling the cooler from the car to the metal bear locker by the picnic table, and her mom was being optimistic about the clouds breaking up before morning. Lily could hear the whole camp settling down, quiet except for a creek somewhere behind the trees.

At breakfast the next day, a ranger walked through the loop checking lockers. She stopped at their site and looked at the picnic table, then at the tent. "Everything with a scent needs to go in the locker overnight," she said. "In Yosemite and parks like it, anything scented counts as food. That includes toothpaste, sunscreen, and trash." Lily's dad thanked her, and the ranger moved on to the next campsite.

Lily sat with her granola bar halfway to her mouth and thought about that. Toothpaste counted as food? It was minty, not edible, at least not on purpose. She tried to imagine a bear caring about sunscreen. The rule seemed strange until she considered how a bear searches, not with its eyes but with its nose, and a nose did not sort things the way a grocery store did. If it smelled like something, it was something.

That evening she offered to transport the last load to the locker herself. She packed the toothpaste, the sunscreen, and the empty wrapper from her dad's sandwich, and she counted the items as she placed them inside, one by one, keeping her own little economy of scents, everything tallied, nothing left over. She zipped the tent empty and walked back under a sky going dark and blue.

"Did we get everything?" her mom called from the fire.

"Every single thing with a smell," Lily said. "The tent is clean."

Isabella slid her notebook across the library table and tapped the page where she had written, in her best cursive, "Dogs are smarter than cats." The writing club had exactly fifty minutes before the librarian kicked everyone out for a chess tournament, and her five-paragraph persuasive essay was due at the next meeting.

"Your thesis looks solid," said Marcus, peeking over. "Mrs. Ruiz called it a working thesis, remember? Because it can change."

"It's not changing," Isabella said. "I have three days of evidence to gather." She opened the library's dog encyclopedia and started copying facts. Dogs guide blind people. Dogs sniff out bombs. That was paragraph two sorted already.

Then she found the cat book someone had left beside the chair, and it ruined everything. Cats solve puzzle boxes. Cats recognize their owners' voices. One study, she read with growing horror, tested both animals on the same puzzle, and the cats finished faster.

"You look like you swallowed a bee," said Priya, sliding into the next seat and handing her a spare pencil without being asked, because Priya always noticed who needed things.

"My evidence says cats are smarter." Isabella turned the book around. "If I ignore this, my essay is a lie. If I use it, my essay argues the opposite of my thesis."

"So argue the opposite," said Marcus, shrugging. "That's why it's a working thesis. If the evidence points somewhere else, you revise it instead of pretending the evidence doesn't exist."

Isabella stared at the page. She crossed out her old thesis with one dramatic stroke, which felt spontaneous and slightly heroic, and wrote, "Intelligence depends on what you measure." Then she paused. "Wait. If my thesis changed, my whole introduction changed too. My first paragraph says dogs are obviously smarter."

"That's why you draft the introduction after the body," Priya said, already delegating jobs around the table with the calm authority of someone with a reputation for finishing essays on time. "Marcus, find her one more cat study. I'll check her conclusion."

Isabella read her new introduction aloud, quietly, testing it like a recipe. The clock above the biography shelf showed ten minutes left. "Cats and dogs can both be brilliant," she whispered, "depending on the test."

Marcus flipped a page and held it up. "Found one. Cats beat dogs again."

"Perfect," said Isabella, and wrote it down.

Christopher sat on Marcus's floor with the phone box in his lap, because tomorrow was the big day and Marcus's dad had picked the phone up early so they could set it together. The plan had one catch, and Christopher had read it four times: two gigabytes of data a month, and that was all. He wanted to know what actually ate the data, since you couldn't watch it disappear.

"It's the videos," Marcus said. "Obviously."

"But Grandpa sends me videos of geese and they barely count," Christopher said. He remembered last fall, when Grandpa texted him a clip of a big migratory flock passing over the lake, and the data meter barely moved. That was the clue. So he borrowed Marcus's phone and ran a test: he played one video with the wifi off and wrote down the number, then played the same video on wifi and checked again. The wifi number stayed flat. It wasn't videos that used data. It was videos without wifi. The hidden rule showed itself, and Christopher felt like he'd pulled a curtain back.

"My dad says there's a poster at the store," Marcus said, pulling up a picture on his tablet. "It's supposed to depict the very first handheld cellular call ever made. Some Motorola engineer named Martin Cooper made it right on a New York street on April 3, 1973."

"Fifty years before phones like this," Christopher said, holding up the slim box. "Pocket phones are older than my parents."

Marcus read a message out loud that his sister had sent from the store: "Kid in front of me asked how long people have carried phones around. Manager said 1973. Kid said, 'That's it?' and everyone laughed."

Christopher texted his dad: I figured out the data. Wifi at home for videos. Regular stuff is fine anywhere. Dad sent back one word: "Deal."

Christopher slid the phone under his pillow like a buried treasure and set his alarm for tomorrow.

Ella set down her fork when Grandpa Marcus slid his phone across the table, screen up. "Look at this. The river's over the road by the mill. They're saying everyone in the low houses has to evacuate tonight." The photo showed brown water swallowing a stop sign, and it was so sharp it could have been taken that afternoon. Marcus wanted to drive over and help his friend Ruben move furniture before the water came, and he was already reaching for his jacket.

Ella's little brother Theo leaned over her shoulder to mimic the face of the frightened man in the photo, but Ella wasn't laughing. Something about the picture tickled her memory. Last summer, when their cousin had forwarded a shark photo that was "definitely this week," Ella had learned about reverse image search from a video she'd watched on a rainy afternoon. You could show the search engine a picture instead of typing words, and it would show you where that photo had appeared online before. If it had shown up years earlier, then someone was passing an old picture off as new. She took Grandpa's phone, pressed the photo until a menu appeared, and chose the search option.

"Dinner's getting cold," Mom said gently, spooning more rice onto Theo's plate because he always ate more when he was nervous. "Marcus, sit. Five minutes." The search results loaded. There it was, the exact same stop sign, the same tilted mailbox, on a news site from years back. "That flood already happened," Ella said. "This photo's from way before today." Grandpa's hand dropped away from his jacket. He called Ruben, and Ruben's voice came through the speaker, warm with relief, saying the river was low and he'd just been down there fishing.

"Where'd you learn that trick?" Grandpa asked, and there was something distinct in his voice, part embarrassment, part pride. "The internet tried to fool you and you caught it." Theo jabbed his elbow toward Ella, then winced and rubbed it, muttering that he'd bruised the cartilage. "That's not where cartilage is," Ella said, but she passed him the last of the bread anyway. Grandpa raised his glass of sweet tea. "To the fact-checker of the family." Ella tapped her fork against her glass until it rang.

Sadie pressed her nose close to the glass wall of the AgZone barn, where the science center kept three pigs beside its farm exhibits. It was the hottest day of the school year, and the field trip had already included a planetarium show and a room full of Tesla coils, but this was the part she had been waiting for. All three pigs lay in a shallow brown puddle, moving so little they looked like statues.

"They're just dirty," said Marcus, elbowing in beside her. "That's all pigs do. Roll in mud because they like being gross."

Sadie wasn't sure. She crouched down and watched. The smallest pig climbed out, trotted to the water trough, drank, then flopped back into the puddle on its side with a satisfied grunt. It did this twice more in ten minutes. The other two never left the shade of the barn roof, but their mud had dried pale and cracked on their backs, and one of them waddled over to the sprinkler line near the fence and stood in the spray. A pig that only wanted to be dirty wouldn't keep choosing water, Sadie thought. There was a rule underneath this, something the pigs knew and nobody had said out loud.

She found a small placard near the trough and read it twice, then walked back to Marcus with the whole pattern clear in her head.

"Pigs have very few working sweat glands," she said. "So they wallow in mud or water to cool off on hot days."

"So the mud is like their air conditioning," Marcus said slowly.

"Exactly. It's not about being dirty at all."

When the class gathered near the bus, their teacher asked someone to summarize the visit for the morning announcements. Sadie raised her hand and gave a quick report, ending with the pigs. On the ride home, Marcus looked out the window at the sun-baked fields and turned to her.

"Next hot day, I'm sitting near the sprinkler too," he said. "Right beside them."

Elliot pushed his peas around his plate while his sister Maya talked and talked. She played forward on the Riverside Ravens, and tonight she had news.

"Guess who has the best shooting percentage in the whole league," Maya said, grinning across the tranquil kitchen. "Me. One hundred percent. The website says so."

Dad raised his eyebrows. "Better than Kelsey Okafor?"

"Better than everybody."

Elliot set down his fork. Kelsey Okafor had scored nineteen goals this season; he'd watched her slot three in one game from the bleachers, hugging his jacket around himself because the wind off the field cut right through it, nothing to insulate him but that thin jacket. He tried to remember Maya ever taking a shot. He pictured game after game, her passing, passing, passing, always looking for the open teammate. He could not recall a single shot.

"How many shots have you actually taken?" he asked.

Maya's grin flickered, just for a second. "That doesn't matter. A percentage is a percentage."

Elliot went and got the laptop from the hall. The league site listed every player, ranked by shooting percentage, and Maya sat at the top with 1 for 1, one hundred percent. Kelsey sat seventh with 46 for 61, which worked out to seventy-five percent. From one perspective the ranking looked like the whole truth. Elliot scrolled and counted the shots column again, just to be sure. One shot. Maya had taken one shot all season.

"You made one out of one," he said slowly. "If you'd taken that one shot in the first game and never played again, you'd still be perfect."

Maya stabbed a meatball. "I'm still ranked first."

"Ranked first on one shot." He turned the laptop toward her. "Kelsey made forty-six. She just missed some too."

Dad leaned over to look, and Maya stared at the two numbers side by side, her finger hovering over the screen. Finally she laughed, a short surprised sound.

"Fine," she said. "Saturday, I'm taking at least five shots."

Brielle sat in the big chair and read the chart on the far wall. The top letter, an E, looked like someone had dragged a thumb through wet paint. She held her book up close and the words smeared the same way, which was the whole reason she was here. It had to be the chart, she had told herself for months. It couldn't be her eyes, because eyes went blurry either near or far, not both. She was optimistic about that theory right up until the second row of letters turned to gray streaks.

The optometrist swung a metal device in front of her face and flipped lenses into it, one click at a time. "Better or worse?" Click. "Better or worse?" At the third flip the E snapped into shape, so sharp and black that Brielle sat up straight. Then the optometrist turned the lens a quarter turn in its frame, and the smear came back, sideways now, like the E had been stretched.

"Try turning it back," Brielle said. The optometrist raised an eyebrow but let her reach up and rotate the lens herself. Sharp. Turn it. Blurry. Sharp again. She did it twice more to be sure. The blur changed with the direction of the turn, which meant it wasn't random. "So it's not the chart and it's not the distance," she said slowly. "It's something about direction. My eye curves more one way than the other, so it smears everything, near or far."

"That's called astigmatism," the optometrist said. "Your cornea is shaped more like an egg than a sphere." She wrote numbers on a pad. "We'll fix it."

A week later Brielle put on her new glasses in the parking lot and stopped walking. The stop sign across the street had letters with edges, actual edges. She read a license plate, then her own hand, then the fine print on a parking meter, just because she could. Her little brother was tugging her sleeve toward the car, where their dad was checking a leaking tire valve, but she stood one more second, staring at a brick wall, counting bricks.

"Come on," her brother said. "You can look at bricks later."

Logan had exactly one class period to figure out why the Egyptians built the pyramids and what the Nile had to do with their farms, because his poster was due tomorrow and so far it said, in giant letters, PYRAMIDS: BIG. He spread three books across the library table and began to monitor his progress with a sticky note he labeled EVIDENCE. So far the note said "grain?" which was not going to impress anybody.

Priya slid into the seat across from him with her own project, a thin old book wrapped in a paper towel. "My grandma lent me this," she said. "It's a settler's diary from her house. I'm supposed to write about the trail years." She opened it carefully. "This guy writes about crossing a river. He says it was the hardest week of his life. Oxen, mud, everything."

Logan leaned over. The handwriting was cramped and brown at the edges. "He crossed a whole nation's land, though. Doesn't he mention who was already living there?" Priya flipped pages. "No. It's all oxen and mud." She frowned. "One guy's diary, one guy's view." She tapped the page. "I guess a settler's diary rarely tells how the Native American nations whose lands the trails crossed saw the same events. I'd need their side too, or I'm only telling half the trail."

Logan sat back so fast his chair squeaked. Half. He looked down at his stack: every book he had told the pharaohs' story, because the pharaohs were the ones who hired the writers. He grabbed a fresh sheet and started again, this time drawing the Nile first. The river flooded every year, so farms got water and rich mud, so there was grain, so thousands of workers could be fed while they stacked stones for a pharaoh's tomb. Then he added a second column: what the workers themselves might have said about it, if anyone had asked them.

"Ms. Ruiz says we have a silverfish problem," Priya whispered, pointing at a trap near the returns cart. "Little parasites that eat the glue in book spines." Logan packed up his poster paper and grinned. "Then let's get out of here before they eat my evidence."

At the French booth at the cultural festival, Penelope clutched her practice sheet and inhaled the smell of butter and melted sugar. Her task: by the end of the afternoon, she had to introduce her whole family and her dog Biscuit in French, using complete sentences, no English allowed. She had practiced all week. "J'ai un chien," she whispered. "Il s'appelle Biscuit."

She spotted the perfect practice partner, a boy about her age waiting at the crêpe stand with a handful of coins. His little sister tugged his sleeve and pointed at a chocolate crêpe. The boy frowned at his coins, then at the price sign, which was smudged beyond reading. Penelope realized he needed to ask the cost, and from the banner above the booth she remembered the phrase written in curly letters: "C'est combien ?" She had also heard the vendor say "Combien ça coûte ?" a minute earlier. Both meant "How much is it?" That was a concept worth testing.

She marched over. "C'est combien ?" she asked the vendor, figuring the boy would hear the answer too. The vendor smiled and said, "Trois euros." The boy's face transformed from worry to relief because he had four euros. "Merci," he told her. "Combien ça coûte ?" he then asked, pointing at a second crêpe, using the other phrase he'd just picked up. "Deux euros cinquante," the vendor answered. The boy counted again and bought crêpes for both of them, one for Penelope, since she'd saved him from a smudged-sign disaster.

Between warm, gooey bites they practiced. "J'ai une soeur," the boy said. "J'ai un frère," Penelope answered, then added, "J'ai un chien. Il s'appelle Biscuit." She rattled off her mother, her father, and her terrible cat in full sentences, and the boy clapped. Later, at the festival stage, when the booth leader asked who could introduce their family in French, Penelope's hand shot up first. She stood tall under the lights and began, "J'ai une famille formidable."

Colton held the thermometer like a sword and pointed it at the chicken thighs sizzling on the grill. "Mom said chicken has to hit 165 degrees Fahrenheit in the thickest part before it's done. That's about 74 degrees Celsius, if you want the fancy version."

His little sister Nadia leaned over the picnic table, chin in her hands. "It looks done. It's all brown. Can we eat now? I want dinner before my show starts."

"Brown isn't the boss of chicken," Colton said. He poked the probe into the biggest thigh, right into the thickest part like Mom had shown him, and watched the numbers climb. 140. 148. The smell was making his stomach growl, and he was optimistic they'd eat within the minute. 151. Then it stopped.

"Stuck," he muttered. Why would it stop? He looked at the grill, and in the context of the flaming coals below, one side was practically a bonfire while the other side had gone gray and cool. He'd stacked all the coals on the left. The chicken over there was racing ahead while the right side lagged behind. He couldn't see heat, but the thermometer could, and it was telling him the truth: uneven fire, uneven dinner.

He slid the slow pieces toward the hot side, moved the fast ones away, and gave it another two minutes. Nadia groaned like a deflating balloon. "Your show will still exist," Colton said. "Raw chicken won't forgive us."

He tested the biggest thigh again. 167.

"Done!" He plated it triumphantly. "Sixty-five plus two for luck."

Nadia bit in, chewed, and paused. "Okay, this is actually amazing. You may cook forever."

Colton took a dramatic bow with the thermometer. "Every meal, madam. That'll be one remote control."

She slid the remote across the table. "Worth it."

Aubrey crouched by the fence with her notebook, drawing the chain she had to turn in Monday: sun, then the tropical milkweed in the corner, then the monarch caterpillars that chewed it, then the mockingbird that patrolled the yard, and at the top, the red-tailed hawk that circled every afternoon. She was halfway through the arrow from caterpillar to bird when she counted the milkweed stems and her stomach dropped. The caterpillars were gone. Every one.

Her little brother Theo came out with a snack, celery in one hand and a folded piece of ham in the other. He bit the celery and it snapped so loud the mockingbird flinched. "Why does this crack like that," Theo asked, "and the ham just bends?" Aubrey took a stalk and pressed it. It resisted, then gave way all at once. She remembered the science book open on her bed: plant cells have a stiff cell wall outside the cell membrane, made mostly of cellulose. "Cellulose," she said, mostly to herself. "Animal cells don't have that wall." Theo nodded like this settled something and wandered toward the garden.

That was when she noticed it. The milkweed was brown at the base, the leaves curling, and she saw the green hose coiled beside it, still dripping. Someone had left the sprinkler aimed there for days, or worse, Dad had sprayed something. She knelt and dug her fingers into the soil. It smelled sour, like the compost bin where the fallen apples slowly decompose. Whatever had killed the plant was still working in the ground.

She tested it the only way she could. She picked one healthy stem from a pot by the porch, the one she'd grown from seed, and set it near the fence where the caterpillars used to cross. Then she waited behind the shed, notebook flat on her knees, pencil still. The mockingbird came first, landed, found nothing, left. The hawk circled at four o'clock, higher than usual, and drifted off toward the creek without stopping.

"Monday," Aubrey said to Theo, tapping her drawing. "I'm going to explain what happens when a link disappears, because I just watched it."

At Sunday dinner, Jaxon's little sister Zoe and his cousin Marcus started fighting before the rolls even hit the table. Zoe wanted the chair by the window. Marcus wanted the chair by the window. Aunt Rosa kept saying "somebody has to give in," which Jaxon knew from experience would end with somebody crying into the mashed potatoes.

He watched them instead of eating. Zoe kept glancing at the window itself, where a cardinal was hopping along the ledge. Marcus kept shifting his plate so it wouldn't sit on the wobbly spot in the table, which the window chair avoided because it was the one chair on solid floor. That was interesting. They both demanded the same seat, but they weren't actually demanding the same thing.

"Hold on," Jaxon said. "Zoe, why the window chair? Not because it's yours. Why?"

"The bird," Zoe said. "I can see it from there."

"Marcus?"

"My plate tips at the other spots. Gravy slides off."

Grandpa, who was buttering bread like the argument was a TV show, raised an eyebrow at Jaxon. "You figured something out, kid. I can tell by your face."

"A position is what somebody demands," Jaxon said. "An interest is the reason they want it."

Grandpa pointed his butter knife. "Now you're cooking."

Jaxon turned the butter dish toward Zoe so the light caught it. "Zoe, take my chair. It's two seats over, and the window's still right there, you can watch the bird fine. Marcus gets the solid spot."
