Zoe moved, the cardinal flared red against the glass, and she actually said thank you, which happened maybe twice a year.

After dinner, Marcus pulled out his phone. "Best of three in Street Racer?"

They were tied at one game each when it happened. Both of them grabbed for the last controller, the good one with the sticky-free triggers. "I won the last round, it's mine," Marcus said. "It's my house," Jaxon said, and then he stopped, because he heard himself doing exactly what Zoe and Marcus had done over the chair.

"Wait. My position is I get the controller. My interest is I want fair triggers so the race is even." He looked at Marcus. "What's yours?"

"I don't care about triggers. My battery's at four percent. My interest is I want a controller that won't die mid-race."

"You're immune to the sticky trigger thing?"

"Completely. I barely notice it."

"So we're not actually contradicting each other," Jaxon said. "We only sound like it." He brought the good controller to the charger by the couch, plugged in the weaker one, and handed it to Marcus. "Yours, charged in ten minutes. Race after."

Marcus plugged it in and grinned. "You're weird now, you know that?"

Jaxon shrugged and picked up the good controller for practice laps, listening for the soft click of the triggers under his thumbs.

Evelyn pressed the last wire into the clip and held her breath. The bulb stayed dark. Somewhere behind her, a boy was shouting at the radar-speed pitching cage, and the noise made her fingers feel clumsy.

"Try jiggling the switch," said the boy, whose name tag read Marcus. He was lanky and loud, and he had been pacing by her table since she sat down at the Build-a-Circuit station. "Mine lit up on the first try."

"I don't want it to light by accident," Evelyn said, turning the switch over in her hand. "I want to know why it lights." She bent the little metal arm and saw it, a gap where the arm touched only air instead of the screw. A circuit was invisible, a loop of something you couldn't watch move, so she had to picture it, like water in a hidden pipe. She slid the screw closer until the arm pressed flat against it. The bulb glowed.

"Your fastball was twenty meters per second," the museum attendant called to Marcus, whose throw had just clocked on the radar screen. "That beats a walker for sure."

"Does it beat a runner?" Marcus asked. "Runners go, like, twenty kilometers per hour. I don't even know how to compare those."

Evelyn had read a placard near the entrance, a small chart half hidden behind a case of glass that refracted the overhead lights into little rainbows on the wall. She hesitated, then said, "To change a speed in meters per second into kilometers per hour, you multiply by 3.6." She did it in the margin of her worksheet. "Twenty times 3.6 is 72 kilometers per hour."

"Seventy-two!" Marcus yelled. "That's faster than cars in a school zone!"

Evelyn smiled and unscrewed her bulb, then screwed it back in, watching the light return. On the far wall, an exhibit about glowing fungus flickered in its dark case, tiny lights like the one in her hand.

"Throw again," she said, picking up a spare ball. "I bet mine's faster."

Lauren had to negotiate for the lamp, because Marcus was notorious for claiming the best equipment and then fiddling with it for the whole period. "You hold the ball," she said, "I get the lamp. Deal?" Marcus considered this, then agreed, which surprised her so much she almost forgot what she was doing.

The ball was their Moon and the lamp was the Sun. Lauren switched it on and dimmed the classroom lights, and Marcus walked the ball in a slow circle around her. That was the plan. The problem started when Priya, watching from her desk, shouted, "It's full!" and Devon, watching from the other side of the room, shouted, "It's new!" They argued until Ms. Okafor said, calmly, "Both of you are looking at the same ball." Lauren stared. Half the ball was lit and half was dark, always, no matter where it stood. The phase you saw depended on where you stood, and whether the lit side faced you or away from you. She made Marcus walk the circle again while she spun slowly in place, and there it was: full, then gibbous, then half, then a sliver, then dark, and back again. "Ha!" she said. "I'm Earth. I'm doing the phases."

Later, at recess, the sprinkler line by the fence had leaked all week, and a little stream ran across the blacktop and into the retention pond. At the edge of the water, Devon pointed at a fan of wet sand, spread out like a tiny triangle. "What made that? The water just stops there."

"The stream slows down when it hits the pond," Lauren said, "and it drops all the sand it was carrying, so the sand builds up and makes new land. That's called a delta."

"That's it? That's the whole trick?"

"Rivers do it too," Lauren said, "when they reach a lake or the sea." She crouched, poked the wet edge of the fan with a stick, and said, "I made half the Moon phases with a lamp and a tennis ball this morning. I'm basically unstoppable."

Marcus snorted. "You negotiated that lamp from me, is what happened."

"Same thing," said Lauren, and drew a delta in the sand with her stick, one careful line at a time.

Arianna stood in the dressing room with her violin tucked under her arm, watching the mirror shake whenever somebody slammed a locker. Tonight was the first school concert she had ever played in, and her hand kept sliding up the neck of the violin because her palm was sweating. Her friend Marcus, who played oboe, sat on the bench eating carrot sticks. "Those are nutritious," Arianna said, mostly to think about something other than the stage. "You're going to be the important one out there anyway."

"How do you figure?" Marcus asked.

"Every rehearsal, nobody plays a single note until you do. Then everyone tunes to that one tone, all at once. I've been watching for three weeks." She pulled the spine of her music binder straight so she could read her own notes, the ones she kept in the margins. "I want to test it tonight. If I tune to you before you play, and everyone else tunes to you after, we should sound exactly the same. If we don't, then I'm tuning to something else and I don't know what."

"What if it doesn't work?" Marcus asked.

"Then I find out why." She had looked it up in the library book about orchestras, and she could cite the page if anyone doubted her: orchestras tune to a concert A played by the oboe, because its pitch is steady and its penetrating sound is easy for everyone to hear. Nobody had explained it to her. She had noticed the waiting, asked the book, and matched the two together like puzzle pieces.

Backstage, the curtain went up and the lights hit the rows of chairs. Marcus stood, lifted his oboe, and played a single A that seemed to cut straight through the whole hall. Arianna set her fingers, tuned her A string to him, and heard the cellos and flutes settle around the same note like birds landing on one wire. When her turn came in the first piece, her entrance was clean, and her spine straightened up on its own.

After the last song, Marcus found her in the wings. "So it worked?"

"Perfect match," Arianna said, and held up her hand for a high five.

The bee was held in the back room of the public library, where the folding chairs smelled like old paper and the radiator clicked in the corner. Rose sat in the second row with her number pinned to her sweater, number fourteen, watching the other spellers take their turns beneath the tall windows.

The moderator was a librarian named Ms. Okafor, who pronounced each word twice and then folded her hands on the podium. When it was Rose's turn, she stood at the microphone and received the word "pinnace," which means a small boat. She knew it was a vessel, not a large one, and she knew the word came from a language she couldn't quite pin down.

"P I N N A C..." She stopped. Her stomach dropped. It needed another N in the middle, she was almost sure of it. But she had already said one N, and only one.

She looked at Ms. Okafor. "Can I start over?"

"You may start the word again," Ms. Okafor said. "But if you change any letters you've already said, that counts as a misspelling."

Rose stood very still. So she could begin again from the P, but the letters had to come out in the same order, the same ones, or she was finished. The rule felt arbitrary to her, like being told you could retrace your steps but not fix where they'd landed. There was no way to sneak the second N in. If she started over, the first N would still be a single N.

She tested it in her head, saying the whole word silently. P, I, double N, A, C, E. If she began again, she'd have to say "P, I, N" and then she'd be trapped in the same spot. Starting over changed nothing. The only question left was whether the word truly had two N's, and she had to decide that now, inside her own head, where nobody could help her.

She thought of the word "channel," which her class had once been asked to categorize as words with double letters or not. Channel had two N's. She thought of how "pinnace" sounded when Ms. Okafor said it, the little hiccup in the middle, pin-nace, the way you'd say "manner" or "dinner."

"P I N N A C E," Rose said slowly, finishing where she'd stopped without starting over.

The bell did not ring. "Correct," Ms. Okafor said, and the boy in the front row clapped once before catching himself.

Rose walked back to her seat, her knees a little watery, and watched the next speller step up to the microphone.

The funeral home smelled like carnations and old hymnals, and Ruby sat in the third pew twisting a tissue into a rope. Grandma June's casket sat near the altar covered in a spray of yellow roses, which would have made Grandma June snort, because she had always said roses were too showy and daisies were the only honest flower. Ruby's mother leaned over and whispered the worst possible sentence: "Pastor Dan wants you to say a few words up there. Just a little eulogy."

Ruby's stomach dropped through the pew and into the basement. She knew people gave speeches at funerals, but she had never heard the word before, and it sounded like a medical procedure. In the front row, her cousin Dex was drawing what appeared to be a shark in the margin of the program, and when Ruby slid next to him he showed her his sketch of "Grandma's spirit animal," a predatory shark wearing Grandma's reading glasses. Ruby laughed once, a small hiccup of a sound in the quiet church, and felt slightly braver for it.

"What's a eulogy?" she whispered. Dex shrugged, but the woman in the next pew, Aunt Fran, leaned in. "A speech praising the person who died," she said softly. "The word comes from Greek roots meaning to speak well of." Ruby turned that over. Praise. That meant one good thing, the best thing, spoken out loud in front of a hundred people whose eyes would all be on her. She started making a list in her head and then, one by one, had to abandon every memory that involved the dress Grandma sewed inside out, or the time she called the pizza place to complain about a pizza she had not ordered from them. Too funny, maybe. Or exactly funny enough.

The pianist finished playing, and Pastor Dan said her name. Ruby stood, walked the long carpet to the lectern, and discovered her legs worked fine, which felt like an anomaly because the rest of her was shaking like a wind chime in a storm. She looked out at the crowd, took a breath, and began.

"Grandma June believed daisies were the only honest flower," she said, "and she made the best grilled cheese in three counties, and she let me have the first tomato every summer even though technically it was her garden." She told about the tomato, how Grandma would hand it over warm from the sun and say, "Taste that and tell me the store sells anything close." Ruby could hear her voice saying it, clear as a bell.

When she finished and sat back down, Dex nudged her and held up the shark drawing, which he had labeled "Swimming Somewhere Warm." Ruby took it, folded it carefully, and put it in her pocket next to the tissue rope. Then she reached over and straightened one yellow rose in the spray, so it stood up straight instead of slumping. "You're still too showy," she whispered, "but you'll do."

The bean plant by the window had drooped overnight, and Alexis had ten minutes before the bell to figure out why. Her lab partner, Marcus, leaned over the pot and said, "That plant is ugly. It's the worst one in the room." Alexis frowned. "That doesn't help. I think somebody forgot to water it, and that's a claim we can actually test." Marcus shrugged. "It's my opinion. You can't prove an opinion wrong." Alexis stopped, spoonful of gravel for drainage in hand, because that sentence was exactly what her older brother had shouted at dinner last night before their mom made them both go to bed.

She scrutinize every part of the setup. The soil was dry and pulling away from the sides of the pot, so the plant had not been watered, that much was certain. But the control plant two tables over had also been skipped and it looked fine. So lack of water alone could not be the whole answer. Marcus tapped the window glass. "This one gets cooked by the sun all afternoon. That window is like a toaster." Alexis checked the blinds, which hung half open, and then felt the leaves. Warm, almost hot. Her reasoning went like this: dry soil plus hot leaves, versus dry soil and cool leaves across the room. The difference was the window.

"We water both plants the same amount," she said, pulling the blinds down on their side only, "and see which one perks up by tomorrow." Marcus wrote it on a sticky note and slapped it on the pot like a tiny flag. When Ms. Ortiz walked past, she raised an eyebrow at the flag, and Marcus pointed at Alexis. "Her experiment. I'm the official note writer. It comes with benefits." Ms. Ortiz moved on, but Alexis noticed she turned down the radiator near their table on her way, which had to mean something.

The classroom grew tranquil as the last students packed up. Alexis snapped a photo of the droopy plant so tomorrow they would have proof, not just a memory of it. On her way out she grabbed the watering can and topped off the control plant too, because fair tests deserved fair treatment. "Tomorrow," Marcus said at the door, holding it open for her, "we find out if I'm wrong." Alexis grinned. "You're wrong about the ugly part either way. That bean plant is my favorite one in the room, and nobody can test me on that."

Joshua's class had come to the courthouse for a mock legislature, and Ms. Ferrante had promised a prize for whoever could explain a bill's journey best. That's what Joshua wanted, the prize and the glory, but first they had twenty minutes to wait in the lobby. He wandered past the security desk and stopped in front of a framed poster. It showed a document with a heading, The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and below the title, a date: proclaimed April 17, 1982. He read it twice. His little sister was eleven in dog years compared to that document. He'd assumed rights were just always there, like air. If the Charter became part of the Constitution in 1982, what had people had before that?

He found Priya by the water fountain and pointed at the poster. "Look at the year. Nineteen eighty-two. That's after our parents were born."

"So it's like a bill," Priya said. "It had to pass through the legislature too, sort of. It didn't just appear."

That gave Joshua an idea. He decided to decompose the problem, break it into pieces the way Ms. Ferrante taught them for word problems. A bill starts as an idea, gets introduced, gets debated, gets voted on, and then, if it survives, becomes law. If he could trace the Charter's path, he'd understand the whole system, because it followed the same rule.

When the mock session started, the guide handed Joshua's team a bill about bike helmets on municipal paths. Joshua argued against it at first, thinking a fun field trip shouldn't involve rules. Then Priya whispered, "Think about the poster. Rights got written down because people debated them." He changed his mind mid-debate, which surprised him, and stood up to speak in favor.

"An idea has to travel through the legislature," he said. "Like the Charter, proclaimed on April 17, 1982, becoming part of Canada's Constitution. It's the irony of rules, we have to debate them to be free."

"The irony," the guide repeated, smiling, "is that the kid who opposed the bill just made the most influential speech of the day."

The vote passed, six to two, and Ms. Ferrante wrote Joshua's name at the top of the scoreboard.

John stood in the middle of Ms. Reyes's studio between two rubber plants she called "the choir" and tried, for the fourth time, to sing the low part of "Emperor of the Popsicle Kingdom" while Priya sang the high part. Every single time, his voice climbed up to join hers, like a dog escaping a yard to chase a squirrel. Ms. Reyes played along on her old guitar, but halfway through the verse she stopped, let the strings ring out, and frowned at the instrument as if it had betrayed her.

"That low string's gone flat again," she said. "Controversial little thing. Here, John, hold the neck and turn that peg while I pluck. I'll tell you when it matches my pitch pipe." John gripped the peg and scrutinized it, turning it slowly one way, then the other. When he twisted it left, the note sagged lower, all droopy and sad. When he twisted it right, tighter, the note rose back up. The string rang against her pitch pipe and finally matched, and John felt like he'd solved a tiny mystery, even if the mystery was only a stubborn piece of wood and wire.

Then came the twist, because Priya was watching him with her chin in her hand like a detective. "Wait," she said. "That's your whole problem. Your voice is like that string. When you get nervous, you go loose, and loose goes lower, except your low part isn't low enough, so your brain drags you sideways into my part instead." John opened his mouth to argue, then closed it. It actually fit. Every time he lost his part, he'd been sagging flat first, then grabbing the nearest safe sound, which was her.

"Tightening a string raises its pitch," John said slowly, "and loosening it lowers it. So I need to tighten. Not louder. Tighter." Ms. Reyes raised an eyebrow, clearly deciding not to rescue him. John planted his feet, imagined an invisible peg behind his ear, and gave it a firm twist to the right in his imagination. Priya started the high part. John held his line, steady and low, and for the first time the two notes stacked together instead of crashing like shopping carts.

"Emperor of the popsicle kingdom, please grant me a fudgy crown," they sang, and it worked, it actually worked, both parts locking together like zippers. At the end Priya pointed at him and said, "You may address me as the emperor now." John bowed so low he knocked over a rubber plant, caught it mid-topple, and set it back upright while Ms. Reyes strummed a dramatic finish.

Naomi stood at the door of the community hall holding a box of dates she had bought with her allowance. Her best friend Samir had invited her to come along with his family, and she had one morning to figure out a puzzle. Last night, when she asked what gift to bring, Samir had said, "Bring dates," but the ones at the store came in three sizes, and she had guessed the small box, because everyone at the hall would surely be saving their appetite for later.

Inside, the long tables were already crowded with plates of samosas, sweet sev, and a mountain of sheer khurma. Samir's grandmother pressed a warm bowl of it into Naomi's hands. Naomi took one bite, then stopped. "Wait," she said to Samir. "Aren't you still fasting until sunset? Should you cease eating right now?"

Samir laughed so hard he nearly dropped his plate. "It's Eid al-Fitr," he said. "That's the celebration marking the end of Ramadan, the month when we fast from dawn until sunset. Nobody's fasting today. That's the whole point."

Naomi felt her face go warm. She looked down at the small box of dates in her bag. She had spent nine dollars on it, expecting a crowd of hungry people who would not touch food until dark. Now she could see dozens of families eating and laughing at ten in the morning, and her gift looked tiny. The gift table stood near the stage, and the volunteers would carry everything to the kitchen at noon, when the games began. She had two hours.

She tried to think of it from Samir's perspective. A month of no food or water between dawn and sunset, and then one morning of feasting. Of course everyone wanted to eat now, all at once, all together. That was the pattern she had missed. So what did a hall full of people who had just finished a month of fasting actually need? She remembered the water station by the entrance, where a line of kids waited for paper cups.

Naomi walked to the kitchen and found a volunteer stacking trays. "Could I trade this box of dates for a job?" she asked. "I could refill the water cups. There's a long line." The volunteer, an uncle with a whiskered smile, said that refilling was the most controversial job in the hall, because last year two boys had argued over who got to hold the pitcher, and he had decided girls poured better. He handed her the big blue pitcher.

For the next hour Naomi carried water to every table, and children cheered each time the pitcher arrived, and Samir's grandmother saved her a second bowl of sheer khurma, this time with extra nuts. When the volunteers finally cleared the gift table, the small box of dates sat alone on the corner, and Samir's little sister grabbed it, tore it open, and announced, "Dates! I get the first one."

Emmett leaned over the kitchen table, where six paper airplanes lay in a row like tired birds. His best flight yesterday had gone seventeen feet, but he'd built it from the heavy poster paper Mom used for signs, and he'd also folded the wings up in a wide V instead of flat. Both changes at once. Now he couldn't tell which one had made it fly farther.

"If it was the paper, I'd want to know," he said to his sister Ruth, who was eating cereal at the counter. "Poster paper is heavy. Heavy could mean it glides better. Or the V wings. Or both. Or neither."

"So do it again and watch," Ruth said, not looking up.

"Watch what? I changed two things. Two." He flipped his notebook open and stared at his scribbled numbers. Flight three: twelve feet. Flight four: seventeen feet. He had no idea why.

Ruth came around the counter and tapped the notebook. "You know what Marcus did with his bean project? He changed the pot and the water at the same time, and the teacher said he couldn't tell which one mattered. She said you're supposed to change only one thing on purpose. That's called the independent variable."

"The one thing you change on purpose," Emmett repeated slowly. The words felt like a key in a lock.

He grabbed two sheets, one notebook paper and one poster paper, and folded them into exactly the same shape, flat wings, matching creases, careful match. Then he threw each one three times down the hallway, measuring with a tape measure and refusing to let Ruth announce the numbers until he'd written them down, because guessing first had become a mandatory rule in his notebook.

The poster paper beat the notebook paper every single throw.

"It was the paper," he said, grinning. Then he paused. "But what about the V wings?"

Ruth rolled her eyes. "Then change only that next."

He folded two fresh poster-paper planes, one flat and one in a wide V, and carried them to the hallway door.

Anais had packed her sleeping bag three times before her cousin Marisol's mom drove her across town to Priya's house. At Marisol's that afternoon, Marisol had been assertive about it: "Take the flashlight. Trust me." Anais had laughed, because Marisol's cousin had told her that at sleepovers, someone always tells a ghost story, and Marisol believed it like a rule of the universe.

Now it was eleven at night, and the rule had come true. Priya's older brother, Devon, had told a story about a figure that stood at the foot of the stairs and counted the steps out loud in the dark. Everyone knew he made it up. He even said so at the end. But when the last word finished, the room went quiet, and Anais noticed her own heart pounding hard and fast, and her breath coming quicker, like she'd run the block to the corner store. Priya's breathing was quick too. Anais could hear it.

Then a stair creaked, right outside the door.

Devon yelped and grabbed a pillow like a shield. Priya shrieked. The door pushed open and Biscuit, the family cat, strolled in, tail up, entirely unimpressed. Devon laughed so hard he fell off his mattress. "It's the cat! It's just the cat!"

Anais laughed too, but she was thinking. She tried to deduce what had made Devon jump, since he'd invented the story himself and knew every word was fake. She watched Priya put a hand on her own chest, still feeling it drum. "Yours too?" Anais whispered. Priya nodded. "And I knew it was made up," Priya said. "I watched him make half of it up on the spot."

So it didn't matter what you knew. Anais sat with that for a while, remembering Marisol's flashlight, which she had decided was silly and left on the dresser. It was in Marisol's room, a whole town away.

"Next time," she said, and clicked off the lamp.

"What?"

"Nothing," Anais said. Biscuit curled up on Devon's pillow and started to purr.

Sebastian had ridden the number 14 bus every school day for two years, and he knew every ad by heart. There was the sneaker poster above the rear door, where the rapper Dash Malloy grinned down and said, "I never step on court without Zooms." There was the soda sign that shouted "Everyone's making the switch!" in letters so big they seemed to push the seats apart. And there was the one for Comet Bars, with the words "pure, honest, real chocolate" glowing like the bar itself was a hero. Sebastian barely saw them anymore, the way you stop hearing a clock.

What he did see was Marcus, three rows up, holding a Comet Bar. That was the problem. Sebastian was trying to get the whole grade to boycott Comet Bars because he had heard, over and over, that the company had dumped waste in Miller Creek. He leaned over the seats. "You're still eating those? They poisoned the creek." Marcus shrugged. A seventh grader near the window said, "Yeah, I heard that too." Two kids at the back chimed in, one after another, like popcorn. By the time the bus lurched around the library, five different people had said it out loud.

A girl named Priya, who was reading a science magazine, looked up. "Can I ask you something? Do you believe the creek thing because you saw proof, or because you've heard it five times?" Sebastian opened his mouth and nothing came out. Priya held up the magazine. "There's a study in here. In 1977, Lynn Hasher and her colleagues found that people rated statements as more likely to be true after seeing them repeated, whether or not they were true." She shrugged. "It just says that. Repetition. That's all it takes."

Sebastian decided to test it. At the next stop he said, loudly, "They're replacing the old trolley with one that has a real conductor in a striped vest." Two stops later he said it again. By the school, a boy he had never met told his friend, "Did you hear? The trolley's getting a conductor," and his friend nodded like it was settled fact. Sebastian felt his ears go hot. He had done the exact thing the Comet Bar ad did, the "pure, honest, real" thing, only faster. That afternoon he walked to Miller Creek himself. The water ran clear over the stones, and a man from the city was posting a notice about a leaking garage upstream, not a chocolate factory. On the ride home he tapped Marcus on the shoulder and held out the last of his own Comet Bar. "I got the creek story wrong," he said. "Split it with me?"

Dad had promised to teach her something on this trip, and by the second morning he still hadn't, so Lily took matters into her own hands. She spread the topographic map of the park across the picnic table, weighed its corners down with pinecones, and frowned at it until Marcus, her little brother, leaned over her shoulder.

"What are you doing?"

"Finding us." She traced her finger along the thin curved lines that looped around a brown blob near the middle of the map. She knew from school that the numbered lines running up and down and side to side were latitude and longitude, and that the town of Fairview sat where two of them crossed. If she could read those numbers, she could tell anyone on Earth exactly where Fairview was. But first she wanted to know how tall the hill above their campsite was, because Dad had bet her a marshmallow that she couldn't figure it out. She counted four lines from the bottom of the hill to the top and multiplied. Two hundred feet per line meant eight hundred feet, which seemed too steep for a hill that had taken them only twenty minutes to climb.

Marcus poked the tiny print along the map's bottom edge. "What's this little box say?"

Lily bent closer. The legend, small enough that she'd walked right past it, said the contour interval was forty feet. "The contour interval," she read slowly. That meant the difference in height between one contour line and the next was forty feet. She redid her count, and the hill came out at one hundred sixty feet, which felt about right for their burning calves and one rest stop. Her first answer had implied the hill was five times taller than it was. She thought about last summer, when she'd guessed the lake was a mile across and refused to check, and Dad had rowed her across it in twenty minutes without saying a word.

"So the hill's smaller than you thought," Marcus said.

"It's exactly the right size. I was the wrong size." She found Fairview's crossing lines, copied the numbers onto her hand, and held it up. "Thirty-four point six north, ninety-eight point two west. Now I can find anything."

"Even the bathroom?"

"Especially the bathroom," Lily said, and folded the map into her back pocket.

Oliver dropped his backpack at the top of the stairs and took them two at a time, because today was the day. Today he and Maya were going to finish their Scratch game, the one where a cat dodges falling donuts and every dodge earns a point. "Did you bring the snacks?" Maya called from the basement couch, already clicking blocks together on her laptop.

"I brought pretzels and a plan," Oliver said, flopping down beside her. On the screen, the cat sprite slid back and forth while donuts rained from the top of the stage. "Now we need the score. Watch this." He dragged out a block that said "change score by 1" and tucked it inside the loop that moved the donuts. Then he added an if-then block: if the cat touched a donut, the score would reset to zero. "So every donut that misses adds a point, but one hit and you lose everything."

They tested it. The cat slid, donuts fell, the score climbed to 7, then 12, then 20, and Oliver pumped both fists. It was working, and it was durable, too, because they ran it five times in a row and the score behaved every single time. "We integrate the high score next," Maya said, opening a second variable. "My brother says that's the fancy word for putting two things together so they work as one."

That was when Maya's brother Dev stomped down the stairs, holding his own laptop and frowning at it like it had insulted him. "My times table quiz is broken," he groaned. "It's supposed to go up to twelve, but it mysteriously stops at eleven. Every time. Eleven times twelve, and then nothing." He turned the screen toward them. Oliver leaned in. At the top of the code sat a line that read range(1, 12).

"Wait," Oliver said slowly. He stared at the line, then at the quiz, then at the line again. Something invisible was going on here, a rule he couldn't see, and he wanted to grab it. "Your table goes to twelve, but it stops just before twelve. What if the second number works like the finish line at a race? You stop at the line, you don't step past it." He reached over and changed the 12 to a 13, so the line read range(1, 13). "Try it now."

Dev hit run. The quiz marched through twelve times twelve, clean and complete, and Maya let out a whoop loud enough that they could hear their mom upstairs. "Oliver, you fixed it with one number," Dev said, shaking his head. "One number. And I've been at this for an hour." Oliver grinned and turned back to the Scratch game, where the donut cat waited. "Okay, high score next," he said, and cracked open the pretzels.

Florence stood at the German club's table at the cultural festival, holding a paper map of a pretend town and trying to remember how to say that her family had two cats and a loud dog. She despised feeling stuck, especially in public, so she kept repeating the sentence under her breath until it came out whole.

Then Marco from her class appeared, dragging a folding chair and a red scarf. "We need you," he said. "Priya is blindfolded, and I'm supposed to guide her through the obstacle course, but I have to go help at the food table. You know the direction words, right?"

Florence did not know the direction words, not really, but she said yes anyway. Priya stood near the stacks of plastic crates, the scarf tied over her eyes, waiting. Marco scribbled three words on a scrap of paper and shoved it into Florence's hand before jogging off. On it were links, rechts, geradeaus.

Here was a puzzle she could actually see, in a way. If Priya turned the wrong way, Florence could guess what she had said. She started easy. "Geradeaus." Priya walked straight between two crates. So that one meant straight ahead. Then, quietly, Marco's little brother Tomas whispered near her elbow, "Links means left." That narrowed it down: if links was left, then rechts, the remaining word, had to be right. She tested it. "Rechts." Priya turned right and bumped gently into a cushioned mat. "Correct side!" Florence called. The pattern held every time after that.

When Priya pulled off the scarf, blinking in the sunlight, she grinned. "Say the family sentence now," she said. "You always stop halfway." Florence took a breath and got through the whole thing, cats and loud dog and all, and it felt almost easy. "Zwei Katzen und ein lauter Hund," she finished, and Priya applauded with two plastic cups from the food table.

Rosalie's best friend Dexter swore that Zip Fuel made him run faster, and he had a witness: himself. "I drank one before the mile and shaved twelve seconds," he said at lunch, twice. Rosalie wanted to believe him, mostly because she had three dollars riding on it.

The problem was that Zip Fuel cost five dollars a bottle, which is why she found herself standing in aisle four of Ridgeway Pharmacy, staring at a shelf of vitamins, sugar-free mints, and a row of plain white bottles behind the counter. Her mother was at the drop-off window arguing with a pharmacist about an insurance settlement for a claim that had been denied twice. Rosalie drifted toward the counter, where a display of gel capsules labeled "Homeopathic Sleep Aid" sat next to a sign that said Non-Drowsy.

"Excuse me," she said to the pharmacist when he surfaced. "Do you sell pills that are just sugar? Like, nothing in them at all?"

He looked at her over his glasses. "We use those in trials sometimes. They're placebos." He set a small bottle on the counter. "Pharmacists can't sell you the real medicine without a prescription, but sugar is sugar."

Rosalie turned the bottle over in her hands and thought about Dexter. Twelve seconds. If the drink really worked, then a fake drink shouldn't work at all, and he'd run his normal time. If the fake drink did work, then maybe the running faster came from believing, not from the bottle. She could empty one of her dad's glass juice bottles, fill it with water, add two drops of orange food coloring, and tell Dexter it was Zip Fuel. He'd never tasted the real one; he'd chugged it cold at the track. To make the test fair, she'd have to exclude every other difference: same day, same weather, same time, same taunting from the eighth graders at the fence.

Her mother was still going with the settlement. "It's the third letter," she was saying. "The third. I'm immune to their apologies at this point."

Rosalie paid for the sugar pills with crumpled ones and a quarter she found in her jacket, then tucked the bottle into her backpack next to the empty juice bottle she'd brought from home. Monday after school, she handed Dexter the orange drink and watched him chug it at the start line, grimacing like a professional. He ran the mile in exactly his usual time, to the second, and spent the cooldown insisting his legs felt "incredibly springy."

"So," Rosalie said, holding up the empty bottle, "about those twelve seconds."

"Test it again," Dexter said. "One more lap. And this time I want the grape flavor."

Isaac spread the giant map of the Roman Empire across the living room floor, weighting one curling corner with a cereal bowl and the other with his sneaker. Tomorrow he had to explain to his class why the empire split and fell, and all he had so far was a map, a red marker, and a little sister named Maya who kept trying to obstruct his view with her sock feet.

"Move your toes," he said. "I'm having a breakthrough."

"You're having nothing," said Maya, but she pulled her feet back, because she wanted something. She wanted to be the audience, complete with a handmade sign that said MAYA'S HISTORY SHOW, and she'd promised to clap only if the show was actually good.

Isaac squinted at the northern border of the empire. The frontier didn't wander like a drunken snake, the way he'd expected. For long stretches it followed two clean blue lines, one flowing west, one curving east, with little fort symbols and soldier markers strung along their banks like beads. He sat up so fast he knocked over the cereal bowl. "They're rivers. The border is rivers." He traced them with his finger. "This one's the Rhine, and this big bendy one is the Danube. Rome stuck forts and soldiers all along their banks." It made a strange kind of sense: rivers were easy to see from anywhere, like a signal fire made of water, telling everyone exactly where Rome ended. No guessing, no arguing, just a line nobody could cross without getting wet.

"That's the whole show?" Maya asked, waving her sign. "Rivers? Clap, clap."

"No, watch." Isaac drew the empire splitting in half with his red marker, east and west, then pretended to crumple one half. "Now imagine the whole thing like Dad's old garden fence. The rain doesn't smash it down in one day. It's slow and corrosive, rotting the posts one at a time, until one morning the whole fence leans over."

Maya considered this, chewing her hair. That evening she slid a note under his door: "Your show was ok. I am starting a museum. You can be the security guard. Bring the map."

Isaac read it twice, grinned, and went to find the pushpins.

Cameron pressed middle C for the tenth time and nothing happened. Well, something happened: a dull thunk, like the piano had swallowed the note and decided to keep it. He was supposed to practice a simple melody for the spring concert tryouts, and the scholarship for summer music camp went to whoever played best, so the thunk mattered.

Mrs. Ruiz had left the classroom open for practice, and Priya was there too, working at the other piano near the windows. She looked over. "That D sounds terrible," she said.

"It's C," Cameron said. "It didn't used to sound like this." He slid his finger along the keys, feeling the cool ivory, and noticed something odd. Middle C sank lower than every other key, almost touching the wood beneath it. He couldn't see anything wrong underneath, so he made a guess: something invisible was blocking it, and whatever it was sat under the front edge. He lifted the little lid over the keys and peeked into the shadowed works inside. A shiny flat something, about the size of a coin, was wedged where the hammer needed room to move.

"Let me guess, a pencil?" Priya said.

"A dime, maybe." He tried tweezers made from two pens, which only shoved it deeper. Then he thought about the key itself, how it rocked on a balance point near the back. If he pressed the very back edge, the front would lift. He reached under and pressed. The front rose, and he slipped the dime out with his fingernail. He hit C again and a clean, round note filled the room, warm as toast.

Priya laughed and came over. "Grandpa's piano doesn't do that, and it's way fancier. It's a standard modern piano, so it has 88 keys: 52 white and 36 black."

"Eighty-eight," Cameron repeated, glancing at the classroom piano, which looked smaller. "This one's an approximate copy, then. Probably why the teacher calls it a compromise."

He set the dime on the music rack, placed his hands on the keys, and played his melody all the way through for the first time without a single thunk.

Elena pressed the marker flat against Maya's kitchen table, where a half-finished poster read "maya's sign language club, thursday, room 12." Her palms had started to perspire, because Maya had handed her the red marker and said, "You do the big title. Your letters are way better than mine." The problem was the word in the middle. Maya had written "deaf coffee chat" in pencil first, all lowercase, then crossed it out and written "Deaf" with a capital D, then crossed that out too.

"Which one?" Elena asked, holding both pencils above the paper like she was about to duel somebody.

"Both feel right," Maya said, pulling her dark curls into a bun. "But it can't be both, right?"

Elena squinted at the crossed-out letters. "Maybe it can," she said slowly. She turned the pencil over and chewed the eraser end, which her mother said was a terrible habit. She was thinking about Maya's brother Theo, who was in the club and had shown Elena once how a sign for a name can carve through the air like a wave. What was different about a community and a condition? Could a single letter really carry all of that? She wrote "deaf" on a scrap and stared at it, then "Deaf," then held them side by side.

"Maya! Theo's home," Maya's mom called from the hallway, and Theo appeared in the doorway with his backpack still on, hands moving fast. Maya signed back, and he came over and read the poster upside down.

"He says ask Priya," Maya translated. "She's Deaf, she'll know." Priya lived two floors up, so they ran upstairs, poster flapping, and found her arranging books on a shelf like a small tidy plateau of paperbacks.

Priya studied the poster, then signed while Maya interpreted. "In 1972 James Woodward proposed writing Deaf with a capital D for the community and culture of sign-language users, and lowercase deaf for the hearing condition itself," Maya translated, and Priya grinned at Elena's face. "So which one does your coffee chat want?"

Elena looked at the penciled words. "The chat. The people. Capital D, then."

Back in the kitchen, she inked the title in her best letters, red and enormous: MAYA'S SIGN LANGUAGE CLUB, DEAF COFFEE CHAT, THURSDAY, ROOM 12. Theo gave her a thumbs-up and signed something quick.

"What'd he say?" Elena asked.

"He said your letters are way better than mine," Maya said, and threw a pencil at her.

Alexandra slid her worksheet toward the middle of the table, where the rest of the math club could see it. Fraction problems covered the page, and she had gotten stuck on the third one: 1/2 plus 1/3. She knew the answer had to be bigger than one half but smaller than one whole, and she said so. "Then test it," said Marcus, tapping her pencil. "Try cutting both fractions into sixths. Two sixths plus three sixths." She wrote it out, added, and got five sixths, which fit between her two bounds, so she grinned and crossed out the wrong answer above it. Mr. Okafor had a reputation for never giving away an answer, and now she saw why.

Across the table, Priya was not grinning. Priya wanted the team's geometry trophy back more than anything, because last spring her older sister had dropped it in the hallway and the club had never won it again. She had spent a week on her proof for the practice meet, and the judge's paper came back with a red circle around one line. "Two sides and an angle," the note read, "but not the included angle."

Alexandra leaned over. "What's that mean?" "I don't know," Priya said. "The angle has to be the one between the two sides. That's the included angle. I used a different one, so it doesn't prove the triangles match." Priya's shoulders sagged.

Alexandra remembered sitting in this same room last fall, when she had glued two paper triangles together because two sides matched, and they had still been different shapes. She had thought she was just bad at geometry. Now she looked at Priya's diagram and noticed the angle Priya had marked sat at the end of both sides, not in the notch between them. "There," Alexandra said, pointing. "Your sides are here and here. The angle between them is that one." She could not see why it worked, only that the judge's rule was explicit about it, so it had to sit in that spot.

Priya erased the mark, drew a new one in the notch, and rewrote the whole line. Then she copied the diagram onto a fresh sheet and slid it across the table to Alexandra. "Check it with me," she said.

Noah had one week to build a model that would illustrate the phases of the Moon, and his science table already looked like a disaster. The lamp stood in for the Sun, a styrofoam ball for the Moon, and a basketball for Earth, but every time he walked the ball around the lamp, his best friend Priya frowned.

"That's not right," she said. "The Moon can't have a shadow on it from that angle. Half of it should be lit no matter where it is."

"Then why do we see phases at all?" Noah asked. He stopped the ball, squinted at the lamp, and turned the styrofoam sphere slowly in his fingers. Half of it was bright white. The other half sat in darkness. He walked around the table himself, watching the ball from Earth's position, and suddenly only a sliver of the lit side faced him. A crescent. When he moved to the far side of the table, the whole lit face swung into view. A full Moon.

"The phases are just my point of view," he said. "The light doesn't change. Where I stand changes."

Priya grinned and wrote it on their poster. But the next day, when Mr. Okafor set a globe on the table for their presentation, Noah noticed an anomaly. The globe was leaning, its pole tipped far from straight up, and nobody had bumped it. He tipped it upright and the globe wobbled back into its tilt on its stand.

"It's supposed to lean," said a girl named Marcus's sister, passing by their table. "Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4 degrees from straight up relative to the plane of its orbit around the Sun."

"That's a weirdly exact number," Noah said, but he wrote it down anyway, because their grade depended on getting details right. He checked the classroom globe with a protractor the teacher lent him, and the tilt matched. On the display screen, a diagram of Earth's path around the Sun showed the same lean, steady the whole way around.

Their presentation time was endangered when the lamp's cord came loose and the bulb flickered, but Priya held the plug in the socket while Noah walked the Moon ball around the basketball globe, calling out each phase as the fifth graders in the audience saw it happen. New Moon. First quarter. Full. When he finished, he pointed at the globe.

"And notice it's leaning," he said. "About 23.4 degrees from straight up relative to the plane of its orbit around the Sun. That's not a mistake. That's just how Earth is."

A boy in the front row raised his hand. "So if we ever move to Mars, will we lean too?"

The morning announcements had barely finished when Mr. Ruiz held up a laminated sheet and said the honor roll was posted by the cafeteria. Olivier walked fast, because his grandfather had made him a bet over Sunday's game: if Olivier could prove that no major leaguer had hit .400 in a season since 1941, when Ted Williams batted .406, the old man would hand over twenty dollars. He had until Friday.

The hallway smelled like floor wax. Through the translucent glass panel beside the cafeteria door, Olivier could see students clustered around the sheet, some cheering, some quiet. His friend Denae stood in front of it with her phone out, taking a picture, because she wanted to make the honor roll so badly she had asked her mom to supervise her homework time every night this quarter. Her name was third in her grade. Third, out of three hundred.

"Third isn't bad," Olivier said, reading over her shoulder.

"Third is a ranking," Denae said. "It squishes three hundred people into one number. It doesn't say I missed honors in math by one point." She scrolled on her phone. "And my average, 94.2, doesn't show the 88 that dragged it down. One number hides everything."

Olivier stared at the honor roll. Every name had a single average next to it, and every average had swallowed a hundred small events, every quiz, every lab, every rushed breakfast before a test. Baseball was the same, he realized. A batting average compressed a whole season of groundouts and line drives into one tidy decimal. Ted Williams batted .406 in 1941, his grandfather had said, and no player had finished a season above .400 since. Not in eighty-some years. Every hitter since had been squeezed under that invisible line.

He grabbed a napkin from his lunch bag and wrote his test plan. He would ask five kids at lunch two questions: who was on the honor roll, and who had improved since last quarter. If most improved kids weren't on the list, then one number really was hiding the story, and his grandfather's favorite hitters weren't slouches, just swallowed by the same kind of math.

By fifth period he had his answers. Four of the five improved kids weren't on the honor roll, including Denae's friend Marcus, whose average had climbed six points. At the library printer, Olivier ran off the honor roll, the category of "most improved" from the gym wall, and his napkin chart. Friday night he spread them on his grandfather's kitchen table next to the twenty dollars.

"See? One number hides everything," Olivier said. "The .406 still stands because every season gets squished down the same way."

His grandfather laughed, counted out the bills, and slid them across the table. "Bet you double or nothing," he said, "that you can't carry my groceries up those stairs without stopping."

Olivier was already reaching for the bags.

Harrison stood in the kitchen holding his speech cards like they might bite. Tomorrow he had to give a two-minute speech in front of the whole class, with an opening hook, three points, and a closing, and every time he practiced, he sped up until the words crashed into each other like dominoes.

"Again," said his sister Priya, munching a granola bar at the table. "You just said your hook and your first point in one breath."

"I know." Harrison dropped into a chair. "I can't figure out where to stop."

Priya shoved her laptop toward him. On the screen was a script from her school play, covered in pencil slashes. "Watch," she said, and pointed at one. "Actors split a script into beats," she said. "A new beat starts wherever a character's thought or tactic changes, and a pause often marks that shift." She tapped a slash between two lines. "My thought changes there, so I stop. New thought, new beat."

Harrison grabbed a pencil. That was the hidden rule he'd been missing. His speech wasn't one long river of words; it was chunks, and each chunk had a job. He spread his cards on the table and hunted for the places where his thinking changed. After the hook, slash. After point one, slash. He marked all of them, then added one more and excluded the part about his uncle's failed business, because it didn't fit any of his three points no matter how much he liked it.

"Ready?" Priya set the kitchen timer for two minutes.

He stood up, took a breath, and started. "What if I told you a lemonade stand could pay for a new bike?" Pause. "That's income, money coming in." Pause. At every slash he stopped, and the stops made the next sentence land harder. Priya grinned so wide her grin looked infectious, and Harrison caught it.

The timer buzzed. One minute fifty-eight.

"You sounded like a person," Priya announced, "not a panicking vacuum cleaner."

Harrison squared his cards. "One more time."

Tyler had the best spot on the couch, the corner cushion nearest the bowl of chips, and he was not giving it up. Aunt Rosa, Uncle Marcus, and his cousin Jayden were packed into the living room with his parents, all of them shouting at the television as the playoff game went to overtime. Every time the camera cut to the trophy waiting in the tunnel, it gleamed under the lights, but it also looked battered, like a dented silver pot somebody had kicked down a hill.

"Why does it look so old?" Jayden asked during a commercial. "Couldn't they buy a shiny new one?"

Uncle Marcus shrugged. "They have the money. Maybe they like it ugly."

Tyler chewed that over. It wasn't just ugly, he decided; it was worn in a way that suggested it had been around for a very long time, longer than any other trophy he could think of. The Super Bowl trophy looked new every year, and so did the basketball one. He tried to distinguish this cup from those in his head, and the difference kept pointing one direction: age. If the cup was the oldest, that might explain the dents, the same way Grandpa's old truck had more scratches than Dad's. He had a rule forming: a trophy passed around for more years should collect more damage. It was a guess, though, and a guess needed checking.

He slid off the cushion. "Hold my spot," he said, and Jayden put a hand on it at once, which was not what Tyler had meant.

At the bookshelf he found the sports almanac Grandpa had left there last summer. The index sent him to a page about hockey's big prize, and the first paragraph stopped him cold. The Stanley Cup was donated by Lord Stanley, Canada's governor general, in 1892, and first awarded in 1893. That made it the oldest trophy in North American professional sports. His guess had been right, and now he had proof.

He carried the book back to the couch. "It looks old because it is old," he announced. "It was donated by Lord Stanley, Canada's governor general, in 1892, and first awarded in 1893. Oldest trophy in North American professional sports."

"Read that part again," Aunt Rosa said, reaching for the book.

"The 1892 part," Uncle Marcus said. "I want to hear that twice."

Jayden held up the almanac page next to the dented cup on the screen. "Almost two hundred years of dents," he said.

"Well, not two hundred," Tyler said. "But a lot."

Uncle Marcus pointed at him. "Objection. The defendant is correcting the witness."

"Sustained," Dad said. "Tyler keeps the nachos."

The buzzer sounded on the television, the third period stats scrolling up the screen, and Tyler reached over and pulled the bowl into his lap.

Alexis stood at the zucchini booth at the farmers' market, holding a recipe card her grandmother had written out in loopy blue ink: Zucchini Honey Muffins, makes twelve. "One dollar each," said the farmer, "or three for two." Alexis counted her coins and picked three, choosing the ones that were small and heavy, the way Gran had taught her last summer.

She could still remember that day clearly. Gran had let her measure the flour all by herself, and Alexis had been so proud that she'd declared the kitchen a monarchy with herself as queen. "Then I hereby classify you as the royal taste tester," Gran had said, bowing so low her reading glasses slid off. They had laughed until the muffins almost burned.

Today was different, though, because Alexis was baking alone. Gran was at the dentist, and the kitchen was Alexis's whole responsibility. She grated the zucchini, cracked the eggs, and stirred until her arm ached. The recipe card said, in Gran's handwriting at the bottom: Preheat oven to 375. Don't skip this. Alexis looked at the oven. The oven looked back, cold and blank. The last time she'd baked with Gran, she remembered, the muffins had come out pale and squat, dense as hockey pucks. Gran had frowned at them and said, "Hmm. What did we do differently?" Alexis hadn't known then.

She thought about it now, turning the wooden spoon in the batter. Gran always put the tray in after the oven had beeped. Alexis, that day, had slid the tray in right away to save time, because waiting was boring. The pale, squat muffins had gone in before the oven was hot. She had never connected those two things until this moment, standing alone in the kitchen with the oven still cold. So that was what preheating meant: waiting until the oven reached the temperature you set before the batter went in, so baking started at the right heat. She turned the dial and sat on the counter to wait, swinging her sneakers against the cupboard.

The wait felt endless, so she cut the last zucchini into diagonal slices and arranged them on the counter like a tiny green fence. When the oven finally beeped, she filled the paper liners, slid the tray in, and set the timer for twenty-two minutes exactly.

The muffins rose into golden domes, crackled on top, and smelled like honey and Sunday morning. She carried them, still warm, to the farmers' market in a basket covered with a dish towel. The zucchini farmer took one bite and closed his eyes. "Your gran's recipe?"

"Mine," Alexis said. "Baked by the queen herself."

He bowed so low his cap fell off. "Then I hereby classify myself as the royal taste tester."

"Get in line," Alexis said, and lifted the towel.

The washing machine at home had died on Tuesday, so on Saturday Mya and her dad carried three baskets of laundry to the Spin Cycle Laundromat, which smelled like warm soap and pennies. Her dad dropped the baskets, fed quarters into two machines, and then handed her a five dollar bill and a short list written on a dryer sheet. "Milk and stamps," he said. "The corner store. You know the way."

She knew the way. She had walked it maybe two hundred times, but always with somebody. The light at Foster Street took forever to change, and the store's bell jangled when the door moved even a centimeter, so you could hear customers coming before you saw them. Still, standing at the laundromat door with the bill folded in her fist, she felt hesitant, like the sidewalk outside had gotten longer since the last time she'd looked at it.

"Your mother walked to that store alone at nine," her dad said, which was supposed to be encouraging but wasn't. Mya thought about her mom at nine, small and fearless, and decided she could manage at twelve. She walked out. At the corner store she found the milk, stood in line, and counted her change twice at the register because the cashier had already turned to the next customer. Two dollars and thirty-one cents. She counted it again on the walk back, lips moving, and it came out the same both times, which felt like passing a secret test nobody had announced.

Back at the laundromat, the first load had finished, and Mya pulled out her white school shirt and winced. It was pink. Not pink like a sunset, pink like a watermelon that had lost an argument. Her dad held it up and said, "Well." In the load there was also one red sock, brand new, that her little brother had insisted needed washing before Monday.

Mya laid the shirt flat on the folding table and stared at it. She hadn't mixed the clothes up; her brother had dropped the sock into the whites basket himself. But something had to have traveled from the sock to the shirt, because the sock had come out barely lighter than it went in, and the shirt had gone in white and come out pink. She thought about the water, how it had sat in the machine with all of it tumbling together for half an hour, and she said, "The new sock let dye go into the wash water, and the water carried it to everything pale in there." Her dad said, "That's why people sort by colour, kid," and she thought, nobody ever tells you why, they just say sort.

She ran a test with the second load, which was her idea. Darks in one machine, whites and pale things alone in another, no new red anything. When that load came out, everything was the color it was supposed to be, and she folded it in stacks, smug, while her dad watched his phone.

Later, walking home with the milk, she turned the pink shirt over in the bag and thought about her brother's sock, which was technically his fault but mostly just a sock doing what new red socks do. She hadn't checked the basket before starting the load, either. She still wasn't sure whose job that was.

"I'm wearing it anyway," her brother announced at dinner. "Pink's my color."

Elena spread her poster board on the picnic table and stared at the blank page. Tomorrow she had to draw a food chain from the sun all the way to a top predator, and then explain what would happen if one link disappeared. Her motivation was simple: Mrs. Okafor had promised the best diagram would hang in the hallway for the whole school year, and Elena wanted that wall more than anything.

She had just drawn a fat yellow sun when her little brother Theo came out carrying their grandfather's old microscope and two mystery slides. "Grandpa said one is leaf and one is cheek cells," Theo said, setting them down beside her crayons. "But he forgot which is which. Can we look?"

Elena cherished afternoons like this, when a problem just appeared out of nowhere. She clipped the first slide under the lens and leaned down. The cells were neat little rectangles, like bricks in a wall, lined up in tidy rows. She switched to the second slide and squinted. These cells were blobby, roundish, scattered every which way like spilled beads.

"Okay," she said slowly. "Plant cells have rigid walls, so they're fixed and boxy, like these bricks. Animal cells only have a flexible membrane, so they come out rounded and irregular." She tapped the first slide. "Leaf. And the blobby ones are from somebody's cheek." Theo made a face. "Grandpa's cheek," Elena said, and they both laughed.

Then she stopped laughing, because something clicked. She pulled the leaf slide out and looked at her poster. "Theo, that's the whole point of my food chain," she said, grabbing a green crayon. "The sun feeds the leaf, and the leaf is made of those boxy little bricks, millions of them. A caterpillar eats the nutritious leaves and gets fat, a robin eats the caterpillar, and a hawk eats the robin. Sun, leaf, caterpillar, robin, hawk." She drew arrows down the page. "Every link is feeding the next one."

"But what if one link disappears?" Theo asked, peeling an orange and handing her half without being asked, because he could see she was on a roll and wouldn't stop to eat.

"Let's find out," Elena said. She drew a second chain, then scribbled the caterpillars out entirely. "No caterpillars means the robins go hungry and leave. Then the hawks lose their food too, and there are way too many leaves with nobody eating them." She sat back. "One missing link, and the whole chain gets weird."

Theo held up the leaf slide to the light. "So these little boxes feed everything?"

"These little boxes feed everything," Elena said, and drew an extra-large leaf right next to the sun.

Sara stood in the living room on Sunday morning with her arms crossed and her hip stuck out, which was her official arguing pose. "The festival is tomorrow, and I still can't get the timing right. I need the video, just for one hour."

Mom did not even look up from her crossword. "You know the rule. Sunday morning until noon is our rest time. No screens, no rushing around, no frantic practice drills. That's the whole point. We slow down so the day doesn't get away from us, and so we notice each other instead of our phones."

"That's a lovely reason," Sara said. "I will notice everyone tomorrow while I'm dancing completely off beat." She flopped onto the couch beside Uncle Kimo, who was visiting from Hilo and had been quietly watching this whole thing like it was a very good show. He was holding something round and brown with a cord around its neck.

"You're dancing the old style, yeah?" he said. "Hula kahiko." He lifted the round thing and thumped it against the floor, and a deep hollow boom rolled through the room. Sara sat up straight. That was the sound from the video, the one she kept missing. "This is an ipu," Uncle Kimo went on, "a gourd drum. The old hula isn't danced to a song at all. It goes with chanting and drums like this. No melody to follow. That's probably why you can't find the beat, cousin. You've been listening for singing that isn't there."

Sara stared at him, then at the ipu, then at the ceiling, where an invisible lightbulb might as well have switched on. All week she had been trying to catch a tune, waiting for a note to tell her when to step. But the timing wasn't hiding inside a melody. It lived in the chant, in the words themselves. It was like hunting for her missing sock under the bed when it was in her shoe the whole time.

"Okay," she said slowly. "Rest time. No screens. But nothing in the rules says no chanting." Mom's pencil paused over the crossword. Sara planted her feet, took a breath, and began, low and shaky at first, the old words about the sea. Uncle Kimo kept time on the gourd drum, and her feet found the boom, boom, then the quick double beat, exactly where they belonged. Little brother Noah wandered in wearing a random cape made from a beach towel and started chanting along, getting every word hilariously wrong, which broke Sara up laughing so badly she had to start over twice.

At noon Mom declared rest time officially over and went to take her antibiotic that had been waiting in the cupboard since breakfast. Sara, dripping with effort, begged Uncle Kimo to dismantle his plan to head home early. "One more hour," she said, and struck her opening pose. Noah, still caped, picked up the kitchen pot and a wooden spoon, and raised both like drumsticks. "Ready, cousin," he said.

Parker stared at the tray of parts in the Build-an-Atom lab at the science museum: fat red balls for protons, gray ones for neutrons, and blue marbles that were supposed to be electrons, though they kept rolling off the table. His ticket said his atom was oxygen, which meant eight protons, and his little sister Josie had appointed herself the jury. "Wrong," she announced before he had attached anything. "You dropped one under the bench."

"This is why I didn't invite you," Parker said, fishing out the runaway proton. He counted again, touching each ball with one finger like a banker counting coins. Eight. Then he had to figure out the neutrons, which were allowed to vary, and the electrons, which had to go in rings, two in the first ring and six in the second. He built it, took it apart, and built it again, because the second ring kept collapsing whenever Josie bumped the table with her elbow.

The real trouble started at the station next door, where a volunteer handed out strips of litmus paper. You dipped them in a mystery liquid, and they turned pink or blue depending on what the liquid was. Parker dipped his strip in cup number three and it went pink, while Josie's went blue in cup five. "That's suspicious," she said. "The paper must be biased against my cup." Parker laughed and told her the paper didn't have opinions, it just changed color, and the color was the clue. It was like the atom model, he realized. You couldn't see the thing itself, so you read the evidence it left behind and worked backward to what had to be true.

The word litmus snagged in his mind, and a memory surfaced from last summer at Grandpa's house. Parker had been scrubbing the garden wall with a brush, complaining about the crusty gray-green patches stuck to the stone, when Grandpa came out with a mug of tea and told him to leave those alone. "That's lichen," Grandpa had said. "Litmus is a dye extracted from lichens, the crusty growths found on rocks and tree bark." Parker had thought that was the strangest fact he'd ever heard, a rock-scab turning into science paper, and now here was the paper, sitting in his hand.

He held his strip up next to the window, where the light was strong enough to show the little fibers. "Josie, guess where this comes from." She shrugged. "A paper factory, obviously." "Lichen. Like the stuff on Grandpa's wall. The crusty stuff on rocks and tree bark." Josie squinted at her strip, then at him, deciding whether to believe a brother who couldn't even keep six electrons in one ring.

The lab assistant walked past and said the museum would enforce the five-items-per-tray rule, so Parker gave back his spare neutrons. Then he carried his finished oxygen atom, both rings wobbling, across the room to the testing station. The checker counted the protons, counted the electrons, and stamped his card. Josie leaned over the card and read the stamp out loud: "Certified oxygen. Congratulations, you just made air."

The morning bus smelled like wet boots and orange peel, and Marcus would not stop talking. "My cousin says the new stadium tax is going to cost every family in town two thousand dollars a year," he announced to the whole back row. "He saw it in an ad. It had graphs."

Gabrielle pulled her backpack onto her lap. Two thousand dollars sounded like a lot, but it also sounded like the kind of number somebody might have invented. Marcus's cousin, last month, had claimed the school was canceling summer, and before that, that the lake fish were all dying from a spill nobody else had heard of. Gabrielle had begun to notice a pattern: the cousin's statements came in two flavors. Some were just opinions, like "the stadium is ugly," which nobody could check. Others were statements about the world, like "two thousand dollars per family," which either matched reality or didn't.

"Is two thousand dollars something you can verify?" she asked.

"What does verify mean?" said Priya from across the aisle. Priya wanted to be class president and had been collecting opinions all week, writing them in a spiral notebook titled WHAT THE PEOPLE WANT. "Because if the people believe the tax is two thousand dollars, that's what matters."

"No," Gabrielle said. "Believing isn't the same as it being true. My mom calls statements like that claims. A claim you can look up. An opinion you can only agree or disagree with." She paraphrased it another way, since Priya was still frowning. "If I say the bus smells like oranges, that's an opinion. If I say we're getting oranges every Tuesday, you could check."

Marcus said his cousin was never wrong. Priya said her notebook had eleven entries against the tax already. The bus lurched around the corner by the pharmacy, where a sign in the window advertised free delivery on prescriptions, and Gabrielle made a plan.

That night she and her dad had watched a TV ad about the stadium, and afterward her dad had looked it up on his phone. "PolitiFact," he'd said. "A fact-checking website, been around since 2007. They rate claims on a scale called the Truth-O-Meter." He'd turned the screen toward her. The ad's tax claim sat there with a little gauge on it, a whole range from True all the way down to Pants on Fire, which meant the claim had failed so completely that the meter had gone silly. The stadium claim, it turned out, was only mostly wrong, which earned it something in the middle.

The next morning Gabrielle boarded the bus holding a printout. "The ad took a number from one county and applied it to ours," she said. "The Truth-O-Meter called that Half True."

Marcus studied the paper. "My cousin's going to say the fact-checkers are biased."

"He can," Gabrielle said. "That's an opinion."

Priya leaned over the seat, pen already out. "So what's the actual number?"

"Ten dollars a year. Per family."

Priya crossed out eleven entries and sighed. "The people," she said, "are going to be so disappointed."

Marcus folded the printout and put it in his pocket. "I'm going to need this at lunch."

Camille pushed her noodles around her plate and stared at the flyer propped against the salt shaker. Saturday's neighborhood garage sale started at eight, and Mrs. Okafor's telescope, the one Camille had wanted all summer, would be gone by nine if she didn't figure out a plan. Her brother Theo slurped his milk and grinned.

"You still moping about that telescope? It's just a tube with mirrors."

"It's not just anything," Camille said. "It's the only one on the whole street. And I only have eleven dollars."

Dad set down his fork. "Eleven dollars for a telescope? She'll want thirty, maybe more."

"Then I'll never get it," Camille said, and her stomach felt tight and cold. But then she remembered something. At the spring sale, Mrs. Okafor had stacked contemporary mystery novels, glossy and new-looking, and priced them at five dollars each. Nobody bought a single one. By eleven she had dropped them to a dollar, and by noon the whole stack was gone. The old battered paperbacks, though, priced at a quarter from the start, had sold out in an hour.

Camille sat up straight. "It depends on how many people want it and how many there are," she said slowly, working it out as she spoke. "If a lot of buyers want something and there's only one, the price goes up. If there's a pile and few takers, the price has to come down until everything sells." She grabbed Theo's napkin and scribbled numbers. "So I'll wait. If nobody else wants the telescope, she might lower the price before noon."

"That's a gamble," Dad said. "Someone else might grab it."

Camille's motive wasn't greed, she told herself; it was math. Saturday morning she hovered near the telescope, hands sweating, while Mrs. Okafor called out lower and lower prices. Ten o'clock: twenty dollars. Eleven: fifteen. At eleven forty, a boy picked it up, and Camille's heart contracted with fear. He put it down and wandered off.

"Twelve dollars," Mrs. Okafor announced, checking her watch. "Sale closes at noon."

Camille held up her eleven dollars and her lucky quarter. "Eleven twenty-five?"

Mrs. Okafor laughed. "Sold. You know, when what buyers want matches what sellers have left, that's the market-clearing price. You found mine."

Camille hugged the telescope all the way home.

The message appeared in the group chat at 4:32 on Tuesday, right between a photo of Marcus's new bike and three rocket emojis from Priya. It was from Ben: "Guys my grandpa signed my birthday card all weird. He wrote Kovacs Peter. He's losing it maybe?" Aaron stared at the screen. His own last name came after his first name, and so did everyone else's he could think of, except the kids in his class whose families were from China and Japan and Korea. Wei Chen. Sato Kenji. He had never thought about it as a rule before, but there it was, a pattern he could see once he looked.

He typed back: "Wait what's his name usually?" Ben answered: "Peter Kovacs. Like always." Aaron pulled up another chat, the one with his friend Dae, whose parents ran the corner market. "Question," Aaron wrote. "In Korean, does the family name go first?" The reply came fast: "Yeah. Mine's Kim Dae. You just never noticed." Aaron sat back. A test began to form in his mind. If Ben's grandpa wrote the family name first, then maybe he was not confused at all. Maybe Hungarian names worked that way too.

"Ben, ask your grandpa if he meant to do that," Aaron typed. Two long minutes passed, with only a random mushroom meme from Priya filling the silence. Then Ben sent a voice note. In it you could hear an older voice in the background, firm and cheerful: "In Hungarian, the family name comes first. Like the Chinese, the Japanese, the Koreans." Ben came back on, laughing a little. "He says I should decompose my own name and figure out which half is which. Also he says if I eat my vegetables it will strengthen my constitution. He says that a lot."

Aaron smiled and typed, "Tell him some of us already knew that. Well, kind of." Ben sent back a picture of the card, the ink neat and sure, the family name sitting proudly in front. "Grandpa says happy birthday to the whole chat," Ben added. Priya sent six rocket emojis. Marcus wrote, "Best card in the thread." Aaron saved the picture to his phone.

The lights went out all at once, and Ava froze in the middle of Gran's kitchen with a half-washed plate in her hands. From the living room, Gran's chair scraped the floor. "Third time this month," Gran muttered, and Ava heard her shuffle toward the hallway closet where the candles lived.

"Wait," Ava called, setting the plate down and drying her hands in the dark. She was thinking about the fire-safety unit from school in the fall. The officer had stood at the front of the room and said safety agencies recommend flashlights rather than candles during a power cut, because a candle can easily start a fire in a dark house. Ava had written it in her notes and even got the citation right on the quiz, the page number from the handbook. Now the sentence came back to her whole.

"Gran, don't light those yet." She felt her way along the counter, found the drawer, and pulled out the two flashlights Gran kept beside the batteries. The first one clicked on, a steady beam. "Flashlights are safer than candles. A candle can start a fire in a dark house." Gran paused, matchbox still in her hand, then laughed a little and put it back.

Ava carried the smaller flashlight to the front window and swept the beam across the street. Every house on the block was dark, so the problem wasn't Gran's old wiring, which Gran was always grumbling about. "It's the whole street," Ava reported. "Maybe a line came down somewhere." She found her phone, checked the power company's outage map, and saw the little shaded patch covering their neighborhood, with a repair time of two hours.

Gran declared they would sustain themselves with ice cream before it melted, and they ate it straight from the carton on the porch steps, watching a distant repair truck's lights blink through the trees. "You're a resilient one," Gran said, handing Ava the spoon. "Most people would have just sat in the dark." Ava aimed the flashlight at the sidewalk and drew a long bright line toward the road.

Victor had promised his best friend Dexter that they would finish their Lunar New Year poster on the same day as the big dinner at the community hall, which meant he had to know exactly when the dinner would be. "Grandma," he said, poking his head into the kitchen, "is the party on February fourth again this year?" Grandma laughed so hard she nearly dropped a dumpling. "February fourth? Last year, maybe. This year the new moon falls somewhere else."

Victor frowned at the calendar on the wall, which had red circles jumping around like startled crickets. One year the celebration landed in late January, another year in the middle of February, and once it had almost coincided with his birthday, which had made for one spectacular cake-and-dumpling double feature. He decided to test an idea. If the date moved, maybe it moved in a pattern, the way his little sister's losing streak at rock-paper-scissors followed a rule only she understood. He wrote down every date Grandma could remember, then grabbed the old calendars from the junk drawer.

His sister Mei leaned over his shoulder. "You look like a detective," she said. "A very hungry detective." He waved her off and kept sorting.
