The dates all sat between January 21 and February 20, and Grandma had said something about the new moon. So the rule, he figured, was this: Lunar New Year falls on a new moon, and that new moon lands somewhere inside those dates. His plan for the poster could still work, as long as Dexter agreed to build it around the dinner instead of a fixed day.

At the hall, the lion dance had just started, drums booming, and Victor found Dexter by the refreshment table, guarding the spring rolls. "Good news," Victor announced. "It's a moving target, but a predictable one. New moon, between January 21 and February 20, every single year." Dexter took a vigorous bite of a spring roll and crumbs flew like confetti. "So we make the poster a detective case," he said. "The date is the fugitive." Grandma, passing by with a tray, sniffed. "In my day we just looked at the calendar." Mei raised her cup of tea like a toast. "The fugitive will strike again next year," she said.

Ariana sat in the guidance counsellor's office with her hands curled in her lap, waiting for Mrs. Okafor to finish writing. She had signed up for this meeting on the voluntary sign-up sheet outside the door, mostly because her stomach had been doing flips all week and she wanted to know why. The posters on the wall said words like anxiety and coping in big calm letters, and she kept reading them while she waited.

"So," said Mrs. Okafor, "the recital is Friday, and your note says the nerves feel huge."

"They feel like they're going to knock me over," Ariana said. "My hands get cold. My heart pounds. Last year I messed up the whole middle of my piece." She had been thinking about it in class, in bed, even at breakfast, and she was starting to wonder if the nerves themselves were the problem, or something else hiding behind them.

Mrs. Okafor slid a paper across the desk. "Stress is the body's response to a demand or a challenge," she said. "People talk about it like it's always bad, but it isn't." Then she leaned back. "That's all I'm going to tell you. What you do with it is yours."

Ariana frowned at the paper. A response to a challenge. So the pounding heart wasn't just noise; it was her body answering the recital. But answer doing what? On Wednesday she decided to run a test on herself. She had a practice performance in music class, and instead of trying to make the nerves evaporate, she let them be there and paid attention to what happened. When her heart started pounding, she noticed something strange: she could hear every note more sharply. The page looked clearer. She caught a mistake in measure twelve before her fingers made it. When she got nervous on the bus, by contrast, with nothing to focus on, the same feeling just rattled around uselessly.

"So the nerves help only when there's something to aim at," she told Mrs. Okafor on Friday morning. "Like a race. My body is getting me ready to play, not to fall apart." They worked out a plan together, a kind of treaty between Ariana and her own pounding heart: she wouldn't fight it, and she wouldn't let it tell her to skip the recital either. She also set a boundary with her cousin, who kept texting "are you nervous yet" every hour; she asked him to stop until after the show. That was her coping plan, and she carried it down the hallway to the auditorium.

Backstage, her heart thundered. Ariana took her seat at the piano, spread her cold fingers over the keys, and thought, there you are. Then she began to play.

Jade sat on her bedroom floor with her shoes off, pressing her heel against the pencil mark she had drawn on the wall two weeks ago. Her sneakers had started pinching at school, so she had marked the wall to check something, and now she leaned forward and squinted. The mark had moved. Not by much, but by enough.

"Mom says shoes are expensive," her little brother Denny said from the doorway, holding his own sneakers, which were also tight. He was nine and had worn the same shoes all year. "I only got new ones in September."

"That's the weird part," Jade said. She pulled out a notebook and wrote down what she knew. Denny had needed new shoes in September, and now in March his toes were pushing the ends again, even though his jeans from September still fit fine. Her own shoes pinched too, and her sleeves still reached her wrists. She tapped the pencil against her chin. Feet and hands first, then everything else. Maybe that was the order.

"How do you know?" Denny asked, doubtful. He came in and sat on her bed, swinging his legs.

"I don't know yet. That's why I'm testing it." She held up her hand against Denny's. "Look. Yours are almost as big as mine now. If it's really hands and feet first, your hands should be big too, even though you're little." Denny spread his fingers, and Jade compared them to her own palm. His fingers reached her knuckles. Last summer they had only reached her first finger joints. She wrote that down too.

"There's a chart in my science binder," she said, jumping up. She carried the binder, heavy with a year of notes, across the room and let it drop onto the bed with a thump that made Denny laugh. She flipped through until she found the page about growing. She read it twice, then closed the binder slowly.

"Hands and feet grow first," she said. "Before arms, legs, and the rest. So shoes stop fitting before anything else does."

"Before jeans?" Denny asked.

"Before jeans, before sleeves, before everything." She looked at her brother, who was still worried about Mom saying no to new shoes. He had worn duct tape on one sole since February, and the resentment on his face whenever kids mentioned sneakers had been building for weeks. She knew that look. "Come on," she said.

They found Mom in the kitchen, and Jade laid out the notebook, the measurements, and the comparison of hands. "He'll keep growing into everything else soon," she finished. "His feet are just early." Mom sighed at the numbers, then measured Denny's foot with the wooden ruler, and drove them both to the shoe store before dinner.

At the store, Denny ran one lap around the aisle in his new shoes while Jade waited by the register, holding his old pair. "Transport these to the donation bin when we get home," Mom said, handing her the bag. In the dry, arid heat of the parking lot, Denny was still bouncing. "Your feet will be next," he told her, pointing at her pinching sneakers. Jade wiggled her toes and laughed. "Already are."

Nathaniel was eating cereal at the kitchen table with his laptop open when the group chat lit up. It was the Robotics Club chat, the one with eleven people in it, and someone named Marcus had just posted a screenshot. Nathaniel leaned closer, crumbs falling onto the keyboard. The screenshot showed a private chat between him and his friend Dev, and in it Nathaniel had written, "Honestly, Priya's robot arm design is garbage and she never listens to anyone." He had sent that two days ago, to one person, in a chat that said Just Dev and Nathaniel at the top.

His stomach dropped like an elevator with cut cables. Below the screenshot, Priya had typed a single line: "Cool. Thanks for that." Three people had reacted with the shocked face emoji. The room smelled suddenly too much like cinnamon cereal, and the fan above the stove hummed like nothing was wrong with the world.

Nathaniel closed his laptop, then opened it again. His first thought was that hackers had gotten in, which made him feel better for about four seconds. But nobody hacks a chat to steal a complaint about a robot arm. He had sent that message to exactly one person. If it was now in a different group chat, then Dev had shared it, because a private message only stays private if the person who receives it keeps it that way. Anyone with the message could screenshot it and pass it along. So the hidden cause wasn't hackers or a glitch. It was Dev.

He decided to test the idea before accusing anyone. He typed a new private message to Dev: "Hey, did you leave your phone unlocked at school today?" If Dev had no idea what he meant, the answer would sound confused. Instead Dev wrote back in eleven seconds: "Ok yeah. Marcus grabbed my phone in the cafeteria and went through my chats. I should've told you. I'm sorry." There it was, like finding the source of a leak in a pipe. Marcus, whose brother drove a delivery truck full of cargo from the airport and who never stopped talking about it, had hijacked Dev's phone and shipped Nathaniel's private words to the group like freight.

Nathaniel took a breath that tasted like cinnamon. First he sent Priya a message, not private this time, right in the group where everyone could see it: "That was a rude thing I wrote and I'm sorry. Your arm design has the best grip strength in the club." Then he wrote to Dev: "Next time change your password, and I'll try writing complaints in a journal made of actual paper."

He hit send, and the little checkmark appeared next to his apology, sitting there in public where everybody could watch Priya's reply load: "Meet me at the workbench tomorrow. Bring your grip strength ideas."

Jordan had been counting down to this beach trip for eleven days, and when the car finally rolled into the sandy lot by the dunes, he was out the door before Dad even killed the engine. Mom handed him the sunscreen tube at the picnic table. "Whole face, ears, back of the neck," she said, and he did it fast, because the waves were calling. That was nine in the morning.

By ten, he was bodysurfing. By eleven, he and his cousin Tessa were digging a trench so long that a jogger stopped to admire it, and the jogger's dog, a lush golden retriever named Biscuit, lay down in the hole and refused to move. Jordan was sweating from all the shoveling. Then he went straight back into the water, and Tessa followed, and they stayed in until their fingers wrinkled, then out for sandwiches, then in again. Nobody mentioned sunscreen once all day. The afternoon sun didn't feel hot in the water; it felt like nothing at all, which Jordan would later decide was the tricky part.

At four o'clock, toweling off, he caught sight of his shoulders in the truck's side mirror. They were pink. Really pink, the color of the shrimps in the cooler. Tessa's nose was peeling already at the edges. "Mom's going to make us read the sunscreen tube as punishment," Tessa groaned, and Jordan, curious now, flipped the tube over and read the back while the wind tried to snatch it.

"Reapply every two hours," he read out loud, "and immediately after swimming or sweating." He counted backward on his fingers, feeling like a detective in one of the memoirs Grandpa was always writing about his Coast Guard days. One application at nine. Swimming by ten. Sweating by eleven. Seven hours with nothing extra. The morning coating must diminish over time, or wash off, or both, and they had never once renewed it. That was the whole mystery solved in one sentence on a plastic tube. "We did everything wrong in exactly the right order," he told Tessa, and she laughed even while pressing cool fingers to her nose.

Aloe gel became the evening's main event. Dad lined them up on the porch of the rental cottage and dabbed it on while Biscuit's owner, who turned out to be staying next door, watched with amusement. Jordan held up the sunscreen tube like a trophy. "Two hours, every time," he announced. "And after swimming. Even sweating counts."

"And tomorrow?" Tessa asked, already grinning.

Jordan shook the tube. It sloshed, half full. "Timer on my watch. First one to remind me gets the last popsicle."

The fourth game of the day, and Payton still hadn't beaten Marcus. They were sitting on the porch of the crafts cabin, the chessboard between them, while everyone else was at the lake. Marcus moved his bishop, grinned, and leaned back like he'd already won.

Payton picked up her knight to think, then set it back down without moving it. "Hold on. I want to look at the whole board first."

"No take-backs," Marcus said immediately. "You touched it, you have to move it."

"That's not a rule. I wasn't even going to move it yet."

They argued for a solid minute, getting louder, until Payton held up a hand. "Okay. Naming the problem: you think touching means committing, and I think only moving means committing. Those are different rules."

"Fine," Marcus said, "but which one is the actual rule?"

Payton looked around. The only chess book at camp belonged to Dolores, the craft lady, who was pretending to weave but obviously listening. "Can we borrow that book? Just to check one thing?"

Dolores handed over a worn paperback with a cracked spine. Payton flipped through it until she found the tournament rules, and there it was, in print. In formal chess, the touch-move rule says a player who deliberately touches one of their own pieces must move it, if that piece has a legal move. "Look," she said. "It even has a name. The touch-move rule."

Marcus read it twice. "So you have to move the knight."

"Right. But now we agree on the rule, so it's fair for both of us. Next time you touch your rook, same thing happens to you."

"That's going to be a disaster for me," Marcus said. "I touch everything. I'm like a raccoon."

Payton moved her knight to the only safe square, which, it turned out, forked his rook and queen. "Interesting," she said, and reached for her water bottle very, very carefully, with one finger.

The Hurricanes had lost every game so far, and they had yelled at each other through all of them. Jake sat on the bench after practice, lacing and unlacing his cleats, listening to Marcus and Dev argue about who should take the free kicks. Marcus wanted to be captain so badly that he had started wearing an armband he made himself, and Dev said the armband meant nothing. The whole team had become a controversy on legs, as Jake's older sister would say.

At home, Jake dug through her old report on teamwork that she had left on the kitchen table. He had to extract the page he wanted from under a stack of her magazines. The report said that a psychologist named Bruce Tuckman had proposed in 1965 that groups go through stages called forming, storming, norming and performing. Jake read the line twice. Forming was when a group first got together. Storming, the report said, was the arguing stage. Norming was when they settled things. Performing was when they finally worked. He thought about the last three weeks of the Hurricanes and felt something click, like a puzzle piece turning over in his hand.

He remembered the very first practice, back when school had just started. Nobody had known anyone's name, so they had all stood in an awkward circle passing the ball politely, saying "nice try" even after terrible passes. That was the forming part, he realized. Then the storming had begun, game by game, argument by argument.

Before the next practice, Jake texted his sister from the kitchen: Do you still have that Tuckman report? We're stuck in the storming stage and I want to know how long it lasts. She wrote back: It lasts as long as it lasts. But it doesn't last forever. Show them the report. So Jake photocopied it and brought the page to the field, where the October grass was damp and the goal nets sagged with morning dew.

He read the four words out loud while the team stretched. "Forming, storming, norming, performing," said Marcus slowly, tugging his homemade armband up his arm. "So we're not broken. We're just in the middle." Dev squinted at the page, then at Marcus. "Fine," he said. "You can call the plays. But I take the free kicks." Marcus nodded once, the way captains do in movies.

The Saturday game was still sloppy in the first half, and the goals they gave up felt like the cumulative weight of the whole season pressing down. But in the second half, when the ball came loose near midfield, Marcus shouted a play without shouting at anyone, and Dev touched it once and slid it to Jake, who was already running into the open space. Jake struck it low, toward the far post, and watched it curl inside the net. The team piled on him in the wet grass, and from somewhere under the heap of players, Marcus yelled, "That's performing, right there!"

Oliver's mother had dropped him at Sunrise Travel for the afternoon because the dentist was next door, and because Mr. Adeyemi, the agent, had known him since he was five. The office smelled of old paper and coffee. On the back wall hung a giant world map with faint lines drawn across it, sideways and up and down, like graph paper wrapped around the world.

"You can find any city on Earth if you can read those lines," Mr. Adeyemi said, resting his coffee cup on the counter. "Latitude lines run sideways. Longitude lines run up and down. A city sits where one of each crosses. Nobody memorizes all the cities. You just read the numbers." He tapped a spot in Africa. "Cairo, about 30 degrees north latitude, 31 degrees east longitude." Oliver leaned close and traced the numbers with one finger, the way he had once traced the letters on his grandfather's frail old globe before it cracked in the move and had to be thrown out. He still felt bad about packing it badly. His grandfather had only said, "Maps outlive globes anyway," and Oliver had never been sure whether that was forgiveness or not.

A woman hurried in with a folder of papers, a customer named Mrs. Okafor who wanted to visit her sister in a city Oliver had never heard of. "Sister keeps saying, come before the heat, come before the heat," she told Mr. Adeyemi, "but she can never tell me why the heat comes when it comes." Mr. Adeyemi began flipping through a fat index of cities, muttering that his filing system was a disgrace and that if he could just win the office pool for most trips booked this month, he would finally buy a proper computerized system and retire the shoebox of index cards under his desk.

Oliver, meanwhile, was not looking up cities. He was looking at the tan patches. The Sahara, the Arabian Desert, the Kalahari, the Australian outback, the stretch across Mexico. He had noticed something at home on his wall map, and now, on this bigger one, he counted again, using the latitude lines like a measuring stick. The big hot deserts were not scattered anywhere. They lined up in two belts, one above the equator and one below, and when he read the numbers, the belts sat near 30 degrees north and near 30 degrees south. He checked one desert after another, and they kept landing on those numbers, as if the map had a rule it was following.

"Where sinking air warms up and dries out," Oliver said slowly, reading aloud from the small print under the map's legend. "That's why the deserts sit there, near 30 degrees north or south of the equator. It's a pattern."

"Find me the pattern for a rainforest, then," Mrs. Okafor said, half joking. Oliver ran his finger along the equator itself, where the green blobbiest jungles lived, past a poster of toucans dipping into flowers for nectar, past a caption about orchids that seemed able to colonize every wet branch in sight.

"Hot and wet at the equator, hot and dry at thirty," Oliver said. "So tell your sister the heat comes because her city sits in the dry belt. Thirty-two degrees north." Mrs. Okafor laughed and booked the ticket. Mr. Adeyemi slid the index card into his shoebox and said, "Two more bookings and that computer is mine."

Oliver went back to the map and put his finger on the empty blue Pacific, right at 30 degrees south, and waited to see if the rule would hold even there.

Emilia's hands were shaking again, and she hadn't even opened the envelope yet. The letter from the science fair committee had been sitting on the kitchen table since Tuesday, and every time she walked past it, her stomach clenched like a fist. She had been nominated for the regional finals by her teacher, which should have felt like winning, but instead it felt like being handed a bomb with a ribbon on it.

"Still not opening it?" her brother Theo asked, sliding into the chair across from her with a bowl of cereal.

"I'm building up to it," Emilia said. "Slowly."

"Nominate you for what, disappearing contests? You've been hiding up in your room all week."

She glared at him, but he wasn't wrong. She thought about last month, before the nomination, when she'd actually liked her science project. She'd spent evenings in the garage testing water samples from the creek, laughing when Theo spilled pH solution on his shoe. Then the letter came, and something in her had switched off. Her stomach hurt. She couldn't sleep. On Friday she'd fallen asleep during math, which she never did.

That afternoon her mother drove her to the clinic because the stomachaches wouldn't quit. Dr. Okafor listened, asked questions, and ran tests that came back normal. Then she leaned forward and said, "I think your body's been running on stress too long. There's a hormone called cortisol, made by the adrenal glands, and it rises during stress. When stress lasts for weeks, cortisol can stay high, and that can leave you feeling run down." Emilia had scribbled it all in her notebook, because facts were easier to hold than feelings.

Now, sitting at the kitchen table, she opened the notebook and read her own handwriting. Her anxiety had started the day the letter arrived. It had lasted weeks. If the doctor was right, her body was still churning out cortisol like a factory that forgot to close. "Theo," she said slowly, "I have a hypothesis. The stomachaches aren't random. They follow the stress. If the stress stops, the cortisol should come down."

"So stop being stressed," Theo said, as if that were obvious.

"That's not how it works. I need coping stuff. Actual strategies." She flipped to a blank page and made a list: breathing exercises, walks by the creek, talking to Mom instead of hiding. At the bottom she wrote one more line in careful letters: I will set boundaries. No practicing past eight o'clock, and no reading the judges' comments fifty times.

She took a breath, picked up the envelope, and tore it open. "I'm in the finals," she said, and her voice came out steady. "Round one's in three weeks."

"Plenty of time," Theo said, raising his cereal spoon like a toast. "Your stress guild will just have to find a new member."

"Not everything's a guild," Emilia said, but she laughed, and her stomach, for the first time in days, stayed quiet. She taped the acceptance letter above her desk, right next to the list, and went outside to the creek with her sample kit.

Zoe arrived at her grandmother's house on Saturday morning with a granola bar hidden in her jacket pocket. Her family had agreed she would try keeping Shabbat for part of the day, from sunrise until three o'clock, the way Grandma did. No phone, no money, no snacks between meals. Zoe had said yes mostly to get her mother off her back, and she planned to eat the granola bar in the garden shed the first time Grandma wasn't looking.

At breakfast, she asked Grandma why rest even counted as doing something. "You're not doing anything," Zoe said. "You're just not doing stuff."

Grandma set down her teacup. "You could put it that way. Or you could say it's a principle, one day out of seven, and the point is to stop," she said. She slid a folded letter across the table. "Your grandfather wrote this the year he died. Read it while the light's good."

The letter was written on translucent paper, the kind that showed the newspaper print beneath it, and Zoe tilted it toward the window. Grandpa had written about his own grandmother, who kept the whole day, sunrise to three stars, and how at first he thought it was empty. Then he described sitting with nothing in his hands and noticing, for the first time, the sound of the kettle and the creak of the third stair. He wrote that the day was like a window that had been painted shut and someone finally pushed it open.

Zoe put the granola bar back in her pocket without taking it out. At noon she went with Grandma to Danny's house, where Danny's family was sitting shiva for his grandfather. Danny was in the kitchen, and Zoe asked him what the word meant that people kept saying upstairs.

"Olam ha-ba," Danny said. "That's what they call the afterlife. It means the world to come."

When they got home, Zoe pulled Grandma's big Tanakh off the shelf and searched for the phrase, flipping through Genesis and the prophets. She found nothing. "It's not in here," she said. "Not even once."

"Not in the Hebrew Bible, no," Grandma said, and went back to her tea.

Zoe sat with that. Grandpa hadn't needed it printed anywhere either; he had written his own letter and left it where she would find it, exactly on the day she needed something to fill the quiet. She stayed past three o'clock without checking the clock, and when the shadows stretched across the kitchen floor, she opened the Tanakh again and started at the beginning.

"I'll read until dinner," she said.

Riley woke to his phone buzzing and a text from school in bright letters across the screen: closed for snow. He pressed his face to the window and saw the park across the street buried in white, the swings wearing thick snowy caps. He had promised Mrs. Okafor next door that he would check on her cat while she was away, and he had promised his friends he would meet them at the sledding hill by ten. He pulled on two pairs of socks and started out.

Halfway across the park, he noticed something odd. Every step he took made a loud squeak, like a rubber duck being stepped on. Squeak, squeak, squeak, all the way past the frozen duck pond. He stopped and pressed his boot down slowly, and the snow cried out under it. He remembered yesterday, when the snow had been soft and quiet and he had rolled it into balls without a sound. The snow had not changed color or shape. Something invisible had changed underneath it.

"The squeak means it got colder," he said out loud, to nobody. He tried an experiment. He stomped hard on a patch of snow, then stepped gently on another patch, and both times the crystals crunched and broke with the same sharp noise instead of squishing quietly like they had yesterday. Warm snow gave a little under his boot. This snow was too hard and icy for that, so it snapped and squealed instead. He looked at the sky, flat and gray, and zipped his coat all the way to his chin.

At the sledding hill, his friend Dara was taking a census of everyone who had showed up, walking around with a mitten full of pebbles and dropping one in her pocket for each kid on the hill. "Twelve," she announced, "but Marcus says thirteen, so we're counting again." Riley told them about the squeaking snow, and they all stomped in a circle like a small thunderstorm until a park volunteer asked them to settle down. They decided to nurture the half-built snow fort near the picnic tables instead, packing the squeaky snow into firm walls that rang under their mittens.

Dara wanted to sled straight down the icy slope that ended near the benches, but Riley shook his head. "That part's frozen solid now, like the squeaky snow. That's why it's squeaking. It would be reckless to hit those benches at that speed." They chose the slower hill instead, and Riley's first run was smooth and quiet, his scarf snapping behind him. At the bottom he looked back up at his boot prints, a dotted line of small dark marks, and heard Dara squeaking her way down after him, laughing the whole ride.

Jaxon stood in front of the bilingual booth at the festival, holding his crumpled worksheet about next year's plans. His teacher had circled one word in red: "teneré." Next to it, a single question mark. The booth had a sign that said "Habla con nosotros," and behind the table sat a girl about his age wearing a shirt with a luminous sugar skull glowing under the string lights.

"Tengo un perro y una hermana," Jaxon said, mostly to prove he could. "Mi perro se llama Biscuit. Mi hermana se llama Dana."

The girl laughed. "Biscuit is the dog or the sister?"

"The dog. Dana would retire from being my sister before answering to Biscuit." He flattened the worksheet on the table. "But I wrote this paragraph about next year, and this one word came back circled in red. I figured you just stick an é on any verb. Tener, teneré. Boom."

She shook her head and wrote on a napkin: tendré. "Tener becomes tendré," she said. "It means I will have. Not teneré."

Jaxon stared at the napkin. So the verb wasn't just getting a new ending; it was changing its stem too, and there was no way to see that coming unless somebody showed you or you caught the pattern yourself. He tested it out loud. "El año que viene tendré trece años. Y Biscuit tendrá... um, much older in dog years."

"Better," she said. "Try the whole paragraph."

He worked through it slowly, fixing verbs one by one, while somewhere behind them a drummer started up and a vendor carried a luminous glass vessel of lemonade past the booth, ice cubes rattling like tiny applause. When he finished, the girl clapped anyway, louder than the ice.

"Next year," Jaxon said, pointing at the napkin, "tendré un perro que habla español mejor que yo."

"Keep practicing," she said, and wrote her number for the language exchange club on the corner of the napkin, right beside tendré.

Grandpa Frank arrived on Saturday with one duffel bag, a jar of his famous honey, and a hearing aid that whistled when he hugged her. Nora had been counting down the days all week. She had plans: board games, pancake mornings, a trip to the creek to look for frog eggs.

The trouble started at dinner. "Grandpa, do you want the butter?" she called from the kitchen while he sat at the table. He didn't turn around. She tried again, louder, practically shouting, and he just frowned at his plate. Mom leaned over and said something to him, and he laughed right away. Nora stared. How could Mom's quiet words work when her loud ones didn't?

She decided to diagnose the problem like a scientist, the way they did in science class. First hypothesis: Grandpa was ignoring her. That seemed plausible until she noticed he answered Mom every single time. Second hypothesis: it was about where Mom was standing. Mom always faced him. Nora ran a test in the living room. From behind him, she asked, "Is it supposed to rain?" Shouting it made him spin around, startled, and guess wrong twice. Then she walked around, looked straight at him, and said it again, clearly and at a normal volume. "Rain? Maybe tomorrow," he said instantly.

"So it's not louder, it's closer and facing you," Nora said, bouncing on the couch cushions. "From my perspective, I thought volume was everything."

"Faces carry a lot," Grandpa said, tapping his hearing aid. "And that whistling thing needs new batteries anyway. I've been guessing half the conversations in this house."

Here was the twist: all week, whenever Nora had muttered, he hadn't been ignoring her. He'd been pretending, nodding along, guessing from context, because he was embarrassed to keep asking people to repeat themselves. She'd thought he was grumpy. He'd thought she was avoiding him.

After that, it became their game. She'd catch herself yelling from the hallway, stop mid-word, sprint into the room, and plant herself in front of him. "Face-to-face squad," she announced, holding up a fist. He bumped it with his knuckles, grinning.

On Friday, her last morning with him, she flipped a pancake high, caught it, and turned to Grandpa before saying a word. "Perfect flip," he said. "Heard the sizzle, saw your face. Didn't miss a thing."

Violet sat at her mother's desk on a Saturday, when the office was almost empty, using the spare computer to hunt for a science project idea. She wanted to build something that would insulate a soda can and keep it cold, and she typed "keep can cold" into the search bar. The first screen full of results was mostly shopping links and a big sponsored box shouting BEST THERMOS. She remembered her mother saying that half of searching was choosing words, so she tried "aluminum can insulation experiment foam." The junk mostly dropped away, and one result from a university engineering page looked real. She noticed the small gray word "Ad" tucked beside the second result and skipped it.

Her friend Marco had come along, and he was supposed to be helping, but he was busy being proud of something else. "Look at my password," he said, turning his phone toward her. "p@ssw0rd. The a is an at sign and the o is a zero. Nobody can guess that." He had changed it that morning so he could log into the project-sharing site they used for science club.

"Ad" or not, Violet couldn't stop wondering about it. She remembered a month ago, when the club's shared account got locked after someone kept guessing at the password, and Mr. Reyes had said guessers work through obvious things fast. She opened a new tab and searched with specific keywords: "password guessing programs dictionary words common substitutions." She skipped the sponsored result and read a short article on a security site.

"Marco," she said. "Guessing programs try dictionary words, names, and common swaps like '@' for 'a' or '0' for 'o' early." She read the line twice to be sure. "So your at signs and zeros add almost nothing."

"No way," Marco said. He looked at his phone. "It looks so tricky."

Violet tested it. She searched "p@ssw0rd common password" and found it on lists of the most guessed passwords in the world. Marco made an abrupt grab for the keyboard, but she was already typing, and she pulled up a page where he could make a longer password out of four random words instead. He typed in "copper foam jar moon" and hit save.

"Fine," he said. "But I'm keeping the can project."

"Then help me search," Violet said. She slid the notepad over and wrote "soda can insulation" at the top of a fresh list of keywords. Marco sighed, pulled his chair closer, and started typing.

Eve typed "jaguar" into the search bar for the third time, and for the third time the first screen was all car dealerships. Her science report was due Friday, and she needed facts about the animal, not a dealership offering zero percent financing.

Her older brother Marcus leaned over her shoulder from the couch, where he had a library copy of a notorious rocker's memoir open on his lap. He wanted to finish it before his book club meeting on Saturday, and Eve's typing was slowing down the wifi he blamed for everything.

"Everything's an ad," Eve said, pointing at the top of the page. "How do I even tell what's real?"

Marcus set the memoir face-down on the cushion. "The ones that say 'Sponsored' in the corner, they paid to be there. And anything trying to sell you a car, that's a clue." He picked the book back up. "This rock guy was notorious for throwing TVs out of hotel windows, by the way. Whole chapter on it."

Eve studied the page. The top three results had "Sponsored" labels and prices. Below them sat a zoo page, a wildlife fund page, and a page titled "Jaguar Cars Reviews." She scrolled past it and found three more car pages, then more dealerships. The animal facts were buried on page two, under a result that looked like it had been written in 2009.

She tried "jaguar animal," which helped a little, but the cars still crowded in. Then she noticed something in the search tips box at the bottom of the screen, small gray text she had skipped twice before. A minus sign placed directly before a word, with no space, removes results containing that word. She tested it, typing jaguar -car, and hit enter.

The dealerships vanished. Every result on the first screen was the animal: a fact sheet, a rainforest site, a page with a range map. Eve bookmarked three of them, then closed the laptop.

"Fixed it," she said.

Marcus held up the memoir. "This guy could never," he said, and went back to his chapter.

The class group chat had existed for exactly one day, and it was already a mess. Norah sat at her computer lab station scrolling through the messages. Someone named SoccerStar09 had written "BE AT THE FIELD AT THREE" in all capitals, and Marcus had replied "WHY ARE YOU YELLING AT ME." Then came twenty minutes of arguing about who was angry and who was not.

"He wasn't yelling," Norah said to Priya, who sat at the next computer. "He just types in capitals. My grandpa does it too. But it reads like yelling, so everyone presumed he was mad."

"Then why does he do it?" Priya asked.

Norah clicked over to a search page. "I want to know if anyone ever wrote actual rules for this. Like, official ones." She typed "official online manners" and hit enter. The results loaded slowly, one blue link at a time. Then she found something odd: a document with a plain, number-like name.

"Look at this," she said. "It's called RFC 1855. It's one of the first written guides to online manners, and it was published in 1995."

"1995?" Priya leaned over. "That's before my parents even had the internet at home."

"Here's the title," Norah said, scrolling. "Netiquette Guidelines." She read a line out loud. "'Don't use all capitals. It looks like you're shouting.' So it's a real rule, and it's old."

Priya pointed at the screen. "You could make it our class rule and say it's official. Nobody would even know where it came from."

"That's biased," Norah said. "If I only show them the one rule about capitals, I'm picking the part that proves my point." She kept reading. The guide said to be careful in public spaces, where lots of people see what you write, and to remember that a message to one person is not the same as a message to everyone. "The chat is public. Our whole class is in it."

They printed the rule about capitals, and Norah pinned it to the corkboard by the door. By the end of the lab period, three people had come over to read it. Marcus copied it into the chat as "RULE ONE." SoccerStar09 replied with "ok ok," all lowercase, and then, a minute later, "i can't find the shift key anymore."

Norah was about to log off when a new message appeared. It was from Ms. Alvarez, their teacher, and every word was in capitals: "GREAT WORK ON THE RULES, EVERYONE."

Priya started laughing before Norah could say anything. "Go tell her."

Norah unplugged her headphones, walked to the front of the room, and held up the printed page. "Ms. Alvarez? You might want to read this."

Brooklyn counted the crumpled bills in her hand again at the counter of her uncle's gas station: four dollars and thirty-five cents. Last month, strawberries at the farmers' market had cost eight dollars a basket, which meant her plan for a strawberry shortcake had collapsed on the sidewalk outside the gym. Behind her, the drink cooler hummed, and Mr. Ruiz, who came every Tuesday for the same ten gallons of gas, was stacking jars of his grandmother's salsa on the counter, hoping Uncle Marco would sell them beside the chips. His salsa needed tomatoes, and good ones, and he wanted them cheap.

"Market day," Uncle Marco said, nodding at the window. The farmers' market shared the gravel lot with the station on Saturdays, and Brooklyn watched a flatbed truck roll in, then another, their beds stacked so high with strawberry baskets that the driver had to regulate his speed over the speed bump to keep them from sliding. A third truck followed. Every farmer seemed to have berries, rows and rows of red in the morning light, and the field behind the station, dark and fertile from all the June rain, had been dotted with pickers all week.

Brooklyn walked out and stood at the first stall. "How much?"

"Four dollars a basket," the farmer said. "It's the peak of the harvest season. Everybody's got the most they'll have all year."

She did the math twice. Half of eight. She tested it at the next stall anyway, and the next, and every sign said the same thing, four dollars, sometimes three fifty. She bought two baskets and still had coins left for whipped cream.

On her way back she stopped beside Mr. Ruiz. "Tomatoes are probably cheap right now too," she said. "Everything's coming in at once." He straightened up, looked at the trucks, and grinned at the baskets in her arms.

"I'll follow you," he said, and carried his empty crate toward the stalls.

Kaitlyn had exactly one night to figure out an opening hook, because Mrs. Parekh had made it very clear: tomorrow, everyone gives a two-minute speech, three points, a closing, and no starting with "Hi, my name is." Kaitlyn's draft began with "Hi, my name is," which she now regarded as evidence of a desolate imagination. She crumpled it into her pocket and wandered toward the auditorium, where the drama club was rehearsing because Mrs. Parekh refused to retire the old tradition of holding the sixth-grade speech contest on the same stage, one night after the actors.

One boy, Dev, stood alone under a single spotlight, saying strange things to nobody. "To be, or not to be," he told the empty air. Kaitlyn sat down in the dark rows and watched. There was no other actor. No reply. Just Dev, pacing, thinking out loud as if the audience were inside his head.

"You missed your cue partner," she whispered to herself, then frowned. There was no partner. So who was he talking to? She tested the simplest idea she had: maybe nobody, and that was the point. She slipped backstage after the run-through and asked him straight out.

"Who are you talking to up there? The stage is empty."

"Exactly," Dev said, peeling off his pretend crown. "It's a soliloquy. The character's alone on stage, and the audience gets to hear his private thoughts."

Kaitlyn walked home fast, turning it over. A speech that let the audience hear her private thoughts. Her topic was "why the school should fix the drinking fountain by the gym," which was, she admitted, not a natural thriller. But what if she started alone in thought, like the boy in the spotlight? She rewrote the opening at her kitchen table while her little brother banged his spoon. "Every day I walk past that fountain and think, not again," she wrote, and underlined it twice.

The next night she stood on the stage, waited for silence, and began, "Not again. That's what I think, every single day, in the east hallway, and I've never told anyone until now." She heard a kid in the second row sit up. She gave her three points, steered the ending like a boat with a good rudder, and closed with, "So tomorrow, when you pass that fountain, you'll know exactly what I'm thinking." Mrs. Parekh wrote something on her clipboard and did not frown. In the wings, Dev gave her a small bow.

The waiting room of Bright Smiles Dental smelled like mint and rubber gloves, and Landon had already read the poster about molars twice. His problem was bigger than a cavity. Next week he had to give a science report on how bees pollinate flowers, standing in front of the whole class, and ever since Ms. Rivera announced it, his hands got clammy and his brain went fuzzy. His mom said everyone gets nervous, which did not help at all.

In the corner, a girl about his age sat tracing something on the armrest of her chair. Up, across, down, across. Slow and steady, like she was drawing a square over and over. Landon watched her do it four times before his curiosity won.

"Are you drawing a map?" he asked.

She looked up like she'd been caught. "It's box breathing. My sister taught me before her recitals." She traced one side with her finger. "You breathe in for four, hold for four, breathe out for four, then hold for four. Then you do the whole pattern again." She demonstrated, sliding her finger up the invisible left wall while she inhaled, across the top while she held it, down the side while she breathed out, and along the bottom during the last hold.

Landon tried it right there, drawing his own square on the magazine cover in front of him. In four, hold four, out four, hold four. By the time the receptionist called his name, something surprising had happened: the fizzy feeling in his chest had shrunk to almost nothing.

In the chair, Dr. Okafor tilted her light and peered at his back teeth. "You're growing fast, Landon. Growing bodies sweat more, which is why showering every day and using deodorant becomes a significant part of the routine around your age. It's not a punishment, just biology." Landon grinned around the suction tube. Growth, sweat, breathing squares: it was a lot of new information, but he felt ready. Monday morning, standing in front of his class, he traced a square on the podium, one side for each count of four, and began: "Bees don't just visit flowers. They pollinate them."

Mathis crouched between the rows of onions with his sketchbook balanced on his knee, and so far the page held exactly one thing: a sun with rays radiating out of it in every direction. His assignment was due Monday. Draw a food chain, his teacher had said, from the sun all the way to a top predator, and explain what happens if one link disappears. The garden was supposed to give him the whole chain for free, but so far it was giving him nothing but dirt under his nails.

"You're staring at an onion," said Priya, dropping down beside him with a bucket of water she was supposed to be carrying somewhere.

"I'm looking for aphids." Tiny green aphids meant the food chain's middle links. Aphids sucked juice from the onions, ladybugs ate the aphids, and the ladybug was his top predator. If he could find the bugs and sketch them, the poster would practically draw itself. He had already tried three plants in vain. Then he spotted them, a whole crowd of green specks clustered on an onion leaf, and right beside them, one round orange ladybug, steady as a stone. He copied the scene fast, before anything hopped away.

Priya leaned over his shoulder. "You made the leaf way too plain. Mrs. Okafor will want the cells. She's got that microscope in the shed, the one the bank donated when the garden almost got sold to pay somebody's mortgage." Mathis had forgotten about the microscope. He picked a thin sliver of onion skin, carried it to the shed, and slid it under the lens. The cells appeared like neat brick walls, each one boxed in. He labeled the cell wall, then the nucleus, easy. Then he reached the label that said cell membrane, and his pencil stopped. There was no line inside the boxes. Nothing. He turned the focus wheel back and forth until his eyes ached. "Maybe onion cells don't even have one," he muttered.

He tried a second slide, then a third. Same thing. The box stayed clean and single-lined, and the missing membrane stayed missing, no matter how he squinted. Then, staring until the brick shapes blurred, he understood. The membrane wasn't gone. It was pressed right up against the inside of the wall, so tight against it that it didn't show as its own line at all. The cell was full, that was all, so full that the membrane had nowhere to be except flat against the wall. He wrote "cell membrane" with an arrow pointing at the very edge of the box, right against the wall line, and drew a small tight second line beside it on his poster version so nobody else would hunt for it the way he had.

On the walk home he thought about the aphids, fat and crowded on that leaf, and the lone ladybug holding the border. Back at the garden, Priya was still watering. "Finished?" she called.

"Almost." He flipped his sketchbook open to the sun. "Watch this." He drew a big X through the ladybug, then over the aphids he wrote, in careful block letters, "100 of them by Friday."

Gavin had thirty minutes before the community center spelling bee started, so he wandered into the little library off the gym, looking for a quiet corner to calm his nerves. On a bottom shelf, wedged between dusty encyclopedias, sat a fat old book with a cracked leather cover. He opened it carefully. The pages smelled like dust and rain, and the words were printed in long, narrow columns. It was a dictionary, but not like the one at school. This one looked ancient.

"Who decided how words are spelled?" he asked Priya, who had followed him in. "I mean, somebody had to. Somebody had to write down that C-A-T is cat and not K-A-T."

Priya flipped the brittle pages with one finger. "Look at the front. There might be a name." There was. A portrait of a stern man in a wig, and printing underneath that Gavin read slowly. "It says Samuel Johnson," he said. "Samuel Johnson's 'A Dictionary of the English Language', published in 1755, helped settle how many English words were spelled." He read the sentence twice, because it seemed like a big job for one man. "So before that, spellings were kind of loose. And this book helped pin them down."

"That's a weird thing to think about," Priya said. "Like, spelling wasn't always a rule?" Gavin tested the idea in his head, the way he tested everything. If spellings were once unsettled, then the weird silent letters he hated, the G-H in "night," must have been locked in by somebody's choice, not by magic. That made them less annoying, somehow. They were history, not tricks.

The bell rang and they hurried to the gym. Gavin sat in the second row of folding chairs and waited through three rounds. A boy named Marcus got "impulsive," spelled it wrong, and shrugged. Then the moderator called Gavin's word. "Larva," she said. Gavin pictured the old dictionary, all those settled letters, and took his time. "L-A-R-V-A. Larva." "Correct," she said.

In the final round the moderator said, "Illustrate." Gavin thought of the stern man in the wig, and of the tiny drawing of a caterpillar in the old book that had seemed to illustrate its own entry. "I-L-L-U-S-T-R-A-T-E. Illustrate." The moderator nodded, and Gavin, holding his blue ribbon, whispered to Priya, "Samuel Johnson would be proud."

The kitchen smelled like garlic bread, but Payton could barely taste it. Her cousins Dez and Marisol had spent the whole afternoon playing their dinosaur card game, and now nobody was speaking except through her. "Tell her the T. rex beats everything," Dez said, jabbing his fork toward Marisol. "Tell him the volcano card wiped out the whole herd, so my raptors win," Marisol shot back. Payton put down her spoon. "Why do you keep telling me? I wasn't even playing."

"Because you're in the middle," Dez said. "You decide who won." Marisol nodded and slid the whole messy pile of cards across the table, waiting. Payton stared at the cards, at the greasy fingerprints, at the volcano card sitting on top of a herd of plastic-coated raptors. If she named a winner, the loser would carry that resentment around for a week, and next Sunday's dinner would be nothing but cold silence and kicked shins under the table. She had seen it happen before, like a species going extinct one Sunday at a time.

Then she remembered the word from the poster in the school hallway, the one about arguments: mediator. "I'm not a judge," she said slowly. "A judge decides who's right. A mediator is a neutral third person who helps two sides reach their own agreement." Dez squinted. "So who won?" "Nobody yet. You two are going to decide, not me." She held up the volcano card. "First we name the actual problem. Marisol, you say the volcano makes the herd extinct. Dez, you say the T. rex wasn't in the herd."

They argued for a minute, but quieter now. Payton tested an idea: what if the rule depended on whether the T. rex card had been played before the volcano? She asked each of them to show the order the cards had gone down, and Marisol checked the app, which transmitted the game log to her phone. The log showed the T. rex had landed last. "So," Dez said, "new rule. Anything played after the volcano survives." Marisol considered it. "Fine. But the volcano can only be used once per game." Dez stuck out his hand. "Deal." They shook over the mashed potatoes. "Same rule next Sunday?" Marisol asked, already shuffling.

Payton slid her phone across the table so her brother Dex could see the text from Nadia. "Fine, it's wrong, but it's just my opinion that the Eiffel Tower is in Berlin." Dex read it twice, then put a piece of broccoli in his mouth and chewed for a long time, as if the broccoli might have an answer.

"That can't be right," Payton said. "If it's an opinion, nobody can check it. Like if I say broccoli tastes like old socks, you can't look that up." She pointed at his plate. "You can be indifferent to broccoli all you want, that's your opinion, and nobody can prove you wrong. But the Eiffel Tower is either in Paris or it isn't. There's one answer. It's a claim." Dex swallowed. "So?" "So it's a wrong claim, not an opinion. It's just a false one." She picked the phone back up and typed: what if I told you my opinion is that you owe me fifty dollars? That's checkable. You can check your pockets.

Dex grinned. "She's going to say that's different." "It's not different." Payton set the phone face down next to her fork, then lifted it again, then set it down again. Their dad, who had been quietly moving rice around his plate this whole time, looked up. "Is this about the France project?" "Nadia put the Eiffel Tower in the wrong city in our group slide," Payton said. "Mrs. Ruiz marked it. Nadia's saying it should count as an opinion so she doesn't lose points."

"Ah," said their dad, and went back to his rice, which seemed to be the most interesting thing at the table.

Payton typed one more message. "The Eiffel Tower is in Berlin is a claim. It can be checked, and it's false. Say you love Berlin, that's an opinion. Say the tower is there, that's just wrong." She hit send and waited, watching the three dots appear, disappear, and appear again. The reply came: "Fine. But I still say broccoli tastes like old socks."

"That part I'll allow," Payton said, and put her phone in her pocket.

Olivia stood at the garage door with a five-dollar bill folded in her pocket, staring down the sidewalk toward the corner store. Mom had said she was old enough to go alone this time, but the trip felt enormous. First she had to find the milk in the back cooler, then pay Mr. Patel, then count her change without letting the line behind her grow impatient. She recited it like a spell: walk, find, pay, count. On the workbench beside her, a note in Grandpa's shaky handwriting lay next to something lumpy and small. "Ran your red sweater through the wash on hot," it said. "Now it would fit a doll. Sorry. It was the sloshing." The sweater that had reached her knees last winter was now the size of a cat.

She picked it up and squeezed it. It was stiff, like felt, not stretchy anymore. On the drive last summer she remembered Grandpa explaining that wool had tiny scales on every fibre, and that heat made the scales open up and grab the neighbouring fibres, pulling the whole knit tighter and tighter. He had called it felting. She turned the little sweater over in her hands. So that's what happened, she thought. Hot, sloshing water, scales locking on, everything shrinking. She wondered if cold water would have left it alone, and decided to ask Mr. Patel, who knew about everything, including wool and milk prices.

The walk to the store was longer than it looked from the garage, but she distinguished the landmarks as she went: the cracked mailbox, the house with the barking poodle, then the blue awning. Mr. Patel was stacking cartons behind the counter. "Milk's three eighty today," he said. "Going up next week, they tell me. Currency never sits still." She handed him the five and counted her coins slowly, one by one, until she had one dollar and twenty cents, exactly right. She almost smiled.

"One question," she said. "If wool goes in a hot wash, and the water sloshes around, do the fibres really lock together?" Mr. Patel laughed. "My mother ruined a sweater that way once. Shrank it to nothing. Felting, they call it." On the way home, milk jug swinging against her leg, Olivia planned to test a tiny corner of the little red sweater in cold water, just to see, and she called over her shoulder, "I'm doing it alone next time too."

Mathis tapped the recipe against his knee and stared at the little propane oven bolted to the corner of the camper. Breakfast was at seven o'clock sharp, because Marcus and Theo were hiking over from the far campsites at six forty-five and would arrive starving. The muffins needed twenty minutes in the oven, and the oven needed fifteen minutes to preheat, plus ten minutes to mix the batter. The eggs, on the other hand, would take five minutes flat. He had been naive to think, when he'd volunteered last night, that everything could just happen at once. Now, with the clock reading six o'clock, he grabbed his pencil and flipped the recipe card over.

He remembered the time last summer when his cousin Priya had invited him for dinner and everything had come out wrong, the potatoes cold, the chicken still pink, the salad sweating on the counter. Priya had shrugged and said, "You start with the one that takes longest and plan backward from the time you want to eat." At the time Mathis had only cared about the pizza they'd ordered afterward. Now, at the picnic table under the pines, he wrote 7:00 at the bottom of the card and started climbing. Muffins out at 7:00 meant they went in at 6:40. Into a preheated oven meant the oven had to be on by 6:25. Batter mixed by then meant mixing at 6:15. Eggs, the quick thing, could wait until 6:55.

He cranked the oven dial and checked the time. Six oh five. Ahead of schedule, for once. Then a gust off the lake rattled the camper and the pilot light went out with a soft pop. The wind had thwarted him. Mathis crouched down, relit it, and dragged the picnic table's windward side against the camper wall as a shield, checking the little blue flame every few minutes after that.

By 6:22 the oven ticked warmly, the batter stood in paper cups, and Theo's voice came up the trail calling his name. Mathis slid the tray in at 6:40 exactly and cracked the eggs into the skillet at 6:55, watching both timers like a hawk. From Theo's perspective, arriving to the smell of baking, Mathis looked like somebody who had done this a hundred times.

At 7:00 Mathis pulled the muffins out, golden and steaming, and set them beside the eggs just as Marcus reached the table. "You're a wizard," Marcus said, already reaching. Mathis slid the plate closer and said, "First one's yours if you get the butter."

Payton set the popcorn bowl between herself and Dad and waited for movie night to begin, but instead of laughing at the funny parts, Dad snapped at her twice for slurping her drink, and he got up three times to pace in the kitchen. That was the fourth grumpy night in a row, and Payton had started keeping a tally in her notebook. Friday: snapped at Mom. Saturday: couldn't focus on fixing the porch step, kept wandering off. Sunday and Monday: more of the same. Something was wrong, and it had started the exact same week Dad threw his vape in the trash and announced, "That's it, done forever."

"It's like he turned into a different person," Payton whispered to Mom while Dad got water from the fridge. "Not a bad person. Just... rattled." She flipped her notebook open on the counter. "Look, I summarized every day since he quit. Grumpy, jumpy, couldn't concentrate on his crossword, and he kept opening the drawer where he used to keep it, like he wanted something that wasn't there." She tapped the page. "I tested an idea, too. On Tuesday I asked him to play cards, and he couldn't sit still for even one round. Then Wednesday I left a note saying I was proud of him, and he got teary over a note. It all started the day he quit."

Mom pulled up an article on her phone and slid it over. Payton read fast, then read it again. "When a dependent person stops using nicotine, withdrawal can bring irritability, anxiety, trouble concentrating, and strong cravings," she read aloud. "Cravings. That's the word. That's what's happening to Dad." She had almost decided Dad was just mad at her, and now she saw her own bias, blaming herself when the pattern pointed somewhere else the whole time.

"So it's temporary?" Payton asked, bouncing on her toes.

"Temporary," Mom said. "And we can help. More popcorn, more patience."

Payton grabbed the bowl, wrote "Day 5" at the top of a fresh page, and drew a big sticker-worthy star next to it. From the living room Dad called, "Coming! Pause it!"

"Don't worry," Payton shouted back. "We saved you the fluffy part!"

The paper in Aurora's hand had a number on it, and she had read it six times since they left the parking lot. "Minus two," she said, staring at the little card. "It says minus two."

Her dad kept both hands on the wheel. The wipers ticked back and forth against a thin rain, and the windshield made everything outside look like it was underwater. He glanced over. "That's your prescription. From Dr. Okafor."

"I know where it's from." Aurora turned the card over, as if the back might say something kinder. "But why is it minus? It's like my eyes took a test and got a negative score." She imagined a big red mark on a paper, the kind her teacher wrote when something was wrong all the way through.

Her little brother, buckled in the back beside her, leaned toward the card. "Minus two. That's worse than zero."

"Nobody's at zero, dummy." But his words landed anyway, and she watched the raindrops slide down the window while she thought. The card listed other things too. There was a word on it, diopters, next to the numbers, and next to that, in the corner, the name of the clinic, which her mom always called the most prestigious one in three counties, the place people drove an hour to reach.

At the stoplight, her dad pivoted in his seat to face her. "You know your cousin Theo wears glasses."

"So?"

"His card says plus something. Plus three, I think. He's farsighted. You're nearsighted, near the opposite. So your numbers go the other way."

Aurora watched the light, red, then green. Her thoughts seemed to revolve around the little minus sign, going round and round it like the cars around the fountain in the town square. Minus for nearsighted. Plus for farsighted. It wasn't a grade at all. It was a direction, like east and west.

"Wait," Theo said slowly. "So a minus doesn't mean bad? It just means which kind?"

"That's what it means," her dad said, and turned back to the road.

The lens strength in diopters, minus two, sat on the card like a small answer instead of a small punishment. Aurora folded the paper along its crease and put it in her jacket pocket, the pocket with the zipper, where important things went.

The glasses would be ready Thursday. She looked out at the rain, at the streetlights she had always thought were fuzzy on purpose, soft glowing blobs that everyone saw the same way. Maybe they weren't. Maybe everyone else had been reading signs and counting leaves all along, and now it was her turn.

"Can we pick the purple frames?" she asked.

"Purple frames," her dad said, and signaled the turn for home.

"Read the smallest line you can," said Nurse Okafor, pointing at the chart, and Rebecca squinted until the letters turned into gray ants marching across the wall.

Her best friend Maya sat on the cot beside her, swinging her legs. Maya had glasses already, and her eyes behind the lenses looked huge, like a cartoon owl's. Rebecca had appoint... no, she had been told to report here three times this week, ever since she'd copied the wrong homework from the board and turned in math about volcanoes.

"You'll get glasses," Maya said. "Then we can be twins. Sort of."

Nurse Okafor flipped lenses into a strange pair of frames, one at a time. "Better? Worse?" Rebecca peered through them at a poster on the near wall. Then, suddenly, the words snapped into focus so sharply she gasped.

"That one! That one's it!"

The nurse wrote a note. "You're nearsighted. Light focuses in front of your retina instead of on it, so far things blur. We fix it with concave lenses, the opposite of Maya's."

"Opposite?" Rebecca grabbed Maya's glasses and held them up next to her trial pair. Maya's lenses bulged outward in the middle, fat like lentils. Hers curved inward, thin in the middle. She looked through Maya's lens at the poster: the words shrank. Through her own: the words grew.

"Yours are convex," Maya said. "Mine are for farsightedness. Light focuses behind my retina, so near things blur."

"So that's why your eyes look gigantic and mine will look tiny!" Rebecca turned to the mirror and laughed out loud. The trial frames made her eyes look like two little buttons.

"Twins, huh," said Maya.

"Opposite twins." Rebecca skipped to the door, then stopped. "Wait. What if I hold your glasses inside mine? Would they cancel out and make everything neutral?"

"Only one way to find out," said Maya, holding out the glasses.

Rebecca stopped at the third marker on the nature trail, where her worksheet was supposed to correspond with the little numbered post that did not, as far as she could tell, correspond with anything. The assignment said to draw a food chain, sun to top predator, using one real organism she could actually find. Her brother Denny, who was a chronic complainer even on good days, had already found three ticks and no inspiration.

"There's grass," Denny said. "Grass eats the sun. Congratulations, food chain, let's go home."

"Grass doesn't eat. It makes food from the sun." Rebecca crouched and sketched the sun, an arrow, the grass. Then a grasshopper, because one flicked past and landed on Denny's sleeve, which he did not appreciate. She drew arrows from grasshopper to the snake she'd seen warming itself on the rocks by marker two, and from snake to the hawk circling overhead, patient as a substitute teacher.

"Question," she said, chewing her pencil. "What if the grasshoppers all vanished?"

"Then the snake starves, then the hawk starves, then the ticks get me instead. See, I'm learning."

"That's three links gone from one." She frowned at her drawing. Every arrow stood for something she couldn't actually watch happen. She wanted to see a chain work, not just believe in it. From her backpack she took the pocket microscope kit she'd brought for reasons she could no longer defend, and the prepared slide of onion cells. The cells looked like neat little bricks, and she couldn't find the membrane anywhere, which ruined her whole "seeing is believing" plan.

Denny, who poked things when bored, added a drop of water from his salty snack lid to the slide. Under the lens, the membranes pulled inward, shrinking away from each cell wall and suddenly, unmistakably, visible.

"It's called plasmolysis," Rebecca said, reading off the kit card, "when salt water draws the water out like that."

"So when one thing leaves, something else shows up?"

"Basically." She handed him the lens, and the hawk screamed once above them, low and bright.

Zachary had come to the bank only because his mom needed a countersigner for a loan, and the waiting area had exactly one interesting thing in it: a first-aid poster next to the vending machine. He read it twice. Apply pressure. Clean the wound. Cover it with a bandage, wrapping firmly but not so tight that fingers turn purple. He practiced on his own knuckle, tearing a bandage from his lunch bag and wrapping it in slow spirals, then doing it again to see if he could replicate the neat result. His second try was better than his first, which felt like actual progress.

He was on attempt three when the doors slid open and Mrs. Okafor from his street came in holding her grandson Danny's hand, along with the leash of her huge brown dog, Biscuit. Danny was crying and shaking his right hand, and there was a red line across the knuckles. "He grabbed Biscuit's ear when the automatic doors banged," Mrs. Okafor said, mostly to the room, the way people do when they're embarrassed. "He didn't mean anything by it."

Zachary leaned closer, wondering. Was that a scrape, or had the skin actually broken? Danny's hand told him one thing and Danny's crying told him another, and crying wasn't evidence. Then Zachary spotted two tiny dark pinpoints on the knuckle, welling up slow. Not gushing, not deep, but broken. The poster's bottom line came back to him, the part he'd almost skimmed: any animal bite that breaks the skin should be checked by a doctor, because bites can carry germs deep into the wound. A scrape you could bandage. This was something else.

"Mrs. Okafor," he said, "the skin's broken. I think it needs a doctor, not just a bandage." She looked at the pinpoints, then at him, and changed her mind about the walk-in clinic being an overreaction. "You're right," she said. Danny sniffled, "Is Biscuit toxic?" and Zachary laughed. "No, buddy. He's just a dog." Danny wiped his nose. "Can I still keep the bandage?" "You can keep two," Zachary said, and pressed one into his hand as they headed for the door.

Brayden sat at the corner desk in his mom's office, squinting at her coworker Dev's laptop. Dev had promised him a soda from the break room if he could figure out why the password "brayden123" was, in Dev's words, "about as safe as a screen door on a submarine." Brayden typed it into a little testing program Dev kept on his desk, and a red bar shot across the screen like it was trying to escape the monitor. "That password would take about two seconds to crack," Brayden read out loud. "Two seconds? Even my gym teacher runs slower than that."

He tried again, this time with something longer, mixing letters and numbers and one of those symbols that looked like a spider fell on the keyboard. The bar turned green and crawled along, slow and stubborn. Then Dev dropped the real trap. "Here's the part most people miss. Say you use that same great password for your game account, your email, and the library site. The library site gets broken into, and now the thieves have your password for everything. One site goes down, they all go down." Brayden thought about it like dominoes standing in a row, invisible until the first one tipped. You couldn't see the connection, but it was there. "So it's like giving every teacher the same key to your locker," Brayden said slowly, "and one of the teachers loses their keys in the parking lot."

Dev grinned. "Exactly. Different password for each door." He handed Brayden a sticky note covered in scribbled fragments, and Brayden built four different passwords out of them, testing each one, watching the green bar stretch out like taffy, elastic and slow, every single time.

"Okay, that earns you a soda," Dev said, "but first, one more mystery." He pulled up a spreadsheet of survey results, rows of numbers about how much coffee each department consumed on Mondays. "My analysis keeps coming out looking wrong. The chart looks sideways. Marketing should tower over Accounting, but instead it stretches across like it's lying down for a nap."

Brayden leaned in. The chart did look odd, every category stretched out horizontally instead of standing up. He remembered a project from school in the fall, when his own chart had come out lying flat and his teacher had laughed and said the class had accidentally picked the wrong one. He scrolled through the chart menu and found two side-by-side options, bar and column, and he noticed the tiny pictures next to the words. One showed flat bars, one showed upright ones.

"Wait," Brayden said, tapping the screen. "Bar chart and column chart. That one's a bar chart, that's why it's horizontal. A bar chart has horizontal bars. A column chart has vertical bars, even though both compare amounts across categories." He clicked column, and Marketing shot straight up like a skyscraper while Accounting stayed low and modest. Dev clapped him on the shoulder, then Brayden pointed at the break room door. "So, about that soda."

The cast on Kate's left arm itched in a place she could not reach, which she decided was the second worst thing about the emergency room. The worst thing was waiting for the doctor to come back with her X-ray. When he finally clipped the film onto the light box on the wall, she forgot about the itch entirely. Her bones glowed white against a gray fog, like ghosts of sticks, and one of them near her wrist had a dark crack running through it.

"Why are the bones white when everything else is basically invisible?" she asked.

The doctor was already halfway out the door, called away to supervise a new patient arriving by ambulance, so he only said, "Calcium," and vanished behind the curtain. Kate frowned at the word. Calcium, like in milk commercials. She stared at the film and turned the clue over in her mind. Calcium must be the reason bones looked different, but that still did not tell her why different meant white instead of gray.

In the next bed, behind a thin blue curtain, a boy was getting a cut on his chin checked. Kate heard his mom say something about a laser pointer, that her son had been waving a counterfeit one, a cheap knockoff from the fair, and that was how the whole fight with his brother had started. Kate was not really listening. She was thinking about light. The X-ray machine shot something through her arm, and whatever it was, some of it got through and some did not, or the picture would not show anything at all. So the white parts must be where the beam stopped. If calcium made bones white, then calcium had to be soaking up the rays, more of them than her skin and muscle did, because those parts showed up as barely-there gray.

She tested her idea against the picture itself. The crack in her bone was darker, almost the gray of the soft tissue. If the calcium was doing the blocking, then a crack meant less calcium in that spot, less blocking, and the gray showing through like a window. The dark line and the white bone fit together like a lock and a key.

"So it's calcium," she said when the doctor came back. "The calcium soaks up more of the X-rays than the soft stuff around it, so the bones print white."

"That's it exactly," he said, and pulled out a marker. "Want me to sign your cast where the break is? I can draw the crack for you."

"Draw it dark," Kate said, holding out her arm. "Like on the film."

The snow started before sunrise, and by seven o'clock the school website flashed the words Nathan had been hoping for all winter: CLOSED. He whooped so loudly that his mother sent him outside before he woke the whole house. At the end of the driveway he ran straight into Mrs. Okoye, who was out with her shovel. "Perfect timing," she said. "I'll pay you in hot chocolate if you clear my walk."

Nathan shoveled fast, but halfway through he stopped and stared at her birdbath. It had frozen solid, and the ice was glassy and clear as a window. Yet her whole yard, made of the same frozen water, glowed pure white. That made no sense at all. He picked up a chunk of birdbath ice and held it beside a mittful of snow, turning both over and over.

"Here's my idea," he announced, because an idea felt too big to keep quiet. "It's not about what the ice is made of. It's about how many pieces it's in." Mrs. Okoye raised an eyebrow, so he emphasized each word by rapping the ice chunk with his knuckle. "One big piece, you can see through it. A million tiny pieces? Maybe not." He carried the chunk to the driveway and smashed it with the back of the shovel, once, twice, three times, until it crumbled into a pile of glittering crumbs. He scooped them up and looked. White. Completely, unmistakably white, and when he pressed them together in his palm they caught the light and sparkled just like snow. "The crystals are still clear," he said, holding one crumb up to the sun so Mrs. Okoye could see through it. "But all those little clear pieces must scatter light and reflect every color in every direction, and all the colors together look white. That's the whole yard!"

Inside, she poured the hot chocolate and let him set a crumb of ice on the warm radiator to watch it melt. "Careful, don't touch," she warned, nodding at the space heater in the corner. "That old thing is flammable near the curtains, so we keep our distance." Nathan didn't mind. Any leftover resentment he had about shoveling had melted faster than the ice. He pressed his nose to the window and watched the falling flakes. "Millions of tiny mirrors," he said. "Every single one of them."

Alyssa pushed the microphone closer and looked at the rows of folding chairs in the town hall basement. Her sixth-grade class had been given five minutes at the meeting to argue for a new skate park, and Councilwoman Reyes had told them that first they had to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature. "No bill, no park," she had said.

Alyssa had practiced the steps all week: a proposal gets drafted, then a committee reviews it, then the whole legislature votes, and if it passes both houses it goes to be signed. But halfway through her speech, a man in the back stood up. "Kids always want rules changed when they lose," he said. "Like voting. You'd complain about the system too, if you understood it."

"My uncle lives in New Zealand," Alyssa said, mostly to buy time while she thought. Then the idea landed. She hadn't known this two weeks ago, but she'd found it while hunting for examples, testing whether any country had really changed its voting system instead of just arguing about it. "They voted in a referendum in 1993 to replace first-past-the-post with a proportional system called MMP. Then they first used it in the 1996 election. So it can be done, through a legal process, by voting."

The man sat down slowly, the way people do when they're changing their minds. Councilwoman Reyes leaned toward her notes. "Could you paraphrase that for our minutes?" she asked. "In one sentence."

Alyssa put it in plain words: New Zealand held a referendum in 1993, switched from first-past-the-post to the proportional system called MMP, and used it for the first time in the 1996 election. The clerk wrote it down under the agenda category marked "Citizen Comments, Youth." The overhead lights made the page luminous under the clerk's pen, bright white and official.

"Motion to draft a bill for a skate park feasibility study," said Councilwoman Reyes. "All in favor?"

"Seconded," said the man from the back, without standing up this time.

Muhammad slid into his usual seat on the bus, third row from the back, and pulled out his phone. The group chat for the science fair team was blinking with new messages. He read the first one and his stomach dropped. Someone had written, about Theo, the new kid who had joined the team on Monday, "Why did we let the weird kid in? He'll just ruin everything." The name on the message was Dylan.

That was the part Muhammad couldn't make fit. Dylan sat two rows ahead of him on this exact bus every morning. Dylan was the kid who held the door for substitute teachers, who said "excuse me" to kindergartners, who had once carried Muhammad's dropped binder half a mile down the hallway to return it. Muhammad leaned forward and watched Dylan laugh quietly at something his seatmate said, polite even in his laughter. In person and on the screen, it was like two different people.

The chat's whole purpose was to organize the project, and if Theo got pushed out now, he would be excluded from the team without ever knowing why. Muhammad wanted to fix it before first period. He typed a reply, deleted it, and tried another. Words on a screen felt different from words in the air, heavier somehow, and easier to throw. He thought about his older cousin Amir, who had told him last summer, "People say stuff online they'd never say to your face. Psychologists call it the online disinhibition effect." Muhammad hadn't believed it mattered much. Now he wondered.
