Sebastian stood in the living room holding a spatula like a microphone and waited for his sister Priya to stop laughing at him. She sat on the couch with her arms crossed, still in her soccer cleats, because he had promised her the last slice of pizza if she practiced with him for one whole hour.

"Fine," she said. "What are we doing?"

"Improv," Sebastian said. "Drama club tryouts are Friday. Mrs. Okafor picks partners and you have to make up a scene together, and she said the kids who get in are the ones who accept every offer with yes, and." He raised the spatula. "I start a scene, you say yes, and then you add something. Then I do it back."

Priya rolled her eyes, but she stood up. "Go."

"Welcome aboard the ship," Sebastian said grandly. "We are sailing to Antarctica."

"No," said Priya. "I don't want to sail anywhere. Let's be on a train."

Sebastian dropped the spatula. "That's the whole point! You have to say yes, and. If you block me, the scene just dies." He had tried it alone all week, playing both parts in the bathroom mirror, and every time his imaginary partner argued, the scene collapsed like a wet tent.

Priya picked the spatula up and handed it back to him. "Okay, okay. Again."

"Welcome aboard the ship. We are sailing to Antarctica."

"Yes, and I've nominated you to climb the mast and check for icebergs," Priya said, and Sebastian nearly hugged her. The scene rolled on for five whole minutes, and they discovered that their ship was powered by a giant turbine, which Sebastian had to look up later, and that they were transporting a hold full of impoverished penguins who had lost their fishing grounds and needed new homes.

At dinner, their dad asked what they'd been shouting about upstairs. Sebastian explained the tryouts, and then, because his dad looked confused, he added, "I have to introduce the scene too, right at the start. That's the hard part."

His dad nodded slowly. "When I give presentations at work, they call the opening line a hook. A hook is the opening line that grabs attention, like a question, a surprising fact, or a very short story." He speared a piece of broccoli. "Mine are usually terrible."

Sebastian thought about that. On Thursday, Priya helped him test it. He stood at the end of the hallway and opened the way he'd planned: "Today I will talk about a ship scene." Priya's gaze drifted to the window within four seconds, and she started fiddling with her shoelace.

"Try again," she said.

"Would you sail to Antarctica with forty penguins and no captain?"

Priya's head came up. "Yes, and the penguins are in the kitchen."

Sebastian grinned and pushed open the kitchen door.

Cameron wanted his street to look like it was actually sinking into the paper, the way the avenues in his favorite graphic novels did, buildings leaning toward each other until they vanished somewhere far below the edge. Ms. Ro had shown the class one-point perspective on Monday: a dot on the horizon, then ruler lines running toward it like ropes. Cameron had forgotten the ruler today, so he had to devise a substitute, and he scavenged through the studio's crowded supply shelf until he found a long wooden stirring stick, straight enough to trust.

He drew the vanishing point first, a small dot that he pretended was a doorway to another version of the street. Every roofline and curb had to aim at that doorway. When he leaned close and sighted along the stick, he could almost see the buildings folding inward, tugging each other down the page like the whole street was sliding into the dot. He tested one idea to be sure the trick was real: he drew a line he guessed would hit the dot, then laid the stick on top, and found it missed by a thumb's width. So the eye was a liar. The ruler-stick was the truth. He erased and redrew.

Across the table, Priya, age nine, was painting a portrait of her cat. She had made the cat's nose an unfortunate shade of green yesterday, let it dry overnight, and today she brushed clean water over it to soften the edges. The green moved. It smeared sideways in a slow tide across the cat's cheek, and Priya gasped like the cat itself had twitched.

"It dried," she said. "Dried things aren't supposed to run. Dried glue doesn't run."

Cameron came over and touched the edge of the smear with his fingertip. It came away faintly green. "Ms. Ro said watercolour paint is pigment bound with gum arabic," he said. "That's why it can dissolve again in water even after it's dried." He watched Priya's face do the same thing his had done when the stick proved his guessed line wrong, that flicker of a hidden rule suddenly becoming visible.

"So it's like it's only pretending to be permanent," Priya said. "A hypothetical cat that stays put until water shows up."

"Exactly. Your cat is a spy who dissolves when the rain comes."

Priya turned the smear into a swirl of whiskers, and the accidental green became grass in a reflection, a cat looking into a puddle. Cameron went back to his street and drew the puddle's edge with lines running to the vanishing point, so that even the reflection obeyed the doorway. He held the stick up to check it one last time.

"Bullseye," he said, and drew the dot's tiny doorframe around it.

Ryan had measured himself against the coat hooks in the hallway every Sunday since September, and today he finally had proof. He stood in Exam Room 4 with his shoes off, staring at the pencil marks on the doorframe of his memory, while Dr. Patel clicked through something on her screen.

"Four inches in ten months," she said. "That's a sprint, even for twelve."

"My mom thinks I'm going to be seven feet tall," Ryan said. "I told her the doorways aren't proportional to that plan, and she said we'd move."

Dr. Patel laughed and turned the monitor toward him. "Want to see why you're growing so fast? This is your left hand from today's X-ray."

The image was ghostly and gray, and Ryan perceived faint dark lines running near the ends of each bone, like tiny gaps in a fence. He leaned closer. "Is that a fracture? Do I have eleven fractures?"

"Those are your growth plates," she said. "Bones grow longer at the growth plates near their ends."

Ryan squinted. "So the middle of the bone just sits there doing nothing, and the ends do all the work?"

"Basically, yes."

He thought about that. The doorframe marks hadn't been even, either. Half an inch one month, an inch the next, then nothing for weeks, then a jump. It was like the erosion on the creek bank behind his school, slow and invisible until suddenly the shape had changed. Then a question landed in his stomach like a dropped marble. "Wait. Do the plates ever stop?"

"Once they close after puberty, a person stops getting taller," Dr. Patel said. "Closed means sealed. Done."

"So there's a deadline." Ryan sat up straighter. "Can you tell from the X-ray how close mine are?"

She tapped the screen. "See how wide and dark those lines are? Wide and open means lots of runway left. Narrow and pale means the countdown's nearly over."

That was all Ryan needed. He asked for the facts, memorized them, and spent the next week running an experiment. He borrowed his friend Desmond's little sister's growth chart app, and he tested a hypothesis: if his dad had stopped growing at fourteen, and his uncle at seventeen, then the family plates closed late, and Ryan had time. He tracked his uncles' heights at Thanksgiving like a detective, and Grandma pulled out a box of old report cards with heights penciled on the back. The data was beautiful. Late closers, all of them.

At his checkup the next June, Ryan had grown another two inches, and Dr. Patel held up the new X-ray next to the old one. The lines were still wide and dark.

"Runway," Ryan said, grinning.

"Runway," she agreed, and printed him a copy to take home. On the way out, he taped it to the refrigerator at exactly his own eye level, which, he suspected, would not be his eye level for long.

Sydney's paper bag of onions slid across the table while the farmer counted her change. "Romanas," he said. "Sweet enough to eat raw, if you're brave."

She wasn't that brave, but she had a plan. Her grandmother was teaching her to make pasta sauce from scratch tonight, and Sydney had exactly one hour to buy onions, garlic, and canned tomatoes before the market closed. She moved through the stalls like a scavenger hunting treasure, sniffing garlic heads, squeezing tomatoes, and wondering why the tropical fruit stall smelled like a vacation even in October.

Then she smelled something else. Butter and cinnamon, drifting from the muffin stand at the end of the row, where a woman pulled a tray of blueberry muffins from a small oven. The timer had dinged, but the woman frowned at the tray. "Tops look pale," she muttered. "They usually brown by now."

Sydney drifted closer, curious. How could anyone know the inside of a muffin without cutting it open? The woman turned the tray, tapped one top, and sighed. Last summer, Sydney remembered, she had bitten into a muffin at camp and hit a pocket of raw batter in the middle, gooey as glue. The cook had shrugged and said the outside had looked done. Looks, apparently, could lie.

"Could you check one?" Sydney asked. "Like, without cutting it?"

The woman tapped her chin. "My grandmother used a trick. Push a toothpick into the centre of a muffin. If it comes out clean, or with a few dry crumbs, it's baked through." She pulled a toothpick from her apron pocket and handed it over. "You try."

Sydney pushed the toothpick straight down into the centre of the biggest muffin, held her breath, and drew it out. Wet batter clung to the wood, glistening. "Not done," she announced, almost triumphantly. The woman slid the tray back into the oven and set the timer again. While they waited, Sydney tested two more muffins; one came out clean, the other showed dry crumbs. "That one's fine too," the woman said. "Crumbly counts." Sydney filed that away, pleased to have a rule that worked. When the timer dinged the second time, she tested the big muffin again and the toothpick came out clean. The woman insisted Sydney take it, still warm.

That evening, in her grandmother's kitchen, Sydney curled her fingers into a claw over the onion she'd bought, knuckles forward like tiny shields, and cut slow, careful slices. "Smart hands," her grandmother said. "You're going to cherish that sauce, and I'm going to cherish not driving you to the emergency room." Sydney laughed so hard she nearly lost her claw grip. The onion sizzled in the pan, going soft and gold, and she took a bite of her muffin on the way past the counter: baked through, every last crumb.

The science lab chat was supposed to be for questions about the digestive system, so when Mr. Ortega posted "Reminder: intestine diagrams due Friday," Leah typed "Great, my favorite organ" and hit send before she thought about it. Three people replied with links about intestinal diseases. Marcus sent her a private message: "Are you okay? Do you actually have a stomach thing?" She stared at the screen. Her joke had traveled like a stone dropped in water, and every ripple had taken it literally.

She tried to clarify with a follow-up post: "I was joking, intestine diagrams are not actually my favorite." That only made it worse, because Priya asked why she would say that if she didn't mean it, and the whole chat scrolled on without her, arguing about whether Leah was being sarcastic or upset. Leah shut her laptop and watched Mr. Ortega sketch the small intestine on the whiteboard, feeling like the whole class had read a different sentence than the one she wrote.

That night she went looking for a way to fix it, and found something better. On a computer history site she read that on September 19, 1982, a computer scientist named Scott Fahlman had proposed the emoticon :-) on a Carnegie Mellon University message board, so readers could tell which posts were jokes. People typing to each other back then had the exact same problem she'd had, and somebody had invented a mark for it. She read the date twice. Her problem was older than her parents. Somewhere along the way she had thought of :-) as obsolete, a thing her aunt used, but clearly it had been doing its job since 1982.

The next morning she asked Marcus to meet her at the picnic table by the gym before first period. "I found out why my joke blew up," she said, and told him about Fahlman, the message board, the smiley meant to flag jokes. "So this afternoon I'm going to post one in the chat. An apology with a :-) at the end, and then a real joke with one too, so people can see the difference." Marcus turned his water bottle in his hands. "Or you could just say it was a joke in plain words." He had a point, and she sat with it for a second, remembering how her plain words had already failed once.

"Both," she decided. "Words first, smiley as backup." Fifth period, she typed her apology, added :-) and watched Priya reply with a laughing face instead of a question. Marcus leaned over from the next desk and typed, "Told you it was a joke," and Leah smiled at the little sideways grin sitting at the end of her sentence, still working after all these years.

Matthew set the stiff brushes on the kitchen table like evidence at a trial. There were five of them, and every one stood up straight, hard as popsicle sticks. He had left them in the studio overnight, and now his poster for history class sat half-finished beside them: a painted diagram of the monarchy, with a king at the top and arrows pointing down to the lords, then the knights, then the peasants crowded along the bottom.

His sister Priya wandered in and picked one up. "It's like a tiny spear," she said, poking his arm with it. "Ow. It actually hurts."

"Put it down. I have to fix them before Mom gets home or she'll say my whole art kit is obsolete." He filled a cup with warm water and dropped the brushes in. His first draft of the poster had taught him something already: when the paint was wet, a splash of water thinned it right out, and he could swirl it around, lighten a color, rinse it clean. So maybe water could rescue the brushes too. He stirred the cup and watched.

Nothing happened. The bristles stayed bent and stiff, like a hedgehog that refused to be friends with anyone. He pressed one against the rim of the cup. The water beaded off it.

"Huh," he said. He fetched a fresh brush, the one good one he'd washed properly last night, and dipped it into his red paint. Then he held it under the tap. The paint dissolved in a pink cloud and swirled down the drain. Same paint, same water. The only difference was that on the ruined brushes, the paint had dried.

"So wet paint washes out," Priya said, leaning over his shoulder, "and dry paint just... stays."

"Forever, probably. Or until I'm thirty." He remembered leaving those brushes on the studio counter, telling himself he'd clean them in the morning, and how easy that had felt at ten o'clock at night. He wondered whether it was worth asking Mom to buy new ones, or whether he'd rather accept the punishment of painting his peasants with a cotton swab. The poster still needed a border, and the peasants were all supposed to be brown, and now he owned exactly one working brush.

He swirled the good brush in the water cup, dried it on a paper towel, and dipped it into the brown. "Rule for the rest of my life," he said. "Wash the brush before it dries."

Priya held up the stiffest one. "Spear number two?"

"Fine. But aim at the trash can."

Nathaniel had a dilemma. His science presentation was due Monday, and he wanted to show how a river could carve a canyon over millions of years, but he couldn't exactly wait millions of years to film it. He stood at the kitchen counter staring at a long plastic tray he'd filled with packed sand and dirt, a jug of water beside it.

"Pour slow at first," his sister Priya said from the doorway. "Rivers don't start out trying to demolish the landscape." She was twelve minutes older than him in twin terms, which she claimed made her an impartial judge of his experiments, though he doubted it.

He tilted the jug and let a thin stream run down the middle of the tray. At first nothing happened. Then a small channel appeared, deepened, and branched. He sped up the water and watched the dirt crumble at the edges of the cut while downstream a little muddy pile grew, spreading out flat like a fan. Erosion there, deposition here. He grabbed his phone and started recording, then poured again, and again, and by the fourth run the channel had widened into something that actually looked like a tiny canyon with a delta at the end. Priya leaned over it. "Okay, that's better than I expected. You should say the river carries the dirt away and drops it where the water slows down."

After she left, he scrolled through his notes and hit a snag. He'd written that summer heat peaked at the summer solstice, the longest day, because that part felt obvious. But when he checked the backyard thermometer log they'd been keeping since June, the highest numbers weren't anywhere near the longest day. The really hot readings, the sweat-through-your-shirt ones, were stacked up weeks later, in the middle of July. He frowned at the notebook, then at the thermometer, then back at the notebook, as if one of them would confess.

He found the answer in one of Dad's old weather books, and it stopped him cold: the hottest weeks usually come several weeks after the summer solstice, because land and oceans take time to warm up. He crossed out his old sentence, feeling his ears go warm too, and rewrote the whole last section. His river worked the same way, he realized. The water needed time, run after run, before the canyon took shape. Nothing big happened all at once.

Monday morning he set the tray on the desk, poured the water, and watched the channel deepen while the class leaned in. "The river did this in four minutes," he said. "A real one takes millions of years, and the hottest part of summer comes weeks after the longest day, because the land and oceans take time to warm up." He pointed at the muddy fan spreading at the end of the tray. "Same idea. You just have to give things time."

Alexander carried the cardboard box across the backyard with both hands, walking like someone balancing a full glass of water. Inside, under a flap of hay, sat a brown and white guinea pig named Biscuit, his first pet ever. His little sister Priya trotted beside him, already arguing that she should be allowed to hold Biscuit first because she had a special way of sitting very still.

"Biscuit is my obligation," Alexander told her, setting the box down by the new hutch under the maple tree. "That means I'm the one who takes care of him." Priya pouted, but she had her own plan. She wanted Biscuit to learn to eat from her hand so he would like her best, and she planned to sit by the hutch every single afternoon until it happened.

For the first week Alexander did what the pet store had said. He filled the bowl with dry pellets every morning and changed the water. The pellets smelled faintly sweet, like toast, and Biscuit crunched them happily enough. Then, on Saturday, Alexander noticed something odd. Biscuit was sitting in the corner of the hutch with his fur puffed up, and he didn't come to the front when Alexander rattled the bag. His eyes looked watery, and he had left his favorite tunnel untouched.

Alexander sat on the grass and thought. What had changed? Nothing, except the food, and the food had been exactly the same all week. He turned the pellet bag over and read the tiny print on the back, squinting in the sun. There it was: a line about added vitamin C. He went inside and searched on the family computer, and what he found made him sit up straight. "They can't make their own vitamin C, like humans, so they need it in their food every day," he read aloud to Priya, who had followed him in. Every day. The pellets had some in them, but Alexander remembered something else from the search, that the vitamin faded from stored feed over time, and their bag had been sitting on a shelf for who knew how long.

So he tested it. He cut a strip of red bell pepper, which the website said was packed with vitamin C, and brought it out to the hutch along with a slice of orange, wondering which one Biscuit would choose. The pepper smelled sharp and green in the cool morning air. Biscuit sniffed it, then snatched it and chewed so fast that crumbs of pepper flew onto the cedar shavings. He ignored the orange completely.

Alexander gave him fresh pepper every day after that, and within a week Biscuit's fur lay smooth again and he raced to the front of the hutch whenever Alexander's sneakers appeared on the grass. He wasn't just fine now; he seemed to thrive, popcorning straight up in the air when the food bowl rattled. Priya got her wish too, though not the way she expected. Biscuit decided the best place to eat his pepper strip was directly from her hand, and she sat by the maple tree every afternoon, giggling as his whiskers tickled her fingers. "He likes me best," she announced, and Biscuit, mouth full, made no argument.

Mila leaned her bicycle against the railing outside the bank and noticed the front tyre was flat, soft all the way around, with a hiss she could not hear but could imagine. She had ridden there to deposit a birthday cheque from her grandmother, and now the deposit would have to wait, because riding home on a flat would wreck the rim. In her backpack she had a repair kit her uncle had sent with a note, and she had never once used it.

She sat on the wide stone step beside the doors and unfolded the note. "Tyre levers go under the bead, three of them spaced around, then spoon the tyre off," her uncle had written in his careful, diligent handwriting. "Find the puncture, patch it, pump it up. You can interpret a flat two ways: bad luck, or a chance to learn something. Your choice." Mila read it twice, then dug out the levers, three curved plastic strips, and the little hand pump.

A security guard came out on his break and watched her work the first lever under the edge of the tyre. "You want to hook that second one a few inches along," he said, "and clip the third to a spoke." She did it, and when all three were set, the tyre popped loose and she could pull the tube out. As she ran her fingers along the rubber to find the hole, a spoke nicked her knuckle and a bead of blood rose up. She stuck it in her mouth.

"Put a plaster on that and let the air at it," the guard said. "Dries out faster that way."

A woman waiting by the doors shook her head. "My nurse said the opposite. A thin layer of petroleum jelly keeps the surface moist, and that helps it heal and can reduce scarring." The two of them went back and forth while Mila held the tube under the fountain by the wall, watching for bubbles. One small stream rose from a spot the size of a pinhead, near the valve. She marked it with the crayon from the kit, roughed it up with the sandpaper, spread the glue, and pressed the patch on until her thumb ached.

Then she took the small jar from the kit's zip pocket, dabbed petroleum jelly on her knuckle, and covered it with a plaster from her pencil case. "I'm going with the moist version," she said, holding up her finger. She tucked the tube back inside the tyre, seated the bead with her thumbs, and pumped until the tyre was firm enough to bounce a little when she pressed it. Inside the bank, she slid the cheque and the deposit slip through the slot at the counter. On the way out she rang the bell on her handlebars once, for the guard, and pedalled home over the bridge with the front tyre humming on the pavement.

Eve had been washing dishes at her uncle's restaurant for two Saturdays, and today she had been promoted, which meant she was standing over a cutting board with an onion and a very sharp knife. "Claw grip," her uncle Rafi said, curling his fingers so the knuckles stuck out ahead of the fingertips. "The knife rides your knuckles. Your fingertips stay under, where the blade can't find them." Eve bent her fingers the same way, decided it made her hand look like a crab, and started cutting. The first slices were uneven. The fifth ones were not.

The lunch rush wanted pasta sauce, forty portions of it, and Rafi wanted it from scratch, which was how Eve ended up with a pan of oil on high heat and a board full of chopped onion and minced garlic. He was called away to the front when a delivery coincided with a health inspector's surprise visit, and he left her with exactly one instruction: "Cook."

She dumped everything in at once. The onions hissed and softened and smelled wonderful, and she felt extremely professional until she tasted the sauce ten minutes later. It was bitter. Not burnt-on-the-bottom bitter, because she'd stirred, but bitter in a way that coated her whole tongue. She tried a second spoonful in case the first spoonful was a mistake. It was not.

She stood there chewing her lip and staring at the pan like it owed her an answer. If it wasn't the bottom, it was something in the pan. The tomatoes were from a can that Rafi himself had opened, so they were probably fine. The oil was fine, the salt was salt. That left the onions and the garlic. The onions looked soft and golden and innocent. The garlic, she noticed, had gone dark around the edges, and when she fished out a piece and ate it alone, it was the exact bitterness from the sauce. The garlic had burned. It had gone in at the same time as the onions on high heat, but the onions were golden and the garlic was black, which meant the garlic had cooked faster and burnt while the onions were still catching up. She felt like she'd solved a crime with only one suspect.

Rafi came back, tasted it, and made a face. "Bitter."

"The garlic," Eve said. "It burned before the onions were done."

He raised an eyebrow, which for Rafi was applause. "So what's your plan?"

"Onions first, on lower heat. Then when they're soft, the garlic goes in after, just for a minute." She was already chopping the second onion, claw grip and all, knuckles leading, fingertips tucked safely away.

"Good. And next time don't leave the pan alone with the whole garlic at once."

"It wasn't the pan's fault," Eve said. "The garlic's just faster." Rafi laughed at that, a real one, and told her that if she kept this up she'd break the stereotype of dishwashers who only break dishes. She said she'd try, and she slid the onions into the fresh oil, watching them turn soft and sweet while the garlic waited on the board, patient as anything, like it had never ruined anything in its life.

When the second sauce came together, Rafi tasted it, then tasted it again, which he never did. "Get me forty containers," he said. "And don't let the garlic fool you twice."

Rosalie pulled the laptop closer and typed her cousin Marcus's favorite player into the search bar, because the argument was still running from dinner and she intended to win it. "Told you," Marcus had said, pointing at the batting average on his phone. "Point two sixty. That's not a great hitter." Her grandpa had hummed at that, the way he did when he knew something, and Rosalie had spent the whole car ride home wondering what the hum meant.

The player page loaded, all numbers stacked in tidy columns. She scrolled past the average to the row of walks, and there it was: a lot of walks, more than half the hits. She clicked to another player, one with a higher average, and counted his walks too. Far fewer. She sat back. "Huh," she said to the empty kitchen, which felt less silly than saying it to nobody at all.

She texted Marcus: come over. He lived two streets away, and luckily his free evening happened to coincide with hers, because otherwise she'd have had to explain it all in messages and he never read long messages. He arrived still holding his phone, still sure of himself.

"Look," she said, spinning the laptop toward him. "Watch what I did." She pulled up both players side by side. "Count these. Hits, and then walks." Marcus counted, lips moving. "So?" he said. "A walk isn't a hit."

"A walk isn't a hit, but it's not nothing either," Rosalie said. "Here's the thing. A batting average is hits divided by official at-bats. And walks don't count as at-bats. So the number gives a batter no credit for walks. Your guy's average looks small because the walks are invisible."

Marcus leaned in, scrolling, checking. He found a third player with a fat average and only a handful of walks all season. "Okay," he admitted, "so the average is squashing everything down to one number and it drops stuff on the floor."

Rosalie thought about the settlement they'd made last summer, when Marcus had traded her his window seat on the trip to the lake in exchange for her last two pieces of licorice, and how she'd regretted it within an hour. Numbers could be like that too, she figured. You agreed to them because they looked simple, and then you found out what they left out. "So your player's underrated," she said. "You were right for the wrong reason."

"That still counts as right," Marcus said, and he pulled the laptop back toward himself, already typing the player's name into a new search. "Grandpa's going to be endangered when I tell him he started this." Rosalie laughed and slid her chair over next to him.

Justin slid the guitar case onto the table in Ms. Reyes's studio and popped the latches like he was opening treasure. One week of lessons, and he already knew three chords, though his fingertips knew something else entirely.

"I'm not quitting," he announced, "but I have to tell you, my fingers feel like I pressed them against a hot stove. Is my guitar broken? Maybe the strings are too tight."

Ms. Reyes set down her coffee. "Play me a G chord."

He pressed down. Even before he strummed, he winced. The tips of his left hand were pink and shiny, and yesterday they had stung through his pencil in math class. He strummed anyway, because quitting before the chord was not an option.

Ms. Reyes held out her own left hand, palm up. "Feel the fingertips."

They were hard, like small pebbles under the skin. "Whoa. What happened to your fingers?"

"Calluses," she said. "Want to know the funny part?"

Justin was already piecing it together, his mind turning on some hidden pivot, the way it did when a math problem suddenly swung from impossible to obvious. "You practice a lot, right? And I've practiced every day for a week, and my fingers are sore. So the soreness comes first, and then..." He stopped, ideas germinating faster than he could line them up. "Then the skin gets tougher, and it stops hurting?"

"Play a chord on my guitar and see how the strings feel."

He took her guitar and pressed a G. His sore fingers ached, but the strings felt different, lighter somehow. "Wait, is your guitar easier?"

"It's not the guitar," she said, grinning.

Justin sat back. If the pain was inevitable for every new player, then it wasn't a sign something was wrong. It was a sign something was starting. "So everybody who ever got good at this went through exactly this week?"

She nodded. He looked down at his pink fingertips and felt like he was holding tickets to something huge. "Then I'm keeping the schedule. Every single day."

For the rest of the lesson he hammered through chord changes, counting them like push-ups, and by the last one he laughed out loud at the sting.

"Same time next week?" Ms. Reyes asked.

"Same time next week," Justin said, and he pressed one fingertip to his thumb, testing it like a tiny promise.

The waiting room clock said 3:40, and soccer tryouts started at 4:30, which gave Jaxon exactly fifty minutes to get the orange cast off his left arm, sign out, and ride his bike across town. He had broken the arm six weeks ago falling off the dock at his uncle's lake house, and ever since then the cast had been the rudder of his whole summer, steering every plan toward "sorry, I can't." Today the rudder came off.

In the exam room, Nurse Diaz rolled a cart toward him with something that looked like a small circular saw. Jaxon's stomach dropped. "Whoa, whoa. That thing spins?"

"That's what I thought too," Jaxon said quickly, before the nurse could answer. He sat up straighter, because he had figured this out at his last appointment and it was worth sharing. "It doesn't spin. The blade vibrates, back and forth, super fast. It cuts through the hard stuff, the plaster and fiberglass, but it won't cut your skin underneath."

The kid stopped chewing his gum. "That's impossible."

"Watch," Jaxon said. His own heart was still hammering from the memory of six weeks ago, when he had gripped the armrest so hard the nurse couldn't excavate his fingers from it, not even with both hands. The flashback made him grin now, though it hadn't been funny then. He held out his casted arm like a man volunteering for a magic trick. "Go ahead. I'll prove it."

The saw whined like an angry hornet, and Jaxon kept his eyes open the whole time. The blade buzzed down one side of the cast, then the other, a line of dust puffing out like a tiny snowstorm. When it was done, Nurse Diaz spread the halves apart with what looked like shoe horns, and there was his arm, pale and skinny and completely whole.

"See?" Jaxon said to the kid in the doorway, holding up his arm like a trophy. "Hard cast, soft skin. Back and forth, not spinning."

The kid looked at Jaxon, then at the saw, then at Jaxon again, and let out a long breath. "Okay," he said, and sat down in the chair like a normal person instead of a person planning an escape.

Jaxon signed out at 4:05, flexing his free arm in the parking lot. Twenty-five minutes. His bike waited by the rack, front wheel tipped to one side, chain guard glinting in the sun.

"Race you to tryouts," he said to nobody, and took off down the sidewalk.

Jeremy slammed his notebook onto the kitchen table so hard the salt shaker rattled. Tonight he was going to write the best short story Mr. Doran had ever graded, one with real dialogue, quotation marks, commas in the right spots, and a climax that actually felt like a climax. He sharpened two pencils even though he was using a pen, because it helped him think, and the smell of cedar and graphite made the whole project feel official.

His sister Maya dropped into the chair across from him with her laptop and a groan. "My essay is broken," she said. "I moved my paragraph about the leaky plumbing to the end because it made more sense there, and now everything feels off, but I can't say why." She spun the screen toward him. The kitchen smelled like the spaghetti sauce simmering on the stove, and somewhere under it Jeremy could hear the faucet dripping, which seemed like a sign.

Jeremy read her first paragraph, then the three body paragraphs, then the first paragraph again. Something clicked. "Your intro says you'll talk about leaks, then bad pipes, then mold. But the paragraphs go bad pipes, mold, leaks." He tapped the screen. "It's like my story problem. My narrator promises trouble in the basement, but the trouble shows up upstairs first."

Maya frowned at her screen. "So the thesis has to name the supporting points in the same order the body paragraphs discuss them?" She highlighted her opening sentence, dragged the list of points around until leaks came last, and read it aloud. It sounded smooth, like fixing a crooked picture frame. "Jeremy, you're a genius," she said, and stole one of his sharpened pencils to circle her revised sentence.

He turned back to his own notebook feeling like he'd found a secret passage. He had been letting his scenes arrive in random order because each one was fun to write, but readers needed the map first. He crossed out his opening line and wrote a new one that promised exactly what would happen, in the order it would happen. Then he fixed his dialogue, comma before the quotation mark, period inside, reading each line out loud in a dramatic voice until Maya threw a folded napkin at him. "The pipe burst at midnight," he wrote, "and water shot across the basement like a fountain."

"Nice climax," Maya said, mouth full of spaghetti.

"Regulate your volume," their dad called from the stove, because Jeremy was now reading the burst-pipe sentence at full volume, both fists in the air.

Evan sat on the crinkly paper of the exam table, rolling up his sleeve for his flu vaccine, when Dr. Okafor paused with the syringe in her hand. "Before I do this, tell me something. Your mom says you've been getting stomachaches. When do they happen?"

"Sunday nights, mostly." Evan watched her give the shot, a quick pinch in his arm. "And Monday mornings. It's weird. I'm not even sick."

"Anything big happening at school on Mondays?" she asked.

That was the question that snagged in his head on the drive home. Mondays meant math, and math meant timed multiplication quizzes. He remembered last Monday: his stomach churning, his palms so sweaty the pencil had slipped, and the Sunday before, lying awake until almost midnight, staring at the ceiling. He'd thought those were three separate things, like three separate bad days. Now he tried to isolate the one thing they had in common. Monday. Every time, Monday.

He dug out a notebook and drew a chart, two parallel columns: one for how his body felt, one for what was coming the next day. Headache, Sunday. Upset stomach, Sunday night. Sweaty palms, Monday morning, right before the quiz. Trouble falling asleep, the night before every single one. When he looked at the two columns lined up side by side, his stomach dropped a little, the way it did in an elevator. The pattern was too neat to be a coincidence. His body was reacting to the quizzes before his brain had even admitted it was worried.

That night was Wednesday, so he decided to test something. No quiz tomorrow, but he practiced anyway, the way Dr. Okafor had shown him in the office: breathe in for four counts, hold it, let it out slow, like he was fogging a window. He also set up a routine, same time every night: pajamas, teeth, ten minutes of a book, lights out. He did it Thursday and Friday and the weekend too, filling in his chart each morning. Sleeping, he wrote. No headache.

Sunday night came, and his stomach tightened at eight o'clock, right on schedule. Evan noticed it, actually noticed it this time, and instead of just lying there waiting for it to get worse, he sat up and breathed. In for four. Hold. Slow fog on an imaginary window. His stomach didn't vanish, but it loosened, like a fist uncurling one finger at a time.

Monday morning he walked into math with dry palms. When the timer started, he took one breath before picking up his pencil, and his hand stayed steady all the way through.

"Feeling okay?" his teacher asked as he handed in his paper.

Evan glanced at the clock, then at his hands. "Ask me Sunday night," he said. "That's the real test."

The Cougars had lost seven road games in a row, and Vincent had started keeping notes in the back of his math binder about it. "We stink everywhere," said Marcus, dropping his bat bag on the bench, "but especially in other people's dugouts." Vincent flipped to a fresh page and wrote Saturday, HOME, then underlined it twice, because today the Cougars were finally playing at Maple Field, their own diamond, with their own ratty net behind home plate and their own crackly scoreboard.

First inning, Marcus robbed a line drive at shortstop. Third inning, their pitcher, Dev, struck out the side. By the fifth, the Cougars were up 4-1, and Vincent felt something weird bubbling up, a feeling he had almost forgotten existed while wearing this uniform. "We're good?" he asked the bench, like he was announcing a scientific discovery. "We're actually good?"

Then it hit him, standing there in the seventh inning with the tying run on second base. It wasn't luck. His notes proved it. Every single away game, ugly loss. Every home game this season, a win. Three straight at home now, if they held on. He turned to Coach Ruiz's nephew, Benny, who kept score and knew everything about baseball. "Benny. Is there a thing where teams win more at their own park?"

Benny didn't even look up from his scorebook. "Home advantage," he said. "Home teams win more than half their games on average. Across a lot of sports, not just baseball."

Vincent's jaw dropped. It was a rule. An invisible, actual rule of the universe, and he had found it with a binder and a bad season. He wanted to test it. If home advantage was real, then the other team's batter, this scary kid named Trevor who had already homered twice in away games against them, should be easier to handle right here. So Vincent, catching, called for a low curveball, a pitch Trevor had hammered on the road. Sure enough, Trevor's swing was late by a hair, and the ball popped up into the gray sky. Marcus caught it. Inning over.

"Your testimony as scorekeeper," Vincent said grandly in the handshake line, "will confirm my theory." Benny rolled his eyes. "It's a scoreboard, not a courtroom. We won 4-2." Marcus put an arm around both of them. "So all we have to do is never leave Maple Field again. I'll write a letter."

In the parking lot, Vincent flipped open his binder one more time and wrote home advantage, big and dark, then drew a box around it. His mom honked from the car. He shoved the binder in his bag, grabbed his bat, and sprinted across the diamond yelling, "Next home game, I'm testing whether it works twice!"

The X-ray photos glowed on the light box, and Abigail leaned forward in her plastic chair, staring at the pale gray bone running down her forearm. Dr. Patel tapped it with a pen.

"Good news," he said. "It's a greenstick fracture."

"A what?" Abigail asked. Her mother was still filling out forms at the counter, so nobody answered for her.

"You can read about it on this sheet," the doctor said, handing her a printout, and then he went to check on another patient.

Abigail read the page twice. The bone had cracked on one side and bent on the other, like a young green branch that snaps partway through but stays connected. It happened mostly in children, because children's bones were more flexible. She looked at the X-ray again. Sure enough, one edge of the bone showed a dark jagged line, and the opposite side curved inward, like it had folded instead of snapped. So her arm was only partly broken. That was strange to think about, like being only partly asleep.

She tried to remember the fall. She had been racing Danny up the hill behind the school, the day after her mother had told her, twice, to slow down and stop showing off. She had shown off anyway. When her feet slipped on the gravel, she had thrown her right arm out to catch herself, and her whole weight had come down on it from one direction. Now that she studied the picture, the crack was on the side that would have been squeezed, and the bend was on the stretched side, exactly the way a branch bends when you push it too far. She felt a small flash of insight: the ground had pushed, and the bone had answered by cracking on one side and folding on the other. Her bones had bent because they were still young, and somehow that made the whole thing less embarrassing, not more. Still, she wondered whether she would have taken the hill slower if her mother hadn't warned her. Maybe the warning was what made her want to go faster. She couldn't decide.

Dr. Patel came back with a bucket of wet casting material and asked her to pick a color. Abigail pointed at the bright orange one, hoping to salvage something good out of a rotten week. The wrap was cool and then warm, like molten wax hardening around her arm, and she held still while it set.

"Can I still write with my left hand?" she asked.

"You'll have to," he said. "For six weeks."

Abigail looked at the orange cast, then at the X-ray still glowing on the box, at the crack and the bend in the branch of her own bone. "Fine," she said. "But Danny has to carry my backpack."

Carson stood behind his science fair table staring at the periodic table taped to the wall, and he could not find sodium. His project, a tray of three cloudy jars labeled "Saltwater Experiment," depended on it, and the judges were already two tables away.

Last spring, his grandmother had narrated her entire garden tour, explaining how an invasive vine had swallowed her tomato plants while she was in the hospital. "The invisible things are the powerful ones," she'd said, pointing at a spot of gray mold on a fence post, "like that microbe eating the wood right now." He hadn't understood what she meant until now, squinting at the tiny numbers crammed into each square. He traced his finger along row three and there it was, Na, with the number 11 sitting on top like a tiny hat. Eleven. He counted the columns and rows again just to be sure he hadn't drifted into magnesium by mistake. Sodium had eleven protons, and the box said so, if a person could learn to read the map.

"Tell me about your project," said the judge, a woman with a clipboard and pen shaped like a thermometer.

Carson picked up the first jar. "Two weeks ago I dissolved salt in water and put it in my bedroom window, the sunny side. I kept a second jar on my desk in the shade, and a third in the fridge." He held up the window jar, which now had white crystals crusty around the bottom and edges. "The water's mostly gone from this one, and look. Salt. The same salt."

"Same salt?" the judge asked.

"That's the twist. I thought dissolving it destroyed the salt and made something new, a chemical change. But when the water evaporated, it left the same salt behind." He touched the jar. "So dissolving salt in water is a physical change. Nothing got destroyed. The salt was just hiding."

The judge smiled and wrote something. Behind her, a small boy in a dinosaur shirt tugged her sleeve and whispered, too loudly, "I thought he was going to show a microbe." A woman at the next table snorted, and Carson's ears went hot, but the judge laughed kindly.

He turned to the periodic table anyway. "See, sodium is number eleven, so every single salt crystal in there has eleven protons in every atom," he said, tapping the square. "I can't see them. Nobody can. But the map tells you where they are, if you know how to read it." The dinosaur boy leaned in, squinting at the tiny numbers. "Whoa," he said. "It's like a treasure chart."

The morning of Grandpa Walt's funeral, Blake sat at the kitchen table with the newspaper open in front of him, pushing his eggs around the plate. Mom had said he could skip breakfast if he wanted, but he made himself take three bites anyway. At the bottom of the page he found a box with Grandpa's name at the top and a picture of him from years ago, back when his beard was still brown. Blake read it slowly, twice.

"It says here Grandpa was a sailor," he said. "On cargo ships. He never told me that."

Mom set down her coffee. "That's the obituary," she said. "It's a published notice that someone died, and it tells about their life. Family, work, what they loved."

Blake frowned at the paper. "But I saw him every summer for six years. He taught me checkers. He hated boats. He wouldn't even get in the paddle boat at the lake." It didn't make sense. Either the paper was wrong, or there was a whole part of Grandpa he had never seen, and that second possibility felt worse, like finding a hallway in a house you thought you knew.

He pushed the eggs away and decided he could not postpone figuring this out until after the funeral. He went to the pantry where Mom kept the old photo boxes, the ones Grandma had left behind, and dug through them while Mom dried dishes behind him. The first box was all babies and weddings. The second box was mostly blurry birthdays. Then, near the bottom, his fingers hit a stiff rectangle.

The photograph showed a man in a white uniform standing on a ship's deck, one hand on a railing, squinting into the sun. It was Grandpa. Young, skinny, and grinning like Blake had never seen him grin, not even when he won at checkers. Behind the photo, in pencil, someone had written: "Walt, first crossing, 1968."

"Mom," Blake called. "Come look at this."

She came over, wiped her hands on the towel, and when she saw the picture she sat down hard in the chair beside him. "I never saw this," she said quietly. "He never talked about it. Not once."

Blake turned the photo over, then back again. "Why wouldn't he talk about it?" he asked. "If I'd sailed across an ocean, I'd tell everybody. I'd tell the mailman."

Mom laughed a small, cracked laugh and put her hand on his shoulder. "Some people keep things," she said. "Maybe it hurt somewhere. Maybe he liked having one thing that was only his."

Blake had felt like despair was waiting for him all week, sitting in the corner of every room, but holding the photograph, something shifted instead. There was a version of Grandpa he had never met, and it wasn't a lie, it was a door. He slid the photo into the pocket of his dress pants, right over his heart, where it made a stiff little square against the fabric.

"Can I carry it into the church?" he asked.

"You carry it," Mom said, "all day."

The lights died at 7:40, right in the middle of Colton's homework. He sat very still in his dark bedroom and waved a hand in front of his face. He could feel his fingers moving, but he could not see them at all. "Great," he said to nobody. "Blind and stuck on fractions."

In the living room his little sister Priya had already lit the emergency candle, and his dad was poking at the breaker panel by the door with his phone flashlight. "Nothing tripped," Dad reported. "Whole building must be out. Probably lost voltage on the whole block." Priya was busy drawing bees on construction paper by candlelight for a school poster. "Bees pollinate flowers," she announced. "That means they carry the powdery stuff around. My poster is going to be intricate. Like, super detailed." "Then you'll need more than one candle," Colton said, and she stuck her tongue out at him.

Colton went back for his phone and found the battery at four percent. He could not waste the flashlight, so he sat on the couch in the dark instead. That was when he noticed something strange. Ten minutes ago he could not even see his own hand. Now, when he waved it, he caught a pale blur against the darker blur of the wall. He turned toward the window, where a sliver of city glow leaked through the blinds, and slowly the coffee table appeared, then the edge of the armchair, then the intricate pattern of shadows the blinds threw across the floor.

"Okay, science experiment," he said out loud. "If I sit here even longer, can I see the whole room?" Priya scooted over to share the experiment, mostly because she wanted to be included. They sat side by side, not talking, staring into the dark while the minutes crawled by. The couch cushions grew clearer. The bookshelf separated itself from the wall. When Colton checked his phone, exactly half an hour had passed since the lights went out. He could make out the whole living room, soft and gray, like an old photograph. "Whoa," Priya whispered. "Our eyes are upgrading."

Colton remembered something his science teacher had mentioned once, about a pigment in the rod cells of the retina, and the word floated back to him. "It's called rhodopsin," he said. "It fades out when there's light, and in the dark your eyes rebuild it. Takes half an hour or more." He counted backward in his head and it matched, almost to the minute. "So the longer we sit here," Priya said slowly, "the better we see?" "That's the rule. Total darkness superpowers."

Then the lights snapped back on, blinding white, and both of them yelped and buried their faces in the couch pillows. From the doorway Dad laughed. "Congratulations, kids. Now your rhodopsin is toast." "Dad!" Priya shouted, eyes squeezed shut. "Turn it off, we weren't done with the experiment!"

The bus dropped Leo's class at the nature reserve just as a fire truck rolled up beside the visitor center, a low brick building donated years ago by an affluent family whose name was carved over the door. "Smoke machine today," said Ms. Ruiz, checking her clipboard. "The firefighters set up a demonstration in the classroom wing, and everyone goes through it."

Inside, a firefighter named Captain Osei explained the drill. A haze machine would fill the room with harmless gray vapor, and each student had to cross from the door to the far window and back. Leo watched the first group go. Priya stood up halfway, coughed on the fake smoke, and had to start over. Most kids walked, heads bent, and bumped into desks they couldn't see. When Leo's turn came, he crouched at the door and paused. The smoke hung in a thick layer above him, and down near the carpet the air looked strangely clear, like the space under a floating blanket. Was the cool air actually down there, or did it just look that way? He had a theory, and a way to test it: he pulled his sweatshirt sleeve over his nose and stood up slowly, inch by inch, like a periscope rising. At knee height, nothing. At waist height, the sleeve went gray and his eyes stung. He dropped back down and crawled the rest of the way, fast and clean, without touching a single desk.

"Best time so far," Captain Osei announced, squinting at her stopwatch. "Anyone know why he kept so low?"

"Because the smoke and heat rise," Leo said, "so the cleaner, cooler air is near the floor. That's why you taught us to crawl low under smoke." He pointed up at the thick gray ceiling of vapor. "I checked, kind of. I stood up slowly to verify where the clean part ended. It's like an invisible line."

"That's some solid logic," the captain said, grinning. "Though next time, verify with your hand, not your face."

That evening Leo wrote a letter to his grandfather, who used to volunteer at a fire station.

Dear Grandpa, You'll like this. Today we crawled through fake smoke at the nature reserve and I found out the clean air hides at the bottom. Everyone else walked through the gray cloud like confused ghosts. Priya says hi. Did you ever crawl for real? Write back and tell me.

A week later the answer came, in shaky handwriting: "Twice, kiddie. Both times the floor saved me. Stay low."

Leo read it twice, then taped it above his desk, right where he could see it from his bed.

Sofia pushed the kitchen chairs aside to make a stage in the living room and set her phone on the bookshelf to record. Tomorrow was her first improv workshop, and she wanted to walk in already knowing how it worked. Her older cousin Denise had agreed to practice with her over video call, and now Denise's face filled the screen, waiting.

"Okay," Sofia said. "You start a scene, and we build it together."

Denise rubbed her hands together like a villain. "Welcome to my store. We only sell one thing: shark teeth."

Sofia froze. She had planned to say something clever, but nothing clever came, so she blurted, "No, we're not in a store, we're on a pirate ship."

Denise dropped the villain pose. "Hold on. You just erased my whole scene. In improv that's like slamming a door in someone's face."

"I didn't like the store," Sofia said. "A pirate ship is better."

Denise tilted her head. "Maybe. But think about what just happened. You proposed the change, and you acted like it was my job to show why your pirate ship was bad. It doesn't work that way. The side that proposes a change carries the burden of proof. That means you have to show why the change is needed instead of me proving it isn't."

Sofia rewound the moment in her head. She had assumed the opposite rule, that whatever she threw out must be accepted until Denise knocked it down. No wonder Denise had looked annoyed. "So if I want the pirate ship, I have to earn it," Sofia said slowly. "I have to build from your shark teeth instead of deleting them."

"Try it again," Denise said.

Denise started over. "Welcome to my store. We only sell one thing: shark teeth."

"Yes, and business is booming," Sofia said, "because the local sharks went predatory and everyone needs proof of what happened."

Denise grinned. "Yes, and a merchant just walked in offering to transport the whole inventory across the harbor for a fee."

"Yes, and the fee is ruining our economy, so we'll pay you in shark teeth instead."

They went back and forth for ten more minutes, building a market, a storm, a smuggler with a peg leg. Twice Sofia slipped and denied an offer, and each time she stopped, rewound, and found a way to say yes to it. The second slip turned into her favorite moment, when Denise's "the harbor is frozen" became Sofia's "yes, and that's why we're racing the ice truck across it."

At the end, Sofia flopped onto the couch and scrolled back through the recording. She watched herself stumble, repair, stumble again, and land the scene. Tomorrow she would walk into that workshop and say yes.

Grayson had one week to turn a primary source into an actual answer, and his grandfather's attic had exactly one box labeled OLD PAPERS. The assignment wanted him to use something written at the time, not a textbook, to explain why people moved west in the 1800s. He had guessed the answer would be gold, because everyone in his class would guess gold, and he wanted something better than the obvious.

Grandpa set the box on the kitchen table beside a rolled-up wall map he'd taken down from the hall. "That map's from my teaching days," he said. "You can spread it out when you need a break." Inside the box, under church programs and a ribbon from a prestigious agricultural fair, Grayson found a small leather book. The handwriting was cramped, and the ink had bled through the thin pages in places, so some words dissolved into pale blue shadows he could only guess at.

The diary belonged to a great-great-something named Elias Ward, and the first entry was dated April 1852. Grayson read slowly, hunting for the word gold. It never came. Instead Elias wrote about a letter from his brother in Iowa, describing soil so dark it "stains the boots," and about a failed mill back east, and about land selling for a dollar and a quarter an acre. Grayson sat back. His easy answer had just collapsed. He decided to test a new one: maybe people moved for cheap land and work, and the gold story was only part of it. He counted the reasons Elias gave across four entries, and land came up in every single one.

When his cousin Marisol arrived to borrow the map for her own homework, the two of them unrolled it on the living room floor. It showed the Roman Empire, not America at all. "You have to trace the biggest border," Marisol said, "for my teacher." Grandpa leaned in the doorway. "Biggest it ever got was around 117 CE, under Emperor Trajan," he said. "Britain in the northwest, all the way to Mesopotamia in the east." Grayson and Marisol ran their fingers along the edge together, from the top corner of Britain across to the far eastern edge, and it took a long time, longer than either of them expected.

Marisol asked whether the empire lasted like that. "No, it got smaller after," Grandpa said, and rolled the map shut, and that single word, smaller, made something click for Grayson. Elias had written that his town back east was shrinking too, mills closing, neighbors leaving. Growing big and then shrinking had a consequence: people went looking for somewhere else. He copied three lines from the diary into his notebook, word for word.

Then he noticed the signature inside the back cover. Not Elias Ward. Ellen Ward, 1852. He flipped to the front again and read the April entry more carefully. "My husband reads this to me and I hold the pen," Ellen had written in the first line, which Grayson had skimmed right past. The settler's diary he needed had been written by the settler's wife, all along. "Grandpa," he called toward the kitchen, "did anyone in the family ever know Ellen wrote this?" Grandpa came back drying his hands on a towel and bent over the page for a long moment. "Well," he said, "they do now."

Ellie swung her bike into the gas station parking lot just as Marcus pedaled in behind her, both of them breathing hard. The afternoon heat shimmered off the pavement, and the drink cooler inside was calling their names. They had exactly three dollars each, saved from dog-walking money they cherished all week for this moment: the giant fountain sodas at Gas-N-Go, the biggest cups in town.

"Race you to the cooler!" Marcus shouted.

They burst through the door and stopped dead. A hand-written sign hung on the cooler: LARGE CUPS, 50 CENTS. Under it, another sign: ICE, SOLD OUT. Beside the register, a small table of last-year's water bottles read $1.75, while a full rack of them by the door read 99 cents.

"Wait, why are those two dollars and those under a dollar?" Marcus asked, pointing. "Same water."

Ellie frowned. The shelves near the register were nearly bare, with only six bottles left. The rack by the door was stacked to the top, so full nobody could reach the back rows. She picked up the 99-cent bottle and turned it over like a detective examining evidence. "Nobody's buying these because they're way over there," she said slowly. "And everybody grabs these because they're right here where you pay. So the close ones cost more because more people want them, and there aren't many left."

"So the store decides the price?" Marcus said.

"No way," Ellie said. "It's us. We decide it by what we'll pay. If we all refused to buy the close ones, they'd have to make them cheaper."

They argued about it all the way to the counter, where the clerk, a teenager named Dana, was taping a fresh price sign over the old one on the fountain machine. "Careful," Dana said. "Large sodas just went up to a dollar. We're almost out of large cups." Behind her, Ellie saw a single sleeve of large cups left, and a line of sweaty customers forming at the door.

"A dollar!" Marcus groaned. "Yesterday it was fifty cents!"

Ellie's mind spun. Then Dana pointed at a mountain of small cups by the syrup machine, hundreds of them, untouched. "Small ones are still fifty cents," Dana said. "We've got a million of those."

Ellie grabbed two small cups. "It's like scissors," she announced, paying Dana. "My grandpa told me about this guy named Alfred Marshall, who wrote a book in 1890 called 'Principles of Economics.' He compared supply and demand to the two blades of a pair of scissors. It takes both to set a price."

"Both what?" Marcus asked, filling his cup from the root beer nozzle.

"Buyers and sellers," Ellie said. "You were right that buyers set the price, and I was right that sellers do. We're both right, like the two blades. Neither one alone can cut anything." She held up her cup triumphantly. "And today, both blades say: buy small, because small is plentiful and cheap."

They carried their sodas outside to the concrete curb, where the air conditioner's thermostat hummed against the wall, keeping the store cool. Marcus took a long sip and grinned. "Best fifty cents I ever spent."

Ellie clinked her styrofoam cup against his like a toast. "To Alfred Marshall," she said, "and his scissors."

The baby had been crying for eleven minutes, which Emilia knew because she was watching the clock on the microwave the way other people watched horror movies. Her cousin Priya had gone to a movie with her parents, and Priya's neighbor Mrs. Okafor had asked if one of them could watch eight-week-old Theo for the evening. Priya had a play rehearsal. Emilia, who was visiting for the week and had never babysat anything larger than a hamster, had said yes mostly to have something to do.

For the first hour it had gone fine. Theo had slept, and Emilia had explored Mrs. Okafor's apartment, which smelled like lavender and had a fridge magnet shaped like a saxophone. Then Theo woke up and began to cry, and nothing worked. She fed him. She changed him, which was an experience she would not describe to anyone, ever. She walked him in circles, sang to him, burped him twice. The crying continued at a volume that seemed to obstruct all rational thought, filling the room so completely that she couldn't hear herself deciding what to try next.

She was standing in the kitchen, bouncing Theo harder and harder on her shoulder, her arms aching, when she noticed the folder of notes Mrs. Okafor had left on the counter. Emergency numbers, feeding times, and a page headed IMPORTANT, which Emilia read while Theo screamed into her collarbone. Never shake him, it said. A baby's neck muscles are too weak to support his heavy head, and shaking can cause serious brain injury. If he cries and cries and you feel yourself getting frustrated, put him somewhere safe and step away for a minute. It's okay. Emilia stopped bouncing. Her arms had been doing something that felt, suddenly, like a bad idea from the future.

She carried Theo to his crib, set him down on his back, and walked to the far side of the room. He kept crying. She stood by the window, hands flat on the sill, and breathed until her shoulders came down from around her ears. It felt like breaking a treaty with herself, leaving him there, but the note had said it was okay, and the note knew more than she did. She texted Priya: "The baby has been screaming for 15 minutes. I put him in his crib and walked away like the note said. Is that normal or am I the worst babysitter in history?"

Priya's reply came fast: "totally normal. he does this. give it 5 min." Emilia watched the clock again, this time without dread. At minute four, Theo's cries slowed into hiccupy gulps. At minute five, the apartment went tranquil, all at once, like someone had lifted a lid off the room. She crept over and looked down. He was asleep, one fist against his cheek, red-faced and furious-looking even in defeat.

She sat on the floor beside the crib with the IMPORTANT page in her lap and read it again. Then she texted Priya one more line: "Tell Mrs. Okafor he slept from 8:40 to now, and I want hazard pay."

Arthur had been waiting for the farm field trip since September, mostly because of the old farmhouse. The bus bumped up a dirt lane between fertile fields, past cows that barely looked up, and stopped at a red barn where a guide in a straw hat was already waving. Arthur's teacher, Ms. Okafor, counted heads twice, then said the magic words: "The farmhouse is a museum now. Everything inside is over a hundred and fifty years old."

Inside, the rooms smelled like dust and wood smoke. Arthur drifted toward a wide oak desk near the window, the kind with little drawers and a worn leather top. His hand was almost on the edge, fingers an inch from the wood, when a girl named Priya grabbed his sleeve.

"Don't touch that!"

"Why not?" Arthur pulled his arm back. "It's just a desk. It looks strong."

"It is strong," Priya said. "That's not the problem. Museums ask visitors not to touch objects because oils and salts from your skin build up over time, and they can stain or damage the surfaces."

Arthur frowned. Oils and salts? From skin? His hand looked perfectly clean. He turned it over and studied his palm like it might be hiding something. Could something invisible really hurt a desk that had survived a century and a half of farmers? A question formed in his mind, the kind he liked best: if the oils and salts built up over time, wouldn't there be proof somewhere?

He wandered the room with his hands jammed in his pockets, looking for evidence. He noticed the banister on the staircase first. The middle of each rail was darker than the ends, a smooth brown stripe exactly where a hand would slide. The doorknob on the pantry door gleamed like a polished coin, while the hinges above it stayed dull and gray. On the desk itself, he leaned close without touching and saw that the front edge, the part a person's arm would rest on, had a soft shine the rest of the wood didn't have.

"There," he said to Priya, pointing. "Look at the banister. It's darker in the middle, right where hands go. And the doorknob's all shiny. That's years and years of hands, isn't it? That's the buildup." He was starting to grin. One kid touching the desk once wouldn't matter, the way one raindrop wouldn't flood a field. But a thousand hands, ten thousand, every one leaving a little behind? That was different. The damage wasn't one moment; it was a pattern, and patterns left marks.

Priya peered at the banister and nodded slowly. "I never thought about it like that."

Arthur still felt a small sting of resentment about the rule, if he was honest. His fingers itched to feel that old wood, and it seemed unfair that a desk could sit there begging to be touched and nobody was allowed. But now he understood the motive behind the sign by the door, the one that said PLEASE DO NOT TOUCH in curly letters. It wasn't about him being clumsy or careless. It was about what he couldn't see sitting on his skin.

At the end of the tour, the guide let them touch one thing, a rough iron horseshoe from the blacksmith shed, and Arthur held it with both hands, running his thumb over the rust. Even this, he realized, would slowly change under a million thumbs.

"Next museum," he told Priya as they climbed back on the bus, "I'm bringing a magnifying glass. I bet I can find the shiny spots from the front row seat."

Alexandra had exactly one week to finish her science project, and the microscope sitting on her grandfather's kitchen table was the most interesting thing on the whole farm. It belonged to her Uncle Theo, who had won a scholarship to study biology years ago and left the heavy black instrument in the attic with a box of slides. Alexandra's project was supposed to be about the finches of the Galapagos Islands, how their beak shapes had changed on different islands until each kind matched the seeds available there. She could write that down, but she wanted to see something real under the lenses.

She pulled out a slide of an onion and dropped it onto the stage. The microscope had three lenses, and she turned the big knob until the longest one, the strongest one, clicked into place. Surely the strongest was the best place to start. She pressed her eye to the eyepiece and saw nothing but a milky blur. She turned the focus wheel, first one way, then the other, and the blur only swam. After ten minutes her neck ached and there were no onion cells anywhere, only fog.

"You look like you lost a fight with that thing," her grandfather said from the doorway.

"It won't show anything. Maybe it's broken." She said it as an accusation, which implied she believed the microscope, not herself, was at fault.

He shrugged and went back out to the barn, and Alexandra slumped in the chair, ready to quit. Then she sat up. The blur wasn't empty. It moved when she moved the slide, just a little. Maybe the cells were there but she was too far off. She clicked the smallest lens, the lowest power, into place, and suddenly the fog resolved into a pale landscape, orderly rectangles edged in faint lines, like a brick wall. There were the onion cells. She found one sharp, clean group in the center, focused carefully, and only then clicked up to the stronger lens. Now the magnified cells filled the view, and the detail was astonishing. She sketched fast, in case it vanished.

Afterward she carried the notebook to the barn, where her grandfather was stacking hay. She showed him her drawing and then flipped to her finch pages, the tracings she had made from Uncle Theo's old book, the thick crushing beaks on one island and the slender probing beaks on another. "Nobody watched the beaks change," she said. "But the pattern is there, the same way the cells were there under the blur. You just have to start in the right place and look."

Outside, the sun was sinking, and the sky over the silo glowed like molten copper. Her grandfather studied the pages for a long moment, then said, "Help me finish this row, and after supper you can tell me the whole thing, start to finish."

The bus smelled of wet raincoats and pencil shavings, and Rosalie had her boots propped on the metal bar under the seat in front of her when she heard the laughing start. Derek was holding his phone toward the window seats so everyone could see the screen. "Look what Milo wrote in the group chat," he said. "Can you even read this? It's like a baby typed it."

Milo sat two rows up, hunched into his jacket, staring at the back of the seat. Rosalie knew about the group chat. She was in it too, and last night she had watched the mean comments pile up under Milo's question about the agriculture project, comments about his spelling and his old shoes. This morning they had all vanished. Derek had deleted them, or someone had, and now there was nothing to point at. Last month something like this had happened to her friend Tessa, and Rosalie had stayed quiet, telling herself the bus wasn't the place. She had regretted it for weeks.

Derek kept scrolling, hunting for the messages. "Wait, where'd they go?" he muttered, tapping the screen. Rosalie's stomach tightened. The evidence was disappearing while everyone watched, and once it was gone, who would believe Milo? Then she remembered her own phone. She hadn't deleted anything. She never did, because her storage was always too full to bother. Last night, before bed, she had taken screenshots of the worst comments, mostly because reading them twice had felt so unfair she'd wanted proof they were real. They were still in her camera roll, time-stamped, eleven o'clock at night.

She stood up in the rattling aisle, gripping a seat back as the bus swayed. Her plan felt small and maybe useless, but she wanted to test one thing: whether Derek would back off if the proof could not be erased. "Those comments you deleted," she said, keeping her voice even, "I have screenshots." She held up her phone from where she stood, not close enough for him to grab, and let the words land. "So deleting them didn't make them never happen."

The bus went quiet except for the engine. Derek dismissed her with a shrug, "Nobody cares," but his ears turned red and he put his phone away. A girl near the window said, "I saw them too." Milo turned around slowly, and his eyes went from Rosalie's phone to her face.

"I'm going to show my screenshots to Ms. Okafor at first period," Rosalie said. "You can come with me or not, but they're not going anywhere." Milo blinked, then nodded and gathered his backpack onto his lap like he was ready for the bus to hurry up and arrive.

Derek stared out the window the rest of the ride. When the doors hissed open, Rosalie waited for Milo in the aisle and said, "Walk with me."

Every August, watering Grandma's tomato beds was a ritual: fill the can at the spigot, haul it down the gravel path, pour, trudge back. Jade had assumed the tomatoes needed her, but by the third trip her arms burned, and she began to think the tomatoes mostly needed somebody with stronger shoulders.

Grandma was at the picnic table with her coffee, reading, while Jade lugged the can again. "My arms are going to fall off," Jade said.

"Farmers along the Nile had the same problem," Grandma said. "They used a shaduf." She pointed her cup at the tool shed. "Your grandfather built one for the pond years ago. It's behind the rakes." That was all she said, and she went back to her book.

Jade found it leaning against the wall: a long pole with a bucket on one end and a heavy stone wired to the other, balanced on a post. She hauled it to the pond, dipped the bucket, and pulled down on the rope. The stone rose, the bucket swung up over the bank, and the water poured out toward the beds. It still took work, but it took half the work, and Jade stood there dripping and grinning, moving bucket after bucket. It was so simple it felt unfair. One heavy thing lifting another, so nobody's arms had to do it all.

Then she remembered Monday. Her history teacher had asked the class to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War, and Jade's rough draft was one flat sentence: the treaty punished Germany after World War I. Mrs. Okafor had written, "But how? Show me." Jade sat down on the gravel, still holding the shaduf rope, and thought about punishment. Germany had been made to carry payments so heavy they never seemed to end, like being handed a watering can that never got lighter. People who feel crushed year after year look for someone to lift the weight, and someone had promised he could. She couldn't see a country or an armistice the way she could see this pole, but the shape was the same, a burden doing something over time. She pulled out her notebook and wrote: imagine carrying the can forever, and imagine the person who says, put it down.

"Did you figure out your homework out here?" Grandma asked, coming down the path with the empty coffee cup.

"I think the treaty is a watering can," Jade said, and hauled up another bucket.

Ryder stood at the counter with a whole onion in one hand and his mom's sharpest knife in the other, glancing at the clock. His parents would be home at seven, and he had promised them a pasta sauce made entirely from scratch. His little sister Nadia sat on a stool nearby, arms crossed, watching him like a judge.

"I'm not eating anything with onion in it," she announced. "Onion is sharp and mean. It bit me once at Maya's house."

"That was raw onion," Ryder said. "This is going to be different." He hoped he was right. He curled the fingers of his left hand into a claw, fingertips tucked behind his knuckles, and guided the knife with his knuckles leading the blade. The first slices were uneven, but none of his fingertips went with them, which he counted as a win. The raw pieces smelled so sharp that Nadia leaned away, fanning the air with her hand.

He melted butter in the pan and turned the heat down low, because the recipe card his mom had written said low and slow, no rushing. He remembered how the tomatoes in their garden thrived when he stopped overwatering them, and he figured onions might have their own hidden rule too. His motive was simple: get Nadia to eat the sauce without complaining. He decided to test one piece on her before he finished, so he fished out a small strip of cooked onion, blew on it, and held out the fork. "One bite. If you hate it, I'll pick every single one out of your bowl."

Nadia eyed it like it might bite back, then took the tiniest nibble. Her eyebrows went up. She took a bigger bite. "It's soft," she said, chewing slowly. "And sweet. It tastes like it got dipped in honey. Why isn't it mean anymore?"

"That's the trick," Ryder said, stirring the pan, where the onions had turned soft and golden brown, their natural sugars showing themselves as they cooked. "Raw onion stays sharp, but if you cook it slowly over low heat, it turns sweet like this." He poured in the crushed tomatoes, added a pinch of salt, and let the sauce bubble while he boiled the pasta, checking the clock. Six forty. Plenty of time.

At seven the front door opened and his parents came in, sniffing the air. Nadia got to the hallway first. "Ryder made sauce from scratch," she reported, "and there's onion in it, and I'm getting seconds."

"Seconds?" his dad said. "You picked onion out of your chili last Tuesday."

"Not anymore," Nadia said. "Ryder, save me the fertile pieces. The golden ones." Ryder laughed and lifted the pot, steam rising as he carried it to the table.

The floorboards in Grandma Ruth's attic creaked as Levi and his cousin Marisol set up two folding chairs. In two hours, the whole family would gather downstairs for Grandpa Joe's seventieth birthday party, and the two of them had promised to perform a five-minute improv scene, even though Levi had never done improv in his life.
