"Rule one," Marisol said, tapping the chair like a game show host. "Whatever I say, you say yes, and then you add something. So if I say, 'We're astronauts landing on a cheese moon,' you don't say, 'No, that's silly.' You say, 'Yes, and the smell is making me hungry.'"

"That sounds easy," Levi said.

It was not easy. Every time Marisol made an offer, Levi's brain revolved around all the things that could go wrong, and out of his mouth came a dodge. "Um, I guess so," he said to the cheese moon. "Uh, okay," he said when she suggested they were being chased by a vacuum cleaner. Marisol pulled a small notepad from her pocket and started making tally marks, one for every um and uh. After ten minutes she turned the page toward him: twenty-three marks.

Levi stared at the tallies like they were evidence at a trial. He had thought his problem was not knowing what to say, but the marks showed a different pattern. The ums appeared exactly when an offer arrived, right at the moment of choice. He decided to run a test. Instead of filling the gap with a sound, he would stay silent for a beat, then say the words "Yes, and" and let them carry him wherever they wanted.

They started the scene again. Marisol said, "Our spaceship runs on pickle juice." Levi paused, silent, letting the pause sit there. "Yes, and we're almost out, so we have to land at the space diner." Marisol's eyebrows shot up. She kept the scene going, and the tally marks slowed, then stopped. By the third run, she put the notepad away entirely and started laughing so hard she fell off her chair.

Downstairs, the smell of Grandpa Joe's lemon cake drifted up the attic stairs. Levi heard chairs scraping, the screen door banging, and Grandma Ruth calling that the show would start in five minutes. Marisol grabbed his arm. "One last treaty," she said. "Whatever happens down there, nobody says no, not even once." Levi shook her hand, and they headed for the stairs, where the first row of relatives, looking cheerful but slightly obstinate about being entertained, was already waiting. Marisol leaned over and whispered, "We're two penguins who opened a lemonade stand in Antarctica." Levi let the pause hang there, took a breath, and said, "Yes, and business is about to pick up."

Rose had babysat plenty of toddlers before, but never a baby, and eight-month-old Ivy weighed almost nothing in her arms, like a bundle of laundry. She followed Mrs. Okafor's directions through the park to the shaded benches near the duck pond, where a stroller ride was supposed to knock Ivy out for her afternoon nap.

"There's a note in the diaper bag," Mrs. Okafor had said before leaving. "Please read it. It's important."

Ivy fell asleep on the third loop around the pond, her fists curled under her chin. Rose wheeled the stroller back toward the bench and dug out the note. The handwriting was small and careful: Back at two. Nap is at one. Safe sleep: on her back only, firm flat surface, no pillows, no blankets, no toys.

Rose frowned. The note sat on the bench beside the diaper bag, which was stuffed with a soft yellow blanket embroidered with a cartoon emperor penguin, its wings spread wide. Rose had planned to spread that blanket on the grass, lay Ivy on it, and tuck the edges around her like a nest. It looked so cozy. She had even imagined the penguin watching over Ivy like a little guard.

But the note said no blankets. And grass wasn't flat exactly, and it wasn't firm either, not the way a floor was firm. Rose looked at the blanket, then at the stroller seat. The stroller seat reclined all the way back until it lay flat, and it had a hard frame underneath. She pushed the lever, and the seat lowered with a click.

"Okay," Rose whispered to the sleeping baby. "You go on your back, on this, and Penguin stays in the bag." She lifted Ivy out slowly, the way you'd carry a full glass of water across a room, and lowered her onto the flat seat. Ivy's eyes stayed shut. Rose clicked the buckle across her, loose and gentle, then stepped back and checked from three angles that Ivy was still on her back. She was.

A woman on the next bench leaned over. "She'll be cold without a blanket, won't she?"

"Mrs. Okafor emphasized back sleeping on a firm, flat surface," Rose said, surprising herself with how steady she sounded. "No pillows, no blankets, no toys. Babies under one are safer that way." She pointed to the note. "It's all right here in her handwriting. I decided I'd rather follow it exactly than guess."

The woman nodded slowly. "I used to put mine on her stomach. That's what everyone did." She watched Ivy sleeping, pink-faced and undisturbed. "You're a careful one."

When Mrs. Okafor hurried back at five of two, Rose handed her the note, the blanket still folded, and the penguin still in the bag. "She slept forty whole minutes," Rose said. "On her back, on the flat seat, nothing in there but her."

Mrs. Okafor let out a breath and put both hands on Rose's shoulders. "Could you come back Thursday?"

Dinner was lasagna, the good kind with the crunchy edges, and Paige pushed hers around the plate in slow circles. Tomorrow morning she had to stand up in front of the whole class and read her poem out loud, and even thinking about it made her stomach feel like it was full of ice water. Her hands were clenched in her lap under the table.

"You're not eating," said her older brother Dex, who was home from soccer practice and working on his third helping.

"I have anxiety about the poem thing," Paige said. "That's what Mom called it last time. My chest gets all tight and my heart goes fast."

Across the table, six-year-old Theo waved his fork. "I'm a herbivore," he announced, stacking his zucchini slices into a tower. "I only eat plants. And garlic bread."

"That's not how it works, but fine," said Dad, breaking a piece of bread that had gone brittle in the oven. It crackled and showered crumbs across the tablecloth.

Dex set down his fork. "You know what my coach has me do before a penalty shot? Goalies and penalty takers, both. You breathe in, then let it out slow, like twice as long as the in breath. Long exhales." He demonstrated, puffing the air out so his cheeks went flat. "It's a coping skill. Whole team does it before a stressful moment, before we even walk on the pitch. It calms the body's stress response down. That's what he said."

"Does it actually work?" Paige asked.

"Try it and see. Can't hurt."

She was quiet for a moment. It seemed strange that breathing could change anything, since breathing was just a thing her body did anyway, like blinking. But there was a way to test an idea, and she knew it. You did it and watched what happened, the same way you'd check whether the toaster was broken or just unplugged. She took a slow breath through her nose, counted to four, then let it out through her mouth, long and thin, like she was fogging a window gently.

"Feeling any better?" Dex asked.

"My heart's not going as fast," Paige said, surprised. She did it again, and this time she paid attention on purpose. In, slow. Out, slower. The ice water in her stomach didn't vanish, but it turned into something more like cold tap water, which she could live with.

Later, in her room with the poem cards spread on the bed, she tried to replicate the exact same thing, in through the nose for four, out for six or seven. She did it three times before practicing the first line out loud to her poster of the solar system. Her voice came out steadier than she expected, and she said the second line to her reflection in the mirror, and then the third.

"Boundaries," she told Mars on the poster, holding up a hand. "You don't get to hear the ending until tomorrow."

At breakfast she set her fork down, breathed in slow, and let the breath out long, watching it fog a little against the cold window. Then she picked up her poem cards and walked out the door.

Jace noticed it at the fridge, where Marcus was standing with the door open without taking anything out. They had been friends since second grade, and Marcus never just stood at a fridge. He grabbed the juice, made a joke, kicked the door shut with his heel.

"You want a snack?" Jace asked.

"I'm not hungry." Marcus closed the fridge and sat down at the kitchen table. He pulled out his phone, then put it back. He picked up a pencil from the counter and tapped it against the wood, four taps, pause, four taps.

Jace sat across from him. Last week Marcus had skipped soccer practice, which he never did, and yesterday he had laughed at nothing Jace said, the fake kind of laugh that comes half a second too late. Jace had been building a theory in his head: something was wrong that Marcus wasn't saying out loud, and the pattern of small changes was the evidence.

In health class, their teacher had put up a poster and told them to read it themselves. Jace remembered the exact words because he'd copied them into his notebook for the quiz. Mental health includes a person's emotional, psychological and social well-being, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. He'd assumed it was quiz material, nothing more. But standing there now, he thought about the "social" part. If friendships counted inside mental health, then what happened between him and Marcus wasn't separate from how Marcus was doing overall. It was part of the same thing.

"Remember in fourth grade," Jace said, "when you got picked for the county math team and your dad called it the most prestigious thing that ever happened to our family?" Marcus's dad had framed the certificate and hung it over the toaster.

Marcus almost smiled. "He still points at it when he makes eggs."

"And then the team got cut because the county ran out of budget, and you were fine about it."

"I wasn't fine," Marcus said. He set the pencil down. "I told everyone I was fine."

Jace waited. In his theory, the missing money part mattered too, so he asked, "Is it your dad's shop?" Marcus's dad repaired bicycles, and the whole spring had been slow. Marcus looked up fast, surprised, then nodded.

"The revenue's been down for months. They might lose the lease. If we move, I change schools." His voice went thin on the last word. "I didn't want to say it out loud because it gets bigger when I say it."

"That's backwards," Jace said. "Stuff gets smaller when you say it. That's how it works with my mom and her stress thing. She calls her breathing exercises coping, and she says I can borrow them if I ever need to."

"My sister says I have anxiety," Marcus said. "She read about it."

"Maybe. You could talk to the counselor about it, and you could also just talk to me. I'm asking for that. Consider it a boundary: no more fake laughs, and no more standing at the fridge pretending you're hungry."

Marcus opened the fridge, took out the juice, and poured two glasses.

The group chat lit up at 7:02 p.m., right after dinner. Maya had posted a screenshot of an email from their teacher, and beneath it, eleven people were typing at once. Ella scrolled through the chaos: someone sent a string of exclamation points, someone else typed in ALL CAPS, and Priya dropped a single thumbs-up. "Guys," Ella typed slowly, "nobody can even tell what we're deciding."

The problem was real. Maya's birthday was in nine days, and she wanted to invite the whole class, all twenty-six kids, by email instead of paper invitations this year. But nobody had everyone's address. Some kids had never shared theirs, and Maya refused to ask people to send their emails to the whole group. "It's not fair to just hand out everybody's address to everybody," she wrote. "My mom says that's how spam lists start."

Ella stared at her phone. She thought about the email her soccer coach sent every fall, the one listing practices and field locations. When she'd hit reply once, the message had gone only to the coach, not to all the other parents, and she'd noticed the To line was strangely short. Somewhere in that memory, a word persisted in nagging at her: three letters, hiding in plain sight near the top of the email form. She opened her own account and started a new message, typing Maya's address in the To field, then looking carefully at the little links beside it. Cc. Bcc.

She clicked Bcc and typed in her own address, then sent a test message to Maya: "Look at the To and Bcc lines and tell me what you see." Two minutes later Maya replied, and then posted in the group chat: "ELLA. This is it." She pasted a screenshot. Ella typed the explanation she'd worked out: "BCC stands for 'blind carbon copy.' People you add in the Bcc field still get the message, but the other recipients can't see their addresses." Maya added, "So I can put everybody in Bcc and nobody's address gets shared with everyone."

The plan still had wrinkles. Maya's first attempt failed because she'd typed half the class into the regular To line by accident, and Priya gently pointed it out: "Same problem, different window. Try again." Maya tried again, and this time the test email arrived in Ella's inbox with a To line showing only Maya's own address. It was like mailing twenty-six sealed envelopes instead of one giant postcard.

The next evening, the invitations went out. Every kid in class got one, and when Dylan replied asking who else was invited, Maya could honestly say he'd have to wait and see. "The mystery is part of the party," she wrote, and Ella laughed out loud at her desk. Then a new message appeared, from Maya only to her: "Chronic overthinker saves the day again. You're getting the first slice of cake." Ella grinned and typed back, "Deal. But I want it in writing."

Victor had one job at Marcus's birthday sleepover: find out where the new kid, Aiden, was from, so they could put it on the team sheet for the international food day. He waited until they were all sprawled on the living room floor with pizza, because asking at the door would have been rude.

"So where are you from?" Victor asked, pencil ready.

Aiden pushed a pepperoni to the edge of his slice. "That's the problem. Singapore for three years, then Germany, then Brazil, and before all that, a place I barely remember. My parents say home is Ohio, but I've never lived there longer than a summer." He shrugged. "I always get stuck on that question. It's like asking a fish which puddle it owns."

The other kids offered guesses. Marcus said Ohio, because that's where Aiden's parents were from. Priya said Singapore, because that's where he'd lived longest. Aiden shook his head at every answer, and Victor noticed his shoulders creeping up toward his ears. The question itself seemed to obstruct the conversation, like a couch blocking a doorway: nobody could get past it to the actual kid sitting there.

Later, when the others had drifted toward the video games, Victor found Aiden alone at the bookshelf, looking at Marcus's mother's old sociology textbooks. Victor had an idea he wanted to test. His own dad had moved from one country to another before Victor was born, and Victor had once overheard a phrase at his aunt's house. "My aunt says there's a name for kids like you," he said. "Third culture kid. An American sociologist, Ruth Hill Useem, made it up back in the 1950s. For kids raised in a culture different from their parents' home culture."

Aiden turned around slowly. "Say the name again."

"Third culture kid."

Aiden said it back, once, then again, like he was trying on a coat that might actually fit. "So I'm not from nowhere. I'm from a third place, the one in between." He laughed, a real laugh this time. "It's a paradox, isn't it? The question made me feel like I had no answer, and the answer is that the in-between is the answer."

Victor wrote it down on the team sheet: Aiden, third culture kid, four countries. Priya read it over his shoulder and said they could make a dish from each place, a little buffet, and it would be the best table in the cafeteria, inevitable really, since no one else would have four flags.

Aiden grabbed the marker and drew a fifth flag with a question mark on it. "For the third culture," he said, and held it up for everyone to see.

Naomi had exactly one hour before the health expo opened, and her model of the brain's reward pathway still looked like a pile of yarn and buttons. "The nicotine goes in here," she said, threading a blue bead along the yarn from the front of her cardboard brain toward the middle, "and it lands on these cells, and they flood the gap with dopamine." Dopamine was the messenger that made the brain say yes, do that again. Nicotine tricked the pathway into saying it about something harmful.

"Is that the formula for addiction?" asked Priya, crouching beside the picnic table. "Like, chemical in, dopamine out, want more?"

"Sort of a formula," Naomi said. "Want to test it?" She held up a marble, a magnet, and a paper clip. She was trying to show how nicotine made the pathway react faster and harder than ordinary rewards did, so quitting felt like losing something. Priya flicked the marble down the yarn track. It bumped past the magnet without stopping. Then Naomi taped the magnet to stand for nicotine, and the paper clip snapped sideways toward it before the marble even arrived. "See? The pull starts before the reward shows up. That's the craving part."

Priya went quiet. She turned a button over and over in her fingers. "Can I tell you something? I've been so anxious this whole session. Like, chest-tight, can't-sleep anxious. I thought I was the only weird one here."

Naomi remembered the binder from the camp office that she'd flipped through while waiting for glue. "You're not. There was this big U.S. survey of teens aged thirteen to eighteen, and about a third of them had had an anxiety disorder at some point. It said anxiety was the most common kind of mental disorder among them." She stacked a third of the buttons from the table into one pile and left the rest scattered. "Look. If this table were the survey, this pile is you."

"One third," Priya said slowly. "That's, like, two other girls in our cabin, probably." She almost smiled. "Where's the binder? I want to see it with my own eyes."

They ran through the lodge together, and Naomi felt oddly competent, like her brain had its own reward pathway lighting up. The binder was on the shelf where she'd left it, but when she opened it, a folded note slid out, addressed to the camp director. Priya grabbed her arm. "That's my handwriting," she whispered. "I wrote that note two weeks ago about my anxiety and never sent it."

"So send it now," Naomi said, holding out a pen.

The driving school shared a parking lot with a laundromat, and Aubrey's mother taught behind the wheel all afternoon, so the basket of family laundry came with them every Tuesday. Aubrey had resigned herself to spending those hours in the back room of Hometown Driving Academy, sorting darks from lights beside the humming dryers, while her mother's voice drifted in through the propped door. "Check your mirror, Mr. Delgado. Mirror, signal, shoulder." Her mother wanted her to have the whole laundry system mastered by summer, and Aubrey wanted the opposite: to be out in the training car, learning something that actually moved.

Today she was determined to get it right anyway. She pulled Aubrey's dad's work shirts from the pile, felt a wet patch, and discovered a red sock hiding inside a white pillowcase, the culprit behind months of pink undershirts. "That's the contradiction," she muttered. "Dad says hot water cleans everything, but hot water is exactly what sets the pink." She wrote it in her notebook: cold rinse, darks, always. Then she reached deep into the basket and something sharp caught the pad of her thumb.

At first it looked like nothing. Then the blood came, bright and steady, and Aubrey's mother hurried in from the parking lot, still holding her clipboard. She grabbed a clean towel from the folded stack and pressed it firmly over the cut. "Keep this on," she said. "Firm, like you mean it." The clock on the wall read 3:12.

Aubrey held the pressure and counted the dryer cycles. Her mother went to the office phone and called for medical help, then came back and crouched beside her. "Ten minutes is the rule," her mother said quietly. "If it's still bleeding after ten minutes of firm pressure, it needs real medical help." Aubrey watched the second hand sweep. At 3:22 she peeled the towel's edge back just enough to see, and the blood was still coming. "It's still going," she reported, and pressed down again, harder, the way she'd been told. Her mother stayed on the line with the dispatcher, one hand resting on Aubrey's shoulder.

The ambulance took eleven minutes to arrive. Aubrey kept the towel pressed the entire time, her other hand steady on top of it, while her mother gave the address twice. When the medics finally knelt down and took over, one of them nodded at the towel and said, "Good, you didn't let up." Aubrey looked at her notebook on the folding table, open to the page about cold rinses and hidden red socks. "Next Tuesday," she said, "I'm finishing that load."

Stella's pencil hovered over the paper, and the paper was winning. In art cabin three, everyone else had already drawn a street with one-point perspective: two rows of buildings whose edges ran uphill and downhill toward a single dot, the vanishing point, where the whole road disappeared. Hers looked like a street built by a drunk giant. The left side tilted one way, the right side the other, and the road climbed instead of receding.

She wanted this badly, because tomorrow the camp was holding a small gallery night, and the pottery instructor, an artisan from the town who sold glazed bowls at the market, had promised to trade one bowl for any drawing she liked. Stella had her eye on a blue-green one with a wobbly rim. She also wanted to beat Marcus, who kept leaning over and saying, "Mine looks like a photograph, Stella. Yours looks like a melted crayon."

She decided to test an idea instead of guessing. First she retraced the road with her ruler and saw the problem: her building lines weren't parallel with each other before they angled in, so they ran to two different vanishing points instead of one. Two vanishing points meant two roads, and two roads meant melted crayon. She marked a single dot with a pushpin, tied a piece of string to it, and pulled the string tight to guide each line. The string made a faint sound, a small humming like a plucked guitar, and she pretended it was the street singing itself into place. Pin to corner, line. Pin to corner, line. Slowly a real street appeared, a candy shop, a lamppost, a mailbox, all obedient, all sliding toward the dot.

But her street was empty, so she added a boy juggling on the sidewalk and, near him, a ball resting on the pavement. The ball looked wrong. No matter how she shaded the rounded side of it, the ball seemed to hover a little above the ground, like it was floating an inch of air, refusing to land. She erased the shadow, drew it again, shaded the whole shadow evenly. Still hovering. Marcus leaned over. "Nice balloon," he said.

Stella glared at the drawing, then at the actual sunny porch step outside, where a soccer ball sat in the sun. She went out and knelt beside it. The shadow on the step wasn't the same darkness all the way across; the outer edge looked soft and gray, but the part right under the ball, in the narrow space where the ball touched the step, went almost black, the darkest shadow of all. She hadn't shaded that spot at all. Back inside, she pressed her pencil down hard in the tiny area where the ball met the pavement, making it the darkest mark on the whole street, and left the rest of the shadow lighter. The ball dropped onto the ground like it had been waiting for permission.

At gallery night the artisan stood in front of her drawing for a long moment. She tapped the place where the ball touched the street and said, "You saw it. Most people never look at the dark part where the ball touches the ground." Stella retrieved the blue-green bowl from the trade table with both hands, and Marcus, standing behind her with his photograph-perfect street, said, "Okay. Fine. That one's better."

The lemonade stand had been Victor's idea, but the notebook on the counter was his sister's idea, and that was the problem. Dana was leaving for college in the fall, and she had put two hundred dollars of her birthday money into something she called an investment account. She wanted Victor to understand it before she went. "Stock or bond," she had said that morning, tapping the notebook. "Pick one, and be able to tell me which is riskier and why. I'll stop by at noon and quiz you."

Victor poured lemonade for a man in a red cap and thought about what he had read the night before. A stock was a tiny piece of a company. A bond was more like lending the company money, and the company promising to pay it back with a little extra. He could recite that. But which was riskier, and why, kept sliding around in his head like ice in a glass.

By ten thirty he had sold nine cups at fifty cents each, and there was a line of four kids from the soccer field. Then his friend Marcus arrived with a wild plan. "Double the price," Marcus said. "A dollar a cup. They're hot out there. You'll make twice the money."

Victor hesitated. He remembered last summer, when he had tried to sell friendship bracelets at three dollars each and nobody bought a single one. He had blamed the bracelets. Now he wondered if he should have blamed the price. "Let's test it," he said. They taped a new sign to the jug: ONE DOLLAR.

The line did something strange. The next kid looked at the sign, dug in his pocket, and walked away. The three behind him turned and drifted back toward the field. For twenty minutes not one person stopped. "It's like they vanished," Marcus said. "Nothing else changed. Same lemonade, same sun." Victor wrote it down in the margin of Dana's notebook: when the price goes up, people buy less, as long as nothing else changes. It wasn't the bracelets last summer. It never had been.

He changed the sign back to fifty cents, and by eleven fifteen, the customers had returned, laughing and spontaneous, splashing quarters on the counter and arguing about who had the driest soccer sock. Victor watched them and turned the stock-and-bond question over again. A company that did badly could skip the extra payment on a bond, but the company usually still had to pay the bondholder back eventually, because the bond was a contract. A stock, though, was just a claim on whatever was left. If the company fell apart, the stock could be worth nothing at all.

At noon, Dana pedaled up the driveway on her old bike, kicked the stand down, and sat on the curb with a cup sweating in her hand. "Okay," she said. "Quiz time. Stock or bond. Which is riskier?"

"Stock," Victor said. "A bond is a contract, so the company owes you. A stock is only worth what the company turns out to be. No promise, no payback order, just the risk." He slid the notebook across the counter, open to his scribbled margin note. "And I figured out something else today. Price up, buyers down. I proved it with lemonade."

Dana read the page, then grinned at him over the rim of her cup. "Okay, one more question, and this one's for double. If you had two hundred dollars, what would you do with it?"

Victor looked at the line of quarters, then at her, and said, "First, I'd buy another bag of lemons."

Autumn had exactly one week to get her science fair project ready, and her only idea was to smear mud on a baking sheet and hope for the best. She sat on her grandmother's porch steps with her chin in her hands, staring at the garden hose coiled by the fence.

"What's the sighing about?" Grandma asked, setting down two glasses of lemonade even though Autumn hadn't asked for any, which was typical.

"I have to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years. Erosion and deposition. It's mandatory for the unit grade, and I can't picture it. A canyon is huge and slow, and I can't even see time." She took the lemonade anyway, because refusing Grandma's lemonade was like refusing a sunrise.

Grandma tipped her head toward the hill behind the garden, where a shallow gully ran down past the compost bin to the creek. "You see that ditch? Your grandfather filled it in twice. Twice. That gully beat him like an old adversary. Every hard rain carved it right back out."

Autumn walked up the slope and crouched at the edge of the groove. It was maybe a foot deep, with pebbles heaped at the bottom where the water had dropped them, and at its mouth, where it met the flat ground, a little fan of mud spread out like a tiny delta. The water had carried dirt away here and dumped it there, and it had done it all without her ever once watching it happen. She grinned, turned the hose on low, and aimed it at the top of the gully.

For an hour she experimented. A trickle barely moved anything, so she pinched the nozzle and made a torrent, and the gully deepened so fast she actually yelped. Then she watched the fan of mud at the bottom grow, layer after layer, and thought about the Colorado River doing that not for an hour but for millions of years. At school they'd read that the Grand Canyon is 277 miles long, 446 kilometers if you measured that way, and over a mile deep at its deepest point. She'd skipped past that number before. Now she stood at the bottom of the garden, looked up at where she'd started at the top of the hill, and tried to picture a mile of rock going down instead of up. Her brain stuttered. A mile was a whole mile, straight into the ground, and the river had done it one rainy afternoon at a time.

"Grandma, was Grandpa really mad about the gully?" she called.

"Mad enough to write it a letter," Grandma said. "I still have it somewhere."

Autumn laughed so hard she nearly dropped the hose, then got an idea so good she jogged back up the hill. She would build the whole project in a plastic storage bin, film the water cutting its channel overnight, and split the screen so the viewers could watch the canyon grow while she narrated in fast-forward. First, though, she washed out Grandma's gully-carved measuring cup, refilled both lemonade glasses, and carried them carefully back down the slope.

"Truce," she said, handing one over. "The gully and I are on the same team now."

The graph paper sat between Aubrey and her partner, Marcus, with two climate charts pinned at the corners. One showed a hot desert: a thin scrub of rainfall bars, barely a few centimeters a year, with a temperature line that climbed high and stayed there. The other showed a rainforest, where the rainfall bars towered so tall that Marcus had needed a second sheet of graph paper to fit them all. Their science teacher had written one instruction on the board: compare the two climates before the bell, because the packets were due at the end of the period.

"Easy," Marcus said, tapping the desert chart. "Desert wins on temperature. Rainforest wins on rain. Can we turn it in?"

Aubrey frowned at the desert's rainfall bars. They looked almost like a mistake, so small she could cover all twelve months with her thumb. "But that can't be the whole answer," she said. "If it rains at all, why is the ground always dry in pictures of deserts? Where does the water go?" Marcus shrugged and started doodling a cactus on the margin, which meant he was done thinking.

Then she remembered something. Last fall, before the unit on decomposers, her cousin Elena in Arizona had sent her a video. Elena had dumped a bucket of water on her backyard patio just to see what would happen, and by lunch the whole puddle had vanished, even though it had only been a drizzle-free morning. At the time Aubrey had assumed someone wiped it up. Now she looked at the temperature line again, flat and burning across the whole year, and a different idea felt plausible. The water had gone up. The sun and the dry air could take far more water in a year than the rain put down.

"I think I've got it," she said. She grabbed a sticky note and wrote across the desert chart: the sun and dry air could evaporate far more water in a year than falls as rain, so the ground stays dry. "So even when it does rain, the desert loses it. The ground can't hold on."

Marcus stopped doodling. "Wait. So the rainforest is the opposite?" He flipped to the second chart, where the rainfall bars looked like a skyline. "The rain comes faster than anything can take it away." He wrote that on a sticky note too and pressed it beside the tall bars. Then he looked at Aubrey. "So for our answer, the desert isn't just hotter. It's a place where the water leaves."

"There's ten minutes," said Priya from the next table, glancing over at them. Aubrey noticed Priya's own packet was still blank except for a title, and Priya's pencil was hovering without moving. "We're stuck on the same question," Priya admitted.

"Take this." Aubrey slid the desert chart across so Priya could see the sticky note, and Priya copied the comparison onto her own sheet while Marcus flipped their rainforest chart around. They each wrote a sentence about which months preceded the heavy rain in the rainforest and how the desert's heat held steady no matter what.

When the bell rang, Marcus handed in the packet with both charts and three sticky notes flapping off the sides. Priya slid hers in right behind his. On the way out, Marcus pointed at the thermometer by the door. "Eleven degrees. If I dumped a bucket outside right now, it would still be there tomorrow." Aubrey grinned and said, "Then let's be glad we don't live in a desert," and pushed the door open into the cold.

The argument started three rows from the back of the bus, which was where most good arguments started. Marcus held up his phone with the district cross-country standings. "Torrance is number one," he said. "Riverview's girl is second. Torrance is obviously faster."

"Obviously by how much?" Ella asked.

Marcus looked at her the way people look when a question is more trouble than it's worth. "By first place. That's the whole point of first place."

Eella wanted the standings for a reason of her own. Her brother Cole ran for Torrance, and their dad had watched the state meet on TV last spring, where the silver medalist in the hundred meters lost by less than a blink. Cole had moped about it for a week, saying the guy was basically as fast as the winner. Their dad, who considered himself Cole's mentor in all things running, had disagreed at dinner every night since. Ella intended to settle it, because she was optimistic about her chances of winning an argument nobody had asked her to join.

She leaned over the seat. "Rankings don't tell you the gap. Torrance's girl could be ahead by a hundredth of a second or by a whole minute. First and second just tells you the order."

"You made that up," Marcus said.

"Then let's check." Coach Peters kept meet times on a clipboard that lived in the equipment shed, and Ella knew it came out of the shed every Thursday, when the equipment cart rolled onto the bus for away meets. Today was Thursday. When the cart rattled aboard at the next stop, she flipped the clipboard open on her knees while Marcus held the phone.

Torrance's top runner had run the two-mile in 11:42.06. Riverview's had run 11:42.07. One hundredth of a second. Marcus stared at the numbers, then at his phone, which said the same two names in the same order and nothing else.

"Okay," he said slowly, "but that's just those two."

She turned the page. Fifth place and sixth place in the standings were two kids from Farmington and Halloway. Their times were 12:10 and 13:05. Fifty-five seconds apart, and the ranking treated that gap exactly the same as the hundredth of a second, which was to say it didn't treat it at all.

Marcus wrote both pairs of numbers in the fog on the window with his finger, as if the glass might disagree too. The glass did not.

That night she told Cole, who took the news the way runners take hills. "So the guy on TV," he said, "could've been a hundredth behind. Or a minute." He picked up his shoes by the door. "I'm going to go run the same time as somebody faster than me."

The sign in aisle six stopped Aaron cold. Storm Cocoa Puffs, the cereal he'd been saving for, had jumped from four dollars to six fifty. The shelf behind the sign was nearly empty, just three battered boxes left. His mom had given him exactly five dollars and told him to pick a box while she grabbed Grandma's prescription at the pharmacy counter.

He picked up a box anyway and turned it over, as if the answer might be printed under the ingredients, next to the part about polymer packaging that kept it fresh. Three boxes left. Everyone in town must want this cereal because of the storm that had knocked out power for two days and kept delivery trucks off the roads. When lots of people want something that's running out, he figured, the store can charge more, and they do.

An older man in a gray coat reached past Aaron for the last box on the top shelf, then paused. "You were here first, son." He held it out. Aaron looked at his five dollars and shook his head. "I can't afford it anymore. It went up." The man's face went vague for a second, then he set the box back. "Everything went up this week. My wife's heart pills went up twelve dollars."

"Are you going to stop buying them?" Aaron asked, then winced, because it sounded rude.

The man laughed, but not meanly. "Of course not. She needs them." He tapped the box on the shelf. "I'll skip this, though." He walked off toward the pharmacy with his small cart.

Aaron wandered that way too, because the cereal he could afford, the store brand, was stocked in the next aisle over, and it was on sale, two for five. Piles of it. Nobody was fighting over it. His theory was holding up: scarce plus wanted meant expensive, plentiful meant cheap. But the pills kept bugging him. Twelve dollars more, and the man didn't even hesitate. He'd compared it in his own head, buying the pills versus skipping cereal, and the pills won without a fight.

At the counter, Aaron found his mom and the pharmacist, Ms. Reyes, sliding a white paper bag across. "Same price as always for the generic," Ms. Reyes said. "The brand-name went up again, but almost everyone keeps buying it anyway." She noticed Aaron listening. "That's called inelastic," she said. "People buy it no matter what the price does."

"Inelastic," Aaron repeated, testing the word.

Ms. Reyes nodded and turned to the next customer.

On the way out, Aaron recounted his finds to his mom: the cereal, the sale, the man with the gray coat and the twelve dollars. She listened the whole way through the parking lot, then stopped by the cart return and held up the pharmacy bag. "So what you're saying is, Grandma's medicine is like a need, and your cereal is like a want."

"Basically." Aaron hugged the two store-brand boxes to his chest. "And next week, when the trucks come, the price of mine drops. The pills won't."

His mom smiled and unlocked the car. "Get in, economist."

The deodorant aisle smelled like a fake pine forest, and Ethan stood in front of it holding two dollars and thirty-seven cents in his palm. His mother had sent him in for cough syrup while she circled the parking lot, but on the way to the register he had spotted the gel deodorant with the lightning bolt on it, the same kind Marcus used, and before he really thought about anything he had it under his arm. Now he was doing the math. The cough syrup cost exactly two dollars and thirty-seven cents, and he had exactly that. The deodorant cost four dollars and fifty cents.

"It's a paradox," his sister Lily would have said if she were there, "wanting to be the kind of kid who buys deodorant and also the kind who brings home the medicine." She wasn't there, but he could hear her anyway, which was annoying. He envied Marcus, who seemed to have everything figured out, deep voice and gym bag and all. Ethan's own voice still cracked in the middle of class like a bad radio.

At the register, the pharmacist, a woman named Dara with reading glasses on a chain, rang up both items before he could decide. "That's six eighty-seven," she said. His face went hot. He mumbled that he only had the two thirty-seven, and that the deodorant had been, sort of, an accident.

While Dara took the deodorant back, his phone buzzed. It was a text from Lily, and attached was a page she had been reading for her health class: a diagram of a brain with a shaded area near the front. The caption said the prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain involved in planning and controlling impulses, keeps developing through the teenage years and into a person's twenties. Ethan read it twice. So the part of him that was supposed to plan ahead and stop himself from grabbing things was still, literally, under construction. That was almost a relief.

"So that's the prefrontal cortex," he said out loud, pointing at the shaded spot, "and mine's still loading." Dara leaned over the counter to look and laughed. "Mine took until about twenty-five, if it's any comfort." She slid the cough syrup across to him and kept the gel deodorant in a small pile behind the register, marked with a sticky note that said HOLD FOR ETHAN.

"For next week," she said. "When you've saved up. Planning ahead, right?" Ethan nodded, put his phone away, and walked out to the car with the change still warm in his hand and a plan already forming for the four dollars and fifty cents he was going to earn mowing Mrs. Okafor's lawn on Saturday.

Naomi had until Sunday night to finish her biology sheet, and the only microscope within forty miles sat in the back room of her grandmother's farmhouse, under a dust cloth. The sheet asked for a drawing of onion skin cells with three labels: cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus. She had peeled a paper-thin layer from an onion that morning, carried it in a jar, and now she waited for her grandmother to finish the milking so she could ask for the key to the back room.

"Third drawer down," her grandmother said, wiping her boots. "Mind the scope, it was your grandfather's." The room smelled of old paper and machine oil. Naomi found the key, unlocked the cabinet, and set the microscope on the table by the window, where the light was best. Then she discovered the problem. Through the eyepiece she could see the cells clearly, little brick-shaped boxes in neat rows, and the thick outer lines had to be the cell walls. But everything inside was pale and blank. The sheet demanded a nucleus, and there was nothing to label.

She sat back and drummed her fingers. Somewhere in this room her grandfather had kept his science notebooks. She pulled a box from the shelf, and that was when she found the loose page folded inside a notebook from his marine course. It described a stretch of Washington State shore where an ecologist named Robert Paine removed a starfish that ate mussels. After that, the mussels took over the rocks and crowded out many other species. "You couldn't watch the starfish matter," her grandfather had written in the margin, "you could only see the shore change and work backwards."

Naomi read the page twice. The important thing had been invisible while it was there; you noticed it only when it was gone. So maybe the nucleus was like that. Maybe it was in her slide, just faint, and she needed to change something, not find something. She remembered the little brown bottle in the kitchen her grandmother used for tinctures, and she fetched it and added one drop to the onion skin.

The suspense while she refocused was almost unbearable. She turned the fine knob a hair at a time, the image swimming, blurring, sharpening. Then it snapped into view: a small dark sphere inside each cell, plain as a stone in shallow water. The nucleus had been there the whole time, waiting for the stain to let her see it. She traced the thin line just inside the wall and labeled the membrane too, then finished her drawing while the afternoon light held.

Outside, a raccoon, one of the nocturnal visitors her grandmother swore about, had already begun prodding at the compost bin, and the chickens would not cease their squawking until someone chased it off. "All right, all right," her grandmother called from the yard. "Naomi, grab the broom."

Naomi spread her graph paper across the kitchen table and wrote "SIMPLE" at the top of one column and "COMPOUND" at the top of the other. She was saving her birthday money, forty dollars a year, and her mother had said, "Five years. Figure out which account pays more." The simple account added three dollars for every hundred, every year, straight across. The compound one added three dollars on whatever was already there, including the interest from before. She worked the simple column fast. The compound column made her stop and squint, because the numbers climbed a tiny bit faster each year, like something growing quietly underground.

Her cousins burst in before she finished. Marcus waved a crumpled certificate. "Toytown stock. Uncle Rick gave it to me last summer." Priya held up a fancy printed sheet. "I got a Toytown bond. Same company." Toytown had gone bankrupt in the spring, and every kid on the block had heard about it.

"Mine's a stock," Marcus said. "Stocks sound bigger."

"I don't even know what a bond is," Priya admitted.

Naomi tapped her pencil. The word bankruptcy had shown up in her mother's newspaper pile, and one afternoon she had read enough of an article to provoke a question she'd been chewing on ever since: when a company died, who got paid first? She had made an inference from the article's grumbling quotes, and now she wanted to test it. "Trade me," she said suddenly. "Straight across. My next two weeks of allowance for your bond."

Priya stared. Marcus laughed so hard he knocked over the lemonade. "You'd trade real money for paper from a dead company?"

"Twenty minutes," Naomi said. "Then decide." She flipped her graph paper over and wrote fast, then handed Priya a note:

"Priya. If we're right about the order they pay people, your sheet is ahead of his in line. Stocks are last in line, and often get nothing at all. I'll still buy it from you either way, but only for a dollar. That way you can't lose much. Your choice. Naomi."

While Priya read, Marcus kept gloating, which provoked nothing but Naomi's patience. Priya looked up. "Last in line? So Marcus's stock is behind mine?"

"Only if my inference is right," Naomi said. "Grandma's neighbor worked at a bank. Let's ask her, but I'm asking, and nobody talks but me."

Mrs. Okafor, three doors down, was watering her tomatoes. She listened, wiped her hands, and said, "When a company goes bankrupt, bondholders get paid back before stockholders. Stockholders are last in line, and often they get nothing."

The walk home was quiet except for Marcus's sneakers. He stopped at the driveway. "Okay. I changed my mind. Your compound interest thing, the one you were drawing? Teach it to me and I'll trade you my stock for Priya's bond. She said yes already." He pointed at Priya, who was grinning and holding out the crumpled certificate.

"Deal," Naomi said, and she cleared a space at the table between her two columns. "Now watch what happens in year three."

Marcus pulled up a chair.

Mia threw her gym shirt into the laundry basket from across the room, and it landed with a satisfying thump, but the smell followed it. That was the problem. Two weeks ago she could wear a shirt twice before washing it. Now, one period of dodgeball and it smelled like a locker room that had given up on life. She was thirteen, officially, as of last month, and apparently thirteen meant her body had signed some secret contract she hadn't read.

The math tutor arrived at four, which gave Mia exactly one hour to solve the sweat situation before Mrs. Palermo sat at the kitchen table and politely pretended not to notice anything. Mia drafted a quick note to herself, in her head: money, store, product. She had eleven dollars from walking Mr. Nebbins's dog, and the drugstore was six blocks away. She told her dad she'd be back before the tutor got there, grabbed her bike, and pedaled off so fast the wheels made a sound like a startled cat.

The deodorant aisle had about nine hundred options, which felt absurd, so Mia made herself slow down and read. The first stick said deodorant in big letters. The second said antiperspirant. She'd always assumed those were just two words for the same thing, but standing there with her thumb on the shelf, she noticed the fine print under "deodorant" talked about odor, not sweat. The antiperspirant label mentioned wetness. She turned both packages over like a detective comparing fingerprints. So one dealt with the smell, and the other actually stopped the sweat itself. Her skeptical brain did a quick test: if she wanted the underarm version of a raincoat, not just a air freshener, antiperspirant was the answer.

She grabbed the antiperspirant, a lavender one, paid, and raced home with the bag swinging from her handlebar. Five minutes before Mrs. Palermo knocked, Mia was in the bathroom applying it, sniffing her shirt sleeve like a sommelier. The phone buzzed. Her best friend Dana had texted: "why are you biking so fast on your mom's tracking app??"

Mia laughed out loud and typed back with one thumb. "NEW DEODORANT ERA. come over after tutoring, I'll show you." Dana replied with twelve fire emojis, which was Dana's way of saying yes to anything.

Mrs. Palermo arrived, and they drilled fractions for an hour, and Mia got seven out of ten right, which felt like a personal holiday. When Dana showed up, they read the antiperspirant label together in the bathroom mirror.

"You're telling me this stuff plugs the sweat," Dana said, holding the stick up like evidence in a courtroom.

"Basically a tiny dam," said Mia, and raised both arms in a victory V.

Charles had a system, and the system had a flaw. The flaw was the letter F.

For three days he had studied the eye chart the school nurse had photocopied and sent home. He could recite it frontwards: E, F, P, T, O, Z, all the way down to the tiny row that looked like ants carrying crumbs. The chart was older than anyone could remember, the nurse said, a dusty poster that had been in the clinic since forever, and Charles planned to recite it perfectly at Saturday's eye appointment so nobody would know his left eye had gone fuzzy. If he passed, he could keep playing goalie without his cousin Marcus announcing, to the entire neighborhood, that Charles couldn't see a soccer ball until it hit him.

His little sister Dee wandered into the kitchen, where the photocopy was taped to the refrigerator. "That's mine now," she said. "I'm starting an eye hospital in the garage. I already have a tongue depressor and half a stethoscope."

"You can't have a hospital with one patient."

"I'll circulate flyers," Dee said. "Everyone on this street has eyes. That's my market."

Saturday morning, the optometrist's office smelled like plastic and peppermint. Charles was ready. The doctor, a small woman with purple glasses, sat him in a chair and pointed at a wall chart.

"Read the top line."

"E," Charles said confidently. Then "F, P, T, O, Z," sailing down the rows without a single mistake, like a boy with vision sharp enough to count a mosquito's eyebrows.

The doctor looked at him. Then she walked to the wall, pressed a button, and the chart rolled up with a snap. A different chart rolled down, one Charles had never seen.

"Read this one."

Charles opened his mouth. Nothing came out. The letters were strangers, blurry gray smudges, like an intestine photograph in his science textbook, all coiled and mysterious and definitely not something he could identify from across a room.

"That chart you memorized," the doctor said, "was Herman Snellen's chart, the rows of shrinking letters he developed in 1862." She smiled. "Kids try it every month. The Snellen chart is older than your great-grandparents. Some of them, older than your great-great-great-grandparents."

"You could have told me there were two charts," Charles said.

"Where's the fun in that?"

An hour later Charles stood blinking in the waiting room in his first pair of glasses, round silver ones, and the world snapped into focus like a TV with the antenna finally straightened. He could read the gum wrapper on the counter. He could read the exit sign. He could read Dee's flyer, which she had apparently made during his exam, circulating it to every seat: DEE'S EYE HOSPITAL, GRAND OPENING, MY BROTHER IS THE FIRST PATIENT.

"You're not touching my eyeballs," Charles said.

"It's unanimous between me and the tongue depressor," said Dee, and she took his hand and marched him toward the garage.

Carter sat on his grandfather's porch with a battered paperback open on his knees. He was supposed to be rehearsing. On Monday, his drama teacher had paired him with Priya for the improv unit, and their rule was simple: whatever your partner offers, you accept it and add to it. "Yes, and," the teacher kept saying. But every time Carter tried it at school, he froze, and Priya was left hanging like a climber whose rope had gone slack.

The paperback was a play he'd pulled off his grandfather's shelf, mostly to have something in his hands. It was by a playwright named Harold Pinter, and at first Carter thought the pages were misprinted. Whole lines were taken up by single words. Pause. Silence. They sat there in the middle of the dialogue like stage directions that had wandered into the wrong job. "Grandpa," Carter called, "did somebody write in this book?" His grandfather squinted at the page from his rocking chair. "Nope. That's how Pinter wrote it. The pauses and the silences are printed in like lines. Part of what the characters say."

Carter turned back to the page and read a scene again, slowly. Two characters were talking about almost nothing, the weather, a cup of tea, and yet the silences between them seemed to fluctuate, swelling and shrinking, sometimes a beat long, sometimes a whole breath and a half. It was strange. Nobody had ever told him that nothing could be written down and performed. He wondered: if a pause could be a line, then was his own freezing in improv really nothing? Or was it something he could use, something he could offer Priya on purpose?

He had an idea, and he wanted to test it. That afternoon Priya came over to practice in the living room, because the Monday performance was two days away and she refused to carry the whole scene by herself again. "Same rules," she said, pushing the coffee table aside. "Yes, and. You take whatever I give you and build on it. Your protagonist can be anyone. Ready?" Carter nodded, but he had a secret plan.

Priya started. "We're two astronauts and the oxygen is running out." Instead of scrambling for a joke, Carter said, "Yes, and there's a light blinking on the console." Then he stopped. He let the silence sit, counting one breath, the way Pinter's pages had taught him, eyes on the imaginary light. Priya blinked, then leaned in and matched him, quiet too, her hand hovering over the pretend controls. The pause wasn't dead air. It was the two of them trapped in a ship, deciding whether to touch that button. When Carter finally spoke, the words felt spontaneous, like they'd risen out of the quiet on their own. "Yes, and," he said softly, "I think it's blinking faster."

They ran the scene three more times, and each time the silences did different work. Once the quiet felt like fear, once like grief for a planet they'd left behind. Priya kept sneaking glances at him like he'd swapped bodies with somebody braver. "Where did that come from?" she asked afterward, flopping onto the couch. "You used to just stand there."

Carter held up the Pinter paperback. "Turns out you can write down nothing," he said. "Pause. Silence. Right there in the script, like lines." Priya grabbed the book and flipped through it, hunting for the single words on the page. "Show me the longest one," she said. "The performance is Monday, and I want a silence in our scene so big the audience forgets to breathe."

Grandpa had dumped a bag of wrapped caramels on the kitchen table and told Nevaeh to count them into piles. "Forty votes," he said. "Green party, sixteen. Gold party, fourteen. Blue party, ten. Now, we've got five seats on this town council. First-past-the-post, you split the town into five districts." He slid the caramels into clumps. "Eight caramels per district."

Nevaeh leaned over the table. In the first district, Green got five votes and Gold got three, so Green won the seat. Same thing happened in the second and third. But in the fourth and fifth, Grandpa shuffled the piles so Gold squeaked ahead each time. "Wait," Nevaeh said. "Green has the most votes in the whole town, but Gold got two seats and Green got three. That's barely fair." She grabbed a napkin and drew it out, wondering what would happen if she stopped dividing the town at all.

"Try it the other way," Grandpa said. "Proportional representation. No districts. Five seats, forty votes, so eight votes per seat." Nevaeh divided each pile by eight. Green got sixteen, which was exactly two seats. Gold's fourteen votes gave it one seat with six left over. Blue's ten gave it one with two left over. She counted on her fingers, then pushed the last caramel back and forth between Gold and Blue. "It doesn't come out even," she said. "Somebody has to get the leftover seat."

"Every system has to decide that somehow," Grandpa said. "The question is which one feels fair to the most people, and which one lasts."

That made Nevaeh pause. "Which one is more durable?" she asked. Grandpa shrugged. "Proportional ones usually match how people actually voted. But a system can be fair and still fall apart if nobody trusts it." Nevaeh tapped the napkin. "So you can't just assume the one with the neatest math wins. People have to believe in the counting." Grandpa grinned and ate one of the caramels, which she pointed out was voter suppression.

Just then her cousin Marcus came in from the porch, still arguing with his friend Deon over the speakerphone. "I'm telling you, freedom of expression means anyone can say anything," Marcus said. Nevaeh opened her mouth, but Deon's voice came through first, steady as a kid reciting something he'd looked up an hour ago. "Section 1 of the Canadian Charter says its rights are subject to reasonable limits that can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society." Marcus stood there with his hand still raised, like the sentence had taken the wind out of it. "So they're limits," he said at last. "Reasonable ones."

Nevaeh looked from her cousin to the caramels, and a question formed slowly, the way the seat math had. "So even rules about talking have to be fair to everybody, like a vote." She slid the leftover caramel across the table to Marcus. "Sit down. You're the tiebreaker."

Ellie set the cutting board on the picnic table at the back of the yard, where the light was good and the smell of chopped vegetables wouldn't fill the kitchen. Tonight was her turn to make dinner, and she had promised her family potato soup with real onions, not the dried flakes from a jar. Her little brother Marcus sat on the grass nearby, sketching on a pad of paper. He wanted to depict the whole meal in a drawing, soup pot and all, so he could hang it on the fridge when the food was done.

She halved the first onion and began to chop. Within a minute her eyes stung and water ran down her cheeks. Marcus looked up from his drawing, alarmed, then his own eyes began to stream too, even though he was three steps away and hadn't touched the onion at all.

"You're crying," he said, wiping his face with his sleeve. "Why does a vegetable make people cry?"

"I'm not crying," Ellie said, sniffling. "I'm mad at this onion." But she kept thinking about it while she chopped. The tears had started only after she cut into it, not before, when the onion was whole on the table. Something had to be coming out of the onion when her knife went through it. She remembered her mother saying the cells inside a plant were like tiny sealed rooms. Cutting must break the cells open and release something, some kind of gas, and the gas had to be reaching their eyes. That would explain why Marcus was tearing up too, sitting nowhere near the cutting board. It would even explain why whole onions in the bag had never made anyone cry.

She decided to test the idea. She carried the board to the far corner of the yard, upwind of Marcus, so any gas drifting off would blow away from him instead of toward him. She made him stay by the picnic table with his drawing while she finished the chopping. From across the yard she called out, "Eyes still burning?"

"No," Marcus called back, surprised. He blinked hard and touched his eyelids. "They stopped. Hey, Ellie, is the gas why the soup in your picture looks like it's steaming? Because that's steam, not crying gas."

"That's steam, you gullible creature," she said, laughing through her own tears. She finished the last onion, dumped everything into the pot, and carried it inside, blinking the sting away.

After dinner, Marcus taped his drawing to the refrigerator, right beside the takeout menu from the tenants who rented the upstairs apartment. He tapped the little onion in the corner of the picture and said, "I'm going to draw tears on it, for science."

The end-of-season party was supposed to be the fun part, but by the time the pizza boxes were half empty, Charlotte noticed that nobody was eating much. Her soccer team, the Parkside Foxes, sat in a loose circle under the pavilion, and everyone kept glancing around like they were counting heads. Marisol was moving pepperoni slices into rows. Benji had his cleats off and was staring into them. Charlotte had been looking forward to this all week, and now the whole thing felt heavy, like the air before a storm that never arrives.

"We lost the tournament," Benji said finally. "That's not why it's weird, though."

"I know," Marisol said. "It's weird anyway."

Charlotte pulled her phone out of her bag, pretending to check the time. What she actually did was search: why does a team feel sad at the end of a season even when nothing bad happened. She scrolled past a bunch of advice columns until she hit a page about how groups develop. Four stages, a man named Tuckman: forming, storming, norming, performing. Then she read the line that made her sit up straight. In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, adjourning, for when a group finishes its work and breaks up.

"Listen to this," she said, out loud, before she could decide not to. "It's a real thing. There's a fifth stage and it's called adjourning."

Marisol looked up. "What does that mean?"

"It's the part where the team ends." Charlotte held the phone so they could see the screen, her thumb covering an ad. "In 1977, Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added it to the other four stages. So this horrible feeling is, like, documented."

Nobody said anything for a second. Then Benji laughed, short and surprised. "You mean everybody gets this? Not just us?"

"Everybody. Every group."

Marisol stopped rearranging the pepperoni. "So we're not falling apart. We're just in the last stage."

The knot in Charlotte's chest loosened a little. It wasn't that the sad feeling went away, exactly. It was more like the feeling had a name now, and named things were smaller than nameless things. She noticed, too, that a low-grade resentment she'd been carrying all afternoon, about her dad showing up late and missing her only goal of the whole season, faded at the same time. Hard to stay mad about small stuff when the whole team was going through an official stage together.

"There's a wasp by the juice," Priya announced, and everyone scrambled. The wasp circled the cups with a predatory patience while five girls armed themselves with paper plates. Charlotte swatted and missed, and the wasp emitted a sharp buzz and looped up through the pavilion rafters, where it hovered like it was thinking it over.

"Next year," Marisol said, watching it go, "we might not all be on the same team. Tryouts get shuffled."

"We're not next year yet," Charlotte said. She stood up on the bench and put two fingers in her mouth and whistled at the whole pavilion. "Everybody grab a slice. We still have a stage to finish."

Brooklyn sat in the back seat of the family car with a paper bag from the eye doctor's office folded on her lap. Inside was her first pair of glasses, and she hadn't put them on yet. "You could try them now," her dad said from the driver's seat. "We're stuck in traffic anyway."

"Give me a minute," Brooklyn said. She was thinking about how she'd figured it out in the first place. Last month she'd been in the back row of science class, copying the board through a fog of blurry letters, while her phone screen an inch from her nose stayed sharp as anything. That made no sense, so she'd run a test. She'd made a hole in a piece of paper with the point of a pencil, held it up to one eye, and looked at the board through it. The letters sharpened. She'd tried the same trick at home with her phone, and it barely changed anything, which meant the problem was with faraway stuff, not near stuff. She'd marched that paper to the eye doctor and asked him why it worked.

He'd looked at the little hole and laughed. "Clever. In nearsightedness, light from distant objects focuses in front of the retina instead of on it. Your eyeball is slightly too long, that's all." He'd tapped a diagram on the wall, and she'd traced the light rays with her finger, meeting too soon and smearing the picture before it ever reached the back of her eye. The paper hole had blocked the sloppy rays, she guessed, letting only the neat ones through. It was like her eye was a camera built one millimeter wrong, and a hole could pretend it wasn't.

"I'm going to look like a librarian," she said now, "or like an artisan who makes tiny violins for mice."

"An artisan of tiny violins," her dad said gravely. "There's a future in that. Now open the bag before I have to pull over."

She slid the glasses on. The world converted itself all at once, the way a blurry photo snaps into focus. She could read the license plate of the truck three cars ahead. She could count the exits still to come. She could see, far down the highway, a billboard that she'd only ever known as a pink smudge. "Dad. Dad, that sign says EXIT ONLY."

"I've known that sign my whole life, Brook."

"It has a little arrow on it. It has always had a little arrow." She pressed her forehead against the window and stared out at everything, wide awake after months of feeling lethargic in class, half asleep behind her own eyes. "Can we take the long way home? There's a hawk or a garbage bag on that pole, and I need to know which."

The screen door banged behind Evelyn, and the smell of Grandma's lemon cake followed her into the kitchen, where Grandma was on the phone with a pencil tucked behind her ear. "Hold on, Ruth," Grandma said, then covered the receiver. "Two of my garden club friends are having a spat. Want to watch? It's better than television." Evelyn flopped onto the stool. Garden club spats, it turned out, were serious business, involving a borrowed trellis and a lot of hurt feelings.

Ruth's voice came through the line like a wasp. "Marjorie said I'm so selfish, keeping all the prize dahlias to myself." Evelyn braced for Grandma to yell back, or to take sides, which is what happened every single time in the cafeteria at school. Instead Grandma said, "So what I'm hearing is, you want a fairer share of the dahlias this year." There was a pause, long enough for Evelyn to hear the clock tick and smell the cake starting to burn at the edges. Then Ruth said, in a much smaller voice, "Well. Yes. That's all I want."

After Ruth hung up, Evelyn slid off the stool. "You changed what she said. She called Marjorie selfish and you turned it into something about sharing." Grandma pulled the cake out, waving away the smoke with a dish towel shaped like a rooster. "That's called reframing," she said. "Now go call your mother back, she's been waiting an hour." Evelyn noticed Grandma hadn't explained anything more than that, so she carried the idea to the porch swing like a warm slice of cake, turning it over. The insult hadn't been repeated to Marjorie at all. It had been caught in midair, the way Dad caught flies with his bare hands, and set down as something harmless.

That was exactly what she needed, because on Monday, Marcus Teague had told half the sixth grade that Priya's synthetic fur jacket looked like a dead raccoon, and Priya hadn't come to lunch since. Evelyn had been trying to figure out a negotiation between them all week, and failing. Maybe the problem wasn't the jacket at all. Maybe it was the word "raccoon," which had traveled from mouth to mouth like a cold germ, getting worse each time. She wondered: what if she could catch it before the next person repeated it?

On Monday she found Tara repeating the raccoon joke near the gym, everybody laughing. Evelyn's stomach did a somersault, but she kept her voice level. "So basically, you think her jacket is too fuzzy for your taste. Noted." The laughter wobbled and died out, like a radio losing signal. Tara blinked. "I guess," she said. The group drifted off, and Evelyn spotted Priya at her locker, watching. Priya walked over and held out half a granola bar. "You want to delegate someone to sit with us at lunch, or should we just go claim the good table ourselves?" Evelyn grinned. "Let's go claim it."

The departure board at Gate 14 flicked from ON TIME to BOARDING, and Jeremy's dad picked up the biggest suitcase before anyone else could grab it. They were flying east across six hours of time zones, which meant that when they landed in the morning, their bodies would still believe it was the middle of the night. Jeremy knew this the way he knew his locker combination, as a fact he'd been told, not something he'd ever felt. His little sister, Priya, was already asking whether the hotel had a pool, and Mom was saying that she'd had to enroll Priya in the kids' activity club before they even left home, because the good spots filled up fast.

The flight was long and pale. Jeremy watched the little airplane on the screen crawl across the map, and he did the arithmetic in his head: six hours forward, so their arrival at nine in the morning would feel like three in the morning. When they landed, everyone was groggy except Priya, who had slept the whole way and bounced through the terminal like it was noon. "I'm starving," she announced. Jeremy's stomach, which knew perfectly well it was three in the morning, said nothing at all.

The first night in the hotel, everyone fell asleep at eight, local time, exhausted. That was fine. The second night was the strange one. At midnight, Jeremy lay in the dark listening to his dad turn over, and his mom sigh, and Priya whisper from the other bed that she was wide awake. Nobody could sleep. It didn't make sense to Jeremy, because they had all been tired, and it was night, and the room was dark and quiet. Something invisible was holding them all upright at midnight, and he wanted to know what rule it followed.

On the third night, Jeremy ran a quiet experiment. He noted the time when each of them finally dropped off. Priya went out around one. He himself fell asleep close to two, he thought, though he couldn't be sure, since being asleep made it hard to record. His parents were still murmuring when he went under. On the fourth night it was earlier, maybe one o'clock for him and midnight-ish for Priya. He wrote the numbers in the back of his notebook, and by the fifth night a pattern had crawled onto the page: each night, sleep arrived roughly an hour earlier than the night before.

He counted on his fingers. Six hours of time difference, one hour of catch-up per day. "So it takes about six days," he said at breakfast, spreading his notebook on the table. "One day for every hour of difference. That's why we were all awake at midnight on day two, and why Priya's getting normal faster than Mom and Dad, because she adjusts quicker than the average." Priya stole a piece of his toast and studied the columns. "Then tonight is night six," she said. "We should be fixed."

They took a family vote on how to spend the last difficult evening, and it was unanimous: early dinner, no screens, everyone in bed by ten. Jeremy lay in the dark and waited to see whether his rule held. Somewhere below, a taxi honked, and Priya's breathing slowed beside him, and then, without noticing the exact moment it happened, he was asleep.

"Nobody in the Rockhound Guild is going to believe a seasons video filmed in a quarry," said Priya, hoisting her backpack onto a flat slab of granite.

Matteo set down the flashlight he'd carried all the way from the parking lot. "That's the point. Mr. Ferreira says if you can explain something in a weird place, you really understand it. I got a C minus on my seasons essay. He wrote that I sounded like I was reciting." He pulled out the round mirror his mother used for canning jars and propped it against a shard of stone. "Earth's axis tilts, so the same sunbeam spreads over more ground or less ground. Watch."

He tilted the mirror and moved the flashlight in a slow arc. The light on the granite stretched into a long, pale oval, then tightened into a small bright circle. Priya crouched and put her hand in the beam. "When it's spread out, my fingers are barely warm. When it's small, it's hot." She looked up. "Okay, that part's good. But you said tilt, and your mirror isn't spinning."

Matteo held the mirror steady against his knee so the angle stayed stable while he swept the flashlight again. "Tilt first, spin later. One thing at a time, or everyone gets confused." He was so focused on the light that he almost put his hand down on the dark pebble Priya had been examining. "What's that?"

"Basalt, I think. It's from the piles over by the crusher." She held it beside the granite slab. The slab glittered with fat, sparkly crystals you could see from a step away. The basalt was plain and dark, its surface almost smooth. "Same quarry, and they look nothing alike."

Matteo turned the pebble in the light, and the flashlight beam refracted off a tiny crystal face, throwing a thin gold thread across the stone. He stared at the granite, then at the pebble, then back. "The granite's crystals are huge. This thing's are so small I can barely see them." He thought about the quarry walls, all that rock sitting deep underground for who knows how long before anyone cut it open. "Granite cools slowly, way down under the surface, so the crystals get big. Basalt cools fast at the surface, so they stay tiny."

"So it's like your seasons thing," Priya said. "The thing you can't see is what makes the difference."

Matteo had been sure the quarry was a dumb location. He looked at the glittering slab, at the small hot circle of light on it, and changed his mind completely. "Start the camera. I'll explain the tilt first, then the crystals."

Priya pressed record. "Go," she said.

The sign at Kwik Fuel read "Bottled Water $1.25" on Monday, and Mya rode past it without a second thought. By Thursday, after the storm knocked out the town's water pump, the same sign read "$4.00," and a hand-lettered note under it said "LIMIT 3 PER CUSTOMER." She stood in front of the cooler with five dollars in her pocket and did the math twice, because the first answer made her mad.

Her little brother Dez needed the water more than she did. Their mom had said to buy whatever she could on the way home from school, so Mya took three bottles and got in line behind a man buying an entire case at the new price without even blinking. "Four dollars," the cashier said. "It was a dollar twenty-five on Monday," Mya said. "Storm," the cashier said, as if that were a whole sentence. Ahead of her, the man with the case shrugged and paid, and two more people came through the door heading straight for the cooler.

At school that week, her social studies class had argued about a question on a worksheet: "Why is water cheap and a diamond expensive?" A boy named Teo had waved his pencil and said it was because diamonds are prettier, and Mya had not been able to come up with anything better. The teacher had written a hint on the board: In "The Wealth of Nations," published in 1776, Adam Smith pointed out that nothing is more useful than water, yet it will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal. Mya had copied it down because it would probably be on a quiz, not because she understood it.

Standing at the register, she understood it. Water was the most useful thing in the store today, everyone in town wanted it, there were only about forty bottles left in the cooler, and the price had jumped to four dollars. Teo's answer had the cause backwards. The price didn't rise because water had become prettier. It rose because it had become scarce, and a line of people stood behind her proving it. She thought about the diamonds in the glass case at the jewelry store downtown, tiny things in a locked box, expensive because there were almost none of them. The town pump, on the other hand, usually pushed out all the water anyone could use, which had to be part of why a bottle used to cost a dollar twenty-five.

She decided to test the idea, because a worksheet answer was one thing and real life was another. "If the pump gets fixed," she asked the cashier, "will the price go back down?" The cashier looked up from the register. "Happened after the ice storm two years ago. Price drops when the delivery trucks come back and I got shelves full of it. Nobody pays four bucks for something there's a wall of." He rang her up. "Twelve dollars even, since you got three."

Mya counted it out and incorporated the change into her plan: two bottles for drinking, one held back for the soup her mom wanted to make. On the walk home she passed the jewelry store, where a diamond the size of a peppercorn sat on velvet with a price that would have bought every bottle in the gas station. In the window's reflection, the store's weekly revenue probably came from a handful of tiny stones, while the gas station made its money on coffee, chips, and, this week, water. Two businesses, two completely distinct ideas about what a thing was worth, both of them right.

On Saturday the pump came back on, and Mya rode her bike to Kwik Fuel just to check. The sign said "$1.25." The cooler was packed, the delivery truck was idling out front, and nobody was in line. She went in and bought one bottle, mostly for proof, and the cashier nodded at it. "Told you."

Piper sat on the low wall by the swings, her left arm stiff inside a bright green cast, and watched the others run the obstacle course she could not join. Three days ago she had decided that jumping off the top of the climbing dome was worth it, and now she had five weeks of sitting still to evaluate that decision. It did not look good so far.

"Green suits you," said Marcus, plopping down beside her. "I wanted orange." He tapped his own cast, the old one, pale blue and full of signatures, on his right leg. "I keep thinking about what Ms. Reyes said at the assembly, when the nurse asked if anyone knew how casts were invented. I raised my hand and got it wrong."

"You did not," Piper said.

"I said casts were invented in America in like 1900. Nobody knew anything, so we all just guessed." Marcus shrugged. "After school I looked it up.
