A Dutch army surgeon named Antonius Mathijsen developed the plaster-of-Paris bandage for setting broken bones, and he published his method in 1852. Before that, people wrapped broken arms in stiff stuff that didn't hold its shape the way plaster does."

Piper turned that over. "So every kid who ever broke an arm before 1852 got the wobbly version."

"Basically."

The bell had not rung yet, and a small crowd was gathering near the fence, where two fourth graders were arguing about whose paper airplane had flown farther. "We'll ask them," Marcus said. "We'll be the jury. Whichever one we pick has to be the winner."

Piper followed him over, holding her casted arm like something fragile and precious. She had not felt fragile before the jump. She had felt certain, which was worse.

The fourth graders, Sam and Bea, each held a plane and a grudge. Piper made them throw again, three times each, and she watched where each plane landed rather than how pretty it looked in the air. Bea's went farther twice. Sam's folded once and dropped like a stone. "Bea wins," Piper announced. "Two out of three."

Sam scowled at his plane. "It's the wind's fault."

"It's the same wind for both of you," said Marcus.

Sam studied the plane for a long moment, then walked to the fence and threw it one more time, watching carefully where it came down. Piper watched too. "Try it backwards," she called out. "Sam, throw it backwards and see if it still curves."

Juliette smoothed her skirt and followed her mother up the wide steps of the gurdwara, where her friend Simran's family had invited them for the celebration of Vaisakhi. She had never been inside one before, and she was doing her best not to stare at everything at once. Inside, the hall glowed with golden cloth and the smell of something warm and bready drifted from a doorway on the left.

"Cover your head," her mother whispered, handing her a thin scarf. Juliette wrapped it awkwardly and tucked her shoes onto a shelf beside dozens of others.

In the main hall they sat on the carpet behind Simran's family, listening to the music. Juliette understood only that it was beautiful, the harmonium humming under voices that rose and fell together. Her stomach growled during a long, eloquent chant, and she pressed her hand against it, embarrassed, until Simran leaned back and whispered, "Hungry? Good. Come on."

Simran led her down a corridor to a vast room where long rows of people sat cross-legged on the floor, side by side, families and strangers and an elderly man in a wheelchair all in the same lines. Volunteers moved between the rows carrying steel buckets. One paused beside Juliette, and before she could speak, a woman had set a steel tray in front of her, then a bowl of dal, then a cup of water.

Juliette caught Simran's sleeve. "Where do I pay? I didn't bring any money."

"You don't pay," Simran said, grinning. "It's called langar. It's a free meal for every visitor, no matter who you are."

"Everybody here?" Juliette looked down the row. A woman in jeans sat beside a grandfather in a turban sat beside a girl in a school uniform. "Even people who aren't Sikh? Even me?"

"Even you." Simran's grandmother, two places down, nodded as if she had heard, and Juliette realized she had probably asked too loudly. Her ears went hot, but nobody seemed offended. If anything, the volunteers looked pleased to have someone new to feed.

Juliette tested it anyway, quietly, in her own way. When the roti came, she asked the boy carrying the bucket for a second one, half expecting him to hesitate or check with someone. He just handed it over and moved on. She ate both, thoughtfully, watching the whole system work. Nobody paid, nobody was turned away, nobody sat above anyone else; everyone was down on the same carpet together, conserving nothing but space, each person scooting over to make room for the next.

When her tray was empty, she stood up and found the boy by the bucket. "Can I help?" she asked. He looked at her tray, then handed her a stack of fresh rotis wrapped in cloth, warm as a sleeping cat.

"Walk the rows," he said. "Give until your cloth is empty, then come back."

Juliette walked slowly, offering roti to each person with both hands the way she had seen him do it. The grandfather in the turban took one and said something to her in Punjabi that made the whole row smile. She didn't understand a word of it, but she understood the smile, and she kept walking, her cloth lighter with every step, until there was one roti left and she placed it in the hands of the girl in the school uniform, who bowed her head and whispered, "Thank you."

Aria set up her easel on the grass beside the shed, where the afternoon light fell evenly across her cousin Marcus's face. He sat on an overturned bucket, holding still the way she had asked, because today she was going to paint his portrait in watercolour. Her art book said to build the picture in thin washes, starting with the palest colour and letting each layer dry before adding a darker one. That meant the shadows around his eyes would come last, and the whole first hour would look like almost nothing. Aria decided she could allocate one whole hour to the light layers and another to the dark ones, and she wrote the plan on her wrist in pen.

Marcus wanted to be useful while he sat, so he was drawing his own bedroom on a clipboard. "I'm going to enter it in the county fair," he said. "My room, from the doorway, so you can see two walls." He worked in silence for a while, tongue between his teeth.

By the time Aria's second wash was dry, Marcus held up his clipboard and frowned. "Something's wrong with it," he said. "It looks like the room is tipping over. Like the whole bedroom is sliding off the page sideways." He tilted the clipboard one way, then the other, but it looked wrong in every direction.

Aria came over, still holding her brush. She looked at the two walls slanting away from the doorway, their edges marching toward faraway points, which was right. Then she looked at the door frame, and there was the problem. He had angled its upright edges too, leaning them toward the same faraway points, as if the door itself were about to fall flat. She held her brush up straight against the drawing, then against the real back door of the house. "Look at the actual door," she said. "The corners go straight up and down." She took his pencil and drew the frame again with its edges parallel to her brush handle, straight and vertical, while only the horizontal lines kept slanting toward their points. When Marcus held the page up, the room stood solidly on the paper.

"That's kind of aggressive shading," Aria said, pointing at his heavy scribbled carpet, and Marcus laughed and softened it. The irony was that her own portrait had a tipping problem too. While she had been fixing his door, her light wash had dried with a hard dark edge across Marcus's forehead where the paint had pooled. She had been so aggressive with the water that it had made a tide mark. She dampened the whole forehead area with clean water and touched in a pale wash over it, and the line softened into skin.

Then she layered the middle tones, his hair, the shadow under his jaw, waiting and waiting for each wash to dry, which was the hardest part of all. When she finally added the darkest darks around his eyes, Marcus leaned in and grinned. "That's me," he said. "That's actually me."

"Fair entry number two?" Aria asked, and Marcus went inside to get the entry forms.

Everly had guessed something was wrong in October, when the words on the whiteboard began to blur unless she squinted. By November she had copied half her notes from the girl next to her, and her mother finally made an appointment. Now she sat in the waiting room of the optometrist's office, holding a slip of paper with her name on it while a machine hummed behind the door.

A boy about eight years old sat across from her, swinging his legs and staring at his own paper as if it might bite him. "Do you know what OD means?" he asked. "It says it right here. Twice." He held the paper out. "And the other one says OS. My sister says they're codes for what's wrong with you. Like a secret diagnosis. My aunt had a paper like this and then she had surgery."

Everly looked at her own slip. Under her name it said OD and OS, each followed by a row of numbers and plus signs. She didn't feel scared, exactly, but the letters did look official, the kind of thing that could hide something. She wanted to know before the doctor called her back, because if the codes meant something bad, she'd rather find out now than standing under the bright lights in the exam room.

She turned the paper over and thought. The letters came in pairs, one line for each. She covered her right eye with her hand, the way she did when she copied the board, and then her left. Two eyes, two lines. If OD and OS each stood for one eye, then the pair had to split left and right somehow. She looked around the room. On the wall hung a poster of an eye chart labeled with the same letters, and beside it a smaller chart of Latin roots for a vocabulary program the office ran with the school. OD could be oculus something. Right, in Latin, was dexter. She'd seen the word dexterity in a spelling list, and right-handed people were called dexterous. So OD was the right eye. That left OS, and sinister had come to mean something dark, but her social studies teacher had mentioned that in Latin it just meant left.

"OD is your right eye," she told the boy. "OS is your left. Oculus dexter, oculus sinister. It's just Latin."

"Latin? Not a code?" The boy looked at his paper again, and his legs stopped swinging. "So mine are just telling which eye is which?"

"That's all it's doing," Everly said. The fear in his face diminished by about half, and then the rest went when the receptionist called his name and it turned out he was only there for a checkup.

When it was Everly's turn, the doctor slid the new glasses onto her face. The room sharpened all at once, and the eye chart across from her showed letters she could name down to the smallest row. Through the open door she saw the boy leaving with his mother, and he waved his paper at her like a flag.

"Hey," he called across the waiting room. "My right eye is the good one. OD. I'm going to tell my sister her code theory is wrong."

Edouard stood in Mrs. Okafor's kitchen holding a page of instructions she'd scribbled before hurrying out to her night shift. Bedtime at eight. Snack at seven. Emergency numbers on the fridge. He was thirteen and this was his first real babysitting job, and the two-dollar word for how he'd gotten it, according to his mother, was that he was "not impulsive like some boys," which he hoped was a compliment.

The child, Poppy, was three and wanted exactly one thing: to excavate the couch cushions until she found the lost button from her purple coat. She had been at it for twenty minutes, dragging cushions onto the floor like a little archaeologist, when Edouard noticed the kitchen had gone silent. Silent was wrong. He counted the sounds he should have heard: no humming, no cushion thumping, no small shoes on tile. He ran.

Poppy stood by the sink with a spray bottle in both hands, cap off, and a shiny wet smear across her chin. The label said all-purpose cleaner. Edouard's stomach dropped, but he crouched down and spoke slowly. "Did you drink some, or just touch it?" Poppy, proud of her honesty, said, "I licked it. Like a lollipop."

His phone was in the living room, and for one terrible second he couldn't remember any number except 911, which felt wrong for a lick. Then he remembered Mrs. Okafor tapping the fridge twice. Taped at eye level was a curled index card: Poison Help 1-800-222-1222. He called it, heart hammering, and a calm woman answered on the second ring. "This is poison control. What happened?" He told her: three-year-old, cleaner, a lick, a few minutes ago.

"Read me the label," she said. He did, squinting at the tiny print while Poppy tried to lick the bottle again and he held it above her head like a chandelier. The woman asked questions, then said a small lick of this one was usually nothing to worry about, but to give Poppy water and watch her for an hour, and to call back anytime, day or night. "Wait, it's almost nine at night," Edouard said. "You're still open?" "Any hour," she said. "Your call goes right to your local poison center."

He gave Poppy water in the good dinosaur cup and watched the clock like it owed him money. By eight thirty she was drowsy and complaining that her chin tasted "spicy," which the woman had said could happen. By nine she was asleep with the excavated button clutched in her fist, and Edouard texted Mrs. Okafor everything, ending with a question he genuinely wondered about: how many parents taped that card to the fridge, and how many never thought to?

When Mrs. Okafor came home at eleven, she read the texts twice, checked Poppy's sleeping face, and pressed twenty dollars into his hand instead of the agreed fifteen. "You called them before you panicked," she said. "That's the whole job." Edouard photographed the index card before he left, so he could make one for his own fridge, then stood on her porch in the cold, wondering whether the woman at poison control was still there, answering, somewhere in the dark.

Rose counted bars under her breath, her fingers resting on the keys of the old upright piano backstage at the Hartwell Concert Hall. In fifteen minutes her small jazz combo would open for the visiting trumpeter, and she had one job in the tune: keep the form. Twelve bars, then around again, chorus after chorus. The trouble was that Dexter, the sax player, had a habit of wandering off somewhere in the middle and never finding his way back.

Last month at the school gym it had been a disaster. Dexter had soloed straight past the end of a chorus, landed his phrases in the wrong place, and finally stopped playing altogether, his face pink under the fluorescent lights. Rose had ended the tune early just to rescue him. On the bus home she had stared at her sheet music, running a quiet analysis of where things fell apart, and she had noticed something she'd never seen before. Near the end of each twelve bars, the bass walked up and the piano hit a chord that felt like a door swinging open. Her teacher never explained it, but the chart labeled it in small print: turnaround.

"They call that part the turnaround," Rose had said to Dexter on the bus, pointing at the page. He had only shrugged.

Now, side stage, Dexter was pacing. "I still get lost," he admitted. "Twelve bars is twelve bars until it isn't."

"Listen for the turnaround," Rose said, adjusting the bench. "It's the end of the twelve-bar form. It usually lands on the V chord, and that chord pulls the music back to the start of the next chorus. When you hear it, you're home."

"What if I miss it?"

"Then you wait twelve more bars. It comes around again. That's the whole trick."

When the lights came up, the tune rolled out smooth for the first chorus. Then Dexter stood to solo. Rose watched him close his eyes, and she knew from his loosening shoulders that he was drifting. But she kept her left hand steady, and when bar ten arrived she leaned into the V chord, letting it ring a half beat longer, pushing the sound toward the top of the form. Dexter's eyes snapped open. His next phrase landed square on bar one, and he built it upward like he had never been lost at all.

Afterward, the trumpeter with the visiting band came over. "Nice mediating," he told Rose, nodding between her and Dexter. "You held the form together without playing over him." The others crowded in to hear the story, and Rose realized the evening felt full instead of thin, nothing impoverished about it. Dexter raised his sax case like a trophy.

"Bar ten," he said. "I heard it. I heard the door open."

Asher had predicted that a marble rolling down a taller ramp would travel farther across the kitchen floor, and for three days the marble had stubbornly refused to agree with him. The ramp made of an old bookshelf board leaned against the counter at four different heights, and every time he raised it, the marble flew off the end, bounced once, and stopped in almost the same spot. His data sheet, which he had decorated with a drawing of the marble wearing a tiny helmet, now showed four nearly identical measurements.

"You look like somebody deleted your game save," said his sister Priya from the doorway, chewing a granola bar.

"My hypothesis is wrong." Asher flattened the data sheet against the table. "The whole poster says taller ramp, longer distance. If I present this, I'll embarrass myself in front of everyone."

Priya picked up the marble and rolled it across the table, watching it drop off the edge. "Maybe the floor is the problem. Or maybe the marble is just lazy."

Asher laughed, but then he stopped. He tried the ramp on the hallway's wooden floor instead of the kitchen tile. Same result. He tried a heavier marble. Same result, so close it was practically the equivalent of a photocopy of the first one. Whatever was happening, it wasn't a fluke, and it wasn't the floor. Something he couldn't see was keeping the distance the same, and that made him almost more curious than being right would have.

At school the next morning he cornered Ms. Okafor before homeroom. "My results prove my prediction wrong. Should I start over with a different project?"

"A result that shows your hypothesis was wrong is still a real scientific result, and it's worth reporting," she said, handing him a fresh poster board.

He stared at it. "So I just... show everyone I was wrong?"

"You show everyone what you found."

That reframing felt like a metaphor for something, though Asher couldn't decide what. At home that evening he rebuilt the poster from scratch. The title now read, in letters he traced twice so they'd look bold: "WHY I WAS WRONG AND WHAT THE MARBLE KNOWS THAT I DON'T." He taped up the data sheet, drew an arrow to the suspiciously matching measurements, and added a question in red marker: "What hidden factor keeps the distance the same?" Maybe the marble lost speed somewhere he wasn't measuring. Maybe the board itself was doing something. He had questions, and somehow that felt better than having answers.

On science fair day, Priya found him at his table, straightening the marble helmet drawing for the tenth time. A kid from another class squinted at the poster and asked, "Wait, so your project is you being wrong?"

Asher slid the marble down the ramp one more time, and they both watched it roll to the exact spot where it always stopped.

Evelyn set her tray down at the end of the sixth-grade table, three seats away from Priya, who was picking at her pizza without looking up. Priya had skipped Evelyn's birthday sleepover on Saturday, and the text she sent had said only "can't come, sorry." No reason. No follow-up. On Sunday Evelyn had decided that Priya was selfish, full stop, and she had walked to school Monday radiating that decision like a heater.

She was also, in a diligent way, reading her older brother's psychology book at lunch, because she had a book report due Friday and no library pass. A page caught her eye. It described blaming someone's behavior on their character while ignoring the situation they were in. That was exactly what she'd done, she realized, except she hadn't ignored Priya's situation, because she didn't know it. Which was the problem. She didn't have the data.

"So what was the situation?" said Marcus, who had leaned over to steal her fries. "You don't know."

"I can find out," Evelyn said. She tore a corner from her brown bag, wrote a note, and folded it into a paper football. Then she flicked it across three seats. It hit Priya's milk carton. Priya unfolded it, read it, and looked over. Evelyn held up the psych book, then pointed at the empty chair beside her. A signal, she hoped, that said "truce, and also I have evidence."

Priya slid over with her tray. "What do you want."

"My brother's book says there's this thing," Evelyn said. "It's called the fundamental attribution error. A psychologist named Lee Ross named it in 1977." She showed Priya the page. "It's when you blame somebody's character instead of their situation. I did it to you. I called you selfish."

Priya stared at the page. "My grandmother had a stroke Friday night. We were at the hospital until Sunday. I didn't want to text the whole story, it felt weird." Her voice wobbled. "And I thought you'd be mad, so I didn't text at all, which was worse. Is she okay? She's okay, by the way. She yelled at a nurse about the jell-o, so she's fine."

"Then why weren't you answering me this morning?"

"I left my phone at the hospital," Priya said. "Mom's picking it up today. That's where I'm going after school, actually, if you want to come. Grandma keeps asking who ate all her grapes, and I need a witness that it wasn't me."

Evelyn closed the book. "I'll bring grapes."

Marcus reached across the table and took one of her fries anyway.

Lucy dumped the duffel bag onto the folding table and stared at the pile of clothes like it was a math test. Mom was at work until six, the soccer jersey had to be clean for tomorrow's game, and Lucy had exactly one hour to figure out laundry on her own.

"Separate the colours," she told herself, sorting into dark, light, and a hopeful little heap of pink things that she finally tucked into the dark pile as a compromise. Whites with whites, she reasoned, or the red sock would turn everything the colour of a sunburn. She fed quarters into the machine, poured in detergent, and watched the drum start to tumble.

Outside the window, a boy about her age was crouched beside his bike, pumping the tire pump like he was trying to inflate a bowling ball. He pumped, checked, frowned, and pumped again. Nothing was happening, and he was getting that red-faced, about-to-kick-something look. Lucy's washer would take forty minutes anyway, so she pushed out the door.

"Your pump is broken?" she asked.

"It's my little brother's bike, and he has a race at five, and I have to get the tire up." He pumped furiously. "It won't take air. I've been at it forever. My arms are getting cumulative tiredness."

"That's not what cumulative means," Lucy said, "but I get you." She crouched down and looked at the valve. It was skinny, nothing like the fat ones on her own bike, and on top of it was a tiny nut. She had read something about these once, in a bike magazine at the dentist's office. She turned the little nut counterclockwise until it wobbled loose, then pressed the pump on. This time when the boy pushed the handle, the tire began to firm up under his hand. He laughed out loud.

"The nut has to be unscrewed before any air can go in or come out," Lucy said. "That kind of valve is a Presta valve. You have to loosen it first."

"You are a genius and I will buy you a snack forever," the boy said, and pumped until the tire rang firm when he thumbed it. "My brother burns through carbs before races anyway. He'd eat your whole snack shelf."

"Carbohydrates," Lucy agreed. "He'll need them."

Her washer's spin cycle was shrieking by the time she got back inside. She moved everything to the dryer, and when the clothes came out warm she folded the jersey first, sleeves tucked in, just the way Mom did it, and laid it on top of the stack like a trophy. At 5:40 the boy pedalled past the window, his brother clinging to the back, both of them waving.

"Good luck tomorrow!" the brother shouted through the glass, holding up a granola bar in salute.

The bell hadn't rung yet, but Mr. Okafor's computer lab was already loud with keyboards. Nathan slid into his seat, logged in, and opened the group chat for the robotics club. The regional qualifier was in nine days, and nobody had agreed on who was bringing the backup battery pack. He typed his question, waited, and watched three other conversations scroll past without a single answer to his.

Across the row, Marcus hunched over his screen, tapping keys like he was squashing bugs. On the chat, a message from him shot to the top: WHERE ARE YOU. It sat there, thick and enormous. Below it, Priya replied within seconds: why are you yelling? i'm right here, chill.

Nathan blinked at the screen. Marcus hadn't been yelling. Nathan had heard him, and the loudest sound in the room was the heater rattling under the window, the same eccentric rattle it made every January. So why did Priya hear shouting? He looked again. Marcus's message was all capitals, every letter. Priya's was all lowercase. Nathan scrolled back through the last week of chat, and a pattern showed up fast: whenever somebody typed in capitals, the replies got defensive, jumpy, short. Whenever they typed normally, people answered calmly, even kindly.

He decided to test it. He typed a second question about the battery pack in regular letters and sent it, then leaned over. "Marcus, try asking again. Not all capitals. Just regular." Marcus gave him a suspicious squint, but he erased his draft and retyped it letter by letter, and Nathan watched him deliberately convert the giant blocky words into ordinary ones. where are you guys, we need to plan.

This time Priya answered in half a minute. here, sorry, was fixing my wheel. i can bring the battery pack if someone grabs the charger. Two more club members chimed in with offers, and within five minutes the whole supply list was sorted. Marcus stared at the screen like a magician had just pulled a rabbit out of it.

"So the caps were the problem," Marcus said slowly. "People read it like you're shouting at them."

"That's what it looked like from here," Nathan said. He felt a small twist of guilt anyway, remembering a message he'd sent his cousin last month in all capitals, and the cold one-line reply that had followed. He'd thought his cousin was just being moody.

Mr. Okafor called for attention and the screens went dark one by one. As they lined up, Marcus nudged Nathan's shoulder. "Next time something weird happens in the chat, you're investigating," he said. "Deal?"

Matthew had been waiting all week for this, and now the whole living room at Mr. Alvarez's house smelled like chili and popcorn, and the pregame show was finally counting down. He grabbed the best seat, the beanbag chair closest to the giant TV, before his cousin Dana could claim it. Mr. Alvarez carried in a bowl of chips the size of a kiddie pool. "This is the year," he announced, "that my team finally goes all the way."

The doorbell rang twice more before kickoff. First came Mrs. Okafor from next door with her famous seven-layer dip, then Mr. Alvarez's brother with his dog, Biscuit, who immediately tried to steal a napkin. Everyone crowded onto the couch, and Matthew's little sister, Priya, squeezed in beside him. On the screen, the announcers kept saying the same phrase over and over: Super Bowl LVIII. "Wait," Priya said, squinting at the logo. "Why are there letters in the title? Where are the numbers?"

Matthew started to answer, then stopped, because he honestly didn't know. LVIII. He knew it was Roman numerals, the kind they carved on old buildings, but why would a football game use them? He thought maybe someone just thought they looked fancy, like when restaurants call a small drink "petite." Dana shrugged when he asked her. Mr. Alvarez's brother said, "Always been that way, I figure." That answer itched at Matthew the way a loose tooth did. Things that had always been a certain way had still started somewhere.

During the first quarter, Matthew borrowed Mr. Alvarez's tablet from the counter and searched for the very first one. He found it fast, and his mouth actually fell open. He tapped Priya on the shoulder. "You're not going to believe this. The first Super Bowl's official name was the AFL-NFL World Championship Game."

Priya gasped like he'd revealed a magic trick. "Then where did 'Super Bowl' come from?" Matthew scrolled a little further, grinning. "The Roman numeral 'Super Bowl I' was added later. Somebody went back and stuck it on." Priya stared at the screen, then at the TV, then back. "So when they say LVIII, they're counting from a game that didn't even have that name?"

"Exactly!" Matthew said, louder than he meant to, and half the room turned. Mr. Alvarez held up a chip like a microphone. "The beanbag chair has an announcement."

Matthew stood up. "The first Super Bowl wasn't called the Super Bowl at all. It was the AFL-NFL World Championship Game, and the Roman numeral one came later." Dana whooped. Priya clapped. Even Biscuit barked, which made the dip wobble dangerously.

On the screen, the halftime show erupted in fireworks. Mrs. Okafor said the year her team lost the big game, she was so upset she let her mood deteriorate for a full week and wouldn't even watch highlights. Mr. Alvarez laughed and said that kind of thinking was toxic, and that tonight, win or lose, everyone was staying for ice cream sundaes. Priya leaned over to Matthew and whispered, "Next year, I'm going to know what the letters say before you do."

"Deal," Matthew said, and shook her hand, chili still on his fingers, as the second half kicked off and the whole room roared.

Ava slid the short story across the library table like it might bite. "Mr. Okafor wants two paragraphs on foreshadowing and symbolism by Friday," she told her friend Dev, "and I don't even know what I'm looking for."

"You're looking for clues," Dev said, popping a cheese puff into his mouth despite the NO FOOD sign looming above them like a threat. "Like when the narrator says the ice on the pond looked thin, and then later somebody falls through. That's foreshadowing. The ice is telling you the future, but quietly, like a gossipy snowman."

"That is the most bizarre description of foreshadowing I have ever heard," Ava said, but she picked up her pencil anyway. The story was called "The Kite," and sure enough, on page one, the kite string was described as frayed. On page three, the kite was red, "the color of the flag on Grandfather's old letter." Ava sat up straight. The frayed string might correspond to something breaking later, and the red flag might connect to something Grandfather had lost or left behind. She flipped to the last page. There it was: the string snapped, and when the kite landed in the neighbor's tree, it hung there like a flag. She felt like a detective who had just found the fingerprint.

"Okay, I've got it," she said, and began writing fast. "The author writes that the kite 'drifted away like a lost balloon.'" She filled half a page, feeling brilliant, then heard Dev's stomach growl like a small angry bear and paused. Something nagged at her. Had she copied that line exactly? She'd written it from memory.

She went back to page three and checked. The real line said "drifted off like a lost balloon," not "drifted away," and it said "a lost red balloon," not just "a lost balloon." Two words were wrong. Ava groaned loud enough that the librarian gave her the look, the one that could cause a concussion from across the room. "Dev, I made up my own evidence. My whole paragraph is built on a fake quote."

"So fix it," Dev said, shrugging. "Just copy it word for word this time. Same spelling, same punctuation, inside quotation marks, exactly like it is on the page."

Ava read the line out loud slowly, one finger under each word, then rewrote it in her notebook, checking every comma like it owed her money. When she was done, the quote matched the book perfectly, and her paragraph about the red balloon as a symbol of Grandfather drifting away actually made more sense with the real words. She closed the notebook with a snap.

"Next time I'm quoting the page before I trust my own brain," she said. Dev held out the cheese puff bag. "Deal. And next time, I'm sitting farther from the librarian."

The stream table in the back of Mr. Okafor's room was just a long plastic tray, a hose, and a bucket of sand, but to Henry it looked like the Grand Canyon waiting to happen. The class had spent two days arguing about how rivers cut canyons, and a small controversy had broken out: Marcus insisted a river could only dig down, while Priya said it also carried the sand away and dropped it somewhere else, which she called deposition. Henry wanted to settle it, and more than that, he wanted to watch a canyon actually form under his own hands.

"Ten minutes of water equals millions of years," Mr. Okafor said, turning the hose on low. "Fast time."

But nothing much happened. The water slid over the sand in a thin sheet, barely leaving a scratch, and Henry began to resign himself to a boring tray of wet sand. Marcus smirked. "See? Rivers can't do it."

That weekend Henry visited his grandpa, who kept a wall calendar in the kitchen and made a small mark on it every evening he spotted the Moon. Henry noticed something odd: on one page there was a dark circle with the word new written beside it, and no mark at all that night, and then the marks began again, a sliver, a half, a full round circle, shrinking back down. He counted the days from that first dark circle to the next one, half expecting it to be a tidy number like thirty.

He counted twice. "Grandpa, is it twenty-nine and a half days?" he asked. "From one new moon to the next?"

"Every time," Grandpa said. "About twenty-nine and a half days. The sky doesn't hurry."

Henry stared at the little marks marching across the calendar. Half a day. The Moon couldn't even be bothered to finish on a whole number. Nothing dramatic had happened on any single night, yet the Moon had gone from dark to full to dark again, one tiny sliver at a time. He thought about his stream table, ten minutes of water that had barely wrinkled the sand. Maybe he had expected a canyon in fast time when he should have expected a sliver.

Monday after school, Henry barricaded the end of the tray with a dam of pebbles and let the hose drip, low and patient, into one narrow channel he had dug with his finger. Priya stayed to watch. "It's going to take forever," she said.

"That's the point," Henry said, defiant against the clock on the wall.

They checked every fifteen minutes. First the channel deepened, a real groove now. Then a curve formed where the water slowed, and sand began to settle there in a tiny, fan-shaped delta. Priya leaned down until her nose almost touched the tray. "It's dropping the sand," she whispered. "It carried it and dropped it."

By the time the custodian knocked on the door, the groove was a canyon, deep enough that its walls cast shadows, and at its mouth a small smooth beach had grown where nothing had been an hour before. Henry turned off the hose and looked at the little delta, then out the window at the pale daytime Moon hanging over the gymnasium roof.

"Twenty-nine and a half days," he said, "and I only needed an hour and a half."

Paisley crouched behind the folding table in the gymnasium and tightened the last screw on the robot's arm while the judges finished their coffee two rows away. The Eastern Valley Robotics Rally gave every team thirty minutes to set up a display, and their display was supposed to be a web page on the big monitor at the back of the table. Except the page did not exist yet, because nobody on the team had ever written one.

"We need something on that screen before the first whistle," said Devon, spinning a spare propeller between his fingers the way he did when he was nervous. "Can you do it?"

Paisley had watched a video about HTML the night before, mostly out of curiosity, and she remembered enough to feel dangerous. She opened the team laptop and typed out tags for a heading and a paragraph, filling them with the team name and a few sentences about the robot. The words appeared on the screen, black and plain, shoved all the way against the left edge like they were hiding from the judges.

"It looks extinct," said Marisol, arriving with a fistful of safety pins for the banner. "Like a page from 1998."

"It needs style," Paisley said. "CSS." She had never actually written CSS, only read about it, so she added a style rule for the heading, saved the file, and hit refresh. Nothing changed. The heading stayed glued to the left. She read the line again, character by character, hunting for the invisible mistake, and spotted a missing semicolon hiding between two properties. She fixed it, refreshed, and the heading slid to the center of the screen with the paragraph below it, suddenly looking like a real page. Devon let out a whoop and gave the propeller a celebratory flick across the table.

Then the laptop chimed. Marcus, running their scoring program one last time, frowned at it. "The prime checker is broken. It keeps saying one is prime, and I can't figure out why."

Paisley leaned over. The program tested numbers by dividing and checking remainders, and one passed every test because one divided everything evenly. She thought about that for a moment. One had never seemed like a weird number before, but calling it prime must be wrong somehow, because the program's whole point was to break numbers down. She remembered the video guy saying something about it, and she tested an idea out loud.

"Try the number six," she said. "Two times three. That's the prime way to build six, right?" Marcus nodded and typed it. "Now try one. How many ways can you write one as a product of primes?"

Marcus stared at the screen. "None. You can't. There aren't any primes in it."

"That's it," Paisley said. "One is not a prime number. Mathematicians exclude it so that every whole number has only one way to be written as a product of primes." Marcus typed a single exception into the code, and the program stopped listing one, though she noticed he kept the rest of the loop exactly as it was. He would not have to eliminate any other cases, because the pattern only broke at the beginning.

The whistle blew. The robot lurched forward on the practice mat, snagged the first block, and carried it toward the goal zone while the centered heading glowed on the monitor behind it. Marisol pressed a safety pin into Paisley's palm like a medal.

"Hold onto that," she said. "You never know when a webpage breaks at regionals."

Parker sat at his grandpa's kitchen table with a laptop open and a stack of survey papers beside him. The whole school had voted on a new mascot, and Parker had promised his class he would show the results in a proper chart. He typed each vote into a spreadsheet, one row at a time, and when he finished he made a pivot table to count the votes by grade. That was when things stopped adding up.

Grade seven appeared twice. One line said "Gr 7" with fifty-two votes, and another line said "Grade 7" with fifty-eight votes. Parker frowned and counted the total in his head. Every other grade showed up once, so why did seven split itself in two? "Grandpa," he called, "did the seventh graders vote twice, or is my spreadsheet haunted?"

Grandpa came over with his mug of coffee and looked at the screen. "A pivot table treats 'Gr 7' and 'Grade 7' as two separate groups," he said, "so answers must be typed consistently before they are summarised."

Parker stared at the two lines. So the votes weren't doubled, they were just sorted into two bins with nearly the same label. He scrolled back through his data and found it: at the top of the stack his friend Dex had filled in half the forms while Parker filled in the rest, and Dex had written "Gr 7" on every one. Parker tested the idea by fixing a single cell, changing one "Gr 7" to "Grade 7", and watched the counts shift. Fifty-one and fifty-nine. The rule was real. "It's a little paradox," he said. "The answer was right in front of me the whole time, but it was hiding in the spelling."

He went through the rest of the rows carefully, changing each "Gr 7" to "Grade 7", and the gradual shift in the numbers felt like watching a tide come in. When he finished, grade seven showed up once, with all one hundred and ten votes. Then he built the formula that added the whole column, checked it against his hand count, and inserted a bar chart. The bars rose across the screen, tall and clean, one for each grade.

Dex texted him a minute later: did the dragon win? Parker looked at the chart, at the tallest bar standing above the others, and typed back, "Come see for yourself. But first, we need to talk about how you write the word grade."

Jake sat at the kitchen table with his notebook open to a page that had only two sentences on it. His pencil hovered, then wrote a third, then stopped. His story was about a kid named Marcus who wanted to win the science fair, but nothing was going wrong for Marcus, and Jake knew that meant nothing was happening at all.

His little sister Nora slid into the other chair with a bowl of cereal and read over his shoulder. "Who's the bad guy?" she asked.

"There isn't one," Jake said. "That's the problem."

"Every story has one." She crunched her cereal like this was obvious.

Jake tapped his pencil against the table. He thought about the word he'd copied from the board at school: protagonist. The protagonist was a story's main character, and the antagonist was the character or force working against them; their conflict drove the plot toward the climax. He had assumed the antagonist had to be a villain in a black mask, something sinister with a cackle and a hidden lair. But the word "force" was sitting right there in his notes, and he kept stepping over it.

He looked at his story again. Marcus wanted to win the science fair. What worked against Marcus? Jake flipped back a page and found his answer: the weather forecast. A snowstorm was coming on the night of the fair, and if the school closed, Marcus would never get to show his project.

Jake sat up straight. "Nora, my antagonist is a snowstorm."

"That's not a person," she said.

"It doesn't have to be. It just has to fight him."

He started writing fast. First he had to calibrate the trouble, like tuning a radio to the right station, so the storm grew from a small worry to a real threat without jumping too soon. At the kitchen window the afternoon light was already going gray, and fat flakes had begun to stick to the glass, which felt like the storm was reading over his shoulder too.

He wrote the dialogue out carefully, checking every comma and quotation mark. "We can still make it," Marcus said. Then he built the climax: Marcus carrying his project through the snow to the school, the doors still open, the judges waiting.

When he finished, Jake read the last page aloud. Nora pushed her empty bowl aside. "So do they call a truce, Marcus and the storm?"

"No," Jake said. "Marcus wins." He underlined the final line, and outside, the real snow kept falling.

Felix's new phone arrived in a box no bigger than a sandwich, and he tore it open on the kitchen table before Dad had even set down his coffee. The screen lit up blue, and Felix grinned at it like it was a door with no locks on the far side. He spent the whole afternoon setting it up, typing in his email password twice, and downloading a game about repairing lighthouses.

That evening, while he was charging the phone beside his bed, it buzzed. A message filled the screen: "Your login code is 471-208. If you didn't request it, ignore this message." Felix stared at the numbers. He hadn't typed his password anywhere since that afternoon. So who had? Somebody, somewhere, must have just tried to get into his account, and the only way to reach that gate was with his password. His stomach did a slow flip.

He ran downstairs holding the phone like evidence. "Dad, I got a code and I didn't ask for one."

Dad leaned in. "That's two-factor authentication," he said. "Good thing you turned it on."

Felix paced the kitchen, thinking out loud. "So the code is a second thing you have to show. It comes right to my phone. Even if somebody stole my password, that alone wouldn't be enough to get in. They'd be stuck at the door without this." He waved the phone. Then he stopped pacing, because a worse thought arrived. "Dad. Somebody has my password. That's the only way they could have triggered a code at all."

They sat at the table and changed it together, and Felix made the new one long and strange, a string no anonymous stranger on the internet would ever guess. Then he thought about where the old password could have leaked. He'd used the same one on a quiz site months ago, a site with pop-up ads that had eventually made him abandon it entirely. That had to be it. His old password, floating around out there like a key somebody found on the sidewalk.

The next morning Felix was ready with a plan, eager to test it. He asked Dad to try logging into the email account from the family laptop using the old password, just to see what happened. Dad typed it in, and a message popped up on Felix's phone: a new code request. The screen on the laptop said, "Enter the code sent to your device."

"See?" Felix said, bouncing on his toes. "The password got them one step in, and then they hit the wall. Without my phone, they're a civilian locked outside."

Dad laughed and closed the laptop. Felix picked up his phone and typed a note to himself, out loud as he wrote: "Rule one, unique password for every account." He read it twice, then held the phone up like a tiny trophy. "Lighthouse level two, here I come."

The annual Marín family picnic had one rule that everybody ignored: bring a dish from your side of the family. Anthony had brought potato salad, which was from nobody's side, and it was already half gone. He was standing near the horseshoe pit when his cousin Dario and Dario's friend Sam started arguing, which was normal, except this time it wasn't about the score.

"Your grandma's from the rez but you live in the city," Sam said, flicking a horseshoe so it landed nowhere near the stake. "You can't just decide you're Native. Somebody has to, like, certify you."

"Certify me?" Dario picked up the other horseshoe. "Who, you?"

Anthony had been thinking about something similar all morning, ever since Great-Aunt Rosa had pinned him by the lemonade and listed every group she belonged to, which took a while, including two she invented herself. Nobody had ever told Rosa what she was. Rosa told you what she was, and then she told you what you were, and then she gave you more lemonade.

"Maybe there's an actual answer," Anthony said. "Like a rule about who decides."

Sam rolled his eyes. "There's no rule. You're so gullible."

But Anthony was already typing on his phone, one-handed so he wouldn't drop his plate. He found it faster than he expected, a United Nations document, and he read the part out loud. "The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted on 13 September 2007." He scrolled. "It says Indigenous peoples have the right to determine their own identity and membership."

"Meaning what?" Dario said.

"Meaning the group decides who's in the group. Not Sam."

Sam made a face like the potato salad had turned on him. "Fine, but does a picnic count? This isn't, like, a council."

"It's Dario's family," Anthony said. "Seems like it counts more than horseshoes."

Later, Anthony told Rosa about the argument while she refilled his cup. She said that in her day people didn't look things up, they just argued longer, and that a good argument could spread through a family like a virus if nobody stopped it. Then she said he should prioritize eating over officiating disputes, since the refereeing didn't pay and the brisket was going fast.

Dario walked over with two forks and handed one to Sam, who took it after a strategic pause. "So membership committee," Sam said, mouth full. "That's a thing now?"

"That's a thing," Dario said, and pointed his fork at the dessert table.

Chase had exactly one goal on Saturday morning: prove to his father that their family's weekly pizza spending was out of control. He had a library card, a computer by the window, and a shoebox of receipts he had smuggled out of the kitchen drawer before anyone noticed.

Ms. Reyes, the librarian, leaned over the keyboard when he waved her down. "You want a spreadsheet," she said. "Type your numbers in one column, click the cell under them, and type equals, S-U-M, open parenthesis, then drag over your numbers." She waited while he did it. When he pressed Enter, the total appeared like magic: 214 dollars in one month. "Now highlight everything, including the words like 'pepperoni,' and pick bar chart," she added. "The chart will evaluate your whole column and draw it for you."

Chase grinned. The bars rose like a tiny skyline, and Friday's "double cheese emergency" towered over the rest. He was adjusting the colors when his father slid into the chair beside him, holding a sticky note covered in scribbles. "Good, you're on a computer. I have to change my office password again and I keep forgetting the new one. It's the fourth time this month, I swear." He typed a new password, hit Enter, and got a red rejection message. He typed another. Rejected again.

"Why do they make you change it so much?" Chase asked.

"Every month, everybody, the whole office," his dad groaned. "Some rule somewhere, probably."

Chase remembered a Saturday a few weeks back, when his dad had missed his grandma's video call because he'd been locked out for a whole afternoon, resetting passwords and waiting on hold. That was the night they'd ordered pizza, which was how the shoebox of receipts had started in the first place. Chase had felt bad watching his dad apologize to Grandma over and over, promising next week, definitely next week. Something about forced password changes kept wrecking things.

"I can look it up," Chase said. He searched "rules about changing passwords" and found a page from NIST, which Ms. Reyes said was the group that made official guidance for things like this. He read it twice, then read the key line out loud. "It says systems should not force people to change passwords on a schedule, only when there is evidence a password has been stolen."

His dad blinked at him. "So all those monthly changes are against the guidance?"

"That's what it says. No schedule. Only if there's evidence it got stolen." Chase pulled up the citation and printed it at the front desk, thirty whole cents of his own money, because his dad's phone battery was being volatile again and died at ninety percent every time it mattered.

His dad emailed the printout to his office's IT person, fully expecting to be ignored. On Monday evening he burst through the door holding his phone like a trophy. "They killed it. The monthly change. The IT guy said you were right, and now nobody has to reset anything unless something actually happens." He dropped a pizza box on the table, then paused, catching sight of the shoebox. "Also, I saw your chart."

Chase winced. But his dad just laughed at the double cheese bar. "Tell you what," he said. "Add a column for 'pizza caused by password problems,' and we'll call that one Grandpa's fault too." Chase opened the spreadsheet, typed a new column, and stretched the SUM formula down one more row.

Bennett had earned a reputation on the fourth floor as the kid who grew tomatoes in a bucket, and this spring he intended to top it. He filled four flower boxes for the balcony railing with potting soil and planted beans, peas, lettuce, and peppers. His little sister Dot watched from the sliding door with a bag of chips. "Beans are boring," she said. "Peppers are boring. Plant candy."

"Beans are the smart choice," Bennett said, and patted the soil. He had read one sentence about them in a library book and it had stuck in his head, though he didn't entirely understand it yet.

For three weeks he was diligent about watering, checking every morning before school and again at dinner. The lettuce came up spindly and yellowish. The peppers sat there doing almost nothing. But the beans and peas shot up so fast they needed strings to climb, and by June the boxes were crowded with vines. Dot came out one evening, chewing, and frowned at them. "Why are the bean ones winning?" she asked.

That was the question Bennett had been circling all month. He had a guess, but a guess wasn't the same as knowing, so he decided to test it. He pulled up one scraggly pepper plant, shook the dirt off its roots, and looked. Smooth roots, white and skinny. Then, feeling a little guilty, he tugged up one bean plant from the crowded box. Its roots were covered in small lumps, dozens of them, like beads on a string. "Would you look at that," he said.

Dot leaned over. "Those bumps are weird. Is it sick?"

"They're called nodules," Bennett said, remembering the word from the book. "The book said beans and peas have bacteria in these little lumps, and the bacteria take nitrogen from the air and turn it into a form plants can use." He held the root up to the porch light. The pepper had no bumps and no luck. The bean had both. That wasn't proof exactly, but it fit, and he anticipated that the peas would show the same thing. He pulled one pea vine, and there they were, the same small lumps. He grinned so wide Dot backed up a step.

"So the beans are cheating," Dot said.

"They're not cheating, they're farming." Bennett pushed the plants back into the soil, watered them, and propped the strings straight. He had been planning to pull the peas out to give the peppers more room, since peppers were the impressive crop, the one worth bragging about. He changed his mind on the spot. "Next year, this whole balcony is beans," he said, and went inside to find a marker and the back of Dot's chip bag, which was, he'd decided, the perfect place to draw the plan.

Alice discovered the lines in the bathroom mirror that morning, two thin pale streaks curving along her hip like someone had drawn them with a very fine pencil while she slept. She had pulled her waistband down twice to check, then three times, as if they might change their minds and vanish. Now she sat in the back seat of the family car with her sweatshirt tied around her waist, even though the heater was making the whole car smell like dusty warm air.

"Seatbelt," her dad said, glancing in the mirror. He was driving her to swim practice, and her little brother Ben was buckled in beside her, chewing a granola bar with his mouth open.

She buckled it, slowly. The problem was the swimsuit. In twenty minutes she would have to stand on a pool deck in front of the whole team, and the suit sat exactly where the lines were. Maybe she could claim she felt sick. The idea gave her a small twist of guilt, because it would be a lie, and Dad had already given up his Saturday morning to supervise her practices all season. He'd told her last week that his old stopwatch had become obsolete now that the team used electronic timers, but he still came anyway, clicking his dead watch out of habit.

"Hey, Dad," she said, watching the wipers push rain across the glass. "When you were twelve, did you ever grow really fast? Like, fast enough to notice?"

"Notice how?" He turned down the radio.

"Like, overnight. Clothes not fitting. Stuff."

He laughed. "Your uncle Matt grew four inches one summer. Why, are your jeans too short again?"

Alice hesitated. Ben was staring out the window, counting horses in the fields. "There are these lines," she said, quieter. "On my hips. Thin ones. I thought maybe something was wrong."

The car slowed at a light. "What do they look like?"

"Like little scratches that don't hurt. Pale."

Dad tapped the wheel, then reached over and turned the radio down the rest of the way. "You know what, your mom has some. I remember noticing them years ago, and she said everybody in her family got them. Want me to ask her at pickup?"

At the pool, Alice changed in the corner stall with the door locked, then stood there a long minute. Finally she pulled the suit strap up on her shoulder and walked out. Nobody looked. Nobody pointed. The pool smelled like chlorine and coconut shampoo, and the water was that impossible blue that made everything seem fine.

After practice, Mom was in the driver's seat with the heater running. She looked at Alice's hip for exactly five seconds and then smiled. "Stretch marks," she said. "Half the girls your age have them. Mine showed up during my big growth spurt, and they fade over time."

Alice buckled in and pressed her palm flat against her hip through the fabric. "So they're just... from growing?"

"Fast growing," Mom said, pulling out of the lot. "You shot up two sizes this year."

Alice leaned her head against the cold window and watched the rain. Maybe by next summer they'd be nearly invisible, and she'd be taller, and her jeans would be too short again.

"I'm ordering new jeans," she announced.

"Large ones," said Ben, and threw his granola bar wrapper at her head.

Grandpa's kitchen table had three bowls of cereal, a stack of old bank statements, and one very upset cousin. Maya, who was sixteen, kept refreshing an app on her phone and groaning. "It's down again. My bond. I paid a hundred dollars for it and now it says ninety-two."

Levi slid his cereal aside. He had come to Grandpa's house to work on his own problem, a chart comparing two savings accounts over five years, one paying simple interest and one paying compound interest. The compound line on his graph climbed in a gradual curve that started slow and then bent upward, like a ramp turning into a hill. The simple line went up straight and boring. He kept poking at the numbers because he could not actually see the interest piling up; he had to trust the pattern.

"Which bond?" he asked Maya.

"A government one," she said. "Grandpa helped me buy it last year for my college money. I'm going to lose everything."

Levi picked up the phone. The app showed the price, the day's change, and a box labeled "Maturity." He tapped it. "It says here it matures in nine years. What does that mean?"

Grandpa came in with his coffee, sneezed twice, and set the mug far from Maya's cereal. "That cat of yours gets on everything," he muttered, rubbing his eyes. "My allergy acts up every visit." He did not look at Maya's phone. He believed kids figured things out better when nobody handed them the answer.

Levi read the screen out loud. "Held until maturity, the issuer pays back the full face value." He frowned, then tapped back to the first page. "The face value here is a hundred dollars. So if you just keep it until the maturity date, you get the whole hundred back, no matter what the price did in between." He said it slowly, testing it. "The ninety-two is just what someone would pay you for it today."

Maya stared at the little chart that had been scaring her all morning. "So the dip doesn't matter? Not unless I sell now?"

"That's what it says." Levi turned the phone toward her.

Grandpa smiled into his coffee and said nothing. Maya slumped back in her chair, relieved, then sat up again and pointed at Levi's graph. "Okay, but explain yours now. Why does your compound line go all bendy like that?"

Levi grinned and pulled his chair over. "Interest on interest. Watch. Year one, it's tiny." He tapped the paper, one square at a time. "By year five, it's the tallest thing on the page."

Camille spread the photocopy of the Charter across the kitchen table and frowned at it. Section 3, the right to vote, was supposed to be the one she explained in her own words for Monday's assignment, but the sentence on the page sat there like a locked door. "Every citizen has the right to vote," she read aloud, "including the right to choose their representatives." She could copy that. Explaining it was the hard part, and Ms. Okafor had been clear that copied words would earn a zero.

The knock on the door came before she got further. It was her friend Deena, still holding her phone, still wearing the scowl she'd had at school. "You saw the class president results?" Deena dropped into the chair across from Camille. "Priya got twelve votes out of thirty. Twelve! Noah got eleven and I got seven, and now Priya acts like the whole class picked her."

Camille pulled a napkin toward her and wrote the numbers on it. Thirty kids, three candidates. Twelve for Priya, eleven for Noah, seven for Deena. She stared at the napkin until something clicked, a small, sharp insight: nobody had a majority. More than half of thirty was sixteen, and Priya didn't have sixteen. She had the most votes, but most votes weren't most people.

"So eighteen of us wanted someone else," Deena said, jabbing the napkin. "That can't be fair. There has to be a rule against it."

Camille took out her phone and searched how elections pick winners. The results mentioned something called first-past-the-post. She read it twice, then looked up. "It's called first-past-the-post," she said. "In our kind of election, whoever gets the most votes in the district wins the seat, even if they didn't get more than half the votes." Deena slumped back in the chair.

"That's the rule? That's actually the rule?"

"That's the rule." Camille tested the idea against the napkin, checking it both directions. Priya had the most, so Priya won. Noah had more than Deena but fewer than Priya, so Noah lost. It wasn't a mistake in the counting; it was how the counting worked. She could try to refute it by finding a case where the most-votes candidate lost, but every example she thought of fit the pattern instead.

Deena sighed. "So objecting to the result won't get me anything."

"Maybe not the result," Camille said slowly. She turned back to the Charter, and the locked sentence came loose. "But here's the thing. The right to vote is the right to have your vote counted in that system, not the right to always get the winner you wanted. That's my explanation. My own words." She copied the napkin numbers onto the back of her homework sheet as evidence.

Monday morning, she stood up in front of the class, held up the napkin, and said, "This is what happened in our election, and this is why it's still legal." Priya, in the front row, raised her hand first.

The folding chairs in the town hall were already half full when Simon found a seat beside his teacher's mock election display. His card with the right to fair representation written on it felt damp in his hand, and he read it one more time under his breath. His class had held their election two weeks ago, and tonight he was supposed to explain that right to the whole room in his own words. The problem was that he had not understood it himself until yesterday.

Yesterday, their class had recounted the same ballots twice. First they had counted the way the old town rules worked, where the party with the most votes in each district won everything, and one party had swept seven of the ten council seats. Then Ms. Ruiz had handed out a sheet that said only one word at the top: proportional. "Recount," she had said, and nothing more. Simon had lined the ballots up in party columns and counted the votes instead of the districts. The Blue party had 30 percent of the votes, and when he divided the seats that way, they got three seats out of ten. He checked it twice, certain he had made an error, because the same ballots had given Blue almost nothing the first time. Under proportional representation, parties win seats roughly in proportion to their share of the vote, so a party with 30 percent of the vote gets about 30 percent of the seats. The Blue party went from being shut out to holding three chairs, and nothing on the ballots had changed at all.

That was the part Simon wanted to disclose to the room tonight, because he had worked out that fair representation was not some vague, subjective feeling of being treated well. It was countable. You could take the same stack of ballots and get two different councils, and one of them looked a lot more like the people who voted.

When his name was called, Simon walked to the microphone. "Fair representation means the council should look like the voters," he said, and his voice steadied as he went. "Our class counted the same ballots two ways. When we did it proportionally, a party with 30 percent of the vote got about 30 percent of the seats. When we counted the other way, they got almost none. Same votes. Different council."

A woman near the front raised her hand. "So which count was right?"

"Both counts were right," Simon said. "The rules were different." Then he pointed at the chart behind him, at the two columns of seats, three in one and nearly empty in the other.

"That's the whole problem," the woman said, standing up with her ballot in her fist.

Florence had promised her cousin Priya that she would participate in the family science fair by video call on Saturday, which meant her model of an atom had to be finished by Friday night. The problem was her model. She had glued four hundred tiny beads onto a foam ball, packing it solid, and now it looked like a lumpy planet instead of an atom. Her little brother Dev strolled into the kitchen, opened the fridge, and said, "You should make it out of cheese so I can eat the leftovers."

"You don't get leftovers of a science project," Florence said, though privately she thought an edible atom might win her points. Instead she turned to the packet of litmus paper she'd been saving. Her teacher had said anyone who finished their model early could try the pH testing challenge, and Florence wanted that challenge badge. She dipped a red strip into a glass of lemonade and watched it turn pinkish, then a blue strip that stayed blue. "Acid," she announced to the kitchen. Dev, who wanted to be declared the official taste tester of anything liquid in the house, said, "What about dish soap? If it's an acid, we shouldn't be putting it on plates."

That afternoon the mail came, and with it a letter from Priya, who loved sending actual letters because she said texting was too easy. Florence slit it open at the counter, still holding her litmus paper.

"Dear Florence," Priya wrote. "Guess what we learned today. There was an experiment with gold foil, run by Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden under Ernest Rutherford. They shot tiny particles at the foil, and most of them passed straight through, which shows an atom is mostly empty space. Mostly EMPTY. I thought of your bead ball immediately. Sorry. Love, Priya."

Florence read it twice, then looked at her four hundred beads. Most of them, apparently, were standing where nothing actually was. She tested one more liquid while she thought, dipping a strip into Dev's soapy water; it turned the red paper blue, which meant base, not acid, and Dev cheered as if he had personally invented soap. The mixture in her testing cup sat translucent and faintly blue, and beside it her brother's collection of "mystery metals," which he claimed included an alloy of two juice-can lids, glinted in the afternoon light.

She carried the foam ball to the trash can, beads and all, and started over with wire and three lonely beads held far apart. "That's it?" Dev said. "That's the whole atom?" "Mostly empty space," Florence said, and skewered a marshmallow where a particle would pass straight through.

Grace slammed the oven door shut and pulled out the third pan of the afternoon. The cookies looked wrong again, thick and dry, more like little cakes, and she winced when she broke one open and saw the crumbly middle. Her grandmother's kitchen smelled like butter and cinnamon, which was the only good news.

"I don't get it," Grace said, dropping into a chair. "I followed Grandma's recipe exactly. Twice."

Her grandmother set down her tea and slid the old recipe card across the table. Grace had copied it out that morning, one cup of flour, half a cup of sugar, one egg, all in her neatest handwriting. She had even made an amendment to the bottom of her copy: bake ten minutes, not twelve, because the first batch had burned.

"Show me how you measure the flour," her grandmother said.

Grace marched to the counter, grabbed her cup, and plunged it straight into the flour bag. She packed it full, tapped it level, and held it up like proof. "See? Perfectly full."

Her grandmother smiled, but not in a mean way. "Try it again. Only this time, weigh what's in the cup."

They dug out the old kitchen scale from under the sink, the one with the dial that Grandpa used for his coffee. Grace scooped another cup the same way and set it on the scale. Then her grandmother fluffed the flour with a spoon, spooned it gently into a fresh cup, leveled it with a knife, and weighed that too.

Grace leaned over the dial. "Mine's heavier. A lot heavier." She scooped again, weighed it, and wrote the numbers in her notebook. Packed cup, big number. Fluffed cup, smaller number. Every single time.

"Scooping straight from the bag packs it down," Grace said slowly, reading her own notes. "So my cup is holding way more flour than the recipe wants. That's why they're dry and cakey." She flipped to a clean page. "Grandma, does your recipe book have weights?"

"Top of every page, honey. Bakers weigh flour because it's more accurate."

Grace measured everything by weight for the fourth batch, double-checking each number like a scientist. When she pulled the pan out, the cookies had spread into golden rounds with crackled tops, and the smell made her mouth water. She carried the plate to the porch where her cousins were waiting, and Grandpa announced that the lemonade was definitely not synthetic, squeezed from real lemons that morning.

"Try one," Grace said, holding out the plate with both hands. "I weighed the flour myself."

Austin had never been inside a polling station before, and the first thing he noticed was how ordinary it looked, folding tables, a coffee urn, and a line of people clutching paper receipts like tickets to something important. His mom went to vote, and he drifted toward a table near the door where a woman with a clipboard was saying "petition" over and over. Curious, he edged closer.

A petition, he heard her tell an old man in a Cardinals cap, is a written request, signed by many people, asking a government body to take a specific action. She slid a sheet toward him. At the top, in bold letters, it said: Petition for a Crosswalk at Maple and Ninth. Austin read it twice. So that was what a petition was. He had assumed it was something lawyers did, or something that happened in courthouses, but here it was on a plain table with a pen tied to a string.

Last spring, he remembered, his friend Dev had tried to get a crosswalk near their school by emailing the city once and then giving up when nobody answered. One email. One person. Austin looked at the petition sheet again, at the columns of names marching down the page, forty-one signatures so far, and a pattern started to form in his mind. Maybe the problem was never that the city didn't care. Maybe one voice was just too quiet to hear, and fifty voices made a sound you couldn't ignore. He wanted to test that idea before it slipped away.

"Can I sign?" he asked the woman.

"You have to be a registered voter to sign," she said, and he felt his shoulders drop. But then she added, "You can read it, though. That's how most people decide."

So he read the whole page, out loud, slowly enough that a couple of people in line glanced over. It said the petitioners requested that the city council direct the traffic department to install a marked crosswalk at Maple and Ninth, and it cited something from the state charter, the section listing rights. He stopped on one line and read it again: citizens have the right to petition their government for redress of grievances. He'd heard his teacher use the word articulate, meaning to put an idea into clear words, and now he understood why that was hard. He chewed on the sentence until he could say it his own way.

"It means," he said to the woman, testing it out loud, "if enough of us ask for something in writing, somebody has to at least look at it. Like, the door doesn't get to stay closed."

She smiled and tapped the clipboard. "That's better than most adults manage."

A man in line overheard and stepped over to sign, and his vigorous scrawl nearly tore the page. "My kid bikes that corner," he said, pressing down hard. Austin watched the forty-second name appear and thought about Dev, who was going to lose his mind.

He borrowed a scrap of paper and wrote: petition equals names equals volume, then circled it. On the walk home he'd stop at Dev's house first. He was already planning what to say when his mom caught his arm at the door.

"Learn anything?" she asked.

"Yeah," Austin said, waving the scrap of paper. "Dev and I have forty-one people to thank and about a hundred more to find."

"Fourteen dollars for one bottle," Marcus said, holding his phone screen toward the seat behind him. "My cousin says AquaPure strips toxins out of your body in nine days. Look at the site. Lab coats, testimonials, everything."

Sophie leaned over the aisle of the rumbling bus and studied the page. It did look impressive: a doctor in a white coat, a chart climbing upward, paragraphs of glowing reviews. She scrolled a little and noticed a small link at the bottom, "Shop Now," and beneath it, in faint gray letters, the name of the company that owned the website. The same company, she saw, that sold the drink.

"That's weird," she said. "The people who made the site are the people selling it." She thought about that for a moment. Judging the site by its own pages felt like asking a used-car salesman whether his car ran well. He would say yes, whoever he was. What she needed was somebody outside the deal.

"Hey, Marcus, hand me your phone a second." She opened a new tab and typed the drink's name plus the word "scam." A news article from a consumer magazine appeared, then a doctor's blog, then a warning from a health agency. None of them had anything good to say. One called the "clinical study" an internal company document that nobody outside could verify. She opened two more tabs to be sure, and the story from outside the site was the same everywhere.

"So it's fake?" Marcus groaned. "I already told my cousin I'd advocate for it at lunch. He gets a cut if we sell six bottles."

"Wait, what's this called, opening other tabs instead of trusting the site itself?" said Priya from the window seat, looking over Sophie's shoulder.

"Lateral reading," Sophie said. "My sister says professionals do it that way."

"Well, you just saved me fourteen dollars," Marcus said. He tapped out a message to his cousin, then frowned at his phone. "He's going to be mad."

"He'll survive," Priya said. "Tell him to read the magazine article."

"I will." Marcus slumped back, then straightened up. "Okay, but my cousin also says our principal used to be in a monarchy's royal guard, and that's why he walks so stiff. Is that checkable or is that just an opinion?"

Sophie laughed. "Whether he was a royal guard is a claim you could check, if you can find records. Whether he walks stiff is just what your cousin thinks." She opened a fresh tab. "Give me his full name."

Marcus spelled it out, and Priya scooted over to share the screen as the bus turned the last corner toward school.

The nurse's office smelled like disinfectus and old paper, and Grace sat on the crinkly paper of the cot while Mrs. Okafor fitted a pair of purple frames over her ears. The little hinge above each lens clicked as the temples folded out, and Grace felt the weight of them settle on her nose like a small, patient animal.

"I can see the poster," she said. The eye chart across the room, which had been a smear of gray all morning, now had letters on it, sharp as typed words. Even the crooked thumbtack in the corner of the sun safety poster was suddenly clear.

Mrs. Okafor smiled. "Dr. Patel said your prescription is mild. Nearsighted, which means the far stuff is blurry." She wrote something on a card. "Signs the paper for your mom, and you can go back to class."

Grace slipped out into the hallway, but instead of turning toward math, she stood still. The drinking fountain down the hall had a dent in it. The trophy case had fingerprints on the glass. All year she had thought the board was smudged and the posters were faded, and it had been her own eyes the whole time. That was the part that bugged her. Her little brother read at midnight with a flashlight and had perfect vision, and she had eaten her carrots and done everything right, or mostly right. She wanted to know the actual reason, and she wanted it before she got home and her mom asked why she needed glasses when Theo didn't.

At lunch she found Dr. Patel's pamphlet still folded in her jacket pocket, the one from the clinic visit last week. She read it at the picnic table outside, in the October sun. Under a heading about nearsightedness it said that studies show nearsightedness is less common in people who spent more time outdoors during childhood. Grace read the sentence twice. Then she did her own test, right there, because it was a thing she could check.

She made a list in her head. Theo played outside constantly, soccer and worms and whatever else. Priya, who sat in front of her and wore thick glasses, had told Grace once that she spent whole weekends gaming and rarely left the house. Grace herself had spent the last two summers indoors, drawing at her desk and postponing every walk because the air conditioning was better. She thought of three more kids with glasses and tried to remember whether she ever saw them at the park. She didn't. The kids who were always outside on weekends, like Marcus and his loud bike, were the ones squinting at nothing in class.

"So it wasn't the carrots," she said out loud, and Priya, across the table, laughed.

"Carrots can't fix weekends indoors," Priya said. "I'm negligent about daylight, according to my mom."

"I'm going outside this Saturday," Grace said. She lifted her new glasses and looked at the trees past the fence, each leaf separate for the first time. "First, I have to postpone my math homework. Somebody has to call my mom about these."

Kate had spent most of October guessing which kids were which by the shape of their hair, so when Coach Ruiz finally said "The scoreboard is right there, Alvarez, and you asked me if we won," she marched herself to the nurse's office before last period.

The nurse, Ms. Okafor, was trying to renovate a cardboard eye chart stand that a kindergartner had body-slammed during a fire drill. "Sit," she said, pointing with a roll of tape. "Letters getting blurry, or is everything a smudge?" Kate explained about the scoreboard, and about how the whiteboard looked like it had melted a little, especially the vertical lines. Ms. Okafor hummed and flipped lenses in a funny pair of frames, asking which looked better, one or two, one or two, until Kate's answers started sounding like a coin flip.

"Astigmatism," Ms. Okafor said at last. "Your eye bends light unevenly, so the lenses have to bend it unevenly too."

"Like a magic trick?"

"Like a very boring magic trick. The district's lens kit takes two weeks, but we have a loaner pair in your prescription." She dug through a drawer that appeared to contain one glove, three lollipops, and a small civilization of rubber bands, then produced a pair of purple glasses.

The world snapped into focus so hard Kate actually said "Oh" out loud. But then she tilted her head to scratch her ear, and the doorframe stretched, tall and skinny, like taffy. She froze, then straightened up slowly, watching the doorframe go back to normal. She turned her head again, and the bulletin board's squarish border leaned and widened like something out of a funhouse.
