The bus lurched around the corner before Logan even reached his seat, and he grabbed the rail so hard his knuckles went white. Four rows back, Dex was laughing with Marcus Chen about something on Marcus's phone. Something that had happened Saturday, apparently, at the skate park. The skate park where Logan had stood alone for forty minutes, checking the entrance, before texting are you coming? and getting nothing.

"Move it, Day," said a sixth grader, and Logan slid into the seat across the aisle, backpack first. He yanked out his notebook, the one with the torn cover, and flipped past his math homework to a blank page. He was going to write it down. The whole thing. And then he was going to say it out loud, tomorrow, in the cafeteria, before his courage restricted itself to zero.

He wrote fast: You ditched me Saturday. You never even texted back. You like Marcus better now. He read it back and his stomach dropped, because even on paper it sounded like an accusation, and Dex had a reputation for shutting down the second anyone came at him. One time in third grade a kid called Dex a cheater at four square and Dex didn't talk to him for a month.

Then Logan remembered something. Last year, rainy Tuesday, library, hiding in the self-help shelf because Ms. Perrin had sent him there during indoor recess. He'd pulled down a dusty orange book just for something to read, and it had said that a psychologist named Thomas Gordon coined the term "I-message" back in the 1960s. The idea was a sentence like "I felt left out" described the speaker's own feelings instead of blaming the listener with "you." Logan had thought it was boring then. Now it felt like a combination he'd been given for a lock he'd been kicking for three days.

He crossed out every you. He wrote: I felt left out on Saturday. I waited and I felt like I didn't matter. It still said the same true thing, but it didn't point a finger. It just opened a door. He copied it onto his hand in pen, where he couldn't lose it, and the bus hissed to a stop at the corner of Fitch Street.

Dex was getting off at this stop too. Logan's heart hammered like he was about to drop in on a half-pipe. "Dex!" he called, squeezing past the sixth grader. "Wait up. One second." He caught him at the mailbox, held out his ink-covered hand like evidence, and read it, fast, before Dex's face could close: "I felt left out on Saturday. I felt like I didn't matter to you anymore."

Dex stared at the ink. "My phone died at my grandma's," he said. "Then my mom restricted me from the park for the weekend because of my grades. I was going to tell you Monday but Marcus made it sound like the best day ever and it got weird." He kicked a pebble off the curb. "You want to come over today? We still haven't landed the stair drop."

"Race you to your door," said Logan, and ran.

Arthur wanted lettuce more than anything else in the garden, because Grandpa's sandwich bread came from the bakery two towns over and the tomatoes were already coming, and lettuce was the missing piece. He measured out three beds behind Grandpa's shed, turned the soil with a fork, and planted one bed with beans pushed deep, one bed with lettuce pushed just as deep, and one bed with lettuce scattered on top of the dirt and patted down.

Every morning he watered all three beds and pressed his palm flat on the soil to feel the warmth. "You're very optimistic about that third bed," Grandpa said from the porch, watching him pat seeds he could barely see. "That's not even planting. That's seasoning."

Nine days later the beans were up in two crooked rows, fat and green. The deep lettuce bed was bare, not one sprout, and Arthur got down on his knees and dug where he remembered placing the seeds. He found them, swollen and pale and going nowhere. The shallow bed had a fuzz of green across the whole surface, tiny leaves lifting like they were stretching.

He sat back on his heels and thought about the pattern. Beans had gone deep and sprouted. Lettuce had gone deep and failed. The difference couldn't be the water, because he had watered everything the same, and it couldn't be warmth, because the dirt was warm everywhere he checked. That implied the depth itself was the thing. But depth meant one thing above all: how much light reached the seed. The beans had come up from the dark without any trouble, so dark wasn't the problem for beans. Maybe lettuce was the opposite kind of seed, a category that needed light to sprout at all, which would mean it had to sit almost on top of the soil to get any.

He tried it again to be sure. He filled two trays on the windowsill. In the first he set lettuce seeds on the surface of damp soil. In the second he buried them half an inch down, then put a shoebox over the tray so it stayed dark but just as warm and just as wet. The surface tray greened up in five days. The covered tray stayed empty until Arthur lifted the box, and then only the two seeds nearest the edge, where a stripe of sun had crept in, put up leaves.

"Beans don't care," he told Grandpa, laying the two trays side by side on the porch table. "Give them water and warm dirt and air, and they'd come up in a coal cellar. But lettuce wants the light on it, so you basically just set the seeds down and dust them over."

Grandpa leaned in and looked at the two trays, then at the green fuzz of the third bed glowing in the evening field.

"Sandwiches in three weeks," he said, and went inside to start the tomatoes.

Connor had inherited exactly two things from his grandfather so far: a watch that didn't run and a Thursday-night tutoring session at the kitchen table. The watch sat in his pocket, dead, while the retake quiz sat in his backpack, alive with danger. Tomorrow, first period. One night to finally understand equations like 3x + 4 = 19, which until now had looked to Connor like a typo.

"You're thinking of the x as a mystery," Grandpa said, sliding the sugar bowl to the middle of the table. "Don't. Think of it as something under a lid. You can't see it, but the equation is telling the truth about it. Your job is to make the lid come off without breaking the truth."

"That sounds like a fortune cookie," Connor said, but he wrote it down anyway.

Grandpa set a kitchen scale on the table, then two piles of pennies. "Whatever you do to one side, you do to the other. Take four off the left, take four off the right. The scale stays level. The truth survives." Connor tried it. He took four pennies from each side, and the little needle didn't move. Then he divided the left pile into three equal stacks and did the same to the right, and suddenly the stacks matched, and there it was, x, sitting in plain sight like it had never been hiding at all. He did three more problems on paper, whispering "same to both sides" like a password, and got every one right.

For the last problem, Grandpa pulled down his own old math notebook from the shelf, the one with the warped green cover, and found a geometry diagram to use as a break. "Old exam question," he said. "Copied off the board in 1961, if you can believe it."

Connor looked at the drawing. It was a triangle inside another triangle, and it was clearly wrong somewhere, because the exam question said two sides had to be equal, and in the drawing, one of them looked almost twice as long as the other. "Grandpa, your diagram is broken. These can't be equal."

"Can't they?" Grandpa said, and went to refill his coffee, which was his way of saying figure it out yourself.

Connor flipped back a page in the notebook and found the same triangle copied again, by Grandpa at fourteen, for practice. In that version, the two sides that supposedly matched each had a single small slash through it, and the two other sides each had double slashes, and two corners each had a little curved arc, one arc on one angle, two arcs on another. In the exam version, sixty years of page-turning had worn the marks away to nothing. Connor leaned close, then sat back. "The little slash marks," he said. "They're tick marks. Matching tick marks show sides that are equal in length." He tapped the two angles with the matching arcs. "And those arcs. Matching arcs show angles that are equal."

"So," Grandpa said.

"So the sides are equal in length even though your drawing makes them look totally different. The marks were the whole message, and they wore off." Connor copied the diagram into his own notebook, carefully, tick by tick, arc by arc, and then wrote 3x + 4 = 19 underneath it and solved it in four seconds flat.

"There's hope for you," Grandpa said, glancing at the clock, which said nine forty. "Bed. And tomorrow, when you copy the board, copy everything. Every mark. Your teacher has a chronic habit of erasing fast."

Connor pocketed the dead watch and climbed the stairs.

Colton had claimed plot fourteen at the community garden because it was the sunniest one, and he had big plans for it: three rows of carrots, two tomato plants, and a zucchini he privately intended to grow to the size of a small dog. His best friend Nadia had claimed plot fifteen, right beside his, mostly so they could argue across the fence without shouting.

Three weeks after planting, the trouble started. Colton's bed had been watered the same day as Nadia's, by the same sprinkler, but by Friday his soil had cracked into a brown checkerboard while hers stayed dark and damp. Worse, little green weed sprouts were popping up all over his rows like uninvited guests at a birthday party. Nadia leaned on the fence and grinned. "Did you plant weeds on purpose? Because they're thriving."

"I didn't plant anything," Colton said, kneeling down. He pressed a finger into her soil, then into his. Hers gave. His did not. He looked from one bed to the other, and the only difference he could see was the fluffy yellow layer of straw spread across hers like a blanket. "That's the mulch Mr. Ruiz gave you, isn't it."

"It's called mulch," Nadia said. "Straw or wood chips, either kind works."

Colton ran a hand over the straw. Underneath, her soil was cool and soft. His was baking in the sun. He borrowed a wheelbarrow, begged two bales of straw off Mr. Ruiz, and spread a layer over his whole bed, tucking it around the carrot seedlings like he was putting them to bed. "Enjoy your monarchy while it lasts," he told the weeds, "because your reign ends today."

Nadia snorted. "Weeds don't have a monarchy."

"Everything with that many subjects has a monarchy," Colton said. "I'm staging a rebellion."

The following week proved him right. When he pulled back a corner of the straw, his soil was damp, his carrots stood in straight little lines, and the only weeds he found were a few stubborn survivors pushing up at the very edge. He plucked those and dropped them over the fence into Nadia's compost bucket, one by one, like trophies.

At the fall harvest, Mr. Ruiz walked the rows with his clipboard and stopped at Colton's zucchini, which had grown to the size of a loaf of bread and was still going. "Now that's authentic gardening," he said. "You want to enter it in the fair?"

"Enter it?" Colton lifted the zucchini with both hands. "I'm going to name it King Mulch the First."

Violet sat at the end of the lakeside dock with her duffel bag squashed behind her knees, waiting for the camp bus. The bus came at noon, her father had said twice, and it was already 11:40. She pressed her palm flat against the warm boards and thought about the fire last night in the backyard, the one she had talked him into. Marshmallows, then water from the hose, then bed. She had not stirred it. She had not checked anything. Somewhere in her stomach the memory sat like a stone.

When the bus arrived, a counselor named Renata climbed out and counted heads. "Cabin Four, we make one stop before check-in," she announced. "Yesterday's group left a fire ring by the shore. We make sure it's dead before we swim or cook or do anything else, and we do it fast. Swim check is at one."

The fire ring was a circle of black stones with a heap of gray ash in the middle. A boy named Declan poked a stick at it. "It's out. It's just ash." He kicked some aside and pale flakes drifted down like dirty snow. Violet crouched and looked closer. The ash was not lying loose the way cold powder would. It was stuck together in crusts, as if something underneath had baked it into a shell, and on the upwind side the crust was thicker. That was a pattern. Something she could not see had made it.

"Renata," Violet said. "Yesterday's group watered it, probably. But look, the ash is compressed into chunks. Can I try something?" Renata handed her the metal rake. Violet broke the crust open, and a red thread glowed inside like a worm hiding in a rotten apple. The others went quiet. "It's not out at all," she said, and her stomach turned as she pictured her own backyard, the hose, the sleeping neighborhood. "My dad taught me you have to drown it, stir it, drown it again, and then feel for heat. If a fire's too hot to touch, it's too hot to leave."

They worked through lunch. Declan hauled the lake water in buckets with vigorous, splashy swings that soaked his sneakers, and Violet stirred until her arms ached, drowning each glowing pocket they uncovered. Renata pointed at the half-burned log and said the boring parts still mattered, since fungus and beetles were decomposers and even the black crumbs fed the soil, so they left the true ash in the ring and only took the danger out. Twice more Violet found hidden heat, once under a stone that had rolled over a coal. The second time, it took her a moment to believe it.

Finally she pulled her sleeve over her hand and pressed it to the middle of the drowned ash. Cool. She pressed every stone, every edge, all the way around, while Declan watched the trail for the swim check. "Cold," she reported. Renata checked behind her, then blew one long whistle blast toward the waterfront.

"Go get your suits," she said. "And Violet, you get the first off the dock."

Theodore sat in the back seat with the glow stick in his fist, trying to look like this was no big deal. Dad drove, Mom checked her mirror every few blocks like a bird watching a migratory flock cross the highway, and the gymnasium lights got closer with every turn.

"Crack it now," Mom said. "It'll be brighter by the time you walk in."

That was the problem. Theodore had cracked his glow stick two nights ago, testing it in his room, and it had already burned half its glow. His best friend Marcus had cracked his the same night, and both sticks had come from the same pack. Marcus's had died completely by morning. Theodore's was still going, but faintly, like a firefly that was getting tired.

He turned the stick over in his hand. Both sticks, same pack, same night. Marcus had kept his in the pocket of a hoodie hanging next to the radiator, the warmest spot in his room. Theodore had left his on the windowsill, where the night air leaked through the old frame. Warm stick, dead by morning. Cold stick, still glowing. He had tested it again with a third stick from the pack, one he'd held against the heater vent for ten minutes after cracking it. That one had blazed like a tiny green flare, brighter than either of theirs had ever been, and it had gone dark before dinner.

So there was a rule hiding in there somewhere. A warm stick shone brighter but ran out faster. A cold one glowed dimmer but lasted longer. If that was true, then tonight the bright sticks everyone else was cracking in the parking lot would be gorgeous for an hour and then nothing. His dim stick, if he kept it cold until the last song, might be the only one still alive.

"Variable," he said out loud, then felt his ears go red.

"What was that?" Dad asked.

"Nothing. Can you turn the AC toward the back?"

"It's forty degrees out, Theo."

"Please. It's for a science thing." That was almost true. He wrapped the glow stick in a napkin and pressed it against the cold air from the vent, budgeting its glow like the last pieces of a candy bar, saving everything for the end of the night. Mom and Dad exchanged a look in the front seat, the kind that said they knew something he hadn't figured out yet, but neither of them said it.

The gym was loud and hot and flashing. Theodore danced badly with Priya from science class, spilled punch on his own shoe, and watched, song by song, as the gym went dark in patches. First the bright orange sticks faded, then the blue ones, and by the time the slow songs started, half the kids were holding dead plastic tubes and complaining about it. When the last song began, Theodore slipped out to the car, unwrapped his stick from the napkin, and cupped it in his hands.

It was still glowing. Faint, green, stubborn, alive.

He walked back through the double doors holding it up, and Priya turned around first. Her own stick had gone black an hour ago.

"How is yours still going?" she asked. "Mine died forever ago."

"Trade secret," Theodore said. "But if you put yours somewhere cold tonight, you can find out in the morning."

"Like where?"

"The freezer," he said. "Meet me at the bus stop. If yours glows even a little, you owe me a pudding cup."

Nicolas crouched at the ramp station in the physics hall, stopwatch in one hand and a meter stick in the other, because today he was going to crack the museum's rolling ball challenge. The rules were posted right there: measure how far the silver ball travels, measure how long it takes, and mark those numbers on a distance-time graph. If his graph came out right, a green light would flash and his name would go on the wall of finishers. His friend Dex had failed twice already, and Nicolas fully intended to get his name up first.

He rolled the ball from the top of the ramp. It traveled two meters in four seconds, and he plotted the point, then rolled again from higher up. Four meters, eight seconds. Same slope. "It's a rule," Nicolas said, tapping the graph. "Distance divided by time gives you the speed, and it's the same every run." He drew a straight line through his points and the machine's screen printed SPEED: 0.5 METERS PER SECOND. The green light flashed. His name went up on the wall while Dex groaned loudly enough that a toddler turned to stare.

"You're good at dividing," Dex said, dragging Nicolas toward the circuit station across the hall. "Fix this for me." Dex had a wire connected to a meter showing 6 volts across it and 2 amps flowing through it, and a screen demanding the wire's resistance in ohms. Dex had typed 12. The screen had blinked red and said TRY AGAIN.

"Twelve?" Nicolas said.

"I multiplied six times two. Multiplying feels right. Numbers want to be multiplied."

Nicolas stared at the screen. It wanted something else. He thought about the ramp, about the principle he had just used there: you take the bigger number on top and divide by the one that tells you how much is flowing through, and what's left is the rate, the thing that resists. Why should this be different? Six volts, two amps. He punched in six divided by two.

"Three ohms," he said, and hit enter. The screen turned green and played a little chime. Dex whooped and slapped the counter so hard the wire jumped.

"That's it? Divide? That's the whole trick?"

"That's the whole trick," Nicolas said. He copied the numbers into his notebook, feeling buoyant enough to float right out of the museum, and under them he wrote the same method twice: distance divided by time, volts divided by amps. On the way out they passed the ramp station again, and Nicolas pointed at the silver ball sitting at the top, waiting for the next kid. "Two meters, four seconds," he told Dex. "You do the math."

The box was small, but Hudson's hands shook a little anyway. Inside was his first phone, dark and cool, with a screen that lit up before he even touched it. His mother had one rule, delivered while stirring soup that smelled of garlic and onions: "The family group chat is free over Wi-Fi, and the plan gives us a shared bucket of mobile data each month. Don't drain the bucket."

By Thursday, the bucket was nearly empty. Hudson knew this because his father sent a screenshot to the group chat with a single emoji, the one with the wide eyes. The numbers showed the family had used almost everything, and the month had a whole three weeks left. Hudson had only done one thing differently: every morning on the bus, he had watched videos while the heater rattled and the windows fogged up around the edges.

He sat on his bed and thought. His sister Zoe had texted constantly all week, hundreds of messages, and her name barely showed up in the usage numbers. He had watched maybe an hour of video total. Something was distinct about his phone use, something invisible. He scrolled back through the chat, counting her messages against the tiny data they used, and the pattern jumped out at him. Texts were like whispering. Video must be like shouting through a megaphone.

He decided to test it. "New plan," he typed into the group chat. "Texts only until the first of the month. No videos unless we're home on Wi-Fi." Zoe replied with a thumbs up and "finally, scientist Hudson." For a week he rode the bus with the phone in his pocket, feeling it buzz with messages, reading them instead of watching anything. He learned to compress his jokes into short texts, because "the dog ate my entire sandwich and also my homework" was funnier than three paragraphs anyway.

When the new month started, his father posted fresh numbers in the chat. With everyone texting instead of streaming away from home, the data bucket barely rippled. "Whatever you did," his father wrote, "keep doing it." Hudson grinned and typed back, "Videos eat data like Zoe eats popcorn. Texts barely take a crumb."

Zoz replied with a photo of an empty popcorn bowl and the words "Rude but accurate." Then, because the family was home and on Wi-Fi, they all pressed play at the same time on the same video, and in three different rooms of the house, the same laugh started up at the same moment.

Gabriella held the phone box on her lap all the way to the mall, tracing the picture of the phone on the lid with one finger. Her mother had one condition: prove she could handle it, and the phone stayed hers. The test started the moment they walked through the sliding doors.

"Meet me at the food court at four o'clock," her mother said, handing over the phone, already set up. "I'll be in the bookstore. If anything goes wrong, call me. That's the principle of the whole thing. A phone is for reaching people."

Gabriella agreed, but she was already distracted, because her best friend Priya was supposed to meet her at the fountain at three thirty, and Priya's mother had asked Gabriella to text when they found each other. That was her first real job with the phone. She wandered past the shoe stores, practicing, and sent Priya three texts full of exclamation points. Then she sat on the fountain's cool marble edge and waited.

Priya showed up at ten after, and they took turns taking ridiculous photos of each other with the giant plastic flamingo outside the candy shop. Then they bought pretzels and tried the game where you tilt the phone to steer a cart through a fruit stand. Gabriella noticed the battery draining fast and found a setting that seemed to save power. She tapped it on without reading carefully. After that, the afternoon blurred into window shopping, and when they finally parted at the escalator, Gabriella checked her messages to text Priya's mother. The message refused to send. She tried again. Nothing. A cold feeling crept up her neck.

At the food court, her mother was already waiting at a table, arms crossed, phone in hand. "I've been calling you for twenty minutes," she said. "Priya's mother called me in a panic because she never got your text. Where have you been?"

Gabriella's mouth went dry. "Right here. My phone just stopped sending things. I didn't do anything." Then she looked at the screen again, at the little airplane symbol in the corner, the one that had appeared right when she tapped the power-saving setting. She thought about how the phone had gone completely quiet, not one message coming in all afternoon, not even the group chat that never stopped buzzing. "Wait," she said slowly. "Airplane mode. It turns off the phone's radio signals, including the cellular connection it uses for calls and texts." She tapped it off. The screen exploded with notifications, missed calls, texts stacking up one after another.

Her mother watched the messages pile in, then held out her hand for the phone. For a long moment neither of them spoke. "You figured it out yourself," her mother said finally. "That's something. But you put the phone in that mode without knowing what it did, and you didn't check it when things went quiet." Gabriella looked down at the tiny airplane still glowing faintly on the screen before it faded away.

"Can I keep it?" she asked.

Her mother slid the phone back across the table toward her.

Carter sat in the waiting room of Dr. Okafor's office, holding his phone low so his mom wouldn't see, typing to Nadia, who had texted him from the pharmacy across the street.

"Guess what I found out," Nadia wrote. "I'm comparing face washes. There's a whole aisle. My forehead started breaking out this year and I wanted to know why, so I read the labels and looked it up. Hormones in puberty make the oil glands in your skin produce more oil. It's called sebum. The extra oil can clog your pores, and that's what leads to acne."

Carter stared at the message. So it wasn't because he'd skipped washing his face after soccer on Tuesday, which was what he'd decided at 2 a.m. last night while poking at the red bump above his eyebrow. Hormones. Things happening inside him that nobody could see, sending instructions to his skin like a radio station broadcasting to a city. He wondered what else the station was telling his body to do without asking him first.

"That's why washing more doesn't fix it," he typed back. "I've been scrubbing like it's dirt. It's not dirt. It's my own skin making too much oil."

"It's not an illusion, it's chemistry," Nadia replied. "Also there are like forty washes and they all say equivalent results on the bottle, which I doubt. Pick your book up, your mom says you're daydreaming."

He shoved the phone in his pocket. His name was called, and he followed the nurse down the hall, past a poster showing cross-sections of skin. In the exam room, Dr. Okafor looked at the bump, then at Carter's chart, then asked him a question that surprised him. "What do you think caused it?"

Carter explained, careful to get it right. Puberty, hormones, oil glands, more oil, clogged pores. Dr. Okafor smiled a little. "Where'd you learn that?"

"My friend Nadia. She was at the pharmacy."

"Well, she did her homework, and so did you." The doctor turned the light toward Carter's eyebrow again. "Here's the thing, though. That's not acne."

"It's not?"

"That's a small cyst, completely harmless, and it's going away on its own. But the acne is coming, Carter, probably starting this winter. Your feet grew two sizes in four months, your voice is doing interesting things, and bacteria that cause breakouts? They thrive right where you're headed. So let's talk about what actually works, and it's a lot easier than scrubbing."

Carter leaned forward. "Wait, say the easy part first."

Dr. Okafor pulled a sample bottle from the drawer and dropped it in Carter's hand. "Wash gently, once a day, with this."

Joshua stood in the drama room with his arms crossed, staring at his partner, Devon, who had just pretended to hand him a pizza. "No, it's not a pizza, it's a hat," Joshua said, and Devon groaned. Ms. Reyes clapped her hands and told the class to freeze, then walked to the shelf and pulled down a book so worn its cover was soft at the corners. She dropped it on Joshua's desk on her way past. "Spolin, 1963," she said. "Look it up tonight. And play the game right tomorrow."

At home, Joshua flipped through the book, Improvisation for the Theater, finding pages of games with names like "Mirror" and "Where." His mom leaned over his shoulder. "Ms. Reyes says people call it the bible of improv teaching," Joshua told her. "It collected all these theater games together, back in 1963." He kept reading, and one phrase kept appearing: accept the offer. When your partner hands you a pizza, the pizza is real because you both agree it is. Joshua wondered if that was the hidden rule behind the whole book, the pattern underneath every game. How could he test it?

The next day he decided to invest one full class period in a simple experiment: say yes to every single offer Devon made, no matter how strange, and add something new to it. Devon started the scene as an astronaut. "Yes, and the spaceship is out of fuel," Joshua said. Devon's eyebrows went up, then he leaned in. "Yes, and the fuel we need is peanut butter." "Yes, and it has to be nutritious peanut butter, for the long flight." They built a whole mission out of nothing, one agreement stacked on another, until Devon declared the spaceship had landed on a planet ruled by houseplants.

Afterward Joshua noticed something odd. When he had blocked Devon's pizza, the scene had died in seconds, like a pond going stagnant. When they kept saying yes, the scene grew, like an ecosystem where everything fed something else. He hadn't seen that rule written anywhere on one page, but it was there under all the games, holding them up.

On Friday Ms. Reyes had them perform in front of the class. Halfway through their scene, Devon grabbed an invisible microphone and said, "Breaking news, everyone, the mayor is a giant squid." Joshua felt the old reflex rise, the urge to say no, that's silly. Instead he took the microphone and turned to the class.

"Yes, and I have an exclusive interview with him right now."

Eli slid his laptop across the table so Priya could see the screen. "The enemy moves ten steps and then freezes," he said. "Every single time. I didn't tell it to stop."

Priya was supposed to be working on her ballot design for the student council election, a bright yellow sheet with checkboxes that she'd redrawn three times already because the spacing looked crooked. She leaned over anyway. "Show me."

Eli clicked the green flag. The little purple sprite marched across the stage, ten steps exactly, then stood there like it was immune to everything happening around it, while the player sprite zipped past and grabbed the coin. Eli groaned. Priya pointed at the script. "What block is that?"

"Repeat ten," Eli read. Around it sat the movement blocks, tucked inside the C-shape. He stared at it for a long moment. "Wait. Repeat ten means it runs what's inside exactly ten times. That's it. Ten, then done." He scrolled down to the player sprite's script, where the same movement blocks sat inside a forever block. The player never froze. He watched it loop again. "Forever keeps going until you stop the whole program. That's the difference. The enemy got repeat ten and the player got forever."

He fixed it in two seconds, dragging the blocks into a forever loop, and the enemy started chasing the coin without stopping. Priya went back to her ballot, muttering that the council would never comply with her suggestion to move elections to Friday, but Eli had already opened a second window. His homework was due last period: a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it's prime. He'd written it once and it printed "prime" for 9, which was wrong, and he'd been stuck since breakfast.

Then he thought about the frozen enemy. His loop checked divisors, but something about how many times it ran had gone wrong, the same kind of hidden mistake, a rule about repetition doing something he hadn't intended. He counted the numbers his loop actually tested, one by one, on paper. It stopped too early, like the sprite. He widened the range, saved, and typed 9. "Not prime." He typed 7. "Prime." He typed 25, then 23, then 97, leaning closer each time.

Priya looked up from her ballot. "Is it right?"

"Try to break it," Eli said, and slid the laptop back across the table.

Nicholas had one job before lunch: pick the photo for the robotics team's page. He scrolled through the folder on the lab computer while his friend Dex leaned over his shoulder, chewing a straw like it owed him money.

"Use the one with the robot's arm up," Dex said. "That looks awesome."

"That's the one where I dropped a piston on my foot," Nicholas said. "Look, I'm mid-hop. Nobody needs to see that." The robot itself was fine. They'd spent three weeks getting the little engine part to pump up and down, and yesterday the arm had finally moved fast enough to make Dex's little brother scream and run in a circle.

They settled on a selfie: Nicholas, Dex, and Priya on Priya's front porch, the robot held up between them like a trophy. Priya was grinning so hard her eyes were closed. Nicholas hit upload, then paused, because something about the photo itched at him. He zoomed in, dragging the image bigger until it blurred.

"What now?" Dex asked.

"Zoom out before my retinas file a complaint." But Nicholas kept going. Behind Priya's head, on the porch railing, sat a little brass number. He traced it with his finger on the screen. Her house number. And over her shoulder, the corner of a green street sign stuck into the frame.

"So?" Dex said.

"So I know her address," Nicholas said slowly. "And we're about to post this where anybody can look at it. Anybody." He thought about how he'd once found a stranger's video and figured out the kid's school just from a logo on a gym banner in the background, and how he'd felt clever, then sort of slimy.

Priya appeared behind them with a juice box. "Why are you staring at my nostrils?"

"Your nostrils are safe," Nicholas said. "Your house isn't. Somebody could zoom in on your house number and that street sign and know exactly where you live." He demonstrated, zooming until the brass numbers filled the screen like glowing digits of doom.

Priya squinted. "Huh. Okay, that's creepy."

"It's fixable," Nicholas said. He tried cropping. That cut off the robot. He tried smudging the number with the blur tool, which made the railing look like it was melting. Dex suggested drawing a mustache over the street sign, which, honestly, was tempting. Finally Nicholas angled it: they went back to Priya's porch after school, took the same photo at the bottom of the steps instead, porch rail and street sign behind the camera, and reposted it.

The new picture got forty likes by dinner. Dex commented, "Team Not-Kidnapped." Priya replied with a robot emoji, immune to his nonsense after three years of robotics club. The next morning, Mr. Alvarez paused at their lab table on his way past.

"Nice post," he said. "Clean frame, too."

Nicholas grinned and opened the folder for next week's photo. "Rule one," he said, dragging the zoom slider out to full, "we check everything at maximum magnification."

"Even my nostrils?" Priya asked.

"Especially your nostrils."

Ethan had lost the eight-hundred-metre race at the district meet twice now, and both times the same thing had happened: a strong first lap, then legs that felt like wet sand on the second. The track was closed for resurfacing, so he dragged his cones and stopwatch to the cracked basketball court behind the rec centre, where the painted lines were almost exactly two hundred metres around if you followed the fence. That was where he met Priya, the eccentric girl who swam laps in the outdoor pool on the other side of the chain-link, in a neon swim cap even when the sky was grey.

"Counting laps?" Ethan asked, watching her churn up and down.

"Counting breathers," she said, hanging on the gutter. "I take a census of the pool every Saturday. Ten swimmers. Want to know what I found?" She didn't wait for an answer. "The ones who lift their heads forward to breathe, every single one of them, their hips and legs sink lower in the water. Watch the man in the blue trunks."

Ethan stood at the fence with his heart still thumping from his timed lap, and he watched. Blue Trunks hauled his face up and forward at every breath, and each time he did, his legs dragged down until his kick was slapping the surface instead of driving under it. Two lanes over, a woman turned her head sideways to breathe instead, and her body stayed flat, cutting through the water like a blade. Priya's census had found a pattern he could see, and a rule underneath it that he couldn't: turn the head to the side, keep the body flat; lift it forward, and everything behind you sinks.

He tried to deduce what it meant for him. He couldn't see his own pacing any more than Priya could see the drag on her own legs. The hidden thing had to be tested. So he set up his plan: first lap controlled, held back, arms loose, breath steady; second lap everything he had left. His first attempt failed because the moment the stopwatch ticked past halfway, fear took over and he sprinted early, finishing empty again. The second attempt, he made a deal with himself. Count breaths, not seconds. Four steps per breath, first lap, no matter what.

He started on the far corner by the bleachers, sneakers slapping the faded paint. Around the backboard, along the fence, past the drinking fountain, and the whole first lap he held himself back while a voice screamed at him to go. Second lap, he let it out. His legs still burned crossing the final line of paint, but they carried him, and when he checked the watch his eyes went wide.

"Priya!" he shouted at the pool. "Negative split. I ran the second lap faster. What's my time? Read it to me!"

The party was in Jayla's backyard, where a strip of grass near the fence had gone arid and brown from the summer heat and the rest was worn flat by feet. Twelve kids circled a folding table set up for the plane contest. Each person launched a rubber-band-powered balsa plane, and whoever's plane stayed in the air longest won the giant chocolate bar. Eli's plane had a bright red propeller that he had wound himself, twisting the band in careful half turns, and it had already outflown everyone on the first round.

Matthew had watched Eli wind that propeller at school too, in the corner of the cafeteria where Eli always sat alone. Some kids called him "Windup" and mimicked his careful, repetitive hand movements. Matthew had laughed once, in September, before he really knew Eli. He had been thinking about that laugh all week, the way you keep poking a sore tooth.

"Second round," Jayla announced. "Same rules as before." Eli rewound his plane. It climbed, stalled, and drifted down so slowly it seemed to change its mind about landing. It beat the next three planes easily.

"We should change it," said Dylan, who had been loud about everything all afternoon. "Longest distance should count, not longest time. Time rewards planes that just float around doing nothing." His eyes flicked toward Eli, and the look conveyed exactly what he meant, even though he never said Eli's name.

A couple of kids nodded. Eli's shoulders drew in, and he started putting his plane back in its box, the cardboard closing over the red propeller like a lid over something embarrassing. Matthew felt the September laugh rise in his own throat, and this time he recognized it for what it was.

"Wait," Matthew said. His voice came out louder than he expected, and everyone turned. "Last summer at camp we changed a rule like that, halfway through a game, and the guy who suggested it won. I didn't say anything then. I just thought it was bad luck." He picked up Eli's box and set it back on the table, keeping it open. "Here's what I figured out. Agreeing on a rule before a game starts is fairer than deciding it mid-game, because nobody yet knows whether the rule will help or hurt them." He looked at Dylan. "You already know distance helps your plane. That's why you thought of it now."

Dylan's mouth opened, then closed. "It was just an idea," he muttered.

"Then suggest it before the next game," Jayla said. "We'll all vote when nobody knows who it helps. Eli, you're up for the final round."

Eli rewound the propeller, his hands steadier than before, and launched. The plane rode a breeze coming over the fence, circled the arid strip of grass twice, and came down past everyone else's marks. "Sixteen seconds," Jayla called. Eli allowed himself a small, quick smile, and Matthew found he was smiling too.

"Alright," Dylan said, pulling his own plane from his backpack. "Before the next game starts, I have a rule to propose."

Lincoln's fingers kept landing on the same three notes, and after the fifth time through the twelve-bar progression, Marcus shook his head from behind the drum kit.

"You're playing it safe, man. That was the solo equivalent of walking in a straight line."

"I know." Lincoln stared at the fretboard of the loaner guitar. Mr. Reyes had told them to improvise over the blues changes, and everyone else in seventh-period jazz band seemed able to just make things up. Lincoln could play anything written down, but the empty bars on the page terrified him, like being told to fill a pool with water you had to invent.

His dilemma was simple: he didn't know which notes were allowed. He'd been hovering on the safe ones, the ones he'd memorized, and it sounded like elevator music.

After class, Marcus stayed behind, tapping out the slow blues rhythm on the edge of the snare. "Try something reckless," he said. "Just once. Worst case, it sounds awful for a second."

Lincoln bent down to the low E string and plucked it, then plucked the A string, comparing them. Then he noticed something. The tuner app was still open on his phone from tuning up, and he held it near the low A string. It read 110. He frowned, then played the A string at the fifth fret, and the app jumped to read 440.

"That's the A the tuner calls standard," he said slowly, "and this low one is 110. Four times smaller." He climbed the frets, testing, until his finger landed on the octave, and the screen flashed 220. The note had the same warm, rounded character as the low one, only brighter. He played them back and forth, low A and high A, and they seemed to coincide perfectly, locking together like two gears.

"Listen," he said. "The low A is 110. The A one octave higher is 220. It's exactly double. If the low one vibrates 110 times a second, the octave vibrates 220." He checked the screen again, grinning. "So the A above the standard A has to be 880 times a second. Same name, double the speed."

Marcus leaned over and tapped the high fret. "So anywhere you find an A, there's a whole family of them?"

"Right." Lincoln closed his eyes and ran the progression again, and this time when the fourth bar arrived, he leapt recklessly from the low A up to its octave, letting the two related notes ring against the chord. It sounded deliberate, like he had planned it for weeks.

"That," said Marcus, hitting the crash cymbal, "is the sound of somebody improvising."

Nolan slid the printed graphs across the lab table and frowned at them. One showed monthly rainfall for the Sonoran Desert, a line so flat it barely rose off the bottom of the page. The other, for a rainforest in Borneo, spiked every single month like a row of towers. The temperature graphs looked almost backwards to him, though. The desert swung from scorching days to cold nights, while the rainforest stayed warm and steady all year. He was supposed to write a comparison paragraph by Friday, and so far his paper held one sentence and a smear of eraser.

"I don't get why the wet place has steady temperature and the dry one goes wild," he confessed to Priya, who sat next to him collecting beakers from the cabinet marked flammable, since Mr. Ruiz had asked her to help straighten up after last period's experiment.

Priya set down a bottle. "Can I see?" She leaned over his graphs, then pulled out a pencil. "Think of it like this. Try flipping what you're looking for. Instead of asking why the desert swings, ask what the rainforest has every single day that the desert doesn't." She tapped the rainfall towers. "Test something. Cover the rainfall graph with your hand and look at just the temperatures."

Nolan covered the towers. The rainforest temperature line rolled along, month after month, barely wobbling. He uncovered the rainfall, then covered it again, comparing. "Water," he said slowly. "The rainforest gets water all year, and the desert gets almost none. So the pattern in one graph goes with the pattern in the other." It wasn't in his textbook paragraph yet, but it was a real connection, and he wrote it down fast before it could evaporate.

"See, you did that yourself," Priya said. "I didn't tell you anything." She had become his unofficial mentor on projects ever since they were lab partners in the fall, and she was generous about it, never making him feel slow.

As he drafted his paragraph, he glanced at her rainforest poster, the one she'd made after her trip. "Hey, what's that line in your photo? The brass stripe on the ground, with all those people standing on it."

"That's the prime meridian," she said. "Zero degrees longitude, right through the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London. An international conference picked it, and get this, the conference was in Washington, D.C., in 1884. I stood on it."

Nolan laughed. "So the world's zero line runs through London, but it was decided in America?" He copied the rainfall numbers into his notebook, lined them up beside the temperatures, and started his second draft, the pencil scratching steadily through the towers.

Owen stood on the Hendersons' back porch with a sticky note in his hand, copying the street address off a letter that sat on the kitchen counter. Mrs. Henderson had her keys out and one foot in her car already, because she and her husband had a long commute to the dinner where she worked, but Owen had remembered something from the babysitting class at the community center. The instructor had said that when you call for help in an emergency, the dispatcher usually asks for the address first, before anything else, so a babysitter should always know the exact address of the house. Owen had gotten that wrong once, on a quiz, and he had never forgotten it. So he wrote 42 Maple Court on his note and taped it next to the phone, just in case.

The little girl he was watching, Priya, was four, and she wanted to be in the backyard immediately. She wore a synthetic superhero cape that made a loud swishing sound when she ran, and she ran a lot. "I'm saving the ants," she announced, crouching by the fence with a magnifying glass. "This one's hurt." Owen knelt beside her. The ant was dragging a crumb and moving fine, but Priya pointed at a spot on its back. "It has a microbe," she said solemnly. Owen had learned about microbes in science, tiny living things too small to see, and he told her that was probably just dirt. She considered this, then decided the ant needed a hospital made from a flowerpot.

They built the hospital. They dug a small hospital sign into the dirt with a spoon. Priya decided the doctor was a pebble. It was going well until she stood up too fast, tripped over the flowerpot, and landed hard on the gravel border. There was a moment of silence, the worst kind, and then a cut above her eyebrow started bleeding and she cried in a scared, gulping way that made Owen's chest go tight.

He carried her inside, pressed a clean towel against the cut the way the class had taught him, and looked at the bleeding and at her pale face. It was longer than a bandage could hold, and he thought it might need stitches. His hands wanted to shake, but he made himself pick up the phone. He dialed the emergency number and said, "Forty-two Maple Court. That's the address of the emergency. A little girl cut her head and she's awake." The dispatcher's voice was calm and steady, and she asked her questions next, and an ambulance came with its lights quiet, no siren.

Mrs. Henderson sent Owen a letter two days later, because she said he wrote things down and she did too. "Priya got three stitches and a popsicle," she wrote. "She told the doctor her ant was also hurt and needed a bed. You called in the address before anything else, and the paramedics said that saved time when it mattered. You will babysit for us whenever you want, and Priya has already asked if the pebble doctor can come too."

The next Saturday, Owen was back in the same backyard, and the flowerpot hospital was still standing in the grass, a little crooked. Priya ran up in her swishing cape with a bandage above her eyebrow and held out her magnifying glass. "New patient," she said, pointing at a beetle. "This one's a big one."

Lily crouched beside the creek with a plastic cup, her brother Marcus pacing the bank behind her with his fishing rod. He wanted the good spot downstream, but she had claimed this bend because the water ran fast over a shelf of packed sand, and she needed to know something before Saturday.

Her problem was real: at the campfire program, each kid had to explain how the river far below the overlook had carved a canyon through solid rock over millions of years. Lily could say "erosion" because the word was on the park sign, but she could not picture it, and she did not want to stand up and recite something she did not understand.

She scooped water and poured it in a thin stream onto the edge of the sand shelf. The water dug a small channel. She poured again at the same spot, and again, and the channel deepened and widened. Bits of sand traveled with the current and settled in a flat fan where the water slowed. Twenty pours later, a miniature canyon curved through the shelf, and a tiny delta of debris sat at its mouth. Tumbling grains, over time, could cut rock the way her cup had cut sand. She wrote the sequence in her notebook: water moves material, drops it where it slows, repeats.

That night, the sun still sat above the pines at nine o'clock, and lights-out came while the sky glowed. Lily's bunkmate Dana complained that bedtime before dark made no sense. Lily pulled the letter her friend Priya had mailed before the trip out of her pack. Priya lived in Chile and had written, "It is winter here. Dark at six. You are tilted toward the Sun, so your days are longer than ours, and the extra hours of sunlight keep warming your ground." Lily read it aloud twice, then said, "Our half of the world is tilted toward the Sun right now. That's why the days are so long and the ground stays warm after dinner." Dana considered this, then pulled her sleeping bag over her ears to insulate herself against the mosquitoes and went to sleep.

At the program, Lily held up her notebook and described the pour test, the channel, the fan of dropped sand, and millions of years. A ranger nodded and added that a canyon is never finished, because every living organism in the soil and every flood keeps loosening more material for the water to carry.

Afterward Marcus said, "Fine, you figured out your rock thing. Can we go now? The fish are biting." Lily packed her cup, and they ran down the trail toward the water.

The Sunset Lake camp newspaper club was supposed to meet for one hour, but today forty minutes of it had already vanished into an argument about whether the club should spend its budget on popsicles or ice cream sandwiches. Jasmine tapped her pencil against her knee and watched Theo, who sat in the corner sketching beetles in his notebook while the other kids laughed about his bug collection. "Theo the roach boy," Drew said under his breath, and two kids snickered.

Jasmine's instinct was to shout at Drew right there, but last summer she'd tried that at school and it had only made the teasing worse, like pouring soda on a campfire and watching it flare. So she forced herself to think instead. Something was off about this meeting. It wasn't just Drew being mean, it was that the whole meeting had no shape, no order, and when there was no order, whoever talked loudest ran everything, and quiet kids like Theo got trampled.

After the meeting she marched to the craft cabin and found a Latin word book on the shelf, because her older sister was always going on about Latin. There it was: agenda, a Latin word meaning "things to be done." A meeting agenda lists the topics in the order they will be discussed. Jasmine read it twice, then grinned so wide her face hurt. That was the hidden rule. Tonight's meeting had gone off the rails because nobody had written down what needed discussing, so snacks ate forty minutes and the club's real business never even started.

The next morning she wrote a plan on a napkin. If she put "club budget" first on a written agenda and "snacks" last, the loud snack crowd couldn't hijack the meeting. And if she added one more item, "Everyone's story ideas," Theo would get a guaranteed turn to speak, in order, without having to fight for it. It was a test, and she couldn't wait to run it.

"Before we start," Jasmine announced that afternoon, holding up her napkin, "I made an agenda. It's a Latin word meaning things to be done, and it lists the topics in the order we'll discuss them." She read it out: budget first, story ideas second, snacks last. Drew groaned about the snacks, but the others nodded, and when it was Theo's turn, he opened his beetle notebook and described how a stag beetle could grip a stick for hours without letting go. "Cool," said one of the kids who had laughed yesterday. Then Theo looked straight at Drew and said, "You can come see my collection after swim time, if you want."

Drew shrugged, but he was already gathering his towel. "Okay. But only if there are snacks."

The Saturday maths clinic at the community centre met in a room with a foosball table nobody was allowed to touch, which struck Bentley as eccentric, since the centre had put it there in the first place. He spread out his worksheet at a wobbly table by the window. At the top, in his teacher's handwriting, was the problem: prove the two triangles congruent by side-angle-side, then show that the third sides are equal without measuring them.

Bentley could do the first part. He had drawn both triangles side by side, marked off two matching sides and the angle squeezed between them, and written his statement in the careful three-column format his teacher demanded. Side, angle, side. SAS. Done. It was the second part that annoyed him. Without measuring. His ruler sat right there in his pencil case, and someone had told him not to use it, which made him want to use it very badly.

Across the table, Priya was building a tower out of borrowing slips. She glanced at his paper. "You've proved they're congruent," she said. "So?"

"So now I have to prove the last sides match, and I'm not allowed to measure."

"That's the whole point, though, isn't it?" Priya dropped a slip on her tower. "If you've proved the triangles are exactly the same triangle, then the rest of it comes free."

Bentley frowned at his drawing. He tried an experiment. He traced triangle one onto tracing paper, then slid it over triangle two. It landed perfectly, corner on corner, line on line. The triangles were the same shape, the same size, identical in every part. He hadn't measured the third side. He hadn't needed to. Once the triangles matched, everything in them matched, including the one side he cared about. There was a principle at work here, and he was fairly sure it had a name, because everything in this unit had a name.

He checked the back page of his textbook, where the glossary lived. CPCTC. He said it out loud once, like a sneeze. "Corresponding parts of congruent triangles are congruent," he read, and under that he wrote the five letters in the reason column of his proof. His teacher would like that. His teacher liked reasons more than answers.

Priya leaned over. "CPCTC," she read off his page. "Sounds like a band nobody's heard of."

"It's better than measuring," Bentley said. "You prove three things, and you get the fourth one for nothing." He looked at the worksheet again, then at the three problems below it, the ones he'd been dreading. Each of them wanted the same trick: prove two triangles congruent first, then use that to drag out whatever else you needed. He began to devise a plan for problem four, which had triangles hiding inside a bigger triangle, like a puzzle inside a puzzle. Find the matching sides and angle. Write SAS. Then let CPCTC carry the rest of the weight.

He worked through the remaining problems while Priya's tower of borrowing slips grew steadily less stable beside him. On the last problem, the two triangles shared a side, and he realized the shared side counted as a matching side all by itself, one less line to write. He underlined his final CPCTC, closed his workbook, and, on his way out, gave the foosball table a slow, respectful spin.

Austin first noticed the ad during math homework, when his phone buzzed three times in a row. The group chat, Titans Forever, had gone from weekend plans to something called Vortex Fuel, a sports drink everyone suddenly had to try. Dev sent a photo of himself holding a can. Then Marcus. Then four other guys in a row, each one typing "everyone's switching" or "you're the only one left, Austin."

He typed back a question mark and got a wall of replies. The messages called the drink "legendary," "insane," "the future." One guy pasted a clip of a basketball player Austin had never heard of saying Vortex Fuel was the only thing he trusted. The chat moved so fast that Austin felt like the last kid on earth who hadn't bought one.

The next morning at school, Mrs. Okafor's class took the bus to the history museum for the World War II unit. Austin trailed behind Dev and Marcus, still hearing about Vortex Fuel, until the class stopped in front of a wall of old posters. One showed a crowd of smiling workers, all marching the same direction. Another used glowing words like "strong," "pure," and "betrayal" for anyone who disagreed. A third had a film star's face on it.

"There's a fact card here," Dev said, reading off the display. "In March 1933, Joseph Goebbels became head of Nazi Germany's new Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda." He said the word "propaganda" out loud, then said it again, slower, like it tasted strange.

Austin stared at the crowd poster. Everyone marching together, no one asking why. Glowing words stacked against plain ones. A famous face doing the convincing. He pulled out his phone and opened the chat, scrolling up through two hundred Vortex messages with new eyes. It wasn't random at all. It was the same moves, just selling a drink instead of a government.

At lunch he ran a test. He posted, "Vortex Fuel is the official drink of people who can't think for themselves," and waited. The replies split. Half the guys kept chanting "everyone's switching." But three of them stopped, went quiet, and one, Priya's brother Sam, sent a private message: "Okay, that poster thing got to me too. I only wanted it because everyone else did."

Austin wrote back, "Same. I almost begged my mom for five dollars last night." He told Sam he'd felt that pull without knowing where it came from, and Sam confessed he'd already bought two cans, both untouched in his locker. After school they traded screenshots of the wildest messages, sorting them into piles: bandwagon, loaded words, celebrity. "Eleven of these just say 'everyone,'" Sam said. "Nine use the word 'weak' for people who don't drink it."

Mrs. Okafor walked past their bench and glanced at the screen. "Homework or mischief?" she asked. Austin held up the phone so she could see the sorted list. She read it, nodded once, and kept walking. Sam typed one more message into the main chat, short and plain: "Drink whatever you want. Just count the tricks first." Below it, Dev replied with a single eye-roll emoji, and then, a minute later, a photo of himself drinking water.

The spreadsheet on Mom's office monitor looked like a city seen from a plane, all neat blocks and numbered streets. Alexis had come to work with her because the school heater had died, though Mom's building kept its thermostat so low that Alexis wore her coat indoors anyway. "I need you busy for an hour," Mom said, "so let me show you something real." She pulled up a list of orders and taught Alexis to type =SUM(B2:B14) into a cell, then click Insert Chart and watch bars rise out of the numbers like a skyline. Alexis made one for fun: her allowance saved each month since September.

She was dragging the bar for November taller when her phone buzzed. A message from the game company, and it didn't sound like the usual cheerful nonsense: "Your account was accessed from a new device at 3:14 a.m. If this wasn't you, change your password and contact support." Someone had spent her gems, all 4,300 of them, saved since summer.

Alexis's stomach dropped. The password on that account was the same one she used on a fan forum, and last month the forum had emailed everyone that it had been breached. She'd shrugged it off then, figuring nobody cared about a site where people argued about dragons. Now she sat very still, staring past the glowing bars.

At the desk across the aisle, Mom's coworker Dev was eating noodles and reading the message over her shoulder, which felt invasive, but his voice was kind. "What's it called when they do that?" Alexis asked, because she half remembered a word from a poster in the hallway here. "Credential stuffing," Dev said, and went back to his noodles.

So that was the rule, she thought, and she could test it like a formula. Attackers take usernames and passwords leaked from one site and try them automatically on many other sites. One reused password could unlock several accounts. She opened a new sheet and made two columns, Site and Same Password, then a third row of bars for how many accounts shared each password. The chart told the truth her memory had fuzzed over: the dragon forum's password sat on four other accounts too, including her email.

She thought about the afternoon she'd set it all up, lazy and pleased with herself, one password to remember. She couldn't decide if she'd been careless or just eleven. Maybe both judgments were true at once.

She changed the password on her email first, then the game, then the rest, typing until her fingers ached. Then she dragged the chart with the four tall bars over to Mom's screen, next to the orders. "Look," she said. "This is why I got hacked." Mom tilted her head, reading the little skyline of trouble, and pulled her chair closer.

Layla had forty dollars and one hour before her mom picked her up at the food court. She wanted the Starlet sneakers, the purple ones with the silver stripe, and she had seen them the second she walked past the shoe store window. Inside, a screen above the shelves played the same commercial over and over: the rapper Dez Flow sprinting down a hallway in the sneakers, saying they were the only shoe he trusted. Two girls beside Layla pointed at the screen. "Everybody at school has these," one said. "You're literally the last person."

The price tag read seventy-five dollars. Layla counted her money again in her pocket. Forty. She could speculate about asking her mom for the rest, but her mom would ask why she needed them, and the honest answer was that everyone had them and Dez Flow said they were great, which even Layla could hear was not much of a reason.

She drifted toward the grocery aisle of the mall's big drugstore, where her little brother Omar was supposed to be picking a cereal with the ten dollars their mom had given him. He stood holding a box with a red banner that shouted ALL-NATURAL GOODNESS across the top. "This one," he said. "It's natural. That means it's good for you." Layla took the box from him and turned it over. The ingredient list ran eleven lines long, and the third word was sugar, followed later by three other syrups. "Natural" was on the front but nowhere on the back, and nothing on the box said what "goodness" meant or how anyone could check it.

"Where'd you learn to do that?" Omar asked. "Mom's hygiene teacher thing," Layla said. "She had a poster. Vague, positive words like natural or freedom that just make you feel good without saying anything specific. Glittering generalities." Omar frowned at the box. "So the front is basically lying." "Not lying," Layla said. "Just not saying anything." She looked at the boxes on either side: PROVEN TRUST, PURE ENERGY, REAL QUALITY. Every one of them sounded strong and meant nothing she could test. She realized the shoe ad had done the same thing. Dez Flow trusted the shoes. Trusted them to do what, exactly? He never said.

Omar put the red box back and picked one whose ingredient list started with whole grain oats and had six lines total. Then he tugged her sleeve. "You still want the purple ones." "Everyone has them," Layla said, and heard herself. The store's own speaker was playing a jingle with the words "Join the movement," which was the same trick in a different hat.

She walked back to the shoe store and found a plain pair, purple without the silver stripe, on the clearance rack for thirty-eight dollars. She tried them on, walked a circle, and paid. Outside the store she sat on a bench, laced them tight, and put her old shoes in the box.

When Omar arrived with his cereal, he pointed at her feet. "Those aren't the ones everybody has." "Nope," Layla said, and stood up. "Race you to the food court."

Payton sat at Grandpa's kitchen table with his old laptop open in front of her, the screen showing the little program she had typed. It asked for a number, then checked every number from 2 up to the one you entered, looking for a divisor. If it found none, it printed "prime." She needed it to work by Sunday, because her computer club was having a showcase and she had promised Ms. Ruiz a demo. Grandpa slurped his coffee behind her, unhelpful and cheerful about it.

She typed 9 and got "not prime," which was right. She typed 7 and got "prime," also right. Then she typed 2, and the screen said "not prime." Payton frowned and leaned closer, as if the answer might change if she stared hard enough. The kitchen smelled like burnt toast from Grandpa's third attempt at breakfast.

"That's wrong," she said. "Two has to be prime." She traced the loop in her mind, the invisible path the program took. Start at 2, divide the input by 2, then 3, then upward. With an input of 2, the first number it tried was 2 itself, and 2 divided by 2 left nothing over, so her code said "not prime." The bug was hidden inside the loop, where she couldn't see it, but she could see its footprint on the screen.

She tried an idea: stop the loop before it reaches the number itself, so the program only tests divisors smaller than the input. She exhale'd slowly through her nose, changed one character, and ran it again. Two came back "prime." She pumped her fist, and Grandpa raised his coffee mug like a diplomat sealing a treaty, which is what he called it whenever she and the computer reached an agreement.

Then she tried 4, and it said "not prime," and 6, and 8, and 10, all "not prime," every single one. Payton sat back and looked at the pattern building up in her notebook, a cumulative list of results running down the page. "Every even number after 2 fails," she said slowly. "Because they can all be divided evenly by 2." Two was the only even prime there was. Her whole notebook suddenly made sense, prime down one column, not prime down the other, and the evens sat stubbornly on the wrong side except for that one lonely 2 at the top.

She wrote a comment in the code so she would remember, then added one more line so the program would say something special when someone entered 2. Grandpa leaned over her shoulder, toast in hand. "Try yours truly's favorite number," he said. She typed in 2 and hit enter, and the screen glowed back at them: "Prime. The only even one."

Ethan had budgeted his Saturday down to the minute: two hours at the community kitchen to bake biscuits for tonight's family dinner, because Mom had picked up an extra shift and there was no money for takeout this week. The kitchen smelled like the bread Mr. Alvarez had left cooling on the rack, and Ethan spread his flour, butter, and the recipe card Mom had written out in her slanted handwriting. Everything was going fine until he opened the tin marked BAKING POWDER and found it empty, except for a few pale dustings on the bottom.

He stared into the tin as if more powder might appear. Under the counter, though, sat a box of baking soda, and on the side of it, in cheerful letters, were the words "bakes up light and fluffy." Close enough, he decided, and measured out exactly what the recipe asked for.

That was his first mistake, though he didn't know it yet.

While he cut the butter into the flour, his friend Dani arrived, dragging her little brother Marcus, who wanted, more than anything in the world, to be allowed to crack an egg. "One egg," Marcus said. "I've cracked an egg at home. Twice." Ethan had seen the results of one of those attempts, a biscuit bowl full of shell fragments, so he handed Marcus a spoon and the job of stirring the milk, which Marcus accepted with the expression of someone being asked to scrub floors.

The dough went into the oven, and Ethan washed up, pleased with himself. It was Dani, peering at the recipe card, who frowned. "Why does it say baking powder here, if you used soda?" Ethan shrugged. "Same thing, basically." She didn't look convinced, and the more he thought about it, the less convinced he got. He remembered last month, when Mom made buttermilk pancakes and reached for the soda box on purpose. Buttermilk. That was tangy. His biscuit recipe had nothing tangy in it at all, just flour, butter, milk, salt, and the powder in question. Something wasn't matching up.

He found Mrs. Okoye, who ran the kitchen on Saturdays, restocking the spice shelf, and asked her point blank. "Baking powder already contains both baking soda and a dry acid," she said, "so it can make batter rise without an acidic ingredient in the recipe." She said it like she was reading a grocery list, then went back to her shelf, leaving Ethan standing there with the whole problem suddenly clear. His soda had no partner. It was sitting in the oven with nothing to react with, as useless as Marcus's spoon.

The biscuits came out flat and dense, like pale hockey pucks. Marcus bit one anyway and announced, "Tastes like glue," which was harsh but not entirely wrong. Ethan refused to be defeated by an obstinate biscuit. He checked the fridge, found a carton of buttermilk someone had donated, and started over, this time swapping the regular milk for buttermilk so the soda would have something to work with. The second batch rose golden and tall, and when he pulled them out, Marcus grabbed the biggest one and held it up like a trophy. "I stirred that," he said.

Samantha had the kitchen table to herself until four o'clock, which was exactly how she wanted it. Her geometry curriculum had reached the chapter on congruent triangles, and tomorrow's math club meeting would be a race. Her friends Priya and Marcus had agreed on the rules: one proof, side by side, first one to finish every reason wins the last slice of Mrs. Alvarez's lemon cake. She set out her paper, drew a vertical line down the middle, and wrote the word STATEMENTS on the left side and REASONS on the right.

"The whole point," Marcus had said at lunch, "is that anyone can check your work. Every statement on the left needs a reason on the right, like a given fact or a rule." He'd waved his fork for emphasis. Priya had nodded so vigorously that her ponytail had knocked over the milk, and the cafeteria lady had to console her about the spilled carton for a full minute before she stopped apologizing.

Samantha wrote her first statement: triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF. Below it she'd need the statements in order, and the reasons across from each one. She had copied a practice problem from the book, two triangles with the marks that showed which sides matched. She knew the rule she was aiming for, side-angle-side, but knowing it and proving it were different animals. On the left she wrote that AB equals DE. On the right, across from it, she wrote "given." Then BC equals EF, and again "given." She paused at the third line, because the angles between those two sides also had to match, and she couldn't remember if the problem gave her that or if she had to earn it.

She tested a simple idea: cover the right column with her hand and read only the left side, like a stranger would. A stranger would see statements but no reasons, which proved nothing. She slid her hand away. Ah. The angle information was a given fact, listed right there in the problem, and she had skipped it in her rush. She added the line, then wrote her final reason: side-angle-side. The triangles had to be congruent, even though she couldn't see them standing in her kitchen, because the rule worked whether the triangles were drawn on paper or hiding somewhere invisible. That was the part she liked best, like a detective proving who took the last cookie without ever seeing it happen.

When Priya and Marcus arrived at four, they set up the race with a kitchen timer shaped like a rooster. Marcus filled his reasons so fast he wrote "given" three times on the same line, then had to cross it out. Priya beat him by a whole statement.

"Side-angle-side," Priya read off her paper, "for the win."

Samantha pushed the lemon cake toward her and started the rooster timer again, just to hear it crow.

The week before camp, Felix had sat in Dr. Okafor's office with his mom, twisting the paper on the exam table while she explained why he'd been snapping at everyone and lying awake till midnight. "It's stress, and honestly, some of it is puberty," she'd said. He'd asked, embarrassed but curious, what actually tells the body it's time for all that. "The pituitary gland," she'd said, tapping her own forehead. "It's in the brain, and it signals the ovaries or the testes to make more estrogen or testosterone." She'd shown him slow breathing, four counts in, six out, and told him sleep liked a routine. He'd rolled his eyes. Then he'd tried it, alone, that night, and slept.

Now it was the second day of the canoe trip, and Felix could feel the same pressure building. His palms were sweaty on the paddle, his jaw was tight, and he kept imagining the rapids around the bend even though their counselor, Raina, had already said the water was calm. He made himself check the evidence instead of the worry: nobody was yelling, the canoes were spaced out, and Raina was paddling backward so she could watch everyone. The danger wasn't imminent. His body just hadn't figured that out yet.

"Water break," Raina called, guiding them toward a gravel bank. While the others refilled bottles, Felix pulled out the note his mom had tucked into his dry bag. "Proud of you for going," he read. "When your chest gets tight, remember: that's your body budgeting for a fight that isn't coming. Spend the energy on breathing instead. Love, Mom." He grinned despite himself. She'd stolen Dr. Okafor's trick and made it her own.

He and Marcus had formed a quiet alliance on the bus, agreeing to share snacks and watch out for each other. Now Marcus slid down beside him on the rocks. "You looked kind of freaked out back there," Marcus said. "Rapids," Felix admitted. "Fake ones. My brain made them up." He held up a hand, breathed in for four, out for six, and did it three times, right there in front of Marcus, which felt braver than any rapid. His shoulders dropped about an inch. "That actually works?" Marcus asked. "Try it," Felix said.

That night at the campsite, Felix set up his routine the way he'd practiced at home: mat flattened, same spot near the fire, phone flashlight dimmed and turned away, one page of his comic, then lights out. His brain still buzzed with the day, but he noticed something. On the night before camp, when he'd skipped the routine and stayed up worrying, the buzzing had won. Tonight, with the breathing already done and the pattern kept, the buzzing thinned out like fog over the lake.

In the morning Marcus plopped down next to him at breakfast, holding out a piece of burnt toast. "I did the four-and-six thing when I heard a raccoon at two a.m.," Marcus said. "Then I slept like a rock." Felix took the toast and grinned. "Told you."

Tyler had one goal in social studies: convince the class to vote for a hot dog stand at the spring fair instead of the usual pizza booth. Ms. Okafor had taped a hand-drawn poster to the dilapidated portable podium, the one with the wobbly leg, and written "Mock Election" across it in blue marker.

"Twenty-four students," she announced. "Four choices on the ballot: pizza, hot dogs, sushi, tacos. First past the post. Highest total wins."

They voted. Pizza got ten, hot dogs got eight, sushi got three, tacos got three. Tyler slumped. "Hot dogs lost by two," he groaned, and his friend Priya patted his shoulder like he was a sad balloon.

Then Lena, whose cousins had enrolled in a school in Munich last fall, raised her hand. "My cousins were telling me about elections in Germany. They use proportional representation, where seats get shared out to match how people actually voted. And their constitution is weird in a cool way. It's called the Basic Law, from 1949, and Article 1 starts with 'Human dignity shall be inviolable.' Like, that's the very first sentence of the whole country."

"Human dignity is inviolable, but my hot dogs got robbed," Tyler muttered, which made Priya laugh so hard she snorted.

Ms. Okafor grinned. "Let's test Lena's idea, then. Tyler, suppose your class of twenty-four gets six committee seats. Proportional representation means you divide the seats by the votes. Try it on the board."

Tyler walked up, marker squeaking. If six seats matched twenty-four voters, then four voters were worth one seat, so ten votes meant two and a half seats, eight votes meant two, three votes meant half. "Pizza still gets the most," he admitted, "but it's not a landslide anymore. Pizza gets two and a half seats out of six. In first past the post, pizza got everything and fifty-eight percent of us got nothing."

"Precisely," Ms. Okafor said. "Different rules, different winners, same voters."

"So the rule is the hidden thing," Tyler said slowly, tapping the board. "It's not that people changed their minds. It's that the counting changed." He looked back at Lena. "Your cousins' constitution puts dignity first. Maybe fair counting is part of that."

"Deep," said Priya. "Still no hot dogs."

At recess Tyler sat on the plateau behind the portables, the flat grassy spot everyone called the Snack Hill, and sketched a new ballot on his binder: rank your choices one to four. "Tomorrow I pitch ranked counting," he told Priya. "Round two."

"Good luck," she said, stealing his last nacho. "Democracy is delicious."

Alyssa had twelve minutes left to draw a labeled cell diagram, and her microscope showed nothing but gray darkness. She had sliced a chunk of onion from the salad container in her bag, laid it on the slide, and pressed her eye to the lens, but no matter how she turned the fine focus, nothing appeared. Behind her, Marcus was already sketching fast, and the clock above the door said 1:48. The bell would ring at 1:59, and Mrs. Okoye collected the lab sheets at the door.

"Move over," said Priya, nudging her. "You probably cut it too thick. Light can't get through a big slab of onion."
