"Then I'll eliminate the slab and try something thinner," Alyssa said. She peeled the onion chunk apart with her fingernails until she found the papery layer inside, the one so thin it was almost invisible, like a scrap of shrink wrap. She snipped a tiny square of it, dropped it on a fresh slide with a bead of iodine, and lowered the cover slip. When she looked again, the gray darkness was gone. Instead, row after row of cells spread across the circle of light, each one a neat brick with a dark dot near its middle.

"It's the inner skin," Alyssa said. "It's only one cell thick, so the light passes through it and you can see single cells." She said it quietly, almost to herself, because she had just figured out why her first slide had failed and this one worked.

"Quick, label it," Priya said. "You have like eight minutes." Alyssa found the outer edge of each cell, the rigid line that kept its shape, and wrote cell wall. Just inside it, she traced the thinner boundary and wrote membrane. Then she tapped the dark dot. "That has to be the nucleus," she said. "It's in every single one, same place." She checked three cells in a row to make sure the pattern held before she committed it to her diagram, because guessing on a lab sheet was the equivalent of not answering at all.

Marcus leaned over from the next stool. "How'd you get yours so clear? Mine's all blobs."

"Use the inner skin, not a chunk," Alyssa said, sliding her spare slide across the counter to him. "You have time. I did mine in six minutes." She went back to her drawing, adding the last labels in careful print as the second hand swept toward the twelve. Mrs. Okoye began walking the aisles, and Alyssa wrote her name at the top just as the teacher's shadow fell across her desk.

"Nice cells, Alyssa," Mrs. Okoye said, tapping the nucleus on her diagram. "This one goes in the portfolio."

"One day I'm going to write a memoir about this class," Alyssa said, "and this page will be chapter one." She handed in her sheet and grinned at Marcus, who was still hunched over his new slide, whispering, "Come on, cell wall, show up."

The moving truck rattled over a seam in the highway, and Madison's box of keepsakes slid an inch toward the back door. She was riding between her mother and a lamp shaped like a flamingo, because the family car had been sold two weeks early and there had been no other seat. Through the gap in the rolled-down door she watched telephone poles flick past like fence pickets, counting them to keep her mind off the last thing her best friend Priya had said: "You'll forget us by Christmas."

At a rest stop, Madison dug through the keepsake box until she found the photograph of Maple Street, all six kids from number 14 through 22 lined up on the curb after the snowball battle of last February. She held it up to the truck's open door so the light could reach it, and to her annoyance her eyes stung and a tear dropped right onto Priya's snow boot. She wiped it with her sleeve and frowned at herself. She was not hurt. Nobody had died. She had simply woken up that morning in a motel with a ceiling she didn't recognize, and the strange ceiling had followed her all day like a shadow.

"Traffic's consistent on this route," her mother said, climbing back into the cab with two bottles of juice. "Stop and go, stop and go." Madison didn't answer. She was thinking about something else, a pattern she was trying to pin down. Her grandmother had cried at the airport when she flew back to Tucson last summer, and by the time she video-called in September she had been laughing about her tomato plants. Her cousin Dev had refused to eat for two days at sleepaway camp, and by day ten he'd been the one leading songs at the bonfire. It was as if the sadness of leaving wasn't about the place itself. It was about being away from familiar people, and it seemed to have a shape, a beginning and a middle and, if you waited, an end.

"It's called homesickness," her mother said quietly, noticing the photograph still in Madison's hand. "It's what being away from home does to you. Almost everybody gets it after a move." Madison nodded and slid the picture back into the box, but she didn't put the lid on. She had a theory forming, and she intended to test it the way she tested things: by collecting evidence.

The evidence would have to come from the new town. They arrived on a Thursday, and the new house smelled like paint and strangers. On Friday Madison sat on her unmade bed and felt the ceiling pressing down, unfamiliar and gray, and she wrote in her notebook: Day One, terrible. On Saturday she met the girl across the street, a tall kid named Rosa who was trying to teach her dog to catch a frisbee in the maple canopy overhead, tossing it low so it skimmed under the leaves. Rosa missed every throw, and the dog just sat down, and somehow this made Madison laugh until she had to lean on the fence.

"You laugh at everything or just at Badger?" Rosa asked.

"Just at dogs who don't catch things," Madison said, and realized she had gone a whole hour without thinking about Maple Street.

By the following week she had filled a page with her data. Day one, terrible. Day three, medium. Day five, she had eaten two helpings of noodles at Rosa's house while Rosa's brothers argued about which birds migrate farther, geese or Arctic terns, and Madison had said terns and been right. Day eight, she had waved at the mail carrier and known his name was Frank. The pattern held exactly the way her grandmother's and Dev's had. The sadness wasn't permanent; it drained away as the town filled up with familiar things, and familiar people, and ceilings she recognized. On day nine she taped the photograph of Maple Street to her wall, right next to a blurry new one of Rosa and Badger and the frisbee stuck in the maple branches.

That evening her phone buzzed. It was a message from Priya: a picture of the old curb, empty, with the caption "You there?" Madison typed back, "Here. You won't believe where this frisbee is stuck," and attached the photo.

The gym smelled like floor wax and pencil shavings, and every folding table held a little paper tent with a school name on it. Lea had come to argue that school uniforms should be required, and she had a binder full of evidence for it. Her first-round opponent, a boy named Owen from Riverside, had already beaten her once in the fall, so she wanted this one badly.

Between rounds, a woman with a clipboard announced a fun event called improv, two debaters per team, no prep time. Lea signed up mostly because her friend Priya dared her to. But when the pairings were posted, Lea saw the twist: her partner was Owen. Her opponent. In the improv round they would have to build a scene together, taking turns adding to it, and the rule on the board said every offer had to be accepted with "yes, and."

They drew the prompt "lost in a museum after closing." Owen started. "We're locked in, and the dinosaur skeleton is winking at us." Lea's instinct was to deny it, to say dinosaurs don't wink, because in debate you attack the other side's claim. Then she thought about the rule. If she blocked his offer, the scene would die right there. So she tried it. "Yes, and the skeleton just pointed at a door marked Staff Only." Owen nodded. "Yes, and the door leads to the security office, where a monitor shows every hallway." On it went, offer after offer, and the scene grew like something neither of them could have built alone.

In the second round, the real debate, Owen stood up with his notes. "Ice cream sales rise in summer, and sunburns rise in summer," he said. "That proves ice cream causes sunburn." Lea froze for a second. Then the pattern from improv clicked into place: two things moving together, and a third thing behind both of them. "Ice cream sales and sunburns rise together, but that doesn't prove one causes the other," she said. "A third factor may cause both. They both go up in summer, and summer is what causes each of them on its own." She heard a judge murmur and write something down. A debater who ignored that, she added, was being negligent with the evidence, treating things that merely happen together as proof. Owen opened his mouth, then closed it and made a small note on his pad.

When the round ended, he walked over to her table. "Good analysis," he said. "You beat me with my own style. The yes, and thing." Lea grinned and slid her binder into her backpack. "Partner for the final round of improv?" she asked. Owen picked up the little paper tent with Riverside's name on it, folded it into a paper airplane, and sailed it toward the recycling bin. "Yes, and this time the museum has a flood," he said.

Jordan leaned over Marcus's basement computer, where the smell of old carpet and popcorn mixed with the hum of the monitor. He wanted his page about poisonous frogs to look real, like an actual website, with the title "Toxic Frogs of the World" sitting dead centre at the top. Marcus had shown him how to type the HTML in a file called frogs.html, and the words showed up fine, but they were jammed against the left edge like they were hiding.

"My grandpa taught me a trick for this," Marcus said, digging through a drawer. He pulled out a floppy disk with a handwritten label and squinted at it. "He made websites back in the day. He gave me his old tutorial." They carried it upstairs to the family computer, which still had a floppy drive, and opened the files. Sure enough, Grandpa's lesson said to wrap a heading in angle brackets around the word center, like a hug: open the tag, write the words, close the tag. Jordan copied it down carefully on a napkin.

Back in the basement, he typed it in and saved. The title stayed stubbornly on the left. He checked for typos, deleted a space, saved again. Nothing. "Maybe the computer's broken," Marcus said, but Jordan shook his head. He remembered a poster from the science fair about how one rotten factor can change a whole experiment, and something told him the computer wasn't the problem. The tutorial was from a different era, like a map of a city before the new highway. Maybe the old trick just didn't work anymore, and the page was ignoring it on purpose.

"So if that tag is out," Jordan said slowly, thinking out loud, "there has to be a new way." He opened a search page and typed what he was trying to do. The answer came up fast. The old center tag had been deprecated in HTML 4, the results said, in favour of something called the text-align property in CSS. He read the line twice. "Dad says 'deprecated' means retired," Marcus offered from the beanbag. Jordan said the word out loud anyway, feeling the shape of it. Then he wrote a style rule for the heading, with text-align set to centre, and saved the file one more time.

He hit refresh. The heading slid to the middle of the page and sat there, balanced and bright, and the whole page seemed to transform from a rough draft into something a stranger might actually visit. Jordan leaned back so fast the chair nearly tipped. "Grandpa's way used to work," he said. "It just got retired." Marcus leaned in to look, then grabbed the keyboard and started typing a second line under the title. "Now we need a picture of a golden poison frog right here," he said.

Annabelle crouched at the top of the skate park bowl with a stopwatch in one hand and a tennis ball in the other. Her science homework said she had to measure the speed of a rolling ball and draw a distance-time graph, and she had until supper, only two hours away, to get it done. She had chalked a line across the concrete every meter, six lines in all. Her plan was simple: roll the ball, click the stopwatch at each line, write the times, and see whether the dots on her graph made a straight slope or a curve. She wondered whether the ball slowed down going uphill on the far side of the bowl, and how she would even tell.

Her friend Dario wanted the bowl for himself. He was filming a trick video to enter an online contest, and the deadline was midnight tonight. "Can't you measure a ball somewhere else?" he asked, rolling his board back and forth. "I need the whole bowl in the shot."

"It's the only smooth slope around," Annabelle said. "My graph would be a disaster on the bumpy path by the library. Give me ten minutes, then it's all yours." Dario sighed and sat down on the coping, but he kept his camera ready, which made her hurry.

She rolled the ball and called out the times. One meter in 0.8 seconds, two meters in 1.6, three in 2.4. The numbers climbed evenly, and when she plotted them, the dots fell along a straight rising line. "One point two five meters every second," she murmured, connecting them. Then the fifth roll went wrong. Her little brother Theo, who had followed her with a toy drum, thumped it right as she clicked, and her time came out wild, far too short.

"Hit it again," she said, "the same as that." Theo whacked the drum hard, and the rice he had sprinkled on the skin jumped high, and the sound was big enough to make Dario cover one ear. "Now soft," Annabelle said. Theo tapped gently, and the rice only shivered, barely lifting. She noticed the sound was quiet, too. She tried it again to justify her hunch, hard and soft, and each time the bigger jump of rice came with the louder boom. So the loudness had to do with how far the drum skin, and the air particles it shoved, moved back and forth. "That's amplitude," Theo announced, reading off a sticker on the drum's side, "Grandpa's pension money bought it and the sticker came with it."

"That's amplitude," Annabelle repeated, writing the word in the corner of her graph. Dario had come over to watch, and he frowned at the drum, then at his camera. "You know what, forget my trick video," he said. "Film your ball rolls instead. Bouncing rice and a rolling ball, that's way more interesting than me falling off a ledge." He set the camera on the coping and aimed it at the bowl. "Roll it once more, Annabelle. This time I'll call the seconds."

The lights went out at Grandma Ruth's farmhouse just as Isla was labeling her science diagram of a frog, its long curled intestine the last part she had left to name. The refrigerator hummed down into silence, and outside the window the whole valley went black except for a few stars. Grandma Ruth felt her way to the junk drawer and found two flashlights, and Grandpa pulled on his boots.

"Generator time," he said, and Isla followed him through the dark kitchen, her flashlight beam hopping across the floor. He opened the door to the garage and Isla heard him fumbling with the pull cord on the big portable generator he used after storms. It sat right there between the car and the workbench, and beside it, propped near the door to the kitchen, was an extension cord already coiled and ready.

"Grandpa, wait." She was hesitant at first, because he had run farms for forty years and she had only read a safety flyer at school last week. "That generator gives off carbon monoxide. You're only supposed to run it outdoors, far from doors and windows. Never in a house or a garage. That's what the flyer said, exactly."

Grandpa stood still with his hand on the cord. "Huh," he said. "My father ran his in the barn."

"Please?" Isla said. "We can run the cord under the garage door and set it way out past the porch."

Grandpa rubbed his chin, then he and Isla wrestled the heavy machine onto a dolly, rolled it down the driveway, and parked it far from the house, its exhaust pointing at the open field. Grandpa had to adjust the choke twice before it coughed to life, and when the lamps came back on inside, Grandma Ruth called from the porch that she was heating water for cocoa on the camp stove out on the steps, not in the kitchen, since she had read the same flyer.

The twist came when Mr. Alvarez from the next farm over trudged up the driveway with his own flashlight. "You folks got power from somewhere?" he asked. "My wife's on one of those breathing machines and the battery won't last the night." Isla remembered something then, a low rumbling she had heard through her window during last spring's storm, coming from the direction of the Alvarez place. "Mr. Alvarez," she asked, "when you run your generator, where do you put it?"

He blinked. "In the garage, with the door cracked."

Isla looked at Grandpa, and Grandpa looked at Mr. Alvarez. "Come on," Grandpa said, picking up the spare gas can. "We'll get yours set up outside, nice and far from your doors, and we'll run you a line."

They crunched off down the gravel together, three flashlights bobbing in the dark.

Charlotte sat at her grandmother's kitchen table with her story draft in front of her and forty-one hours until the contest deadline, which was Saturday at noon. The story was about a peasant girl who hides a wounded horse during a war, and Charlotte thought it was almost good, except for the part she couldn't name. Something about the sentences felt lumpy, like dough that hadn't been kneaded enough, but when she read the pages silently the problem stayed invisible.

"Do writers have anyone read their work before they send it out?" she asked her grandmother, who was drying plates at the sink.

"Mine used to circulate stories to her friends in the mail," Grandmother said. "They mailed them around the village, each woman reading aloud to the next, and they caught each other's worst sentences that way." She set a plate in the cupboard. "Try it yourself. Out loud. This kitchen has heard stranger things than a girl talking to horses on paper."

Charlotte remembered then, a memory arriving uninvited. Last spring, at the writing club, Marcus had read his story aloud and stumbled three times on the same sentence, tripping over "the wind blew the leaves blew the wind" like a stair with a step missing. He'd laughed, embarrassed, but Mrs. Okafor hadn't corrected him. Marcus had crossed the line out himself and rewritten it on the spot, and afterward his story placed second in the district contest. Charlotte had assumed he was just lucky. Now she wondered if the stumbling had been the whole point.

She took a breath and read her draft aloud, slowly, letting each word reach the kitchen air. The first paragraph went fine. Then she hit the line "The stable door creaked open and the stable girl stepped into the stable dark," and her tongue tangled on it like feet in a jump rope. She read it again and stumbled in exactly the same place. A third time, same stumble. It was strange, because silent reading had slid right past that sentence, but her own voice kept snagging on it, and the snagging made the clumsiness impossible to miss. Farther down she found two more spots where every sentence had the same rhythm, boom-boom-boom, like a drum with one pattern only, and hearing them made her wince out loud.

"Bad?" Grandmother asked.

"Helpful bad," Charlotte said, already crossing out words. She read the draft to the end, marking every place her voice tripped or dragged, and the smudged pages looked messier than before but felt truer. Outside, the afternoon light was going amber on the garden fence, and she had a rewrite ahead of her and a deadline breathing down her neck. She read the stable sentence once more, out loud, and stumbled again on cue.

"You," she told the sentence, and reached for the pencil.

On Saturday morning Lucy stood in her own driveway, staring at a truck parked beside the garage, and felt a little intimidated by the crowd already forming down the sidewalk. Her mom had signed them up to host a mobile food pantry, which meant strangers would carry boxes of groceries through their yard all day. Lucy hadn't wanted this. She had wanted a quiet weekend, and she said so twice at breakfast, until her mom pointed out that Mrs. Okafor next door had asked for help and couldn't lift heavy boxes anymore.

"You can be in charge of the check-in table," her mom said, dragging two folding tables onto the lawn.

Lucy sorted cans and wrote tally marks, but something kept catching her eye. The first truck that arrived was from a food bank in their own city, and on its side was a blue logo with a bowl shape. An hour later a second truck rolled up, from two towns over, and it wore the exact same logo. Then a third, from a city an hour away. Same blue bowl. At first she thought it was an illusion, that she was seeing the design wrong, that no two different places would paint identical marks on their trucks.

She asked the driver of the third truck, a man with flour on his sleeves. "Why do all the trucks have that same picture?"

"That's the network," he said, hoisting a crate down. "It's called Feeding America. It's a nationwide network of more than 200 food banks."

"Two hundred," Lucy repeated, and thought about that while she worked. It explained the boxes, too. Every carton she opened had the same logo stamped on the corner, even though the trucks came from different cities. The rule she'd been guessing at wasn't a rule at all; it was a system, invisible until you noticed the same mark three times.

A boy her age, Marcus, showed up with his grandmother, who wanted oranges but couldn't see the crate at the far end of the table. He kept asking Lucy if there were any left, because his grandmother wouldn't eat the canned peaches, and he wanted to find her something fresh. Lucy had been about to say no, the oranges were gone, when she remembered the unopened crate still sitting in the garage. She carried it out, and Marcus's grandmother chose three, careful as a jeweler, and thanked Lucy twice.

"So this is okay?" her mom asked at the end of the afternoon, nodding at the emptied driveway, the folded tables, the neighbors walking home with bags.

Lucy looked at the last truck pulling away, blue bowl on its side, bound for some other city she'd never visit. "Can we do it again next month?"

Daniel had been dreading the party for a week, ever since his mother announced that Kenji's grandparents were flying in from Osaka and everyone was gathering at Aunt Rosa's house. Kenji had been Daniel's best friend since September, but Daniel had never met the grandparents, and he wanted badly to make a good impression. The problem was that he didn't know the rules. At his own family gatherings, you shook hands or hugged, you brought a plate of something, and you waited for Grandma to sit down before anyone ate. Kenji's family, he suspected, ran on a different program.

He stood on the porch holding a wrapped box of maple candy, which he had chosen himself, and listened to the doorbell chime. When the door opened, Kenji's grandfather bowed. It wasn't a little head nod like Daniel's uncle gave at church; the man bent from the waist, slowly, and held it. Daniel stuck out his hand at the same moment, so his hand floated in the air between them while the old man's face pointed at the floor. Kenji's grandmother bowed too, a smaller, quicker bow, and then they were both straight again, smiling, and Daniel's hand dropped to his side like a shot bird.

Inside, the folding tables had been pushed together into one long line that filled the whole living room. Kenji's grandmother presented Aunt Rosa with a bundle of cloth-wrapped packages, and Aunt Rosa hurried to the closet to dig out the gift she had hidden there, as if she had forgotten that giving went both ways. Daniel watched from the kitchen doorway and started counting. When the grandfather greeted Aunt Rosa, he bowed about fifteen degrees, brief and light. When he turned to greet Aunt Rosa's father, the oldest person in the room, the bow went deep and slow, almost to the table's edge, and stayed there long enough for Daniel to count to four. There it was, a pattern: the deeper and longer the bow, the more respect it carried. The fifteen-degree one was pocket change; the deep one was a gold coin.

Daniel had a plan to test before dinner. He waited until Grandfather Ota settled into a chair by the window, then walked over, held out the candy with both hands the way Kenji's grandmother had offered her packages, and bowed. He bent as far as his balance allowed and held it, counting silently, one, two, three, four. When he straightened, the old man's eyes were bright. He said something to Kenji, who laughed.

"He says you bow like a resilient young reed," Kenji translated. "Also, sit with your palms up, not on the table like a hammer. Grandmother hates that."

Daniel looked down at his hands, already flat on the table, and flipped them over. "Like this?"

Megan's bean plants stood in two rows on the science fair table, and the ones that had spent three weeks next to the speaker looked exactly as sorry as the ones that had grown in silence. She had wanted this project to work so badly. First prize was a summer camp scholarship, and without it the camp would be out of reach, an expense her family could not manage twice.

Priya leaned over the pots, frowning. "So music doesn't help plants grow?"

"That's not what I can say yet," Megan said, turning her notebook around. Her data table showed heights for both groups, nearly identical. "Mr. Okafor said our whole write-up is wrong because we never decided what no effect would look like. We just hoped the music plants would be taller."

Priya picked up the notebook and read the red comment at the top of the page. "Define your null hypothesis before you test it." She looked up. "What's that?"

"It's the statement that there's no relationship between the things you're studying," Megan said. "Music and growth, for us. The experiment doesn't prove music helps. It tries to reject that statement."

Priya set the notebook down slowly. "So if we'd written it down first, the null would say the two groups grow the same."

"And then our data would either knock it down or not," Megan said. She pointed at the rows of numbers. "Right now they're so close that I can't reject it. The plants grew the same either way." She felt her throat tighten and kept talking anyway. "But that's still a result. Judges want to see how you decide, not just whether you win."

They rebuilt the display board right there between the volcano and the homemade lava lamp. Megan wrote the null hypothesis across the top in careful block letters, then drew the height chart beneath it with both groups' bars nearly even. A boy from the next table wandered over, saw the board, and asked whether music had helped. "Not that I can show," Megan told him. "They look about equal, so the null stands."

When the judge stopped at their table, she asked Priya what they would change. Priya said, "We'd decide in advance what difference would signify a real effect, so we wouldn't just be hoping."

The judge nodded and made a mark on her clipboard. "Resilient beans, too," she said, tapping a pot. "They survived three weeks of my daughter's playlist."

Megan laughed, and straightened the tallest plant in the silent row. "Round two next year," she said. "Quieter music, bigger pots."

Gabriel's mother handed him a small framed photo the moment they reached the park gate. "Don't bend it," she said. "It's the only one of your abuela we have for today." The cultural center had set up tables under the pavilion, and Gabriel's class was helping build the altar for the Día de los Muertos celebration. He knew the holiday happened on the first and second of November, because his mother had circled both dates on the kitchen calendar, and he knew it was a way of honoring family members who had died. What he hadn't expected was that his own family would be part of it.

Mrs. Ruiz from the center gave them instructions. "We are building an ofrenda," she said, pointing to the wooden tiers. "That's what the altar is called." Gabriel watched Sofia from his class place a photo of her great-grandfather on the top tier, smoothing the frame with two fingers. His mother had told him the ofrenda was like the ones families made in their homes in Mexico, though his family had never made one before.

Then his cousin Mateo bumped him from behind, chasing a soccer ball, and Gabriel's hands were suddenly empty. The photo had gone. He knelt and swept his fingers through the grass. Nothing. The irony was sharp: the one object his mother had trusted him to carry, and he had lost it in the first five minutes.

He made himself stop and think instead of running in circles. The wind had picked up right when Mateo hit him. It came from the direction of the pond, steady and strong. A thin photo frame would slide on dry grass, and the ground sloped downhill toward the water. If he guessed right, the wind would have accelerated the frame along the slope, not across it. So the photo should be somewhere along a line between the pavilion and the pond, and the slope would make it drift faster and farther than it could have gone on flat ground.

He walked the line slowly, squinting. Leaves had blown into a drift against the base of an invasive bush, some kind of spiky plant with red berries that Mrs. Ruiz had complained about at the last cleanup, and there among the leaves was a corner of silver frame.

Gabriel lifted the photo out, checked the glass for cracks, and carried it back with both hands. He set it on the second tier, next to Sofia's great-grandfather. His mother came over from the food tables and looked at the altar for a long moment.

"There she is," she said. "Your abuela would have liked this. She always wanted us to do it properly, both days, not just one."

Sofia leaned over and straightened the frame so it faced the crowd. "Now we wait for tomorrow," she said.

Alexa sat in the back seat with her new orange cast propped on a pillow, staring at the place where the doctor had taped a copy of her X-ray to the folder in her lap. Mom pulled out of the parking lot and pointed the car toward home. "You did great in there," Mom said. "The nurse said most kids cry when they set a bone."

"I did cry," Alexa said. "Just before the medicine." She turned the X-ray toward the window light. Two pale stripes ran down her forearm, side by side, and only one of them had a dark crack in it, like a hairline in a windshield. She couldn't tell which stripe was which, and that bothered her more than the ache did.

In her mind she replayed the doctor's voice while he pointed at the film. "The forearm has two bones," he had said. "The radius, on the thumb side, and the ulna, on the little-finger side." Alexa laid her good hand flat on her knee and copied it with the cast arm, slow and careful, the way she was being meticulous about every movement now. The crack in the X-ray sat closer to the thumb stripe. So the broken one should be the radius. But her thumb side barely hurt. The worst ache ran down by her little finger instead, and that didn't fit.

"Mom, can we stop at the pool office?" she asked. "I have to enroll for the swim team before Friday, or the spot goes to the next kid on the list." Mom glanced in the mirror. "You heard the doctor. Six weeks, no swimming." "He said no swimming with the cast," Alexa said. "He didn't say anything about being on the team. Priya said they let injured kids do the dryland drills, the stretching and the running, until they're cleared." She had built her whole plan on that premise, and she knew Mom would try to poke a hole in it.

She tested her idea in the seat, wiggling first her thumb, then her little finger. The thumb moved almost freely. The little finger sent a thin wire of pain up the outside of her arm, and she hissed through her teeth. That settled it. The cracked stripe in the picture wasn't the radius at all, because the doctors had turned the film around when they handed it to her; the image was flipped, like a mirror. It was the ulna that was broken, the little-finger bone, which explained exactly where it hurt. "Two minutes at the office," she told Mom. "I'll sign the form left-handed."

Mom sighed and put on the blinker. "Two minutes. And don't you dare take that pen out of the cast pocket with your teeth." Alexa grinned, tucked the X-ray folder under her good arm, and reached for the door handle before the car had fully stopped.

Eleanor had exactly one weekend to finish her science project on water quality, and she had just found the most bizarre website of her life. It showed photographs of a green, murky pond turning crystal clear in three days, all because of a special powder sold by a man named Dale. "One scoop a week and your water worries are over," Dale wrote beneath a picture of himself holding a jar. Eleanor leaned closer to the screen, her cat Pixel hopping onto the desk beside the keyboard. Her teacher had said every claim in the project needed a reliable source, and this one seemed too good to be true.

She typed "Dale's Clear Water Powder" into the search box and found something unexpected: a real science journal article about pond water, written by three researchers. On the first page, in small print, the article said it had been reviewed by two other experts before publication. Eleanor had never noticed a line like that before. She scrolled back to Dale's site and read every word, but nowhere did it say anyone had checked his work. It was just his own story, one person's experience with his own pond.

At dinner she told her older brother, Marcus, about the difference. "The journal article says experts looked at it before it got published," she said. "It's called peer review." Marcus nodded between bites of pasta. "So Dale's site is just him talking," he said. "Nobody checked anything." Eleanor pushed her noodles around her plate, thinking. The consequence of trusting Dale could be a bad grade, or worse, a project full of nonsense.

She wanted to document the difference properly, so she set up her own small test in the kitchen. She filled two identical jars with cloudy water from the fish tank filter, added a pinch of ordinary baking soda to one and nothing to the other, and labeled them with masking tape. Then she took photographs each morning and wrote down what she saw. By Sunday, both jars looked almost the same, which told her something real: a single scoop of anything was not a magic fix, and one person's glowing story proved nothing.

On Monday she turned in her project with both sources side by side, explaining which one had been examined by experts and which had not, and what her own jar test showed. Her teacher wrote "Excellent comparing" at the top in green pen. That afternoon, Eleanor opened her laptop and, out of curiosity, checked Dale's site one more time. There was a new comment at the bottom of the page, from someone named Ponds4Life: "Tried it for a month, my water's still green." Eleanor grinned and closed the lid.

Bentley pushed his bike toward the rack outside First Neighborhood Bank and heard the soft flop of ruined rubber. The back tyre was flat as a pancake, and he groaned, because a flat had plagued him twice already this month and Dad always fixed it while Bentley watched.

Not this time. He had promised himself he would learn.

Inside, the lobby smelled of lemon cleaner. A man in gray coveralls was scrubbing the floor near the windows, and Bentley approached him, since the guard at the desk looked busy. "Excuse me. Do you have a pump? My tyre's dead."

The janitor, Mr. Okafor, smiled and pointed to a supply closet. "There's a bike pump in there, and a little kit with tyre levers. My daughter left it. Help yourself."

Bentley carried the kit to the rack. He pried one lever under the bead of the tyre, then a second, and the tyre popped off the rim like a lid coming off a jar. He found the culprit, a tiny thorn, pulled it out, and pressed a patch over the hole. When he pumped, the tyre rose firm and round. He had done it, all of it, himself.

He went back in to return the kit. Mr. Okafor was standing at a mop bucket with two bottles, and Bentley noticed one was chlorine bleach and the other said ammonia right on the front, big as anything. He remembered a warning from a safety sheet at school.

"Stop," Bentley said. "Don't mix those."

"Why not?" Mr. Okafor asked, bottle tipped over the bucket.

"Chlorine bleach must never be mixed with cleaners containing ammonia," Bentley said, reading the fine print on the bleach label out loud, "because together they release chloramine, a toxic gas."

Mr. Okafor straightened up and read the label himself, his eyebrows climbing. "Well. I've been cleaning banks for fifteen years and nobody ever told me that." He set the ammonia bottle far away on the counter. "That's a sophisticated bit of chemistry, young man. You may have just saved my lungs."

Bentley grinned and handed back the kit. "My dad always says I should nominate someone for a citizen award if they help me. Can I nominate you?"

"Only if I can nominate you right back," Mr. Okafor said. "Come on, I'll walk you out. I want to see that tyre."

Outside, Bentley spun the back wheel and watched it blur, steady and true. "Fixed it myself," he said.

"Then you'd better ride it," said Mr. Okafor, and held the door.

Marcus had one job on Friday: bring a snack to share for the international foods lesson, and not embarrass himself in front of Wei's grandmother, who was visiting from Hong Kong and coming to watch. He had brought a box of grape juice and a bag of pretzels. It felt thin.

When Wei invited him over Thursday evening to practice, Marcus said yes mostly because Wei's building had the fastest elevator in town. They rode up together, and Marcus pressed the button for Wei's floor. That was when he noticed the panel. The buttons went one, two, three, five. He counted them twice, dragging his finger along the row to be sure.

"Your building doesn't have a four," he said. "That's not a mistake? Buildings don't just skip numbers."

Wei looked at the panel like he was meeting an old acquaintance. "My grandma says in Chinese, the word for four sounds like the word for death," he said. "So some buildings in East Asia skip the fourth floor." Then he shrugged, as if floors were only floors, and the doors opened.

Marcus tested the idea in his head on the way down. If the number were bad luck, it would be missing in other buildings too. In his own building, the fourth floor was right where it should be, home to Mrs. Okafor and her parrots. So it wasn't a law of nature. It was a custom, the way his own family hugged hello and Wei's family bowed slightly, palms together, which Wei had demonstrated that morning with the gravity of a chess move.

At the lesson, Wei's grandmother brought egg tarts in a tin, and Wei passed them out with both hands, which Marcus copied and nearly dropped doing. When he handed one back to say thank you for a second tart, she waved it off and pressed it toward him again, and it took him three tries to understand that refusing once was polite and accepting twice was the point. The whole class ended up eating with their hands or with chopsticks or, in Marcus's case, with a pretzel used as tongs, which even he had to admit was not thriving.

After school, Marcus walked home the long way, parallel to the creek, and thought about how his street had houses from a hundred years ago, one of the oldest settlements in town, and how nobody could see that just by looking. Customs were like that. Hidden floors in an elevator you hadn't ridden yet.

He stopped at the corner store and bought a box of mooncakes, which the label said were red bean. He would bring them Monday, with both hands.

"Mrs. Okafor is on four," he told his dad at dinner. "Of a building with no four in it."

His dad blinked twice. "I'm going to need you to start from the beginning."

"Mom, I can do it myself," Alexis announced, holding the family laundry basket like a trophy. Her mother raised an eyebrow, handed her a twenty-dollar bill, and said that a competent laundry-doer needed to buy her own detergent first. "Aisle six. And no, the candy aisle is not on the way."

At the store, Alexis found a bottle that said it fought stains, brightened whites, and emitted a fresh mountain breeze, which she figured meant it smelled like pretend pine. It cost $7.35. She carried it to register two, where a boy about her age was counting his change with a frown. "You gave me a five and I only got back two dollars and thirty cents," he told the cashier. The cashier slid the coins and notes across the counter, and Alexis watched the boy work it out loud, starting at the price. "Nine seventy-five," he said, tapping the quarter, "ten," tapping a dollar coin, "eleven," tapping another, "twelve," tapping a ten. "That's twelve dollars, but I gave you fifteen. You're three short." The cashier blinked, apologized, and handed over three more dollars. Alexis filed that away like a receipt in her pocket: start at the price, add each coin and note handed back, and you should land exactly on the amount you paid.

When it was her turn, she paid with her twenty and got back a two-dollar coin, a loonie, two quarters, and a dime. Seven thirty-five plus two is nine thirty-five, she thought, plus one is ten thirty-five, plus fifty is ten eighty-five, plus fifty is eleven thirty-five, plus ten is eleven forty-five. She looked up. "I think you gave me too much. I only bought this." The cashier had punched in fifteen dollars instead of twenty by mistake, so the extra fifty-five cents was Alexis's to return. The boy waiting behind her gave her a slow clap, which she accepted with a bow.

At home, Alexis sorted like a scientist: whites in one pile, darks in another, and a suspicious in-between pile she decided to call "the maybes." She measured the detergent, chose the cycle, and stood guard over the machine as it rumbled. She was feeling extremely capable until she opened the dryer and found her white socks had turned a soft, deliberate pink.

She pulled everything out and studied it, sock by sock, like a detective. Nothing pink had gone in, so something pink must have been hiding inside something else. She shook out a pillowcase, and out dropped a single red sock, small and smug as a parasite that had spent the whole cycle feeding on her clean white load. "You," she said, holding it up to its little cotton face.

Her mother came in, saw the pink socks, and pressed her lips together to keep from laughing, which did not work at all. "It's a look," she offered. Alexis sighed, folded the socks into a neat pink stack, and dropped the red sock into a jar on the shelf, labelled in marker: EVIDENCE. "Next week," she said, "the maybes get their own load."

The waiting room of the veterinary clinic smelled like dog shampoo and coffee, and Asher spread his homework across two chairs while his terrier mix, Biscuit, waited for her shots. His assignment was due tomorrow: explain how finches on different islands ended up with different beak shapes, and why. He had a bag of birdseed and a pile of tweezers, pliers, and chopsticks from the kitchen drawer, because he had a plan. If he was going to understand natural selection, he wanted to see it happen in front of him.

He dumped two kinds of seed on a paper tray. Sunflower seeds sat whole and hard, and a pile of tiny millet grains scattered like sand. "Biscuit," he said, holding up the pliers, "you're a big-beaked finch." Biscuit wagged. Asher used the pliers to crack a sunflower seed in four seconds, then tried to pick up a single millet grain and chased it across the tray until it shot onto the floor. The tweezers grabbed millet instantly but squeezed the sunflower seed uselessly, like biting a rock with a straw. He wrote the times down, grinning. Tools matched to food. That was the whole game.

A boy about his age sat across from him with a rabbit carrier and watched the whole seed chase. "Why are you doing that in a vet's office?" the boy asked. Asher told him: on islands with hard seeds, birds whose beaks could crack them survived and had chicks with those beaks, and over many generations the whole island ended up with thick beaks. On islands with small soft seeds, the opposite happened. "Nobody planned it," Asher said. "The food did the choosing." The boy nodded slowly, like the idea had finally clicked into place.

Then the boy squinted at Asher's notebook, where Asher had scribbled a messy timeline from the science museum field trip last week. "That part's wrong," the boy said. "You wrote that animals were declared to be made of cells first." Asher looked. He had guessed animals came first because animals seemed more complicated and more important, so surely scientists studied them first. But at the museum he had stood in front of the timeline wall for ten whole minutes, and now he remembered. "No, wait," Asher said, flipping his notes over. "In 1838, the German botanist Matthias Schleiden proposed that all plant tissues are made of cells. Plants came first, and animals came after." The boy changed his mind about the notebook being useless and pulled out his phone to double-check, and it matched. Plants had gotten the cell theory jury's first verdict, a whole year before anyone said it about animals.

"Your old guess is obsolete," the boy said, and Asher laughed and crossed it out. A seed had to fit a beak, and a fact had to fit the evidence, and his guess hadn't fit either one. When the tech called Biscuit's name, Asher swept the seeds into his bag, thinking he'd nurture the finch idea into a full report tonight. Biscuit trotted through the door ahead of him, nose down, hunting crumbs off the floor.

Gabriella sat on the spinning stool at Bright Eyes Optical and swung her legs, waiting for her new glasses to be made. Her mother was filling out forms at the counter, which meant Gabriella had time to text her cousin Dev, who had just moved from London.

"How did your eye test go?" she typed.

"Perfect," Dev wrote back. "The doctor says I have 6/6 vision."

Gabriella stared at the screen. Six out of six? That sounded like a grade, and not a good one. If 20/20 was perfect, then 6/6 had to be way down the chart, like getting a six on a twenty-point quiz. She typed, "Only 6?? I'm getting glasses because my eyes are 20 something. Are you okay?" Dev replied with a row of laughing faces, which was no help at all.

Fine. She would investigate. Gabriella spun her stool toward the exam room, where the optometrist was hanging a new eye chart, and stood in the doorway with her chin lifted in a way her mother called her ambassador face, the one she used when about to ask for something. "Excuse me," she said. "If someone has 6/6 vision, is that terrible?"

The optometrist laughed. "Where's this someone from?"

"London. England. He just moved."

"That'll do it. Countries that use metres write normal vision as 6/6 instead of 20/20. Same eyes, different measurement."

Gabriella did the math in her head, sort of. So 6/6 was not a failing grade; it was perfect vision wearing a different coat. Dev hadn't been bragging badly or hiding a disaster. He'd been bragging correctly. She felt her cheeks go warm, then decided to be defiant about it and blame the eye drops. She marched back to the waiting area and typed, "You have perfect vision, you smug show-off."

"Naturally," Dev wrote. "Are those glasses emojis supposed to be you?"

Before she could answer, the technician called her name and handed over the new glasses, purple frames with tiny stars on the hinges. Gabriella slid them on, and the whole store sharpened like someone had finally focused a camera. She could read the tiny price stickers on the lens cleaner. She could see that the poster of an eye near the ceiling had eyelashes, which seemed like showing off.

She walked to the counter, where her mother was signing the last form. "Mom, guess what. Dev sees six out of six, which is the same as my twenty out of twenty, except his is in metres."

"His what is in metres?"

"His vision. His perfect, annoying vision." Gabriella pushed the glasses up her nose. "Also, I've decided to enroll in optometry school so I can put those little letter charts on people's walls."

Her mother paid, shaking her head. Gabriella waved at the optometrist on the way out. "Six out of six!" she announced to the whole parking lot.

Isabella had to finish her science homework before Friday, or she could not enroll in the after-school robotics club, which required all assignments to be current. The assignment said to roll a ball across the floor, time it, and draw a distance-time graph. Her little brother Marco kept stealing the ball, so she waited until he fell asleep, which had become a nightly ritual: he went down at eight, and she started her experiments at five past.

She laid a tape measure along the hallway floor and marked positions with masking tape at every half meter. Using the stopwatch on her mother's tablet, she rolled the ball and clicked the timer each time it crossed a mark. The numbers looked messy. At one meter she had 1.2 seconds, at two meters 2.5 seconds, at three meters 3.7 seconds, at four meters 5.0 seconds. She could not tell from the list whether the ball had sped up, slowed down, or done anything consistent at all.

She plotted the points on graph paper, distance up the side and time along the bottom, the way the worksheet showed. Then she held a ruler across the page and found that every dot sat on one straight line, slanting upward from the lower left to the upper right. She checked twice with the ruler's edge. The line did not curve anywhere, not even at the end where she had thought the ball was slowing.

She knocked on her mother's door and brought the graph in. "Look, the ball on the hallway floor did this," she said. "The line is straight the whole way."

"A straight sloping line means constant speed," her mother said, glancing at it between folding laundry. "That's what your sheet says, isn't it?"

Isabella went back to the hallway to test it. If the line was straight, then equal distances should take equal times, no matter which part of the roll she checked. She rolled the ball again and timed only the stretch between the two-meter mark and the three-meter mark: 1.2 seconds. Then she timed only the stretch between three meters and four meters: 1.3 seconds. Close enough, given her thumb on the button. The ball really was keeping the same speed the whole way, even though it had felt faster at the start.

She copied the graph neatly for the worksheet and wrote her conclusion underneath it. Then she picked up the tape measure, wound it back into its case, and peeled the masking tape off the floor one strip at a time, balling each piece in her fist. In the morning she would ask her teacher one question: whether a graph of Marco running down the hall would be straight, too.

At dinner, Charlotte's little brother slammed his fork down and pointed at her. "The poster at the community center is two faces," he insisted. "Two faces looking at each other. I saw it today."

"It is a vase," said her mother, ladling soup into bowls. "A white vase on a black background. I walk past it every Tuesday."

Charlotte stopped with her spoon halfway to her mouth. That was strange. Her mother and Dex had looked at the exact same poster, in the exact same hallway, and they had come home with completely different pictures in their heads. "Can you both see the other thing?" she asked. "Mom, can you see the faces? Dex, can you see the vase?"

Dex squinted at the ceiling as if the poster were painted up there. "Sort of? If I try really hard. But then the vase goes away."

"It's like a treaty," their mother said, smiling. "You can only have one at a time."

Charlotte pushed her bread around her plate, thinking. After dinner she found the community center's website and searched for the poster. There it was: black and white, and once she knew what to look for, she could make the white part pop out as a vase, or let the black part take over and become two faces in profile, nose to nose. It flipped. She made it flip again. But no matter how hard she tried, she could not hold both pictures at once, the way you could look at a picture of a dog and a cat together. It was vase, or it was faces. Never both.

Underneath the image she found a caption. "This is called a Rubin vase," she read aloud, and Dex leaned over her shoulder. It said the Rubin vase was introduced by a Danish psychologist named Edgar Rubin in 1915, and that it could be seen as either a vase or two faces, but not both at the same moment.

"So Mom was right," said Dex.

"So you were both right," said Charlotte. "That's the weird part." She was skeptical of one thing, though. Maybe it only worked because they expected it to. Tomorrow at school she would nominate the poster for show-and-tell, draw it big on paper, and ask her class to call out what they saw without any hints. If kids who had never heard of it still saw only one picture at a time, then it wasn't just her family being strange. It was something about how seeing itself worked, some hidden rule in the brain you couldn't watch directly, only test from the outside, like guessing what was inside a wrapped present by shaking it.

The next afternoon she stood at the whiteboard with her marker squeaking, filling in the black around the white vase shape. "First person to raise a hand," she said, capping the marker, "tell me what you see."

The sticky note appeared on Isabelle's desk before she even sat down. It said, in tiny handwriting, "Whatever you do to one side, do to the other." She looked around Room 4 of the tutoring centre, but everyone was bent over their own workbooks, and the tutor, Mr. Rowan, was helping a boy two tables away. Isabelle crumpled the note into her pocket. She had until Friday to pass the retest, and if she failed, she would be the only one in her class who had to migrate down to the grade seven math group, which everyone called the slow table.

The problem on her page stared back at her: 3x plus 2 equals 11. She tried subtracting 2 from the left side only, got 3x equals 9, and then, feeling her bias toward doing things the fast way, wrote x equals 9 over 3 anyway. Something felt off, like a shelf with one bracket missing. She pulled the crumpled note out and smoothed it flat. She rewrote the problem, subtracted 2 from both sides, and watched the 2 on the right shrink the 11 to a 9. Her pencil hovered. She divided both sides by 3. x equals 3. She checked it, 3 times 3 plus 2, and yes, 11. The rule had weight to it, like the beam of the playground see-saw she and her cousin used to fight over.

Then came the fraction problem, and the see-saw wobbled. Two-thirds cup plus one-half cup. Her grandmother had asked for exactly that last weekend while they baked, and Isabelle had poured them together and announced five-fifths cups, which made her grandmother laugh until she had to sit down. Five-fifths would have been a whole cup, and the batter had clearly not gained that much. Now, at the table, she wrote one-half plus one-third and stopped. She drew a circle, cut it into halves, then another cut into thirds. The pieces were different sizes. You could not count them together straight, because a third was smaller than a half. She converted both to sixths, three-sixths plus two-sixths, and got five-sixths. She looked at that number for a long moment.

"Who left this note?" she asked Mr. Rowan, holding it up.

He turned around slowly, and she noticed for the first time how young his face was. "I did," he said. "I flunked this exact test in grade eight. I'm in grade ten. I volunteer here on Tuesdays."

Isabelle stared at him. "You're not a real tutor?"

"I'm the closest thing you've got before Friday." He tapped her page. "And you just caught your own mistake with the cups. That's cumulative progress, you know. It stacks."

Isabelle looked from the note to her five-sixths, then flipped her pencil around and wrote a new problem on his side of the table. "Solve this one, then," she said, "if you're so smart."

The rain had finally stopped, though the sky outside the kitchen window still looked ominous, and Eleanor stood at the counter with a package of chicken thighs and a head of lettuce, determined to make dinner before Mom got home. Dad had said he would handle the ride to pick up her little brother, so the meal was hers alone. She wanted it to be good, not just edible, and she had even planned to elaborate on the usual Tuesday menu by adding a salad and garlic bread instead of plain rice.

She rinsed the chicken, patted it dry, and chopped it into strips on the big wooden cutting board. Then she slid the pieces into the pan, where they sizzled and popped, and turned to the lettuce. She was about to tear off the outer leaves and start chopping when she paused. The board in front of her still had faint smears from the raw chicken, and the knife lay beside it, damp from the meat.

Something tickled at the back of her mind, a memory of a poster in the cafeteria about keeping foods separate. She looked at the board, then at the lettuce, which nobody would cook. The chicken would spend ten minutes in a hot pan, but the salad would go straight from board to bowl to mouths. If the raw chicken had left something behind on the wood, it would ride the lettuce straight to the table. She could not see anything wrong. The board looked almost clean. But whatever the poster had been about, it was clearly about things you could not see.

Eleanor pulled open the drawer beneath the counter and found the green plastic board, the one Mom used for bread. She washed her hands, took a clean knife from the rack, and set up a whole separate station by the sink. "Separate boards," she said to herself. "Raw meat on one, ready-to-eat stuff on the other, so nothing spreads over."

Her neighbor Tomas appeared at the back door, drawn by the smell of garlic, and watched her juggle two boards. "Why not just use the one?" he asked.

"Raw chicken, then salad on the same board," Eleanor said. "That's cross-contamination."

"Sounds like a science project," Tomas said, and stole a piece of cucumber.

By the time the headlights swept the driveway, the chicken was golden, the salad was crisp in its blue bowl, and the two boards were drying on opposite sides of the sink. Mom came in with wet boots, sniffed the air, and dropped her bag on the chair. "You made all this?"

Eleanor slid the salad to the middle of the table. "Sit down before it gets soggy."

Lucy stood at the long steel counter of the community kitchen, staring at three recipes she had copied onto one index card. The windows looked out over the estuary, where the river fanned out wide and brown before it met the gray sea. She liked watching the two waters slide past each other without mixing, but today she had a bigger puzzle: rice, curry, and flatbread all needed to be done at the same moment, and each one took a different number of minutes.

"If the rice takes twenty and the flatbread takes two per piece," she said to her friend Dara, ticking numbers with her pencil, "then flatbread has to go last. But the curry has to simmer for fifteen. When do I start?" Dara shrugged and kept kneading her own dough. Lucy decided she could deduce the answer by working backward from the end. If everything should be ready at noon, the rice went on the stove first, then the curry, then the flatbread, one piece at a time, straight onto the hot pan.

She started the rice at eleven forty. While it absorbed its water, she chopped onions for the curry, her eyes streaming so much that Dara laughed and slid her a pair of swimming goggles from the lost-and-found box. "You look exceptional," Dara said, and Lucy grinned behind the foggy lenses and kept chopping.

The curry went into the pot at eleven forty-five, and Lucy stirred it and thought about a dinner she'd had at Dara's house last month. Dara's mother had made a smooth white sauce, flour and butter in the pan first, then milk poured in slowly while she whisked. It had turned silky and thick, nothing like the lumpy glue Lucy once made at home. She had been wondering about it ever since. "What did your mom call that white sauce?" she asked.

"Béchamel," Dara said. "A roux thickened with milk makes béchamel, one of the classic mother sauces of French cooking." Lucy rolled the word around. Mother sauce. As if all the other sauces were its children, the way the estuary outside fed a hundred little channels. She wondered what else in cooking had a family tree, and whether the curry bubbling in front of her belonged to one too.

At eleven fifty-five the rice was resting, the curry was simmering on low, and Lucy divided her dough into balls and rolled the first one thin. It hit the pan and puffed up in the middle like a small balloon, and she flipped it and watched it brown in spots. One by one the flatbreads stacked on a plate under a towel. At noon exactly, she looked around her. Rice, steaming. Curry, thick enough to coat the spoon. Flatbread, warm and stacked. Everything at once, like she had planned it, though her heart was still going quick.

They carried the pots to the long tables where the Saturday lunch crowd was already gathering, and Dara's mother found a seat near the window. Lucy ladled curry over rice and handed her a flatbread. "You made this?" Dara's mother asked, tearing off a piece.

"All three, ready at the same time," Lucy said. "I worked backward from noon. And tomorrow I want to make béchamel."

Sara curled her fingers into a claw and set her knuckles against the onion, exactly the way Chef Ana had shown her. "Knuckles guide the blade, fingertips stay out of trouble," she murmured to herself, and the knife ticked down through the layers in even, parallel cuts. The kitchen smelled of garlic and tomatoes, and somewhere behind her the radio muttered the weather.

Her friend Marcus stood at the counter with his phone raised. He was trying to film a chapati for his cooking channel, but the flat circle of dough just sat on the hot pan, browning slowly, refusing to do anything interesting. "It's supposed to puff," he groaned. "I saw a video where it blew up like a balloon. Mine just lies there." He poked it with a spatula and it stayed stubbornly flat.

Sara carried her chopped onion to the stove, but she kept glancing at the pale disc in the neighboring pan. Why would a flat circle balloon at all? Nothing was pushing on it from outside. Something had to be pushing from inside, but she couldn't see inside. She thought about steam curling off the pasta water, invisible until it hit the cool air near the window. Maybe the dough had water hidden in it, and on the heat the water turned into steam. Steam took up more room than water. That could be the push. She filed the idea away and softened her onions in olive oil, listening to the whispering sizzle.

When Ana slid a fresh chapati onto the pan, Sara leaned in close. After a few seconds a small bubble rose at the edge, then another, and suddenly the whole thing swelled into a golden dome. Marcus gasped. "How? It's flat dough! Where does the air even come from?"

"Watch," Sara said. She rolled a little dough herself, but she made one small tear in the top before laying it on the pan. That one rose only halfway, sagging where the steam leaked out, while Ana's next chapati beside it puffed perfectly. A leaky one couldn't hold the push. That fit her idea. "I think it puffs because water in the dough turns into steam," she said. "I tested it. The one with the hole can't hold it in."

Marcus lowered his phone. "You tested it. On a stove. While making sauce." He looked at her bubbling pan of tomatoes and onions, then at the two chapatis. "Okay, I have to confess something. My channel has four subscribers and two of them are my mom." He turned the camera toward Sara's experiment, chapati still domed and steaming beside its flat, torn twin. "Tell them again what the steam does, but slower this time."

Justin sat on the bench beside the pharmacy counter, sniffling into a tissue that had gone soft as an old sock. He was on day two of the flu, and although his fever had finally packed its bags, his nose had not. His mother stood at the window waiting for his prescription while the pharmacist typed with the speed of someone defrosting a freezer.

"I'm going to Dev's party on Friday," Justin announced, mostly to the ceiling.

"You're going nowhere," his mother said without turning around.

An old man in a plaid jacket who was also waiting looked over. "Big party?"

"Backyard, fourteen people, a taco bar," Justin said. "I'm the only one bringing hot sauce. It's a big responsibility."

The pharmacist slid a white bag across the counter. "Prescription for Marsh," she said, then, glancing at Justin's red nose, added, "Flu? Then listen, kid. You're most contagious during the first three days of your illness. After that it drops off." She rang up the old man's cough drops and moved on, as if she hadn't just handed Justin a mystery.

He did the math right there on the pharmacy bench, tapping his finger against his knee. Today was Tuesday, day two. Wednesday would be day three, Thursday day four, and Friday would be day five. The germs were like unwanted houseguests who only trashed the place for three days and then got bored. But if he sneezed on the taco bar on Friday, that would be fine. If he sneezed on it Wednesday, half of seventh grade would be home by the weekend. His original plan, going to the party early to prove he was fine, suddenly seemed like a terrible idea.

He tested his reasoning on the walk home, carrying the prescription bag like evidence. "So Wednesday's the danger day," he said to his mother. "Friday I'm practically harmless."

"That's not what the pharmacist said," his mother replied, "but I'll admit it's closer to the truth than your last argument."

Justin texted Dev from the couch, wrapped in the blanket where viruses clearly failed to thrive because he was already improving. He proposed moving the taco bar from Wednesday to Friday, citing the pharmacist like a lawyer citing a witness. Dev replied with a single thumbs-up and the message "my mom says yes, she says you're the only kid who ever researched a party."

The twist came Thursday, when Dev texted again: taco bar postponed, he had the flu now. Justin laughed so hard he started coughing, then called him. "What day are you on?"

"Day one," Dev groaned. "Why?"

Justin grinned at the ceiling. "You've got three days of being a walking sneeze. Mark your calendar. And save me a spot at the taco bar on day five."

Jaxon stood at the kitchen table with a poster board, a bag of marbles, and his older cousin's phone number written on a sticky note. His health teacher had assigned him the hardest topic in the class: explain how nicotine hooks people, right down to the brain. He could not see a brain working, and that was the problem. He had to narrate something invisible to a room full of seventh graders, and he wanted it to be good.

"Got a minute?" he said when his cousin Dre picked up. Dre had quit vaping last spring, and Jaxon had been meaning to ask him about it for a week. Dre talked while Jaxon spread the marbles across the table like a handful of random pebbles. "It wasn't one big decision," Dre said. "It crept in. Good feeling first, then needing it just to feel normal." Jaxon pushed a marble along a track he had drawn on the poster, a curve labeled REWARD PATHWAY, and watched where it rolled.

Later that afternoon his little sister Riya came in from her checkup and dropped her jacket on a chair. She was quiet in a way Jaxon recognized, because two years ago he had sat in that same beige exam room, in that same squeaky chair, and asked Dr. Okafor why every other boy in gym class seemed to be changing and he wasn't. He remembered staring at the paper on the wall while the doctor talked, too embarrassed to look up. He remembered exactly what it said, too, because he had read it four times.

"Everything okay?" he asked Riya now. She shrugged. "I asked the doctor if something was wrong with me because I haven't started yet, and Ava already has." Jaxon told her what the wall chart had told him, the thing he had tested in his own head that day in the exam room. "Puberty usually starts between ages eight and thirteen for girls and between nine and fourteen for boys," he said, laying out the marbles into two rows, one shorter, one longer, the way he had pictured it back then. "So girls can start as early as eight, boys as early as nine, and starting anywhere in those ranges is normal. You and me, we're both inside the lines." Riya picked up a marble from the girls' row and held it to the light. "So Ava just started early," she said, "and I'm not late at all."

Jaxon looked at his rows of marbles, then at the curving track on his poster, and smiled. Ranges and pathways, both invisible, both working quietly whether anyone saw them or not. For his presentation he would roll one marble down the track for the first cigarette, then a handful for the tenth, showing how nicotine kept hitting the reward pathway until the brain expected it, the way Dre had described. Riya set her marble back in its row. "Can I watch you practice after dinner?" she asked. Jaxon picked up the bag and shook it, listening to the click inside. "Sure," he said. "You can be the audience."

Grandma's piano sat in the front room under a window full of ferns, and Jade had been dying to play it all summer. On Monday morning she found a piece of sheet music on the stand with markings everywhere: piano, forte, crescendo, ritardando, like the notes were being shouted at. "That's Grandma's old solo," said Cousin Marcus, who was staying there too. "It has dynamics and tempo changes. I want to learn it for the talent show Friday, but I only know keyboard from school." Jade wanted the same thing, and there was only one piano, so they made a deal. "I'll practice in the morning, you take afternoons," she said. "And we can delegate the lunch dishes to whoever doesn't practice." Marcus agreed fast, because he hated dishes even more than he wanted the solo.

That evening a letter came from Mrs. Okafor, who directed the church choir Grandma sang in. "Friday's show will open with a round," Jade read aloud. "Tell your grandmother the choir needs every voice. Row, Row, Row Your Boat, first group, second group, third group." Marcus frowned. "If everyone sings the same song at the same time, how is that interesting?" Jade shrugged, but the question stuck in her head all through dinner, which was frugal but good, rice and beans and greens from the garden out back.

Tuesday morning she tried the solo and got the loud parts and the speeding up, but the music felt flat, like something was missing under the melody. Then she remembered the letter. At the piano she played Row, Row, Row Your Boat with her right hand. When she reached the second line, her left hand came in on the same melody at the very beginning. She held her breath. Where the two lines crossed, they made harmony. Same melody, different starting times. That was it. She grabbed her phone and called Marcus in from the porch, where he was reading a comic about a giant herbivore dinosaur. "Come listen. Every group sings the same melody but starts at a different time, and that's what makes the harmony." He dropped the comic and ran.

They tried it with voices in the kitchen, Jade going first, Marcus jumping in on "gently down the stream," and Grandma arriving home from the store right in the middle. Instead of hushing them she set down her bags and held up one finger, waiting for her spot, then slid in as the third group. The three lines braided together so well that Marcus whooped and knocked over the cereal box.

On Friday the choir opened the show with the round, three groups stacked like stairs, and then Jade played Grandma's solo with every crescendo and ritardando in place, Marcus turning pages beside her. When the last chord faded, Grandma stood up in the second row and cupped her hands around her mouth. "Again," she called. "From the top."

Maria raised her hand so fast her chair squeaked, and Mr. Doran still didn't call on her. He was busy writing "INTERPRETATION" on the board, which was the topic she wanted to argue about, because the topic was the reason she was in trouble at home.

It had started yesterday in the hallway. Her little brother, Theo, had come home from school and announced, "Dad asked me how fast you smashed into that kid by the lockers." Maria had barely brushed past a boy named Dev; her shoulder had touched his backpack and his water bottle had fallen. Yet Theo described her "running him over," and now she was grounded for the weekend, which meant missing the pool party, unless she could change her father's mind by dinner tonight.

"Here's your exit question," Mr. Doran said, checking the clock. "Ten minutes. Everyone saw the same video of the car accident on Monday. So why did half of you say the cars were going forty and half said twenty?"

Nobody answered. Maria looked around. Same video, same room, same morning. That made no sense to her, and things that made no sense bothered her the way a splinter bothered her thumb.

"Can I ask the class something?" she said. When Mr. Doran nodded, she stood up. "When I asked you to write your estimate, did anybody say the word smashed to you? Like, did I say, how fast did they smash into each other?"

Priya frowned at her paper. "You said smashed to our row. It was on my slip."

"It was on your slips?" Mr. Doran turned around, and Maria's ears went hot, because she hadn't planned to confess. But the clock gave her seven minutes, so she went on. "I handed out two versions. Half the slips said smashed and half said hit. I wanted to see if it mattered. It's for my dad. He thinks I did something I didn't."

"It mattered," said Priya, flipping through her notes. "We said forty and fifty. That's so sinister, actually. Just one word."

Marcus, whose slip had said hit, held up his paper. "I said twenty." Three other kids near him nodded.

Mr. Doran pulled a book off the shelf and set it on Maria's desk, open to a page. "Read the third paragraph out loud. Quietly, just to yourself." She read it twice. In 1974, two researchers, Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer, had asked people how fast cars smashed into each other, and those people gave higher speed estimates than people asked how fast cars hit. Same films, different word. She looked up, and Mr. Doran was already collecting the exit questions, because there were two minutes left.

At dinner she laid the book on the table, open to the page. "Dad, what exact words did you use when you asked Theo about the hallway?" Her father paused with his fork in the air. "I asked how fast Maria smashed into that kid. It was just a question."

"That's what the researchers found," Maria said. "One word, and the speed goes up. Dev dropped a bottle, Dad. Ask him. I'll install a tracking app on my phone if you don't believe me, but call his mom tonight."

Her father picked up his phone and dialed. Maria waited, watching Theo push peas around his plate, while the word extinction ran through her head, the way her science teacher used it, the dying out of a thing that used to exist. Maybe her bad reputation could go extinct too.

Her father hung up and set the phone down next to the open book. "Dev's mother says it was nothing. You're ungrounded." He looked at Theo. "And tomorrow I'm asking you different questions."

The line outside the Riverside Pavilion stretched past the bakery and around the corner, and Raphael had been standing in it since six in the morning. Ahead of him, a man in a gray jacket moved down the queue, saying the same words to every group he passed. "Box office tickets, eighty apiece. Limited number. Cash only."

Raphael counted his money again. Fifty-two dollars, saved from mowing lawms all June. The box office price was supposed to be forty, but the sign taped to the window that morning had changed things: "Limited tickets available." When he'd bought tickets for this same band last year, the line had been short and the seats had sat empty in whole rows.

"Eighty," the man in gray said again, closer now. "Going fast."

Behind Raphael, two girls were whispering. "My mom did this with chips last month," one of them said. "Her favorite brand jumped to six dollars a bag, so she just bought the store brand instead. It does the same job, basically. She calls it a substitute." Her friend laughed. "Your mom and her economics." Raphael turned the word over in his mind. Substitute. A similar thing that does the same job.

He looked down the street. Three blocks away, a smaller theater had put up a banner that morning: a tribute band, same songs, same night, tickets fifteen dollars, and the sign under the window read "Plenty of seats available." The line there had only eleven people in it. As he watched, a boy from the concert queue peeled off and walked toward it. Then a couple followed. Then a family of four. It was contagious, the way the little line began to grow while the big one barely shrank.

Raphael's heart pounded. If he stayed, the man in gray might sell out before he reached the window, and he'd have nothing. If he left, he'd see the songs performed, but not the real band. He made himself wait ten more minutes, watching, testing his idea. The concert line stayed long and hungry. The tribute line kept growing. When the man in gray shouted "Last four tickets, eighty each," four hands shot up at the front, and that settled it.

He walked the three blocks, bought a ticket for fifteen, and still had thirty-seven dollars left. Ahead of him in the new line, the two girls from the concert queue had appeared, and the one who'd talked about chips grinned at him. "You switched too?"

"Substitute," Raphael said, holding up his ticket.

The doors opened, and the line surged forward.

The microscope had come from her uncle, secondhand, in a box labeled FRAGILE in three languages, and Nevaeh's science worksheet was due tomorrow morning. The instructions were simple. Look at onion skin under the microscope, then label the cell wall, the membrane, and the nucleus on the diagram. She had a single onion from the crisper drawer and a plan, which was more than she'd had an hour ago.

The hard part was the skin. She cut the onion in half, peeled off a papery layer, and dropped it into a splash of water on the slide, but through the lens she saw nothing except a gray blur, like weather. She tried the thin skin from between two layers instead, pressing the cover slip down until bubbles skated sideways. That, at least, was something.

Her little brother Desmond appeared at her elbow, breathing near her ear. "I want a turn. I've been waiting my whole life."

"You've been alive seven years."

"That's my whole life." He held up a spoon. "I'll trade you my lucky spoon."

Nevaeh decided to assume he would go away if she gave him a job. "Fine. You're my assistant. Hold this flashlight." Desmond held the flashlight with enormous seriousness, steady as a soldier, which surprised them both.

At forty times magnification, shapes appeared. At one hundred, the shapes sharpened into rows and rows of pale rectangles, neatly stacked, one against the next, a wall going on and on across the whole field. Nevaeh sat back. Her heart sank a little. She had peeled the wrong thing. Somehow she was looking at the onion's actual wall, the structure itself, like bricks in a garden fence. She had no onion wall. She had onion skin. This was a disaster, and it was almost bedtime.

Desmond leaned in anyway. "Whoa. It's like a brick wall in there."

"It IS a brick wall," Nevaeh said. "Except." She stopped. Except onions didn't have brick walls, and even if they did, a brick wall wouldn't be on the thin skin from between the layers. She looked again, closer.
