Alexis did not take the phone. She had spent the school year failing Spanish, and she had decided the class was useless, so she left the phone on the table to prove she could manage without it. She walked three blocks carrying the bag of clothes she was meant to donate, and then the streets stopped matching anything Abuela had told her. A man was sweeping in front of a shop with green awnings. She stopped, and the dilemma was simple: ask in English and get nowhere, or try the Spanish she had decided she didn't have.

"¿Dónde está Calle Rosa?" she said.

The man answered fast, too fast, and then slowed down. "Sí. La primera calle a la izquierda." He pointed with his broom, but the street split ahead into two left turns, and she could not tell which one he meant. She knew izquierda meant left, that much had stuck. But which left came first?

She tried the other half of what her teacher had drilled into them, the part she'd thought she'd never use: repeat it back. "¿La primera calle a la izquierda?"

"Sí," the man said. "La primera." He held up one finger.

Alexis looked at the split. One left turn was really just a driveway into a parking area. The other was an actual street with a sign. If the driveway didn't count as a street, then the real street was the first one, the one with the sign. She said "Gracias," walked on, and watched. The driveway went into a lot full of cars. It was not a street. The sign at the second left said Rosa.

The bin stood at the corner, next to a bakery. She pushed the clothes in, and the bakery door swung open behind her. It was the man with the broom, holding a paper bag. "You found it," he said in English. "First street on the left."

"You speak English?" Alexis said.

"All my life." He shrugged. "Your grandmother asked me to keep an eye out. She said you'd refuse the phone." He held up the bag. "Come, she ordered bread. And she says I make the best empanadas in the city, but that is subjective."

Alexis laughed and followed him down Rosa. On Monday, she decided, she would ask Abuela to speak only Spanish at breakfast. She took out her phrase list on the walk home and read it twice.

The pitch counter app on Coach Alvarez's phone was still a prototype, a rough version his brother had built, and it glitched whenever someone's shadow crossed the screen. Brooklyn had volunteered to keep count on a clipboard instead, because she liked numbers better than surprises. She sat on the bench behind third base, marking every pitch Marcus threw, and by the fourth inning she had a funny feeling in her stomach. According to her sheet, Marcus had thrown sixty-one pitches. According to the coach's phone, he had thrown forty-four.

"Coach," she said quietly, jogging over between batters, "the app might be missing some. It freezes when it's sunny, and it was sunny all inning." She showed him her clipboard, where she had also noted which warmup tosses she had counted and which she had left out, so he could check her reasoning himself.

Coach Alvarez looked at the numbers, then at Marcus on the mound, then called time. He walked out, put a hand on the boy's shoulder, and led him back to the bench. "You're done for today, bud. You hit your pitch limit."

Marcus dropped his glove in the dust. "I don't even feel tired."

"That's not what the limit is about," Coach said. Brooklyn expected a lecture, but he just sat down next to Marcus and rubbed his own elbow like an old memory lived there.

Marcus stared at the dirt. "My cousin plays high school ball and throws a hundred pitches a game."

"That's because his bones finished growing," Marcus's older sister, Delia, called from the fence. She was a sophomore and had driven him to practice. "Yours haven't. You've still got growth plates, areas of growing cartilage near the ends of your bones. They're weaker than the bone around them, so young pitchers have limits on how much stress we can put on them." She shrugged. "I learned it in health class after I wrecked my shoulder swimming."

Brooklyn wrote that down too, in the margin, because it suddenly made everything make sense. The limits weren't about being tired. They were about something you couldn't see, working quietly inside a person's arm, and the pitch count was the only way to see it from the outside. She decided to test her idea. She flipped back through her sheets from the last three games and found that Marcus had also been participating in every throwing drill at every practice, on top of his games. When she showed him the tally, his face changed.

"Okay," he said. "Maybe I'll catch on drill days."

He picked up his glove, walked over to the cooler, and came back with two cups of water, handing one to Brooklyn before he sat down to watch the rest of the inning.

The drive to the coast had taken six hours, and Ethan had spent most of it reading the state park brochure he found in the glove box. His sister Maya said he was biased because he'd already decided the beach would be better than their trip to the mountains last summer. "You only like it because you found that sand dollar," she said. Ethan put the brochure in his back pocket anyway.

That evening a ranger named Ms. Okafor gathered everyone at the fire ring behind the dunes for a talk about national parks. "Whoever answers the final question wins a junior ranger badge," she announced. "The question comes in ten minutes, at sunset, so talk it over now." Ethan's dad immediately claimed he knew everything about parks. Maya said the first one was probably Yosemite. Dad shook his head and said the Grand Canyon, since it was the biggest.

Ethan didn't shout out a guess. Instead he thought about what he'd read in the brochure while the waves hissed in the dark behind them. There had been a whole paragraph about Yellowstone, and he was almost sure he'd seen a date there, and a president's name. It felt like remembering where he'd left his shoes: he couldn't see the page, but he could picture sitting on it. He tested the memory by saying it out loud under his breath. "March 1, 1872. Grant." It sounded like something he'd actually read, not something he'd invented.

The sun touched the water and Ms. Okafor held up her hand. "Final question. Yellowstone became the first national park in the United States on March 1, 1872, when which president signed it into law?" Dad whispered "Roosevelt." Maya whispered "Lincoln." Ethan raised his hand so fast he knocked over his cup of cocoa.

"Ulysses S. Grant," he said. Ms. Okafor smiled and pinned the badge to his jacket. Dad threw his hands up. "I was going to say Grant," he said. "You were going to say Roosevelt," said Maya. "I was collecting my thoughts," said Dad, and everyone laughed, even Ethan.

Walking back to the cabin, Maya poked the badge. "Fine, the beach trip is better than the mountains. For now." Ethan crouched by the tideline, where a dead crab was slowly starting to decompose among the kelp, and picked up a spiral shell. "Trade you," he said, holding it out. "Badge for shell." Maya snatched it and ran up the dunes shouting, "No take-backs!"

Nora slid her vocabulary list across the desk and sighed. Fifteen word histories by Friday, and the definitions in the back of the book were so tedious that her eyes kept sliding off the page. The last word was "propaganda," and she almost skipped it, except that word had been bothering her all week. Marcus's posters for class president were everywhere, and something about them felt off, like a picture hung slightly crooked.

One poster said EVERYBODY'S CHOOSING MARCUS, with a long line of smiling kids drawn underneath it. Another called his opponent's ideas "dangerous" and "reckless," words that sounded exciting but meant nothing exactly. The biggest poster of all showed TJ, the eighth grader who could dunk, holding a thumbs-up: "TJ says Marcus is the real deal." Nora couldn't point to a single lie in any of them, and that was what made her uneasy. She flipped to the library's dictionary of word origins and ran her finger down the page.

There it was. The word came from a Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith, the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622. Nora read the line twice, then copied it into her notebook. She raised her hand before she could talk herself out of it. "Mr. Reyes, I found where propaganda comes from. The Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, a Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith, set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622." A boy near the window snickered, and Nora felt her face go hot, but she kept going. "So it just meant spreading an idea around. It didn't start out as a bad word."

That night she tested a theory. If Marcus's posters worked by making people feel like everyone else had already decided, then a poster that pointed at the trick itself might break the spell. She made her own poster, plain and loud: "WHY DOES IT SAY EVERYBODY? ASK SOMEBODY." Underneath she drew a tiny panda chewing bamboo, with the caption "Pandas are herbivores. They eat facts, not hype." It was a strange joke, and she knew it, but she taped it up anyway, right between two of Marcus's.

By lunch, kids were standing in front of it. "What's a fact panda?" someone asked, and Nora said, "It only eats things that are actually true." Priya, who had been on the fence for a week, laughed and said, "Okay, that poster just got my vote for best poster. Marcus's are all sparkle and no sandwich." Marcus himself came down the hall, stopped, and read it twice. He peeled off his EVERYBODY'S CHOOSING MARCUS poster and looked at Nora over the top of it. "So what would a poster look like," he asked, "if I actually told people what I want to do?"

The graph in George's lap was supposed to keep him busy until Flagstaff, but it had turned into an argument instead. He had printed two rainfall charts at the library before the trip, one for the Sonoran Desert and one for the Hoh Rainforest in Washington, and his older sister, Priya, riding shotgun, kept glancing back at him instead of the map. "You're going to wrinkle the airport," she said, meaning the fold where the Sonoran bar column looked like a row of flat pennies. The Hoh's bars were tall blue towers, some of them taller than George's thumb.

"Look at this," George said, holding the sheets up. "The desert gets barely anything. Like, the whole year is shorter than one rainforest month." Priya's stomach rumbled audibly from the front seat, and Dad took the next exit toward a diner with a gravel lot and a sign shaped like a saguaro. Outside the window the actual desert slid past, all rust and pale green, smelling of hot dust through the cracked vent.

At the diner, the waitress refilled their waters and noticed the graphs spread across the table next to the ketchup. "Homework on vacation," she said, and George felt his ears go warm, because the graphs had been his own idea. Last summer he had refused to do the workbook pages Mom bought him, and she had ended up donating the whole thing, which he still thought about sometimes without deciding whether he'd been right. "What are you comparing?" the waitress asked.

"Rainfall," George said. "A desert is a place that gets less than about 250 millimeters of rain a year. Ten inches." He tapped the Sonoran sheet. "That's how scientists define it, not just sand and heat."

The waitress laughed and set down a basket of fries. "Then you know what's funny? Where I grew up, in Antarctica's dry valleys, they call that a desert too. Cold one. Snow barely falls there at all." George stared at her. Snow. A desert. Priya pulled out her phone and started reading, and for ten minutes the only sounds were ice clinking and the fryer humming behind the counter.

Back in the car, George took out a fresh index card and drew a temperature graph next to the rainfall bars, the Hoh's line mild and level, the Sonoran's line a jagged climb. The two places were opposites in every way except that both had living things that had found a way. He thought about the estuary they had visited on the Oregon coast last spring, where the river met the sea and everything depended on the balance of fresh and salt, and how his class's influential poster about it had won the hall contest even though it had almost no numbers on it. Numbers mattered, he decided, pushing the pen harder. He would add Antarctica to the card, a cold desert with a line that dove below zero while rainfall stayed under ten inches. "When we hit Washington," he told Priya, "I'm going to stand in the rain and measure it."

"You'll need a bigger cup," she said.

At dinner Tyler kept glancing at his older sister Priya, who was shoving noodles around her plate with a textbook propped against the milk carton. "Chapter five," she groaned. "There's this test from 1985, the Sally-Anne test, and there's a quiz on it tomorrow."

"Sally Anne is a doll," Priya said. "Sally puts her marble in a basket and leaves. While she's gone, someone moves the marble to a box. Then kids have to say where Sally will look for it." She tapped the page. "Kids from about age four usually say she'll look where she left it, the basket, not where it was moved. Little kids just can't believe Sally could be wrong about something."

Tyler looked down the table at their cousin Marcus, who was four and a half and busy building a tower out of sugar packets. "Wait," Tyler said. "You mean Marcus doesn't know that other people can be wrong?"

"He doesn't know that other people can believe something false," Priya said. "Nobody at this table believes the same thing about the meatloaf, and we all heard Mom's opinion on the school funding census at the last town meeting, so you know we're all capable of opposing each other politely." She grinned at Mom, who had spent two weeks arguing for a recount.

"Marcus," Tyler said, sliding a fork out of the drawer and hiding a sugar packet under it. "I'm putting my treasure under the fork. Watch." Marcus watched with enormous eyes. "Now I'm going to the kitchen. Don't touch it." Tyler walked out, stood against the refrigerator for ten seconds, and listened. When he came back, the fork was in exactly the same place, but Marcus's elbow was suspiciously close and one sugar packet was missing from the tower. Tyler knelt down. "Marcus. Where am I going to look for my treasure?"

Marcus pointed at the drawer. "You're gonna look in the drawer, 'cause you didn't see."

Tyler sat back on his heels. He'd been sure Marcus would point at the fork, because that's where Tyler had put the treasure, and that's what mattered, right? But Marcus had tracked the whole thing: Tyler left, Tyler didn't see the move, so Tyler's mind still held the old picture. Four and a half years old, and he already knew that what you saw wasn't the same as what somebody else knew. Priya was the one who'd gotten it wrong, at least about Marcus.

"Priya," Tyler called. "Wrong kid. He passed." He turned back to Marcus, took the fork, and lifted it slowly. The sugar packet was gone from underneath, and in its place sat a folded napkin with "SORRY" written in wobbling crayon letters.

"You can have this instead," Marcus said, holding out the sugar packet with both hands. "I only borrowed it."

The lights went out while Alicia was watering her grandmother's tomato plants, and the porch swallowed itself into darkness so fast it felt like the evening had decided to accelerate. She stood in the backyard holding the dripping can, listening. No hum from the air conditioner. No glow from the kitchen window.

"Grandma?" she called, and heard shuffling inside. Her grandmother found her at the back door with a flashlight, its beam small and unimpressive next to the extravagant chandelier that hung, useless and dark, in the hallway. Grandma's cordless phone sat in its cradle on the counter, and when she picked it up and pressed talk, nothing happened. Not even static.

"Battery must be dead," Grandma said, tapping it against her palm.

Alicia took the phone and turned it over. "It's plugged into the wall," she said slowly. "The base is, anyway. If the power's out, maybe the phone isn't dead. Maybe the outlet is." Grandma raised an eyebrow, which was her way of saying go on. Alicia set the handset down and stood still, thinking. The phone needed the house's electricity. That part made sense. But something nagged at her, an old memory of phones with curly cords and no plugs at all. How had those ever worked? It seemed like a paradox, a thing with no power cord that still had power. Unless the power came from somewhere else.

"Grandma, did you ever have one of those wall phones? The kind with the cord?"

"Kitchen. Still there, behind the biscuit tin. I keep it because I hate throwing away anything that works."

Alicia pushed the tin aside and found it, a heavy cream-colored phone bolted to the wall with a cord coiled like a spring. No plug, no battery compartment. She lifted the receiver and held it to her ear, half expecting silence. Instead, a dial tone buzzed, steady and alive, as if the power cut had never happened. She nearly dropped it.

"Grandma! It works!" she shouted. "The line gets its power from the phone company, not from our house. That's why it still works."

"Well, I'll be," Grandma said, and then, because she was Grandma, "Call your mother before she worries."

Alicia dialed, and when her mother answered on the first ring, breathless and already reaching for her car keys, Alicia had to talk fast to keep her from driving over in the dark. "We're fine. We have flashlights, the stove is gas, and I found a phone that doesn't need electricity at all." Outside, a neighbor's generator roared to life, and somewhere down the block a dog barked at it. Alicia sat on the kitchen floor, the coiled cord stretching to reach her, and told her mother about the tomato plants she'd been watering when the world went dark. The dial tone hummed softly under her voice the whole time.

The science quiz was fourth period, which gave Rosalie exactly one lunch break to figure out the giant poster of the periodic table that Mr. Okafor had hung above the chalkboard. "The atomic number tells you the number of protons," her notebook said, in her own handwriting, copied off the board yesterday. That part seemed almost too easy. Carbon was number 6, so carbon had six protons. But then why did the table have all those weird gaps, and why did some squares sit lower than others, like the whole thing had been built by someone who ran out of room?

She stood in front of the poster with her sandwich in one hand, tracing columns with her eyes. "They're called groups," said Dev, appearing beside her with a juice box. He pointed at the tall rows running up and down. "My cousin says elements in the same group tend to have similar chemical properties." Rosalie chewed on that along with her sandwich. Similar properties. She scanned the far right column and noticed helium, neon, and argon stacked one above another like beads on a string. What could a super light gas and a heavier one possibly have in common? She had a sudden, wild idea: maybe it was the protons. Maybe columns were secretly proton patterns.

She tested it right there. Helium was 2, neon was 10, argon was 18. She wrote the numbers on her napkin and stared at them until her eyes crossed. Two, ten, eighteen. It was like a secret code, and for one glorious moment she felt like a spy cracking it. Then she checked a different column, lithium and sodium, numbers 3 and 11, and the pattern faltered. If protons alone made the columns, the numbers should march in tidy steps everywhere, and they didn't. Her whole theory was less credible by the second. She glared at the napkin as though it had personally set out to hinder her, which, in a way, it had.

"Time check," Dev announced. "Eight minutes till the bell." Rosalie flipped her notebook to the study sheet. Question one: How many protons does oxygen have? She found oxygen, atomic number 8, and wrote 8, fast. Question two: Name two elements in the same group. She wrote neon and argon, then hesitated. Mr. Okafor's voice drifted back to her from some Monday long ago: the periodic table is organized by patterns, not by accident. Maybe the principle wasn't that each column shared proton numbers, but that sharing a column meant something else, something about how the elements behaved. She added a note: "similar properties," and underlined it twice.

The bell rang as she was writing question three. Then came the twist: Mr. Okafor walked in carrying a stack of papers and announced, "Change of plan. Open notebook quiz today." Rosalie looked down at her napkin, covered in numbers and arrows, sitting beside her notebook like a treasure map. She slid it under the notebook's cover, and Dev whispered, "Best sandwich investigation ever."

Hudson wheeled his bike through the door of the Spin Cycle Laundromat because it was the only place on Marsh Street with a roof and a bench, and his back tyre had gone flat two blocks ago. He had a patch kit, two tyre levers, and a small pump in his backpack, all of it bought with his own money, none of it ever used. His mother was three washers down, feeding quarters into a machine, so he set the bike against the folding table and got to work.

First came the levers. He slid one under the edge of the tyre, then the second, and the rubber fought him until he learned to pin the first lever under a spoke. The tube came out pale and wrinkled, like a long balloon after a week. He could not see any hole. He knew one had to be there, though, because air had leaked out and air could only leave through an opening, so he decided to test it. He carried the tube to the utility sink in the corner, held it underwater, and pumped a little air in with the hand pump. Somewhere near the valve, a thin thread of bubbles rose up through the water like a silver string.

He was marking the spot with chalk when the man at the change machine called out. "Kid, come here a second." The man had sold Hudson a bottle of milk from the little shelf by the dryers, part of the laundromat's strange side commerce in snacks and soap. "I gave you the wrong change before, I think." He counted coins into Hudson's palm. "One fifty-five."

Hudson looked at the coins. He had paid with a five dollar bill, and he had done the subtraction in his head while the washers hummed. "That's too little," he said. "The milk was two sixty-five. Five minus two sixty-five is two thirty-five."

The man counted again on the counter, slowly, lips moving. "Two sixty-five from five." He opened the register and added coins until the pile came right. "Eighty cents more. You're not as gullible as my nephew." He laughed at that, and Hudson pocketed the coins, which would prolong his afternoon by exactly one ice cream.

Back at the folding table he roughed the chalked spot with the sandpaper from the kit, spread the glue, waited until it went tacky, and pressed the patch down hard with his thumb. Then he worked the tube back inside the tyre, tucking the last stretch over the rim with his thumbs, and connected the pump. The stroke that seemed useless at first gradually stiffened. The tyre rose round and firm against his palm.

Hudson spun the wheel and watched it turn, steady and true, in the fluorescent light.

"Ready?" his mother asked, closing the dryer door.

"Ready," he said, and lifted the bike toward the street.

Gabriel had babysat exactly nobody before Saturday, which was why Mrs. Yi leaving him alone with eight-month-old Penny felt like being handed a live grenade and a smile. The instructions on the fridge ran to two pages, front and back, in handwriting so small he had to lean in until his nose nearly touched the paper. Behind him, from the playpen, Penny made a sound like a small, judgmental owl.

Everything went fine for an hour. Penny ate her cereal, gravity took its usual cut, and Gabriel learned that a baby could inhale a fistful of banana faster than he would have believed possible. Then Penny stopped eating. She pressed her lips together and turned her face away from the spoon with the determination of a soccer goalie defending a net. Gabriel tried the airplane trick, the choo-choo trick, and the desperate humming trick. Nothing. He looked at the cereal, which was plain oat mush, and thought the problem was obvious: it was boring. He got the honey jar from the pantry and had the lid half off when he noticed a line at the bottom of page two, underlined twice.

No honey, it said. Not until she's over 12 months. Bacteria spores in it can grow in her gut. That last word had sent Mrs. Yi's pen skidding. Gabriel stood there with the jar, rereading it. He'd never once thought of honey as something that could hide trouble. It just sat there looking golden and harmless, like a trap designed by someone with a grudge against toast. He put the lid back on and returned it to the pantry, feeling the embarrassment arrive about one second too late to stop him from having opened it in the first place.

Penny still refused the cereal, so Gabriel got systematic. If the problem wasn't taste, maybe it was temperature. He touched the bowl: cold. The instructions said warm it for twenty seconds, and he'd been so busy with airplanes he'd skipped that step. He tested the idea, microwaved the bowl, stirred it, and offered the spoon again. Penny considered him with the flat stare of an emperor, then opened her mouth like a garage door. The entire bowl vanished in four minutes.

Mrs. Yi came home to find the kitchen clean, the honey jar in its exact spot in the pantry, though it was turned two degrees from where it had been, and Penny asleep in the playpen. "How was she?" she asked.

"Fine," Gabriel said. "Great, actually." He did not mention the honey, or page two, or the fact that his heart had gone briefly extinct in his chest when he'd read it. He took his twenty dollars, and at the door he paused. "Next time could you underline that honey part at the top? Maybe in red."

Zack flattened the big sketchbook on the kitchen table and sharpened his pencil until the shavings curled like tiny scrolls. He was going to draw Draper Street, the whole thing, with the buildings leaning toward each other and every edge sliding back to one dot. His art book called it one-point perspective, and the dot was the vanishing point. Last week his drawing of the street had looked like cardboard boxes glued in a row, and he was not doing that again.

He remembered Saturday morning, standing at the corner with his friend Marcus. The smell of the bakery's cinnamon rolls had drifted down the block, and a bus had rumbled past so close the sidewalk buzzed under Zack's sneakers. "Just draw what you see," Marcus had said, and they had both tried, sitting on the curb with their knees bumping the curbstone. Today Zack wanted to get it right, so he drew a straight line across the middle of his page first, laid out the street, and let every roofline and curb run toward his vanishing point on that line. He leaned back. It looked like a street. He actually shouted, "Yes!"

Then Marcus knocked on the door, holding up his own drawing. "Trade check," Marcus said, which was their rule: you had to find one thing wrong with the other person's art, because otherwise the checking would be Zack's monopoly, since he found mistakes faster than anybody.

Marcus stared at Zack's street. "Where's the sun? Where's the sky? Mine has half a page of sky." He spread his drawing next to Zack's. His horizon line sat way up near the top of his page, and his buildings rose from the bottom edge like towers. Zack's horizon sat low, near the bottom, with walls rising above it on both sides.

"Where did you draw from?" Zack asked.

"My bedroom window. Upstairs." Marcus tapped his page. "You?"

"Curb. Saturday, with you." Zack's mouth went dry with excitement, because he was starting to see it. "So the horizon is low when you're down low, and high when you're up high." He flipped to a new page fast. "Draw mine again but pretend you're on the roof."

They knelt side by side, pencils scratching, the kitchen smelling of pencil wood and the leftover cinnamon toast Zack had eaten. Zack put his new horizon even lower than before, almost at the bottom edge, and suddenly his street felt the way it had felt sitting on that curb: small and huge at once, buildings looming, sky pressing down. "Look," he said, holding it up next to the first one. "A low horizon makes it feel like a kid's view."

"And mine implies you're floating above the bakery," Marcus said, grinning at his tall, towering street.

Zack ran for the stairs, sketchbook under his arm, intricate ideas crowding his head. "Come on, we're doing the roof next!"

"Race you," Marcus said, already two steps up.

Clara spread the two flowcharts across her grandfather's kitchen table, weighting the corners with jars of homemade pickles. The assignment was due Monday: pick one right from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, put it in her own words, and explain it to the class. But her teacher had also promised bonus marks for describing how a bill becomes a law, and Clara had never gotten that far before.

"Still working on the homework?" her grandfather asked, setting down two mugs of tea. He was a veteran who had served overseas decades ago, and he kept a framed photograph of his old regiment in the hallway. "You've been at that table all afternoon."

"I picked section two," Clara said. "Freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression. My own words for it are: you're allowed to think what you think and say what you think, without the government stopping you." She frowned at the flowcharts. "But I'm stuck on the bill part. The federal chart says a bill goes through the House of Commons and then the Senate, and then the Governor General gives royal assent. The provincial chart just stops after one box."

Last weekend, she remembered, she had complained that the assignment was pointless. She had wanted to quit and write about her weekend instead, and her grandfather had said, "People obstruct laws they've never read, Clara. Read this one." Then he had slid a worn booklet across this same table, and she had opened it just to be polite. The first line had caught her before she could pretend to be bored.

Now she traced the provincial chart with her finger. "That can't be right. Every law should have to pass both houses. Otherwise it's too easy to pass something bad."

"Draw it again," her grandfather said. "Count the boxes yourself. Don't trust the chart."

Clara counted. The federal chart showed two chambers, first one and then the other, before the Governor General. The provincial chart showed one chamber only, and after that single chamber the bill went straight to the lieutenant governor, who gave royal assent. She checked the provincial government website on her laptop, then checked a second site because she was skeptical of anything she found only once. Both said the same thing.

"Grandpa, look. All Canadian provinces have one-chamber legislatures. So a provincial bill passes only one house before the lieutenant governor gives royal assent." She said it slowly, testing each word. "That's why the chart isn't missing anything. It's just shorter."

"So will you change your mind about the shorter chart?" he asked.

"It's not wrong, it's just different," Clara said. She was thinking of the boy in her class, Daniel, who had insisted last week that provincial laws took twice as long to pass as federal ones because there were more provinces. She had believed him then. Now she had a page of counted boxes that said otherwise, and she intended to wave it at him on Monday.

She copied the two flowcharts side by side onto a fresh sheet, wrote "one house, not two" beside the provincial one, and underlined it twice.

"There," she said. "Now for section two."

Georgia had measured her bean plants twice, and both times the numbers made her stomach drop. The six pots on the windowsill, the ones she had watered every morning with the special fertilizer her grandmother sent, had grown three inches in two weeks. That was the good part. The bad part was the question her friend Priya had asked at lunch: "Grown three inches compared to what?"

Now, in the kitchen, Georgia laid her science notebook on the counter and stared at her chart. Six plants, all fertilized, all tall. Beside the sink her little brother Theo was gluing popsicle sticks into what he claimed was an authentic Viking longship, though it looked more like a raft with ambitions. "You keep frowning at that notebook," he said. "Is it going to bite you?"

"Priya says my project doesn't prove anything. Maybe the beans would have grown three inches anyway." Georgia tapped her pencil against the page. Her instinct told her the fertilizer worked, but instinct wasn't allowed in the results section. "If I can't compare them to something, I can't tell."

Theo set down his glue. "Compare them to what, the Viking ship?"

"No. Beans." She went quiet, and then the idea landed all at once, so big she actually laughed. "More beans. I'll start six new pots, same soil, same window, same water, everything the same. The only difference is the fertilizer. That way, if the fertilized ones grow more, I know it's the fertilizer doing it, and not the window or the soil or dumb luck."

Theo's eyes lit up. "Can I be in charge of the new ones? I'll water them at the same time you water yours. We can coordinate it, like eight o'clock every morning before the bus." He was already pulling the bag of dried beans from the cupboard, the one Mom used for soup, and lining up six clean yogurt cups on the counter. He filled them with soil from the same bag Georgia had used, patting each one down twice, checking her old pots to match the depth.

"Careful," Georgia said. "The new ones get plain water only. Not one drop of the fertilizer, or it ruins everything." Theo nodded so seriously she believed him. He had wanted his own job for the project ever since she'd started it, and now he had one that actually mattered.

Two weeks later, they knelt side by side at the windowsill with the ruler between them. The fertilized plants had grown three and a half inches. Theo's plain-water beans, the ones nobody had fed anything special, had grown two. Georgia wrote the numbers down twice to be sure, then grinned at him. "Yours are the control group," she said. "The ones treated exactly like mine except for the fertilizer."

Theo straightened up like a soldier receiving a medal. "The control group," he repeated, tasting the words. "Can I put that on the label? In Viking letters?"

Tristan discovered the problem at seven o'clock on Tuesday morning, in the driveway, with the car still cold. He had been singing along with the radio, loudly, the way nobody could hear him, when the word "tonight" came out in two pieces. The "to" was high and normal, and the "night" dropped straight down into some gravelly cave he had never visited before. He tried it again. "Tonight." It cracked again, right in the middle, like a stick snapping.

In the car on the way to school, his sister Maya noticed him experimenting. "Why do you keep saying 'ahhh' like a dying robot?" she asked, buckling her seatbelt. Tristan ignored her, which was not easy, because the car was small and Maya was never indifferent to a chance to tease him. He was busy. He hummed a low note, then a high one, then the note in between where the break lived. It was like there were two voices inside him, an old one and a new one, and no bridge between them yet.

By Thursday he had begun to classify the evidence. Low notes worked fine. Talking worked fine, mostly. High notes were the problem, and the break always happened in the same narrow spot. Dad drove them to choir practice that evening, and Tristan spent the whole ride testing his newest idea: if he sang quietly enough, maybe the crack couldn't get enough air to happen. He whispered scales in the back seat. Maya put in her earbuds. "It still cracks," Tristan reported, half thrilled, half annoyed. "Just quieter."

At practice, Marcus got the solo in the new song, and Marcus sailed through the verse and then hit the big high note at the end, and his voice split exactly the way Tristan's had. Mr. Ruiz raised one hand. "Marcus's larynx is growing," he said, "so the vocal folds inside it are getting longer and thicker, and they may crack while that happens." Marcus turned red, but Tristan nearly fell off the riser. Folds. Longer and thicker. That was it. That was the hidden machine.

On the drive home, Tristan leaned forward between the front seats. "Dad, the vocal folds get longer and thicker, and that's why the voice drops. It's like a guitar string, kind of. Except inside." Dad glanced at him in the mirror. "A metaphor," Dad said. "Sure. Every guy in this car went through it." Maya pulled out one earbud. "Even Dad cracked?" "Ask your grandmother," Dad said. "I once scared the dog."

Tristan sat back. The car hummed along the dark road, and he hummed with it, low, in the new voice, the one with no cracks in it at all. He was already planning the choir solo for next year. "Marcus," he said to the window, "your solo is mine in October."

Evelyn did not cherish Tuesdays, and she especially did not cherish Tuesdays that began with a lab sheet titled Resistance of a Wire. The instructions seemed simple enough: connect the wire to the power pack, measure the voltage across it, measure the current through it, then divide. R equals V divided by I. Her partner, Marcus, read it out loud twice, as if saying it again might make the numbers behave.

The thick copper wire went first. The voltmeter said 1.5 volts and the ammeter said 0.30 amps. Evelyn wrote both down and did the division on the corner of the sheet. Five ohms. She checked it twice, because a number that neat felt suspicious, like it was trying to win her trust.

Then they swapped in the thin wire, the same copper, the same length, and the ammeter barely twitched. 0.10 amps. Marcus tapped the meter with one finger, the universal cure for instruments. "It's not broken," Evelyn said. She wrote the current down anyway and divided. Fifteen ohms. She looked at the two answers sitting side by side on her page, five and fifteen, and frowned at them.

"Same wire stuff, same length," Marcus said. "How can it be three times as much?"

Evelyn laid the two wires on the table next to each other. The thick one was like a piece of spaghetti; the thin one was more like a thread from her mom's sewing kit. She thought about the hallway outside, the one everybody jammed into at the bell, and how the wide stairwell never backed up. "More room to flow," she said slowly, mostly to herself, and Marcus grinned at her with the infectious delight of someone who has just watched an idea arrive.

For their last trial she chose a thick wire again, from a different spool, and got four ohms, which was close enough to five to feel like testimony: the thickness was the thing, not the spool. When Mr. Reyes walked past, he glanced at her data table and raised an eyebrow at the last column, where she had written thick, thin, thick beside each trial like evidence tags.

"Nice control," he said, and moved on before she could decide whether to be proud or to wonder how teachers always knew which student had actually figured something out.

At the bell, Marcus stacked the wires in the bin by thickness. "So the skinny ones are the stubborn ones," he said, holding up the thread-thin copper.

"Exactly," said Evelyn, and clipped the meter leads together one last time, just to see the needle jump.

Megan sat at her grandmother's kitchen table with the laptop open and a deadline hanging over her: the student council meeting was at four o'clock, and she had promised to bring a summary of the field trip survey. Grandpa hovered behind her with his own want, which was to get the kitchen back for his bread baking before the dough overproofed.

"Five minutes," she negotiated, tilting the screen away from his flour-dusted elbow.

The spreadsheet held 212 rows, one for each student who had answered the survey. There was a column for grade, a column for the activity they chose, and a column where everyone rated the trip from one to five. Megan had figured out pivot tables the night before, mostly by clicking things at random until a gray panel appeared and dragged fields into boxes. She put Grade in Rows, and the count of students appeared neatly for each grade. Sixth grade, 74. Seventh, 68. Eighth, 70.

But the count told her nothing about whether anyone had actually liked the trip. She scrolled through the ratings and saw a wall of threes, fours, ones, and fives with no order she could detect. There had to be a pattern in there somewhere, a rule hiding inside the numbers, but it was invisible while the ratings sat scattered down the column.

She clicked into the values area of the pivot table and found a dropdown. Sum was selected, which made no sense; summing ratings would just give giant useless numbers. She changed it to Count, which she already had. Then she saw Average. That had to be it. The whole column of one-to-five ratings would turn into the mean rating for each grade. She clicked it and the table rebuilt itself. Sixth grade, 4.2. Seventh, 3.1. Eighth, 4.6. She sat back. The eighth graders had loved the trip, the seventh graders had barely tolerated it, and now she could say so with actual numbers instead of a shrug.

Megan tested it once to be sure, dragging the Activity field into Columns so the average rating showed for each activity within each grade. The pattern held: seventh graders who chose the museum averaged 4.4, while the ones stuck with the walking tour averaged 2.3. The tour was the problem. That was worth saying at the meeting, and she could even propose fixing it for next year.

"Done," she said, and slid the laptop aside as Grandpa slid the loaf pan in. "Grandpa, you're my spreadsheet mentor now, by default."

"Only if mentoring means standing here eating bread," he said, and set a warm slice in front of her.

The synagogue smelled of old wood and honey from the year before, when someone had spilled candy behind the radiators. Noemie sat in the back row with her prayer book open, though her eyes kept drifting to her cousin Ari, three seats ahead. Ari had diabetes, and today was Yom Kippur, the day everyone fasted. He had his water bottle tucked under his jacket like something illegal.

Noemie was supposed to be thinking about the service, which talked a great deal about being written into the Book of Life. Instead she was thinking about her friend Priya, who went to the Hindu temple across town. Last week Priya had explained reincarnation over pizza, drawing little circles on her napkin. "Your soul comes back," she had said, "again and again, until it doesn't need to anymore." Noemie had drawn arrows. She wanted to compare it with what her own tradition said, and she had promised to bring an answer by Saturday.

The problem was Ari. He looked pale, and halfway through the morning service he swayed and grabbed the pew in front of him. Noemie's mother hurried over. So did Rabbi Wolk, an eccentric old man who wore two different socks and carried a clock that didn't run. Noemie expected him to tell Ari to be brave and push through. Instead he leaned close and said, "You need to eat something now."

Ari blinked at him. "But it's Yom Kippur."

"Jewish law waives the fast when health is in danger," the rabbi said. "In that case you're actually required to eat or drink. So drink, please. It's the religious thing to do." He said it quietly, without ceremony, the way you'd tell someone to buckle a seatbelt.

Ari drank his juice, and the color came back into his face within minutes. Noemie watched him negotiate a deal with their grandmother, who kept insisting he take a second granola bar, and who won. Meanwhile Noemie turned the rabbi's words over in her mind like a stone. She had thought fasting was simply what you did, no exceptions, the way you don't talk during the silent prayer. But the rules had hidden doors in them. She tested the idea against Priya's tradition, where exceptions and levels and second chances seemed to be everywhere too. Maybe, she thought, every system for describing things nobody can see has to make room for real people, in real bodies, on real days.

At the break, she found Ari eating crackers behind the social hall, his fatigue already gone. "Does it feel strange?" she asked. "Eating when everyone else isn't?"

He shrugged and brushed crumbs off his lap. "A little. But the rabbi said it counts as observing the holiday."

"I'm telling Priya that," Noemie said, pulling out her phone to type a note. "She's going to love it. Her tradition has exceptions for sickness too." Ari held out the cracker box, and she took one.

Austin stood in the bathroom at Grandpa's house, leaning close to the mirror and studying the red bump on his chin. Tomorrow he had to give a science talk on how nicotine hooks people through the brain's reward pathway, and his face had picked this exact week to rebel. He raised two fingers toward the pimple, ready to squeeze it flat before anyone had to see it.

His older cousin Marisol banged on the door. "Don't do that. Squeezing or popping pimples can push bacteria deeper into the skin, and it can leave scars." Austin lowered his hand and opened the door. "Then what am I supposed to do, submerge my whole face in ice water?" Marisel grinned. "No. You wash it and leave it alone, and it fades. Patience, remember?" She flicked his shoulder and went back downstairs.

Patience. That was the word that had been missing from his notes all afternoon. Austin sat at Grandpa's kitchen table surrounded index cards, a rubber band stretched between his thumbs, and a bowl of peanuts Grandpa had set down without comment. His problem was simple and frustrating: nicotine was invisible. He couldn't show the class a molecule or a brain pathway, so his talk kept sounding like a dictionary reading aloud.

He tried his speech on Grandpa, who was fixing a leaky faucet under the sink. "Nicotine gets into the brain and trips the reward pathway, the system that normally reacts to food and stuff that keeps you alive. So the brain learns nicotine is important, and it starts to want it, and wanting it gets stronger every time." Grandpa's voice echoed up from the pipes. "Like me and these peanuts," he said, rattling the empty bowl. "One handful yesterday, two today. Tomorrow I'll want the whole jar." Austin sat up straight. That was it. Not a definition. A person, wanting something more and more, without seeing why.

He grabbed his rubber band and stretched it, feeling it pull against his thumbs. Every dose of nicotine was like a stretch, and an elastic band that got stretched again and again stopped bouncing back the same way. He wrote that on a card, then hesitated. It wasn't perfect, and he was pretty sure a rubber band didn't really work like a brain. But it was something a class could see with their own eyes.

He looked back at the mirror on his way to bed. The pimple was still there, small and stubborn, and he left it alone. Some things got worse when you forced them, and some things only faded with time and patience. He set his index cards on the nightstand, put the rubber band on top of them, and turned off the light. "Tomorrow," he told the ceiling, "we stretch."

The pharmacy smelled like soap and cough drops, and Kate stood by the shelf of shoe inserts while her mother picked up a prescription. In the basket under her arm sat a box of plasters, a comb, and the money she had saved for the display rack behind the counter. That was the problem: the pharmacy sold arch supports, but it did not sell what she actually needed, which was a reason her brother Tom's shoes had stopped fitting twice since September while his jeans still fit fine.

Kate turned the idea over while her mother talked to the pharmacist about antihistamines. Her premise was simple: if Tom's feet were growing, the rest of him should be growing too, at the same time. That was how she had always assumed growing worked, everything at once, like inflating a balloon. But the evidence did not fit. His trainers were pinching again, and his school trousers still hung the same as they had in autumn. She looked down the aisle as if the shelves could settle it.

She tested her idea on the pharmacist, a woman named Ruth with reading glasses pushed up into her hair. "If someone's feet got bigger twice this year but their legs didn't get longer at all," Kate asked, "would that mean the feet are broken?"

Ruth laughed. "No. Hands and feet usually grow first, before the arms and legs and the rest of the body catch up."

"So the legs will catch up," Kate said. "Later."

"That's the usual order," Ruth said, and rang up a packet of plasters for the woman behind them.

Kate stood there doing the sums. Two new pairs of shoes in one school year was a lot of money, and their family budget was not rich this winter; her mother had called it an impoverished month just last Tuesday, waving the electricity bill. So Kate made a decision she could defend. Instead of buying the sparkly display rack comb, she put her money toward Tom's next pair of shoes, and she wrote a note on the fridge: DO NOT BUY HIM JEANS YET.

When they got home, she found Tom in the hallway trying to jam his heel into the trainer he had outgrown a second time. "Save your trainers," she told him. "And don't ask for new jeans, because your legs are next."

Tom looked at her, then at his feet. "How do you know?"

Kate tapped his shoe with her own. "Your feet told me."

Lily slid three dollars across the lunch table and watched Maya count out the last two bracelets from her shoebox. By Tuesday they were gone, and Maya had raised almost enough money to enroll in the Saturday art class she'd been talking about since September.

On Wednesday, four sixth graders walked into homeroom with sandwich bags full of woven bracelets, each one tagged with a price of three dollars. By Friday there were nine sellers, and the hallway outside the science room looked like a tiny market. Nobody was buying much, though, because everyone who wanted a bracelet already had one, or was now making them at home from leftover embroidery thread. Maya sat on the radiator, staring at her empty box and then at the crowded hallway. "Nobody wants mine anymore," she said, "and I still need eight dollars for art class."

Lily couldn't stop watching the sellers, wondering what had changed. Nothing about the bracelets themselves had changed. Was it just that there were so many now? She pulled out her notebook and did something systematic: a column for each seller, the price they asked, and how many bracelets they sold that day. A pattern jumped out by afternoon. The kids charging three dollars sold almost nothing. One boy who had dropped his price to one dollar had sold five. The same bracelets, the same hallway, different numbers. It was like the model wind turbine in Mr. Okafor's room, which spun faster or slower depending on something you couldn't see from across the room, the wind. Lily couldn't see a "price," but she could see what it did.

She shared the notebook with Maya. "When your bracelets were three dollars and there were only a few, everybody wanted them. Then the high price made selling seem worth it, so a bunch of people started making them. Now there are tons." Maya squinted at the columns. "So there's too many for the price they're asking." Lily nodded. "And that boy with the one-dollar sign sold out."

Monday morning, Maya taped a new sign to her shoebox: BRACELETS, ONE DOLLAR, PICK YOUR OWN COLORS. She let buyers choose thread from a box, since everyone else's were the same three patterns. By lunch she had sold eleven, and two of the three-dollar sellers had quietly crossed out their signs and written smaller numbers. After school Maya counted her crumpled bills on the bus, smoothed them flat, and grinned. "Nine to go." Lily looked out the window at the turbines spinning on the ridge past the soccer field, their long white arms turning at different speeds, and started a fresh page in her notebook.

Sophie wanted to win the school science fair more than she wanted her braces off, and she had decided the way to do it was to settle, once and for all, which classroom surface had the most bacteria. Mr. Ruiz had given each table four agar plates, and Sophie's table got the pencil sharpener, the doorknob, the sink faucet, and the teacher's keyboard. "You can't see bacteria," said her lab partner, Marcus, peering at his plate. "So how do we know the shiny stuff isn't just soup?" Sophie pointed at the dots already blooming on the plate they had swabbed that morning. "We can't see them, but we can see what they do. That's the whole trick."

While they waited for colonies to grow, Marcus flipped through a magazine and held up a page. "Look at this ad. Germ-Away wipes change lives," he read. "Wow. Changes lives." Sophie squinted at it. "Fine, but how would you check that?" Marcus shrugged. "You'd have to find a bunch of lives, wipe them, and see." The table cracked up, and even Priya from the next table leaned over to see what was so funny.

Sophie couldn't stop thinking about it, though. She took out her notebook and wrote two columns. In one she put claims like "Germ-Away kills more bacteria than plain soap," which she underlined twice, because Mr. Ruiz had a bottle of each and a whole drawer of plates. You could swab, wipe, wait, count. In the other column she put "changes lives," and after a minute she also put her mother's favorite, "these vitamins make you feel unstoppable," because she could not imagine any plate, anywhere, that could ever prove that wrong. It was like an opinion wearing a lab coat.

"The kill-more-bacteria one is checkable," she told Marcus. "The changes-lives one gives us nothing to test. Not even in principle, whatever principle means." "It means it just can't be done," Marcus said, "even if you had a million plates and a robot." Priya nodded solemnly. "My brother wrote an algorithm that sorts true facts from false ones for his homework," she offered, "and even his algorithm chokes on stuff like that."

Sophie had to confess something then. "I was going to put 'Germ-Away is the best' on my poster, because it sounds strong." Marcus pretended to faint against the sink. "Be strong and checkable," Sophie added, writing it at the top of her column, right under the date.

The next morning the plates had turned into tiny, fertile gardens, gray and orange colonies crowding the pencil sharpener's plate worst of all, which made everybody groan and nobody surprised. Mr. Ruiz stopped at their table and looked a long time at the notebook with its two columns and the circled words "nothing to test." He tapped the page. "Whose is this?" Sophie raised her hand, braced for trouble. He wrote something in his binder instead. "Sofia," he said, "remind me to show you what Karl Popper did with this idea. You'll like him. He was even crankier than you."

Sophie grinned. "That's an opinion, Mr. Ruiz."

"Checkable," he said, and moved on to the next table.

Sawyer refreshed the page for the eleventh time that afternoon. The sneakers he wanted, the white ones with the orange stripe, had been forty dollars two weeks ago. Now the lowest listing read seventy-five, and the little bar under the search filter said only three pairs remained. He had waited because he wanted to spend his lawn-mowing money on a concert ticket instead, and he was still not sure that had been the right call.

"Still checking those shoes?" his dad asked from the kitchen doorway. "Come on, we need gas."

At the station, the sign glowed in the fading light, each number luminous against the dark sky like something from a movie marquee. Sawyer noticed the price first because his dad groaned at it. "It was cheaper last week," his dad muttered, easing the nozzle into the tank.

A kid about Sawyer's age was standing by the next pump, squinting up at the sign. "Why'd it go up since Saturday?" the kid asked nobody in particular. "The gas is the same gas."

Sawyer found himself answering before he thought about it. "My uncle drives tankers, and he says crude oil is usually the biggest single part of what a gallon costs. Like, one chunk, bigger than any other chunk. So when crude gets more expensive, pump prices mostly go up too." He paused. "I think that's how it works, anyway."

The kid shrugged and wandered off, but Sawyer kept turning it over while the numbers climbed on the pump display. It was the same thing happening with his sneakers. Lots of people wanted them, hardly any pairs were left, and the price had shot up. When the warehouse restocked and there were hundreds of listings, the price would sink back down. He couldn't see the wanting or the scarcity itself, only the numbers moving, but the numbers were like footprints. Last month he had tested the idea by watching a different shoe, a pair everyone had said was finished, and he had watched the price fall for nine straight days until it hit nineteen dollars. His technique was simple: check morning and night, write the lowest price in a notebook, and never buy on the first day of a spike.

"Done," his dad said, hanging up the nozzle.

Back home, Sawyer opened his notebook to a clean page and wrote two columns, one labeled shoes and one left blank for now. Seventy-five dollars was too much, and he knew it. But restocks happened, and he could wait. He set an alarm for six in the morning, put the notebook by his pillow, and clicked the refresh button one more time. Two pairs left.

The restaurant smelled of ginger and scallions, and Claire's stomach growled before the waiter had even set down the menus. Mei's family owned the Golden Lantern, and tonight Mei's grandmother had insisted on cooking "something special," which turned out to be seven dishes that all seemed to revolve around one enormous pot of rice in the middle of the table. Claire wanted more than anything to make a good impression. Her plan was simple: eat everything, compliment everything, and not knock anything over.

The trouble started with the dumplings. They were slippery, and Claire needed both hands to fish one out of the shared platter. Without thinking, she planted her chopsticks straight up in her bowl of rice like two little flagpoles and reached across the table. The chatter around the table stopped. Mei's grandmother went very still, and her eyes flicked to the bowl and then quickly away, as if she had seen something she did not want to see.

"Nan, what's wrong?" Mei asked her grandmother in a low voice. Then Mei followed the old woman's gaze, and Claire watched her friend's face change from confusion to understanding. Mei leaned over and whispered, "Don't leave your chopsticks standing in the rice. It looks like incense offered to the dead." Claire pulled the chopsticks out so fast she nearly launched a grain of rice into the soy sauce. "Oh no. Oh no, I'm so sorry," she whispered back. Mei's grandmother said something in Chinese, and Mei laughed for the first time since the dumpling incident. "She says you have good reflexes. She once knocked over a whole teapot doing the same thing at her own grandmother's table."

Claire laid her chopsticks across the top of her bowl the way she saw everyone else do, resting them side by side like a pair of quiet birds. Then, because she wanted to be sure, she watched Mei's father closely through the next three courses. He never once left his chopsticks planted anywhere, not even when he answered his phone about some argument with the landlord over the leaking roof. Every time he needed a free hand, down the chopsticks went, flat beside the bowl. Claire tested her theory by pretending to need both hands for her napkin. Resting the chopsticks, she decided, was the safe pattern, the invisible rule that everyone at this table knew and she had just learned the hard way.

After dinner, Mei's grandmother pressed a small red envelope into Claire's hands. "For luck," Mei translated. "She likes you. She says anyone who apologizes that fast can come back anytime." At the door, Claire turned and held up the envelope with a grin. "Same time next month? I promise my chopsticks will lie down like well-trained puppies." Behind her, she heard Mei's grandmother laugh, a sound like small bells.

The festival filled the park with tents and flags, and Edouard moved through the crowd with a folded card in his back pocket. His grandmother had pressed it into his hand that morning before he left, saying in their family's language, "This is for you, but read it at the lantern table, not before." Edouard understood every word she said. He had been answering her in that language since he was small, at Sunday dinners and on the phone every Thursday. But the card itself was written down, in looping script he could not read at all.

He found the lantern table near the fountain, where volunteers were handing out translucent paper shades for people to decorate and hang on the long strings overhead. Painting a message on a lantern before hanging it was the closing ritual of the festival, and his grandmother had done it every year since they arrived. Edouard unfolded the card, hoping that seeing the whole thing would somehow help. It didn't. The letters sat there like a fence he could walk beside but never get through. He spoke the language, and yet the writing was a stranger to him.

At the next table, a girl about his age was chatting easily with an elderly woman in a language Edouard recognized as the same one. Then the woman handed her a small note, and the girl's face went pink. "Halmoni, I can't read this," she admitted. "I can talk to you fine, but reading it is different." The older woman laughed kindly and read it aloud herself. Edouard drifted closer. "Same thing happens to me," he said. "I chat with my grandmother all the time, but I can't read a word she writes."

The girl, whose name was Naomi, nodded like she'd been waiting for someone to say it. "My cousin calls ours a heritage language," she said. "Because we speak it at home, but out here everyone uses the community's main language." She tapped the note. "So kids like us can speak it and still not read it." Edouard looked back at his card. It wasn't that he was bad at the language. It was that speaking it and reading it were two different skills, and only one of them had ever been needed at his house.

He had an idea. If the grandmother could read the note aloud, maybe he could test whether his ear could do the work his eyes couldn't. He asked Naomi's grandmother, politely, if she would read his card to him. She unfolded it, smiled at the looping script, and spoke the words slowly. As she read, Edouard followed along, and the sentence opened like a door: "Write your wish for the year on your lantern, in our language, any way you can."

His grandmother hadn't asked for perfect spelling. She'd only asked him to try. Edouard picked up a brush, dipped it in the deep blue paint, and, letter by careful letter, copying from the card in front of him, began to write.

Penelope tapped her pencil against the gym door and counted the seconds until Coach Ruiz stopped talking. He was explaining the wall chart again, the one with every girl's free-throw percentage ranked from best to worst, and Penelope's name was near the bottom. Again. She shot every day at the park, sometimes fifty times, and her ranking never moved. Something was wrong with the chart, or something was wrong with her, and she intended to find out which.

That Saturday, her uncle Marcelo took her to Riley's, the sports bar near his apartment, because her parents were at a conference and somebody had to supervise her while they were gone. Uncle Marcelo wanted the place mostly for the nachos, which he claimed were the best in the county, and he wanted them extra hot. On the big screen, two baseball announcers were arguing about a player. One of them kept saying "on-base percentage" like it was a magic spell.

"That guy's boring," the other announcer said. "Everyone knows home runs win games."

Uncle Marcelo laughed through a mouthful of chips. "There's a book about this. Came out in 2003, written by Michael Lewis. It's called Moneyball. The 2002 Oakland Athletics, the whole team, they didn't have money like the rich teams. So they used statistics like on-base percentage to find players nobody else wanted. Cheap players. Undervalued, that's the word. And they competed anyway."

"You mean the team with the least money won?" Penelope asked.

"Competed," her uncle said, holding up a nacho like a professor's chalk. "That's the important part." Then he ordered a second plate and forgot the whole conversation, but Penelope didn't.

Monday after school, she sat in the library with the chart numbers she had copied into her notebook and a library copy of the book itself, which was thicker than she expected and, she discovered by page thirty, kind of tedious in places. The idea underneath it wasn't tedious at all. Home runs and total points and rankings were just the loud numbers. There were quieter numbers that told you what a player actually did over and over, game after game.

She found a table where her friend Dree was drawing a poster for the pet club, some cartoon herbivore munching leaves. "Dree," Penelope said, "you know the book report you did on dolphins? Where'd you get the database?"

"Library site. Why?"

Penelope borrowed the computer and typed in the coach's practice log, which was posted online every week. She felt like she was doing something slightly against the rules, even though it wasn't. The log had everyone's attempts and makes for three whole weeks. The chart on the gym wall only showed one number per player, and Penelope's number looked bad because she took the most attempts of anyone on the team. Sixty-one attempts. The captain, Roni, had taken twelve and made nine, which put her first on the chart.

Penelope did the division four times to be sure. Over the three weeks, Penelope's percentage was higher than Roni's. Not by much. But higher.

The next morning she asked Coach Ruiz if she could show him something, and she laid her notebook on his desk next to his coffee. He frowned at it for a long moment, the way he frowned at blown plays. "Where'd you get this?"

"The practice log. And a book." She pointed at the column of divisions. "The chart squishes everything into one number."

Coach Ruiz rubbed his jaw. Then he stood, walked to the gym wall, and drew a second column in green marker next to the old one. "Practice attempts logged, three-week average," he announced to the arriving team, and the room went quiet the way it did before a close game's final shot.

Roni stared at the new column, at her name, and then at Penelope's name sitting two lines above it. "How long have you been shooting sixty a day?"

"Since October," Penelope said.

Roni picked up a ball from the rack and bounced it once, hard. "Fine. Then race me to a hundred makes."

Gabriella crouched at the edge of the halfpipe with a battery, a coil of wire, and her older brother's multimeter, while her best friend Devi rolled back and forth on her board above her.

"Are you seriously doing homework at a skate park?" Devi called down.

"It's not homework, it's a mission." Gabriella held up the little black box. "Coach Reyes says the wiring in our float for the parade keeps failing, and nobody knows why. I'm going to find out. Today I learn to measure resistance." She clipped one probe to each end of the wire and read the screen. "Voltage is six. Now the current." She switched the dial, and the numbers crawled into place. "Zero point five amps. So resistance equals voltage divided by current. Six divided by zero point five. That's twelve ohms."

"Twelve what?"

"Ohms. That's how much the wire fights the current." Gabriella jumped up, thrilled with herself. "I can't see resistance, but I can calculate it from things I can see. That's the logic of it. Measure voltage, measure current, divide."

Devi rolled down the ramp and stopped in a spray of gravel. "Show me on the float."

They dragged the float, a decorated trailer with three lights strung along one side, into the shade of the bleachers. Gabriella assessed the problem bulb by bulb, pressing each one and checking her numbers. Then she traced the wire with her finger and stopped.

"Wait. There's only one path. All three bulbs share one loop through the battery." She tugged a bulb loose, and all three lights went dark. She stared at it, then at Devi, then grabbed her notebook. "That's the whole problem! One bulb breaks at the parade, everything goes black. Every time."

"So add more batteries?"

"No. Rewire it." Her hands were already moving, unplugging and reconnecting the synthetic insulation she'd stripped back, looping each bulb to the battery on its own. When she finished, she pulled out the middle bulb. The other two stayed lit. She pulled a second one. The last one still glowed.

"Whoa," Devi said. "They don't care."

"Because each bulb has its own path to the battery now, so the others stay lit if one breaks." Gabriella screwed the bulbs back in and all three blazed against the bleachers, bright enough that a kid on the ramps turned to look.

"Test it again," Devi said, grinning.

Gabriella unplugged, replugged, unplugged, replugged, faster each time, the lights stubbornly staying on. Then she measured the voltage and current on the new wire, did the division in her head, and wrote the resistance in her notebook in big letters.

"Twelve ohms," she announced to the whole park, "and unbreakable lights. Parade's on Saturday. Be there."

The bus smelled like vinyl seats and peanut butter crackers, and Grace ran through her word list for the fourth time even though she knew every entry cold. In thirty minutes the regional spelling bee would start, and only the champion would go to nationals. Second place got a dictionary, which felt to Grace like getting a towel after swimming halfway across a pool. Across the aisle, Marcus leaned his head against the window and watched the fence posts go by.

"You look like you're going to be sick," Grace said.

"I might be," Marcus said. "If I come in second again. Last year I got out on 'rhubarb.' Do you know how it feels to lose to a vegetable?"

Grace opened her mouth to say she didn't care about his rhubarb, then closed it, because the truth was she had thought about little else all week except coming in second herself. She reached into her backpack and pulled out a folded note her older sister had left on her pillow that morning. She smoothed it out on her knee.

"If you get 'presume' in the bee, it's p-r-e-s-u-m-e," her sister had written, "because you presume you're right before you check. Don't presume. Ask for the definition every single time. Also eat something, you spelled better after breakfast at the last one. Love, Tessa." Grace smiled and passed the note across the aisle so Marcus could read it too.

At the bee, the rounds burned down from forty spellers to six, then to three, then to Grace and Marcus alone. He spelled "agile" without a hitch. She spelled "anomaly," asking for the definition first, exactly as the note said, and got it right. Round after round followed, and nobody missed. The pronouncer kept pulling fresh words from the box, and Grace noticed something she had never seen before: there was no rule for ending this. She remembered a fact her sister had mentioned once, and she raised her hand.

"Is it true that the 2019 Scripps National Spelling Bee ended with eight co-champions, because the spellers kept getting every word right?"

The pronouncer blinked. "That's correct."

"So if we both keep spelling everything right," Grace said, "there doesn't have to be a loser?"

The officials conferred in the corner, and Marcus caught Grace's eye across the microphone. He was grinning now, not green at all. Two rounds later, after Grace sailed through "moratorium" and Marcus handled "vitreous" without a stumble, the pronouncer lifted his hand.

"We are declaring two co-champions," he announced. "Both of you will advance to nationals."

Marcus held up his fist across the stage, and Grace ran over and bumped it with hers. In the back of the hall, her sister was already on her feet, waving the empty note envelope over her head like a flag.

Jake's fingers slid off the strings for the eleventh time, and the note came out sour, like a door complaining on its hinges. His grandfather's old guitar had a warm, honey-colored body that smelled faintly of lemon polish, and Jake loved everything about it except the fact that he couldn't play it. He had been at Grandpa's house every Saturday for a month, working through the same song from start to finish, over and over, and measure seventeen still collapsed every single time.

He set the guitar down and wandered into the kitchen, where Grandpa was folding a frugal lunch of half a sandwich and the last three crackers in the box. "Can I confide something?" Jake asked. "That song hates me."

"Songs don't hate people," Grandpa said, sliding the plate toward him. "But something in it might not like your fingers."

Jake chewed the cracker and thought about that. What exactly was going wrong? He hummed the piece in his head and noticed something odd. The beginning was smooth now. The ending, the big climax with all those ringing chords, was almost easy. Only four measures in the middle, the quick jump from the third string to the first, kept snapping like a trap. So why was he practicing the whole song, start to finish, when the whole song wasn't the problem?

He carried the guitar back to the porch rocker and tried a different idea. He would play only measures seventeen through twenty. Nothing else. He looped them slowly, slower than the song actually went, watching his fingers make the jump, missing, backing up, trying again. Then a little faster. Then faster still. Was this how real players did it? He wondered whether hours of playing a piece mattered less than aiming straight at the weak spot, like fixing the one broken stair instead of walking the whole staircase a hundred times.

After forty minutes his left hand ached and his fingertips had grooves in them, but the jump was starting to feel automatic, almost like blinking. He played the whole song once, and when measure seventeen arrived, his fingers simply knew where to go. He laughed out loud at the empty porch.

"That sounded different," Grandpa said from the doorway, holding two glasses of lemonade. "You fixed it."

"I fixed four measures," Jake said. "Just those."

Grandpa grinned. "Then tomorrow we'll find out what happens when you aim at the next four."

Mya sat cross-legged on her bed with her phone six inches from her face, watching the group chat light up. The project was due Friday: make a page about where your family came from. Jordan had already typed three messages about presenting first because he wanted the class to remember his slide before anyone else's, and Priya had sent a photo of her grandmother's cookbook. Mya hadn't sent anything yet, because she had a problem. Her cousin Lena was visiting from abroad, and last night at dinner Lena had laughed so hard she nearly knocked over her water glass when everyone kept saying she'd flown in from Germany.

"It's Deutschland," Lena had said. "We never call it Germany. That's your word for us, not ours." Then she'd told Mya the names for the two kinds of words, and Mya had written them on the back of her math homework so she wouldn't forget.

She typed into the chat: "Hypothetical question. If we call a country one thing and the people there call it something else, which name should go on my poster?" Jordan answered fast: "Ours, obviously, it's for our class." Priya sent a shrug emoji. Mya tried a different approach, the way she'd test a rule in science: collect data. She messaged her uncle, her grandmother, and Lena's mother, asking each one what their family called the country in their own language.

The answers came in through the evening. Her grandmother wrote back a whole text about the village, and then added, "Here we say it our way, there they say it theirs, both are true names." Lena's mother sent one line: "Deutschland, always." Mya copied the messages into a document for her citation page, so her teacher could see where each name came from. She noticed a pattern: every family member used their own word, and not one of them used the English one, unless they were talking to someone outside.

"So which one wins?" Jordan asked, when she posted her draft. He still wanted his slide first and had moved on to arguing about presentation order, but Priya had gone quiet, and then sent: "Wait. My mom calls our family's country something different too. I just never thought about it. Can I put both on my page?"

Mya looked at Lena, who was leaning in the doorway in her borrowed sweatpants, reading over her shoulder. Lena tapped the screen where Mya had typed both names side by side, then the two labels underneath them. "A name a group uses for itself is called an endonym," Lena said, "and a name outsiders use is an exonym." Mya added the last line to her poster and hit send. Priya replied within a minute: "Doing it. Mine's going up first, Jordan."

"Fine," Jordan typed. "But I'm still going before the bell invades my free time."

Hannah crouched beside the boardwalk on the Willow Creek trail, her notebook open to a page titled "BIRD EVIDENCE" in fat letters. Her mission for the morning was to watch one bird for ten whole minutes and record what its beak did. Her little brother Marcus wanted only one thing: to reach the frog pond before anyone else in the history of the world. "Slow bird-watchers restrict the pace of fast civilians," he announced, drumming his heels on the boards.

"Shh. I think it's a wren," Hannah whispered, pointing at a stubby gray bird prying something out of a seed head. She drew the beak, small and curved like a bent nail. Then she checked her field guide, and her stomach dropped. The bird on the page had a straight, thick, seed-cracking beak. Her "wren" was a finch, and her whole page of careful notes now belonged to the wrong bird. She flopped back against the railing. "This is hopeless. Even Darwin's birds got mixed up, and I can't even tell a finch from a wren."

Marcus stopped drumming. "Darwin messed up birds? The Darwin?" He sat down, suddenly very interested in the idea of a famous genius being wrong.

Hannah flipped to the back of the guide, where a timeline ran along the bottom of the page. She ran her finger along it and stopped. "Listen to this. In 1837, an ornithologist named John Gould told Darwin that his Galápagos birds, some of which Darwin had taken for wrens or blackbirds, were a new group of closely related finches." She read it twice, and something clicked into place. "So Darwin collected them and labeled them wrong. Gould looked at the beaks and saw what Darwin missed."

"Who's John Gould?" Marcus asked.

"Bird scientist. The one who figured it out." Hannah turned back to her notebook. On the Galápagos islands, she remembered from class, the finches on different islands had different beak shapes, each one matched to a different food. The beaks themselves were the evidence, sitting right there on the birds' faces. If a beak was thick, it cracked hard seeds. If it was thin, it grabbed insects. Nobody could watch the beaks changing over generations, but you could read the pattern, like footprints left by something you never saw. Maybe, she thought, mislabeling one bird wasn't a disaster.
