Mei laughed and told a story about Grandpa hiding plum candy in his coat sleeve, a chronic habit, so reliable that the cousins used to check his pockets first thing at every visit.

The sky was turning gray, and their mothers called from down the hill that the storm would arrive within the hour, so they had to finish before the paper lantern soaked through. Mei and Alexis brushed the last leaves from the base of the stone together, and Alexis pressed her palm flat against the cool granite, once, the way she used to press her hand into Grandpa's before a staring contest.

"Why do you think the bird flies?" Alexis asked, watching the lantern bob in the rising wind.

Mei folded a small crease in its wing. "Maybe it's looking for someone to deliver the oranges to."

"Then it better hurry," Alexis said, and lifted it up into the first fat drops of rain.

Hannah stared at the lopsided bean plants along the back fence and knew her science fair poster was doomed. It said, in fat green letters, Plants Like Music, and her teacher had written one question in the margin: How could that be tested? The beans had grown next to the speaker she dragged outside every afternoon, but her brother Theo had watered them whenever he felt like it, so maybe they liked the water, not the music. Nobody at the fair would believe a poster built on a guess she could not check.

"We can fix it," Theo said, plopping down beside her on the back steps with a peanut butter sandwich. "Mom says I have to collaborate with you anyway, since I did the watering."

"You collaborated too much," Hannah said. "That's the problem." She pulled her notebook out of her back pocket and flipped to a page with the word HYPOTHESIS circled twice. She had found it in her science book the night before. "It says here hypotheses are often written as 'If, then' statements. Like, if I make a change, then I predict a result. The change and the prediction both go right in the sentence."

"So write one."

"Fine. If I play music to one tray of beans and no music to another, then the music tray will grow taller." She said it out loud twice, and it sounded like a real experiment instead of a poster with a blob of glue on it. "But both trays get the same water, same spot, same everything else. Only one thing changes."

They set up two trays of new seeds on the picnic table, counted out twenty seeds apiece, and marked the music tray with a strip of tape. Their father's toy sailboat sat at the end of the table, waiting for its broken rudder to be glued, and Hannah moved it out of the way so the shadow would not fall on either tray. "Sorry," she told the boat. "You're extinct until Saturday." Then she plugged in the speaker, faced it at tray one, and pressed play.

Every afternoon after school they measured. Theo held the ruler while Hannah wrote the numbers, and they argued about half millimeters until their mother called them in for dinner. By Friday the no-music tray was winning by three centimeters, and Hannah felt her cheeks go hot even though nobody was watching. She had predicted the wrong result.

"Poster's ruined," Theo said.

"No, it's better." Hannah turned the notebook around so he could see the graph she had started. "The test overturned my hypothesis, which means it was a real test. I'll write what actually happened." She picked up the green marker, crossed out Plants Like Music, and wrote underneath: If no music, then taller beans. "Guess the plants like quiet," she said, and pinned the page to the fence beside the trays.

Laurence set her easel on the grass beside her cousin Dev, who had decided that anyone could paint a portrait in one afternoon. She had her grandmother's old box of watercolours, the pan nearly gone in the yellow corner, and a photograph of her grandmother propped against the fence. "You don't just draw it once," she said. "You start with the palest wash and let it dry, then add darker ones. Light to dark. You can't go backwards."

Dev frowned at his paper. He was more interested in the fence behind his drawing of the shed, and he had pressed so hard with his pencil that every guide line had carved a groove. "I'll just erase these later," he said.

Laurence remembered last winter, sitting at the kitchen table while her mother winced over a drawing of the living room. Her mother had pressed hard too, back when she was learning, and no eraser had lifted the lines. The finished room had stayed covered in them, faint rails running across the ceiling and floor, because the guide lines for perspective are drawn lightly with a hard pencil so they can be erased once the room's real edges are darkened in. Her mother had said, "You have to trust that the lines are there even when you can barely see them." Laurence had thought that was strange advice for drawing, and stranger still for everything else.

She laid her first wash, the palest peach, over the whole face and let the sun do the drying. While she waited she watched Dev scrub at his paper with the eraser until it pilled and tore. The grooves stayed. He flipped his board over, and she noticed the lines showed through the back, like bones under skin. "Try drawing the fence again on a fresh sheet," she said, "but press like you're drawing on a soap bubble."

Dev gave her the look he saved for advice from girls, the stereotype that art was her side of the family, some hereditary thing that had skipped him. But he picked up the hard 4H pencil she handed him and drew so lightly he had to tilt the sheet to see his own lines. "That's not drawing," he complained. "That's whispering."

"That's how it's supposed to look," Laurence said. She touched her brush to the second wash, a deeper rose along the jaw, and watched the first layer glow up through it. Dev leaned over her shoulder, holding his whispery fence up beside it.

"Okay," he said. "Teach me the faces next."

The lights went out at 8:40, right in the middle of Brooklyn's game, and the screen died to black. Her little brother Theo groaned from the couch. Their mom found the candles in the kitchen drawer, the ones shaped like pinecones that smelled like a fake forest, and set three of them on the coffee table. The flames leaned sideways whenever anyone walked past, throwing wobbly shadows up the wall.

"I was about to beat the whole level," Theo said.

"Beat it tomorrow." Brooklyn stared at the dark television. Then she remembered something her cousin Dev had told her last summer, after a storm knocked out power across his whole network of streets. He had lost his desktop computer that night. When the electricity came back on, he said, a surge of power had shot through the house and fried the machine. Emergency agencies told people to unplug their computers and other electronics during a power cut, because when the power returned, the surge could damage them.

"I didn't believe him at first," she said out loud, crouching behind the TV. "I thought he spilled juice on it and made up the surge thing." She pulled the console's plug from the wall and coiled the cord around her hand. Next she went to the desk in the corner and unplugged the desktop computer, then the router blinking dark on the shelf, then the microwave in the kitchen. Theo followed her with a candle, dripping wax onto a plate he carried like a waiter.

"What if the power comes back on while you're asleep?" he asked.

"That's the point. It can come back any time, and everything plugged in gets hit." She pointed at the lamp by the couch. "That one too, please."

The power stayed off until after 10. They played shadow puppets on the ceiling, and Theo made a shape he claimed was an authentic wolf, though it looked more like a rabbit with big ears. Brooklyn drew a map of the neighborhood in her notebook, trying to depict which streets might be dark, guessing it was just their block since the kitchen window showed lights glowing two houses down.

At 10:20 the ceiling fan spun once, the lamps blazed on, and the refrigerator started humming in the kitchen. The television screen stayed black and quiet, its plug lying on the floor where Brooklyn had left it. She smiled at it, then went around the room picking up her candles.

"Tomorrow, level twelve," Theo said. "Nobody fried."

"Nobody fried," Brooklyn said, and blew out the last pinecone.

The rain moved in after lunch on Wednesday, so Cabin 6's whole afternoon revolved around the battered Monopoly box that黛黛 the craft closet. Leah sat cross-legged on the floor between Priya and Marcus, whose family hosted the camp's exchange weekend last spring, so she knew the Rendell house rules. Those rules did not include money on Free Parking.

Priya threw the dice, landed on Free Parking, and reached for the center of the board with a grin. "Payday." When her hand found nothing but dust, she frowned. "Where's the pot?"

"There isn't one," Marcus said, not looking up from his railroads. "Free Parking is just free. It doesn't do anything."

"Everybody plays it with the taxes in the middle," Priya insisted. She sounded certain, the way people sound about things that revolve quietly through every game night at their own house.

"Maybe at your house," Marcus said. "It's a house rule, not one of the official rules." He shrugged. "That's why people from different homes fight about it."

Across the circle, Jake laughed. "Priya's never read the rules. Priya thinks the money just appears, like magic. Maybe she thinks a memoir about Monopoly would explain it." A couple of kids chuckled. Priya's ears went pink and she stared at the board.

Leah wanted to say something, but she'd learned in fourth grade that shouting "be nice" at Jake mostly made things louder. So she tried a smaller door. "Priya's right that most people play it that way," she said, keeping her voice level. "My family does the pot too. It's like half the fun." Then she turned to the box lid. "Hey, the rules are printed on the inside. We could just look."

They did. Marcus read the Free Parking entry out loud, and it was exactly as short and boring as he'd claimed: nothing happened, no money, no pot. Priya read it herself, twice, and Leah watched the pink fade from her ears. "Okay," Priya said. "But next game we vote on house rules before we start. Write them down."

"Deal," said Marcus. "As long as we also vote on whether Jake has to stop being obstinate about the banker job."

"I'm the best banker," Jake said, clutching the box of money to his chest like a rescued kitten.

Leah slid a pencil and the back of the camp schedule across the floor to Priya. "You write. Rule one: pot on Free Parking, taxes and everything, all cash in the middle."

Priya printed it in big careful letters while Marcus pretended to faint and Jake pretended to catch him. Then Priya rolled, landed on Free Parking again, and held out her hand. "That one's free," she announced. "I'm keeping track."

Jayden slid the last of his birthday money across his desk and counted it twice. Eleven dollars, and he needed three mangoes for the smoothie he was making Mom on Sunday, because she had said once, quietly, that mango smoothies tasted like a good day. At the grocery store he walked straight to the produce section and stopped cold. A small handwritten sign sat in an almost-empty bin: Mangoes, $2.50 each. He touched the sign as if it might be a mistake, but the plastic was cool and permanent. Two empty crates leaned against the wall behind the bin, and a stocker with a name tag that read ROSA was carrying the third away.

"There was a frost down south," Rosa said, not slowing down. "We get what we get." Jayden did the math in his head. Three mangoes would be seven fifty, which left him nothing for the orange juice, and without juice there was no smoothie, just a bowl of pulp. He stood there while a woman in a gray coat picked up four of the last six mangoes without even looking at the price. Four. Jayden watched her walk off and felt something click, a concept forming: lots of people wanted them, there weren't many, and the price was high. The three things went together.

That night his phone buzzed. A message from his friend Zoe: "Garage sale tomorrow on Elm. Mr. Ruiz is selling 20 skateboards he imported. Come early, it'll be huge." Jayden texted back that he was saving for mangoes, and Zoe replied, "That's the boringest sentence anyone has ever sent me." But he went anyway, because Zoe said the skateboards were five dollars each, and five dollars for a skateboard was like finding money on the ground.

It did not go how Zoe promised. At nine in the morning Mr. Ruiz's driveway was crowded, but his sign said twelve dollars, and people picked up the boards, looked at the price, and set them back down. By ten there were still fifteen skateboards, and Mr. Ruiz had crossed out the twelve and written nine. By noon only six were left, and the sign said seven. Zoe bought one and Jayden hung around to watch Mr. Ruiz change the sign one more time, to five fifty, and the last boards vanished in under twenty minutes. Not one left over, and not one buyer who walked away wanting one. "My son taught me that," Mr. Ruiz said, sweeping the empty driveway. "He says the price where the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers have is called the equilibrium price. Also market-clearing, because it clears you out exactly."

Sunday morning Jayden walked back to the grocery store. The mango bin was full, stacked into a wobbly orange pyramid, and Rosa was squeezing past crates of them. The sign read $1.25 each. His pulse seemed to accelerate as he grabbed three, then the orange juice, then paid with money to spare. The price had come down to meet the buyers, and it felt stable now, the way Mr. Ruiz's five fifty had felt, like the exact right number sitting still.

He carried the bag home and put everything on the counter, then set the leftover four dollars beside the blender. "That's for next time," he said, and got out the knife.

Brody stood at the edge of the gym with his phone out, typing into the family group chat while the DJ played a song nobody danced to yet.

"Nobody's dancing," he sent. "I'm basically a coat rack with shoes."

His sister replied first, as always. "Then be the first coat rack to dance."

His mom sent a thumbs-up, which helped exactly zero percent. His grandpa typed slowly, in fragments, so Brody knew a message about "back in my day" was coming, and he would get it in about ten minutes, sentence by sentence.

He remembered the chat from last week, when the permission slip had come home. His mom had written, "He says he's not going," and his sister had answered, "He said that about the bake sale too, and then he ran the cash box." That had actually been the best part. He liked handling the commerce part, counting change, making sure the fundraiser earned what it should. His grandpa had replied, "The boy understands commerce. He'll be fine." Brody had gone to his room and smiled at that, though he'd never admit it.

Now the gym lights dimmed, and a single spotlight clicked on, aimed at the mirror ball hanging from the ceiling. Brody watched the beam hit it, and suddenly hundreds of small spots of light began to sweep across the floor, the walls, the bleachers, sliding over everybody's faces. It was like the whole room had started to glitter. Some kids stopped pretending not to care and just looked up.

A girl near the wall was watching the spots too. She wasn't dancing either. She pointed at one spot on the floor and followed it with her finger until it vanished, then found a new one. "Okay, wait," she said to nobody, then seemed to decide that Brody counted as nobody. "There's one spotlight. One. So why is the whole floor covered?"

Brody looked up. Each little mirror tile on the ball caught the beam and threw it somewhere different, so every tile made its own spot, and because the ball spun, the spots moved. One spotlight in, hundreds of moving spots out, because each mirror tile reflected the beam in a slightly different direction.

"Want me to demonstrate?" he said. He held up his phone with the flashlight on, angled it at his watch face, and a little white spot of light jumped onto the girl's sneaker. He tilted the watch a tiny bit and the spot slid away across the floor. She laughed.

"So the whole ball is just a bunch of watches," she said.

"A bunch of really organized watches."

The DJ started a song people actually liked, and the floor began to fill. The spots of light kept sweeping over everyone, faster now, like the room was breathing. The girl stuck out her hand.

"I'm Priya," she said. "That was the most fundamental thing anyone's said to me all night. Come on, you can explain the smoke machine next."

Brody put his phone in his pocket, where the group chat buzzed on, unread, and followed her onto the floor.

The group chat lit up at 4:32 on a Tuesday. Marisol sent a screenshot of an old blog with a purple background and a clipart frog in the corner, followed by three crying-laughing emojis. "WAIT," she typed. "This is Dani's blog from third grade. It's still ONLINE."

Jonathan tapped the link. Sure enough, there was Dani's handwriting, scanned in, a whole page about her dream of owning forty-two hamsters. Below the frog, small gray letters said the page had been saved by something called the Wayback Machine. "What is that," he typed, "a time machine for frogs?"

"It's real," Dani answered, and he could tell from her short replies that she was not laughing. "Since 1996 the Internet Archive has been saving copies of public web pages, and anyone can look at old versions of sites. My mom just showed me. That's how Marisol found it."

Marisol apologized right away, typing fast. Jonathan scrolled down the old page instead. Near the bottom, under a post about the class talent show, Dani had written her old address and a map to her house so friends could come to her birthday party. Forty-two hamsters, he thought, and one home address, sitting in an archive where anybody could read it.

He remembered his own post from last spring, the video of his dog Biscuit in the backyard, with the school name visible on his gym shirt in the background. He had deleted the video in June. He typed to the chat: "Meet me in the library computer lab tomorrow. I want to test something." Then, because it was Dani's page that started this, he added, "Bring that link. I want to see how far back it goes."

The next day, four of them crowded around one screen. They opened the archive and searched for Dani's blog. There it was, captured over and over, year after year, like a photo album nobody had asked for. Jonathan felt his stomach go quiet. "So deleting doesn't really delete," he said. "If a page was public, a copy might live there anyway." He tried to mimic the casual voice of someone who had known this all along, but nobody was fooled. Marisol put her hand on the back of his chair.

He pulled up his own deleted video account next, searching in a systematic way, page by page, checking dates. Not there. He let out a breath, then stopped himself, because Dani was still staring at her old address on the screen. He slid the keyboard toward her. "You could write to them," he said. "There's a contact page."

That night Dani sent the group a photo of the message she had submitted, asking politely if the page could be taken down. Two days later came her reply: "It's gone. And my new blog has hamsters, no frogs, and no addresses." Jonathan typed back, "Forty-two hamsters deserves a fresh page."

Mila slid the onion skin onto the stage and clamped it down, her heart doing a little drumroll. Today was the day she would actually see a cell, a real one, and she had already promised herself she would get the focus perfect on the first try. Ms. Reyes had written three words on the board: cell wall, membrane, nucleus. "Your job," she had said, "is to find all three and label them in your drawing."

She leaned into the eyepiece. Gray nothing. She turned the coarse knob one way, then the other, and still nothing but a pale fog. Behind her, Devon shouted that he could see his cells already, which felt unfair, since his onion sample was so thick it could have been a slice of pizza crust.

"Mine's too thick," Mila muttered. She pulled the razor blade from the tray, peeled a paper-thin layer from the inside curve of a fresh onion ring, and laid it flat in one drop of iodine. The new sample looked almost invisible, like a ghost of an onion, and that gave her a sudden idea. If the fog was just layers and layers of cells stacked on top of each other, then one thin layer should let the light through. It was like the difference between one window and ten windows glued together.

She focused slowly this time, saving the fine knob for last, and the image bloomed all at once. Bricks. Dozens of them, each one a tidy rectangle with a dark dot near the edge. "Look, the wall goes all the way around each one," she said, pulling Devon over by his sleeve. She traced the dark outline of a cell, then the thinner line just inside it. "That thinner one's the membrane, and the dot's the nucleus." She was so excited she nearly knocked the microscope sideways drawing it.

"The nucleus is the part that gets passed down," Devon said, squinting at his own slide. "My cousin has my grandpa's exact nose. My mom emphasizes it every Thanksgiving, like it's the climax of the whole year." He drew a nose in the margin of his lab sheet, a big one with a bump.

Mila laughed, then stopped, because the nose reminded her of something from a documentary she had watched with her dad about birds on islands. "Hey, the finches," she said. "There was a drought in 1977, and only some birds survived, and the ones that made it had big beaks. Then their babies had bigger beaks on average than the birds before the drought. Because the beaks got passed down, like your grandpa's nose." She tapped her drawing, right on the nucleus of cell number three, and labeled it with a hard push of her pencil.

"Exactly like the nose," Devon said solemnly, and drew a beak next to it.

Ms. Reyes stopped at their table, looked at the two labeled drawings, and pointed at the extra beak. "Nice," she said. "Now find me a cell that's vulnerable, one with a broken wall, and draw what's inside spilling out." Mila bent back over the eyepiece, hunting.

Gabrielle slid a folded paper across the dinner table, past the mashed potatoes, until it stopped against her brother Marcus's glass of milk. "Read the first line," she said.

Marcus picked it up with his fork hand. "'The city should paint a crosswalk at Fifth and Maple.'" He lowered the paper. "That's your opinion. The council gets a hundred of those a week."

"It's not just an opinion." Gabrielle pulled a crumpled notebook from her backpack and opened it to a page covered in tally marks. "I sat at that corner after school on Tuesday and Thursday. I counted eleven times when somebody almost got hit because there's no place to cross. Eleven near-misses in two days."

Their dad set down his serving spoon. "You counted near-misses? For how long?"

"Forty minutes each time." She tapped the tallies. "So when I say the city should paint a crosswalk, it's still my opinion, right? But an opinion with evidence behind it is more convincing than one with no reasons at all. Marcus's opinion is just words. Mine has eleven tallies."

Marcus frowned at the notebook. "Fine, it's more convincing than mine. But the council meeting is tomorrow at four. That's your deadline, right? You need signatures tonight."

"That's the problem." Gabrielle pushed her peas around her plate. "I thought I'd get spontaneous support, people just signing because it's obviously dangerous. But Mrs. Okafor next door said no. She wants proof. And I have proof, I just don't know if it's enough to sustain a whole argument, or if it's only a start."

"What else could you count?" her dad asked.

Gabrielle stared at the tally marks, then out the dark window toward the corner she couldn't see. She wondered whether more cars sped up on that stretch than on Oak Street, and whether you could even measure that without a radar gun. What about the number of kids who crossed there every day because the bus stop is on the wrong side? She flipped to a clean page and started writing questions faster than her handwriting could keep up.

"Slow down," Marcus said, watching her. "You have until four tomorrow, not four tonight."

"The bus comes at 7:10 tomorrow morning." Gabrielle was already standing, notebook in hand, chair scraping back. "If I'm there before school, I can count every kid who crosses. Then I'll have two kinds of proof."

She ran for the stairs, then stopped halfway and turned around. "Marcus, bring your watch. I need someone to time the forty minutes."

He sighed and drained his milk. "Fine. But you're carrying the clipboard."

Theodore discovered the disaster the moment he unzipped his backpack on the train. Crumbs everywhere. His bag of salt-and-vinegar chips had burst along the seam sometime during the flight from Denver, and now his paperback, his headphones case, and even his spare socks were saturated with grease and shattered chip pieces. His little sister Maya leaned over from her window seat and burst out laughing.

"It's not funny," Theodore said, fishing out the limp, exploded bag. "I packed it sealed. It was fine at home. Then we get on the plane, and somewhere over the mountains it just blew up." He turned the bag over in his hands, frowning at it. Maya stopped laughing, because she could tell he was in one of his figuring-it-out moods, and those usually ended with something interesting.

"Remember the pretzel bag I bought in the airport?" she said. "The lady at the shop had to squeeze it into my tote because it was so stiff and puffed up. I thought she'd overfilled it."

Theodore pulled the crumpled in-flight magazine out of the side pocket of his backpack, where he had shoved it before landing. He flipped through it, past the maps and the duty-free pages, until he found the paragraph he had half-noticed during the flight. He read it aloud slowly. "Airliner cabins are pressurized, but under regulations the cabin air pressure may be as low as it would be at 8,000 feet, about 2,400 meters, above sea level." He looked up. "Eight thousand feet. That's like being on a tall mountain, even though the plane is way higher than that."

"So the air outside the bag, inside the cabin, gets thin," Maya said, catching on. "But the air inside the bag was sealed in back home, at normal pressure. So the bag puffs out, and if it's already full of chips, it pops."

Theodore grabbed his notebook. "We can test it," he said. "There was some controversy at school last month when Mr. Reyes said planes aren't really sealed like spaceships, and half the class didn't believe him. Conventional wisdom says the cabin is just like sea level, but it isn't, not exactly." He wrote out the plan in his careful block letters: one fresh sealed bag of chips in the backpack, one in the carry-on, checked at takeoff, mid-flight, and landing. If his idea was right, both bags would puff up hard somewhere over the ocean on the way home, then go soft again after they landed.

Their mom, who had been pretending to read her novel across the aisle, handed them a bag of peanuts without a word. Maya held it up. "Sealed at the factory," she said. "Want to save it for the flight home?" Theodore took it and tucked it into the front pocket of his backpack, right next to the notebook, and wrote one more line at the top of the page: Peanut bag, trial number one.

Jaxon pressed down on the tomato, and the knife skated sideways off the slick skin and landed on the cutting board with a clatter. Chef Marisol looked over from the stove, where a pot of curry was already bubbling. "Let me see that blade," she said, running her thumb along the edge. She pulled a different knife from the magnetic strip, handed it over, and went back to stirring.

Jaxon set the tomato on the board again, expecting the same fight. Instead the sharp blade slid through the skin with almost no pressure at all, and the slices fell open in neat red half-moons. He tried the next one, barely pushing, and it cut clean too. So that was the trick. The dull knife had needed all that force, and the force was what made it slip. He lined up the rest of the tomatoes and worked through them slowly, letting the edge do the work.

"Rice, curry, flatbread, all on the table at six o'clock," said Priya, the other student, reading the order ticket. "How is that even possible?" Jaxon glanced at the clock, then at the three stations. The rice would take twenty minutes in the pot, the curry needed fifteen to simmer, and the flatbread cooked in ninety seconds a piece. It wasn't arbitrary, he realized; the timing had a pattern to it, like a schedule hiding inside the recipe. If he started the rice first, then the curry ten minutes later, then rolled the dough while everything simmered, the flatbread could come off the pan last, hot, right as the rice rested.

"Twenty minutes for rice, fifteen for curry," he said out loud, checking his math. "That works if I start now." Priya nodded and lit the burner under the curry pot while Jaxon measured rice and water. The two pots refused to cooperate at first; the curry threatened to boil over while the rice sat stubbornly hard. Jaxon slid the curry to a cooler corner of the burner and lowered the flame under the rice until both settled into a steady simmer.

By ten to six he was rolling dough, dusting it with flour, watching Priya lay the first flatbread in the dry pan. It puffed and blistered, and she flipped it with a confident snap of the wrist. "You're the defendant in this kitchen now," she told the flatbread, "and the jury finds you guilty of being delicious." Jaxon laughed and rolled the next round, glancing at the clock, then at the rice, which had finally absorbed all the water.

At six exactly they carried everything to the serving window: a pot of fluffy rice, a pot of curry, and a stack of warm flatbread. Chef Marisol sampled a bite, then a second one, then said, "Same time next week. You're on onions."

"With the sharp knife," Jaxon said, already washing the blade.

Grandpa's laptop smelled faintly of coffee and old paperbacks, which was odd, because Grandpa drank tea. Christopher sat at the kitchen table with his own notebook open, copying lines of Python while Grandpa hovered behind him like a large, hopeful shadow.

"So the program asks for a number," Christopher said, typing, "and then it tells you if it's prime." Grandpa had tried to recruit him for this project all summer, promising unlimited snacks, and Christopher had finally given in because prime numbers were actually kind of fun. You couldn't see primeness. A number just sat there, looking innocent, and you had to hunt for hidden factors like a detective checking an alibi. "Seven," Grandpa guessed immediately. Christopher ran the program, typed 7, and the screen said prime. Grandpa cheered as if his team had scored.

While Grandpa tested every number he could think of, including his age and his old street address, Christopher glanced at Grandpa's other project, a homepage for his beekeeping club. The heading, BEE HAPPY, ran along the left edge of the page like it was trying to escape through the margin. "Grandpa, your title's squashed against the side."

"It's been like that for days," Grandpa admitted. "I thought the internet was punishing me for something."

Christopher leaned over and paged through the file. Somewhere in the jumble of styles he found a rule that matched the heading, and he tested a simple idea: he added one short line. "h1, curly brace, text-align colon center, curly brace," he murmured, saving the file. He refreshed the page, and BEE HAPPY slid to the middle of the screen like it had been waiting for permission. Grandpa gasped so loudly that Grandma called from the garden to ask whether somebody had won the lottery.

"That line centers the top-level heading," Christopher said, feeling a little smug. "The big h1 one. Every one on the page, actually."

"Every one?" Grandpa said. "Then watch this." He added a second top-level heading, NECTAR FOR SALE, HONEST, beneath the first, and refreshed again. Sure enough, it sat dead center too, right beside the picture of Grandpa in his bee suit holding a jar. "Although," Grandma said, coming in with dirt on her hands and reading over their shoulders, "that honey you bought from the county fair was counterfeit. It was corn syrup with a bee sticker on it."

"Then we'll sell the sticker," Grandpa said, and clicked publish.

The bleachers smelled like hot dogs and cut grass, and Violet's whole family had claimed the middle rows for the championship game between the Riverside Rockets and the Northside Bears. Her uncle Marco was already hoarse from yelling, and the game had not even started. "The crowd wins games," he kept shouting, drumming his fists on the railing. "That's the whole point of home field!" Violet frowned. She wanted the Rockets to win, and she wanted to believe Uncle Marco, but something about his claim bugged her, like a math problem with a step missing.

She thought back to two winters ago, when she had watched football at her grandmother's apartment during the year of the empty stadiums. The TV had shown rows and rows of vacant seats, and the games had felt strange and quiet, like a forest with no birds. Grandma had read the season totals out loud from her newspaper at the time, and the numbers had stuck in Violet's head ever since. She pulled out her phone now and searched until she found the page again, just to be sure.

"Uncle Marco," she said, tugging his sleeve during a timeout. "You know the season when almost nobody was allowed in the stadiums? Home teams finished 127 wins, 128 losses, and one tie. There was basically no home advantage at all." Marco blinked at her. Her cousin Jayden leaned over. "Wait, so cheering does nothing?" Violet shrugged. "It did nothing that year, at least. Maybe it's something else about home field. Maybe it's the players, not us." Marco looked wounded, like she had told him his cooking was bad. "Fine, science girl," he said. "Test it. Next few plays, nobody cheers. Then everybody goes wild. See what happens."

Violet felt a little thrill. An experiment, right here in the bleachers. She asked the families around them, and even a man with a foam finger agreed to stay silent for the next three plays. The stadium went oddly quiet, and the Rockets gave up a sack. Then she raised both arms, and the whole section erupted. The next play, the Bears intercepted the ball anyway. Marco threw up his hands. "That proves nothing!" Jayden laughed. "You need way more plays than that. That's the point, isn't it? One moment can't tell you anything." Violet nodded. Three plays was noise, not a pattern.

So they kept going, quiet then loud, loud then quiet, marking each result in her notebook, and by the fourth quarter she had a messy little chart that proved absolutely nothing except that the Rockets were aggressive on defense no matter what the crowd did. When the final interception sealed the win, Marco swept her up in a hug anyway. "All right," he admitted. "Maybe the cheering is for us." Violet grinned and waved her notebook above her head like a trophy. "Best data I ever salvaged from a blowout," she said, and Jayden said, "Save me a seat for the rematch."

Isabelle knelt on the concrete floor of Messina's Garden Center, a paper packet of carrot seeds in one hand and a packet of bean seeds in the other. The rules for the community plot said every vegetable had to be in the ground by Sunday, and today was Friday. She shook a carrot seed onto her palm, where it sat like a fleck of dust, then shook out a bean seed, fat as her fingertip.

"These can't go in the same depth," she said to her friend Marcus, who was hauling a bag of soil toward the register. "Look at them."

He set the bag down and peered at her hand. "The bean is like ten times bigger."

Isabelle turned the seed packets over, hunting for instructions. The carrot packet said "sow shallowly," which told her almost nothing. The bean packet said "plant two inches deep," but when she checked a carrot packet from another rack, that one just said "keep moist." She frowned at the shelf, where packets were sorted by category, and pulled out a radish packet, a pea packet, and a sunflower packet too.

"Okay, listen," she said, laying the packets in a row on the floor. "Big seeds say deep. Little seeds say shallow. Radish, tiny seed, half an inch. Pea, pretty big, one inch. Sunflower, huge, two inches." She tapped each packet. "So there's a rule hiding in here."

"Like the seed tells you how deep to bury it?" Marcus asked.

"Plant a seed about two to three times as deep as the seed is wide," Isabelle read aloud. She had found it on a laminated card hanging from a hook by the seed rack, worn soft at the corners from people thumbing it. "That's the rule. The bean is about an inch wide, so two or three inches down. The carrot seed is barely anything, so barely any dirt on top."

They carried their bags out to the community plot behind the garden center, where the air smelled of wet earth and cut grass. Isabelle measured with her finger, pressing the bean seeds into holes about three knuckles deep, then scattered the carrot seeds and dusted them with the thinnest layer of soil, thin as salt on fries. Marcus dug the fence posts for the pole beans, because raccoons, nocturnal thieves that they were, had emptied three plots last summer. The plot committee would not permit any harvest from unfenced beds.

Every morning before the bus, Isabelle walked over to check. On the fourth day, a haze of green threads showed where the carrots slept, so fine she almost breathed them away. The beans took longer, and she worried she had buried them too deep, until the eighth morning when fat hooked stems shouldered up through the soil like divers surfacing.

Marcus crouched beside her, mud on his knees, grinning at the bean sprouts. "So the little ones and the big ones both made it."

"Both came up," Isabelle said, and she traced a careful circle in the dirt around the strongest carrot seedling, marking it with a Popsicle stick.

Isabelle spread the photocopied page of Arabic across her grandmother's kitchen table, weighted the corners with teacups, and glared at it as if it might surrender. In two weeks, at the gathering her parents were calling her coming-of-age ceremony, she would recite Surah Al-Mulk from memory, all thirty verses, in front of forty relatives. So far she had four.

"You look like your grandfather watching the kettle," Grandma said, sliding a plate of dates toward her. "It boils when it boils."

"That's the problem, it doesn't boil at all." Isabelle tapped the page. "I keep starting at the beginning, and by verse five my brain is tired, so I never get to the end. Maybe I should build it backward, like a countdown." She grabbed her notebook and began sketching boxes and arrows, verses feeding into verses, testing order like a pattern she couldn't see directly. "Grandma, what if I memorize the last verse first? If a pattern works, it should work from any direction, right?"

Grandma laughed and said something in Farsi about stubbornness skipping a generation, which Isabelle took as a yes.

She tried it that afternoon on the porch steps, recording each verse on her phone and playing it while she hung laundry. Last verse, then second-to-last, then snapping the two together. By evening she could chain six verses from the back, and when she recited them for Grandma, word perfect, they both shrieked so loudly the neighbor's cat bolted off the wall.

That night her phone buzzed with a message from Priya: working on my project, need your help. Priya's world religions assignment was on reincarnation, the idea that a soul returns in many lives, life after life. Isabelle sat cross-legged on Grandma's guest bed texting back and forth, and suddenly she noticed something that made her sit up straight. The verses she was memorizing kept returning to a Day when everything hidden would be laid open, when people rise again to be judged, and then paradise or hell. One life, then one judgment. Priya's project had many lives, cycling on and on.

"Grandma!" Isabelle called, padding into the hall in her socks. "The surah I'm memorizing, it talks about the Day of Judgment, Yawm al-Qiyamah. Everybody gets raised up and judged, then sent to paradise or hell. Priya's project has souls coming back over and over instead. Isn't that the biggest difference you could imagine?"

Grandma leaned out of her bedroom doorway, hairnet crooked, eyes bright. "So tell me, then. Which one is the assignment?"

"Yours isn't an assignment. Yours is mine." Isabelle was already turning back toward the guest room, phone in one hand, photocopied page in the other. "I'm going to finish the last third before breakfast."

Ellie had been to Fairhaven Cemetery twice before, both times for her grandfather's funeral, when she was too small to remember anything but the cold. Today she came with her grandmother Nani, who carried a small brass pot of water and a bag of marigolds, and with her mother, who carried nothing and kept looking at the ground. They found the flat gray stone with DAVID OKAFOR carved into it, and Nani set the marigolds in a neat ring around the edges.

"His family was Christian," Nani said, arranging the flowers. "The minister said he is in heaven now, resting."

"That's it? He just stays there?" Ellie asked. She was working on a comparison for her world cultures class, and heaven was one half of her notes. The other half she was supposed to get from Nani, who had grown up in Varanasi.

"For them, yes. Forever, in peace." Nani touched the stone the way she touched Ellie's head when checking for a fever. "In what I was taught, a soul is born again. And again. Many times."

Ellie wrote reborn? in her notebook, then thought about it. "Wait. Is being reborn good? Should you hope for it?" She tested the idea out loud, the way she tested answers in math: pick one, see if it breaks. "Because if Grandpa gets to come back, that seems better than lying here."

Nani laughed, a short sound in the quiet. The recession had cut the cemetery's grounds crew to two men, and their negligent mowing had left tall grass between the rows, so the laugh carried farther than it would have otherwise. A man in a suit, two graves over, glanced over at them.

"No, beta. You hope to escape it." Nani sat down on the dry grass beside the stone, careless of her sari. "The wheel goes around and around, birth after birth. The highest thing a life can do is get off the wheel."

"It has a name?"

"Moksha."

Ellie wrote the word carefully. Liberation from the whole cycle of rebirth, she added, and underlined it, and then sat back on her heels. So the two faiths pointed in opposite directions, as far as she could tell. One wanted a soul kept safe forever in one place, and the other wanted it free of the road entirely. She looked at the marigold ring, then at the tall grass bending in the wind past the edge of the mowing, out toward the fence and the fields beyond it.

"Can I try the water?" she asked.

Nani handed her the brass pot. Ellie poured a slow line of it along the top of the stone, watching the water run into the carved letters and gather in the O of OKAFOR, filling it until it shone.

Kayla laced her sneakers at the kitchen table while her mom buttered toast, because today was her first day volunteering at the River Street Food Bank. "Remember when you were six," her mom said, "and you cried because we threw out the jack-o'-lantern?" Kayla laughed. She had wanted to keep it on the porch forever, and when it softened and collapsed, she had buried it under the maple tree with a popsicle-stick marker. She still couldn't stand seeing food thrown away, which was exactly why she had signed up to volunteer.

The food bank smelled like cardboard and oranges. A supervisor named Dara handed Kayla a box of donated groceries from Hartman's Market: lettuce with brown edges, apples with dents, peppers that had gone soft in spots. "Sort the good from the not good," Dara said. "Blemished is fine. Rotten is not."

Kayla worked down the row, but a question kept nagging her. These vegetables weren't rotten, they were just ugly or slightly old, and the store had gotten rid of them anyway. She counted the box quickly: forty-two items, and thirty-one were still perfectly good if you cut around the spots. That was more than half saved from the trash. She wondered how big that number would get if you counted every store, every kitchen, every school cafeteria in the whole country.

She found Dara stacking cans. "Do you know how much food in the whole United States just gets wasted, never eaten?" Dara smiled. "Actually, yes. The Department of Agriculture estimates between 30 and 40 percent of the U.S. food supply is wasted." Kayla stared. Out of every ten boxes like this one, three or four never fed anybody at all.

She wanted to test it. At home that afternoon, she pulled everything out of her own refrigerator and counted: sixty items. If the estimate held for her family too, somewhere between eighteen and twenty-four of them would end up in the garbage. She made a plan, writing it on the whiteboard by the fridge. Leftover rice became fried rice. Soft apples became applesauce. The half-onion went into soup. By the end of the week the trash can was nearly empty, and her little brother, Marcus, who usually complained about leftovers, asked for seconds of the applesauce and said it tasted better than the store kind, almost like something from the artisan bakery downtown, the way the whole house smelled like cinnamon.

At her next shift, Kayla told Dara about the experiment, and Dara gave her a new job: teaching the sorting table to keep slightly blemished fruit out of the discard bin. "You have a distinct talent for this," Dara said, handing her a permanent marker to label the rescue crate. Kayla wrote RESCUED on the side in big letters, then set a rescued apple on top, where everybody could see it.

Owen set his pencil down and glared at the paper. His street looked like a street that had been through a landslide. The buildings on the left leaned one way, the buildings on the right leaned the other, and the road between them wandered off the page like a snake that had lost its glasses. He wanted to draw the view from his grandmother's front porch, the one she said she might have to sell, so he could give her the picture before the moving truck came. He had one week.

"You're frowning at that paper like it insulted you," his mom said, setting a lemon on the counter. She turned it over, squinted, and muttered, "Is that fungus? I think that's fungus." She dropped the whole thing in the trash and came to stand behind him.

"Perspective," Owen said. "You're supposed to make lines go to a vanishing point, and I get that, but my street won't cooperate."

His mom pulled out the chair across from him. "Did I ever tell you about the nail hole? In the Last Supper?" She waited while he shook his head. "The single vanishing point is at Christ's head, and a nail hole Leonardo used to stretch his guide strings is still visible there."

Owen looked up. "A nail hole? In one of the most famous paintings in the world? You can still see it?"

"Still there."

He sat with that for a second. Strings, from a nail. Strings that stretched out from one spot to guide the lines. So Leonardo hadn't just eyeballed it, and he hadn't started with the walls or the ceiling either. He had started with the one point, the point at Christ's head, and let every line grow outward from there like spokes on a wheel.

Owen flipped to a fresh page. This time he drew nothing but a small dot first, halfway up the paper, right where the street should disappear. He pressed the pencil tip so hard it nearly poked through, then found a thumbtack in the junk drawer, set it exactly on the dot, and looped a piece of sewing thread around it. He pulled the thread taut and drew along its edge, then moved it and drew again, line after line radiating out from the tack like rays from a tiny sun.

"Why the actual thread?" his mom asked.

"Because my hand curves. The thread doesn't."

When the lines were done he took the tack away and built the street on top of them, storefronts, windows, a mailbox. The buildings stood up straight and tall. The road ran true and narrow and went exactly where it was supposed to go, shrinking toward the dot until it vanished. In the middle of the road, far down where everything converged, the paper held one small, dark pinprick where the tack had been.

Owen leaned close to it. "I'm leaving it," he said. "Grandma can find it."

Eli had been a tenant of Birch Cabin for exactly six days, long enough to learn which bunks squeaked and which counselor snored, and long enough to notice something odd. Every afternoon, Owen from Fox Cabin got teased at the boathouse, always at the boathouse, and never anywhere else. Dex would mimic the way Owen's words caught and stuck, and the other boys would laugh, and Owen would pretend to search the water for his paddle as if he'd lost it. Eli wondered about that. Why the boathouse? He watched, and the answer slowly formed: no adult ever came down the dock after lunch. The teasing had a hidden rule, a time and a place where it was safe, and once Eli saw the pattern, he couldn't stop turning it over.

He tested his idea the next day. At lunch, when a counselor stood two feet away, Dex was all grins, passing Owen the ketchup like they were friends. An hour later, at the boathouse, Dex was doing the stuttering voice again. The pattern held. So the problem wasn't Dex exactly, Eli thought, chewing his lip; it was the empty dock. If the teasing needed a hidden spot, then maybe he didn't have to fight Dex at all. He just had to take the hidden spot away.

That evening Owen sat alone by the fire pit, and Eli went over. "I keep reporting it and then deleting it," Owen said, poking a stick at nothing. "Marcus said I'm a snitch."

"It's not tattling if you're trying to keep someone safe, not trying to get him in trouble," Eli said. He'd been chewing on that distinction all through dinner, and saying it out loud made it feel solid. "Tattling is when you want Dex to get busted. This is different. The goal is to protect you."

"So what do we do?"

Eli told him the pattern, the boathouse, the hour when no adult walked the dock. Then he went to find Renata, the waterfront counselor, retrieving his sandals from under the bench as he went. He didn't say Dex's name first. He said, "Nobody watches the dock between one and two, and stuff happens down there that kids are afraid to report." He waited, curious whether the pattern alone would be enough, the way a fishing line works even when you can't see the fish take the hook.

Renata looked at him for a moment, then nodded and pulled a whistle from around her neck. The next day she scheduled paddle practice for one o'clock sharp, right at the boathouse, with eleven boats on the water and her standing on the dock. Dex opened his mouth once, glanced up, and closed it. Owen capsized his kayak on purpose and came up laughing, and from the water he looked at Eli and raised his paddle like a flag.

Florence had one lunch period to build a three-point argument about why the school should restrict phone use in hallways, and her notebook page still held nothing but the word "phones" circled three times. She sat at the back table of the library, where the writing club met on Tuesdays, and stared at the assignment sheet. Thesis statement first, then the outline, then the draft. The draft was supposed to come last, which felt backward to her, like decorating a cake before baking it.

Across the table, Marcus was taping a strip of paper above his laptop. Florence leaned over to read it. "Omit needless words," the strip said, in Marcus's careful block letters.

"Whose rule is that?" she asked.

"It's from William Strunk Jr.'s writing guide, The Elements of Style, written in 1918," Marcus said, smoothing the tape. "Mrs. Pell keeps a copy in the reference section. I copied it out this morning."

Florence got up, found the slim little book on the shelf, and carried it back. Nineteen eighteen. People were writing rules about cutting words before her grandmother was born. She flipped it open anyway, half hoping for a secret chapter on thesis statements, and found rule after rule about sentences, all of them blunt and short, like the book was following its own advice.

Then she looked down at her circled word and tried an experiment. She wrote her first attempt at a thesis: "I think that maybe phones in the hallways are kind of a problem that could possibly be solved." Twenty words, and most of them were hiding the actual point. She crossed out "I think that maybe," then "kind of," then "could possibly be." What remained was "Phones in the hallways are a problem that can be solved." Twelve words, and the sentence stood up straighter, like it had a spine now.

"Marcus, listen." She read it aloud, then read her original. He pointed at the taped strip without saying anything, which in Marcus language meant she had gotten it right.

The outline came faster after that. Point one, phones slow foot traffic in narrow halls. Point two, they make collisions more likely at the stairwell doors. Point three, a hallway phone rule would not restrict phone use at lunch, so students would keep most of their freedom. She numbered the three points, and under each one she jotted two pieces of evidence she could hunt down in the encyclopedia shelf before the bell.

At 12:45 the library lights blinked, the signal for five minutes left. Florence copied her thesis onto a clean page in her buoyant, looping handwriting and slid the notebook into her backpack. The blank page had been her adversary all lunch, and now it wasn't.

"Same table Thursday?" Marcus asked, packing up his laptop.

"Same table," Florence said, and zipped the bag shut.

Aiden carried two paper cups of punch across the community hall, scanning the folding tables for his grandmother's church group. The hall had been split in half for the interfaith evening, with hymnbooks on one side and a cloth-covered table on the other, where a Sikh family was arranging a small stand wrapped in saffron fabric. Aiden's assignment for school was due Monday: compare how two faiths explain what happens after death. He had planned to just look things up online, but his grandmother had said the community hall evening would demonstrate more than any website could.

At the Sikh table, a boy about his own age sat copying something into a notebook in careful Punjabi letters. His name tag read Vikram. When Aiden set a cup of punch down beside him, Vikram grinned and covered his page. "You can look. It's not secret." The page was covered with lines of Gurmukhi script, the same lines over and over.

"That's a lot of copying," Aiden said.

"It's Japji Sahib. The morning prayer." Vikram tapped the notebook. "I have to know it well, because I'm getting ready for my initiation."

Aiden frowned. "Like a ceremony?"

"It's called Amrit Sanchar," Vikram said, and then his little sister tugged his sleeve and he went to help her with her shoes, leaving Aiden staring at the notebook.

Aiden wandered back to the church side, where his grandmother was stacking chairs. She had retired from the post office last spring, and now that she drew a pension, she volunteered at events like this almost every weekend. Aiden asked her what she thought happened after death, and she said what she always said, about heaven and being with God. Then she asked what the family across the hall believed.

"I don't know yet," Aiden admitted. "They said something about the soul merging with God, like a drop going back into the ocean. But I got interrupted."

He remembered then, suddenly, a funeral he had attended two years before, for his grandfather. After the service, in the church basement, a man had stood up and described reincarnation so vividly that several of the mourners had leaned forward, listening to something completely different from the minister's sermon. Aiden had been eleven and had thought the man was simply wrong. Now he wondered whether he had been biased that day, hearing only what he already expected to hear.

He marched back across the hall, punch sloshing. "Vikram. For my project. Does Japji Sahib say anything about what happens after you die?"

Vikram's mother looked up from the cloth-covered table and smiled. "Ask him what he's reciting it for," she said, and went back to smoothing the fabric.

"I'm reciting it because it's part of the ceremony," Vikram said slowly, working it out as he spoke. "And the prayer talks about the soul's journey. So I guess learning it is like practicing for the whole thing, the life after this one too." He looked surprised at his own sentence, then pleased.

Aiden wrote fast, filling half a page. "Can I ask you one more thing on Monday? After you've thought about it more?"

"Bring two cups of punch," Vikram said, and turned back to his notebook, pencil moving through the letters one more careful line at a time.

The lights went out at 7:42, and Eve knew the exact time because she had been watching the clock, counting the minutes until her cupcakes came out of the oven. The oven went dark too, along with the refrigerator, the hallway light, and the whole city block outside the window. Her little brother Theo crawled out from under the kitchen table with a flashlight and nominated himself Chief of Darkness, which meant he got to hold the flashlight and shine it wherever he wanted.

The real problem, as Eve saw it, was the freezer. Mom was stuck at work until ten, and the note on the counter said leftovers, chicken, peas, be careful. Eve stood in front of the closed freezer door and reasoned it out. Cold air sinks, she thought, so every time someone opened the door, the coldest air spilled out the bottom like water from a cracked glass. The rule she made up was simple: nobody opens the freezer, not even Chief of Darkness, not even to check. Theo agreed, mostly because Eve let him nominate the flashlight as an official member of their alliance against the blackout.

They ate crackers and cheese on the living room floor and watched the building across the street, where some apartments still glowed with candlelight. Theo asked questions about whether the ice cream would melt, and Eve said she didn't know yet, which was the honest answer. She put her hand flat on the freezer door now and then, as if she could feel through the porous old seal, but of course she couldn't. What was happening inside was invisible, and she hated that.

At 9:15 the lights came back, all at once, and the refrigerator hummed like it had never stopped. Mom arrived twenty minutes later with a phone in her hand and worry in her face. "How long was it off?" she asked, and Eve told her, an hour and a half. Mom bit her lip. "The chicken. If it's thawed, it has to go."

"Wait," Eve said, and pulled out the bag of chicken. It was still hard as a brick, with frost on the plastic. Then she took out the peas and opened the bag so Mom could see. Inside, among the loose green dots, tiny ice crystals glittered in the kitchen light.

"Look," Eve said. "Still ice crystals. I found it on the food safety site while the power was out, on my phone. Thawed food can be refrozen if it still has ice crystals, or if it's forty degrees Fahrenheit or below."

Mom felt the chicken with her fingers, then held the phone and read the whole line herself, including the part about four degrees Celsius. "Alliance of the freezer," she said, and held up her hand for a high five. Theo shined the flashlight on the peas one more time, like a soldier inspecting his troops, and slid the bag back onto the shelf.

Lea had exactly one job at the polling station: hold the "Vote Here" sign without whacking anyone with it. She was failing. The sign was nearly as tall as she was, and every time a voter walked past, the cardboard corner lunged at somebody's hat.

"I saw that," said Marcus, her best friend, who was supposed to be handing out sample ballots. "Your sign is attacking Mrs. Okafor. Again."

"The sign has a mind of its own. I'm just the camouflage, hiding its sinister plans." Lea wrestled the cardboard into a corner and propped it against the wall like a sleeping dragon.

Their civics class had sent them here to participate in Election Day, which mostly meant standing in the hallway of the community center for two hours. Their teacher, Ms. Reyes, had assigned a worksheet that Lea had stuffed in her back pocket: Read a right listed in the Constitution, then explain it in your own words. She'd been avoiding it all morning.

"Did you do the worksheet?" she asked Marcus.

"I wrote that the Constitution is a big paper that tells the government what it can't do. Very inspiring. Ten out of ten."

Before Lea could argue, a man with a clipboard hurried over. He was from the local newspaper, and he was upset. "They moved me to the parking lot," he said to the poll manager. "I need to photograph inside."

"Rules are rules," the manager said. "No cameras past this line."

Lea watched the man retreat, muttering. Something nagged at her, a pattern she couldn't quite see yet. Marcus had said the Constitution tells the government what it can't do. So what stopped the government from shutting down a newspaper entirely?

She pulled out her phone and searched. The First Amendment. She read it twice, lips moving. It protected freedom of religion, speech, the press, peaceful assembly, and petitioning the government. Five things, all in one amendment. The press. There it was, printed plain as a cereal box label.

"Marcus," she said, yanking his sleeve. "The First Amendment protects the press. And speech. And religion. And peaceful assembly, and petitioning the government. That's why that reporter gets to be annoying at all."

"So the government can't just squish newspapers?"

"Apparently not." Lea flipped her worksheet over and wrote fast, in her own words: The First Amendment means the government can't tell people what to believe, what to say, or what to print, and it can't stop us from gathering peacefully or complaining to its face.

Marcus read over her shoulder. "Complaining to its face. Truly your finest work."

The reporter came back through the doors, camera bouncing on his chest, having negotiated a spot near the door. He raised the camera toward the check-in table, and Lea, without thinking, yanked her sign out of the corner to hold it high and proud.

The cardboard corner clipped his clipboard, and his pen flew across the floor.

"You're attacking the press now," Marcus said. "The exact press we just learned is protected."

Lea chased the pen, held it out to the reporter, and grinned. "Freedom of the press," she said. "And freedom of my sign. Somebody should write an amendment about that one."

Emmett slid the phone box across the kitchen table, but his mother held her palm over it. "Rules first," she said. The lamplight caught the syrup bottle and the folded newspaper, relics of a Saturday breakfast that had ended an hour ago.

"One hour on school nights," she said. "It charges in the kitchen at bedtime, not in your room." Emmett argued that everyone in seventh grade took their phones to bed, and she argued back that she wasn't everyone's mother, and that after the recession had chewed through their savings, a phone at all was a gift they'd had to be frugal to manage. That word landed on him like a wet towel. He stopped trying to justify keeping it upstairs and signed the paper she pushed toward him, a contract with his own shaky signature.

For five nights the phone sat in the kitchen drawer at bedtime, and for five nights Emmett fell asleep within minutes of his head hitting the pillow. He didn't notice anything, because there was nothing to notice. On Friday night his mother was out, and he crept downstairs, opened the drawer, and lay on the couch in the dark scrolling through videos until nearly midnight. When he finally climbed the stairs, his eyes felt like they'd been rinsed in cold soda, wide awake behind his lids. He lay in bed listening to the furnace tick, counting to five hundred, then starting over. His sister's slow breathing came through the wall. Two o'clock. Then almost three.

At breakfast he fell asleep sitting up, his cheek drifting toward the cold table. His sister poked his arm. "What did you do last night?" she asked, and he told her, defensive at first, then quieter, because a pattern was forming in his head like dots on graph paper. Dark room plus no phone equaled sleep. Dark room plus glowing screen equaled staring at the ceiling for hours. "It's the screen," he said slowly. "It only happens on screen nights."

"You want to know the word for what you messed up?" his sister said, chewing. "Melatonin. It's the hormone that makes you sleepy." She said their science teacher had explained that blue-enriched light from screens can reduce or delay melatonin being released in the evening, and Emmett had been bathing his eyes in it until midnight.

Saturday night he put the phone in the drawer himself, before anyone asked. He set his alarm the old way, on the clock radio shaped like a rocket, and lay in the dark listening to his own breathing slow down, the hallway light a thin gold line beneath his door. From downstairs, faintly, came the drawer sliding shut, his mother's hand, then nothing at all.

Marcus's kitchen smelled like burned popcorn, and his mom was already laughing about it, so the two of them sat on the translucent glass porch table with the phone between them, watching the screen like it was a fishbowl. That was where Tyler had put it, face up, after Marcus threw it there.

"She's mad," Marcus said. "Look at it. She texted 'Okay.' and that's it."

"It says okay," Tyler said. "Okay is like the friendliest word there is."

"With a period." Marcus tapped the screen once, hard. "Kayla doesn't use periods. Kayla uses like forty emojis and the word 'okay' means fine. 'Okay.' means I'm dead to her."

Tyler picked up the phone and looked at the message again. Last month he'd sent his cousin "See you there." with a period, and his cousin had replied "why are you mad at me," and Tyler had spent a whole evening trying to figure out what he'd done wrong. Maybe nothing. Maybe it was the period itself. He couldn't see the difference, the way you couldn't see the start of an infection until the finger swelled up, but the difference was still in there, working.

"I read something," Tyler said. "A study. Binghamton University, 2016. Small one." He scrolled, found the page, held it out. "Same message, with a period and without. The one with the period came across as less sincere."

Marcus read it twice. "So I'm right."

"You're not right, you're a lab result. Let's test it." Tyler typed "that's cool" and sent it to Marcus's other phone, then sent "that's cool." right after. "Which one would make you panic?"

Marcus pointed at the second one without hesitating. "That one's cold. The first one's just talking."

"So to fix it with Kayla, you eliminate the period." Tyler deleted the period from a draft reply and turned the phone around. "Try this."

Marcus stared at the draft for a second. "Feels too easy."

"So send the emoji too," Tyler said. "Cover all the bases." He thought about his cousin again, about whether he should have just asked what was wrong instead of lying awake making up reasons. Maybe he'd message him tonight. Maybe with no period. Maybe with a whole parade of emojis.

Marcus hit send. The porch light buzzed, the popcorn smell drifted out through the screen door, and then Kayla's reply lit up the glass: "okay!! see you at 7" followed by a string of tiny dancing ghosts.

"There," Marcus said. "Saved. You're a genius."

Tyler slid the phone back across the table. "I'm going to go fix my cousin," he said.

At the first turn of the track, Madison bent to retie her shoe even though it didn't need it, because bending gave her an excuse not to look at the girl stretching beside her. That girl was Priya, the fastest eighth grader in the county, and in twenty minutes they would both toe the line for the eight hundred metres, the race Madison had bombed at twice already.

"You went out too fast last time," Priya said, not unkindly. "I watched. First lap like a rocket, second lap like a walk."

"I know," Madison said. The embarrassment still stung from the meet where she'd led at four hundred metres and then been passed by six people, one by one, her legs turning to wet cardboard. The trouble was she couldn't feel it happening. Everything seemed fine until suddenly it wasn't, which meant the problem was hidden somewhere she couldn't see, in the way she spent her energy, like a bank account draining without receipts.

Her brother Dev, who swam, had run into a version of the same puzzle last summer. "Freestyle," he'd told her, frowning at the television. "You'd think everyone would pick something different, right? Like, it's free. Any stroke you want."

"So why doesn't anyone?"

"I asked my coach. Almost all swimmers choose front crawl in freestyle races, because it's the fastest of the competitive swimming strokes. It's just faster. That's the whole answer." Dev had shrugged. "But you still have to swim it smart, because if you go out too hard, even front crawl won't save you."

Madison had rolled her eyes at the time. Now, standing at the line under an ominous gray sky, the idea came back to her from a new angle. The swimmers didn't win by choosing the fastest stroke alone; they won by managing the fastest stroke. Maybe pace worked the same way. The first lap of an eight hundred wasn't the race at all. It was an investment, and if she poured everything into it, there'd be nothing left when the actual race began.

So she made a plan she could test: on the first lap she would stay three steps behind Priya, no closer, no matter how easy it felt. If the plan was wrong, she'd lose again and know it. If it was right, the second lap would tell her.

The gun cracked. Priya swept to the front, and Madison sat three steps back, her legs begging to go, the whole field stringing out behind them. Four hundred metres. The bell. Then, coming off the final turn, the gap ahead of her began to shrink, one step at a time, like the second half of a race she'd never actually run before. She surged. Twenty metres out she was even with Priya's shoulder, hearing her own breath like a drum.

"Where did you come from?" Priya gasped.

Madison didn't waste the air to answer. She just leaned forward and ran through the line.

Anna sat cross-legged on the worn rug in her grandmother's living room, a practice book open on her knees. In three weeks she would chant from the Torah for her bat mitzvah, and her portion looked back at her like a puzzle: Hebrew letters in neat columns, tiny vowel dots below them, and curling symbols stacked above and below like musical birds on wires.

"You have the ambition," her grandmother said, setting down two glasses of mint tea, "now you need the patience." Anna traced one of the little curls with her finger. "What are these marks, Savta? They weren't in the email Rabbi Feld sent." Her grandmother just smiled and said Anna would find out herself at Thursday rehearsal, which felt like being handed a wrapped box and told not to open it.

All week Anna tested an idea. She covered the vowel dots with a strip of paper and tried to read a verse cold. The letters sat there, silent and stubborn. When she uncovered the dots and chanted the melody from the marks above, the words flowed again. So the little birds carried the tune, she reasoned, and the dots carried the sounds. Both of them were her crutches. What would happen if she had to read without crutches? The question itched.

On Thursday, in the sanctuary that smelled of wax and old wood, Rabbi Feld unrolled the Torah scroll on the long desk. Anna leaned over it and her stomach dropped. No vowel dots. No curling birds. Nothing but bare letters marching in parallel columns, the same words she had practiced, stripped of every clue she'd leaned on. "Where did the marks go?" she whispered.

"They were never there," Rabbi Feld said. "The scroll is written without vowels or musical marks."

Anna stared at the bare letters. So that was why her practice book existed at all. She had assumed the book was a convenience, a softened copy for kids. Now she understood it was the opposite: the only place the tune lived. She had to carry the melody and the vowels in her head before she ever touched the scroll. Every night until the ceremony, she would be negotiating between her eyes, which wanted the dots, and her memory, which had to supply them.

She went back to her grandmother's house and tried again with the paper strip, covering the vowels, then covering the melody marks, then both, chanting louder each time. Her grandmother turned the pages of her own book in the corner chair, tapping her foot to Anna's rhythm.

On the third try, the whole verse came out whole and unaided, rising and falling in the right places. Anna lifted the strip of paper like a flag. "Did you hear that?" she said. "No marks. All me."

Arianna sat at the kitchen table with two printed graphs spread in front of her: monthly rainfall and temperature for the Sonoran Desert and for a patch of Amazon rainforest in Brazil. Her science tutor had promised that by Thursday she had to be able to compare them without looking, and Thursday was two days away. The rainfall bars for the rainforest towered over the desert's flat little stubs, month after month, and she kept losing her place.

Her little brother Marco leaned over her shoulder, chewing a granola bar. "Why is there a lake in that picture?" He pointed at her open textbook, where a photo showed bright green rice plants rising out of a sheet of standing water.

"That's not a lake, it's a field," Arianna said. She turned back to her graphs.

"It's a lake with plants in it." Marco was obstinate about it. "Look, there's water between every row."

Arianna looked again. He was right that it looked like a shallow lake. Rice growing in flooded fields seemed strange to her, since her graphs said nothing about rice anyway. She flipped to the caption and read it aloud: "Rice is usually grown in flooded fields called paddies." That was the whole caption, no reason given.

"See, paddies," Marco said. "Told you it had a name."

"But why would anyone flood it on purpose?" Arianna asked. "Water that just sits there, everywhere, all season." She stared at the photo, then at her rainfall graph for the rainforest. The Amazon bars showed heavy rain nearly every month, a hundred and fifty to three hundred millimeters, and warm temperatures that barely moved between 25 and 28 degrees Celsius. The desert graph was the opposite: almost no rain most months, and temperatures that swung from baking days to cold nights, 40 degrees down to 5. Then it clicked for her, a slow turn like a key. Rice came from places like the rainforest side of the graph, places where water arrived constantly. The standing water in the paddy wasn't a problem for the rice, and the caption's last line gave her the rest: the standing water helps keep many weeds from growing. So the flood was doing a job.

"So the water is like a weed barrier?" Marco asked when she said it out loud.

"That's what the caption says. The water keeps the weeds down." Arianna had thought the flooded field was a mistake or a waste, and now she thought it was clever. She copied both graphs onto one sheet of paper, desert bars in orange and rainforest bars in green, because drawing them herself was the only thing that ever propelled the patterns into her memory.

Marco tapped the desert bars. "Nothing could grow rice here."

"Not outdoors," Arianna said, and slid the pencil across the table to him. "Here, color the cold nights blue."

Luke signed his name at the folding table outside the old hardware store, where the neighborhood cleanup had started at nine sharp. He wanted the volunteer hours for school, but he also wanted to matter, and a trash grabber seemed like a small way to matter. He worked the chain-link fence along the alley, pulling out a flattened soccer ball, a boot, and a strip of pink insulation that somebody had wedged between the fence posts, probably to block a gap. It crumbled in his hands and made him itch, so he dropped it in the bag fast.

By eleven, the pile of filled bags stood taller than he did. A woman in a green polo shirt backed a van up to the curb and started loading them, and Luke noticed the words on her shirt: Riverside Community Food Bank.

"You take the trash?" he asked.

"We take everything we can. The city drops the bags at the transfer station, and we compost the food scraps for the community garden." She held out her hand. "I'm Dana. You're the kid who did the whole fence line."

"Luke." He helped her lift the last bag, and then, because the van was still half empty, he asked what else went in it. She told him she was heading back to the food bank to shelve Saturday's delivery. "Sweet potatoes," she said. "A whole bin of them."

Luke frowned. "Where do sweet potatoes come from in October? Nobody around here grows them."

"Want to come see? We need hands tomorrow morning."

He rode along. The food bank occupied a low building with a loading dock and shelves that looked like a grocery store, except everything was free. Dana showed him where the canned goods went, then pointed to a bin of sweet potatoes with dirt still on them. "Saturday morning we go out to the Hartwell farm. You in?"

Luke said yes before he really thought about it. On the drive home that night, though, he turned the problem over. The bin had been full. Farmers sold their crops. Why would a farmer hand over perfectly good sweet potatoes to strangers? He was pessimistic about the whole thing, and he decided he would test it the only way he could: he would go, watch, and count.

Saturday morning the field was brown and stubbled. A machine had already gone through, and at first Luke saw nothing but dirt. Then he spotted one, half buried like a stone. Then three more within a step. The harvester couldn't get every potato, and the ones it missed were still good. He filled a bucket, then another.

Dana knelt beside him with her own bucket. "It's called gleaning," she said, "gathering what's left in the field after harvest."

"And it all goes to the food bank?" Luke asked.

"Every bit. Mr. Hartwell calls us when the machine's done, and we send volunteers out."

Luke counted his buckets. Eleven, by noon, and that was just him. The truck took them back, and at the food bank he helped Dana integrate the new sweet potatoes into the produce section, sliding them in beside the onions so the shelf looked full.

A woman came through the line with two kids and took a bag of them. Luke watched her put them in her cart, and then he grabbed one more bucket from the stack by the door and headed back to the truck.

Carter stood at the counter with the recipe spread out between a bag of onions and a can of tomatoes, and the clock on the microwave said 5:12. His mom would be home at 6:30, and he had promised, actually promised, that dinner would be on the table when she walked in. He wanted to prove he could do this without her hovering, without the word "careful" repeated eleven times.
