The onion intimidated him more than the sauce did. He remembered her hand over his once, knuckles curled under, fingertips tucked back like a bear's paw. "The claw grip," she'd said. "Fingertips down, so the blade rides your knuckles." He set his hand on the onion like that, took a breath, and cut. The first slice was crooked, but nothing bled. He went slower, and by the time the onion was diced, his eyes were streaming and his knuckles were whole.

His little sister Maya banged through the back door at 5:40 with a bag of blueberries and an announcement. "Bake sale tomorrow at seven a.m. I have to make muffins tonight, and you have to share the oven." She was meticulous about her recipe, leveling each cup of flour with a knife, cracking eggs into a separate bowl to check for shells. Carter made room, his sauce simmering behind them, and watched her stir.

She stirred forever. Carter watched her go around and around until every last lump vanished and the batter was perfectly smooth and glossy. "It looks like cake batter now," she said, proud.

They slid the muffins in alongside a covered pot, waited, pulled them out golden at 6:15. Maya split one open and her face fell. It was chewy, almost rubbery, and inside, instead of a soft crumb, there were long tunnels running through it like wormholes. "They're ruined," she said. "The bake sale is in thirteen hours."

Carter turned the muffin in his hand and thought about the batter. Hers had been overworked. His sauce had gotten thicker the longer it simmered, but flour wasn't tomatoes; maybe stirring did something different, something you couldn't see until it baked. "Make another batch," he said. "Stir it maybe fifteen seconds. Leave it lumpy. Lumpy is fine." Maya scowled at him. "Lumpy looks wrong." "Your smooth ones came out wrong," he said. "Try it my way once."

At 6:28 the second batch was in the oven and the sauce was done, deep red, onions melted into it completely. Their mom's key scraped the lock at 6:31, and while she hung up her coat, the timer buzzed. Maya yanked the pan out, split a warm muffin, and held it up: tender, no tunnels. "Carter," she shouted toward the door, "dinner smells amazing and I take back everything I said about lumpy batter."

Aiden opened the group chat for the Science Olympiad team at 7:03 p.m. and found forty-one unread messages, which was never good. The facts, as far as he could piece together from the wall of text, were these: Marcus had left his weather station project at home, Priya had told Mr. Okafor that the missing data had been collected when it hadn't, and she'd done it because Marcus had covered for her little brother the week before when the brother got caught sneaking into the gym. Everyone agreed on all of it. Nobody agreed on anything else.

"she LIED to a teacher," Devon typed. "the rest of the team worked hard on real data and she faked ours. that's a fairness thing. rules apply to everyone or they apply to no one."

"she was paying back a debt," Zoe answered. "Marcus protected her brother. you don't drop people who helped you. that's loyalty, devon, look it up."

Aiden read it twice. That was the strange part. Devon and Zoe weren't fighting about what had happened. They were fighting about what it meant, using the exact same forty-one messages as evidence. He thought about how light bends through a prism and comes out in different directions depending on the glass, how the same beam refracts into colors that weren't visible before. Same light in, different light out. He had a hypothesis: the facts weren't the problem at all. He decided to test it.

He typed: "devon, name one fact you and zoe disagree about. an actual fact."

The chat went quiet for a full minute, which in this group was like a year. Then Devon wrote, "okay. none. she did it, marcus owed her, okafor believed her. we agree."

"so you agree on every single fact," Aiden typed, "and you still land on opposite sides."

"yes???" Zoe sent, followed by the confused emoji and then, "oh."

Aiden's mom knocked on his door and said something about the weather forecast, precipitation moving in overnight, did he have his rain jacket by the door. "Yeah, in a minute," he said, because something was happening in the chat. Devon had sent a screenshot of the team rulebook, and Zoe had sent a photo of the poster in the gym that said WE TAKE CARE OF OUR OWN, and they were now arguing about which document mattered more, which was, Aiden realized, the same argument wearing a new shirt.

He tried one more test. "imagine priya covered for someone who was NOT her friend. devon, would you be madder or less mad?"

"same," Devon said.

"same," Zoe said, "but because it would be pointless loyalty."

Aiden laughed out loud, alone in his room, at two people typing "same" about opposite feelings. He typed, "wait. you both just said priya values something different than you do. devon you value fairness. zoe you value loyalty. nobody's wrong about the facts. you're not even wrong about the values. you just have different ones."

There was a long pause. Then Marcus, silent for the entire fight, finally appeared.

"guys. I'm quitting the team either way. I don't want priya taking heat for me," he wrote. "also aiden you type like a documentary narrator but you're right."

Zoe sent, "we could split into two teams. one for fairness, one for loyalty."

Devon sent, "that's the dumbest idea I've ever heard. I love it."

Aiden looked at the rain starting against his window and went to get his jacket, and when he came back there was a new chat, created by Zoe, named Team Loyalty, and another one already created by Devon, named Team Fairness, and both of them had added him at the same time.

Elena stared at her phone in the kitchen, waiting for Priya to reply. Three days now, and nothing, not even the eye-roll emoji. They used to text forty times a day. Then Priya made the soccer team and Elena joined robotics, and somehow the replies got shorter and slower until they stopped coming at all. Elena typed "u up?" into their thread, deleted it, and opened the family group chat instead, because if she kept watching the empty thread she was going to throw her phone into the sink.

"Question for the group," she posted. "How do you fix a friendship that's already broken?" Her dad replied with a thumbs up and the words "have you tried apologizing," which was useless. Her grandmother sent a voice memo, and Elena played it while stirring her after-school snack. "In my day we wrote letters," Grandma said, "and I'll tell you, the friendships that lasted were the ones where we stayed similar. When Terez and I got different jobs, that was the end." Her cousin Marco, who was in college, replied next: "Actually there's real research on this. A 2015 study followed 573 friendships formed in seventh grade. Friends who were less alike were more likely to see the friendship end."

Elena sat with that. She and Priya had been practically the same person in seventh grade, both obsessed with the same dumb cartoon, both terrible at dodgeball. Now they were less alike. So maybe the silence wasn't because Priya was mad. Maybe it was just the pattern doing what patterns do. She thought of her uncle, who owned a building downtown, always saying a good tenant helped the whole place thrive, but a volatile one could ruin everything, and the landlord had to act fast either way. Elena decided to act. If being less alike was the problem, then the fix wasn't to apologize for nothing. The fix was to find something new they both still cared about.

She scrolled back through months of Priya's messages looking for it, hunting for a topic that had survived the teams and the clubs. There. Eleven months ago Priya had gone on for two full screens about a mural going up near the library, the artist, the colors, everything. Elena had barely answered at the time because she'd been cramming for a math test. She opened a news app, found out the artist was painting another one this Saturday, and typed: "the mural artist you liked is doing a new one by the library sat. want to go watch and judge it really loudly?"

The typing bubble appeared. It disappeared. It appeared again. Elena held her breath so hard she got dizzy.

"I thought you were mad at ME," Priya wrote. "I was mad at YOU," Elena sent back, then: "we're both idiots." The reply came fast: "obviously. saturday. I'll bring snacks, you bring the loud judging." Elena dropped the phone on the counter and did a small, embarrassing victory spin in the kitchen, and behind her the group chat lit up with her grandmother writing, "so did my advice work."

The vase had been on the mantel since before Abigail was born, and by Sunday dinner it was in six pieces on the floor. Everyone in the kitchen had a different story. Her older brother Marcus said the cat knocked it off while chasing a moth. Her grandmother insisted the shelf had been wobbling for weeks and it was bound to fall. Her little cousin Theo, still catching his breath, said he only touched it with one finger, just one, and it jumped. Aunt Rosa blamed the draft from the open window. Four stories, one broken vase, and no way to check any of them, because the cat was asleep, the moth was gone, and the window was shut now.

Abigail kept quiet through dinner, turning the pieces over in her mind. In class on Friday, Mr. Okafor had mentioned a film, and she had written the name in her notebook: Rashomon, from 1950. A boy named Daniel had leaned over and said, "It's a crime told four times, by four witnesses, and every version contradicts the others." She hadn't thought much of it then. Now she did.

On Monday, during the class discussion, she raised her hand. "I want to test something," she said. "This weekend a vase broke at my house. I got four stories and they can't all be true." Mr. Okafor tilted his head, and she hurried on before he could speak. "I think it matters who tells each story. So I made a chart." She held up her notebook. "Theo is the only one who was alone in the room right before it broke. Marcus blamed the cat, but the cat was locked in the basement all afternoon, because Grandma is allergic. Grandma blamed the shelf, but I checked, and it's solid." She paused, and the room went still. "Aunt Rosa blamed the wind, but the window was only open for two minutes, and it faces away from the room."

"Which leaves Theo," Daniel said slowly.

"I didn't say that," Abigail answered, though she had thought it hard all Sunday night. "Theo said he touched it with one finger. That's actually the most plausible story, because it's the only one where the teller makes himself look worse, not better."

"That's exactly the Rashomon problem," Daniel said. "Everyone shades the story."

"It's more than shading," Abigail said. "Every candidate had a reason. Marcus didn't want to be blamed for leaving the basement door open. Grandma didn't want Theo crying at dinner. Aunt Rosa likes a mystery." She tapped her chart. "Nobody lied, exactly. They just saw different true things."

Mr. Okafor asked what she thought actually happened. Abigail looked down at her notebook, then up.

"Theo touched it, the shelf was fine, the cat was downstairs. I asked him last night, just us two, no audience. He said, 'It was warm from the sun and I just wanted to hold it.'"

The class was quiet, and Abigail closed her notebook gently, like the vase was still whole inside it.

Amelia slid her copy of To Kill a Mockingbird across the library table so the worn cover faced the circle of folding chairs. It was her turn to lead book club, and she had drafted her notes on three index cards, which now stuck together in her nervous hands. She peeled them apart and cleared her throat.

"Okay, so, symbolism," she began. "My cards say a symbol is when an object stands for a bigger idea, but I want to try something instead of just reading that. Everybody, think about the title. Why mockingbirds?"

Dev, who had eaten half a cookie already, raised his hand even though nobody needed to. "Because they're in the book? Atticus says something about them."

"That's the thing," Amelia said, flipping to the page she had dog-eared the night before. She read aloud: Miss Maudie explains that it is a sin to kill a mockingbird because mockingbirds do nothing but sing their hearts out for us. She looked up. "So they don't hurt anybody. They just give you music. And they're innocent."

Priya leaned forward, bouncing her chair onto its back legs. "So which characters are the mockingbirds? That's like a scavenger hunt."

"Exactly," Amelia said, her acute attention locking onto the circle of faces. "That's what I did last night. I made a list." She turned over the third index card. "Tom Robinson, first. He never hurt anyone, and they destroyed him anyway. And Boo Radley. He leaves presents in the tree, he saves the kids, and people made up scary stories about him for years."

"Him too?" Dev said. "I only thought of Tom."

"Try it yourself," Amelia said, grinning. "Who else just gives and gives and gets nothing back?"

The room went quiet except for the radiator clicking, which somebody had set by twisting the thermostat until the librarian came over and turned it back down. Then Marisol, who almost never spoke first, said slowly, "What about the kids themselves? Scout just... exists. She gets attacked for something her dad did."

The whole circle erupted at once, everyone talking over each other, and Amelia held up her hands. "Wait, wait, test it like a scientist. Does the person do harm? No. Does somebody try to punish them anyway? If yes, mockingbird."

Dev counted on his fingers. "Tom, yes. Boo, yes. Scout, yes. Man, this whole book is a nest of mockingbirds."

"That's the pattern," Amelia said. "The title isn't just a bird. It's telling you from page one who to watch and who's going to get hurt." She wrote the three names on the whiteboard and underlined them twice.

Priya jabbed a finger at the board. "Next meeting, can we do foreshadowing? I want to find every warning we missed."

"Bring sticky notes," Amelia said, and passed the cookies.

Dex slammed his backpack onto the bench and slid into his spot at the table before Mom had even set down the lasagna. "You guys hear about Ridgemont's point guard? Flunked his math class, so he's off the roster for the playoffs." He tore a piece of bread in half, grinning. "Their whole season is toast."

Nora's fork stopped halfway to her plate. If it was true, her school's team, who had lost to Ridgemont twice this year, might actually have a shot at the city title. "Who told you?"

"Marcus heard it from some kid at the arcade."

"That's like four people away from anyone who knows anything," Nora said, though a warm, satisfying feeling was already spreading through her chest. Of course the guy was failing. Ridgemont players were exactly the type.

Mom sprinkled parmesan on her pasta and said she'd believe it when she saw it, since her commute home ran past Ridgemont and there had been players shooting on the outdoor courts, same as always. Nora ignored that. She wanted the story to be true, so it felt true, like a sweater that already fit.

That night, in her room, she pulled up the league website on her laptop, telling herself it would take two minutes. The site posted eligibility lists every Friday. She scrolled, chewing the inside of her cheek, and found the current roster. The point guard's name was still there, plain as anything. Then she checked the stats page, where the league listed every player's scoring next to the median for the whole league. He was three points above the median and playing Friday night against her school. She sat back, the warm feeling gone, replaced by something colder. She had repeated the story at lunch today to two friends, confidently, and she hadn't checked a single thing. She'd just believed it because it fit what she already thought about Ridgemont. In science class there was a poster about exactly this, and now she said the phrase out loud to her dark ceiling: "Confirmation bias."

The next morning she caught Dex at the bus stop. "That thing about the point guard isn't true. He's on the roster, and he's playing Friday."

Dex squinted at her. "You actually looked it up? Man, don't be so gullible about Marcus."

"I was gullible," Nora said. "I believed it because I wanted it to be true. That's the whole trick of it." She pulled out her phone and showed him the eligibility list, then made him watch while she texted the two friends she'd told: not true, sorry, I checked the league site.

At dinner that night, Mom asked how the lasagna was, and Dex shrugged and said the point guard had dropped thirty points on their team, so thanks a lot, Nora. She laughed so hard she nearly knocked over her water glass. "Next time I'll hope for a better rumor," she said, and speared another piece of lasagna.

The flyer on the community centre door said Free Math Help, Tuesdays Until 4:30, and Nicolas had twelve minutes of Tuesday left. He had missed the placement test twice already, and tomorrow morning was the last sitting before the school authorized him into the advanced stream. No pass, no advanced stream, and everybody knew Mr. Ellis's retest was notorious for being harder than the original.

"You're late," said Priya, the student volunteer at the corner table. She was already packing her calculator into a canvas bag printed with sailboats. "I can give you ten minutes. Sit."

Nicolas sat. He slid his practice sheet across the table. The last problem was 2x + 3 = 11, and beside it, half erased, his answer of x = 5.

"Show me how you got five," Priya said, but she didn't wait. She pulled the sheet back and drew a quick set of axes in the margin. "Do the algebra first. Whatever you do to one side, do to the other."

Nicolas took the pencil. He subtracted 3 from both sides and got 2x = 8, then divided both sides by 2. x = 4. He stared at it. Five minutes ago he had simply moved numbers around until something looked right, and now the steps had carried him somewhere he hadn't chosen.

"Okay," he said. "But why does that work? Where does the four come from?"

Priya glanced at the clock. 4:21. Instead of answering, she drew a line rising steeply through the axes and labelled it y = 2x + 3. "Look at your equation again," she said. "You're finding where the line y = 2x + 3 reaches a height of 11."

Nicolas bent over the graph. He traced the line with his finger, slow, because the clock was ticking and he could hear the caretaker unlocking the storage closet down the hall. The line climbed through the grid. He followed it up and up until it crossed the height of 11, then dropped straight down to the axis below.

"It lands on four," he said quietly. "The same four. Both roads get there."

"Both roads," Priya agreed, zipping her bag.

"But that's not just this problem," Nicolas said, flipping to a fresh page. "It's a rule. Any equation like this, there's a line, and the answer is where it hits the height." He started sketching another set of axes without waiting for permission, plotting, checking, and the pencil kept moving even as the lights in the far half of the hall flicked off.

The caretaker leaned in the doorway. "Centre's closing, kids."

"One second," Nicolas said, still drawing. He followed his new line up to where it crossed, dropped his finger to the axis, and grinned. "Priya. It works. It works every single time, doesn't it?"

She smiled from the doorway and pulled it shut behind her. "Find me Thursday and tell me how the test went."

The community hall smelled of incense and burned milk, and Arthur had forty pages of Sanskrit to get into his head before Sunday. His grandmother had promised him that if he recited the prayer without stumbling at his thread ceremony, she would finally let him carry the brass lamp, the one his older brother had carried. He wanted that lamp. So he sat at the back table under the noisy ceiling fan and whispered the verses to himself, line by line, covering the page with his hand and trying to pull the words up from memory alone.

The hall was busy that evening, which made it worse. Two families had booked the space, one at each end. Near the stage, an old man's family arranged marigolds around a photograph. Near the kitchen, a smaller group stood around a tiny cot with white cloth draped over something no bigger than a bundle of firewood. Arthur stopped mid-verse. He watched the old man's sons carry a bamboo stretcher out toward the river path, where the smoke always rose in the evenings, and he knew what happened there. The body was burned, and the ashes went into the water.

But the small group at the kitchen end began digging. Actually digging, in the corner of the courtyard where the neem tree grew. Arthur frowned. Same hall, same evening, same prayers floating over both parties, and yet one family was heading for fire and the other for earth. He wondered if the two families were angry at each other, or if one had made a mistake. He leaned toward the man handing out tea and asked, "Why are they burying? I thought everyone burns."

The man lowered his voice. "The little one was only four." That answered nothing, so Arthur turned it over while he mouthed the next verse. He thought of the sadhu who used to sit outside the temple, the one everyone called holy, and remembered the mound of earth that had appeared behind the wall after he died. No fire, no smoke. So it was not one rule for everyone. It was a pattern: the old man went to the flames and back to the five elements, while the child and the holy man went into the ground. Fire was for the ones in between. He tested it against everything he had ever seen at the river, every plume of smoke, every mound of earth, and the pattern held.

"Water, earth, fire, air, sky," he murmured, and the verse he had been fighting all week suddenly dissolved into something he could feel rather than memorize, like a door swinging open. His cousin bumped his shoulder. "You've got that look again," she said. "What now?"

"Nothing," Arthur said. "I just figured out who gets the fire."

"Who?"

He nodded toward the neem tree. "Not them." Then he picked up the brass lamp waiting on the shelf, polished it with his sleeve, and set it back down where he could see it from his chair.

"Read it again," Marcus said, leaning over the glass case outside the visitor center at the war memorial. "The part about the mill."

Arianna held the photocopied page of the settler's diary steady. Her history assignment was due Monday, and she needed one primary source to explain why people moved west in the 1800s. The diary belonged to a man named Elias Crane, who had marched past this very hill in 1849. She had expected a story about farmland. Instead, the third line stopped her cold: "Left the farm to Samuel. Gold will do what corn never could."

"He left his farm," Marcus said. "He wasn't going west for land at all. He wanted money."

"That's just one guy," Arianna said. "One anecdote doesn't prove anything." She flipped to the back of the packet, where the park ranger had stapled a timeline. Her finger moved down the dates. Elias Crane had packed his wagon in the spring of 1849, months after something had happened in California. She found the line in the timeline: gold discovered at Sutter's Mill in January 1848.

"That's it," she said. "He read the news, then he left. The diary, the timeline, they fit together." A suspicion began to germinate in her mind, small but persistent. If Crane had left because of gold, how many others had done the same?

"Okay," Marcus said, "but you can't see gold fever in a diary. It's not like he wrote I have a disease."

Arianna pulled her notebook from her backpack and wrote two columns. LEFT FOR GOLD and LEFT FOR LAND. Then she walked along the memorial wall, where plaques listed the names of travelers who had passed through. Beside each name was a destination. Nearly every one said California. She counted eleven out of fourteen.

"They're all going the same direction," she said. "Same year, same place. Crane's diary says gold, and everyone else is headed to the same territory." She tapped the wall. "That's the pattern. That's my evidence."

Marcus squinted at the notebook. "So your whole report is, they weren't farmers, they were dreamers?"

"It's a primary source plus data." She copied the last name from the wall, then reread Crane's line about gold doing what corn never could. "He walked away from a farm he already owned. That tells you something."

The sun dropped behind the hill and the wall went cold and gray. Arianna zipped her notebook into her backpack and stood a moment longer at the plaque for Elias Crane. Somewhere past this hill, he had kept walking.

John had until Sunday night to finish his math project, and he had promised his grandfather he would do it at the kitchen table where the light was good. The assignment said to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years, and John had brought his notebook, two sharpened pencils, and a bad mood, because the numbers refused to feel like anything real.

"I don't get why I should care," he said, sliding the notebook aside. "It's just money sitting there."

Grandpa set down his coffee and pulled a folded paper from the drawer beside the fridge. It was a credit card statement, and the interest rate printed at the top was 24 percent. "Care about it now," he said. "I let a balance ride on this thing once, back when I was buying lumber for the porch. Never again."

John stared at the number. Something about it bothered him, an invisible rule he couldn't see. "How fast would it grow? Like, if you just left it?"

"Couldn't tell you," Grandpa said. "That's your department. Mine's the porch."

John flipped through the banking book Grandpa kept on the shelf, a fat one with a cracked spine, and found a page with a tiny headline: The Rule of 72. He read it twice, then grabbed his pencil. He narrated his steps out loud, the way his teacher liked, because saying them helped him check himself. "Seventy-two divided by the rate. At 24 percent, that's three years to double." He checked it against the compound table on the next page and it matched, close enough to make him grin. Three years, and the debt would be twice as big. That he could picture.

"You look like you found buried treasure," Grandma said, coming in with a plate of peanut butter cookies still warm.

"Sort of the opposite." John showed her the arithmetic, and she leaned over his shoulder, one hand resting light on the back of his chair.

For the next hour the kitchen was quiet except for pencil scratches. John built two five-year tables, one where interest stacked on interest and one where it didn't, and the gap between them widened every year like a slow door opening. The compound row pulled ahead by the third year, and he thought of Grandpa's lumber bill doubling in exactly that time. When he finished, he slid the notebook across the table. "Objective proof," he said. "Compound wins. That's my whole conclusion."

Grandpa read it, nodding slowly. Then he stood, went to the hall, and came back with a small green passbook with John's name on it. "Been putting twenty dollars a month in this since you were eight. The rate's 24 percent on the statement you were reading, and I made every payment, so no doubling trick works against us." He tapped the balance at the bottom of the page, which was almost exactly twice what John would have counted in deposits.

"Five years," Grandma said softly, taking John's empty mug before he could ask for more cocoa.

"Your bike money," Grandpa said, and set the passbook down beside the cookies.

Naomi had to give her science presentation on Tuesday, and by Monday her body was already acting strange. Her hands were cold, her stomach hurt, and she kept snapping at her little brother over nothing. She wanted the weirdness gone before she had to stand up in front of everyone.

That afternoon, her class did a lab on solvent safety, and Mr. Ruiz held up a bottle marked flammable. "Keep this away from the hot plate," he said. Naomi copied the warning into her notebook, and next to it she doodled a little flame. Then she wrote, in smaller letters, stress feels like that. One spark and everything catches. It was a strange thing to notice, but it made her think that maybe her racing heart had rules too, the way the solvent did.

At the dentist's office that evening, waiting for her checkup, she watched a boy about eight years old sit across from her. He was gripping the armrests and breathing fast. His mother leaned over. "Count your breaths out, nice and long," she said. "Watch what your heart does." The boy breathed out slowly, counting, and then said, "It slows down when I breathe out." His mother nodded. "And it speeds up a little when you breathe in. That's just what hearts do." Naomi sat very still. She put two fingers on her own wrist, breathed in, and felt her pulse tick quicker. She breathed out long and slow, and it settled.

On the bus home she kept testing it. In, faster. Out, slower. Long out-breaths made the settling last longer. She figured the pattern was real, not luck, because it worked every single time she tried.

Tuesday morning she woke at five and could not get back to sleep, which she knew was a factor in how bad she felt. So she made a plan instead of lying there. She did ten slow breaths with the long outs, the way the boy had counted, and her heart stopped hammering. Then she set her alarm fifteen minutes earlier for the rest of the week, put her phone across the room so she would not mess with it after lights out, and kept the same bedtime three nights running. By Thursday she was falling asleep faster and waking less.

When her turn came, she stood at the front with her poster, the one she'd used to illustrate the solvent data with a bar graph. Her heart started to race. She breathed in, felt it climb, then let the air out slowly through her mouth, counting to six, and felt it drop. She did it twice more while Priya was setting up the laptop, and nobody even noticed.

Her voice came out steady. She pointed at the graph, said her first line, and moved on to the flame warning at the bottom of the poster.

At dinner Jaxson slid his phone across the table before his mother could tell him to put it away. "Read this headline," he said. "Kids who eat oatmeal get better grades. It's all over the internet today."

His older sister Priya leaned over, noodles still twirling on her fork. "So we should eat oatmeal every morning? Lucky you, you already do."

"That's the thing." Jaxson set down his fork. He had eaten oatmeal almost every day since second grade, and his grades were fine, but plenty of kids in his class who ate sugary cereal had better grades than he did. Something about the headline itched at him. "I want to know how they know it's the oatmeal."

"Maybe they asked a bunch of kids what they eat and what their grades are," Priya said.

"Okay, but what else do oatmeal kids have in common?" Jaxson pushed his peas around his plate while he thought. The steam from the pot of rice fogged the kitchen window, and his father was ladling out seconds, but Jaxson barely noticed. He kept seeing the chart from the article, two lines rising together like teammates. He remembered something else with two rising lines he'd seen in a video last month. "Wait. Ice cream sales go up in summer, and sunburns go up in summer, but ice cream doesn't cause sunburns. Hot weather causes both."

"So what's the hot weather here?" his father asked, sitting back down.

Jaxson grabbed a napkin and drew two wobbly arrows pointing at the same box. He speculated out loud, throwing out ideas faster than he could test them. "Maybe oatmeal kids have parents who make breakfast, and parents who make breakfast also check homework, and that's the actual thing. Or oatmeal is cheap and fast, so maybe those families just have calmer mornings."

"That would be tedious to check," Priya said, "but you could try. Ask your class."

The next day Jaxson did an annoying but simple thing. Between classes he asked eleven kids two questions: what they ate for breakfast, and whether anyone at home helped them study. He tallied the answers in the back of his notebook during lunch, then again after school because he smudged the first page. The pattern surprised him. The breakfast foods were all over the place, cereal, oatmeal, leftover pizza, but the kids with the best grades almost all had someone checking in about school, whatever was on their plates.

At dinner he laid the notebook on the table between the rice pot and the salad. "The oatmeal might not be doing anything. Both things could be caused by something else." Priya tapped his chart of arrows and grinned.

"From your perspective, does that mean I can stop making oatmeal?" his mother asked.

"Keep the oatmeal," Jaxson said, spooning up another bite. "I just want the headline to say the true thing."

Juliette had until fourth period to explain, out loud, the difference between a stock and a bond and which one was riskier, and so far her notecard said only "stock = part of a company, bond = loan, help." Her friend Priya slid into the seat across from her at lunch and read the card upside down.

"That's it? Mr. Okafor said we lose points if we just read definitions."

"I'm not going to read them. I'm going to explain why a stock is riskier. I just don't have a why yet." Juliette looked past Priya at the cafeteria fruit line, where a handwritten sign had appeared that morning: STRAWBERRIES $7. "Wait. Wasn't that sign $3 last week?"

Priya turned to look. "My mom would call that robbery."

Juliette got up, walked over, and asked the lunch lady why the price had jumped. The lunch lady shrugged and said the grower had lost half the crop in that late frost two weekends ago, so what was left cost more. Juliette stood there holding her tray, not moving, until the boy behind her cleared his throat.

On the way back she talked it through with Priya. "The frost ruined part of the crop. Less supply. So the berries that survived are worth more. Nobody had to decide that, it just happened." She set her tray down hard enough to slosh the milk. "That's the part I was missing. A stock's value moves around like that because of things nobody controls. Weather. Or whatever the company equivalent of weather is. A bond just pays you back fixed amounts. It doesn't ride up and down."

"So you'd verify that how?" Priya asked, spearing a fry. "You can't exactly ask a stock about its frost."

"I can ask my brother. He bought one bond and one stock last year with his birthday money." Juliette had meant to text him days ago and kept forgetting. She did it now: did ur stock and bond act different this year? His answer came back before she finished her juice: bond same every month, stock down then up then down. She turned the phone so Priya could see.

"That's your whole presentation," Priya said. "The frost is the show part."

Fourth period arrived faster than felt fair. Juliette stood up with her one sad notecard and told the class about the strawberry sign, the frost, the surviving berries costing more, and how a stock moved like that, sometimes badly, for reasons nobody controlled, while a bond mostly sat still. "So the stock is the riskier one," she said. "It can drop because of something like weather. The bond just keeps paying."

Mr. Okafor wrote something in his book without looking up. "Nice use of the berry stand."

After class, Marcus from the second row caught her at the door. "My dad's company stock just fell," he said. "Is it, like, endangered?"

"Ask the weather," Juliette said, and walked on.

Grandpa's kitchen smelled like butter and old newspapers. Andrew sat at the table with a chemistry book open to the periodic table, tracing his finger down the squares while the pan hissed on the stove. He was supposed to be learning something for science class, but mostly he was stalling, because Grandpa was making eggs and Andrew was hungry.

"You keep staring at that chart," Grandpa said, cracking an egg into the pan. The white spread out, clear and wobbling, and then the edges went white.

"Number eight," Andrew said. "Oxygen. It says the atomic number is eight, so I think that means eight protons. But I can't see protons. Nobody can. How do I know the chart isn't just making it up?"

Grandpa chuckled and tilted the pan. "I worked at the power plant thirty years, boy. Tended the turbine that spun the generators. I never once saw the steam push it, but I watched the needle climb every time it did. You trust the pattern, not the sight of it."

Andrew turned back to the chart. Carbon was six, so carbon had six protons. Gold was seventy-nine, which seemed like a lot of protons for one atom, but the pattern held all the way down: whatever the atomic number said, that was the protons. It was like the chart was a code, and the number was the key to each square. He tested himself, covering the name and guessing from the number alone, getting helium right and messing up nitrogen, which was seven, not six. He'd have to evaluate his guesses more carefully next time.

The egg was done. Grandpa slid it onto Andrew's plate, and Andrew stared at the solid white part, fork hovering. He remembered being little, maybe seven, and watching Grandpa cook while he waited for the egg to turn clear again when it cooled. He'd actually cried about it once, and Grandpa had said something he hadn't understood back then.

"It's permanent," Grandpa said now, as if reading his mind. "Heat changes the proteins in the egg white for good. It turns solid and white, and it stays that way. It's a chemical change. Frying an egg is a chemical change, because heat permanently changes those proteins."

"So it can never go back." Andrew poked the white with his fork. "Not even a little?"

"Not even a little."

Andrew looked from his plate to the chart. Invisible protons you could count anyway, invisible protein changes you could prove with a fork. Atoms changing their partners, eggs refusing to turn back. He cut a piece of egg white and ate it.

"Okay," he said. "But nitrogen is seven. Say it with me so I don't forget."

The living history museum smelled like wood smoke and wet wool, and Colton had exactly forty minutes before the bus left. His assignment was due Monday: use a primary source, an actual document from the time, to explain why people moved west in the 1800s. He had tried the library, but the books just said "economic opportunity," which told him nothing he could picture. Here, in the museum's archive room, there was a glass case holding a settler's diary with pages a volunteer had copied so kids could handle them.

"Careful with those," said the volunteer at the desk. She pointed to a cast-iron pump in the corner. "If you want water, that pump still works, but you have to open the valve at the bottom first." Colton nodded and sat down with the copied pages. The handwriting slanted and crowded, and the ink had faded to brown, but he could read it. He was looking for one thing: a reason.

He found it on the third page. The settler wrote that the fields back home had grown poorer every year, and that a neighbor had written from the west describing soil so dark it stained his hands. The settler wrote, "We are not restless people. We are hungry people." Colton copied the sentence into his notebook. Then he noticed something else, a pattern he hadn't expected. Half the diary was about weather. Too much rain, then none, then too much again. The family's whole year turned on water, when it came and when it didn't.

That reminded him of the argument two girls from his class were having at the next table over a poster for their Egypt project. "Why did they only have three seasons?" one complained. "Everyone has four." Colton leaned over. "I read the plaque in the Egypt room," he said. "It went by the Nile. Akhet was the flood, Peret was the growing season, and Shemu was the harvest." The girls stared at him. "Three seasons of water, then," Colton said slowly, "like this diary. Their year turned on water too, just a different river." He hadn't planned to say that out loud, and it surprised him a little.

He decided to revise his plan for Monday. Instead of one paragraph on soil, he would write about water: the rain the settler waited for, and the flood the Egyptians waited for, and how people built their whole calendars around whatever their land gave them. It felt like a more sophisticated idea than "economic opportunity," and it had come from a brown-inked page and a lucky argument at the next table. On his way out, Colton turned the little valve on the old pump, worked the handle three times, and watched clear water spill over his stained hands.

Aurora had sixty-two dollars in her pocket and one hour before her mom picked her up at the food court, and she intended to spend both on the new Drift sneakers everyone at school was suddenly wearing. She had saved since March, skipping the fall festival and two movie nights, and last week she had even told her grandmother the money was for "plumbing repairs" on her locker, which still made her wince when she thought about it. She crossed the shiny tile floor toward the shoe store, past a kiosk where a sign shouted, "The hoodie EVERYONE is talking about!" Above it, a TV screen showed the rapper Zay Marlow holding up the same hoodie and saying it was the softest thing he'd ever worn. Aurora slowed down. She had almost bought that hoodie in September, until she saw the price.

Inside the shoe store, the Drifts glowed on a backlit wall like something holy. A banner read "LIMITED. LEGENDARY. LOVED BY MILLIONS." She turned a display box and found Zay Marlow's face on that too, grinning, with the words "Zay says: unstoppable." Last month she would have carried the box straight to the register. But something had changed after Saturday, when she was scrolling reviews for a phone case she wanted.

She'd been watching a girl named FoxiiBee raving about the case, calling it flawless, calling it life-changing, and Aurora had been one tap from buying when she noticed the tiny "#ad" in the caption. She'd looked it up, frowning at her phone in the kitchen, and learned that in the United States, the Federal Trade Commission requires influencers and celebrities to clearly disclose when they were paid or given free products to promote something. She'd scrolled back through three more of FoxiiBee's videos. Two had the tag. The video for the phone case did not, and neither did a blurry story that said "gifted!!" with no other marking.

Now, in the store, she asked a clerk with a silver nose ring, "Does Zay Marlow actually buy these shoes, or did Drift just send them to him?" The clerk laughed. "They send him a whole pallet. He's under contract. There's supposed to be a disclosure somewhere, you know, so it complies with the FTC rule. It's on their website, I think, in tiny print." Aurora picked up the box and studied the back, angling it so it sat perpendicular to the shelf edge, letting the light catch the fine print near the barcode. There it was, smaller than the size chart: "Compensated endorsement."

She stood there weighing the shoes in her hands. They were well made; she could feel that. Millions of people did love them, though that banner also told her exactly what the company wanted her to think. Maybe Zay liked them too. Maybe he'd have liked anything they paid him enough to like.

At the register, she set the box down and then, slowly, slid it back toward herself. "I'll take them," she said, "but I'm going to wear them because I like them, not because a rapper got a pallet." The clerk grinned and rang her up. As she walked out, she passed the hoodie kiosk again and shot the sign a look. "Everyone," she muttered, "except me."

Kaitlyn crouched between the tomato rows with her notebook open on her knee, and the tomato on the healthy plant stared back at her like it knew something she didn't. Two rows, same seeds, same soil, planted the same afternoon in April. The left row stood tall and green. The right row drooped, its leaves curling under like old paper. Something invisible was at work, and she intended to find out what.

Her first guess was water. "It's a hypothesis," she told her little brother, Danny, when he wandered over with a popsicle. "A testable guess. I have one, and I'm going to test it."

"Sounds trivial to me," Danny said, working on the popsicle with great concentration. "They're plants. They droop. Big deal."

The bee numbers were down this year, everyone at the garden said so, the whole population in a recession, and Kaitlyn had already ruled out pollination, since the bees that did show up seemed happy to pollinate both rows equally. It wasn't the bees. She was almost sure it was the water, since the drooping row sat closer to the fence, where the sprinkler's arc might fall short.

So she tested it. She dragged a watering can down the droopy row every morning, a good soaking, and within a week the plants perked up. Case closed, she wrote in her notebook. Except they didn't stay perked. They sagged again, worse, and one of them turned yellow at the bottom. Kaitlyn stood there feeling like the notebook had lied to her.

Then she noticed the hose. Her mother had been rinsing the compost bin on the far side of the fence, and the runoff pooled near the drooping row every evening, standing in a low, sunken patch of ground. Kaitlyn's extra morning watering had landed on top of evening runoff, and the sick row was sitting in mud while the healthy row drained fine. Too much water, not too little. Her test had told her the wrong answer, and she wanted to know why. She looked at her notebook, then at the two rows, and saw it. In her test, the two rows had not been treated the same except for the water. The sick row also had the sunken ground, the afternoon shade from the fence, and the runoff. Everything was different, so the test had proved nothing at all.

She started over with two pots of the same seeds, same size, same soil from the same bag, set side by side on the flat part of the patio where the shade fell evenly. Same amount of water, measured to the line on a jar. Same spot, so the temperature stayed the same for both. Same timing, morning and morning, seven o'clock sharp, because that was the part Danny was in charge of, and Danny took the job suspiciously seriously for someone who called the whole project trivial. Two weeks later one pot stood green and the other, the one she'd doubled the water for, drooped in exactly the curling-paper way.

She wrote a single line at the bottom of the page and turned the notebook toward Danny. "Same amount, same temperature, same timing, everything the same except the one thing I'm testing," she read out loud. "And now the answer's actually the answer."

Danny licked the last of his popsicle off the stick. "So it was too much water all along?"

"It was too much water all along," Kaitlyn said, and closed the notebook with a snap.

The gymnasium was a turbulent mess of folding tables, extension cords, and tri-fold boards, and Adam's spot was between a potato battery and a volcano that kept threatening to erupt sideways. His own display sat in the center of the table: two hammers, one orange with flaking rust, one clean and gray, both labeled. His board read WHY? in letters he had traced twice to emphasize the question.

He had found the rusty hammer in Grandpa's garden bed, half buried in the dirt, and the clean one on a nail inside the dry shed. Same hammers, bought the same summer, now completely different. His board explained what he had tested: he had set a third hammer outside in a jar with water, a fourth outside under a roof where rain couldn't reach it, and a fifth in the shed. After two weeks of a damp towel and misting bottle, only the wet one outside had started turning orange. Something in the air plus water did it, and the something didn't reach the shed one much. But when the judges asked "what is the orange stuff, actually," he froze, because he didn't have a word for it.

"It's not just dirty metal," the first judge had said, tapping the rusty head. "It changed into something else. What would you call that?"

Adam flipped through his notebook so fast the pages tore. He found his sketch of the periodic table, taped into the back cover because he thought it looked official. Iron was number 26. He knew that meant 26 protons, and he had written it on the board like it mattered, but right now it wasn't answering anything. He ran his finger across the row anyway, looking for a second element, one that might pair up with iron in the rust. Oxygen, number 8, eight protons, a gas, everywhere in the air and dissolved in water. He circled it twice.

"It's iron and oxygen together," Adam said. "The iron in the hammer reacted with oxygen, but only where there was water. The one in the dry shed never got wet, so it stayed fine. It's a new substance." He paused, remembering the word from the encyclopedia he'd flipped through at eleven the night before. "It's called iron oxide."

The judge wrote something down. "And the protons?"

"Iron is atomic number 26, so 26 protons. Oxygen is 8, so 8 protons. They're still iron and oxygen even after they combine, just arranged into something new." He lifted the rusty hammer and held it beside the clean one. "This one's iron oxide now. Same iron that started here, plus oxygen it pulled out of the water and the air."

Behind him, the volcano finally erupted sideways, and a girl two tables over grabbed her towel and muttered, "Every year. This is not a democracy, Justin, move your project." Adam grinned and set both hammers down in front of the judge, side by side.

The planetarium smelled like dust and old carpet, and Hailey had exactly forty minutes before her demonstration to the astronomy club. Her problem was simple and terrible: she still could not explain why Earth's tilt caused the seasons, and Mr. Ruiz expected her to stand under the dome and teach it to twelve kids who would ask questions. She had volunteered three weeks ago, confident, and every night since, her notecards had become more confusing instead of less.

In the corner of the exhibit hall stood a giant globe with a lamp on an arm, the kind that could swing around it like a slow planet. She dragged it toward the middle of the floor, and something rattled inside the stand. Two thin dotted lines circled the globe's middle, one above the equator and one below, like rings of plumbing pipe wrapped around a water tank. She traced the top one with her finger and frowned. She had never noticed them before.

"What are those lines for?" said a small voice. A boy, maybe nine, had wandered over, dragging his own backpack like a suitcase. He pointed at the dotted circles. "Are they roads?"

"I don't actually know," Hailey admitted, which felt dangerous to say out loud. She knelt and read the tiny printed label near the base. Tropic of Cancer, the top one said. Tropic of Capricorn, the bottom one. "Those are their names," she told him. She turned the lamp on and swung it toward the globe. The label was no help at all. She spun the globe slowly, and the boy watched the light slide across oceans.

Then she noticed the small calendar dial on the lamp's arm. She clicked it forward, month by month, and stopped. In late June, the lamp's beam hit the globe dead straight, and when she crouched to eye level, her stickpin shadow at the Tropic of Cancer vanished to nothing. The noon Sun was directly overhead there. She clicked the dial on and on, through autumn, and in late December the shadow disappeared again, but at the other line, the Tropic of Capricorn. She sat back on her heels. The lamp hadn't moved up or down much. The globe was tilted, leaning like a tired person, and its lean never changed as it traveled. The beam struck each tropic straight on at those moments, and everywhere else it arrived slanted.

"So the light's more direct there," she whispered. The boy leaned in.

"More direct where?"

"At the top line in June," she said, "and the bottom line in December. Around June twenty-one the noon Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Cancer. Around December twenty-one it's directly overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn." She pushed the stickpin into Missouri, where they lived, and clicked the dial. In June the shadow lay short and stubby. In December it stretched long across the Pacific. Short shadow, steep light, heat. Long shadow, slanted light, cold. Her notecards suddenly seemed like a tranquil lake she could finally see the bottom of. The whole thing could transform from a jumble of facts into one swinging lamp and one leaning globe.

Mr. Ruiz's shoes squeaked in the hallway. Twelve kids were coming, and the boy was already raising his hand with a question, the one about the roads she never answered.

Arthur sat on the living room floor with his laptop balanced on the coffee table, two news articles open side by side. His class project was due Monday, and he had promised his partner Nadia he would find two stories about the same event so they could compare them. He had picked the downtown march from last Saturday, the one his mom had driven past on her way to the store.

The first headline read, "Thousands Gather in Peaceful Protest for Cleaner Parks." The second read, "Rioters Disrupt Downtown, Businesses on Edge." Arthur scrolled down. Both articles described the same street, the same afternoon, the same crowd. Both mentioned a broken window at a bakery and a crowd estimate near four thousand. He read them again, then leaned back against the couch and stared at the ceiling fan.

He noticed something odd. When he read the first one, he pictured people holding signs, maybe singing. When he read the second, he pictured shouting and running, even though the article said almost the same things had happened. He tested it. He covered the headline on the first article with his hand and read only the body. Then he covered the second headline and did the same. The paragraphs underneath felt almost identical. The difference was the words on top.

"Protesters," he said out loud. "Rioters." He wrote both words in his notebook, then wrote "crowd of about four thousand" between them. If a word could make him picture two opposite scenes from the same facts, that was worth putting in the project. He could deduce that the writers had chosen those words on purpose, or at least that the words did work the facts alone didn't do. He underlined the pair twice.

Nadia came over at four, dropping her backpack by the door and flopping into the armchair. He turned the laptop toward her. "Read this one, then this one. Same day, same street." She read for a minute, frowning. "The second one makes me feel like it was dangerous," she said. "The first one makes it sound like a picnic."

"That's the thing," Arthur said. "They're loaded words." She raised an eyebrow, and he pointed at the screen. "Same crowd, but the word choice pushes you one way or the other." Nadia pulled out her phone and started typing notes.

"Wait," she said, "there's more. Look at this ad that keeps popping up before the video I need." On her screen, a basketball player Arthur recognized from the playoffs held up a sneaker and said everyone was wearing them this season. Arthur counted the tricks in his head. A famous athlete, a claim that everybody already had them, and the words " revolutionary" and "pathetic" in the on-screen text, describing the shoe and its rivals. "Athlete, bandwagon, loaded words," he said. "All three in fifteen seconds."

"It's like a simile that only goes one direction," Nadia said, tapping the screen. Arthur laughed, then opened a blank slide and typed the headline at the top. "Probable headline of our project," he said, reading it aloud: "How the Same Crowd Becomes Two Different Stories."

"The crowd was never two crowds," Nadia said, and hit save.

Kaitlyn sat on the low wall by the swings, her right arm resting in its blue cast like something she was babysitting. Three weeks ago she had fallen off the monkey bars, and now she watched the bars from a distance, the way you might watch a dog that had bitten you. Her best friend Priya swung back and forth beside her, pumping her legs.

"You're staring again," Priya said.

"I'm not staring. I'm thinking." Kaitlyn turned the cast so the signatures faced the sun. Near her wrist, under the plaster, she could feel a firm lump she had noticed two days ago, a ridge that had not been there before. It worried her at first. Then she remembered the follow-up visit, when the doctor had held up the new X-ray against the light and pointed to a fuzzy shadow spanning the break. "That's your callus," he had said, and her mother had smiled, so Kaitlyn had figured it was a good thing. She'd read the report in the folder when nobody was looking: as a broken bone heals, the body forms a callus, a mass of cartilage and new bone that bridges the gap between the broken ends.

"Thinking about what?" Priya dragged her feet to stop the swing.

"About whether the lump means it's working in there. It's like a bridge being built where you can't see it. Cartilage first, then new bone." She pressed gently on the ridge through the cast. It did not hurt, which she decided was probably a good sign.

Priya hopped off the swing. "So if the bridge is halfway built, could you hang from the bars? Just for a second?"

"No. The doctor said no weight on it for six weeks."

"You could use just the left hand and sort of balance with the cast."

"Balance is a polite word for falling." Kaitlyn slid off the wall anyway and walked to the monkey bars, keeping a careful distance, like a scientist approaching a skunk. Priya followed, and by the time they reached the bars, half the fifth grade had gathered, because a kid in a cast near forbidden equipment is the most interesting thing a playground can offer.

"She's going to do it," a boy named Marcus announced.

"She's not," Kaitlyn said. "I came to look, not to swing." But she stood there measuring the distance with her eyes, and she had to admit her motivation was not entirely scientific. Part of her wanted to prove the bars hadn't won.

"Your arm won't cooperate even if you tried," Priya said. "It's still knitting."

Kaitlyn flexed her fingers inside the cast. They cooperated fine. That was the strange part. The fingers worked, the wrist was stiff but alive, and underneath it all, invisible crews were laying down cartilage and new bone across the gap, closing it a little more every day. She tried an experiment. She raised her left hand, gripped the first bar, and hung, letting the cast hang loose beside her, touching nothing. Her body swung. It felt almost like flying. Three seconds later she dropped down onto the wood chips, and the crowd groaned with disappointment.

"You didn't even try the cast hand," Marcus said.

"That was the experiment. One hand, no weight on the broken side. I'm not falling off these bars twice in one lifetime." She looked up at the row of rungs glinting in the afternoon light. Six weeks from now, when the cast came off, she would come back and cross every single bar.

Just then the bell rang, and everyone turned to run inside. Marcus, sprinting for the line, caught his sneaker on the edge of the wood-chip border and went down hard, holding his wrist, his face going pale.

Kaitlyn crouched beside him and did her best not to smile. "It hurts, right? Wrong place, wrong angle?"

"Really bad," Marcus whispered.

"Well, here's the good news. In about three weeks you'll feel a lump, and it means a bridge is going up in there." She patted her cast. "The bad news is I get the swing wall and the good seat at lunch for the next month, because that's how the cast club cooperates."

Marcus stared at her, then down at his swelling wrist, and said the words every kid on that playground was already thinking. "I should have stayed by the swings."

Florence had until Sunday night to build a model of a river canyon for Monday's science fair, and so far all she had was a plastic tub, a bag of sand from Grandpa's shed, and a smooth gray stone she'd found in the creek behind his house. The stone bothered her. It was perfectly round, like an egg, with no sharp edges anywhere, and she wanted to know what had polished it, because whatever did that was probably the same thing that had carved the real canyons in her textbook.

"Supper's at six," Grandpa called from the porch. "And I need that tub back by Sunday, I'm mixing concrete Monday morning." That gave her two days.

Florence sat on the back steps and turned the stone over. The creek was barely ankle deep. How could something that small cut through rock? She remembered the textbook's two-page spread, a canyon with striped walls and a caption about millions of years, but the caption never said how. Maybe, she thought, the water itself was just soft and harmless, like a shower. So the water couldn't be doing the work. Something in the water had to be.

She went inside and came back with a mayonnaise jar, a fistful of creek sand, three pebbles, and a scrap of soft chalk from Grandpa's garage. She dropped the chalk and everything else into the jar, filled it with water, and shook it hard for a count of one hundred. When she fished out the chalk, its edges were worn and there was a gritty white smear in the water. She shook it again, longer this time. The corners had gone rounded. She was still holding it when Grandpa came out with two glasses of lemonade.

"It's called abrasion," he said, peering into the jar. "That's what the old-timers around here always called it, the sand and stones grinding the bed." He tapped her stone. "Little creek did that, one grain at a time."

Florence spent Saturday building her model. She tilted the tub, lined it with a layer of sand and clay, and poured a slow trickle from a watering can at the top. The water picked up sand, dragged it downstream, and dropped it in a fan where the slope flattened out, which her textbook said was deposition. On Sunday morning she cut the trickle and studied the channel. It was deeper. Not much, but deeper, and the deepest part was where the most sand had traveled over the clay. She propped a luminous orange sign beside it, MILLENNIA IN A TUB, and packed her rounded stone in a sock so she could show it at the fair. Grandpa waved from the porch as Dad's car pulled out Monday morning, and Florence held the model steady on her lap all the way to school.

Paisley crouched between the tomato beds at the community garden, holding a slice of onion skin so thin she could almost see through it, like a scrap of cloudy glass. Mr. Ruiz had left the garden's old microscope on the picnic table before driving off to the hardware store, and Paisley wanted more than anything to see the cells before he came back. Her lab sheet had three empty blanks waiting for labels: cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus. She had never labeled anything under a microscope before, and she only had one shot at the prize for the summer science contest, a packet of heirloom seeds that everybody wanted.

Her friend Donte arrived on his bike, dropped it in the gravel, and peered over her shoulder. "My cousin said onion cells look like bricks in a wall," he said. "That's why they're easy to start on."

Paisley switched on the light and pressed her eye to the rubber eyepiece. The onion skin bloomed into view, a patchwork of little boxes, each one edged in a darker line. She drew a rectangle in her notebook and marked the outer edge. Cell wall. But where was the rest? Everything looked flat and faint, like a photograph underwater. "The nucleus should be a darker dot," she murmured. "Is it hiding, or is it just too small?"

"Maybe you need to turn it up higher," Donte said, squinting at the dial on the side. He spun the nosepiece until a longer lens clicked into place. "There. That one says forty."

Fifty times bigger sounded plenty to Paisley, but Donte shook his head. "It's the eyepiece times the objective," he said. "The top part says ten times, and this one says forty times, so it's four hundred times bigger, not fifty." Paisley lifted her head, checked the numbers stamped on both lenses herself, and did the multiplication on the corner of her page. Ten times forty was four hundred. Donte was right, and that meant her cells had been tiny ghosts before, too faint to hold a nucleus.

When she looked again, the patchwork sharpened. A pale dot floated near the center of one brick, and around it, just inside the dark wall, she could make out a thinner line hugging the edge like plastic wrap. Cell membrane. She labeled all three blanks, pressing hard enough to dent the paper, then taped the onion skin into her notebook to conserve it for the contest judges.

Donte leaned in for his turn, adjusted the fine focus with great care, and frowned. "Paisley. Are we sure these aren't the sinister ones?" He pointed at a cluster of cells near the edge of the skin, blotched and collapsed where her fingernail had squeezed too hard. "Looks like an infection got them." Paisley snatched back the notebook, but it was too late to salvage that corner. She grabbed the whole onion from the picnic table and started peeling off a fresh layer, layer after layer, saying, "Good thing onions have more skins than I have patience."

Elena sat on the crinkly paper of the nurse's cot and squinted at the eye chart taped to the cabinet door. The top E was easy. The second line was a smear of gray. The third line might as well have been spilled ink.

"You failed the screening twice," Nurse Patel said. "The optometrist is already here for the sixth graders. Come on."

The optometrist's folding chair sat under the window, next to a rack of trial lenses. He flipped lenses in front of her eyes, one after another. "Read the line with the T."

"O, maybe D, then something with a tail."

"Better or worse?" He slid a new lens in.

"Better. The letters aren't smearing sideways anymore." Elena leaned forward. "Wait. Why did they smear? I thought you're either nearsighted or farsighted. My friend Marcus is nearsighted, and his stuff is blurry only far away. Mine's blurry everywhere."

"That's a different thing," the optometrist said. "It's called astigmatism."

"But what is it?" Elena asked, because Nurse Patel was no help and he kept flipping lenses.

He shrugged, already reaching for the next lens. "Your cornea, or maybe the lens inside the eye, is slightly egg-shaped. Curves more in one direction than the other. Blurs things at any distance."

Elena went still. An egg. She thought of the way light came through the porous curtain in her bedroom and stretched into ovals on the floor. If the curve was uneven, the light wouldn't land in one point. That would smear the letter sideways, near and far both, which was exactly what she'd been seeing since October, when the whiteboard turned to fog and she'd copied Marcus's notes out of desperation and felt a hot spike of resentment when he called her a cheater.

She had a theory to test. "Hold on. If it's egg-shaped, the blur should have a direction, right? The same direction everywhere?" She held up her hand and curled her fingers slightly, like a tunnel tilted one way. She looked at the chart through the gap. The letters stretched sideways. She tilted the gap the other way. They stretched the other way. "So a lens curved unevenly would smear the E left or right depending on which way the egg sits. Mine smears left. Every line, near and far."

The optometrist stopped flipping lenses and looked at her. "Try this one."

The third line snapped into focus. F, Z, B, D, 4. She read it clean to the bottom, and her eyes stung because she hadn't known letters had that many sharp edges.

Nurse Patel wrote something on a slip. "Glasses in a week."

"A week?" Elena said. "Can I at least keep the chart?"

Jack had been looking forward to the aquarium field trip for weeks, mostly because it meant a whole day away from regular classes. He and his best friend Marcus claimed the seats at the back of the bus, and by the time they rolled into the parking lot, they had already planned to see the shark tunnel first, the octopus second, and the jellyfish room whenever they felt like wandering.

Near the entrance stood a trivia station with a big spinning wheel. A volunteer handed Jack a card. "Answer three questions right and you win a behind-the-scenes tour of the seal exhibit." Jack spun the wheel, which landed on what looked like a completely random category: Farm Facts. "Odd choice for an aquarium," the volunteer admitted, "but everybody eats, right? First question: true or false, every dairy cow in a milking barn has had a calf."

Jack opened his mouth to say false, because in his head cows just made milk all the time, like a faucet. Marcus elbowed him. "Guess," he whispered. Before Jack could, Priya, the quiet girl from his science class who almost never spoke on trips, stepped up beside him. "A dairy cow only produces milk after she has given birth to a calf," she said. "So it's true. Every one of them." Jack repeated her answer, the volunteer stamped the card, and they moved to the next question, which Jack got wrong, and the third, which Marcus got right.

"You know cows," Jack said to Priya as they collected their tour passes. She shrugged. "I live on a dairy farm. I've watched it my whole life." Jack felt his ears go warm. He had sort of assumed she was quiet because she didn't know much about anything fun, and that was a stereotype he hadn't even noticed he was carrying. He was about to resign himself to being the dumb one on this tour when Priya added, "Don't feel bad. Half my cousins argue with me about it at Thanksgiving."

Behind the scenes, the seal keeper led them past tanks and buckets of fish, and Jack actually asked questions, three in a row, and one of them made the keeper say, "Huh. Good eye." At the last tank, a silvery fish with a black stripe kept bumping the glass. "That one's totally random," Jack said. "Just swimming into the wall over and over."

"That's a kelp perch," Priya said. "They feed at the edge of things, right where the glass is." The keeper nodded, impressed, and Jack turned to Marcus. "Remind me to sit near Priya on the way home."

Emmett had one job at the mall: find a birthday gift for his grandmother while his mom picked up shoes at the other end. He had twenty dollars and forty minutes, and he was already wasting both at the phone repair kiosk, where his friend Rico worked weekends. His problem was simpler than it sounded. Grandmother had once mentioned a mug with a red fox painted on it, and Emmett could not remember where she had seen it. He pulled out his phone and typed his own name into the search box, on a hunch that he had once looked it up and saved the link.

The search results filled the screen, and near the top was something he did not expect: a comment he had written three years ago on the mall's public page, complaining about the arcade closing early on a Sunday. Anyone searching "Emmett" could read it, including strangers, and it even showed which mall location he had been at that day. He stared at it, then scrolled and found the same comment copied on a second site he had never visited.

"How is it on there twice?" he asked Rico, holding up the phone. "I only wrote it once."

Rico leaned over the counter. "Search engines use automated programs called crawlers to copy and index public web pages," he said, wiping a smudge off the screen. "So anything posted publicly can turn up in search results." He shrugged, like it was just weather. "Even old stuff. Even with your name on it."

Emmett tested the idea right there. He found the original comment on the mall's page, edited it to conceal his last name and the location tag, and then searched again an hour later, while eating a pretzel by the fountain. The old copy on the second site still sat there, unedited, because he had no way to reach it. His own fix worked only halfway, and he understood now that a public post was less like a note passed in class and more like something pinned to a board anyone could photograph. He typed a fresh comment under the mall's post, asking if anyone knew a shop that sold fox mugs, using only his first initial this time.

The reply came while he was standing outside the pet store, watching a small owl blink at him from behind the glass. The sign said it was nocturnal, which explained why it looked half asleep under the bright mall lights, while the monitor lizard beside it, according to the sign a carnivore, tracked every movement near its tank with wide-open eyes. Emmett's phone buzzed. A stranger named Doris had answered: try the kitchenware shop on level two, third store past the escalator. He walked toward the escalator, reading the message a second time, and said, "Thanks, Doris," out loud to nobody in particular.

Charlotte slid the phone box across the kitchen table like it might explode, which, in a way, it already had, because her little brother had knocked over a glass of juice and the box had saved the table from a lake of purple.

"Careful, that's the whole reason we're still dry," she said, and Owen grinned like a supervillain.

Mom sat down with a slice of cold pizza, which was her way of making any ceremony feel less like a ceremony. "Okay. Ground rules before you turn it on."

"Twelve texts a day," Charlotte guessed.

"Use your brain, not a number," Mom said. "Rule one: nobody gets in trouble for telling me something weird that happened online. Rule two: the phone charges in the kitchen at night. Not your room. The kitchen."

"That's so you can check it," Charlotte said.

"No, it's so I can see the screen glow at two in the morning and know exactly which child to confiscate it from."

At the store that afternoon, a kid named Dev had been waiting behind them, bouncing on his heels, and he'd asked the salesman a question Charlotte couldn't stop thinking about: how long have people actually had phones in their pockets? The salesman had said the first call from a handheld cellular phone was made by a Motorola engineer named Martin Cooper, right on a New York street, on April 3, 1973. Dev had whispered, "Fifty years and my mom still calls me during class," and Charlotte had laughed so hard the display rack rattled.

Now she turned the phone over in her hands. Fifty-some years since Martin Cooper stood on that street. Her whole life, phones had just existed, like plumbing, invisible until something went wrong. She tried to picture a world where carrying one was brand new, where people on the sidewalk stared. It was like trying to picture the ocean before water.

"Are you having a trance?" Owen asked. "You look tranquil. It's creepy."

"I'm thinking about 1973." She set the phone down. "Okay, I want to test something. Rule one says tell you weird stuff. So here's weird: yesterday at school, before I even had this phone, some account named SunnyDeals42 started texting me on Mom's old tablet. It said I'd won something."

Mom put down her pizza. "What did it want?"

"A code. It said the prize would arrive once I confirmed my address." Charlotte spread her hands. "I didn't reply. But I was thinking, it knew my name. I never entered anything anywhere. So either someone gave it my name, or it's guessing names at random and waiting for somebody to say yes."

"That's called phishing," Mom said slowly. "You already did the right thing, and I'm not even going to pretend to be calm about how right you did it."

"I want to reply," Charlotte said.

"You what?"

"Not with real information. One word: nope. Then I watch what happens. If it gets pushy or weird, that proves it's a pattern, a machine hunting. If it writes back like a normal person, maybe it's a person. Either way we know more than we did."

Mom studied her for a long moment, then pushed the tablet across the table. "One word. That's it."

Charlotte typed nope and hit send. Eleven seconds later the reply landed: URGENT!!! PRIZE EXPIRES TONIGHT!!! CLICK HERE!!!

"Machine," they said at the same time, and Owen fell off his chair laughing.

"Blocked and reported," Charlotte said, feeling like Martin Cooper must have felt on that New York street, holding something that changed everything, except hers was slightly sticky from purple juice. "Mom. Can we look up what he actually said on that first call? Please tell me he said something cooler than nope."

The banner over the community centre doorway read Heritage Festival, and Bennett slipped past a cluster of kids to evade the line forming at the entrance table. His project board was due by four o'clock, and the caption still wasn't finished. He carried it under one arm, the glue drying in streaks, the last line blank except for a pencil mark where a word should go.

The problem was Mr. Okafor's note, folded into Bennett's pocket: "Check your wording before you submit." Bennett knew which wording. His caption read: "Drummer and throat singer, performances by an Inuit." He had copied the phrase from a library book, but something about it had started to nag at him on the bus, the way a pebble in a shoe does.

Inside, the hall smelled of fried plantains and cardamom. A woman in a printed headwrap was explaining a wall of photographs to two teenagers: "We call ourselves Igbo," she said, "not tribe, if you can manage it." Nearby, a Scottish pipe band tuned up with a sound like an argument between geese. Bennett walked the aisles, half listening, half rehearsing what he might ask a stranger.

At the northern tables, a man was arranging carvings of seals and a kayak paddler. A card beside the display said Inuit Artists Collective. Bennett stood there a moment, then made himself speak. "Excuse me. I'm doing a school project. Is it right to say a performer is an Inuit, or is there another word?"

The man set down a carving of a loon. "Inuit means 'the people,'" he said. "So it works for the group. One person is called an Inuk." He tapped the card. "That's why it says Artists, not one name. You wouldn't say an Inuit any more than you'd say a the-peoples."

Bennett wrote it on his palm in letters he could still read: one person, an Inuk. The man showed him how the word sat in Inuktitut, sounds Bennett tried and mangled, and the man laughed, not unkindly, and said the second try was better.

At four o'clock exactly, Bennett propped his board on the submission table at the back of the hall, where a judge with a clipboard was already moving down the row. He uncapped his pen and, in his most assertive handwriting, printed the new caption: "Drummer and throat singer, performances by an Inuk and by Inuit from across the north." The pipes started up behind him, swelling toward what had to be the climax of their set, and the judge paused at his board, clipboard steady, and read the last line twice.

"Nice fix," she said. "Half the entries get that wrong."

Chase sat cross-legged on the floor of his aunt's guest room with a photocopy of the Havdalah blessing spread in front of him. In three weeks he would stand in front of ninety people at his Bar Mitzvah and recite it by heart, and right now he could not get past the fourth line. He tried again, mouthed the words, lost the thread, and flopped backward onto the rug.

Downstairs, his cousin Priya was arranging a plate of laddus on the kitchen counter. Her family had come to stay for the week after Grandpa Joe's funeral, and the house still smelled like casseroles and incense from two different traditions. Chase wandered in and slid the photocopy onto the counter. "How do you memorize a whole prayer? I keep forgetting the middle."
