Kaitlyn rewrote it: "Novak Anna, my great-grandmother, who wrote her name the Hungarian way." Then she sat back and looked at the corrected card, and a small ache settled in beside the satisfaction. She had solved the puzzle, but the woman who wrote that postcard was gone, and would never know that a great-granddaughter in a library had finally understood her.

"Friday night, you're reading this out loud," Dani said, tapping the postcard. "Both of us. Our grandfathers would like that."

Kaitlyn slid the postcard to the center of the table, next to Min's scroll, and left it there.

Beatrice set the catapult on the kitchen table, loaded a marshmallow, and pulled the release arm. The marshmallow sailed across the room, bounced off the refrigerator, and landed in the fruit bowl.

"That's forty-two inches," said her little brother Oscar, holding the tape measure at arm's length like it might explode. "Can I have the marshmallow?"

"It touched the floor near the bowl. No." Beatrice wrote 42 on her data sheet under Trial 1, then frowned at it. Forty-two was great. Forty-two would probably win the science fair, or at least beat Dwight Yang's volcano, which had won for three years straight mostly because it glowed in the dark.

She reset the arm and launched again. This time the marshmallow went eleven inches and rolled off the table into Oscar's shoe.

"You wrote eleven," Oscar said, reading over her shoulder. "That's terrible. You should erase it and keep the forty-two."

Beatrice didn't erase it. Something about the two numbers bothered her. Same catapult, same marshmallow weight, same angle, and yet one throw went almost four times farther than the other. Either her machine was haunted, or one of those numbers was lying. She thought about the coin-flip unit from math class, how a single flip told you nothing but a hundred flips started showing something true. One launch might be a fluke. A fluke was exactly the kind of illusion that could win you a ribbon on Friday and embarrass you in front of the whole gym on Saturday, if the judges asked you to repeat it.

"I'm going to run it ten times," she announced.

"That's boring," said Oscar.

"Then count."

She launched, and launched, and adjusted the spoon cup a hair after trial six when it started rattling loose, and marked every distance down. The numbers wandered all over the place, 19, 33, 26, 15, 38, and none of them was 42 again, which made 42 look more and more like a freak. When she finished, she added all ten distances, divided by ten, and wrote the average at the bottom of the sheet: 27.4 inches.

"There," she said. "That's my real number."

"That's smaller than forty-two," Oscar pointed out. "You made your project worse on purpose."

"It's not worse, it's true. One lucky throw is just one lucky throw. If I run it ten times, the weird flukes kind of cancel out, and the average is what the catapult actually does." She tapped the 27.4. "That's the fundamental number. That one I can prove."

Oscar ate a marshmallow anyway when she wasn't looking, which she knew, because trial eleven had been sitting on the scale.

The next morning she brought the catapult to school in a shoebox. Dwight Yang was already in the hallway, plugging in his volcano. Beatrice looked at 27.4 on her data sheet, looked at the judges' table, and set up her first launch of the day.

Florence had typed and deleted her message to Marisol three times before her little brother Theo leaned over her shoulder. "You're doing the typing thing again," he said, flopping onto the couch with his tablet. She shooed him away, but gently, because Theo had spent all morning quiet and pale after his recital video had gone up on the school's music page and someone in the comments had called his solo "a crime scene." Florence's plan was to reply to that comment with something clever and cutting. The trouble was that every version she typed sounded either mean or desperate, and she couldn't tell which one it would be until after she posted it.

Instead of sending anything, she opened a new tab and looked up the school's music page itself. There was Theo, mid-note, under the headline "Winter Concert Highlights." An idea nudged her. If the video weren't public anymore, the comment couldn't keep stinging him every time someone Googled his name. The music teacher, Mr. Adeyemi, ran the page, but Florence knew from the contact line that he only checked email on Sundays. She noticed something else while she scrolled: a link at the bottom of the page, small and gray, to an archive site she'd heard kids mention, the Wayback Machine.

"Watch this," she told Theo, pulling him up by the sleeve. She pasted the music page's address into the archive's search box. A whole timeline appeared, row after row of dates going back years, like snapshots taken of the page while nobody was looking. "It says it's saved more than one trillion web pages," Theo read, his voice going up on the last word.

Florence clicked one of the older dates, and there was the page from two autumns ago, before Theo was even in band. It looked almost the same, except the photos showed kids who had graduated. She felt the idea settle into place, cold and clear. Even if the video came down tomorrow, an old copy might still be sitting in that trillion-page pile, waiting for anyone who went looking. Deleting something public didn't mean it vanished. It meant it vanished from one place.

"So my plan doesn't work," Theo said slowly.

"Your plan was to hide. My plan is different." She scrolled back to the current page and found the email link for Mr. Adeyemi. She drafted a message that didn't try to be clever, that didn't invade his inbox with drama, just said: the comments on the Winter Concert video are hurting my brother, and kids at school are sharing screenshots. Could the comment section be turned off? She read it aloud to Theo so he could hear how it sounded, because tone in an email was like tone in a voice, easy to get wrong without a face to check against.

He nodded, then pointed at her screen. "Add that he practices an hour a day. So Mr. Adeyemi knows the crime scene thing is a lie."

Florence typed the sentence in, and Theo, satisfied, went back to the couch and put his tablet face-down on the cushion, which he only did when he was done worrying about something. She hovered over the send button, then clicked it before she could start deleting again.

"Done," she said. "Now we wait until Sunday."

Juliette stood in front of the bathroom mirror with her chin tilted up, counting. Three on her forehead, one beside her nose, and a new one forming on her chin, red and tender. Last year her face had been clear, and this year it wasn't, and she wanted to know why.

At the pharmacy after school, she found the aisle with the face washes and started reading labels. "Oil-free," one said. "For acne-prone skin," said another. She turned a bottle over and squinted at the back. It mentioned unclogging pores. Pores, oil, pimples. Those three words kept coinciding on every label, and she didn't think that was an accident.

Her little brother Marcus appeared beside her, eyeing the candy shelf across the aisle. "Why are you reading shampoo for ten minutes?"

"It's not shampoo." She held up the bottle. "It says it fights pimples by unclogging pores. So pores get clogged with something."

"With dirt," Marcus said.

"Maybe. Or oil." She set the bottle down and picked up another, a scrub with the word "vigorous" splashed across the front, promising a deep clean. On the back, in smaller letters, it mentioned excess oil. She thought about her own face, shiny by lunch even when she washed it in the morning, and about her cousin Leo, who was eleven and whose face was never shiny at all. The difference was that Leo was younger. Something about getting older had changed her skin, and whatever it was, it was making more oil.

"Marcus, if I washed my face five times a day, would that fix it?"

He shrugged. "You'd be very clean."

She felt some skepticism about that plan herself. Washing had never stopped the shine before, so plain dirt didn't seem like the whole story. She took out her phone and typed carefully: why do teenagers get pimples. She scrolled, then stopped at a line that made everything click into place. Puberty hormones made the oil glands in her skin produce more oil, and the extra oil could clog pores, which led to acne.

"It's oil," she said. "There's even a word for it. Sebum."

"Sounds like a potion ingredient."

"It's the stuff clogging my pores." She put the vigorous scrub back, because scrubbing harder wouldn't change how much oil her glands made, and chose instead a gentle wash marked "non-comedogenic," which the label explained meant it wouldn't clog pores. Two weeks, the bottle suggested, before anyone should expect results. That felt long, but at least now she had a real reason for what was happening instead of just blaming herself for being careless.

At home, she set the new bottle on the sink where she would actually see it, morning and night. Her chin still had the tender spot, and her forehead still had its three, but she uncapped the wash, wet her hands, and started anyway. "Twenty-eight washes till the verdict," she told the mirror. "I can wait."

Avery spread the two graphs across the library table and weighted the corners with pencils before the air conditioning could send them fluttering. One showed monthly rainfall in the Sonoran Desert, a flat line that barely lifted off the bottom of the page. The other showed a rainforest in Borneo, where the bars towered so high they looked like a solid wall. The clock above the reference desk read 4:12, and the library closed at five. Her project was due first period tomorrow, and she still didn't have the answer to the question her teacher had posed: why does the same crop fail in one wet place and thrive in another?

She needed a picture of a rainforest farm for her poster. Her younger brother, Marcus, sat across from her with a bandaged thumb he would not stop examining, ever since Mom had warned him that a cut could get an infection if he kept picking at it. He flipped through a book about Asian agriculture while Avery hunted for photographs.

"Wait," Marcus said. "This doesn't make sense. This farmer is planting rice seedlings in a little bed, like a garden. And then these other people are sticking rice plants into a flooded field. Are they planting it twice?"

Avery was hesitant to believe him, because Marcus got things wrong constantly, like the time he insisted fog was smoke from the ocean. But she leaned over and looked. On one page, seedlings crowded together in a small nursery bed, green and stubby as new grass. On the facing page, rows of people bent over a flooded paddy, pushing young plants into the water one by one, by hand. She turned the pages back and forth. Same crop. Two plantings.

"So they start it in a nursery bed," she said slowly, "then transplant it into the flooded field." The pieces began to click against her graphs. The rainforest's enormous rainfall, the flooded fields in the photographs, they belonged to the same story. She grabbed a marker and wrote it out: rice grown first in a nursery bed, then transplanted, often by hand, into flooded paddies. The desert graph, with its stingy slivers of rain, could never flood a field like that. The rainforest could.

"Does that help?" Marcus asked, sounding worried the answer might be no.

"It fixes everything," Avery said. The clock said 4:47. She taped the graphs onto her poster, added the photograph of the farmers bent over the water, and wrote her headline in tall letters: WHERE THE RAIN GOES. A librarian began wheeling a cart toward the shelves, locking the cabinet doors one by one, and Avery slid her poster into her backpack just as the lights over the reference desk blinked twice.

"That's a five-minute warning," the librarian called out.

Avery zipped the bag and held it against her chest. "Race you to the door," she said.

The October sun radiated warm across the empty football field, though the bleachers threw long shadows by the time Jeremy arrived. His right arm hung in a cast that itched in the afternoons, and under his jacket he had hidden something folded twice: the X-ray film from his wrist, taken three weeks ago at the clinic. He wanted Marisol to see it, because Marisol wanted to be a radiologist someday and because she had promised to tell him the truth about how his bones were knitting.

He found her sitting on the bottom row of the bleachers, lacing her cleats. "You brought it," she said, not looking up. Around them the goals stood with their nets sagging, and an ominous bank of gray cloud was stacking up over the far end zone, but the air was still calm.

Jeremy unfolded the film and held it up against the low sun. "Look at this. The bones glow like they're lit from inside. My skin's barely there, just a gray smudge. Why does the picture work like that?"

Marisol took the film and tilted it. "Because of the calcium. Bones show up white on an X-ray because the calcium in them absorbs more X-rays than the softer tissue around them. The soft stuff lets the rays pass through, so it hardly shows at all."

Jeremy sat down beside her and studied the white bones again, the two broken edges of his radius angled toward each other like friends about to shake hands. "So the dark gap between them," he said slowly, "that's where the rays went straight through. That's the break."

"Right. No calcium bridge yet, so no white." She pointed to a faint haze already forming at the edges of the gap. "But see that? That's new bone starting to fill in."

Jeremy's dilemma had been simple all week: the coach wanted him at practice throwing left-handed, and Jeremy wanted to sit out entirely until the arm was whole. Now he traced the haze with his finger, thinking. If white meant calcium, and calcium meant bone, then the way to know whether he was healing was to see whether that gap kept getting whiter. He couldn't watch it, not without another X-ray, but he could test the idea a different way. "They took two pictures," he said, pulling the older film from his jacket, the one from the day of the break. He laid them side by side on the metal bench. In the first, the gap yawned wide and black. In the second, it had narrowed, and the haze of white crept further along both broken edges.

"It's working," Jeremy said. "It's actually closing." He looked up, and the first cold drops of rain dotted the films, so they gathered them quickly and ran for the equipment shed, Jeremy holding both X-rays flat against his chest with his good hand, Marisol laughing and pulling her hood up as they ran.

The rain hammered the roof of Grandpa's house so hard that Naomi could barely hear herself think, which felt like a joke, since her homework was about rain. On the kitchen table she had spread out two printed climate graphs, one for Cairo, Egypt, and one for Iquitos, Peru, each with twelve bars for rainfall and a jagged line for temperature. Her assignment was due Monday, and it asked her to decide which city belonged to a tropical rainforest climate and to prove it.

The rule from her textbook sat in her notebook, copied in her own handwriting: in the Koppen climate system, a city counts as a tropical rainforest climate only if every single month averages at least 18 degrees Celsius and at least 60 millimeters of rain. Every month. One failure and the whole thing fell apart. That word "every" was starting to feel like a trap.

Cairo was easy. She ran her pencil along the rainfall bars and watched them shrink to almost nothing for months at a time. The temperature line climbed high, but the rain simply ceased to exist for half the year. Desert, no question.

Iquitos should have been easy too. The temperature line never dipped below eighteen degrees, hovering somewhere in the twenties all year. The rain bars stood tall and green, most of them well over a hundred millimeters. Then she reached August, and her stomach dropped. The bar looked small. She held the graph close to the window light. Fifty-eight millimeters. Maybe. Two millimeters short, if she was reading it right, and two millimeters was enough to kick Iquitos out of the rainforest entirely.

"That looks like a graph trying to pick a fight with you," Grandpa said, setting down a mug of cocoa.

"It's picking a fight and winning," Naomi said. "One month might be under sixty."

She refused to guess. The bars were drawn by hand on the printed sheet, thin and slightly smudged, and a shaky bar could fool anyone. So she tested it. She fetched Grandpa's clear ruler from the junk drawer and measured the tallest bar on the page, the one labeled March, which the data box said was exactly 160 millimeters. Then she measured every other bar against that scale, marking each one on scrap paper. March was 32 millimeters tall, so each printed millimeter equaled five real ones. July measured just over twelve printed millimeters. Twelve times five was sixty. She measured August twice, then a third time with the edge of the ruler flat against the paper. Sixty-one.

Every month held. Every single one cleared both hurdles, the temperature and the rain. She wrote her verdict at the top of the page, and it felt like something she had earned with a ruler and a scrap of paper. Then she added the sentence the assignment asked for, about the Koppen system and its requirements, and thought it was almost eloquent, for homework anyway.

"Verdict?" Grandpa asked, leaning over her shoulder.

"Rainforest," Naomi said, "by one millimeter of rain, and I measured it three times."

Keira slid her phone across the dinner table before Dad could start on the green beans. "Look at this dress. What color is it?" She kept her voice flat, like it was a quiz with no stakes, but her knee was bouncing under the table.

Dad squinted. "White and gold. Obviously." Mom leaned over, took the phone, tilted it, and frowned. "Blue and black. Dad, your eyes are broken." Dad laughed and pulled the phone back, holding it at arm's length. "White and gold, and I'd bet the house." Keira's little brother Dev grabbed it next and shouted "Blue and black!" before he'd even looked, which meant nothing, because Dev once swore the neighbor's cat had winked at him.

It was a photo from the internet, one her friend Priya had sent with the message "family destroyer, good luck." Keira had looked at it in her room and seen white and gold, plain as milk and honey. Then Mom had seen blue and black on the same screen. Same photo, same screen, same kitchen light. Keira felt a small, itchy suspicion that something invisible was going on, a hidden rule nobody in this family knew. She decided to test it. "Everybody close your eyes. Count to ten. Then look again."

They humored her, even Dev, though he counted wrong. When they opened their eyes, Dad still said white and gold, Mom still said blue and black, and nobody had switched. Keira tried passing the phone around the table, person to person, watching each face. Same split, every time, like the family had been cut down the middle with scissors. "Priya says this photo went everywhere back in February 2015," Keira said. "It went viral because people couldn't agree. Some people see it as blue and black and some see it as white and gold."

"Which is it really?" Dev asked, mouth full. Keira had an answer ready, because she had persevered through fifteen minutes of searching after Priya's text, wading past jokes and arguments and one site that swore the dress was magic, which she refused to be gullible enough to believe. She'd finally found a news story with the actual dress in it. "The real dress is blue and black," she said. "That's a fact. The photo came out in February 2015, and it broke the whole internet."

Mom smugly tapped her own temple. Dad stared at the screen, jaw tight, the suspense dragging out while Dev chanted "blue and black, blue and black." Then Dad set the phone down and exhaled. "Fine. I've been defeated by a picture of a dress. I saw white and gold the whole time, and I'll say it louder: white and gold." He pointed his fork at Keira. "But you saw it that way too, until you didn't. So what color do you see right now?"

Keira looked down at the dress one more time. Gold faded, white turned pale blue, and the dark bands settled into black, like something swimming up through water. She turned the screen toward her father. "I see blue and black now. Same photo you're looking at."

Ryder spent twenty minutes deciding between his conventional blue shirt and the green one nobody had ever seen him wear. He picked green, then changed his mind, then changed it back. His little sister, Nadia, watched from the doorway with a bowl of cereal. "I nominate the green one," she said. "You look like somebody who's about to do something interesting." Ryder frowned at the mirror. "It's just a dance, Nadia." But he kept the green shirt on.

The gym smelled like floor wax and punch, and the music hit him before he even got through the doors. Marcus was waiting near the refreshment table, waving him over. "You came! Okay, the eighth graders are on that side, the seventh graders claim the far wall, and Priya said she might dance with anybody who asks nicely. That's the factor that decides your whole night, basically." Ryder laughed, but his palms were sweating, and not only about Priya.

They drifted toward the stage, where two speakers taller than Mr. Hobbes stood on either side of the DJ booth. The bass thumped in Ryder's chest like a second heartbeat. After one song, his ears felt strange, a tight, fuzzy pressure, and he noticed Marcus rubbing his ear with the heel of his hand. "Yours too?" Ryder asked. Marcus nodded. "It's like they're full of static."

Ryder's phone had an app he'd opened once for a science homework option, a sound meter. He pulled it out and held it up. The number on the screen wobbled around 88 near the speakers. He remembered the chart from that same homework, the one about safe listening: exposure to 85 decibels was okay for eight hours a day, but each 3-decibel increase cut that safe time in half. So 88 wasn't just a little more than 85. It was half the safe time, four hours. And if the meter was reading low, if they were really at 91, that would be two hours. They had been standing there for maybe twenty minutes, and his ears already felt like static. "Let's test something," Ryder said. "We walk toward the far wall and check the number."

They walked. Ten steps, the number dropped to 85. Ten more, and it hovered at 82. By the seventh grade wall, it read 79, and the pressure in Ryder's ears loosened like a fist unclenching. "Whoa," Marcus said, staring at the screen. "So three points is half? That's wild. My brother stands by those speakers all night." Ryder pocketed the phone. "Not me. I plan to hear things when I'm eighty." Marcus grinned. "You're the most careful reckless person I know."

Priya appeared beside them with two cups of punch, holding one out. "You two look like scientists at a concert. What are you studying?" Ryder took the cup, and the fuzzy feeling in his ears was almost gone. "Acoustics," he said. "Want me to tell you about it?" She sipped her punch and shrugged. "Only if you tell me while we dance." Ryder set his cup down on the table and held out his hand.

Arthur had lost the same race twice, and both times the same way: a blazing first lap, then legs that felt like wet sand on the second. Today at Riverside Park he set a plan. He would run his first lap slow on purpose, hold something back, and let the second lap decide everything. The track looped past the basketball courts, so his friend Marcus timed him from the fence while a pickup game roared behind them.

On the first try, Arthur panicked. When Marcus shouted the split, Arthur was six seconds behind his usual pace, and he sped up to fix it, burning everything early again. He finished with nothing, gasping by the water fountain.

"That's the opposite of the plan," Marcus said, clicking the stopwatch. "You gotta trust the slow part."

Arthur walked it off, thinking. The problem wasn't his legs. It was something he couldn't see, the shape of the race itself, hiding underneath the numbers. If the second lap was where races were lost, then the first lap's job was only to save fuel. He could infer his pace from the split times without feeling it in his legs, because his legs lied. They always felt great early. That was the trap.

While he rested, the basketball game behind them erupted. "They keep scoring," Arthur said. The taller team ran the same few plays, and every time, one of them bellowed "Screen left!" or "Back door!" loud enough for the whole park. The other team jumped the play every single time, stealing the ball at midcourt.

Marcus waved at his cousin Dev, who played on the losing side. "Why do you guys call it out loud like that?"

"Because how else does everyone know the play?" Dev said, wiping sweat.

Arthur shrugged. "Point guards often call plays with a hand signal, a number, or a code word, so teammates know the play while the defense does not."

Dev looked at him with flat skepticism, like Arthur had suggested they play in dress shoes. But his teammate, a quiet kid in a gray hoodie, said, "He's right. My travel team does it. Two fingers means the double screen." Dev chewed on that, then walked back to the huddle. Within two possessions they ran a silent play, three raised fingers, and the kid in the gray hoodie cut hard along the diagonal from the wing to the basket, caught the pass, and laid it in. The defense never moved. Dev pumped his fist and shot a thumbs-up across the court at Arthur.

Arthur stepped back onto the track. First lap, controlled. Second lap, everything. When Marcus called the split, the number sounded slow, and every muscle begged him to surge, but he remembered that his legs were liars. He held the pace until the far curve, then let it all go. He crossed the line three seconds faster than he'd ever run, bent over, laughing at the grass between his shoes.

"Same time next Saturday," Marcus said. "And Dev wants you at the courts after."

Arthur grinned, still catching his breath. "Tell him I'll bring the signals."

The car smelled like grandma's house anyway, because the paper lantern Logan held in his lap had been hers, folded flat and tucked in her dresser for years. Outside, huge white wind turbines turned slowly above the hills, each blade sweeping past like a slow hand waving. Dad had the gearshift in neutral at the long red light, his face set and careful, and Mom kept her eyes on the map even though she already knew the way.

"You're sure it's tonight?" Dad asked.

"That's the whole point," Logan said. "It's mid-August. Obon is mid-August. That's when her spirit comes home for a visit, so if we're going to put the lantern out at her house, tonight is when it counts." He had worked this out over three days, checking the calendar twice, deciding he had to prioritize this over the soccer camp he'd already paid for. Coach Ray had not been happy. That was the cost, and Logan had agreed to pay it.

At Grandma's dark house, Dad unlocked the front door and Logan went straight for the kitchen drawer where she kept her old datebooks. He wanted proof, some sign she had done this herself. The summer before she died, in her careful handwriting, was one word: Obon. But it was written in July, not August, and in the datebook from the year before, July again.

"July," he said out loud, feeling the floor tilt under the plan he'd built. "Most places do it in mid-August, but her hometown was one of the places that did it in July. All along, I was a month off. I missed it. I missed it for this year."

Mom crouched beside him. "You didn't miss her," she said. "You just missed the date."

So the lantern went up anyway. Logan unfolded it on the porch steps, and Dad lit the small candle inside, cupping the flame against the breeze coming off the hills. The paper glowed warm orange, and somewhere down the valley one of the turbines caught the last sunlight and flashed. It was the wrong week, maybe even the wrong month, and the house behind them was empty and would be sold by fall.

"Want to say something?" Dad asked.

Logan thought about it, then shook his head. "She'd rather hear the game anyway." So he sat on the steps and told the lantern, quietly, how the team had done without him this week, and how he'd kind of ruined a penalty kick, and how she would have laughed.

The candle fluttered, then steadied.

Eleanor had five dollars and one goal: the box of old comic books on the far table. She had circled the garage sale twice already, pretending to look at lampshades, because the man next to her kept pulling comics out one at a time and reading them. When he finally wandered off toward the record crates, she darted in and grabbed the box, only to hear the seller say, "Those are three dollars each now."

"Each?" Eleanor said. "The sign says a dollar."

The seller shrugged and flipped the cardboard sign over, where a new price was written in fresh marker. "That was before four people asked about them in the last half hour. Only two full boxes left. Somebody just offered to buy a whole box." His prices were volatile, changing whenever the crowd around a table thickened or thinned, and Eleanor had watched a stack of encyclopedias drop from ten dollars to two when nobody touched it for an hour.

She was still holding the box when she noticed a thin old book at the bottom, wedged under the comics. The cover was cracked leather, and inside, in faded ink, someone had copied a passage. It began: "Nothing is more useful than water, yet it will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal." Eleanor read it twice. She carried the book to the seller. "What is this?"

"'The Wealth of Nations'," he said. "Published in 1776. My grandfather acquired it at an estate sale, and it's the one thing here I'm not discounting."

Eleanor looked at the sentence again. Water was the most useful thing there was, and it cost almost nothing, while a tiny diamond could buy piles of stuff. She looked at the tables around her: the comics, scarce and fought over, climbing in price; a whole driveway of drinking glasses, dozens of them, marked down to a quarter. She thought of the treaty of comic collectors who had apparently agreed, without ever meeting, that these particular issues mattered. Something invisible was setting every price on this lawn, something she couldn't see but could almost touch now.

"I'll give you my five dollars for this book and two comics," she said, holding her breath.

The seller studied her, then the thinning crowd, and said, "Four dollars, because it's almost noon and you're the only one who asked about that book all morning."

Eleanor counted out the bills, tucked the book under her arm, and walked home reading as she went.

Claire dragged the cardboard box across the garage floor and set it under the workbench light, where the bulb swung a little every time the wind pushed at the door. Her little brother Marcus followed her in, carrying a printout of the periodic table that he had flattened against his chest like a treasure map.

"I already decided," Claire said. "Carbon. Not gold, not oxygen, carbon."

"Because it's in pencils?" Marcus asked.

"Because Mrs. Ruiz said the model has to be an element we can explain, and I can explain carbon." She pulled a shoebox of Ping-Pong balls from the shelf, then a hot glue gun she wasn't supposed to use without asking, which she had decided was a compromise between asking and not asking, since Dad was in the driveway and could see her through the open door.

Marcus spread the periodic table on the hood of the lawnmower and squinted at it. "This thing has letters and numbers all mixed up. C, and then a little six above it. What's the six?"

"That's the atomic number." Claire said it quickly, then stopped. She had said the words before she had really thought about them, the way you can recite something and still not own it. She took the paper from him and looked at the small six sitting above the C. "Every carbon atom has exactly six protons," she said slowly. "That's what it's counting. Protons, in the nucleus."

"So the number tells you the protons."

"That's the whole point of it." She tested the idea, because reciting wasn't the same as knowing. She moved her finger two boxes to the right, to oxygen, and its little eight. "So oxygen has eight protons. Every single one. In every oxygen atom anywhere." She looked up. "That's actually wild. Nobody can see a proton. Nobody's ever going to hold one. But they counted them anyway, and the number's just sitting there on a chart in a garage."

"You're making six of them," Marcus said, holding up the printout again. "For carbon. Six balls."

She had been planning to use all the Ping-Pong balls and glue a big swirling electron cloud around the outside, something impressive and lopsided. Six protons meant building a nucleus first, a tight little knot in the middle, and that was harder to make look good. "I wanted the cloud to be the big part," she said.

"So make the nucleus the big part."

Claire looked at the six balls he had already counted out and lined up on the workbench, waiting. It was a plausible plan, actually, better than hers, though she wasn't going to say that out loud. She plugged in the glue gun and held the first two balls together until the glue grabbed.

"Hand me number three," she said, and Marcus did.

The nature trail behind the school had a wooden bench near the creek, and that was where Isla set up the field kit her science teacher lent her: a pocket microscope, a razor blade, a dropper of iodine, and an onion she had carried in her backpack all morning. Her assignment was due Monday. She had to peel a thin layer of onion skin, stain it, and draw the cells with the wall, the membrane, and the nucleus labeled. She could have done it in the lab after school on Friday, but she had chosen the trail instead, the way she had chosen a solo hike last summer instead of going with her friends. She still wasn't sure that had been the right call, but this one felt like it might be.

Her friend Marisol found her there, as she somehow always did. "You really brought an onion on a nature walk," Marisol said, sitting down on the bench without waiting for an invitation. Isla peeled a translucent strip of skin from the onion's fleshy layer, laid it on the slide, and added a single drop of iodine. Under the pocket microscope, the cells appeared like pale bricks in a wall, each one bordered and neat. She began to draw them in her notebook, labeling the thick outer wall first, then the thin membrane pressed just inside it. The nucleus showed up as a darker dot once the stain soaked in, and she marked that too.

"That's good," Marisol said, looking over her shoulder at the finished drawing. Then she flipped back a page and stopped at Isla's comparison chart from last week's homework. "Wait. You wrote mitochondria as animal-only." Isla's pencil hovered, hesitant, over the chart. She had been proud of that chart. She remembered arguing her logic at the dinner table: animals eat food, so animal cells would need something to release energy from it, and plants make their own food, so they wouldn't need any such thing. At the time the reasoning had seemed airtight.

"Plants have mitochondria too," Marisol said. "Both plant and animal cells have them. They release energy from food." Isla frowned at her drawing of the brick-shaped cells. "But plants make their own food," she said. "Yeah," Marisol said, shrugging. "They still need mitochondria anyway." Isla turned back to the microscope and looked again at the onion cells, imagining the tiny structures she could not see at this magnification, working away inside a layer of skin thinner than paper. She couldn't justify leaving the chart the way it was. She crossed out the animal-only box and rewrote the column.

"It's kind of irony," she said slowly, "that the plant makes its own food and still needs the thing that gets energy out of it." Marisol raised an eyebrow. "That's not really how you use that word." "It's close enough," Isla said, and bent over the slide again, because the light had shifted and a row of nuclei had come into view, each dark dot sitting inside its cell like a seed inside a translucent fruit. She drew them one by one, pressing hard enough that the pencil nearly went through the page.

Theo's problem was the blank index card on his desk. On Friday, Mr. Ruiz would pick three students to explain, out loud and in full sentences, how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War, and Theo had exactly nothing written down.

He flipped back through his notebook to the Oregon Trail unit, where he and Priya had read a settler's diary last month. They had made two columns on the whiteboard, arguing the whole time about which reason went where. "Crops failing, that pushes them out of Missouri," Priya had said. "Free land in Oregon pulls them west." Their teacher had stood back and let them fight it out, which Theo now appreciated, since he remembered every word. Push factors drive people away from home, he thought, and pull factors attract them to a new place. The diary family had both: a failing farm behind them and a promise ahead of them.

So what if a whole country could work like that? He tried it. After the treaty, Germany had crushing reparations, lost territory, and a military shrunk to almost nothing. Those pushed Germans away from their own government, away from the Weimar Republic that had signed the paper. And something pulled them too: Hitler promising jobs, pride, and someone to blame. Theo wrote it out and stared at it. It actually held together.

On Thursday he tested it at lunch, because Priya was the toughest audience he knew. "Pretend I'm clueless," he said, unwrapping his sandwich. "Explain the war."

"Okay. The treaty pushed Germans, the way bad crops push settlers. Then somebody offered them a new home, basically, and they went." He slid the notebook across. "Push factors and pull factors, but for a country instead of one family."

Priya chewed slowly, which was her thinking face. "So the treaty didn't cause the war by itself," she said. "It made people desperate enough to follow anyone pointing at a door." She tapped the page. "You should say the reparations were proportional to what Germany could actually pay. It couldn't. That's your push."

"You just gave a whole speech," Theo said.

"I delegated the thinking to you first. You did the work." She handed the notebook back. "Also your handwriting looks like a spider fell in ink."

Friday came. Mr. Ruiz paced the rows, and when he reached Theo's desk he paused. "Theo. Go."

Theo took a breath and started with the diary family leaving Missouri, then widened the lens until the family was a nation of millions, pushed by the treaty's terms and pulled by a voice offering restoration. When he finished, the room was quiet for a second.

Mr. Ruiz nodded once. "That's the clearest version I've heard today." Then he moved on down the row, and Theo drew a small spider on the corner of his index card.

Peyton had until five o'clock tomorrow to submit a short story to the library's summer contest, and she had promised herself she would not postpone it again. She spread her notebook across the table by the window, where her friend Marcus was already reading comic books.

"Read my opening," she said. "It has dialogue, but I don't know if I did the punctuation right." She read aloud: "'This beach is nice,' said the grandmother. 'It was a good trip,' said Jules." Marcus squinted at the page. "The commas are in the right place," he said. "But I can't see the beach. Or the trip. What was nice about it?"

Peyton frowned. Something about his question tugged at her memory. Last spring, her grandmother had come over with a bag of postcards, and when Peyton said her class trip had been interesting, her grandmother had leaned forward and asked what exactly was interesting about it. Peyton had stammered something about the bus and then, finally, described the moment a hawk had landed on the fence outside the planetarium and stared at them through the glass while everyone was still arguing about lunch. Her grandmother had laughed and said she could see the whole thing, hawk and all. "Nice" had shown her nothing; the hawk had shown her everything.

"So the vague ones," Peyton said slowly, tapping her pencil, "words like nice, good, interesting. They give me my opinion without showing anything." Marcus nodded. "Right. A concrete detail lets me picture it and judge for myself." She crossed out "nice" and wrote, "The grandmother picked up a wet feather and rolled it between her fingers." Then she crossed out "good trip" and wrote that Jules had counted forty-one dead jellyfish on the sand and kept the number in his head like a prize.

Now she needed a climax, the moment everything turned. She had been avoiding it because it felt ambiguous, like she couldn't tell what her story was really about. "Maybe that's the problem," Marcus said. "The climax has to be the moment it turns. Yours is just people talking on a beach forever."

They formed an alliance: Marcus would read every page out loud, and Peyton would not defend anything until he finished. When he read the jellyfish line, he stopped. "The grandmother should find one that's still alive," he said. "Right there. That's your turn." Peyton wrote it: the grandmother kneels, the jellyfish pulses once against her palm, and Jules has to decide whether to leave it for the tide.

At four the next day, she handed the printed pages to the librarian at the front desk, one minute before the deadline. "First entry this year," the librarian said, stamping the corner. Peyton smiled, took back her copy, and on the way out she stopped to look through the window at the parking lot, where a crow was standing on the hood of a silver car, watching the doors like it was waiting for someone.

Olivia had been postponing the question all afternoon, but at three o'clock it caught up with her: what do you bring to dinner at a house where you don't know the rules? Her new friend Nadia had invited her over for her birthday, and Nadia's family had moved to town from Malaysia only two months ago. Olivia's own family was eccentric enough that her grandmother kissed strangers on both cheeks and refused to let anyone start eating before a toast, so she knew that every household ran on its own invisible rules. She just couldn't see these ones yet.

She brought a small box of chocolates, wrapped hastily in gold paper, and stood on the porch rehearsing a greeting. When Nadia's father opened the door, he smiled and offered his right hand. Olivia shook it and passed him the gift, also with her right hand, mostly because that was the hand she used for everything. He accepted it the same way, thanked her warmly, and said, "In Malaysia, where we come from, we give and receive with the right hand, as a sign of respect."

In the dining room, Olivia noticed a pattern. Every dish was passed right hand to right hand, and when Nadia's little brother reached across the table with his left, Nadia caught his wrist and switched it for him without a word. Olivia filed that away and watched harder. Nobody said anything about it. The rule was quiet, like her grandmother's toast.

Then the rice arrived, and Olivia realized she had been holding her fork in her left hand all evening, the way her uncle had taught her, scooping with the spoon on the right. Her stomach dropped. Had she been rude for the last twenty minutes without knowing? She considered the probability that no one had noticed and decided it was low, because Nadia's grandmother kept glancing at her plate. Olivia had a simple idea: she would test it. She set the fork down, picked up the spoon with her right hand alone, and took the next bite.

Nadia's grandmother smiled at her, a real smile with crinkled eyes, and pushed the chicken dish toward her side of the table. Olivia reached out with her right hand and served herself. Across the table, Nadia gave her a tiny nod.

After dinner, Nadia pulled her into the kitchen and whispered, "Grandma says you have good manners. She wants to know if you'll come for Hari Raya in the spring."

"Only if you come to my grandmother's house first," Olivia said. "She has rules too. There's a toast, and there's a zero percent chance of escaping it."

"Deal," said Nadia, and handed her the last chocolate from the box, with her right hand.

The clock above the whiteboard read 2:45, and Sadie's rice still needed twelve minutes, the curry eight, and the flatbread, according to her recipe card, exactly four minutes per side. She wrote the numbers in the margin of her notebook and worked backward from 3:15, when Mr. Okafor would ring the bell and expect all three dishes on the table, hot, at the same time. If she started the flatbread last, it would come off the pan just as the curry finished, but the rice would have to go on the burner before anything else. She filled the pot, set it on high, and told herself that timing was just math with consequences.

At the next station, Marcus was draining a pot of pasta over the sink, steam rolling up toward the vent fan. "Stop!" Sadie said, almost knocking over the salt container as she leaned across the aisle. "Save some of that water. A cup."

Marcus stared at her like she had accused him of a crime. "It's pasta water. It's garbage."

"It's not. It's starchy. The pasta lets starch out into the water while it cooks, and if you splash a bit of that into your sauce, the sauce gets thicker and sticks to the noodles instead of pooling at the bottom of the bowl." She wasn't sure where she had read it, some cooking blog at two in the morning, but she was sure of it the way she was sure seven times eight was fifty-six.

Marcus wanted the blue ribbon for Best Sauce at the class showcase on Friday more than he wanted recess, and his sauce was currently thin and watery, sliding off a test noodle like rain off a leaf. He looked at the cloudy cup Sadie had scooped from the pot, then at his saucepan, then back at the cup. "Fine. But if it's gross, that's on you."

He poured a splash in and stirred. The sauce turned glossy and began to cling, coating the spoon the way nectar coats a spoon, slow and heavy. Marcus held the spoon up to the light and actually grinned. "It's clinging," he said. "It's actually clinging."

Sadie turned back to her own station, where the rice was boiling and the curry needed its coconut milk now. The flatbread dough was still a soft ball under a damp towel, waiting its turn. It was probable that something would still go wrong; her last attempt at this had produced gummy rice and cold curry, and the memory of it sat in her stomach like a stone. But she had her timeline written down, and the pot was already bubbling, and Marcus was spooning sauce over noodles at the next table like he'd discovered treasure. She pinched off a round of dough, patted it flat, and dropped it onto the hot pan, where it puffed up in one small, perfect bubble.

Nolan pushed the shopping cart past the cereal, doing math in his head. Two hundred forty dollars. That was what he had in his savings account, and the blue bike in Mr. Herrera's window cost three hundred ninety-nine. "If I add five dollars a week," he muttered, "that's... a lot of weeks."

"Did you say weeks?" his dad asked, tossing in a bag of rice. "Because I was going to tell you about years. The bank pays you interest for keeping money there. Simple interest is a slice of your original amount every year. Compound interest is a slice of your original amount plus all the interest you've already earned. It grows on itself."

"Show me," Nolan said, so at the dairy aisle his dad pulled a receipt from his pocket and flipped it to the blank side. He wrote out five years of simple interest on two hundred forty dollars, then five years of compound, keeping the rate the same. By year five the compound column pulled ahead, and by year ten the gap looked like a small canyon. Nolan stared at the numbers. "So if I just leave it alone, the money does extra work without me?" "That's the idea," his dad said. "Patience pays, and it pays more every year it waits."

In the juice aisle they ran into Priya from Nolan's class, who looked like a plague had swept through her lemonade stand, which in a way it had. "Strawberry lemonade disaster," she groaned. "We charged three dollars a cup because the strawberries cost so much. Everybody wanted the regular lemonade at one dollar. We're stuck with four jugs of strawberry nobody will buy."

Nolan thought about the paper in his dad's pocket, about numbers lined up in columns. High price, lots left over. "So if you charge less," he said slowly, "more people will actually buy it, and you won't be swimming in strawberry." Priya frowned. "But we paid a lot for the strawberries." "But you'll end up with money instead of jugs," Nolan said. "Right now the high price is leaving you with stuff nobody wants." Priya tested it that weekend. At two dollars a cup, the strawberry lemonade sold out by Saturday afternoon. She texted Nolan a photo of an empty cooler with the words "You were right, money boy."

The next Saturday, Nolan stood in the cereal aisle again, this time holding a pencil and the back of a receipt. He wrote his two hundred forty dollars at the top, then added his five dollars a week, then added the little extra the bank would pay on the growing pile, year after year. Somewhere around the third column he grinned. His dad leaned over. "Calculating the bike fund?" "Calculating the bike fund, the second bike fund, and the fund after that," Nolan said, and boxed the final number with a flourish. "Move over, compound interest. You've got company."

Marcus's basement smelled like lizard and old carpet, and his gecko, Godzilla, watched from his tank while the two boys hunched over a laptop on the ping-pong table. Tyler had come over to learn HTML, but Marcus had other plans. "I already built the page," Marcus said, spinning the laptop around. "It's about Godzilla. I just need the heading centred and the prime game to actually work. Then I can show it to Ava. She thinks I'm, like, an influential tech genius. I want to keep it that way."

Tyler leaned in. The heading "GODZILLA: REPTILE OF THE BASEMENT" sat stuck in the corner of the page, and below it was a box where you typed a number and the page told you if it was prime. Tyler typed 97 and pressed the button. The page froze. The cursor spun. Godzilla stared, unblinking, a true carnivore waiting for something to move. "It does that on big numbers," Marcus admitted. "Ava's going to think my page is broken. This could demolish my whole reputation."

Tyler added text-align: centre to the heading first, because that part he actually knew, and watched the title glide to the middle. Then he turned to the prime checker. Marcus's code tested every number from 2 up to the one you typed, one at a time, asking each, "Do you divide it evenly?" On a huge number that was millions of questions. Tyler traced the code with his finger, line by line, and noticed something odd: right after the code checked whether the number was divisible by 2, it kept testing 4, then 6, then 8, all the even ones, all the way up.

He had a guess, but he wanted proof before he said anything out loud. In a new file he tried 15 with only the odd tests, 3, 5, 7, 9, and it still said not prime, correctly, because 3 caught it. He tried 21, 35, 49. All found, all by odd divisors. He could not make it fail. "Skip the evens," he said finally, deleting half the checks. "After checking whether a number is divisible by 2, you only need to test odd divisors. An odd number can never be divided evenly by an even one." Marcus squinted at the screen. "That's it? That's the whole trick?" "Run it."

Marcus typed 999,983 and pressed the button, and both boys held their breath, because if the page froze now, everything was over. The answer appeared before Godzilla could even blink. Prime. The heading beamed from the centre of the screen like a trophy. Marcus grabbed his phone to text Ava, then stopped, staring at the instant result. "It's done already? But she loved watching it think." He typed 999,983 again, slower this time, and waited for a freeze that never came.

Leo knelt on the muddy bank and peeled a papery layer off the onion he had smuggled from his mother's kitchen. "The trick is getting a piece thin enough for light to pass through," he said, mostly to himself, because thin things were the whole point of today.

Maya waded close to the edge and scooped pond water into a jar. She had agreed to accompany him on the condition that they look at pond creatures too, so the jar went into her backpack next to the microscope Leo's uncle had lent him. Back at the picnic table, Leo dropped the onion skin onto a slide, added one drop of iodine, and pressed the cover glass down with his thumb. Then he cranked the microscope's knob with vigorous little turns, too fast, and the image blurred past focus twice before a lattice of brick-like cells swam into view.

"There," Maya said, leaning in. "Draw it before you touch anything."

He drew fast, then slowed down. The cell walls showed as the rigid outer edges of every brick. He remembered the membrane as a thin line just inside the wall, hugging it like a second skin. But the nucleus, the dark blob his worksheet wanted labeled, was nowhere obvious. He tested a simple idea: if the iodine stain made some structures darker, maybe he had not used enough. He made a second slide with two drops instead of one. The consequence was a purplish blob in each cell, plain as a thumbprint. He labeled all three parts and sat back, feeling like he had unlocked something.

"So the worksheet says every food chain starts with the sun," Maya said, squinting at the jar of pond water, where green specks clung to the glass. "The algae in here make food from sunlight, the water fleas eat them, and so on. Sunlight first, always."

"That's what I thought too," Leo said. "Then my sister watched this documentary." He told her what it said: in 1977, scientists in a submersible named Alvin found deep-sea vent communities down in total darkness, and the food chains there start with bacteria that use chemicals from the vents, not sunlight.

Maya frowned at the jar. "So if we sealed this in a dark box, everything would die. But down there, it wouldn't."

"It's like the vents have their own starting point," Leo said. He held the slide up to the light anyway, where the little stained cells glowed faintly purple. "Same rule, different first step."

Maya tilted the jar so the green specks caught the sun. "Draw them next," she said, "before they swim away."

The sign at Miller's Gas Station said REGULAR $3.49, but the handwritten tape over it said $4.25, and the line of cars stretched past the car wash. Kate stood by the ice freezer with her bike helmet under one arm, watching her neighbor Mr. Alvarez feed the pump like it might run out any second. She had only stopped for a bottle of water, but the whole station felt like a swarm.

"They're saying the refinery in Baytown might shut down," Mr. Alvarez told her, waving his receipt. "Everybody fills up at once, and boom, the price jumps. Scarce and wanted, that's all it takes."

"Then why is the water still a dollar?" Kate asked. He shrugged toward the rack, which was crammed with bottles, rows and rows of them. Plenty of something, cheap price. Scarce something, high price. She turned that over all the way home, because it reminded her of something, and the something made her stomach hurt.

At school, everyone had been trading Stellarbeast cards since September. Kate owned the rarest one, a Moonfang Holo that Tavo had offered forty cards for in December, back when the hallway trades got so loud that Mrs. Okonkwo had to move desks to obstruct the flow of kids crowding around the card tables. Kate had almost said yes that day, but she'd been impulsive before and regretted it, so she held out. In January, Tavo offered sixty. Moonfang Holos were barely circulating anymore; nobody would trade theirs away. It was like a principle she couldn't quite name, something invisible pushing the numbers up and up.

That night she looked it up for a history project and found a strange page about the Dutch Republic, where prices for rare tulip bulbs had soared in the winter of 1636 to 1637. People trading bulbs in taverns, paying fortunes for a single flower. Then the page said the whole thing collapsed in February 1637, when buyers stopped showing up. Kate read it twice. Nobody had banned tulips. Nobody had burned the bulbs. The buyers had just stopped coming, and that was enough.

The next morning she found Tavo by the gym and made her offer before she could lose her nerve. "Forty cards, today, for the Moonfang." Tavo stared at her like she was a step behind. "Nobody's trading those anymore. Devon's selling his for ten. Dax gave his away yesterday." Behind him, Kate could see the corner where the trading crowd used to gather. Two kids sat there now, doing homework. She traded anyway, took Tavo's best twenty for it, and put the Moonfang in her backpack next to her history notes, where the doomed tulips sat on their printed page, beautiful and worthless at exactly the same moment. On the way out, she passed the vending machine, still selling water for a dollar.

Ryder had watched Mrs. Okafor's apartment exactly twice before, and both times the worst thing that happened was a cat knocking a plant off the sill. Tonight was different. Tonight he was alone with Theo, who was two, and Theo had just produced a smell that no two-year-old should be able to produce.

Ryder laid out the changing mat on the living room rug while Theo's toy trucks continued to orbit the coffee table, as if nothing catastrophic had occurred. The diaper change itself went worse than any video had promised. By the end, Ryder had wipes stuck to his elbow and Theo was laughing like a hyena.

"Okay, buddy," Ryder said, carrying Theo toward the kitchen, which marked the frontier between the disaster zone of the rug and the place where lunch was supposed to happen. He set Theo in the high chair, then looked down at his own hands. He remembered his mother drilling it into him before his little cousin's birthday party: after a diaper change and before touching food, you scrub with soap for at least twenty seconds. Not a rinse. A scrub.

He turned on the tap and started humming the chorus of Theo's favorite song, the one about the shark family. Once through wasn't enough, he decided, so he hummed it twice, working the soap between his fingers and around his thumbs the whole time. Theo kicked his feet and shrieked the melody along with him.

Then Ryder noticed something. Theo had gone quiet, and his small fists were clenched around the tray of the high chair. His face was doing the thing right before crying, the trembling chin. Ryder had been sure the problem was hunger, but Theo wasn't acting hungry. He was staring past Ryder's shoulder, toward the living room.

Ryder followed his gaze. The changing mat still lay open on the rug, and beside it sat the empty wipes container, rocking slightly. The cat from downstairs had slipped in through the balcony door Ryder had left cracked for air, and it was now crouched over the mat like a dragon guarding treasure.

"Ah," Ryder said. "That's your spot, huh."

He dried his hands, shooed the cat out, folded the mat away, and slid it into the diaper bag, zipping it shut. When he turned around, Theo's chin had stopped trembling. Ryder washed up one more time, humming the song through twice again, and then sliced a banana and spread toast with the exact jam Theo pointed to.

Theo ate like a woodchipper. Ryder sank onto a kitchen chair and watched him go.

"You're going to be asleep by seven," Ryder told him.

Theo answered by putting a banana slice on his own nose.

Nathaniel spread the wires across the kitchen table and counted them twice. Copper, nichrome, and the steel paperclip he had straightened that morning, each one meant to carry current to the same small bulb. The science fair was Thursday, and his data sheet was a mess.

He clipped the copper wire to the battery holder, and the bulb glowed a steady yellow. He wrote down "bright." Then he swapped in the steel wire and a different bulb, because the first one had rolled off the table and he could not find it. The new bulb glowed pale and dim. He wrote "dim" and stared at it. Steel should have been worse than copper, but was the dimness the wire, or the other bulb? He had no way to know. He slammed the notebook shut, and his little sister Maya looked up from her cereal.

"You broke it already?"

"No. I don't know what I measured." He unrolled the crumpled handout from his back pocket and smoothed it flat. Maya leaned over her bowl and read the top line out loud. "Independent variable, the one thing you change on purpose. Dependent variable, what you measure to see the effect."

Nathaniel read it again, lips moving. He had changed two things. The wire and the bulb. That was the problem, sitting there in his own handwriting. "I changed the wire on purpose," he said slowly, "but I also changed the bulb by accident. So the brightness doesn't tell me anything about the wire."

"That's what you get for using my bulbs without asking."

He ignored her. The heater had been running all morning and the air in the kitchen felt arid enough to make the tape crackle when he peeled it off the table, but he kept working. He needed one bulb, the same bulb, every single trial. He searched under the table, found the runaway bulb in the shadow of the chair leg, and taped it down so it could not escape again. Copper went in. Bright. Steel went in, same bulb, same battery. The glow weakened to a dull orange, and this time the difference had to be the wire, because nothing else had moved.

For the last test he used the knife to strip the insulation and expose an inch of the copper, then the steel, then the nichrome, laying the bare metal in a neat row so the clips would touch clean conductor every time. Same battery. Same bulb. Three trials, three honest numbers. Maya slid her empty bowl toward him.

"You still owe me a bulb."

Taylor's motivation for spending her Saturday behind Mr. Alvarez's pasta stand was simple: he had agreed to teach her to cook, and her mother had agreed to stop burning water if someone else took over. The lesson started with onions. "Curl your fingers like a claw," Mr. Alvarez said, tapping her knuckles. "The blade rides against your knuckles, and your fingertips stay out of trouble." Taylor curled, chopped, and produced something closer to onion gravel than onion pieces, but all ten fingers survived, which she counted as a win. She could feel herself begin to perspire under the market canopy, and she blamed the onions entirely.

Two stalls down, Rosa from Rosa's Oven was staring into her display case with the expression of someone whose oven had betrayed her. "Same thing every week," she told a customer. "The tops of my muffins come out golden brown and the insides stay pale. I don't touch the recipe."

Taylor kept chopping, but her mind snagged on it. Golden tops, pale insides. Same batter, same oven, two different results. What was different between the top of a muffin and the middle of one? She turned a cup of Rosa's muffin over in her head while her hands worked the claw grip through a second onion. The top was the part the heat hit first and hardest, the part with no paper wrapper between it and the air. The middle was protected, buried in itself.

She had a theory, and theories needed testing. On her break she bought two of Rosa's muffins, and she borrowed a strip of foil. She wrapped the top of one muffin, set both on a tray in the corner of Mr. Alvarez's little pizza oven, and waited, watching through the glass. After ten minutes she pulled them out. The unwrapped muffin's top had gone golden brown again. The wrapped one's top stayed pale, while the sides that peeked out from under the foil had browned instead. So it was the heat hitting the surface directly, doing something to whatever was in the batter at that surface. She remembered Mr. Alvarez grumbling last week about his bread crust. "Sugars and proteins," he'd said, cutting a distinct line through the crust with his knife. "They react in the heat. That's the Maillard reaction."

Taylor carried the two muffins to Rosa's stall and laid them side by side. "Your recipe's fine," she said. "The tops turn golden brown because the sugars and proteins react in the heat. The insides stay pale because they never get hot enough at the surface." Rosa looked at the pale-topped muffin, then at Taylor, then shouted over three stalls, "Mr. Alvarez! Your apprentice solved my case!"

Mr. Alvarez waved his chef's knife in salute. "Good. Now get back here. You're on onions until you can make them distinct cubes instead of gravel."

Taylor returned to the cutting board, curled her claw, and discovered that onions, at least, had not gotten any easier while she was busy being a detective. She chopped. The pile looked exactly like gravel.

Nicolas stabbed at his broccoli while his older sister Dani scrolled through her phone at the other end of the table. "Mom," she said, "Keisha says Priya's at the shoe store on Maple, the one by the fountain. Can we go after dinner?" Their mom frowned. "How does Keisha know that? Did Priya text her?" Dani shrugged. "She just knows." Nicolas put his fork down. That was the second time this week. Last Saturday, Keisha had known he was at the arcade the moment he walked in, and when he'd asked how, she'd only laughed and said, "Check your map."

He hadn't checked. It had seemed like a joke, and anyway the smell of pizza and the sound of the pinball machines had distracted him before he could think it through. But now the memory plagued him, circling back like a mosquito he kept failing to swat. He looked around the dinner table, at the steam curling off the mashed potatoes and the clink of Dani's fork against her plate, and decided he was done guessing. He had a phone in his pocket, and a test would take thirty seconds.

"Can I be excused for a sec?" he asked. In the hallway he opened the app and found the little map. There was the mall, drawn in simple shapes, and there was a tiny version of Priya's face glowing on the map, right on top of the shoe store by the fountain. It even moved, a small dot drifting toward the corner of the store, as if she were browsing. The map was, in effect, the equivalent of a window that looked directly into everyone's afternoon, except the window worked from anywhere, and it never shut.

He walked back to the table slowly. "Dani, does Keisha see all her friends like that? On a map?" Dani looked up, surprised he'd figured it out. "It's called Snap Map," she said. "Everyone's on it, Nicky. It shows where people are right now." Nicolas sat down, his chair scraping the floor. "Right now, right now? Like, if I went to the park, people would see me at the park?" "Well, your friends would," Dani said, as if this were the most ordinary thing in the world.

Nicolas thought about how many strangers could end up seeing a map like that if one friend shared it with another, and then another, a chain he couldn't see but could now picture clearly. The trouble wasn't one thing he could point to; it was the invisible pattern underneath, and ignoring it would only hinder him from fixing it. He took out his phone again, right there between the potatoes and the broccoli, and opened the settings, his thumb hovering over the map.

"What are you doing?" Dani asked.

"Going ghost," Nicolas said, and tapped the button.

The lights went out at seven, right in the middle of Emilia's homework, and the living room went dark except for the two candles her mother found under the sink. Emilia moved her history notes to the coffee table and tried to keep working by candlelight, but her mind kept drifting to the kitchen. The freezer. She and her brother had eaten through half the frozen food that week because they were too lazy to shop, and now the whole street was black and the fridge wasn't humming anymore.

"Mom, how long is this going to last?" she asked. Her mother, on the couch with her phone held up to the window, shook her head.

"The power company says tomorrow evening at the earliest."

Tomorrow evening. Emilia counted on her fingers. If the outage ended at six tomorrow, that would be almost twenty-three hours from now. She opened her notebook and tried to classify the situation like a math problem: known things, unknown things, things she could test. The known thing was the freezer, sitting in the dark kitchen with its door shut. The unknown thing was how long the food inside could survive.

She remembered a leaflet that had come taped to the freezer years ago, before they owned it, something the previous owners had left in the drawer. She dug through the kitchen junk drawer while her candle dripped onto a saucer, and found the paper folded behind the takeout menus. It said a full freezer holds a safe temperature for about forty-eight hours without power, and a half-full one for about twenty-four hours, if the door stays closed. Twenty-four hours. Her arithmetic from a minute ago had been almost exactly right, and only if nobody opened that door.

Emilia called her family into the kitchen. "We can't open the freezer until tomorrow evening," she said. "Half full, it's only good for about a day. If it were packed full it would be two days, but we ate everything."

Her brother groaned. "The frozen dumplings are in there."

"And they'll still be fine tomorrow at six if you don't stand there with the door open staring at them." She took a roll of masking tape from the drawer and ran a strip across the freezer door and down the side of the cabinet, sealing it shut like crime-scene tape. Then she wrote on the tape with a marker: DO NOT OPEN UNTIL TOMORROW EVENING. Her brother signed his initials under it to make it official, sulking, and their mother wrote hers too.

They went back to the living room, and Emilia read her history notes out loud by candlelight while her brother listened, sprawled on the rug in his synthetic fleece jacket because the house was cooling down. They were supposed to be studying the lives of medieval peasants, who got along without electricity their whole lives, and her brother pointed out that at least the peasants hadn't had a freezer full of dumplings to worry about. Emilia snorted and turned the page, and outside the window the street stayed dark all the way to the corner.

Hannah slid her essay prompt across the library table so Marcus could see it. "Argue for or against a change at our school," she read aloud, "using a thesis and three supporting points. Draft due Friday." The deadline felt imminent, and she had nothing.

"Easy," Marcus said. "Write that we should have a hockey team. Thesis: our school has no hockey team."

Hannah wrote it down. Then she stared at it. "Marcus, everyone knows we don't have one. Nobody's going to argue with that."

"So? It's true."

She flipped to the page their writing club packet had open on the table, the one about thesis statements. She read it twice, then a third time, because something in it kept snagging. A strong thesis makes a claim a reasonable person could disagree with. A statement nobody would dispute, like a plain fact, gives an essay nothing to argue.

"That's the problem," she said slowly. "My thesis is just a fact. There's no argument in it. If nobody could disagree, what am I even defending?"

Marcus shrugged. "So make it something people would fight about."

She tapped her pencil against the table, thinking through the hallway outside the library, the water fountain by the gym that had been shut off since October with a plastic bag taped over the valve. Students had started saying a repair was coming, but it never came. She tested the idea out loud. "Our school should spend its facilities budget fixing the gym water fountain before buying new bleachers."

"Disagree," Marcus said immediately. "Bleachers seat everybody. One fountain is one fountain."

Hannah grinned and started listing points on a fresh page. She abandoned the hockey idea completely, crossing it out so hard the pencil tore a little. Point one: the fountain by the gym is the only water source on that side of the building. Point two: repairs cost less than bleachers. Point three: attendance in PE might drop when students leave class just to get water. She wrote fast, filling the outline before she could lose the thread.

At the next club meeting, their advisor had them read thesis statements aloud. When it was Hannah's turn, she said, "Our school should fix the gym water fountain before buying new bleachers."

Mrs. Okafor raised an eyebrow. "I'd push back on that. The bleachers are a safety issue."

"Good," Hannah said. "That means I have something to argue."

Later, Hannah caught Marcus by the lockers and handed him her outline. "Read point two," she said. "I found the repair estimate from last year's newsletter."

Marcus read it and nodded slowly. "Okay. That's actually pretty convincing."

"Convincing enough that you'd still disagree?"

He zipped his backpack. "Ask me Friday."

By ten in the morning, Hannah had sold two paperbacks and a single mitten, and the sun on the driveway made her perspire through the back of her shirt. Her card table held everything she owned that she could bear to part with: old sunglasses, a stack of comics, a lava lamp glowing a toxic shade of green, and one volume of poetry with a cracked spine. Across the driveway, at the neighbors' table, a crowd had formed, because Mrs. Delgado had only six pairs of vintage sunglasses left and had just raised the price from three dollars to eight.

"Eight dollars?" a woman muttered, putting a pair down. "It's just sunglasses." One by one, the buyers drifted away from Mrs. Delgado's table, and then, to Hannah's astonishment, they drifted to hers. A man picked up her two-dollar sunglasses and turned them over. "Same job, way cheaper," he said, and bought both pairs. Within twenty minutes, her whole box of sunglasses was gone, and she had eleven more dollars for the telescope she'd been saving toward since March.

She sat back on the warm concrete and thought it through. Nobody had announced anything. The price at one table had gone up, and people had simply walked to the other table and bought the thing that did the same job. She wondered if it would work the other way, so she made a quiet plan. She picked up the poetry book, found her favorite stanza, and read it under her breath to steady herself, then turned her attention to the lava lamp. Two boys had been circling it all morning, but nobody would commit at five dollars, because three other families on the street were selling lamps today.

"Three dollars," she called out, tapping the lamp. One of the boys sprinted back from two houses down, coins already counted into his palm. "My brother wanted one, but the lady up the street is asking ten for hers," he said, handing over the money. "So now he can have this instead." Hannah watched him carry the lamp away like a trophy, and something clicked into place: the other family's high price had sent buyers straight to her table, exactly like the sunglasses, exactly like she'd guessed. The rule was invisible, but she had caught it twice in one morning.

When her mom came out with lemonade, Hannah counted her cash box with careful fingers. "Fourteen dollars toward the telescope," she reported. Her mom raised an eyebrow at the empty space where the lamp had been. "You want to split this lemonade?" Hannah asked, then grinned. "Better hurry, before the neighbor's table raises their price and everyone comes running to ours."

Penelope had been practicing her backward crossovers for two weeks, and today was the day they had to work, because Marcus was picking her up at the rink at noon for their first date. She circled the rink once, testing the ice, then caught the boards as her skate slid out from under her.

"Smooth," said Dana from the snack bar window, where she was supposed to be working but mostly watched the skaters and ate pretzels she wasn't allowed to consume on shift.

"Ten minutes," Penelope said. "I have ten minutes to fix this."

She thought about it while she skated. It wasn't the ice, because Dana had been out earlier and hadn't slipped. It wasn't her skates, because she'd had them sharpened Friday. It had to be the left edge, and it only failed on the crossover, which meant she was leaning wrong, putting her weight somewhere she couldn't see. So she tried an experiment: she crossed over slower than slow, counting, and felt it. Her hip dropped a beat before the turn. When she held the hip up, the edge held too.

Marcus arrived at 11:58 with his helmet under his arm and his little sister, Ruby, trailing behind him like a shadow with opinions.

"She has to come," he said. "Babysitter canceled. Is that weird? Tell me if it's weird."

"It's weird," said Ruby. "Also, I want to see the vampire movie at four, and you said I could pick, and now you're saying I can't, which is lying."

"Ruby wants the one with all the fangs," Marcus said. "I keep telling her no."

Penelope glided a lap while they argued. She'd heard her dad mention once that the vampire one was rated PG-13, and Ruby was only nine. Her dad had said the rating came out on July 1, 1984, right between PG and R, as a new step, because apparently PG and R were too far apart for some movies. She filed that away.

"What's it rated?" she asked.

"PG-13," Ruby said. "I checked twice."

"There's your answer. It's not PG and it's not R. It's the one in between, the step they made in 1984, on the first of July. Nine-year-olds can't just walk in."

Ruby narrowed her eyes like she suspected a trap. "Fine. The panda movie. But I get popcorn, a large, and you carry it."

Penelope demonstrated the crossover, clean and slow, then fast, and it held. Marcus applauded with his helmet, which made a hollow bonk sound, and Ruby laughed so hard she had to sit down on the skate rental counter.

"So," Marcus said, wobbling onto the ice and grabbing her elbow immediately. "Show me that backward thing? Before we both need knee surgery or whatever that bendy part is called."

"Cartilage," Penelope said. "And my grandma says bad knees are hereditary, so be careful. I come from a long line of people falling down."

She set her hip, took his hand, and started the turn.

Grandpa's living room smelled like popcorn and radiator dust, and every seat was taken except the piano bench, which nobody wanted because it wobbled. Jeremy dragged it in anyway. On the screen, two teams he didn't recognize were fighting for a ball in the rain, and Uncle Ray was shouting at the referee in two languages.

"Argentina," Uncle Ray announced during a commercial. "First World Cup, Argentina won it. My father told me a hundred times."

"Nope." Grandpa shook his head slowly, the way he did when he was about to enjoy being right. "Uruguay."

"Uruguay?" Aunt Sofia nearly dropped her chip bowl. "Ray, Uruguay hosted it. That doesn't mean they won it. There's a difference."

"Hosts don't win," Uncle Ray said. "It's practically a rule of sports. Ironic, isn't it, the home crowd choking like that."
