Jeremy ate his popcorn and thought about that. He didn't know who was right, and nobody in the room seemed able to prove anything. They just got louder. His cousin Marco slid down behind the couch and pretended to be asleep, which was his standard move during family arguments.

Then Jeremy remembered something. Grandpa's den had a shelf of old almanacs and sports annuals, the kind with tiny print and cracked spines. During the next commercial he slipped out of the room. Nobody noticed, which was fine by him. He found a world sports record book from the 1950s and flipped through the soccer section, running his finger down page after page until he hit a table of World Cup results.

There it was. First tournament, 1930, held in Uruguay. Final: Uruguay 4, Argentina 2. He read it three times to make sure he had it straight, then copied it onto the back of an envelope from Grandpa's desk. It felt like holding a card nobody else at the party had seen.

He walked back in and stood in front of the TV. "I have a message from the den," he said, and held up the envelope like a telegram. "To Uncle Ray, from the year 1930. It says: Uruguay hosted, Uruguay won, final score Uruguay 4, Argentina 2. Signed, a book older than everybody in this room."

Marco sat up from behind the couch. "Grandpa wins the argument AND a thirteen-year-old did the research. Ray, that's a double loss."

"Let me see that envelope," Uncle Ray said. He squinted at it, then at the doorway to the den, as if the almanac itself might be lying to protect Grandpa. "Huh."

"Four to two," Grandpa said, holding out his hand. Uncle Ray slapped five coins into it, though Jeremy had never heard a bet announced. On the screen, someone scored, and everyone who had been arguing two minutes ago jumped up and yelled at the same instant.

Avery set the portable grill table at the far end of the backyard, where Dad said the smoke wouldn't drift into the neighbors' windows. Tonight was her turn to cook, and she had promised chicken drumsticks, a green salad, and lemonade for the whole family. Mom was home from work late, so Avery wanted everything ready by the time she walked through the gate, tired and hungry.

She carried out two plastic cutting boards, the knife block, the chicken, and a fat head of lettuce. Her little brother Theo trailed behind her with the salad spinner, which he insisted on operating even though it was mostly empty. The backyard table was sparse, just their supplies and a roll of paper towels, so Avery laid everything out in a line: chicken first, closest to the grill, then the board, then the lettuce at the far end.

She trimmed the drumsticks on the board, salting each one while Theo handed her pieces of lemon peel for the marinade. When the chicken went onto the grill, she washed her hands at the garden spigot and reached for the lettuce. Then she paused. The board still held faint streaks from the raw chicken, even after she wiped it with a paper towel. She couldn't see anything alive on it, but she remembered last summer, when half her class got sick after a class party, and her friend Maya had said the culprit was a virus too small for anyone to perceive, spreading from food to food. Certain things moved invisibly, and wiping a surface didn't mean it was clean.

"We need the other board," Avery said, and she ran inside for the clean one from the dish rack.

"Why?" Theo asked, spinning an empty bowl on his finger.

"Raw chicken and ready-to-eat stuff like salad have to stay on separate boards," she said. "It's called cross-contamination, when bacteria spread from one food to another."

Theo nodded solemnly, as if she had described a dragon, and stationed himself as the board inspector. He brought out only the blue board for vegetables and guarded the chicken board with the tongs. Together they tore the lettuce, sliced tomatoes, and squeezed lemon into the pitcher, and by the time the gate creaked, the table held grilled drumsticks, a cold salad, and four glasses sweating in the evening air.

Mom set down her bag and looked at the table, then at them. "You did all this?" Avery pointed at Theo. "He was in charge of boards." Theo lifted the tongs like a knight raising a sword and said, "Nobody contaminates anything on my watch."

The street festival two blocks from the gurdwara smelled like fried dough and cardamom, and Asher's little cousin Priya kept tugging his sleeve toward the bouncy castle. His mother had one instruction before she disappeared into the crowd of aunties: take Priya to the gurdwara open house at four, when the langar meal was served. Asher didn't mind. Last year a volunteer there had let him help stir a pot of dal big enough to bathe in.

Outside the gurdwara's front steps, Asher noticed a wall of shelves piled with shoes, sneakers and sandals and one pair of glittery flip-flops. He watched a family in mosque clothes, the mother in a long abaya, set their shoes on the shelf and go in barefoot. A group coming from the Hindu temple down the street, flower garlands still around their necks, did the same thing. Then his friend Dev jogged up, cap on backwards, and Asher felt a flash of skepticism. Dev had never been inside a place of worship in his life.

"You have to take your shoes off," Asher said, pulling off his own sneakers. "Everybody does here. At mosques and Hindu temples too, I think. It's like a rule everywhere."

Dev shrugged and unlaced his high-tops, but a smiling uncle at the door held up a hand before they could step inside. "And your heads, boys. In the gurdwara everyone covers the head, not just the Sikhs." He offered a basket of thin cotton scarves. Asher picked an orange one and knotted it, feeling like a pirate. Dev wrapped his around so crookedly that Priya giggled and fixed it for him, folding the fabric into a neat triangle the way their grandmother had illustrated for her at last year's festival.

Inside, volunteers moved down the long carpet rows with steel buckets of kheer, and the three of them sat cross-legged with their palms cupled, collecting warm rice pudding. Priya whispered that the man stirring the giant pot had been stirring since dawn, and Dev, who usually claimed all free food was somehow a trick, went back for seconds and then thirds. On the way out, Asher felt proud of how smoothly the day had gone, how he had known exactly what to do at every turn.

That was when he reached the shoe shelf and stopped. His sneakers were gone. Vanished into the mountain of footwear, along with, apparently, his ability to find anything. Dev held up the glittery flip-flops, size six. "Could be worse," he said. "These are kind of cute on you." Priya was already laughing so hard she had to sit down on the steps, her orange scarf sliding over her eyes.

Norah had spent four dollars on a hot chocolate she wasn't drinking, because holding the cup gave her hands something to do while she stood at the fence waiting for Eli. The marching band was pivoting on the field in stiff, perfect lines, and the scoreboard buzzed with the end of the first quarter. When Eli arrived, out of breath from biking, he said, "Sorry, my chain fell off twice."

"Twice?" said Norah. "Do you think the derailleur's bent?"

Eli blinked. "You know about derailleurs?"

She didn't, not really. Her older brother lectured about bikes constantly and she had absorbed it the way a sponge absorbs dishwater. But Eli lit up and talked about gears for the next ten minutes, and then about his uncle's motorcycle, and then about how he wanted to invest in a dirt bike by saving mower money this summer. Norah nodded and smiled and said "yeah" at the right pauses. Somewhere in the second quarter she realized he hadn't asked her a single question, and, worse, that she hadn't noticed for a surprisingly long time because his voice was nice to listen to. That was the humiliating part.

She tested a small idea. Instead of waiting for a gap to talk about herself, she asked, "What made you want a dirt bike instead of, like, a road bike?" Eli stopped mid-sentence and looked at her, actually looked, and said, "Nobody ever asks me that," and then told a story about a trail behind his grandmother's house. Norah put her cold cup down on the fence rail and leaned in. When the crowd roared over a touchdown, neither of them turned around.

She remembered, then, a poster in the guidance office: ACTIVE LISTENING. Her friend Priya had once demonstrated it on her, asking a follow-up question about something Norah had said the week before, and Norah had felt heard for the rest of the day. That was the whole trick, she saw now: give someone your full attention, then prove you heard them. She had done the attention part. She tried the proof. "So is your grandmother's trail still there, or did they build on it?"

"She sold the house," Eli said. "I keep meaning to ask her for a photo before her attic gets cleaned out."

"Ask her tomorrow," Norah said. "She'd probably love that you care." He nodded slowly, like the idea was new.

By the fourth quarter they were both shivering, and Eli offered her his jacket, which smelled like sawdust and was too big. She never did tell him about the science fair ribbon in her backpack, the thing she'd rehearsed saying all week. He biked off into the dark waving, promising to text, and she stood at the fence holding the empty cup, having learned exactly one thing about him and zero ways to explain who she was. She dropped the cup in the trash and said, to nobody, "Photo. Ask about the photo."

Dylan had one weekend to figure out linear equations before Monday's retake, and Grandpa's kitchen table was the only quiet place left. He spread out his homework while Grandpa sorted through a crate of wooden triangle tiles for the birdhouse mosaic he was building.

"You're doing the tiles wrong," Dylan said, watching Grandpa hold two triangles side by side and squint.

"Am I." Grandpa stacked one triangle on top of the other. The edges lined up exactly, corner to corner, no sliver of wood showing anywhere. "These two match. All three pairs of sides, all three pairs of angles, equal all the way around."

"There's a word for that," Dylan said, flipping through his math book. "Congruent. Same shape and same size, so everything matches." He took two more triangles from the crate and stacked them. One corner stuck out past the other like a dog-eared page. "Not these."

"Classify them into piles, then," Grandpa said, sliding the crate across the table. "Matched ones on the left, misfits on the right. I need ten pairs by Sunday."

Dylan got to work, stacking and sorting, and somewhere around the fourth pair he noticed something. When he placed a tile on top of another tile, he couldn't see either one anymore. He could only see the top tile, and whether the bottom one peeked out. The matching was invisible unless it failed. He slid his algebra paper closer and read the problem again: x plus seven equals nineteen. The x was like the hidden bottom triangle. He couldn't see it. But if he did the same thing to both sides, the way stacking treated both tiles the same way, the hidden thing would have to show itself. He subtracted seven from the left side and seven from the right, and wrote x equals twelve. It felt like the corner peeking out.

"Found a use for your homework already?" Grandpa asked.

"It's the same trick," Dylan said. "You do the same thing to both sides and whatever's hiding has to show up. With the tiles I stack them. With the equation I subtract from both sides."

That evening a letter came from Grandpa's brother Leo, who never called because he said phones were an illusion of closeness. Grandpa read it aloud: "Dear Walt. Heard you're tiling again. Still cutting them by hand like a man indifferent to the existence of saws? Your brother, who owns a saw." Grandpa snorted and put the letter under the sugar bowl.

Sunday morning, Grandpa fit the last matched pair into the mosaic's roofline. Dylan checked his homework pile one more time, then folded it into his backpack and tapped the page. "Stay solved," he told it. Grandpa picked up a misfit triangle, the one with the crooked corner, and dropped it into the scrap bucket.

The alarm went off at 3:40 in the morning, and for a moment Cooper forgot where he was. Then he remembered: Uncle Yusuf's house, the spare room with the lumpy futon, and the folded paper on the nightstand with the first three lines of Surah Al-Fatiha written in Arabic letters, the ones he had to have memorized by Friday.

He found the kitchen already lit. Auntie Safa was cracking eggs, and his cousins Hamza and Laila shuffled in behind him, hair flattened on one side, eyes half shut. Nobody looked cheerful, but nobody complained either.

"Sit, sit," Auntie said, sliding plates across the counter. "Suhur time."

"Suhur?" Cooper whispered to Hamza as he took a seat.

"Before the dawn prayer, we eat," Hamza said, yawning. "Then nothing till sunset. No food, no water, nothing."

Cooper stared at his eggs. Nothing until sunset meant his stomach would be growling by math class tomorrow. But that wasn't what worried him. What worried him was the paper upstairs, the verses he'd read forty times without them sticking. He tried reciting them in his head while he chewed, and they slipped away like water through his fingers.

After the dawn prayer, when the sky outside the window had turned from black to thin gray, he had an idea. He watched Laila pull a blanket over her head on the couch and realized the whole house had gone quiet and hungry at the same time, together, on purpose. Maybe that was the trick. His brain wasn't holding the words because he'd been studying alone in a noisy room at home, half watching videos. Here, the words had a reason to matter, a place to fit. So he tested it. He went back to the spare room, set his phone to record, and recited the three lines out loud into it, listening once, reciting again.

By breakfast the next morning, which was 3:40 again, Auntie's eggs again, he had six lines memorized. He recited them for Hamza between bites of toast, and Hamza nodded along like he was checking a receipt. Cooper thought about his grandmother, who had taught these same verses to Uncle Yusuf somewhere across an ocean, and how she probably never transmitted them through a phone recording. He decided that didn't make his way worse. Just different. Though maybe by Friday, when he stood up in front of everyone, he would wish he'd started earlier, alone in his room instead of complaining about it for two weeks.

"Seven lines today," he told Auntie, holding out his plate for more eggs.

"Seven," she said, and cracked two more.

The gym smelled like floor wax and old rubber. Zachary stood in the line of boys by the bleachers, holding his sneakers in one hand, and watched Coach Reyes clip a stack of yellow forms to a clipboard.

"Basketball tryouts start in ten minutes," the coach called out. "If you're not on my list, come see me now."

Zachary's name was third on the list. He had turned in his sports physical form two weeks ago, signed by the nurse practitioner at the clinic downtown. His mother had driven him there on a Tuesday, and he remembered waiting forty minutes past his appointment. He was set.

The boy ahead of him in line, Deshawn, was not set. Deshawn dug through his backpack, pulled out a binder, a hoodie, and a sandwich, and then went still.

"I had it," Deshawn said. "I know I had it."

Coach Reyes walked over. "Had what?"

"The physical form. The signed one. My mom took me to the doctor last month."

The coach shook his head. "No form, no tryout. That's not my rule. The school requires a physical before anybody can practice or try out with a team. A doctor or a clinician has to sign off on it. You could be the best player in this gym and it wouldn't matter."

Deshawn zipped his backpack. "It's at home. On the printer."

Zachary thought about that. The tryout was tonight, one night only, and the next round was tomorrow at four. He looked at the clock on the wall. It was 3:35. School let out at 3:15, so the buses were still loading, and Deshawn's house was the one on Miller Street, eight minutes on a bike. Zachary knew this because he'd ridden past it a hundred times, usually slowing down to look at the hoop nailed above the garage.

"Does a photo of it count?" Zachary asked.

Coach Reyes tapped the clipboard. "If I can read the signature and the date, yes. The office just needs proof a clinician signed it."

Zachary turned to Deshawn. "Call your mom. Have her send a picture of the form to your phone, then forward it to the coach."

The gym was being renovated next month, so half the floor was stacked with rolled mats and the bleachers on the far side were already gone, which made the whole space echo. Deshawn's phone call bounced around that empty wall as he pleaded with his mother, who was apparently in a meeting. Two minutes passed. Five.

"Tryouts begin," Coach Reyes said. "Layup lines. Go."

The boys ran. Zachary caught a pass, planted his left foot, and spun into a pivot that shook his defender, then laid the ball off the glass. The tryout drills were fertile ground for showing off, and everyone knew it, so half the squad tried flashy passes and threw them out of bounds. Zachary stuck to the simple stuff: boxing out, calling screens, hitting the open man.

Near the free throw line, he saw Deshawn sprint in from the hallway, phone held up like a hall pass. Coach Reyes read the screen, squinted, and nodded. "Get in line."

Deshawn got a rebound and scored twice before the scrimmage ended. When Coach Reyes read the list of names moving on to the second day, he read Zachary's name, then Deshawn's.

Deshawn grabbed Zachary's shoulder on the way to the water fountain. "You knew my mom would answer eventually?"

"I figured she checks her phone in meetings," Zachary said. "My mom does."

"And the picture thing?"

Zachary shrugged. "Worth testing."

Coach Reyes walked past them with his clipboard. "Zachary, one thing. Your physical form I have on file says it expires before the season ends. You'll need a new one by Friday." He kept walking, and the gym doors swung shut behind him.

Annabelle got to the microscope station second, right behind Marcus, which meant she had to watch him hog the good scope for five whole minutes while she waited with her onion and her lab sheet. On the sheet, three words waited for arrows: cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus. She had already peeled a paper-thin layer of skin off the onion with tweezers, and it lay on her slide like a ghost of an onion, pale and wrinkled.

Her first slide was a disaster. She dropped the coverslip flat onto the skin, the way you would clap a book shut, and when she looked through the eyepiece she saw dozens of round black-edged circles clustered everywhere. She drew them quickly, three of them, and labeled one "nucleus" before a doubt crept in. They were awfully round. And awfully empty.

"Those aren't cells," said Priya from the next station, leaning over. "Those are air bubbles. You've got a whole sky of them."

Annabelle sat back. Bubbles. She had trapped a pocket of sky between glass and glass, and she had almost turned it in for a grade. She pulled the elastic band off the slide box, snapped it once around her wrist, and thought. The bubbles had to be air that got in when she dropped the coverslip straight down, trapping it under. So maybe the trick was not to drop it flat. Maybe she could let one edge touch first and lower the rest slowly, like closing a door instead of slamming it.

"Try it," Priya said, though Annabelle hadn't said anything out loud. "You look like someone about to advocate for a big idea."

"I am advocating for it," Annabelle said. "Angle. One edge first." She took a fresh piece of onion skin, laid it flat, added the drop of stain, and touched just the edge of a new coverslip to the liquid. Then she lowered it slowly, hinged on that first edge, letting it settle across the skin like a slow shield coming down.

Through the eyepiece, the circles were gone. Instead the field filled with boxes, rows and rows of brick-shaped cells stacked together, their walls outlined clean and dark. Near the center of one cell sat a denser dot, round and small. She found it in the next cell too, and the next. That had to be the nucleus, and the dark border around each box had to be the wall, with the membrane just inside it, thin as a whisper.

She drew it all, arrows and labels, while Marcus complained that his slide looked like a meteor shower. "Bubbles," she told him, turning her drawing around. "Lower it at an angle, one edge first. Want to see mine?" She slid off her stool and waved him toward her scope, and Priya crowded in behind, and above them the ceiling fan spun like a propeller, stirring the smell of onion through the whole lab.

The folded note from Coach Ruiz landed on the bleacher beside Jeremy's gym bag: "You're authorized to call the plays Friday. Point guard means the game runs through you." Practice started in ten minutes, and Jeremy still could not decide how to run the pick and roll against Eastside, whose big men switched every screen.

He dribbled at the foul line, imagining it. Marcus would slide over and set the screen. Jeremy would rub shoulders with him, and either the defender switched and Jeremy passed to a rolling Marcus, or nobody switched and Jeremy drove. The problem was that Eastside always seemed one step ahead, and Jeremy could not see why. There had to be a pattern in their switches, something hidden in how they moved.

Before the scrimmage, Coach had the team run hurdles along the sideline. Jeremy clipped the third hurdle and stumbled through it, landing flat-footed. Marcus sailed over every one, but Derek, the fastest sprinter on the team, kept knocking them down or floating so high in the air that he landed slow, well past the hurdle, his lead leg swinging up stiff and straight like a plank. "You're hanging up there," Jeremy said. Derek tried again and hung there again.

Jeremy watched him closely. Marcus bent his lead knee and drove it over the hurdle first, then straightened the leg on the way down, and he came off each hurdle low and quick. Derek swung his whole leg up rigid, and that lifted his body too high, so he drifted over the top instead of running through it. "Lead knee first," Jeremy called. "Then straighten it." Derek nodded, drove the knee, straightened, and snapped down over the fourth hurdle without touching it. "That's it," Derek shouted, already three hurdles clear.

Jeremy chewed on that through a water break. The thing that ruined Derek's hurdling was not slowness. It was doing a stiff, obvious move that pushed him too high and left him floating where everyone could read him. At the whiteboard he texted his older cousin Rene, who had played point guard at Wilson High: "Eastside reads my drives. What do I do?" Rene's reply buzzed back fast: "If they see the play coming, you've already lost. Make the screen look like one thing, then let it become another. You have until Friday. Figure out the pattern in their switches; every team has one."

So Jeremy made his screen look stiff and obvious, a plank of a move, the same screen every time, for three possessions in the scrimmage. He watched. The switching big man always floated toward the ball, high and slow, sure of himself, reading the obvious move. On the next possession Jeremy called " forty-one," sent Marcus to the wing, and came off a screen that looked like the same plank play, except he bent it, changed direction at the last instant, and hit the approximate gap between two slow-moving defenders. Marcus rolled, Jeremy flicked the pass, and the ball dropped through without touching iron. "That," Derek yelled from the sideline, one hand raised mid-hurdle, "looked nothing like the other ones."

Cameron was halfway through his pasta when his phone buzzed against the table leg. His mother gave him the look, so he angled the screen under the edge of the table like a skilled artisan of not getting caught. It was a photo from Dex: his new bike leaning against a garage, captioned "guess who saved up all summer."

"Phone on the counter," his mother said. Cameron slid it over, screen up, which was a tactical error.

His little sister Priya grabbed it before it stopped moving. "Why is there a map on Dex's bike picture?"

"There isn't," Cameron said. "Photos don't have maps."

"There is a little pin thing. It's showing a street." She turned the phone toward their mom. "It says Maple Court."

Cameron reached for it, and Priya, being Priya, held it out of reach and read aloud. "Photo taken at, then a bunch of numbers. Then it says location on."

Something cold crawled up the back of his neck. He took the phone, opened the photo, and tapped the little "i" in the corner himself. Sure enough, there was the map, and there was the pin, sitting squarely on Maple Court, which was where Dex lived, which Dex had told the whole group chat never to share because his older brother said people online were naive about exactly this kind of thing. Cameron had laughed at that. Now he was looking at a map to his friend's house that Dex had transmitted to eleven people without knowing it.

"Language," his mother said mildly, because apparently he had said something out loud.

"Mom, when a phone takes a photo with location services on, it can write the exact GPS coordinates of where the photo was taken into hidden data in the file," Cameron said. "Dex told me yesterday. It's called EXIF metadata. I thought he was making it up."

"So every photo knows where it was taken," Priya said, chewing bread.

"Ours do, apparently." Cameron was already scrolling. Two weeks ago he had posted twelve pictures of the tree fort he and Dex had built behind his grandfather's shed, and he had captioned them "secret fort, no girls, no adults, no exceptions," which at the time had seemed hilarious. Every one of those photos had a map pin on his grandfather's back acreage, down to which tree, basically. Anyone who looked at the file's details could find it. Anyone at all. Strangers. He had felt like the fort was hidden because it was behind a shed, which now struck him as roughly the level of planning that went into hiding a sandwich by putting a napkin on it.

He texted Dex: check the i on your bike photo. Then delete it. Then he went through his own posts, one by one, and removed the fort pictures while his pasta went cold and Priya narrated his facial expressions to their mother.

"Regret," she announced. "With a side of horror."

Dex's reply arrived as Cameron was carrying his plate to the sink. "DELETED. also I'm telling my brother he was right. he's going to be insufferable forever."

Cameron typed back, "worth it," deleted that too, and wrote, "meet at the fort tomorrow. new rule: location services off before the door opens."

Naomi had drafted the plan three times on the back of her homework: movie in the living room, popcorn, her little brother banished to upstairs, Marcus picked from a short list of candidates that included Theo from science class and Dara's cousin. Marcus had won because he laughed at her jokes without looking around to see if anyone else had heard them. He was coming at four, and it was already three forty.

At three fifty she stood in the kitchen arguing with herself out loud. "If he tries to hold my hand, what do I do?" Her little brother, sneakers on the stairs where he'd been eavesdropping, said, "Just let him, obviously."

"Obviously nothing," Naomi said. She tested the idea the way she tested everything, by flipping it over. If she didn't want to hold hands, would she have to anyway, just because it was a date? And if Marcus didn't want to, could she make him? She decided the answer was no, in both directions, and that neither of them owed the other a hug or anything else just for showing up. She didn't say it to her brother. She just shooed him upstairs.

Marcus arrived with the popcorn, which they'd agreed he'd bring, and they watched half of a monster movie with the bowl between them like a wall. When the monster dragged a helicopter into the lake, their hands met in the popcorn and both of them pulled back laughing. Later, on purpose, Naomi slid her hand over and rested it next to his on the couch cushion, not touching, just near. Marcus looked at it, then at her, and moved his hand two inches away.

"Okay," she said, and she meant it. Her face went hot, but she kept her eyes on the screen. He hadn't said no in words, but the answer was the answer, and she wasn't going to push it or ask why.

At six, when his mom's car pulled into the driveway, Marcus stood up and held out his arms for a hug. Naomi stepped back. "Not today," she said, and watched to see what he would do with it. He dropped his arms, easy, no sigh, no begging, no leaning in anyway. "See you Monday," he said, and picked up his jacket.

From the top of the stairs her brother called, "You didn't even hug him?" Naomi held the door open, and the cold air came in around her. "Nope," she said. "And he didn't mind."

The gym smelled like floor wax and nervous sixth graders, and Alexander was one of them. A theater teacher had come to run a workshop before the debate tournament on Saturday, and she had just written two words on a portable whiteboard: yes, and. "Whatever your partner offers, you accept it and add to it," she said. "No blocking, no denying." Alexander's partner was Priya, who had beat him in the school debate final last month, and he was determined not to embarrass himself in front of her.

They started a scene about explorers discovering a lost city. Priya held up an imaginary shovel and said, "I found a door buried in the sand!" Alexander's whole brain wanted to say "that's just a rock." Instead he said, "Yes, and it opens into a room full of gold microbe samples under glass!" Priya's eyes lit up. "Yes, and one of the slides is still alive!" The scene took off like a rocket, and Alexander felt something click: every time he accepted her offer and built on it, the story got stronger, the same way a good argument did when you backed it up.

Saturday, at the tournament, it all connected. In the final round Alexander argued that school lunches should include more fresh vegetables. When a judge asked how he knew fresh food was healthier, he gave his data, then his reason connecting it, and the judge nodded and said, "Good warrant." Afterward a kid from the other team caught him by the water fountain. "Where does the word warrant even come from?" the kid asked.

Alexander didn't know. But his older sister had a shelf of debate books, and that night he dug through them until he found a battered paperback called The Uses of Argument. He flipped the pages fast, and there it was: a model of argument with claim, data, and warrant, laid out by the British philosopher Stephen Toulmin in 1958. Alexander read the page twice, then raced downstairs to extract a promise from his dad to drive him to Priya's house so he could tell her before he forgot a single detail.

The next Monday in the gym, the theater teacher started a new scene, this one set in a contemporary art museum. "I'm the security guard," Priya announced, "and this painting just moved!"

Alexander stepped forward, grinning. "Yes, and the paint is alive, because the artist mixed in microbes!"

"Yes, and they only eat the color blue!" Priya shouted, and the whole gym burst out laughing.

The sprinklers at Millbrook Park had a way of turning on without warning, which was why Aurora was standing behind the drinking fountain with damp sneakers, holding her phone like evidence in a trial. Marisol had told Sam what Aurora said about the eighth-grade dance, and now Marisol was sitting on the third swing, dragging her toe in the wood chips, waiting for whatever Aurora was going to say. Aurora had a whole speech drafted in her notes app, and every line of it began with "you always" or "you never," which felt satisfying to type but somehow wrong to say out loud.

She thought about her aunt's paperback on the picnic table at home, the one with the marriage researcher's name on the spine, John Gottman. Aurora had flipped through it mostly to be nosy, but one page had stuck. A complaint, the book said, was about one specific action. Criticism attacked a person's character with words like "you always" or "you never." Her notes app was basically a museum of criticism. She deleted it all and started over, condensing her fury into a single sentence with a date attached.

"Okay," she said, walking over. "You told Sam what I said on Friday about the dance. That's it. That's the whole accusation."

Marisol stopped dragging her toe. "That's it? No 'you never keep secrets, you're basically a walking megaphone with good hair'?"

"I considered the megaphone angle," Aurora admitted. "It had a certain style. But I'm trying something." The sprinklers hissed on across the field, and two little kids shrieked through them like it was a national holiday.

"Good," Marisol said, "because here's the twist. I didn't tell Sam." She pulled out her own phone and showed a text from Friday night, time-stamped 9:42. "Sam was sitting behind us on the bus. She heard you herself. I got blamed for the leak you did out loud, in public, at full volume, which is very on brand for you."

Aurora stared at the screen. So her whole case had rested on a biased theory, built from one clue: Sam knew, and Sam and Marisol texted constantly. But the pattern had another shape hiding inside it, and she'd never tested it. She had marched over here ready to fracture a five-year friendship over a leak she'd caused with her own loud mouth.

"I'm going to lie down in the sprinklers," Aurora announced, "to convey remorse through dramatic dampness."

"You should also apologize to Sam."

"I will. After the dampness." She ran, and Marisol was right behind her, yelling, "If you splash me, that's a complaint about one specific action, and I will forgive it!"

Kaitlyn set her brushes in Grandma's kitchen sink and looked at the small canvas propped on the counter. She had painted the birch tree in Grandma's backyard, its white bark and the dark door behind it, using the oil paints from the wooden box Grandma kept in the closet.

"The bus leaves at four," she said. "I can carry it home in my backpack."

Grandma was peeling an apple, the spiral of skin getting longer and longer. "You can carry it. Whether that's wise is another question."

Kaitlyn touched the edge of the canvas with one finger, near the corner where she hadn't painted. The painted part was tacky, like a sticker that had lost half its stick. She pressed her fingertip to the birch tree trunk and lifted it away. A faint whorl of her fingerprint stayed in the green.

"It's already dry-ish," she said.

"It's not water paint, dear. Nothing evaporates."

Kaitlyn frowned. With watercolors, the wet shine faded and the paper was dry. This paint stayed glossy and soft. She opened the window over the sink and held the canvas in the breeze, then set it on the table in the sun coming through the curtains. After twenty minutes of washing brushes and eating apple slices, she touched the trunk again. It was no different.

So the air moving over it was doing something, but slowly, and warmth was not speeding it up much. She turned the canvas over and felt the back of the canvas board, which was dry and plain. Then she understood: the wet side had to stay open to the air, and it was the air itself that was doing the drying, whatever the oil was doing with it. That meant covering the surface, even softly, would stop it.

"It has to breathe," she said. "Both sides can't touch anything."

"Precisely why carrying it in a backpack is not feasible," Grandma said. "The straps, the books, your lunch. It would take days to dry anyway. Perhaps longer."

Kaitlyn counted on her fingers. Days. Longer than days, maybe. The art show at school was Friday, five days away, which might just barely work. She looked at the canvas, then at the shelf above the fridge, wide and empty, out of reach of Grandma's two cats.

"Can it stay here until Thursday? I could walk over after school and carry it flat, both hands, the whole way. I know it's a lot to ask."

"You may leave it," Grandma said. "I'll feel an obligation to keep the cats out of this room, which they will resent."

Kaitlyn laughed and carried the canvas to the high shelf, setting it face-up where the air could reach every painted inch. She stepped back and looked at it from below.

"Bye, tree," she said. "Breathe."

The Herreras' kitchen smelled like cinnamon and dish soap, and the baby would not stop screaming. Laurence had been bouncing Marisol for twenty minutes, singing every song she could remember, walking loops past the refrigerator and back. The crying got louder. Her arms ached, and something hot and tight was building behind her ribs.

She remembered her mother's voice on the phone last night, quick and firm between the everyday instructions about bottles and bedtimes. "If she won't stop crying, put her down somewhere safe and walk away for a minute. Never shake her. A baby's neck muscles are too weak to support that heavy head, and shaking can cause serious brain injury." At the time Laurence had said yes, fine, obviously, the way you say things to get to the end of a phone call. She was hearing the words differently now, standing in this kitchen with her ears ringing.

The logical move, she told herself, was the crib. Marisol was fed, changed, and warm, so the crying had some hidden cause Laurence couldn't see, and she couldn't fix what she couldn't find. She carried the baby down the hall, laid her gently in the crib, checked that the blanket was tucked below her arms, and stepped back out into the hallway. Through the monitor on the counter, the screaming continued, muffled now, like a storm heard from inside a house.

Laurence gripped the edge of the counter and breathed. She had invested one whole evening in this job, her first real one, ten dollars an hour, and she'd already planned how she'd spend it. Now she wondered whether she should have taken it at all. Her friend Dara babysat all the time and made it look easy, but Dara had two younger brothers and some built-in hierarchy of who fusses over whom. Laurence was an only child. Babies were a country she didn't speak the language of.

She counted to sixty, watching the monitor. Somewhere in the fifties, the crying shifted, wobbling, thinning out. Then it stopped. Not a sudden stop, a draining one, like water leaving a sink. Laurence held her breath and listened to the small wet sounds of a baby settling herself.

She tiptoed down the hall and stood in the doorway. Marisol lay with her fists up by her ears, eyes open, watching the mobile turn. She wasn't asleep. She was just quiet, and Laurence didn't know what she'd done, or whether she'd done anything at all.

The front door clicked. Mrs. Herrera came into the kitchen, keys in hand, and found Laurence standing there with the monitor held against her chest like evidence. "How was she?" Mrs. Herrera asked.

"Fine," Laurence said. "She's awake. She's just lying there, looking at things."

Arthur had taped his graph to the whiteboard at the back of the science classroom, and it had taken him twenty minutes to stop being proud of it. The problem was the line. Every group that tested battery brands was supposed to get a clear winner, but his line ran sideways, and Mr. Okafor had circled the graph in green marker and written only, "Look again."

"I don't get it," Arthur said. "The data's right. I checked it twice." His friend Priya leaned against the lab table next to him, holding two wires she was supposed to be returning to the drawer.

"Then it's not the data," she said. "It's how you put it on the paper."

He pulled the graph down and laid it flat between the sinks. Along the bottom he had written "Minutes of flashlight time," and up the side, "Battery brand." He had made four bars, one per brand, arranged from longest time to shortest. That seemed fair. It irritated him that something invisible kept telling him he was wrong, because he could not argue with a feeling.

Priya set the wires down and tapped the side of the paper. "You put what you chose on the side that's supposed to show what happened," she said. "You picked the brands. The time happened because of the brands." Arthur stared at her. In his notebook, back at his desk, he had written it out on the first day: change this, watch that. The brands were the thing he changed. The time was the thing that answered.

"So the thing I change goes on the bottom," he said slowly. "By convention, the independent variable goes on the x-axis, and the dependent goes on the y." Priya shrugged like it was obvious, which somehow made it easier to believe.

He started over on a fresh sheet, labeling the bottom "Battery brand" and the side "Minutes of flashlight time." The bars rose in a new pattern, and suddenly the emperor brand, the one with the shiny gold label that everybody said was the best, was one of the shortest on the page. Priya laughed out loud at that.

"Everyone's going to fight you," she said. "Half the class swears by Emperor."

"Good," Arthur said. "A controversial result is still a result." He taped the new graph up where the old one had been, stepped back, and tilted his head at the shape the bars made now. Behind him, the classroom door opened, and the first students coming in after lunch were already drifting toward his board.

Hayden pressed his museum badge flat against his chest and walked into the Hall of Earth Science, where a giant globe hung from the ceiling, tilted, with a spotlight fixed at its center. In three hours he would give his first talk as a junior docent, and the topic was the one he had drawn by unlucky chance: why we have seasons. He knew the wrong version, the one half the visitors believed, that summer happens because Earth is closer to the sun. He had even repeated it to his little sister last week. He needed something better than that.

His grandfather had driven him here this morning, same as every Saturday since Hayden started volunteering, but today Grandpa had sat down in the café and said he would wait, because his knees were resigning from long walks, as he put it. That was new. Grandpa used to march through every hall, quizzing Hayden on exhibits until the guards knew them both by name.

Hayden circled the globe. The spotlight stayed still, but the globe spun, and its axis leaned at a steady angle that never changed. He grabbed a floor model of the sun and Earth and carried it to a bench, tilting the little Earth with his thumb and walking it around the lamp. When the north end leaned toward the light, he touched the tabletop and found it warm; when the same end leaned away, the light spread thin and slanted across his hand. It wasn't distance. It was the angle, and the tilt pointing one hemisphere at the sun, then away, all year long. He said it out loud twice, quietly, the way he would have to say it to strangers.

Near the bench hung a photograph of the Grand Canyon, wide and red, with a caption beside it. Hayden read it twice: scientists estimate the Colorado River began carving the Grand Canyon about 5 to 6 million years ago. Five to six million years. He thought of the postcard on Grandpa's fridge, the one from the trip Hayden had been too young for, and how Grandpa used to say rivers were patient workers.

A girl about nine stopped at his bench and poked the model Earth. "Why is it crooked?"

"That's the tilt," Hayden said. "Watch." He orbited it once for her, then twice, and her face changed the way faces do when something clicks.

She ran off to tell her mother, and Hayden began carrying the model back. On his way he passed the café window. Grandpa was sitting alone, turning his coffee cup in slow circles, staring at nothing Hayden could name. They had made a good team once, an alliance of two museum wanderers, and today Grandpa couldn't even come in with him.

Hayden lifted his hand to the glass. Grandpa blinked, then waved, slow and a little unsure, and Hayden mouthed, "Five to six million years," because he was going to tell him everything later, and Grandpa would want to hear it from the start.

Elizabeth had one goal for the field trip to Marsh Hollow Nature Reserve: photograph the elusive green heron for the school's nature journal, which was offering a whole page to whoever got the best shot. Her friend Dev had a different goal, which was to control the entire snack supply. He had packed a gallon bag of trail mix, peanuts, and dried apricots, and he doled it out one piece at a time like a greedy dragon.

"You have a monopoly on the trail mix," Elizabeth said, holding out her hand.

"Correct," said Dev, and gave her exactly one peanut. "Peanuts are nutritious, you know. You should thank me."

Their teacher, Ms. Okafor, herded them down the boardwalk trail toward the reserve's small visitor center, where an old barn had been converted into an exhibit hall. Inside, the first room was bright and full of taxidermy raccoons in comic poses. But the second room was so dim that Maya, from the back of the group, groaned out loud. "I can barely see anything! Why would they hang a hundred-year-old quilt in a room this dark? That's like putting a birthday cake in a safe."

A guide passing through paused at the doorway. "Light slowly fades the dyes and pigments in textiles, paper and some paintings," she said. "That's why many museums keep delicate items in dim rooms." Then she went back to her desk, and Elizabeth stood in the gloom, staring at the quilt's faded roses, feeling something click.

If light faded paper, then the pressed-flower scrapbook in the bright room, the one lying open in the window bay, was in trouble. She dragged Dev and Maya over to it. The book held pages made by schoolkids each spring for thirty years. Elizabeth turned to the spring pages from ten years ago, then found the ones displayed in the sunny bay versus the same year's pages in a shaded case by the wall. The bay pages were washed out, pale as weak tea, while the shaded ones still held color. Same flowers, same year, different light. "Look," she whispered. "It's not age doing this. It's the window."

Maya squinted at the two pages. "How do you interpret that, detective?"

"Interpret it?" Elizabeth said. "I don't have to interpret it. I caught it red-handed. Well, pink-handed." Dev laughed so hard he dropped his trail mix bag, which spilled across the floor, ending his monopoly forever. Maya immediately claimed three apricots as tax.

Elizabeth brought the pages to the guide, showed her the fading, and the guide's eyebrows went up. "Well, you're hired," she said, and moved the scrapbook to the dim room next to the quilt. She even let Elizabeth label it, in careful letters: Please keep out of bright light.

On the walk back, the green heron finally appeared, standing in the reeds like a grumpy old man in a gray coat. Elizabeth raised her camera just as Dev, still brushing trail mix crumbs off his shirt, sneezed. The heron bolted. The photo showed a blur of wings, a startled frog, and half of Dev's elbow.

Maya patted her shoulder. "It's a great action shot."

"It's an elbow," said Elizabeth.

"An elbow," said Dev solemnly, "that will be remembered for a hundred years, unlike that quilt."

Asher had told his lab partner Priya he didn't need the practice session at the community garden, and for three days he had regretted it, because Monday's quiz asked him to label a cell wall, a membrane, and a nucleus, and he had frozen. So on Saturday he brought his worksheet and his grandfather's old microscope to the garden shed, where the garden club kept a crate of onions from the harvest bin.

He pulled a papery skin off an onion layer, laid it flat on a slide, and lowered the lens. The cells showed up like brickwork, pale and neat. He found the wall, the rigid outer edge, easy. The membrane hugged it, thinner, harder to be sure of. The nucleus was a dark dot near the edge of one cell. He drew them on his sheet, then stopped. In the middle of every cell sat a huge pale bubble, taking up most of the space, and it was on no line of his diagram.

A draft slid through the shed and rattled the clipboard, and he shut the window with his elbow, afraid the slide would dry out. His little sister Nadia had followed him, as she always did, and leaned on the table. "What's the giant bubble in the middle?" she asked.

"It's not on my sheet," Asher said, "so it shouldn't matter." But he couldn't let it go, because a bubble that big would crowd everything he was supposed to label. He remembered the science museum trip, the room of giant models. A kid there had asked the guide the same question about the plant cell model, and the answer had drifted past him while he was messing with his phone. He turned to Nadia. "The guide called it a vacuole. She said many plant cells have one large central vacuole, a water-filled sac that can take up most of the cell." He paused, working through it. "Animal cells only have small vacuoles, if any. That's why I never saw one when we did the cheek-cell lab." That was the test, really. Cheek cells had been scattered gray dots with a nucleus and no big bubble. These were swollen with water from the garden's rain barrel.

Priya came in carrying a tomato and stopped at the microscope. "That's a radical slide," she said. "Better than the polymer one Mr. Doyle showed us, that plastic-bag demo." She peered down. "You didn't come to practice."

"I thought I had it," Asher said.

Priya picked up his worksheet and studied the empty middle of his drawing. "You left the biggest thing in the cell off your diagram because it wasn't on the list." She tapped the paper. "Mr. Doyle said the vacuole is the bonus question."

Asher looked from her to the slide, where the pale sac filled each cell like a held breath, and slid the worksheet across the table. "Draw it in for me?"

Louis had a spot on the community center volleyball team, and he had a problem named Dre. Dre trained every single day, Saturdays included, and lately he was getting slower. His spike times in the coach's notebook had dropped for three weeks straight, even though he stayed after practice to run stairs while everyone else went home. Louis kept the stats, so he was the only one who noticed the pattern.

The center's snack bar, impoverished since the budget cuts, sold only water and stale granola bars, so the two of them sat on the bleachers after Thursday practice splitting a bar and arguing about it. "He works hardest and gets worst," Louis said. "That's backwards." He turned it over all evening, and by the time he got home, he had one idea: something was happening to Dre's legs on the days he didn't train, and never happening at all, because there were no days he didn't train. He couldn't see it, so he'd have to test it.

He had to inhale twice before he said it out loud, because Dre was proud. "Take two days off before Saturday's time trial," Louis told him. "No stairs, no sprints, nothing." Dre stared at him. "Muscles get stronger in recovery after training, not during the workout itself," Louis said. "Rest days are part of getting better. I read it, and the numbers in the notebook back it up. You never recover." Dre argued, but Louis had the notebook, and the notebook had losing times in Dre's own handwriting.

Those two days, Dre took over the scoreboard and wouldn't let anyone else touch the controls, holding a monopoly on the timer buttons like it was real work. He fidgeted through both evenings. Saturday morning, the gym smelled of rubber and floor wax, and the whole team lined up for the trial.

Dre ran first. His time was the best of the season, better than his old best, and the coach wrote it down twice to be sure. Then Kwan, who had trained every day that week because he wanted to beat Dre, ran two tenths slower than his own record and stood there breathing hard, confused. The coach looked from one boy to the other. "Whatever you're doing, Kwan, keep doing it," he said, tapping Kwan's extra drills. "And Dre, whatever changed, keep doing that."

"Easy," Dre said, lacing up his shoes. "I did nothing."

Sophie had been at city hall for forty minutes, and her petition to keep the community garden open on Sundays already felt heavy in her hands. Nine kids from her block had signed it. She'd counted the signatures three times on the bus.

"You can't hand that to the council tonight," the woman at the front desk said, pointing at the agenda board. "See, item six? A group's petition gets sent to a committee first. The committee studies it and recommends whether the full council should approve it."

"A committee," Sophie repeated, writing it on the back of her hand.

"Room 2B. They meet at seven."

That gave Sophie ninety minutes, and she used them badly at first, pacing the marble lobby and practicing a speech nobody had asked to hear. Then she noticed the table near the council chamber doors, where a man in a gray cardigan was laying out papers with a ruler.

"You're the garden girl," he said. "I'm Arun. I run the mock election demo for the schools." He slid a stack of ballots toward her. "We're teaching the students tomorrow how votes become seats. Want to test it? You look like you need something to do with your hands."

There were thirty paper ballots, and three pretend parties, Red, Blue, and Green. First they counted first-past-the-post: the city was split into five districts, and in each district whichever party got the most votes won the one seat. Sophie scrutinized the tally sheet, frowning. The Greens had nine votes out of thirty, almost a third, but their voters were spread thin, so they lost every district. Zero seats.

"That doesn't seem fair," she said.

"Then do it the other way," Arun said. "Proportional representation. Ignore districts. Count all thirty together."

Sophie did the division. Under the proportional count, the Greens got three seats out of ten. Nine votes had turned into real representation, simply because the rule for counting had changed. She sat back. Nothing on the ballots had moved. Only the system underneath, the thing nobody could see on a single ballot, had made the difference.

"You look like you just found a hidden door," Arun said.

"It's like the committee thing," Sophie said slowly. "Same petition, but where it goes first changes what happens to it."

At seven, she stood up in Room 2B, and her speech about tomatoes and Mrs. Okafor's grandchildren came out too fast and slightly squeaky. Two committee members leaned forward anyway. When the chair asked whether anyone opposed, nobody raised a hand, and then the youngest member said, "I move that we recommend approval."

"Seconded," said a voice behind her, and Sophie turned to find Arun standing in the doorway, holding up one of the Green ballots like a ticket.

The banner had been leaning against the porch rail since noon, painted in blue letters: "Honoring Our Diaspora." Autumn's cousin Milo had made it for the cultural festival next weekend, and when she finally asked him what the big word meant, he shrugged and looked at his shoes. "It's on all the flyers," he said. "It sounded right." Their aunt guessed it meant food. Their grandfather said something about dancing. Nobody at the picnic table could say for sure, which bothered Autumn more than she expected, since Milo planned to stand in front of the thing for two whole days.

She found the family dictionary in the hall bookshelf, wedged between cookbooks. The entry was short, but she read it three times, mouthing the words so they would stick. It came from a Greek word meaning scattering, and it described a people living spread out far from the homeland of their ancestors. She carried the dictionary back outside, but instead of announcing her answer, she decided to test it first, the way she tested a formula in math class: plug in what she knew and see if it held.

She walked the length of the backyard and counted. Great-Aunt Rosa lived in Lisbon. Uncle Theo called from Toronto every Sunday. Her mother's cousins were scattered across three continents, and every one of them had flown or driven here for this reunion, to a yard where the picnic tables had been pushed together into one long line. Autumn stood at the end of that line and looked down it, at faces she saw once a year if she was lucky. Scattered, and gathering anyway. The word fit like a key turning.

"It means scattering," she told Milo, sitting down beside him. "It's Greek. It's for people living spread out far from the homeland of their ancestors. Like us." She turned the dictionary toward him so he could see it himself, because she knew he'd want to check. He read the entry twice, then grinned and wiped his sauce-sticky fingers on a napkin before touching the page.

"Can you paint it on the banner?" he asked. "Small, at the bottom. So when people ask, we can point to it instead of standing there looking dumb." He fetched the blue paint and a thin brush, and Autumn knelt on the porch boards, writing the definition in careful letters while Milo held the banner steady against the wind. Their grandfather came over to watch, then went inside without a word and returned with two glasses of lemonade, setting one beside each of them.

At the festival, a woman stopped at their booth, squinted at the banner, and asked, "So what's this diaspora mean, then?" Milo opened his mouth, but Autumn was already turning the banner around to show the small blue words at the bottom. "Read that part," she said. "It says it better than I could."

"Curved fingers, knuckles forward, and keep the fingertips tucked," Violet told herself, gripping the onion like a claw the way Grandma had shown her that morning. The knife ticked against the cutting board, and the onion fell into neat little cubes instead of the ragged mush of her first attempt. "Grandma, look! No blood!"

Grandma leaned over from the stove, where a pot of water was churning toward a boil. "Beautiful work. Now sweep those into the pan before they dry out." Violet scraped the onion into the hot oil and heard the hiss rise like applause. This dinner was her whole plan: pasta with sauce from scratch, made entirely by her own hands, for her parents arriving at seven.

While the onion softened, Grandma set a bowl of flour on the counter. "While that cooks, we'll do biscuits. Measure me a cup and a half." Violet plunged her measuring cup into the bag and scooped, packing the flour down tight, the way she always did. Grandma stopped her with a raised hand and said only, "Hold on. Do you remember those muffins you told me about, yours and Priya's?"

Violet froze with the cup halfway out of the bag. She had thought about those muffins for weeks. Same recipe, same oven, but Priya's muffins were tall and tender while Violet's sat on the plate like small brown stones. She had blamed her oven, then her mixing bowl, then the universe. Now she stared at the cup in her hand. The flour in it was pressed hard, solid as a brick, and she suddenly remembered watching Priya spoon flour gently into the cup and swipe the top flat with a knife.

"Wait," Violet said slowly. "I dig the cup straight into the bag. That shoves more flour in there, doesn't it? Extra flour the recipe never asked for." She turned the cup over and dumped it out, then tried it her way: she spooned flour into the cup, loose and light, and leveled it off with the back of a knife. Then she weighed both cups on Grandma's little kitchen scale. The scooped cup was heavier by a truly significant amount, enough to wreck a whole batch of muffins.

"Priya's weren't luck," Violet said, laughing. "They were technique!" She measured the rest of the flour the new way, stirred the biscuit dough, and set the biscuits in the oven just as the onions turned golden. She crushed in the canned tomatoes with her hands, seeds squirting between her fingers, and let the sauce bubble while steam fogged the window above the sink. Beyond the glass, the estuary glinted in the evening light, and a heron stalked the mudflats like it was hunting for its own dinner.

At seven o'clock sharp, headlights swept the driveway. Violet drained the pasta, folded it into her sauce, and carried the big bowl to the table with her chin high. Her mother took one bite, then another, then put down her fork. "You made this? All of it?"

"Every single cube of onion," Violet said, and slid the biscuits out of the oven.

Quinn had spent six weeks learning to write left-handed, and now her right arm came out of the sleeve pale and thin as a folded sheet of paper. The nurse, whose badge said ROSA, carried the cast saw to the counter like it was nothing, which to her it was. In the next chair a boy of about seven stared at the saw with his whole body rigid.

"It spins," the boy whispered. His mother squeezed his hand.

Quinn had thought the same thing six weeks ago, before Dr. Patel had turned the saw on and pressed it straight against her own palm to show her. The blade didn't spin at all. It vibrated, buzzing back and forth so fast it looked blurry, and that was how it cut through the hard plaster without cutting the skin underneath. Rosa had let Quinn touch the flat of it, and it had only tickled, like a phone buzzing against her hand.

"It spins," the boy said again, louder now, yanking his arm away from his mother.

Quinn pulled the crumpled pad from her backpack, the one she'd used for notes all month since she couldn't talk in class with her arm propped up. She wrote slowly, because writing was the one skill that would contract to nothing the moment the cast came off and she went back to typing.

The note said: "Ask her to put it on her hand first. Watch. It doesn't spin. It wiggles so fast it cuts the hard stuff but not your skin. I touched it."

She leaned over and held it out. The boy read it twice. When Rosa picked up the saw again, he lifted his chin like someone deciding to be braver than he felt. "Put it on your hand first," he said. "Please."

Rosa grinned and did exactly that, pressing the humming blade flat against her own palm, then letting the boy press his finger against it, quick, like testing a stove that turned out to be cold. He laughed one surprised syllable, and after that he sat perfectly still while the cast came off in curling strips.

Quinn's turn came next. The saw buzzed, the plaster split, and there was her arm, thin and strange and hers. She flexed her fingers and they obeyed, stiff but willing. On the counter lay a note her best friend Priya had slipped into her backpack that morning, and she read it while Rosa finished: "Sad you're better. Nobody else lets me draw on their cast. Coming Saturday? Bring markers anyway."

Quinn smiled, then didn't. Six weeks of signatures and jokes and a tiny dragon on her wrist, all of it about to go into the trash, and only Priya had thought that was worth mourning. She folded the note and put it in her pocket.

Rosa carried the broken cast toward the bin.

"Wait," Quinn said. "Can I keep it? Just for a while."

Rosa paused, then handed it back, plaster dust and all.

Audrey pressed her pencil against the sketchbook, shading the wing of a paper hummingbird, while her cousin Marcus sat as far from her pencil case as the art room stools allowed. Marcus was nine and had refused to pick up a pencil all morning. "I'm not touching those," he said, pointing. "Chewing on them gives you lead poisoning. Tyrell said so."

"Tyrell also said the cafeteria hamsters are robots," Audrey said. But she wondered. Could a pencil really poison you? Kids chewed pencils constantly, and none of them glowed green or anything. She turned her pencil over and read the side of it, where the words had started to wear away. "Graphite, clay, polymer," she murmured. The barrel was wood, the yellow coating was some kind of polymer paint, and the gray core was graphite. No lead anywhere on the label. So why did everyone call it lead?

She flipped open the classroom dictionary, the big one that lived next to the glue sticks. Under "lead," she found a note that made her laugh out loud. Early writers had mistaken graphite for a kind of lead ore, and the wrong name had stuck ever since. So the stuff inside a pencil had never contained the metal lead at all. It was like calling a hot dog a dog, except this mistake was five hundred years old.

"I need proof," Audrey said. Marcus wanted proof too, though his real want was to draw the dragons he kept folded in his back pocket. "Tell you what. Draw one dragon, and if you're not poisoned in an hour, you owe me nothing. If you are, I'll take the blame."

Marcus eyed the pencil the way you'd eye a strange dog. "What's the gray stuff called, really?"

"Graphite," Audrey said. "A mineral. Not the metal lead."

He took the pencil and drew. He drew fast at first, ready to drop it, then slower, then not thinking about it at all. By the end of class he had filled two pages with dragons, and Audrey's hummingbird sat finished on the drying rack beside them. Mr. Okafor paused at Marcus's work and turned it toward the light.

"Nice crosshatching," he said. "Who taught you that?"

"Nobody," Marcus said. "I was trying to conceal where the wings attach because I couldn't make them look right."

"Keep it," said Mr. Okafor. "That's style."

Marcus walked out waving his pages, and Audrey realized the twist only as she packed up: Tyrell had been half right. The name really was lead. The metal wasn't in the pencil, but the mistake was in the word, hiding there the whole time. She snapped her pencil case shut and ran to catch Marcus at the door. "Hey," she called. "Does Tyrell know the hamsters?"

Sarah stood at the door of the church hall clutching a loaf of banana bread wrapped in a tea towel, wondering if she had made a mistake. Her mother had said never visit anyone's house without food, but Sarah had never been to Aunty Wiki's church before, and she did not know which rules traveled and which ones stayed home. At her own church people shook hands and said good morning. Here, the elders pressed their noses and foreheads together, one after another, and Sarah could not see any pattern to who did it and who didn't.

The new student, Tama, arrived beside her, jet-lagged and blinking. He had moved from Samoa two weeks ago, and Mrs. Pale had paired them for the welcome lunch. "Do I bow?" he whispered. "Shake hands? I don't want to be rude."

"That makes two of us," Sarah said.

They watched Aunty Wiki greet an elderly man, noses and foreheads touching, unhurried, like it was the most natural thing in the world. Sarah noticed that everyone who came through the door got the same greeting, young and old, strangers and family. Her idea formed quickly: maybe it was not about who you were. Maybe it was about arriving. She decided to test it by walking in exactly when Tama did, so whatever happened to him would happen to her too.

"Kia ora, you two," Aunty Wiki said, folding them toward her. Tama looked sideways at Sarah, panic accelerating across his face. She gave the smallest nod, and they both leaned in. Aunty Wiki's nose touched Sarah's nose, warm and brief, and then her forehead, and then the same for Tama.

"What is it called?" Tama asked afterward, rubbing his nose. "Back home we kiss the cheek."

"The hongi," Aunty Wiki said. "Sharing the breath of life."

Sarah felt something loosen in her chest, an infectious kind of calm that spread to Tama too, because he grinned and said, "Then you and I have officially shared breath, so you have to sit with me at lunch."

At the long tables, Sarah watched before she ate, the way her grandmother had taught her at dim sum. Here nobody reached across; the food was passed, and the elders were served first, always. When the roast vegetables came around, Tama piled his plate, then noticed everyone else taking a little and passing on. "Am I a herbivore now?" he whispered, holding up a stack of kumara. "Is that the rule?"

"I think the rule is take less, more often," Sarah said. She slid the basket of banana bread down the table, and it traveled all the way to the far end and came back empty, which her mother would have called a good sign.

Aunty Wiki caught her eye and raised an eyebrow. Sarah raised her tea towel in reply, like a flag.

The lights went out at 7:40, right in the middle of Nicholas's homework. He sat still and listened. No wind outside, no crash, no siren. The whole street was dark, every window on the block, so the problem was somewhere upstream, a line or a substation he would never see. His mother found the candle box in the hall closet and set two on the coffee table.

"Dinner's a loss," she said. "The oven's electric."

"I'll make sandwiches," Nicholas said. He held his hand in front of his face and could barely make out his fingers. The candlelight reached about a foot and then quit. He walked to the kitchen with one hand on the wall, found the bread by touch, and came back with a plate.

His little sister Marta accused him of taking the last of the peanut butter, which was true, so he gave her his second sandwich and didn't argue. They ate on the couch. Marta wanted to play a board game, but by candle flame the board was just a blur of shadows, and the pieces kept getting mixed up.

"It's not fair," Marta said. "Owls can hunt in the dark. Why can't we?"

"We're not nocturnal," Nicholas said. "But wait." He had noticed something while carrying the sandwiches. Twenty minutes ago he had to feel his way along the wall. Now, from the couch, he could see the outline of the armchair, the shape of the bookshelf, the dark rectangle of the doorway to the hall. He hadn't lit another candle. Nothing had changed except time.

He set his phone timer and told Marta to watch the room, not the candle. "Tell me what you can see," he said every few minutes. At first she said nothing, just the couch. Then the lamp. Then the lamp and the window. He remembered a line from a library book about deep-sea divers and dark caves, something about the eyes building back a pigment in the rod cells. "It's called rhodopsin," he said. "It takes half an hour or more to come back. That's the mechanism, I think. Your eyes get more sensitive the longer you sit in the dark."

By the time the timer hit thirty minutes, Marta could count the game pieces on the table without leaning over them. They set up the board, moved their pieces by the gray light, and didn't knock anything over. Somewhere outside, a truck rumbled past, and the street stayed dark, but in the living room Marta moved her piece to the final square and said, "Checkmate."

Felix's grandfather had died on Tuesday night, room 414, with the TV still murmuring a weather report nobody was watching. Felix had been in the waiting room, doing his homework on fungi for science class, which felt wrong and then, strangely, like the only thing holding him together. His grandfather, a retired biology teacher, had taught him that mushrooms were decomposers, the quiet clean-up crew of the forest. "Nothing wasted," he used to say, tapping the page with two careful fingers.

The funeral was Thursday. Afterward, relatives streamed through Felix's house for what his mother kept calling shiva. He finally asked his cousin Ruth what the word meant. "Shiva is Hebrew for seven," she said, ladling soup. "It's seven days of mourning after the burial, and visitors come to comfort the family." Seven days, Felix thought. A deadline, like the fungi unit test at school.

The problem was that Felix couldn't make himself say anything to anyone. Guests hugged him and told stories, and he nodded like a broken gate. He decided to test an idea: if he couldn't articulate his sadness, maybe he could just be present, standing in the room, listening, the way visitors were apparently supposed to comfort them anyway. So on day five he parked himself beside his great-aunt Miriam, who told a story about Grandpa accidentally setting his own beard on fire at Hanukkah, 1979. Felix laughed so hard that soup nearly came out of his nose, and then, because laughing and crying turned out to run on the same wire, he ended up doing both at once. Great-aunt Miriam patted his knee as if this were perfectly normal, which, in that living room, it was.

His meticulous plan for the eulogy he'd never given, three drafted pages folded in his desk drawer at home, began to feel less necessary. On day six, Mr. Okafor from the hospital, the nurse who had let Felix sneak Grandpa extra pudding, knocked on the door holding a paper bag. "He told me you were studying decomposers," Mr. Okafor said. Inside was a field guide to fungi, with a sticky note in Grandpa's cramped handwriting: For the kid who asks why about everything.

Day seven arrived too fast. Felix sat on the porch steps with Ruth as the last visitors' cars pulled away, the house suddenly quiet in a way that had teeth. Seven days hadn't fixed anything; the deadline just ran out and the sadness kept going. But he opened the field guide to a bracket fungus and read aloud the description of how it slowly turns a dead log into soil for new seedlings, and Ruth leaned her head on his shoulder and said, "He would have made that a whole lesson." "Two lessons," Felix said. "Minimum."

Elizabeth wanted the drama scholarship more than she had ever wanted anything, and the audition required improvising a scene with a partner, which was the one thing she could not practice alone. Her partner was Marcus, who happened to be the best debater in eighth grade and the worst improviser in the room. Every time Elizabeth offered him something, he knocked it down.

"Welcome to the moon base," she said, stepping onto an imaginary platform.

"There's no air on the moon, so we'd be dead," Marcus said. "Scene over."

They tried again with a pirate ship, then a haunted library, and both scenes died the same fast death. Elizabeth flopped onto the stage steps and tried to infer what was actually going wrong. It wasn't that Marcus was shy. He argued like someone whose job was to find the flaw in every statement, and on stage, that meant he murdered every offer she made.

Then she remembered lunch on Tuesday, when Marcus had been showing off for the debate team. Someone said all kids hate homework, and Priya raised her hand and said she actually liked math homework, and the whole claim collapsed with one counterexample. Marcus had laughed and said, "That's why you need a qualifier, a word like 'usually', 'most' or 'probably', that limits how strongly you say something." He had lost the round anyway, but the words stuck in Elizabeth's head now. A qualifier made a claim harder to knock down. Maybe it could make a scene harder to knock down, too.

She stood up and grabbed his arm. "One more time. You're going to say yes to whatever I say, then add something. Yes, and. That's the only rule."

"There's no way that works," Marcus said.

"Yes, and that's why we're doing it anyway," Elizabeth said, and pulled him to center stage. "We're astronauts, we probably just landed on Mars."

"Yes, and the door is stuck," Marcus said, before he could stop himself. His eyes went wide, like he'd surprised himself.

"Yes, and I have a versatile space hammer in my boot." She knelt and pretended to pry open an airlock, and Marcus reached through an invisible gap and pulled out a flag made from somebody's lost gym sock. They built the scene for two whole minutes, rescue ships and suspicious red dust and a Martian who mostly wanted directions, and when Ms. Okafor called time, the other kids actually clapped.

"That was not terrible," Marcus admitted, still holding the sock.

"Yes, and tomorrow we're rehearsing again," Elizabeth said, and wrote her name at the top of the audition list.

Annabelle opened the spreadsheet and typed her aunt's numbers into column A: clicks by day, fourteen days of them. Her aunt Rosa ran a bakery two towns over, and last month the ad bill had jumped to ninety dollars, almost triple the usual. Rosa had told her on the phone, "Every click costs me money. It's called pay-per-click. We bid in an auction for keywords, and we only pay when someone clicks the ad." Annabelle had stared at that sentence afterward, an idea beginning to germinate: if clicks cost money, then somebody could cost her aunt money just by clicking.

In the computer lab, the teacher had shown them how to build a formula. Annabelle selected the cell below her last number and typed =SUM(A2:A15). The total appeared: 612 clicks in two weeks. Way too many for a bakery that usually got sixty a week. She highlighted the column, clicked the bar chart button, and the graph snapped onto the screen, tall gray rectangles towering over the first week's short ones. The pattern was unmistakable. The bars climbed sharply starting on a Tuesday, all fourteen days after that nearly the same height, like a fence.

"Looks weird," said Marcus, leaning over from the next computer. "Like somebody turned a faucet on."

"That's what I think." Annabelle clicked on the tall bars one at a time. Real customers wouldn't click the same amount every single day. But a person trying to drain an ad budget would, the way you'd water a plant on a schedule. She needed proof, not just a hunch. She added column B: days of the week. Then she sorted. The tall clicks fell on every day, including Sunday, when the bakery was closed. Nobody searched for closed bakeries at a steady rate all week long.

She pulled up her aunt's ad account and checked which keyword the clicks came from. One phrase, "heritage sourdough starter," had 400 of the 612 clicks. Her aunt's famous starter, passed down through three generations, was barely searched at all before. Annabelle screenshot everything, pasted the chart into an email, and wrote: "Somebody might be clicking your ad on purpose. Check if the clicks come from one location." She hit send and sat back.

Marcus read over her shoulder. "Could you be wrong?"

"Could be. That's why I sent the chart, not an accusation." She saved the file twice, once to the school drive and once to her flash drive, because a spreadsheet with one good formula deserved protecting.

The reply came before the bell. Rosa had checked the account and found the clicks clustering in one town, the same town as a rival baker. She'd already emailed the ad company. The last line said: "Come Saturday. Free cake. The class voted on your flavor, and it was unanimous: lemon."

Annabelle grinned and closed the laptop. "Marcus," she said, "I'm getting cake."

The cemetery gate had a sensor that beeped when someone walked through, and it beeped now for Autumn and her mother and the urn of white flowers they had recruited Aunt Rosa to help arrange. Grandma Pearl's grave was halfway up the hill, the stone still new enough to look like it did not belong yet, standing perpendicular to the slope the way the crew had set it.

Autumn set the urn down and stood with her hands in her pockets. One week ago she had gone to the movies with Priya, four days after the funeral, and she had laughed so hard at some scene about a raccoon in a mailbox that she'd cried. Then she'd stopped, right there in the dark theater, because it felt wrong. Grandma Pearl was in the ground and Autumn was laughing at a raccoon. She hadn't told anyone, not even Priya, who had noticed anyway and asked if she was okay.

"Turn it toward the road," her mother said, tilting the urn so the flowers faced downhill. "That's how she'd want it. Showing off."

"She never showed off," Autumn said.
